ai.json: Introduction to AI, ML, and deep learning. AI vs ML vs DL, narrow vs general AI, history of AI, real-world applications across industries including healthcare, finance, transportation, and entertainment.

Different categories of AI systems based on capability: Reactive Machines (limited memory), Theory of Mind, Self-Aware AI. Also categorized by functionality: Narrow AI (specialized), General AI (human-level), and Super AI (beyond human).

Fundamental approaches to AI problems including search algorithms, constraint satisfaction, optimization, and decision theory. Covers breadth-first search, depth-first search, A*, hill climbing, and genetic algorithms.

The role of data in AI systems. Structured vs unstructured data, data quality, data preprocessing techniques, feature engineering, data augmentation, handling missing values, and the importance of diverse and representative datasets.

Ethical considerations in AI development: bias, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, responsible AI practices. Understanding algorithmic bias, fairness metrics, interpretability, and regulatory frameworks like GDPR and AI Act.

Essential linear algebra concepts for AI: vectors, matrices, matrix operations, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, singular value decomposition (SVD). These are fundamental to neural network computations, dimensionality reduction, and data transformations.

Calculus concepts essential for machine learning: derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients, the chain rule (critical for backpropagation), and optimization. Understanding how gradients enable model training through gradient descent.

Probability theory fundamentals for AI: probability distributions (normal, binomial, Poisson), Bayes theorem, maximum likelihood estimation, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and statistical significance.

Optimization algorithms for machine learning training: gradient descent variants (SGD, Adam, RMSprop), learning rate schedules, momentum, second-order methods. Understanding the optimization landscape, local vs global minima, and convergence.

Supervised learning: training models on labeled data. Covers regression (linear, polynomial, ridge, lasso) and classification (logistic regression, decision trees, SVM, k-nearest neighbors). Understanding bias-variance tradeoff and model capacity.

Unsupervised learning: finding patterns in unlabeled data. Covers clustering (K-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture models) and dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP). Applications in customer segmentation and anomaly detection.

Evaluating machine learning models: train/test split, cross-validation (k-fold, stratified), confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC curves, AUC, bias-variance decomposition, overfitting vs underfitting detection.

Combining multiple models for better performance: bagging (Random Forests), boosting (AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM), stacking, voting classifiers. Understanding ensemble diversity and bias-variance reduction.

Creating and selecting features for ML models: feature extraction, feature selection methods (filter, wrapper, embedded), normalization and standardization, one-hot encoding, handling categorical variables, polynomial features, and automated feature engineering.

Building neural networks from scratch: perceptron algorithm, activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, softmax), forward propagation, backpropagation, loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy), and the universal approximation theorem.

Convolutional Neural Networks for image data: convolution operations, filters, stride, padding, pooling layers, feature maps. Major architectures: LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, Inception, EfficientNet. Transfer learning with pre-trained CNNs.

The transformer architecture that powers modern AI: self-attention mechanism, multi-head attention, positional encoding, layer normalization, feed-forward networks. Understanding encoder-decoder architecture and how transformers process sequences.

Leveraging pre-trained models: fine-tuning, feature extraction, domain adaptation. Using models pre-trained on large datasets (ImageNet, GPT, BERT) for new tasks with limited data. Understanding when to freeze layers vs fine-tune.

PyTorch deep learning framework: tensors, autograd for automatic differentiation, neural network module (nn.Module), optimizers (SGD, Adam), data loaders, GPU acceleration with CUDA, saving and loading models.

Understanding large language models: GPT architecture, transformer decoder-only design, scaling laws (Kaplan, Chinchilla), emergent abilities, in-context learning. How LLMs process and generate text at massive scale.

Deep dive into attention mechanisms: self-attention, causal/masked attention (for autoregressive generation), cross-attention (for encoder-decoder models), multi-head attention, sparse attention, FlashAttention for efficiency, and grouped-query attention.

Training LLMs from scratch: training data collection and filtering, tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece), next-token prediction objective, compute requirements, distributed training, data parallelism, model parallelism, and pipeline parallelism.

Adapting pre-trained LLMs for specific tasks: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on instruction datasets, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), direct preference optimization (DPO), instruction tuning, and multi-task fine-tuning.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), QLoRA (quantized LoRA), Adapters, Prefix Tuning, Prompt Tuning. These methods enable fine-tuning large models with consumer-grade hardware by updating only a small fraction of parameters.

Crafting effective prompts for LLMs: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, tree-of-thought (ToT), system prompts, role prompting, output formatting, temperature and top-p sampling parameters.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: connecting LLMs to external knowledge sources. Vector databases for semantic search, document chunking strategies, embedding models, retrieval strategies (dense, sparse, hybrid), reranking, and context injection.

Evaluating LLM outputs: benchmark datasets (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K, HellaSwag), automated metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, perplexity), human evaluation, hallucination detection, factual accuracy, and model comparison methodologies.

Building autonomous AI agents: goal-oriented agents, reactive vs deliberative agents, hybrid architectures. Understanding the perception-action loop, environment interaction, and how agents make decisions to achieve goals.

Giving AI agents access to tools and APIs: function calling, tool definitions with OpenAI/Anthropic APIs, search capabilities, code execution, calculator, database queries. Understanding tool selection, argument generation, and error handling.

Coordinating multiple AI agents to solve complex tasks: agent communication protocols, task decomposition, role assignment, hierarchical vs flat organization, orchestration patterns, and conflict resolution between agents.

Advanced reasoning patterns for AI agents: ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) pattern, chain-of-thought reasoning, plan-and-execute architecture, self-reflection, task decomposition trees, and recursive reasoning for complex multi-step problems.

Popular frameworks for building AI agents: LangChain (chains, agents, retrievers), AutoGen (multi-agent conversations), CrewAI (role-based agents), OpenAI Assistants API, Anthropic tool use, and custom agent implementations. Comparing frameworks and choosing the right one.

Deploying ML models to production: model serving with FastAPI, TorchServe, TensorFlow Serving, Triton Inference Server. Serverless deployment, edge deployment, containerization with Docker, and API design for ML services.

Building production ML pipelines: data validation (Great Expectations), feature pipelines, training pipelines, model registry (MLflow), pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow), and automated retraining triggers.

Monitoring ML models in production: data drift detection (population stability index, KS test), concept drift, model decay, prediction monitoring, performance metrics tracking, alerting systems, and automated rollback and retraining workflows.

Tracking ML experiments systematically: MLflow, Weights & Biases, Neptune.ai. Logging parameters, metrics, artifacts, and model versions. Experiment comparison, reproducibility, and collaboration features.

Building LLM-powered applications with LangChain: chains, agents, retrievers, memory systems, document loaders, output parsers, streaming. Understanding the LangChain expression language and LangGraph for stateful agent orchestration.

Vector databases for semantic search and RAG: Pinecone (managed), ChromaDB (local), Weaviate (hybrid), Milvus (distributed), Qdrant (Rust-based). Understanding embeddings, ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF), similarity metrics (cosine, dot product, euclidean).

Running LLMs locally with Ollama: model management (pull, run, stop), OpenAI-compatible API, custom Modelfiles, quantization (Q4, Q5, Q8), GPU acceleration, and building local AI applications without cloud dependencies.

Using OpenAI models via API: chat completions, embeddings, function calling, vision capabilities, text-to-speech, assistants API, fine-tuning API. Understanding token pricing, rate limits, streaming, and best practices.

The Hugging Face ecosystem: Transformers library for model access, Datasets for data handling, PEFT for efficient fine-tuning, Tokenizers for text processing, Hub for model sharing, Spaces for demos, and AutoClasses for model agnostic code.
angular.json: Introduction to Angular and its ecosystem.

Components are the fundamental building blocks of Angular apps, each consisting of a TypeScript class, HTML template, and optional CSS styles. They control a view via a decorated class with @Component metadata.

NgModules organize an Angular app into cohesive blocks of functionality by declaring components, importing dependencies, and providing services. Every app has a root module (AppModule) as the entry point.
Angular templates extend HTML with custom syntax including interpolation ({{ }}), property binding ([ ]), event binding (( )), and structural directives (*ngIf, *ngFor) for dynamic views.
Angular Router enables navigation between views in SPAs with URL-based routing, nested routes, lazy-loaded modules, and route parameters. It integrates with the browser's history API.
Lazy loading loads feature modules on demand when the user navigates to their routes, reducing initial bundle size. Use loadChildren in route config to point to a module imported via dynamic import.

Route guards control navigation using interfaces like CanActivate, CanDeactivate, and Resolve. They prevent unauthorized access, prompt for unsaved changes, and pre-fetch data before a route activates.
Working with data and APIs in Angular.
Jasmine is a behavior-driven development framework for testing JavaScript code with a clean, readable syntax. It provides describe/it blocks, matchers (toEqual, toContain), and spies.
Karma is a test runner that executes tests in real browsers, providing fast feedback loops and reporting. It's the default test runner in Angular CLI projects via ng test.

TestBed is Angular's primary testing utility for configuring and creating component test environments. It manages module compilation, dependency injection, and provides ComponentFixture for interaction.
Angular's dependency injection system provides dependencies to classes via constructor parameters. The injector hierarchy creates singleton or per-component instances of services automatically.
Services are singleton classes decorated with @Injectable that encapsulate business logic, data access, or cross-cutting concerns. They are the recommended way to share logic between components.

Providers configure the injector with dependency recipes, controlling how services are created and scoped. They can be registered at module level, component level, or using providedIn: 'root' for tree-shaking.
Template-driven forms rely on directives in the template like ngModel for two-way data binding. They are simpler but less scalable than reactive forms, suitable for basic form use cases.
Reactive forms provide a model-driven approach with form control instances created programmatically, offering more predictability, testability, and advanced validation capabilities.
Angular forms support built-in validators (required, minLength, pattern) and custom async validators. Validation state is exposed through CSS classes (ng-valid, ng-invalid) and component properties.
HttpClient is Angular's built-in HTTP client with typed request/response, interceptors, and automatic JSON parsing. Methods return Observables supporting RxJS operators for transformations.
Interceptors sit between the application and the backend, transforming outgoing requests or incoming responses. Common use cases include adding auth tokens, logging, and error handling.
Error handling in HTTP requests is done via RxJS catchError operator, retrying failed requests, or displaying user-friendly error messages. Global error handling can be centralized in interceptors.

Angular offers three types of directives: components, structural directives (alter DOM layout), and attribute directives (change appearance or behavior). Custom directives encapsulate reusable DOM manipulation.
Pipes transform data in templates for display, such as formatting dates, currencies, or filtering lists. Angular provides built-in pipes and you can create custom pure or impure pipes.
Decorators are TypeScript features used extensively in Angular for metadata. Custom decorators can extend component behavior, add logging, or transform class properties at design time.
Angular's default change detection checks every component in the tree when any data changes, ensuring consistency. It uses zone.js to patch browser APIs and trigger checks automatically.

OnPush change detection strategy reduces unnecessary checks by only running detection when input references change, events fire, or observables emit. It's essential for large lists and performance-critical views.
Angular supports code splitting through lazy-loaded modules and ES dynamic imports. The CLI generates separate chunks per lazy route, and the router loads them on demand when the user navigates.

Standalone components, directives, and pipes are self-contained without needing NgModules. Created with the standalone: true flag, they import dependencies directly and can be lazy-loaded via the router.
Applications can bootstrap directly from a standalone component instead of NgModule. The main.ts calls bootstrapApplication with the root component and optional provider configuration.
Standalone components load lazily with loadComponent in the route config, eliminating the need for feature modules. Each route points directly to a component with its own imports.
Signals are reactive primitives that notify consumers when their value changes. Writable signals created with signal() expose get/set/update methods for synchronous state management.
Computed signals derive values from other signals with lazy evaluation and caching. They only recompute when dependent signals change, replacing manual ChangeDetectorRef calls.
Effects run side effects automatically when their signal dependencies change. They are used for syncing state to localStorage, logging, or triggering imperative DOM operations.
Signal-based inputs replace @Input with input() and input.required(), providing reactive input values without lifecycle hooks. They integrate natively with the change detection system.
The Angular CLI generates components, directives, pipes, services, modules, and more using ng generate. Schematics customize generation with options for style, inline template, and routing.
Custom schematics automate project scaffolding by generating files, modifying existing code, and installing dependencies. They are published as npm packages and run with ng generate.
Builders extend the Angular CLI build pipeline with custom build, test, or deploy logic. They replace Angular's default builder to support custom tooling like custom webpack configs.
Deferrable views (introduced in Angular 17) lazy-load component dependencies with @defer blocks. They improve initial bundle size by deferring heavy components until a specified trigger.
Defer triggers control when lazy content loads: on viewport (enters viewport), on interaction (user clicks), on immediate, on idle (browser idle), or on a custom timer.
Deferred components and their transitive dependencies are split into separate JavaScript chunks. Angular loads these chunks asynchronously when the trigger condition is met, reducing initial payload.
The inject() function provides a programmatic alternative to constructor-based dependency injection. It can be called in the class body, making DI more flexible and reducing boilerplate.
inject() must be called within an injection context such as a constructor, class field initializer, or factory function. Outside these contexts it throws, ensuring predictable DI resolution.

Angular Signals provide reactive state management with fine-grained reactivity. Unlike Zone.js-based change detection (which checks the entire component tree), Signals track dependencies automatically and update only affected consumers. Key APIs: signal() creates a writable signal, computed() creates derived values, effect() runs side effects when signal values change. The new control flow (@if, @for, @switch) replaces *ngIf, *ngFor, and ngSwitch with better type narrowing and performance. Standalone components are now the default — NgModules are optional.
.Angular Signals & New Control Flow.Angular Routing & Lazy Loading[0]

Angular Router enables SPA navigation with lazy-loaded feature modules/routes. Routes are defined as an array of Route objects with path, component or loadComponent (standalone) / loadChildren (modules). canActivate, canDeactivate, and canLoad guards protect routes. Resolve fetches data before route activation. Route params (paramMap, queryParamMap) are accessible via ActivatedRoute. PreloadingStrategy (PreloadAllModules, custom strategies) balances initial bundle size with subsequent navigation speed. Router events (NavigationStart, NavigationEnd, NavigationError) enable loading indicators.
.Angular Signals & New Control Flow.Angular Forms & Validation[0]

Angular provides two form approaches: Template-driven Forms (simpler, suitable for basic forms) and Reactive Forms (more flexible, suitable for complex forms, better testing). Reactive Forms use FormControl, FormGroup, and FormArray with explicit validation via Validators. Custom validators extend validation logic. Async validators call servers (e.g., checking username availability). Form arrays handle dynamic form fields. ValueChanges observable enables reactive form interactions. Typed forms (Angular 14+) provide strict typing for form values.

Angular Testing uses TestBed for configuring modules, creating components, and injecting services. ComponentFixture provides component instance and debug element. async() and fakeAsync() handle asynchronous operations. HttpClientTestingModule and HttpTestingController mock HTTP requests. Use By.css() for DOM querying and DetectChanges() to trigger change detection. Component harnesses (CDK) provide a stable API for interacting with components in tests. Override providers in TestBed to mock services. E2E tests use Playwright or Cypress.

Angular performance optimization: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush reduces change detection to only when inputs change or events fire. trackBy in @for/ngFor prevents unnecessary DOM re-creation. Lazy loading reduces initial bundle size. @defer (Angular 17+) defers loading of heavy components until viewport or interaction. provideZoneFlush with NoopZone enables zoneless change detection with signals. pure pipes prevent recalculation. Server-Side Rendering (SSR) with Angular Universal improves initial load. Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) guide performance targets.

export function useCounter(init = 0) { const count = ref(init); const inc = () => count.value++; const dec = () => count.value--; return { count, inc, dec } }  // reusable counter composable

export function useFetch(url) { const data = ref(null); const error = ref(null); const loading = ref(true); watchEffect(async () => { loading.value = true; try { data.value = await (await fetch(url.value)).json() } catch (e) { error.value = e } finally { loading.value = false } }); return { data, error, loading } }  // async data fetching composable

export function useLocalStorage(key, initial) { const value = ref(initial); watch(value, v => localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(v)), { deep: true, immediate: true }); return value }  // localStorage composable

export function useEventListener(target, event, handler) { onMounted(() => target.addEventListener(event, handler)); onUnmounted(() => target.removeEventListener(event, handler)) }  // event listener composable

export function useMediaQuery(query) { const matches = ref(window.matchMedia(query).matches); onMounted(() => { const mq = window.matchMedia(query); mq.addEventListener('change', e => matches.value = e.matches) }); return matches }  // responsive media query composable
export function useMouse() { const x = ref(0); const y = ref(0); useEventListener(window, 'mousemove', e => { x.value = e.clientX; y.value = e.clientY }); return { x, y } }  // track mouse position
export function useInterval(fn, delay) { onMounted(() => { const id = setInterval(fn, delay.value); onUnmounted(() => clearInterval(id)) }) }  // interval composable
export function useDebounce(fn, delay) { let timer; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay) } }  // debounce composable

A compiler is a program that translates source code written in one language into another language — typically from a high-level language (like Python or JavaScript) into low-level machine code, bytecode, or another high-level language. Think of a compiler as a translator between you (the programmer) and the computer. You write code in a human-readable language; the compiler converts it into instructions the computer can execute. Why do we need compilers?
  • Computers only understand machine code (1s and 0s)
  • Writing machine code is impractical for humans
  • Compilers let us write in readable languages and still run on hardware
  • Compilers can optimize code to run faster
  • Compilers can catch errors before the program runs
Compilers vs Interpreters:
  • Compiler: Translates all code at once, produces an executable file (C, Go, Rust, Zig)
  • Interpreter: Executes code line by line (Python, JavaScript, Ruby)
  • JIT (Just-In-Time): Compiles code at runtime for speed (Java JVM, V8 for JavaScript)
Try this: Click "Pipeline ▶" in the Compiler mode below the editor to see how code gets tokenized and parsed step by step.

Tokenization (also called lexical analysis or lexing) is the first stage of compilation. It breaks source code into meaningful chunks called tokens. A token is the smallest unit of meaning in a programming language — keywords, identifiers, operators, numbers, strings, punctuation, etc. Examples of tokens:
  • let — keyword token
  • myVariable — identifier token
  • = — operator token
  • 42 — number token
  • "hello" — string token
  • ; — punctuation token
  • // comment — comment token
How tokenizers work:
  1. Read source code character by character
  2. Group characters into tokens based on patterns
  3. Classify each token (keyword, identifier, number, etc.)
  4. Output a token stream for the parser
Why tokenization matters:
  • Simplifies the parser (works with tokens, not raw characters)
  • Catches basic errors (invalid characters, unterminated strings)
  • Removes whitespace and comments from the parse stream
  • Maps source positions for error reporting
Try this: Write code in the editor and click "Tokenize ▶" to see every token the compiler finds in your code.

Parsing (syntax analysis) takes the flat token stream from the lexer and builds a tree structure called the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). An AST represents the grammatical structure of your code as a tree. Each node in the tree represents a construct (variable declaration, function call, expression, etc.) and its children represent the components. Why an AST?
  • Captures the hierarchy of code (blocks inside functions inside classes)
  • Ignores syntactic sugar (semicolons, parentheses in some cases)
  • Makes it easy to transform or analyze code
  • Enables optimizations and code generation
Common AST node types:
  • Program — the root of every AST
  • FunctionDeclaration — a function definition
  • VariableDeclaration — declaring a variable
  • BinaryExpression — a + b, x > 5
  • CallExpression — calling a function: foo()
  • Block — a group of statements in { }
  • ControlFlow — if, for, while
Parsing strategies:
  • Recursive Descent: Most common for hand-written parsers. One function per grammar rule.
  • LL/LR Parsers: Generated from grammar definition. Used in production compilers (GCC, Clang).
  • Operator Precedence: Specific technique for parsing expressions with operator precedence.
Try this: Click "AST ▶" to see the tree structure the compiler builds from your code.

Code generation is the final stage of the compiler pipeline. It walks the AST and produces output code in the target language. For most compilers, the output is machine code or bytecode. In this Compiler Explorer, you can see how the same code would be compiled to different output representations:
  • JavaScript: Same as input (JS is interpreted)
  • Machine code view: Conceptual translation to low-level instructions
  • Structural output: What the compiler "sees" in your code
What code generators do:
  1. Walk the AST (depth-first or breadth-first)
  2. For each node type, emit appropriate output code
  3. Track context (scope, registers, variable locations)
  4. Optimize the output (peephole optimization, register allocation)
Example walk: For let x = 5 + 3
  1. Visit Program node → start new line
  2. Visit VariableDeclaration → emit let x =
  3. Visit BinaryExpression → emit 5 + 3
  4. Visit number "5" → emit 5
  5. Visit operator "+" → emit +
  6. Visit number "3" → emit 3
  7. Finish line → emit ;
Real compiler optimizations:
  • Constant folding: 5 + 3 → 8 (evaluated at compile time)
  • Dead code elimination: Remove code that never runs
  • Inlining: Replace function calls with the function body
  • Loop unrolling: Duplicate loop body for performance

This Compiler Explorer analyzes code from all 15+ languages in Kodex's Lab! The tokenizer and AST builder adapt to each language's syntax. How it works across languages:
  • Comment styles: // (JS/TS/C/C++/etc.), # (Python/Docker), -- (SQL)
  • String delimiters: ", ', backticks, """ (Python/Kotlin)
  • Block structure: { } for most languages, indentation for Python
  • Keywords: Per-language keyword sets for accurate token classification
  • Operators: Universal operators plus language-specific ones (-> in Go/C, => in JS)
Switch languages and click Pipeline to see! The tokenizer recognizes language-specific syntax including:
  • Python: def, class:, indentation-based blocks
  • Go: func, defer, go routines
  • Rust: fn, match, impl, trait
  • SQL: Case-insensitive keywords, SELECT, FROM, JOIN
  • Docker: FROM, RUN, CMD
  • Git: Commands and flags
  • MongoDB: Query operators $match, $group

Semantic analysis is the compiler stage that checks whether code makes logical sense — beyond just syntax. While parsing checks structure (grammar), semantic analysis checks meaning. This is where the compiler catches real bugs. What semantic analysis checks:
  • Type checking: Are operands the right types? "hello" - 5 is syntactically valid but semantically wrong in most languages.
  • Scope resolution: Does each variable reference point to a valid declaration?
  • Name binding: Are functions, types, and variables used before declaration (where required)?
  • Type inference: Can the compiler deduce types without explicit annotations?
Type systems spectrum:
  • Dynamic: Types checked at runtime (Python, JavaScript) — flexible but error-prone
  • Static: Types checked at compile time (C, Go, Rust) — catches errors early
  • Gradual: Mix of both (TypeScript, Python with type hints)
  • Strong: No implicit type coercion (Python, Rust)
  • Weak: Implicit coercion allowed (C, JavaScript)
Semantic errors vs syntax errors:
  • Syntax error: let 5x = 3; — the grammar doesn't allow this
  • Semantic error: let x: number = "hello"; — grammatically valid, but type mismatch

Compiler optimization transforms code to run faster, use less memory, or consume less power — without changing its meaning. Most optimizations are conservative: the compiler only applies them when it's sure the program's behavior won't change. Categories of optimization:
  • Constant folding: x = 5 + 3 → x = 8 (evaluate at compile time)
  • Constant propagation: If x = 5, replace all uses of x with 5
  • Dead code elimination: Remove branches that never execute or variables never read
  • Loop unrolling: Duplicate loop body to reduce overhead of the loop control
  • Function inlining: Replace function call with the function body itself
  • Strength reduction: Replace expensive ops with cheaper ones (e.g., x * 2 → x << 1)
  • Common subexpression elimination: Compute a value once and reuse it
Optimization levels in GCC/Clang:
  • -O0: No optimization (fastest compile, slowest code)
  • -O1: Basic optimizations (good balance)
  • -O2: More aggressive (recommended for release builds)
  • -O3: Very aggressive (may increase code size)
  • -Os: Optimize for size (embedded systems)

Between the high-level AST and the low-level machine code, most compilers use one or more intermediate representations (IRs). IRs bridge the gap between the source language and the target hardware, making the compiler easier to port to new architectures. Common IRs:
  • Three-Address Code (TAC): Simple instruction format: t1 = a + b
  • Static Single Assignment (SSA): Each variable assigned exactly once — enables powerful optimizations (used by LLVM, GCC)
  • LLVM IR: A low-level, typed IR used by Clang, rustc, and many others
  • Bytecode: Portable IR for virtual machines (JVM bytecode, Python bytecode, WASM)
  • C as IR: Some compilers output C code and let the C compiler handle machine code generation
Why multi-level IRs?
  • Frontend (language-specific) → high-level IR → mid-level IR → low-level IR → machine code
  • Each level enables different optimizations
  • New language backends only need to generate IR, not full machine code
LLVM's architecture: The most popular compiler infrastructure uses this exact pattern. Language frontends (Clang for C/C++, rustc for Rust) all emit LLVM IR, which LLVM optimizes and compiles to native code.

.Number Systems and Data Representation.Binary Numbers[0]

Computers use binary (base-2) with digits 0 and 1. Each position represents a power of 2. A byte is 8 bits (0-255). A nibble is 4 bits. Binary addition: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1. The LSB is bit 0, MSB is bit 7. Binary is the foundation of all machine-level operations.
.Number Systems and Data Representation.Hexadecimal System[0]

Hexadecimal (base-16) uses digits 0-9 and A-F. Each hex digit represents 4 bits (a nibble). Hex is the standard notation for assembly: addresses, opcodes, and data. Two hex digits = one byte. Prefix: 0x (C/ASM) or h (MASM). Converting hex to binary is trivial: F=1111, A=1010, etc.
.Number Systems and Data Representation.Two's Complement[0]

Signed integers use two's complement. The MSB is the sign bit (0=positive, 1=negative). To negate: invert all bits and add 1. Range for N bits: -2^(N-1) to 2^(N-1)-1. For 8 bits: -128 to +127. The CPU doesn't distinguish signed vs unsigned — the same ADD instruction works for both; the programmer interprets the result.
.Number Systems and Data Representation.Boolean Logic[0]

Boolean algebra operates on true (1) and false (0). AND: both must be 1. OR: at least one is 1. XOR: exactly one is 1. NOT: invert. NAND, NOR are complements. De Morgan's laws: NOT(A AND B) = NOT(A) OR NOT(B). Truth tables define all combinations. Assembly provides AND, OR, XOR, NOT, TEST instructions.
.Number Systems and Data Representation.Bit Shifting[0]

SHL/SHR shift bits left/right by a count. Each left shift multiplies by 2; each right shift divides by 2 (unsigned). SAR preserves the sign bit. ROL/ROR rotate bits through a circle. RCL/RCR rotate through the carry flag. Shift counts can be an immediate or CL register.
.Number Systems and Data Representation.ASCII and BCD Numbers[0]

ASCII digits: '0'=0x30 through '9'=0x39. To convert ASCII to binary: subtract 0x30. To convert binary to ASCII: add 0x30. Unpacked BCD stores one decimal digit per byte (0x00-0x09). Packed BCD stores two digits per byte (high/low nibble). DAA adjusts after ADD for packed BCD. DAS adjusts after SUB. AAA/AAS/AAM/AAD are legacy ASCII adjust instructions.
.Number Systems and Data Representation.Endianness[0]

Endianness describes byte order in memory. Little-endian (x86): LSB at lowest address. Big-endian: MSB at lowest address. x86 is little-endian: 0x12345678 stored as 78 56 34 12. Network protocols use big-endian. BSWAP instruction converts endianness in registers. MOVBE (mov big-endian) on newer CPUs.
.Getting Started with Assembly.Environment Setup[0]

NASM is the assembler of choice for x86-64 Linux. Install: `sudo apt install nasm` (Debian/Ubuntu), `sudo yum install nasm` (RHEL/Fedora), `brew install nasm` (macOS), or download from nasm.us (Windows). Assemble: `nasm -f elf64 prog.asm -o prog.o`. Link: `ld -o prog prog.o`. Run: `./prog`. For libc programs: `gcc -no-pie -o prog prog.o`. Debug: `nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf prog.asm`. Use make or shell scripts for multi-file projects.
.Getting Started with Assembly.Basic NASM Syntax[0]

NASM syntax: `[label:] instruction [operands] [; comment]`. Labels mark positions and are symbolic addresses. Local labels start with a dot (`.loop`) and are scoped to the preceding global label. Sections: `.data` (initialized data), `.bss` (uninitialized), `.text` (code). Directives: `global` exports symbols, `extern` imports, `equ` defines constants, `times` repeats. The entry point is `_start` for standalone or `main` for programs linking with libc.
.Getting Started with Assembly.Memory Segments[0]

An ELF binary has segments loaded by the OS. `.text` — executable code, read-only, mapped with RX permissions. `.data` — initialized global/static variables, mapped RW. `.bss` — uninitialized data, zero-filled at load time, mapped RW (occupies no disk space). The stack — temporary data (local vars, return addresses), grows downward from high addresses. The heap — dynamically allocated memory via brk/sbrk or mmap, grows upward from low addresses.
.Getting Started with Assembly.Variables[0]

Variables are named memory locations declared with DB (byte), DW (word), DD (dword), DQ (qword), or DT (10 bytes). Initialize with a value or comma-separated list for arrays. Use TIMES for repeating patterns. Access with `mov reg, [var_name]` for load, `mov [var_name], reg` for store. NASM doesn't have typed variables — the assembler just associates a name with an address; you must use the correct instruction size.
.Getting Started with Assembly.Constants[0]

NASM constants are evaluated at assembly time, not runtime. `EQU` assigns a name to a value (cannot be redefined). `%assign` defines a numeric constant that can be redefined. `%define` is a textual macro replacement (like C's #define). Constants improve readability and maintainability — use them for syscall numbers, buffer sizes, flags, and masks. They consume no memory and have no runtime overhead.
.Getting Started with Assembly.Build Tools & Makefiles[0]

Use Makefiles to automate assembly workflow. Pattern rules handle .asm → .o → executable. Common targets: all (build), clean (remove artifacts), debug (with DWARF symbols), run. The `$@` (target), `$<` (first dep), `$^` (all deps) automatic variables streamline rules.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.CPU Architecture Overview[0]

The x86-64 CPU has: ALU (arithmetic logic unit), control unit, registers (fast on-chip storage), cache (L1/L2/L3), MMU (memory management unit), FPU (floating-point), and SIMD units. Execution pipeline: fetch decode execute memory access write-back. Long mode (64-bit) allows 64-bit addressing, 16 general-purpose registers, and SSE/AVX.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.General Purpose Registers[0]

x86-64 has 16 GPRs: RAX (accumulator), RBX (base), RCX (counter), RDX (data), RSI (source index), RDI (dest index), RBP (base pointer), RSP (stack pointer), R8-R15 (extended). Sub-registers: RAX EAX (32) AX (16) AH/AL (8). In 64-bit mode, writing to a 32-bit subregister zero-extends to 64 bits.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.Special Purpose Registers[0]

RIP (instruction pointer) points to the next instruction. RFLAGS stores condition flags: CF (carry), PF (parity), AF (adjust), ZF (zero), SF (sign), OF (overflow), IF (interrupt), DF (direction). Control registers CR0-CR4 manage system state. Segment registers (CS, DS, ES, FS, GS, SS) are largely vestigial in 64-bit mode.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.Stack and Calling Conventions[0]

The stack grows downward (RSP decreases on push). PUSH decrements RSP then stores; POP loads then increments RSP. The System V AMD64 ABI: first 6 args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9; return value in RAX. RSP must be 16-byte aligned before CALL. CALL pushes return address; RET pops it. The red zone (128 bytes below RSP) is scratch space.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.Memory Addressing Modes[0]

x86-64 addressing: [base + index*scale + displacement]. Scale can be 1, 2, 4, 8. Modes: register (mov rax, rbx), immediate (mov rax, 42), direct (mov rax, [addr]), register indirect (mov rax, [rbx]), base+displacement (mov rax, [rbx+8]), indexed (mov rax, [array+rbx*8]), RIP-relative (mov rax, [rel msg]). 64-bit uses RIP-relative by default for data access.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.Segment & Control Registers[0]

Segment registers (CS, DS, ES, FS, GS, SS) are mostly vestigial in 64-bit. FS is used for thread-local storage (TLS). GS is used for processor-specific data on some OSes. Control registers: CR0 (protection enable, paging), CR2 (page fault address), CR3 (page table base), CR4 (extensions). Read via MOV from CRn (privileged). EFLAGS/RFLAGS register controls CPU behavior.
.x64 Architecture and Registers.SIMD Register State[0]

SIMD state: MMX uses MM0-MM7 (64-bit, legacy). SSE uses XMM0-XMM15 (128-bit). AVX: YMM0-YMM15 (256-bit). AVX-512: ZMM0-ZMM15 (512-bit). MXCSR controls SSE rounding/exception masks. VZEROUPPER clears upper YMM bits when mixing SSE/AVX. XSAVE/XRSTOR save/restore full SIMD state.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Hello World[0]

NASM syntax: label: instruction operands ; comment. Sections: .data (initialized data), .bss (uninitialized data), .text (code). The `_start` label is the ELF entry point. Use `nasm -f elf64 file.asm && ld -o file file.o`. System calls use `syscall` with the syscall number in RAX and arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8, R9.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Data Types and Directives[0]

NASM data directives: DB (byte), DW (word = 2 bytes), DD (dword = 4), DQ (qword = 8), DT (10 bytes), DO (16), DY (32), DZ (64). TIMES repeats data. EQU defines constants. $ is the current address. RESB/RESW/RESD/RESQ reserve space in .bss.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Moving Data[0]

MOV copies data between registers, memory, and immediates. MOV cannot do memory-to-memory directly. MOVZX (zero-extend) and MOVSX (sign-extend) for smaller to larger sizes. XCHG swaps values. LEA loads effective address without accessing memory. CMOVcc (conditional move) avoids branches.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Arithmetic Instructions[0]

ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV for arithmetic. ADD/SUB work on any operand size. MUL unsigned: RAX = RAX * rm. IMUL for signed. DIV unsigned: RAX / rm  quotient=RAX, remainder=RDX. IDIV for signed. ADC/SBB include carry. INC/DEC increment/decrement. NEG negates.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Control Flow and Branching[0]

Unconditional: JMP. Conditional: JE, JNE, JG, JL, JGE, JLE, JA, JB, JAE, JBE, JO, JS, JC, JP. Based on RFLAGS set by CMP or arithmetic. CMP subtracts operands, sets flags, discards result. TEST performs AND, sets flags, discards result. Jcc checks specific flags.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Loops[0]

The LOOP instruction decrements RCX and jumps to a label if RCX != 0. LOOPE/LOOPZ (loop while equal) also checks ZF=1. LOOPNE/LOOPNZ (loop while not equal) also checks ZF=0. For more control, implement loops manually with a counter register, CMP, and conditional jump. Nested loops require saving/restoring the outer loop counter.
.NASM Assembly Basics.Stack Operations[0]

PUSH decrements RSP then stores. POP loads then increments RSP. PUSHA/POPA (all regs) are 32-bit only. PUSHF/POPF save/restore RFLAGS. ENTER/LEAVE create/destroy stack frames (rarely used — prefer manual frame setup). Stack grows toward lower addresses. In 64-bit mode, PUSH/POP default to 64-bit operands.
.Procedures and the Stack.CALL and RET[0]

CALL pushes the return address (RIP) onto the stack then jumps to the target. RET pops the return address and jumps back. Near calls (within same segment) are standard in 64-bit. CALL can be direct (call label) or indirect (call rax, call [table+rcx*8]). RET can take an immediate to pop extra bytes.
.Procedures and the Stack.Passing Arguments[0]

System V AMD64 ABI: integer args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 (left to right). Additional args on the stack. Return value in RAX. Callee-saved: RBX, RBP, R12-R15. Caller-saved: RAX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, R8-R11. Stack must be 16-byte aligned before CALL.
.Procedures and the Stack.Stack Frames[0]

A stack frame is created with `push rbp; mov rbp, rsp`. Local variables are allocated by subtracting from RSP: `sub rsp, 32`. RBP provides a stable reference: parameters at positive offsets [rbp+16+], locals at negative offsets [rbp-8]. Leave instruction: `mov rsp, rbp; pop rbp`.
.Procedures and the Stack.Recursion[0]

A recursive procedure calls itself. Each call creates a new stack frame with its own parameters, local variables, and return address. Must have a base case to terminate and a recursive case that progresses toward the base. Deep recursion can overflow the stack (default ulimit ~8MB). Use the stack to save state across calls. Factorial and Fibonacci are classic examples.
.Procedures and the Stack.Macros[0]

NASM macros: %define (single-line) and %macro (multi-line). %define can have parameters: `%define mulby2(x) x*2`. Multi-line: `%macro name paramcount` ... `%endmacro`. %rotate cycles through parameters. %assign for numeric macros. Conditional assembly: %if, %elif, %else, %endif.
.Procedures and the Stack.Multi-File Programs[0]

Large programs split into multiple .asm files and link together. Use `extern` to declare symbols from other files, `global` to make symbols visible. Assemble each file separately, link together. `nasm -f elf64 util.asm -o util.o && nasm -f elf64 main.asm -o main.o && ld -o prog main.o util.o`. Avoid name collisions with LOCAL labels (.label).
.Procedures and the Stack.Stack Alignment & Red Zone[0]

System V AMD64 ABI: RSP must be 16-byte aligned before CALL. The stack is 16-byte aligned at _start. After CALL (pushes 8-byte return address), RSP is 8 mod 16. Subroutines adjust RSP to maintain alignment. The red zone is 128 bytes below RSP — safe for scratch data (not affected by signals/handlers in leaf functions).
.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Flag Register[0]

RFLAGS is 64-bit but only lower 32 bits are used. Key flags: CF (carry), PF (parity), AF (adjust), ZF (zero), SF (sign), OF (overflow), DF (direction), IF (interrupt). LAHF/SAHF transfer flags to/from AH.
.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Comparison and TEST[0]
CMP = SUB that only sets flags. Used before conditional jumps for signed (JG, JL, JGE, JLE, JE, JNE) and unsigned (JA, JB, JAE, JBE). TEST = AND that only sets flags. Used for bit testing.
.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Conditional Moves[0]
CMOVcc combines comparison and move: CMOVZ, CMOVNZ, CMOVG, CMOVL, CMOVGE, CMOVLE, CMOVA, CMOVB. Avoids branch mispredictions. SETcc sets a byte to 0/1 based on condition.
.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Logical Instructions[0]
AND, OR, XOR, NOT, NEG, TEST. AND for bit masking. OR sets bits. XOR toggles. XOR same register is idiomatic zero. AND with 1 checks parity. NOT flips all bits.
.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Bit Manipulation[0]

BT (bit test), BTC (bit test and complement), BTR (bit test and reset), BTS (bit test and set). BSF/BSR (bit scan forward/reverse). POPCNT counts set bits. LZCNT/TZCNT (leading/trailing zero count). SHLD/SHRD (double precision shifts).
.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.SETcc & Bit Test Instructions[0]

SETcc sets a byte register to 0 or 1 based on a condition. SETZ/SETE (zero), SETNZ/SETNE (non-zero), SETG (signed >), SETL (signed <), SETA (unsigned >), SETB (unsigned <), SETS (sign), SETO (overflow). BT/BTC/BTR/BTS test and optionally modify specific bits. Bit test is atomic with LOCK prefix.
.Strings and Data Structures.String Instructions[0]

String instructions use RSI (source) and RDI (dest). MOVSB/MOVSW/MOVSD/MOVSQ (move). LODSB/LODSW/LODSD/LODSQ (load from [RSI]). STOSB/STOSW/STOSD/STOSQ (store to [RDI]). CMPSB/CMPSW/CMPSD/CMPSQ (compare). SCASB/SCASW/SCASD/SCASQ (scan). REP repeats RCX times. REPE/REPNE repeats while equal/not equal.
.Strings and Data Structures.Arrays and Addressing[0]

Arrays are contiguous memory. Element access: base + index * element_size. Word: `mov ax, [array + rbx*2]`. Dword: `mov eax, [array + rcx*4]`. Qword: `mov rax, [array + rdx*8]`. LEA calculates addresses. Multidimensional arrays use row-major ordering.
.Strings and Data Structures.Structures and Records[0]

Structures group related data. NASM uses STRUC/ENDSTRUC with RESB/RESW/RESD/RESQ for fields. Initialize with ISTRUC/IEND. Field access with `[struc_variable + field_name]`. Alignment: naturally align fields. PADDING between fields maintains alignment.
.Strings and Data Structures.Buffers and I/O[0]

Buffers are memory blocks for data transfer. .bss reserves uninitialized space with RESB. For file I/O, use sys_open (rax=2), sys_read (0), sys_write (1), sys_close (3). sys_open returns fd in RAX (-1 on error). Buffered I/O: read chunks into buffer, process, write output.
.Strings and Data Structures.String Comparison and Search[0]

String compare: CMPSB/CMPSW/CMPSD with REPE/REPNE prefix. REPE CMPSB compares until mismatch or RCX=0. String search: SCASB scans for a byte. REPNE SCASB finds a byte. For null-terminated strings use `repne scasb` to find length.
.Strings and Data Structures.Linked List Traversal[0]

Linked lists are dynamic data structures. Node = data pointer + next pointer. Traverse by following next pointers until NULL. Operations: insert (update prev.next and new.next), delete (update prev.next to skip node), search (linear traversal). Assembly list: careful with memory dereferences and pointer arithmetic.
.Floating Point and SIMD.x87 Floating Point[0]

The legacy x87 FPU uses a stack of 8 registers (ST0-ST7). Instructions: FLD (load), FST/FSTP (store/pop), FADD, FSUB, FMUL, FDIV, FCHS, FSQRT, FCOM (compare), FTST (compare with 0). x87 is mostly superseded by SSE but still used in legacy code.
.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Scalar Operations[0]

SSE provides XMM0-XMM15 (128-bit) registers. Scalar: ADDSD (add scalar double), SUBSD, MULSD, DIVSD, SQRTSD. MOVSD moves scalar double. CVTSI2SD converts integer to double, CVTSD2SI converts double to integer. UCOMISD compares scalars.
.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Packed Operations[0]

SSE processes multiple elements at once: packed add/sub/mul/div on 2 doubles or 4 floats. ADDPS (packed single), ADDPD (packed double). SUBPS, MULPS, DIVPS. Also: MAXPS, MINPS, SQRTPS. HADDPS (horizontal add) sums adjacent pairs. MOVAPS/MOVUPS for aligned/unaligned moves.
.Floating Point and SIMD.AVX and Advanced SIMD[0]

AVX extends XMM to 256-bit YMM registers (YMM0-YMM15). Three-operand syntax: `vaddps ymm0, ymm1, ymm2`. Non-destructive sources. AVX2 adds gather, FMA. AVX-512 extends to 512-bit ZMM. VZEROUPPER clears upper bits when mixing SSE and AVX.
.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Integer and Conversion[0]

SSE2 adds 128-bit integer ops in XMM: PADDB/W/D/Q, PSUBB/W/D/Q, PMULLW/D. PCMPEQB/W/D (compare equal). PCMPGTB/W/D. PAND, POR, PXOR, PANDN. PACKSSWB/PACKUSDW (pack with saturation). PMOVMSKB creates integer mask from byte MSBs.
.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Data Conversion & Shuffle[0]

SSE conversion: CVTSI2SD (int→double), CVTSD2SI (double→int), CVTTSD2SI (truncate), CVTDQ2PS (int→float), CVTPS2DQ (float→int). Shuffle: PSHUFD (dword shuffle), SHUFPS (float shuffle), PUNPCKLDQ (interleave low dwords), PACKSSDW (pack with saturation). Shuffle masks select source elements.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.Linux System Calls[0]

Linux syscalls: RAX = syscall number, RDI/RSI/RDX/R10/R8/R9 = args, syscall invokes the kernel. Return in RAX. Common: 0=read, 1=write, 2=open, 3=close, 9=mmap, 12=brk, 60=exit. Syscall numbers differ between x86 and x64. See /usr/include/asm/unistd_64.h.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.Calling C Library Functions[0]

Link with gcc instead of ld to use libc: `nasm -f elf64 prog.asm && gcc -no-pie -o prog prog.o`. Libc provides printf, malloc, fopen, etc. The C runtime expects `main` instead of `_start`. RSP must be 16-byte aligned before CALL.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.Command Line Arguments[0]

When linked with libc and using `main`, argc is in RDI, argv is in RSI. argc = argument count (program name counts as 1). argv = array of char* pointers, null-terminated. Environment variables (envp) are in RDX.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.File I/O with syscalls[0]

File operations: open (returns fd), read/write, close, lseek. sys_open: path in RDI, flags in RSI, mode in RDX. Flags: O_RDONLY=0, O_WRONLY=1, O_RDWR=2, O_CREAT=0x40, O_TRUNC=0x200, O_APPEND=0x400. Always check return values: negative = error.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.Memory Management[0]

sys_brk (12) allocates heap memory. Call with RDI=0 to get current break, then RDI=new_break to allocate. More flexible: sys_mmap (9) maps anonymous memory. mmap args: addr=0, length, prot=3 (PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE), flags=0x22 (MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS), fd=-1, offset=0. munmap (11) frees.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.Debugging with GDB[0]

Assemble with debug symbols: `nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf prog.asm`. GDB commands: break, run, stepi, nexti, info registers, x/Nx addr (examine memory), disas (disassemble), backtrace. Use layout reg for register view, layout asm for disassembly.
.Interfacing with C and Linux.Dynamic Linking & Shared Libraries[0]

Create shared libraries: `nasm -f elf64 -dPIC lib.asm && gcc -shared -o libfoo.so lib.o`. Use from C or ASM. GOT (Global Offset Table) holds addresses of global symbols. PLT (Procedure Linkage Table) enables lazy binding. Position-independent code (PIC) uses RIP-relative addressing for shared libraries.
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Performance Optimization[0]

x64 optimization: minimize memory access (load once, reuse), align code/data to cache lines (64 bytes), avoid branch mispredictions (use CMOV, bit manipulation), use SIMD for parallel processing, unroll loops carefully, prefer register args over stack, avoid partial register stalls (use movzx not mov+and), use LEA for arithmetic when possible.
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Inline Assembly (GCC)[0]

GCC inline assembly: `asm("instructions" : outputs : inputs : clobbers)`. Extended asm: `asm volatile("add %1, %0" : "+r"(a) : "r"(b))`. AT&T syntax (src,dst) vs Intel (dst,src). Use `-masm=intel` for Intel syntax. Constraints: r=register, m=memory, i=immediate.
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Interrupts and Exception Handling[0]

x86-64 has an IDT (Interrupt Descriptor Table). Linux exceptions: #DE (divide error, vector 0), #DB (debug, 1), #BP (breakpoint, 3), #GP (general protection, 13), #PF (page fault, 14). The `int` instruction triggers software interrupts (syscall is preferred on x64).
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.PIC and Position-Independent Code[0]

Position-independent code (PIC) is required for shared libraries. Use `lea rax, [rel symbol]` instead of `mov rax, symbol`. NASM's `default rel` sets RIP-relative addressing as default. For shared libraries: `nasm -f elf64 -dPIC lib.asm && gcc -shared -o lib.so lib.o`. GOT and PLT enable dynamic linking.
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Multithreading and Atomic Ops[0]

Atomic operations prevent race conditions. LOCK prefix: `lock inc dword [counter]`, `lock xadd`, `lock cmpxchg`, `lock bts`. CMPXCHG (compare and exchange) is the core of lock-free programming. MFENCE/LFENCE/SFENCE for memory ordering. POSIX threads (pthreads) can be called from assembly via libc. Thread-local storage (TLS) uses the FS segment register in x86-64.
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Loop Optimization & Unrolling[0]

Loop optimization: unroll to reduce loop overhead (dec/jnz). Partial unrolling for non-multiple iteration counts. Software pipelining: reorder instructions to hide latency. Align loop entry points to 16/32 bytes. Use registers instead of memory for loop counters. Prefer `sub rcx, 1; jnz .loop` over `loop .loop` (LOOP is slower on modern CPUs).
.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Data Alignment & Prefetching[0]

Data alignment: CPUs access aligned data faster. Natural alignment: 2-byte data on 2-byte boundaries, 4-byte on 4-byte, etc. Misaligned access causes penalty (or fault on some architectures). Use ALIGN directive: `align 16`, `align 64` (cache line). Prefetch: PREFETCH0/PREFETCH1/PREFETCH2/PREFETCHNTA bring data into caches before use. Prefetch avoids cache misses on predictable access patterns.
.Macros & Preprocessing.Multi-Line Macros[0]

NASM %macro defines multi-line macros with parameters. %1-%9 access parameters, %10+ need braces. %rotate cycles parameters. %rep/%endrep repeats blocks. %exitmacro exits early. Use %macro for complex code generation that would be tedious to write manually.
.Macros & Preprocessing.Conditional Assembly[0]

Conditional directives: %if, %elif, %else, %endif. Conditions: %id (defined), %nid (not defined), %idef (defined, case-insensitive), numeric expressions. %ifdef/%ifndef for simple existence checks. %ifctx/%ifidn for context stack. Useful for platform-specific code, debug builds, and feature toggles.
.Macros & Preprocessing.Context Stack & Advanced Preprocessing[0]

NASM context stack: %push, %pop, %repl. %ifctx checks context name. Useful for scoped macro state and block matching. %[+/-]contextname for context-local labels. %strlen, %substr, %strcat for string operations at assembly time. %arg, %local, %stacksize macros (from macro package) simplify stack frame creation.
.Macros & Preprocessing.%include & File Organization[0]

%include inserts another source file at assembly time (like C #include). Use for shared constants, macros, and structure definitions across multiple ASM files. Paths relative to current file or include search path (`-I` flag). Guard against double inclusion with %ifndef.
.Debugging & Profiling.GDB Advanced Techniques[0]

Advanced GDB: conditional breakpoints (`break func if rax==42`), watchpoints (`watch var`), reverse debugging (record/replay), checkpoint/restart. examine: `x/20gx $rsp` (20 qwords as hex), `x/s $rsi` (string). display: `display/8i $rip` (show instructions each step). define custom commands with `define`.
.Debugging & Profiling.Profiling & Performance Counters[0]

Performance counters via `perf stat ./prog`, `perf record ./prog` + `perf report`. Linux perf events: cycles, instructions, branch-misses, cache-misses. rdtsc/rdtscp reads the timestamp counter. Read PMCs (performance monitoring counters) via RDPMC (privileged). Use-p stat for basic counts. perf top for live profiling.
.Debugging & Profiling.Valgrind & Sanitizers[0]

Valgrind finds memory errors without recompilation: `valgrind --tool=memcheck ./prog`. Tools: memcheck (leaks, invalid accesses), cachegrind (cache profiling), callgrind (call graph), helgrind (thread races). AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) for C-linked code. For pure assembly, check syscall parameter correctness manually.
.Debugging & Profiling.GAS & Other Assemblers[0]

GNU Assembler (GAS) uses AT&T syntax by default: `mov src, dst` (opposite of NASM). Register prefix: `%rax`. Immediate prefix: `$42`. Memory: `disp(base, index, scale)`. GAS with .intel_syntax noprefix matches NASM syntax. Other assemblers: MASM (Windows), FASM (flat assembler, portable), YASM (NASM-compatible rewrite). GAS is the default for GCC/LLVM.
.Crypto & Security.AES-NI Instructions[0]

AES-NI provides hardware-accelerated AES: AESENC (encrypt round), AESENCLAST (final round), AESDEC (decrypt), AESDECLAST, AESKEYGENASSIST (key expansion), AESIMC (inverse mix columns). PCLMULQDQ for carry-less multiplication (GCM). Instructions are constant-time, mitigating timing side-channel attacks.
.Crypto & Security.Constant-Time Code[0]

Constant-time code prevents timing side channels. No secret-dependent branches (use CMOV). No secret-dependent memory access (use bit masking). Use XOR/AND/OR/CMOV for conditional logic. Avoid lookup tables indexed by secret data. CPU instructions should execute in the same number of cycles regardless of operand values.
.Crypto & Security.CRC & Hashing Instructions[0]

CRC32C instruction (SSE4.2) accelerates CRC-32C checksums. CRC32 reg, mem/reg. Used in iSCSI, ext4, network protocols. Also supports: SHA extensions (SHA1RNDs4, SHA256RNDs2) on newer CPUs. PCLMULQDQ enables fast GHASH (GCM mode). These hardware instructions are much faster than software implementations.
.System Programming.Signal Handling[0]

Signals are software interrupts sent to processes. Register handlers with sigaction syscall (13) or libc's signal(). Common signals: SIGINT (2), SIGTERM (15), SIGKILL (9, cannot be caught), SIGSEGV (11, segfault). SA_RESTART flag re-starts interrupted syscalls. Signal handlers run on an alternate stack (sigaltstack) for SIGSEGV handling.
.System Programming.Process Creation & Syscalls[0]

Linux process creation via sys_fork (57) or sys_clone (56). fork: returns 0 in child, PID in parent. execve (59) replaces process image with a new program. waitpid (61) waits for child. exit_group (231) exits all threads. POSIX libc wrappers: fork(), execvp(), wait(), system().
.System Programming.Shared Memory & IPC[0]

Inter-process communication (IPC) via shared memory (shmget/shmat), pipes (pipe syscall), FIFOs (named pipes), message queues (msgget/msgsnd/msgrcv), and sockets. mmap with MAP_SHARED creates shared memory mappings. semaphores provide synchronization. Use futex for fast user-space mutual exclusion.
.x86-64 Architecture Deep Dive.Registers & Calling Conventions[0]

x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers: RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RBP, RSP, and R8-R15. Each register can be accessed in 64-bit (RAX), 32-bit (EAX), 16-bit (AX), or 8-bit (AL/AH) modes. The System V AMD64 calling convention (Linux/macOS) passes first 6 integer args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, then stack. Return value goes in RAX. Callee-saved registers (RBX, RBP, R12-R15) must be preserved. Stack alignment to 16 bytes is required before calls. Microsoft x64 on Windows uses RCX, RDX, R8, R9 for first 4 args.
.x86-64 Architecture Deep Dive.Condition Codes & Control Flow[0]

x86-64 uses the RFLAGS register for condition codes. CMP and TEST instructions set flags without modifying operands. Key flags: ZF (zero), SF (sign), OF (overflow), CF (carry). Conditional jumps use these flags: JE/JZ (jump if equal/zero), JNE/JNZ (not equal), JG/JNLE (signed greater), JL/JNGE (signed less), JA/JNBE (unsigned above), JB/JNAE (unsigned below). SETcc sets a byte to 1 based on condition. CMOVcc conditionally moves data. The LEA instruction computes effective addresses without accessing memory.
.x86-64 Architecture Deep Dive.Stack Frames & Function Prologues[0]

Function prologues and epilogues manage the stack frame. Standard prologue: push rbp; mov rbp, rsp saves the old base pointer and sets up a new frame. Local variables are allocated by subtracting from RSP: sub rsp, 32 (allocate 32 bytes). The epilogue reverses: mov rsp, rbp; pop rbp; ret. Red zone (128 bytes below RSP) can be used without adjusting RSP in leaf functions. Stack canaries guard against buffer overflows. Frame pointers can be omitted (-fomit-frame-pointer) for performance using RSP-relative addressing instead.
.x86-64 Architecture Deep Dive.SIMD & Vector Instructions[0]

SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) processes multiple data elements in one instruction. x86-64 provides SSE (128-bit XMM registers), AVX (256-bit YMM registers), and AVX-512 (512-bit ZMM registers). XMM0-XMM15 (SSE), YMM0-YMM15 (AVX/AVX2). Basic operations: MOVDQA (aligned move), MOVDQU (unaligned move), PADDB/PADDW/PADDD (packed add), PMULLD (packed multiply), PSHUFB (shuffle bytes), PCMPEQB (compare equality). Auto-vectorization by compilers generates these instructions automatically. Manual SIMD optimization can outperform compiler-generated code by 2-4x for specific algorithms.
.ARM64 Assembly.ARM64 vs x86-64 Comparison[0]

ARM64 (AArch64) is a RISC architecture with key differences from x86 CISC: fixed 4-byte instruction size, 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers (X0-X30), load-store architecture (only load/store access memory), conditional execution via CSEL instead of flags, and no variable instruction length. X30 is the link register (return address). X29 is the frame pointer. Stack pointer is a special register (SP). ARM64 uses BL/RET for calls. First 8 args in X0-X7. Return value in X0. ARM64 dominates mobile devices (Apple Silicon, Qualcomm) and is growing in servers (AWS Graviton, Ampere). Understanding both ISAs is valuable for performance-critical development.
.ARM64 Assembly.ARM64 NEON SIMD[0]

ARM64 NEON provides 128-bit SIMD with 32 registers (V0-V31). Each register can hold 2x64-bit, 4x32-bit, 8x16-bit, or 16x8-bit elements. Key instructions: LD1/ST1 (load/store multiple), ADD/SUB/MUL (vector arithmetic), FMLA (fused multiply-add), EXT (extract), TBL/TBX (table lookup). NEON is particularly efficient for audio/video processing, image manipulation, and machine learning inference. Apple's Accelerate framework and libraries like sleef provide optimized NEON routines.
aws.json: EC2 provides virtual machines. Instance families: general (t3, m6i), compute (c6i), memory (r6i, x2gd), storage (i3, d2), GPU (p4, g5). Purchase options: On-Demand (pay per hour/sec), Reserved (1-3yr, up to 72% off), Spot (up to 90% off, interruptible), Dedicated Host. User data runs at boot. Placement groups control instance placement for low latency or HA.

Security Groups are stateful firewalls attached to ENIs. Rules: allow only (no deny), evaluate all rules. NACLs are stateless firewalls at subnet level (allow/deny, rule numbers). Elastic IPs are static public IPs. ENIs are virtual network cards. VPC Flow Logs capture traffic metadata.

Auto Scaling maintains desired instance count. Launch template specifies instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking (e.g., keep CPU at 50%), step scaling, scheduled scaling. Health checks replace unhealthy instances. Cooldown periods prevent rapid scaling. Lifecycle hooks run custom actions during scale events.

ALB (Application LB): HTTP/HTTPS, path-based routing, host-based routing, WebSockets. NLB (Network LB): TCP/UDP/TLS, ultra-low latency, static IP. Gateway LB: transparent inspection of traffic. Target groups route to instances, IPs, or Lambda. Sticky sessions via cookies. Health checks detect failures. Cross-zone load balancing distributes evenly.

Lambda runs code without servers. Runtimes: Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, custom (provided.al2). Triggers: API Gateway, S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge, Kinesis. Max execution 15 min, max memory 10GB, max ephemeral storage 10GB. Concurrency limit per account (1000 default). Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity. Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm. Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations.

ECS runs Docker containers at scale. Launch types: Fargate (serverless, no EC2 to manage) and EC2 (control over instances). EKS is managed Kubernetes. ECR stores container images. Task definitions describe containers (CPU, memory, ports, env vars). Services maintain desired task count with load balancer integration.

Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS — upload code, AWS handles provisioning, load balancing, auto scaling, monitoring. Platforms: Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, PHP, Ruby, Go, Docker. Environments: Web tier (ALB + ASG) and Worker tier (SQS + background jobs). Customize with .ebextensions config files. Easy for MVPs and standard web apps.

EC2 Image Builder automates AMI creation. Pipeline steps: source image, build components (install packages), test components (validate), distribute to regions. Golden AMIs ensure consistent instances. Systems Manager Parameter Store tracks latest AMI IDs. Automate AMI refresh in Auto Scaling via lifecycle hooks.

Amazon S3 is object storage with 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability. Storage classes: Standard (frequent access), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-cost optimization), Standard-IA (infrequent), One Zone-IA (lower cost, single AZ), Glacier Instant (archival, ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible (min retrieval), Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, 12hr retrieval). Versioning protects against deletes. Lifecycle policies transition between classes. S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda/SQS/SNS.

S3 security: Block Public Access (account/bucket level). Bucket policies (resource-based). IAM policies (identity-based). ACLs (legacy). Encryption: SSE-S3 (AES-256, AWS managed), SSE-KMS (KMS keys, audit trail), SSE-C (customer provided key), client-side encryption. Object Lock (WORM — write once read many). S3 Access Points simplify managing access for large datasets.

EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage for EC2. Volume types: gp3 (baseline 3000 IOPS, 125 MB/s, max 16000 IOPS), io2 (provisioned IOPS, 99.999% durability), st1 (throughput optimized, HDD), sc1 (cold HDD). Snapshots are incremental backups to S3. EBS Multi-attach for clustered workloads. EBS Fast Snapshot Restore for instant snapshot hydration. Instance Store is ephemeral (data lost on stop/terminate).

EFS is managed NFS for Linux. Elastic — grows/shrinks automatically. Performance modes: General Purpose (default, latency-sensitive) and Max I/O (high-throughput, parallel). Throughput modes: Bursting and Provisioned. Lifecycle management moves files to EFS IA after N days. EFS Replication for cross-region DR. FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, AD integration) and FSx for Lustre (high-performance, HPC/AI).

CloudFront is a global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, Lambda Function URL, HTTP server. Behaviors route by path pattern. Price classes: All, 200 (most), NA+EU only. SSL/TLS termination via ACM. Geo-restriction (whitelist/blacklist countries). Lambda@Edge for custom logic. OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. Real-time logs to Kinesis. WAF integration for DDoS protection.

VPC is your isolated network in AWS. CIDR block defines IP range (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets divide the VPC (public for internet-facing, private for internal). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway (IGW) for public internet access. NAT Gateway for private subnets to reach internet (outbound only). VPC Peering connects VPCs within or across accounts. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-prem. Endpoints (Gateway: S3/DynamoDB; Interface: other services) provide private access without IGW.

Route53 is a DNS service (authoritative + resolver). Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verify), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources — free, works at zone apex). Routing policies: Simple, Weighted, Latency, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multi-value. Health checks monitor endpoint health and route away from failures. Private hosted zones for internal DNS. DNSSEC for security.

AWS WAF is a web application firewall that protects HTTP endpoints. Rule groups: IP set, SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo-match, regex patterns. Managed rule groups from AWS (Core, SQL DB, Admin Protection, Known Bad Inputs). Shield Standard is free, protects against DDoS (L3/L4). Shield Advanced ($3k/mo) adds L7 DDoS protection, cost protection, DRT (DDoS Response Team). WAF integrates with CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync.

KMS manages encryption keys. Customer managed keys vs AWS managed keys. Automatic annual key rotation. Envelope encryption: generate a data key to encrypt data, encrypt the data key with a KMS key. Key policies control who can use/administer keys. Grant allows temporary access. Secrets Manager stores secrets (DB passwords, API keys) with automatic rotation via Lambda. Parameter Store (free) stores config data and secrets.

Create an AWS account at aws.amazon.com. Root user has full unrestricted access — enable MFA immediately. Never use root for daily tasks. Create IAM users and roles instead. Set up billing alerts. Use AWS Organizations to manage multiple accounts centrally. Enable CloudTrail in all regions.

IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls access. Users are individuals. Groups organize users with shared permissions. Roles are assumed by services (EC2, Lambda) or federated users. Policies are JSON documents with Allow/Deny effects. Follow least privilege. Use managed policies when possible.

IAM policies have: Version (2012-10-17), Statement list with Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (service:operation), Resource (ARN), and optional Condition (IP, time, MFA, tags). Use policy variables ${aws:username}. Managed policies vs inline. Permission boundaries limit max permissions. Service Control Policies (SCP) in Organizations.

AWS Organizations centrally manages multiple accounts. Root OU contains all accounts. Create OUs for structure (Production, Staging, Sandbox). Service Control Policies (SCPs) restrict max permissions across accounts. Consolidate billing for volume discounts. Use AWS SSO for user access across accounts.

AWS has 30+ regions worldwide (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1, etc.). Each region has 3-6 Availability Zones (AZs) — isolated data centers. Edge Locations are CDN endpoints (400+). Use multiple AZs for HA. Choose region based on latency, compliance, cost, and service availability. Some services are global (IAM, Route53, CloudFront).

RDS manages relational databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Multi-AZ: synchronous standby replica in another AZ for HA (failover is automatic). Read replicas: async replication for read scaling (up to 15). Automated backups with point-in-time recovery (up to 35 days). Manual snapshots persist beyond retention. Enhanced Monitoring (CloudWatch metrics per second). Performance Insights for query analysis. RDS Proxy for connection pooling.

Amazon Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible with cloud-native architecture. 6-way replication across 3 AZs — only 1/6 of data written (quorum). Auto-scaling storage from 10GB to 128TB. Aurora Serverless v2 scales to 0 ACUs (pay per second). Global Database: 1 primary region, up to 5 secondary regions with <1s replication. Backtrack: rewind DB to a specific time without restore. Parallel Query pushes analytics to storage layer.

DynamoDB is fully managed NoSQL key-value/document DB. Single-digit ms latency at any scale. Primary key: partition key (HASH) or composite (HASH + RANGE). Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, auto-scales) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, auto-scaling). DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Global Tables are multi-region, multi-writer (active-active). Streams capture changes for Lambda triggers or Kinesis. TTL auto-expires items.

ElastiCache provides managed Redis and Memcached. Redis: multi-AZ, replication, persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets, streams, Lua scripting. Memcached: simple, multi-threaded, no persistence. Cluster Mode shards data across nodes (up to 500 shards). Global Datastore for cross-region replication. MemoryDB is Redis-compatible, durable (write-ahead log), for microservices requiring both speed and durability. Use cases: session store, caching, rate limiting, leaderboards, message queues.

Redshift is cloud data warehouse (petabyte-scale). Columnar storage, massively parallel (MPP). Node types: DC (dense compute), DS/RA3 (managed storage). Distribution styles: KEY, ALL, EVEN. Sort keys define data order per block. Redshift Spectrum queries data directly in S3 without loading. Automatic workload management (WLM) prioritizes queries. Concurrency Scaling handles burst queries. Materialized views for pre-computed aggregates. Unload data to S3 for analysis.

CloudFormation is IaC (Infrastructure as Code) on AWS. Templates written in YAML/JSON. Resources define AWS components. Parameters allow customization at deploy time. Outputs export values for cross-stack references. Change sets preview changes before applying. Nested stacks compose complex infrastructure. Drift detection checks if real-world resources match the template. StackSets deploy across accounts/regions via Organizations. DeletionPolicy controls resource retention on stack delete.

CodePipeline automates build-test-deploy. Source: CodeCommit, GitHub, Bitbucket, S3. Build: CodeBuild (managed build server, pay per minute). Deploy: CodeDeploy (EC2, Lambda, ECS), Elastic Beanstalk, CloudFormation. Stages run sequentially with manual approval gates. Artifacts stored in S3. CloudWatch Events trigger pipelines on source changes.

CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms. Metrics: CPU, memory, disk, network, custom metrics. Alarms: threshold-based, composite (multiple conditions), anomaly detection. Logs: agent collects from EC2, streams to log groups. Logs Insights queries logs with SQL-like syntax. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors (IPs, endpoints). Synthetics (Canaries) monitor endpoints with Node.js scripts. ServiceLens traces requests across services (X-Ray integration). Dashboards visualize metrics in one place.

EventBridge is a serverless event bus. Sources: AWS services, SaaS (Datadog, Zendesk), custom apps. Rules filter events and route to targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions). Pipes connects sources to targets with filtering and enrichment. Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows (visual state machine). Standard Workflows (up to 1-year duration) vs Express (up to 5-min, high volume). States: Task, Choice, Parallel, Map, Wait, Succeed, Fail. Error handling with retries and catch.

AWS Budgets track spending and send alerts. Types: Cost budget, Usage budget, Savings Plans budget, Reservation budget. Budget actions can apply IAM policy or stop EC2 instances when threshold is exceeded. Cost Explorer visualizes spend. Compute Optimizer recommends right-sizing. Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker) offer discounts for commitment. Trusted Advisor checks cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits. Consolidated billing aggregates usage across accounts.

VPC is the foundation of AWS networking. Subnets (public/private) segment IP ranges. Route tables direct traffic to IGW (public) or NATGW (private). NAT Gateway enables outbound internet for private subnets — costs ~$0.045/hr + data processed. VPC Peering connects VPCs directly (no transitive peering). Security Groups (stateful, allow-only) vs NACLs (stateless, allow/deny, rule numbers). Common mistake: forgetting NACL rules are stateless — must configure both inbound and outbound rules separately. VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata for analysis. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs/on-prem via a hub. Use VPC endpoints for private access to S3/DynamoDB without NAT/IGW.

Route53 is AWS's DNS service. Hosted zones contain DNS records for a domain. Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (cannot be used at zone apex), MX (mail), TXT (verification), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources, works at zone apex, free). Routing policies: Simple (single record), Weighted (A/B testing), Latency (best performance), Failover (active-passive DR), Geolocation (by user location), Geoproximity (by resource location). Health checks monitor endpoints. Common mistake: using CNAME at zone apex — use Alias instead. Enable DNSSEC for DNS spoofing protection.

CloudFront is AWS's global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Distributions define content delivery configuration. Origins: S3 buckets, ALBs, EC2, custom HTTP servers. Behaviors route by URL path pattern. Lambda@Edge executes code at edge locations (viewer/origin request/response) — use for A/B testing, URL rewrites, authentication. Price classes: Price Class All (all edges), Price Class 200 (most, cheaper), Price Class 100 (US+Europe, cheapest). Invalidations clear edge caches (charged per path). OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. WAF integration for DDoS. Common mistake: caching sensitive data — set appropriate Cache-Control and Cookie/QueryString forwarding policies.

DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL with single-digit ms latency. Tables contain items (up to 400KB each). Primary key: Partition Key (HASH) alone or Composite (HASH + RANGE/Sort Key). GSIs (Global Secondary Indexes) have different partition/sort keys — eventually consistent, add after table creation. LSIs (Local Secondary Indexes) same partition key, different sort key — created only at table creation, strongly consistent. DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is an in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, best for variable traffic) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, cheaper for predictable traffic). Streams capture changes for 24h. TTL auto-expires items. Common mistake: scanning instead of querying — always Query with a partition key.

SQS is fully managed message queuing. Standard queues: unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO queues: exactly-once processing, first-in-first-out, 3000 msg/s max (with batching). Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail after maxReceiveCount retries. Visibility timeout hides messages during processing — set longer than your processing time. Long polling reduces empty responses and costs. SNS is pub/sub messaging. Topics fan out messages to subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS). Fan-out pattern: SNS sends to multiple SQS queues for parallel processing. Message filtering with filter policies. Common mistake: forgetting to delete messages from SQS after processing (they reappear after visibility timeout!).

Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows as state machines. Standard Workflows: up to 1-year duration, exactly-once execution, billed per state transition. Express Workflows: up to 5-min duration, at-least-once, billed by execution time/memory. State types: Task (invoke Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SQS), Choice (if/else), Parallel (fan-out), Map (iterate array), Wait (delay), Succeed/Fail (terminate). Error handling: Retry (exponential backoff, maxAttempts) and Catch (redirect to fallback state). Timeouts prevent stuck executions. Heartbeats for long-running tasks. Common mistake: not setting appropriate timeouts — workflows can hang indefinitely.
