Symbol tables map identifiers to their attributes. Scopes are nested; inner scopes can access outer scopes. The most-closely-nested rule governs name resolution.
Three-Address Code (TAC) decomposes expressions into simple operations with at most three operands. Each instruction is a quad (op, arg1, arg2, result). TAC exposes data flow for optimization.

Static Single Assignment (SSA) assigns each variable exactly once. Phi functions merge values at control flow joins. SSA simplifies constant propagation, dead code elimination, and register allocation.
A CFG represents all paths through a program. Nodes are basic blocks (straight-line code). Edges represent control flow. Dominance, natural loops, and data-flow analysis use the CFG structure.
Graph coloring assigns virtual registers to physical registers. Variables with overlapping live ranges interfere and cannot share a register. Uncolorable variables are spilled to memory.
Instruction selection matches IR operations to target instructions. Tree rewriting, maximal munch, and DAG-based selection are common approaches. LLVM uses DAG-based matching.
Constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time. x = 2 * 3 becomes x = 6. Constant propagation replaces variables that are always constant with their values.
DCE removes instructions whose results are never used. In SSA form, trace back from output-producing instructions and mark everything else as dead.
Key loop optimizations: invariant code motion, induction variable strength reduction, loop unrolling, fusion, fission, and vectorization. Loops are the primary optimization target.
Yacc and Bison generate LALR(1) parsers from grammar specifications. ANTLR generates LL(*) parsers. Tree-sitter provides incremental parsing for IDEs.
LLVM provides a modular compiler infrastructure: Clang frontend, LLVM IR middle-end, and target-specific backends. Rust, Swift, and Julia use LLVM. MLIR extends LLVM for domain-specific compilers.

Type systems range from nominal (Java) to structural (TypeScript, Go). Gradual typing mixes static and dynamic checks. Rust's ownership model uses linear types. Algebraic data types with pattern matching provide safe sum types.
cpp.json: C++ is a powerful, statically-typed systems programming language that extends C with object-oriented, generic, and functional features. It gives fine-grained control over memory and performance.
Major standards: C++98 (original), C++11 (modern), C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23. Each adds features. Compile with -std=c++17, -std=c++20, etc. Always check compiler support.
Major compilers: GCC (g++), Clang, MSVC. Build systems: CMake (most common), Make, Ninja, Bazel. CMake generates build files for your platform.
Typical layout: src/ for .cpp, include/ for .hpp/.h, lib/ for dependencies, tests/ for unit tests. Use header guards (#pragma once) to prevent double inclusion.
Namespaces prevent name collisions. `std` is the standard library namespace. Nested namespaces (C++17): `namespace A::B::C {}`. Never `using namespace` in headers.
Semicolons terminate statements. Blocks use braces. `//` single-line, `/* */` multi-line comments. `std::cout` output, `std::cin` input. `#include` for headers.
`auto` deduces type from initializer (C++11). `decltype` yields the type of an expression. `auto&` deduces reference, `const auto&` deduces const reference.
`auto` strips references and top-level const (unless you use `auto&` or `const auto&`). `decltype(auto)` preserves exact type (C++14). Template deduction follows similar rules.
`nullptr` (C++11) is the type-safe null pointer. `<cstdint>` provides `int32_t`, `uint64_t`, etc. with guaranteed sizes. `size_t` for sizes/indices.
`const` for runtime constants. `constexpr` (C++11) for compile-time constants. `constinit` (C++20) guarantees static initialization. `consteval` (C++20) produces compile-time only.
`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (modulo). `++`, `--` (pre/post). `&&`, `||`, `!` short-circuit. Compound: `+=`, `-=`, etc. Integer division truncates toward zero.
`&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift). Useful for flags, bitfields, low-level protocols.
Operators can be overloaded for user types. `operator+`, `operator<<`, `operator[]`, `operator()`, etc. Keep semantics intuitive. Some cannot be overloaded (::, ., ?:, sizeof).
Suffixes for literals (C++11). `operator""_suffix`. Common: `std::string` literal `s` (C++14), `std::chrono` literals. Must begin with underscore for user-defined.
Conditional branching. C++17 added `if constexpr` for compile-time branching in templates. C++17 init-statements: `if (init; cond)`.
Switch on integral/enum types. Each case needs `break` or `return`. `[[fallthrough]]` suppresses warnings. C++20 added init-statement for switch.
`for`, `while`, `do-while`. `break` exits, `continue` skips iteration. Classic for uses init;cond;incr pattern.
Simplified iteration over containers (C++11). Works with arrays, STL containers, and anything with begin/end. Use `auto&` to avoid copies, `const auto&` for read-only.
Compile-time conditional (C++17). Unused branch is discarded, not compiled. Essential for template metaprogramming. Replaces SFINAE in many cases.
Decompose tuples, pairs, arrays, structs into individual variables (C++17). Works with `auto`, `auto&`, `const auto&`.
Variables scoped to if/switch/for (C++17). Reduces scope, improves safety. Combined with structured bindings for powerful patterns.
Declaration (prototype) tells compiler about name/return/params. Definition has the body. Default arguments go in declaration. `void` means no return.
Multiple functions with the same name but different parameters (overloading). Default arguments must be at the end. Resolved at compile time.
Anonymous functions (C++11). `[]` capture by value, `[&]` by reference. Generic lambdas (C++14): `[](auto x)`. `mutable` allows modifying captured values.
`auto func() -> type` (C++11). Useful when return type depends on parameter types. `decltype` in trailing return enables complex type computation.
`noexcept` declares function won't throw. Optimizer can skip exception handling. `noexcept(condition)` for conditional noexcept. `noexcept` is part of function type.
`consteval` (C++20) forces compile-time evaluation (immediate function). `constinit` (C++20) guarantees static initialization order. Both complement constexpr.
Function-level try block catches exceptions from constructor initializer lists and function bodies. Primarily useful in constructors for logging/re-throwing.
Dynamic, safe string from `<string>`. Methods: `length()`, `substr()`, `find()`, `rfind()`, `replace()`, `append()`, `insert()`, `erase()`. Concatenate with `+`.
`std::string_view` (C++17) is a non-owning reference to a string. Zero-copy. Perfect for function parameters. No null terminator guarantee.
Raw literals (C++11) preserve backslashes and newlines. `R"(text)"`. Delimiter optional: `R"delim(text)delim"`. Great for regex, file paths, JSON.
Convert between strings and numbers. `std::to_string()`, `std::stoi`, `stol`, `stod`, `stof`. `std::stringstream` for flexible formatting.
C++11 added `u8"..."` for UTF-8 strings. C++20 made `char8_t` a distinct type. `<codecvt>` is deprecated. Use ICU or platform APIs for full Unicode support.
Classes bundle data and methods. Access specifiers: `public`, `private`, `protected`. Constructors with initializer lists. `this` points to current instance.
Derived classes inherit from base. `virtual` functions enable dynamic dispatch. `override` keyword ensures correct override (C++11). Base class should have virtual destructor.
Base class must have virtual destructor to ensure derived destructors run when deleting through base pointer. `= default` for compiler-generated version.
Pure virtual `= 0` makes class abstract (cannot instantiate). Derived classes must override. Interface-style classes have only pure virtual methods.
Solves diamond problem where multiple bases share a common ancestor. `virtual` in inheritance specifier ensures only one copy of base subobject.
Provide strong exception safety for copy-assignment. Implement copy constructor and destructor normally. Assignment operator takes by value (copy) then swaps.
If you define any of destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment, define all five. Or =default/=delete.
Move transfers resources without copying (C++11). `std::move` casts to rvalue. Move constructor/assignment use `&&`. After move, source is in valid but unspecified state.
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. Constructor acquires, destructor releases. Smart pointers, `std::fstream`, `std::lock_guard`, `std::thread` all follow RAII.
Dynamic array with O(1) amortized push_back, O(n) insert/erase. Contiguous memory. Methods: `push_back`, `pop_back`, `emplace_back`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`.
Ordered associative containers (red-black tree). O(log n) lookup. `map<K,V>` key-value, `set<T>` unique values. Iterate in sorted order.
Hash-based containers (C++11). O(1) average lookup. Keys need hash function. No order guarantees. `reserve()` for pre-allocation.
Double-ended queue. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Non-contiguous memory (chunks). Slightly slower than vector for index access.
`std::list` doubly-linked, `std::forward_list` singly-linked (C++11). O(1) insert/erase anywhere with iterator. No random access. Higher per-element overhead.
`std::stack` (LIFO), `std::queue` (FIFO), `std::priority_queue` (max-heap). Built on underlying container (default deque or vector).
Fixed-size array wrapper (C++11). Stack-allocated. Knows its size. Safer than C arrays. `at()` for bounds checking. Compatible with STL algorithms.
Core algorithms from `<algorithm>`. `sort()`, `stable_sort()`, `find()`, `find_if()`, `transform()`, `for_each()`, `copy_if()`. Work on iterator pairs.
Binary search on sorted ranges (O(log n)). `lower_bound` returns first >= value. `upper_bound` returns first > value. `binary_search` returns bool. `equal_range` returns both.
`partial_sort` sorts first N elements, rest unsorted. `nth_element` places N-th element in correct position, partition around it. Both O(n log k) or O(n).
`std::accumulate` (<numeric>) sums/reduces a range. `std::iota` fills with incrementing values. `std::inner_product`, `std::adjacent_difference`, `std::partial_sum`.
`count_if` returns count matching predicate. `for_each` applies callable to each element. C++17: `for_each_n`. `all_of`, `any_of`, `none_of` for boolean checks.
Templates parameterize types and values. `typename` or `class` for type params. Non-type params: `int N`. `auto` non-type params (C++17). Template specialization.
Full specialization provides specific implementation for particular types. Partial specialization for some parameters. Used for type-specific optimization.
Template parameter that is itself a template. Allows passing container templates. `template<typename> class Container`. Works with template template arguments.
Templates with variable number of arguments (C++11). `typename... Args`. Pack expansion with `...`. `sizeof...(Args)` for count. Recursive or fold-based processing.
Unary and binary folds over parameter packs (C++17). `(... op args)` unary right fold. `(args op ...)` unary left fold. `(init op ... op args)` binary fold.
Substitution Failure Is Not An Error. `std::enable_if` controls template overload resolution. `<type_traits>` provides type predicates. Largely replaced by concepts in C++20.
Compile-time constraints on template parameters (C++20). Standard: `std::integral`, `std::floating_point`, `std::ranges::range`, `std::convertible_to`. Custom with `concept`.
Composable, lazy range algorithms (C++20). Pipe syntax `|` for composition. Views: `filter`, `transform`, `take`, `drop`, `reverse`, `join`. `std::views` namespace.
Stackless coroutines (C++20). `co_await`, `co_yield`, `co_return`. Compiler generates state machine. Need library support (cppcoro, or custom promise/awaiter).
Modern replacement for headers (C++20). `export module`, `import`. Faster compilation, no header guards, better encapsulation. Not all compilers fully support.
Three-way comparison operator (C++20). Returns `std::strong_ordering`, `std::weak_ordering`, `std::partial_ordering`. `= default` generates all six comparison operators.
`std::views` provide lazy, composable transformations. No allocations. `std::span` is a non-owning view over contiguous memory (C++20). `std::string_view` for strings.

std::expected<T, E> (C++23) represents a value or an error, like Rust's Result. No exceptions needed. Methods: has_value(), value(), error(), value_or(). Monadic: and_then, or_else, transform, transform_error. Header <expected>. Useful for fallible operations where exceptions are banned or overhead unacceptable. Unlike optional, expected carries error info.
Deduce the reference qualifier of `this` for member functions. Allows lambda-like syntax for member functions. Eliminates need for const/non-const overload pairs.
Contiguous-storage associative containers. `std::flat_map<K,V>` sorted vector<pair>. Faster iteration, less memory, but O(n) insertion. From `<flat_map>`.
Multidimensional array view (C++23). Non-owning, layout-polymorphic. Supports strides, extents, subspan. From `<mdspan>`. Replaces manual index calculation.
Exclusive ownership. Non-copyable, movable. `std::make_unique` (C++14). Custom deleter as template parameter. Automatic memory management with zero overhead.
Reference-counted shared ownership. `std::make_shared` allocates control block and object together (one allocation). Thread-safe ref count.
Non-owning reference to shared_ptr. Breaks circular references. Lock to get temporary shared_ptr. `expired()` checks if object still exists.
CRTP base class that lets object safely create shared_ptrs to itself. Requires object is already managed by shared_ptr. `shared_from_this()` method.
Smart pointers accept custom deleters (callable). For non-memory resources: file handles, sockets, C resources. Stored in control block (shared_ptr) or as part of unique_ptr type.
OS thread wrapper. `join()` blocks until completion. `detach()` lets run independently (careful with dangling). `std::this_thread::sleep_for`, `get_id`.
`std::mutex` protects shared data. `std::lock_guard` RAII lock. `std::unique_lock` more flexible (defer, try, timed). `std::shared_mutex` (C++17) reader-writer.
`std::async` launches async tasks. `std::future<T>` gets result once. `std::promise<T>` manually sets value/exception. `std::packaged_task` wraps callable.
Joining thread (C++20). Automatically joins on destruction. Cooperative cancellation via `get_stop_token()`, `request_stop()`.
`std::latch` (C++20) single-use countdown. `std::barrier` (C++20) reusable synchronization point. Both from `<latch>` and `<barrier>`.
Signaling mechanism (C++20). `std::counting_semaphore<max>` with `acquire()`, `release()`. Binary semaphore alias `std::binary_semaphore`. Good for producer-consumer.

C++20 added std::latch (single-use countdown), std::barrier (reusable phase sync), std::counting_semaphore, std::binary_semaphore. std::latch: wait for N events. std::barrier: synchronize threads at a point, repeated. std::semaphore: limited resource access. All in <latch>, <barrier>, <semaphore>. Lower-level than std::async but more flexible than manual atomics.
File streams: `ifstream` (read), `ofstream` (write), `fstream` (read+write). RAII: closes in destructor. Open modes: `app`, `binary`, `in`, `out`, `trunc`.
Filesystem library (C++17). Path manipulation, directory iteration, file status. `std::filesystem::path`, `directory_iterator`, `file_status`. Cross-platform.
In-memory string I/O. `std::stringstream`, `std::istringstream`, `std::ostringstream`. Works with `<<` and `>>`. Useful for parsing and formatting.
Reading/writing raw bytes. `read()`, `write()` on streams. `reinterpret_cast` for type punning. Endianness and portability concerns.
Exception handling with `try`, `catch`, `throw`. Stack unwinding calls destructors. Catch by reference. `catch(...)` catches all. Re-throw with `throw;`.
`noexcept` promises no exception. `noexcept(condition)` conditional. `noexcept` operator checks. Violation calls `std::terminate`. Optimizer can improve code.
Standard exception classes from `<stdexcept>`. Base: `std::exception`. Derived: `logic_error`, `runtime_error`, `bad_alloc`, `bad_cast`, etc.
Lightweight error handling without exceptions. `<system_error>`: `std::error_code`, `std::error_category`. `std::errc` for standard POSIX errors.

noexcept specifies a function won't throw. Compiler may optimize: no stack unwinding overhead. If noexcept function throws, std::terminate() called. Conditional: noexcept(expr). noexcept operator checks if expr is noexcept. Move constructors should be noexcept for optimal container performance. Essential for swap, move operations. noexcept is part of function type (may affect overload resolution).
Modern CMake (3.x): targets, properties, generator expressions. `target_link_libraries`, `target_include_directories`, `INTERFACE/PUBLIC/PRIVATE`. FetchContent for dependencies.
C++ package manager by Microsoft. Manifest mode (`vcpkg.json`). Integrates with CMake via toolchain file. Ports for 2000+ libraries.
Decentralized C/C++ package manager. `conanfile.txt` or `conanfile.py`. Supports multiple generators (CMake, MSBuild, etc.). Profiles for configurations.
Ninja (fast parallel builds), Make (classic), Bazel (monorepo), Meson (Python-based). C++20 modules require build system support.
Cross-platform framework for GUI, networking, SQL, etc. Key modules: QtWidgets, QtCore, QtNetwork, QtQml, QtQuick. Signal-slot mechanism for communication.
Peer-reviewed, portable C++ library collection. Key: Boost.Asio (networking), Boost.Beast (HTTP/WebSocket), Boost.Filesystem, Boost.Test, Boost.PropertyTree, Boost.ProgramOptions.
UE uses C++ with reflection macros: `UCLASS`, `USTRUCT`, `UPROPERTY`, `UFUNCTION`. Gameplay classes, Actors, Components, GameplayAbilitySystem.
Testing and benchmarking. GTest: `TEST`, `EXPECT_EQ`, `ASSERT_TRUE`. GMock for mocking. Google Benchmark for performance measurement.

`std::optional<T>` holds a value or nothing. Avoids sentinel values (-1, nullptr, empty string). `has_value()`, `value()` (throws `std::bad_optional_access` on empty), `value_or(default)`. Monadic ops in C++23: `and_then`, `transform`, `or_else`.

Type-safe union from `<variant>`. Holds one of several types at a time. `std::visit()` dispatches based on current type. `index()` returns which alternative is active. No undefined behavior unlike raw unions. `std::monostate` for empty variant.

Type-erased container (like `void*` but type-safe). From `<any>`. `any_cast<T>()` throws `std::bad_any_cast` on type mismatch. `has_value()`, `type()` for RTTI. Prefer `variant` when types are known at compile time.

`<type_traits>` provides compile-time queries: `is_integral`, `is_floating_point`, `is_pointer`, `is_same`, `remove_reference`, `decay`, `enable_if`. `static_assert` for compile-time checking. `if constexpr` (C++17) simplifies template code.

C++17 extends `inline` to variables, allowing header-only definitions without ODR violations. Previously, static class members and global constants needed a `.cpp` definition. `inline constexpr` works too. All translation units share one address.

`[[nodiscard]]` (C++17) warns if return value is discarded. C++20 adds `[[nodiscard("reason")]]`. `[[maybe_unused]]` suppresses unused warnings. Essential for error-returning functions, RAII guards, and stub/hook points.

`std::clamp(v, lo, hi)` from `<algorithm>` constrains a value to [lo, hi]. `std::gcd` / `std::lcm` from `<numeric>` compute greatest common divisor and least common multiple. All are constexpr-friendly.

Execution policies from `<execution>`: `seq` (sequential), `par` (parallel threads), `par_unseq` (parallel + SIMD), `unseq` (C++20, vectorized single-thread). Apply to `sort`, `transform`, `for_each`, `reduce`, etc. Backend: Intel TBB or compiler-specific.

PIMPL (Pointer to Implementation) hides private members from the header, reducing recompilation dependencies. The header only has a forward-declared struct pointer (`Impl*` or `unique_ptr<Impl>`). The .cpp file defines the implementation struct.

Strategy: encapsulate algorithms behind a common interface, selected at runtime. Observer: one-to-many notification on state change. C++ supports both via virtual interfaces, `std::function`, and smart pointers for ownership management.

Catch2: header-only (v2) or compiled library (v3), BDD-style with SECTIONs. GTest: xUnit-style, `TEST()`, `EXPECT_EQ`, `ASSERT_TRUE`. Both support matchers, fixtures, and parameterized tests. Integrate with CMake: `enable_testing()` + `add_test()`.

From Professional C++: 1) Move semantics avoid deep copies. 2) Reserve vector capacity upfront. 3) Pass by const reference, not value. 4) CRTP avoids virtual dispatch in hot paths. 5) Profile first (Google Benchmark, perf). 6) Small-string optimization.
A reference (`T&`) is an alias to an existing object. Cannot be null, must be initialized, cannot be rebound. Used for function parameters (pass by reference) and return values.
Pointers hold memory addresses. Declared as `T*`. Dereference with `*`, get address with `&`. Can be null (`nullptr`). Support pointer arithmetic.
Dynamic memory allocation. `new` allocates + constructs, `delete` destructs + deallocates. Array forms: `new[]`, `delete[]`. Prefer smart pointers in modern C++.
Memory allocated with `new` that is never `delete`d. Causes: lost pointers, exception before delete, circular shared_ptr. Tools: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer.
C++ memory model defines how threads interact through memory. `std::memory_order` for atomics. Sequential consistency, acquire/release, relaxed.
Objects are created (constructor), live, then destroyed (destructor). Storage durations: automatic (stack), static, thread, dynamic (heap).
Compile-time cast between related types. Numeric conversions, upcasts/downcasts in class hierarchies, `void*` to typed pointer.
Runtime-checked cast for polymorphic types. Requires at least one virtual function. Returns null for pointers on failure.
Adds or removes `const`/`volatile` qualification. Modifying a const object through const_cast is UB.
Unsafe cast that reinterprets the bit pattern. No type checking. Used for serialization, hardware access.
Run-Time Type Information. `typeid` returns `std::type_info`. `dynamic_cast` also uses RTTI. Disabled with `-fno-rtti`.
UB: program can do anything. Common: null dereference, buffer overflow, signed overflow, use-after-free, data races.
Argument-Dependent Lookup (Koenig lookup): searches namespaces of argument types when calling a function.
Compilers encode function signatures into linker symbols. Different across compilers => no ABI compatibility. `extern "C"` disables mangling.
Preprocessor directives (`#define`, `#ifdef`, `#pragma`). Text substitution before compilation. Modern C++ prefers `constexpr`, templates.
Declaring a symbol before its full definition. Reduces compilation dependencies, breaks circular references.
Scope controls name visibility. Storage duration: automatic (stack), static, thread, dynamic (heap). `::` for global scope.
A class can inherit from multiple base classes. Syntax: `class D : public A, public B`. Can lead to diamond problem.
Two classes share a common base. Virtual inheritance (`virtual public`) creates one shared subobject.
Each polymorphic class has a vtable. Each object has a vptr. `virtual` function calls dispatch through vtable at runtime.
Runtime polymorphism via virtual functions and base pointers/references. Enables substitutability.
GNU Debugger: step through code, inspect variables, backtrace. Commands: `run`, `break`, `next`, `step`, `print`, `backtrace`.
`-g` flag embeds debug info (DWARF on Linux, PDB on Windows). Levels: `-g0` none, `-g3` extra.
Google sanitizers catch memory errors and UB. `-fsanitize=address` (ASan), `-fsanitize=undefined` (UBSan).
Profiling measures where time is spent. `perf` (Linux), Google Benchmark, `gprof`.
Four stages: 1) Preprocessing, 2) Compilation (C++ -> assembly), 3) Assembly (asm -> .o), 4) Linking.
GCC (`g++`): mature, extensive optimization. Clang (`clang++`): faster, better error messages, great tooling.
Microsoft Visual C++: Windows-only, `/std:c++latest`. MinGW: GCC port for Windows.
Linker combines object files into executable/library. Link-Time Optimization enables cross-TU inlining.
Curiously Recurring Template Pattern: derived class passes itself as template parameter to base. Static polymorphism, no vtable overhead.
Delete copy operations to prevent unintended duplication. Essential for RAII wrappers owning unique resources.
`remove`/`remove_if` moves elements to end, returns new logical end. Pair with `erase`. C++20 `std::erase` simplifies.
Defer copying until a write is attempted. Less beneficial with move semantics.
Type-safe time library. `duration`, `time_point`, `clock`. C++20 adds calendar and time zones.
C++11 `<random>`: engines (mt19937) and distributions (uniform_int, normal). Better than `rand()`.
Five categories: Input, Output, Forward, Bidirectional, Random Access. Higher categories support more algorithms.
Fast, safe formatting library. Basis for C++20 `std::format`. Type-safe, extensible.
Fast, header-only logging library. Async logging, rotating files, multiple sinks.
Protocol Buffers: language-agnostic serialization. gRPC: RPC framework using protobuf + HTTP/2.

fmtlib: fast, safe formatting library (format string syntax). Basis for C++20 std::format. Supports positional args, custom types, chrono. spdlog: header-only logging library, extremely fast. Levels: trace/debug/info/warn/error/critical/critical. Sinks: console, rotating file, syslog, daily. Pattern formatting, async mode. Zero-overhead when disabled at compile time.
cs.json: .Getting Started.What is .NET?[0]

.NET is a free, cross-platform, open-source developer platform. It includes .NET Core (modern), .NET Framework (Windows-only legacy), and .NET 5+ (unified). Choose the right runtime for your scenario.
.Getting Started.Project Types & Templates[0]
.NET provides project templates via `dotnet new`: console, classlib, web (ASP.NET Core), mvc, webapi, blazor, xunit, maui, worker, and more. Each generates the right .csproj structure.
.Getting Started.IDE & Editor Choices[0]
C# development works in Visual Studio (full IDE), Visual Studio Code (lightweight with C# Dev Kit), JetBrains Rider (cross-platform), or the CLI with any editor. The .NET CLI is universal.
.Getting Started.Top-Level Statements[0]
C# 9+ top-level statements eliminate boilerplate Program class and Main method. The compiler generates them automatically, enabling script-like entry points.
.Getting Started.File-Scoped Namespaces[0]
C# 10 file-scoped namespaces remove one level of indentation. Use `namespace X;` syntax at the top of the file instead of a block. All declarations in the file belong to that namespace.
.Getting Started.Project Structure & SDKs[0]

.NET projects use SDK-style `.csproj` files. SDKs: `Microsoft.NET.Sdk` (console, lib), `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` (ASP.NET), `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Worker` (background services), `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Maui` (cross-platform). Project structure: `Program.cs` entry point, `.cs` classes, `Properties/launchSettings.json`, `appsettings.json` for config. Use `TargetFramework` (`net8.0`, `netstandard2.0`). Multiple targets with `<TargetFrameworks>`.
.Variables & Types.Primitive Types[0]
C# has built-in value types: integral (byte, short, int, long), floating-point (float, double, decimal), character (char), boolean (bool). Each maps to a .NET struct in System namespace.
.Variables & Types.var & Implicit Typing[0]

The `var` keyword tells the compiler to infer the type from the right-hand expression. It is strongly typed at compile time. Use it when the type is obvious from context, but prefer explicit types for public APIs.
.Variables & Types.object & dynamic[0]

`object` is the universal base type (requires casting). `dynamic` bypasses compile-time type checking and resolves at runtime. Use `dynamic` sparingly — it sacrifices safety for flexibility (COM, JSON, DLR scenarios).
.Variables & Types.Nullable Value Types[0]
Value types (structs) can be made nullable with the `?` suffix (e.g., int?, bool?). Nullable<T> wraps the value with HasValue/Value properties. Use null-conditional operators to handle null safely.
.Variables & Types.Nullable Reference Types[0]

C# 8+ nullable reference types enable compile-time null-state analysis. Types are non-nullable by default; use `?` suffix to allow null. Enable via `#nullable enable` or in .csproj. The compiler emits warnings for unsafe dereferences.
.Variables & Types.Null-Forgiving Operator[0]
The `!` postfix operator (null-forgiving / dammit operator) suppresses nullable warnings when you know a value isn't null despite the compiler's analysis. Use cautiously.
.Variables & Types.Constants & Readonly[0]
`const` is a compile-time constant (implicitly static, no modifiers). `readonly` is a runtime constant set in the constructor. `static readonly` is like a constant that can be computed at runtime.
.Variables & Types.Tuple Types[0]
C# 7+ tuples provide lightweight multi-value grouping with named fields. ValueTuple structs avoid heap allocation. Tuples are great for internal use; prefer records for public APIs.
.Operators.Arithmetic & Assignment[0]

Standard arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) work on numeric types. Assignment can be combined (+=, -=, etc.). The increment (++) and decrement (--) operators have prefix/postfix forms with different evaluation order.
.Operators.Comparison & Equality[0]

Comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) work on value types. For reference types, == compares references by default; override Equals and == for value semantics. Records have built-in value equality.
.Operators.Logical & Bitwise[0]

Logical operators (&&, ||, !) short-circuit. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) operate on integer bits. Use `&&` instead of `&` and `||` instead of `|` for boolean logic to benefit from short-circuit evaluation.
.Operators.Null-Conditional Operator[0]
The `?.` operator safely accesses members of a possibly-null expression. It short-circuits to null if the left operand is null. Chain multiple `?.` or combine with `??` for fallback values.
.Operators.Null-Coalescing Operators[0]
`??` returns the left operand if it's not null, otherwise the right operand. `??=` (C# 8+) assigns the right operand to the left only if the left is null. Both short-circuit.
.Operators.Switch Expressions[0]

C# 8+ switch expressions provide concise, expression-based pattern matching. Unlike switch statements, they produce a value. Supports type patterns, when guards, property patterns, discards, and relational patterns.
.Operators.Conditional Operator[0]
The ternary `?:` operator evaluates a boolean condition and returns one of two expressions. Use for inline conditional values; avoid nesting for readability.
.Control Flow.if / else if / else[0]
Standard conditional branching. Use `if` for boolean conditions, chain with `else if` for multiple paths, and `else` as the fallback. Can use pattern matching in conditions with `is` expressions.
.Control Flow.Switch Statement[0]

Switch statements evaluate an expression against multiple case patterns. C# 7+ added type patterns, when guards, and the `_` discard. Cases can fall through with `goto case`, but typically each case has a `break`.
.Control Flow.Pattern Matching[0]

C# pattern matching includes type patterns, property patterns, positional patterns (with deconstruction), var patterns, discard patterns, relational patterns (`<`, `>`, `>=`), and logical patterns (`and`, `or`, `not`).
.Control Flow.for Loop[0]

The classic `for` loop uses an initializer, condition, and iterator. Perfect for indexed iteration, reverse loops, and scenarios where the iteration count is known. Declare the counter variable inline for scoped access.
.Control Flow.foreach Loop[0]
`foreach` iterates over any type implementing IEnumerable or IEnumerable<T>. The iterator variable is read-only inside the loop. For arrays, the compiler optimizes with a `for` loop internally.
.Control Flow.while & do-while[0]
`while` checks the condition before each iteration (zero or more runs). `do-while` checks after (always runs at least once). Use when the iteration count isn't known upfront.
.Control Flow.break, continue, goto[0]
`break` exits the current loop. `continue` skips to the next iteration. `goto` jumps to a labeled statement (use rarely). `return` exits the method entirely. Use `break` in loops and switch cases.
.Control Flow.using Declaration[0]
C# 8+ using declarations automatically dispose resources when the variable goes out of scope. Eliminates the nesting of traditional `using` statements. Works with IDisposable and IAsyncDisposable.
.Methods.Method Basics[0]

Methods encapsulate reusable logic. They have a signature (name, return type, parameters), a body, and an access modifier. C# supports method overloading (same name, different parameters). Methods can be static or instance.
.Methods.Parameter Modifiers (ref, in, out)[0]

`ref` passes a reference to the variable (read-write). `in` passes by reference but is read-only (avoids copying for large structs). `out` passes by reference for returning values; the method must assign it before returning.
.Methods.params Keyword[0]
The `params` keyword allows a variable number of arguments. The parameter must be a single-dimensional array and must be the last parameter. The compiler generates the array automatically.
.Methods.Optional & Named Parameters[0]

Optional parameters have default values and can be omitted. Named arguments let you specify parameters by name, enabling skipping optional ones and improving readability for boolean/optional parameters.
.Methods.Expression-Bodied Members[0]
C# 6+ expression-bodied members use `=>` for concise single-expression methods, properties, and operators. Available for methods, get-only properties, constructors, finalizers, and operators.
.Methods.Local Functions[0]

C# 7+ local functions are nested methods inside another method. They capture variables from the enclosing scope, support generics, async, and even attributes. Great for helper logic that shouldn't leak.
.Methods.Return Values & Multiple Returns[0]

Methods return a single value. Return multiple values using tuples, out parameters, or a custom class/record. Tuples are lightweight; records are better for public APIs. Use `ValueTuple` for zero-allocation returns.
.Methods.Delegates & Lambda Expressions[0]

Delegates are type-safe function pointers: `Func<T,R>` (return), `Action<T>` (void), `Predicate<T>` (bool return). Custom: `delegate int Transformer(int x)`. Lambda syntax: `(param) => expr`, `(param) => { stmts }`. Closure captures outer variables. `async` lambdas: `Func<Task> f = async () => await Work()`. Multicast delegates chain multiple handlers. Event pattern built on delegates.
.Classes & OOP.Classes & Objects[0]

Classes are reference types that serve as blueprints for objects. They encapsulate data (fields, properties) and behavior (methods). Use `new` to create instances. Classes support inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.
.Classes & OOP.Fields & Properties[0]

Fields store internal state. Properties expose fields with get/set accessors, enabling validation, computed values, and lazy initialization. Auto-properties generate backing fields automatically (C# 3+).
.Classes & OOP.Init Setters & Required Members[0]

C# 9 `init` setters enable object initializer-only property assignment (immutable after construction). C# 11 `required` members force callers to provide a value during initialization. Both support object/collection initializer patterns.
.Classes & OOP.Primary Constructors[0]

C# 12 primary constructors allow parameter declaration directly on the class/struct/record. Parameters are in scope throughout the class body. For classes, they don't auto-generate properties (unlike records). Capture them explicitly if needed.
.Classes & OOP.Record Types[0]

C# 9 records provide value semantics by default: positional construction, immutable properties (with init), value-based equality, `with` expressions for non-destructive mutation, and concise deconstruction. Use `record class` (reference) or `record struct` (value).
.Classes & OOP.Inheritance[0]

C# supports single class inheritance. Use `:` to derive, `virtual` for overridable methods, `override` for specialization, `abstract` for forced implementation, `sealed` to prevent further inheritance. Base class constructors chain via `: base()`.
.Classes & OOP.Polymorphism[0]

Polymorphism allows derived types to be treated as base types. Virtual method dispatch calls the most derived override at runtime. Interface polymorphism enables unrelated types to share contracts. Use `is` and `as` for type-safe casting.
.Classes & OOP.Abstract Classes & Sealed[0]

Abstract classes cannot be instantiated, serving as base types with partial implementation. `abstract` members have no body and must be overridden. `sealed` on a class prevents inheritance entirely; on a method it stops further overriding.
.Classes & OOP.Static Members & Classes[0]

Static classes contain only static members and cannot be instantiated. Static members belong to the type, not instances. Static constructors run once per type before any static member access. Extension methods must be in static classes.
.Classes & OOP.Object Initializers[0]
Object initializers set properties/fields at creation without requiring a constructor. Collection initializers add items inline. Works with `init` setters and `required` members (C# 11+).
.Interfaces & Generics.Interface Basics[0]

Interfaces define contracts with methods, properties, events, and indexers. A class/struct can implement multiple interfaces. Interfaces enable loose coupling, polymorphism, and dependency injection. C# 8+ allows default implementations.
.Interfaces & Generics.Default Interface Methods[0]

C# 8+ default interface methods allow adding members to interfaces without breaking existing implementations. Implementations can override the default. Useful for API evolution and trait-like patterns. Not available in .NET Framework 4.8.
.Interfaces & Generics.Generic Constraints[0]

Constraints restrict type parameters: `where T : class` (reference), `struct` (value), `notnull` (non-nullable), `new()` (parameterless constructor), base class, interface, or `unmanaged` (blittable). Multiple constraints are stacked.
.Interfaces & Generics.Covariance & Contravariance[0]

Covariance (`out`) allows using a more derived type in output positions (e.g., `IEnumerable<Dog>` as `IEnumerable<Animal>`). Contravariance (`in`) allows less derived input (e.g., `IComparer<Animal>` as `IComparer<Dog>`). Only applies to interfaces/delegates with reference types.
.Interfaces & Generics.Generic Methods[0]

Type parameters can be defined on methods (not just classes). The compiler infers types from arguments. Generic methods enable type-safe algorithms without boxing. Combine with constraints for additional capabilities.
.Interfaces & Generics.IDisposable & IAsyncDisposable[0]

IDisposable defines a deterministic cleanup pattern. The `using` statement ensures Dispose() is called even on exceptions. `IAsyncDisposable` (C# 8+) enables async cleanup with `await using`. Implement the dispose pattern properly for classes holding unmanaged resources.
.Interfaces & Generics.Variance: in/out[0]

C# generics support covariance (`out`) and contravariance (`in`) for interfaces and delegates. `out T`: can use as return type (produce). `in T`: can use as parameter type (consume). Covariant: `IEnumerable<out T>` — `IEnumerable<string>` is `IEnumerable<object>`. Contravariant: `Action<in T>` — `Action<object>` is `Action<string>`. Only safe in one direction.
.Collections & LINQ.Arrays[0]

Fixed-size, zero-indexed collections of elements of the same type. Arrays are reference types with a fixed length set at creation. Supports multi-dimensional (rectangular) and jagged (array-of-arrays) forms.
.Collections & LINQ.List<T>[0]

List<T> is a generic dynamic array that grows as needed. Provides O(1) index access, O(n) insert/remove at arbitrary positions. Use for ordered collections where size changes. Implements IList<T>, ICollection<T>, IEnumerable<T>.
.Collections & LINQ.Dictionary<TKey, TValue>[0]

Dictionary provides O(1) key-value lookups via hash table. Keys must be unique and properly implement GetHashCode/Equals. Use TryGetValue for safe access. Use ConcurrentDictionary for thread-safe scenarios.
.Collections & LINQ.HashSet<T> & SortedSet<T>[0]

HashSet<T> is an unordered set with O(1) add/remove/lookup. SortedSet<T> maintains sorted order (O(log n)). Both implement ISet<T> with set operations: UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith, SymmetricExceptWith.
.Collections & LINQ.Queue<T> & Stack<T>[0]
Queue<T> is FIFO (Enqueue/Dequeue/Peek). Stack<T> is LIFO (Push/Pop/Peek). Both use arrays internally with O(1) amortized operations. Use for breadth-first vs depth-first processing patterns.
.Collections & LINQ.LINQ Basics[0]

LINQ (Language Integrated Query) enables querying any IEnumerable<T> with SQL-like syntax. Query syntax (`from x in xs where ...`) or method syntax (`.Where().Select()`) produce the same IL. Deferred execution until enumeration.
.Collections & LINQ.LINQ Methods Deep[0]

LINQ provides projection (Select, SelectMany), filtering (Where, OfType), ordering (OrderBy, ThenBy, Reverse), grouping (GroupBy, ToLookup), joins (Join, GroupJoin), aggregation (Sum, Average, Min, Max, Count, Aggregate), set ops (Distinct, Union, Intersect, Except), partitioning (Skip, Take, SkipWhile, TakeWhile), and element ops (First, Last, Single, ElementAt, DefaultIfEmpty).
.Collections & LINQ.LINQ GroupBy & Joins[0]

GroupBy partitions sequences into groups with a key. Join performs inner joins on matching keys. GroupJoin creates a hierarchical result (left outer join). Zip combines two sequences element-by-element. All support custom equality comparers.
.Collections & LINQ.Concurrent Collections[0]

System.Collections.Concurrent provides thread-safe collections: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,T> (lock-free ops), ConcurrentQueue<T> (FIFO), ConcurrentStack<T> (LIFO), ConcurrentBag<T> (unordered), BlockingCollection<T> (bounded producer/consumer).
.Collections & LINQ.PLINQ (Parallel LINQ)[0]

PLINQ automatically parallelizes LINQ queries via `AsParallel()`. Uses partitioning and thread pooling. Control parallelism with `WithDegreeOfParallelism`, `WithExecutionMode`, `WithCancellation`. Results can be unordered (`AsUnordered`) for better performance.
.Error Handling.try / catch / finally[0]

Structured exception handling: `try` guards code, `catch` handles exceptions (specific or general), `finally` always executes (cleanup). Exceptions bubble up the call stack until caught. Unhandled exceptions crash the process.
.Error Handling.Exception Filters (when)[0]

C# `catch` with `when` filters exceptions without unwinding the stack first. Log or conditionally catch: `catch (Exception ex) when (Log(ex))`. Filter runs before the catch block; false skips to next handler. Useful for distinguishing error types by runtime data. Can catch by type and filter on `ex.Data`, `ex.HResult`, or custom properties. Stack trace preserved since stack isn't unwound if filter returns false.
.Error Handling.Custom Exceptions[0]

Create custom exceptions by inheriting from Exception. Follow best practices: end class name with `Exception`, implement the three standard constructors, use serialization if needed, provide additional properties for rich error data.
.Error Handling.Guard Clauses & Argument Validation[0]

Validate arguments early using guard clauses. Use `ArgumentException`, `ArgumentNullException`, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. C# 11 lets you specify the nameof parameter. Consider using `ThrowHelper` patterns or a library like Ardalis.GuardClauses to reduce inlining.
.Error Handling.Throw Helpers[0]

Throw helpers are `static` local/member methods that throw exceptions. The JIT sees `throw` as a cold path and doesn't inline the helper, reducing method size and improving performance. Use for validation-heavy APIs.
.Error Handling.Result Pattern (Functional Error Handling)[0]

Instead of exceptions for expected failures, use a Result type to return success/failure explicitly. Common in domain-driven design. Integrates with `switch` expressions for exhaustive handling. Libraries like FluentResults or OneOf formalize this pattern.
.Async & Concurrency.async / await Basics[0]

async/await enables non-blocking asynchronous code. async methods return Task, Task<T>, or ValueTask<T>. Await suspends the method without blocking the thread. Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code to avoid capturing SynchronizationContext.
.Async & Concurrency.Task & Task<T>[0]

Task represents an async operation. Task<T> produces a value. Tasks can be awaited, combined (WhenAll, WhenAny), or continued (ContinueWith, but prefer await). Status tracks lifecycle: Created, WaitingForActivation, RanToCompletion, Faulted, Canceled.
.Async & Concurrency.Cancellation[0]

CancellationToken from CancellationTokenSource enables cooperative cancellation. Pass to async methods. Throw OperationCanceledException when cancelled. Use Register for callbacks. Linked tokens combine multiple sources.
.Async & Concurrency.ValueTask & ValueTask<T>[0]

ValueTask<T> (C# 7+) is a struct that can wrap a synchronous result or a Task<T>. Avoids allocation when the result is already available. Use only for hot paths where sync completion is common. Can only be awaited once (use AsTask() for multiple).
.Async & Concurrency.Async Streams (IAsyncEnumerable)[0]

C# 8+ async streams enable async iteration with `await foreach`. Methods return `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` using `yield return` with `await`. Supports CancellationToken, ConfigureAwait, and LINQ via System.Linq.Async.
.Async & Concurrency.Channel<T>[0]

System.Threading.Channels provides thread-safe producer/consumer queues. Bounded channels (backpressure) limit capacity; unbounded grow indefinitely. ChannelReader exposes ReadAllAsync() for async streams. Perfect for pub/sub and pipeline patterns.
.Async & Concurrency.Task Parallel Library (Dataflow)[0]

System.Threading.Tasks.Dataflow provides actor-like message passing blocks: BufferBlock<T>, ActionBlock<T>, TransformBlock<TInput,TOutput>, BatchBlock<T>, JoinBlock<T1,T2>. Link blocks into pipelines with completion propagation. Fine-grained parallelism control.
.Async & Concurrency.Thread Synchronization[0]

Use `lock` for mutual exclusion (Monitor syntactic sugar). For finer control: Monitor (Wait/Pulse), Mutex (cross-process), Semaphore/SemaphoreSlim (counting), ReaderWriterLockSlim (read-heavy), Barrier (phased), CountdownEvent, ManualResetEvent. Prefer higher-level primitives.
.Async & Concurrency.Parallel.For / Parallel.ForEach[0]

System.Threading.Tasks.Parallel provides parallel loops: Parallel.For (indexed), Parallel.ForEach (enumerable), Parallel.Invoke (multiple actions). Controls degree of parallelism and supports thread-local state (overloads). Use for CPU-bound parallel work.
.File I/O & Serialization.File & Directory Operations[0]

System.IO provides File (static methods), FileInfo (instance), Directory, DirectoryInfo, and Path. Read/write text, bytes, or lines. Use async methods for I/O-bound work. Guard against path traversal and IO exceptions.
.File I/O & Serialization.StreamReader / StreamWriter[0]

StreamReader/StreamWriter provide text-level access over streams. Support different encodings, buffer sizes, and async operations. Use `using` for proper disposal. FileStream provides raw byte-level access.
.File I/O & Serialization.System.Text.Json[0]

System.Text.Json (high-performance, UTF-8) serializes/deserializes JSON. Supports source generators (AOT-friendly), custom converters, ignore/modify serialization via attributes, JsonDocument (DOM), and JsonSerializerOptions for configuration.
.File I/O & Serialization.System.Text.Json Source Generators[0]

C# 9+ source generators for System.Text.Json eliminate runtime reflection. Declare partial classes with [JsonSerializerSerializable] (or [JsonSourceGenerationOptions]) for compile-time serialization. Enables native AOT, reduces startup, avoids reflection.
.File I/O & Serialization.XML Serialization[0]

XmlSerializer serializes to/from XML. Control output with attributes ([XmlElement], [XmlAttribute], [XmlIgnore], [XmlArray]). Supports complex object graphs. XDocument/Linq to Xml provides LINQ-friendly XML manipulation.
.File I/O & Serialization.Binary Serialization (obsolete)[0]

BinaryFormatter (now obsolete/unsafe) serializes object graphs including private members. .NET 8+ throws PlatformNotSupportedException. Use JSON, Protobuf, or MessagePack instead. Never use BinaryFormatter in new code due to security risks (deserialization vulnerabilities).
.File I/O & Serialization.Protocol Buffers (Protobuf)[0]

Google.Protobuf provides compact, cross-language serialization via .proto definitions. Much smaller/faster than JSON. Use with gRPC. Generate C# classes from .proto files. Ideal for high-performance internal services and wire protocols.
.Memory & Performance.Span<T> & ReadOnlySpan<T>[0]

Span<T> is a stack-allocated ref struct providing safe, allocation-free views over contiguous memory (arrays, strings, native memory). No heap allocation. Ideal for high-performance string parsing, buffer manipulation, and slicing operations.
.Memory & Performance.Memory<T> & ReadOnlyMemory<T>[0]

Memory<T> is the heap-friendly counterpart to Span<T>. Can be stored in fields, async methods, and lambdas. Use Span<T> for synchronous processing, Memory<T> when the buffer needs to survive on the heap or cross async boundaries.
.Memory & Performance.ref struct & readonly ref struct[0]

ref struct types are stack-only (cannot be boxed, used as generic type args, stored in heap, or be a field of a class). Used by Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>. `readonly ref struct` ensures all fields are readonly. Enables safe stack-only memory handling.
.Memory & Performance.stackalloc[0]

stackalloc allocates memory on the stack (fast, no GC pressure). Use with Span<T> for safe access. Available in unsafe and safe contexts (via Span). Be mindful of stack space (~1 MB per thread). Best for small temporary buffers.
.Memory & Performance.Unsafe Code & Pointers[0]

C# supports pointer operations in `unsafe` blocks. Enables direct memory access, pointer arithmetic, and fixed memory. Use for interop and performance-critical code. Requires `/unsafe` compiler option. Prefer Span<T> over raw pointers when possible.
.Memory & Performance.Ref Returns & Ref Locals[0]

ref returns allow methods to return references (avoiding copying). ref locals alias existing variables. `ref readonly` returns read-only references. Useful for performance in large struct manipulation and array-like data structures.
.Memory & Performance.Memory Pool & ArrayPool[0]

ArrayPool<T> reuses arrays to reduce allocation and GC pressure. MemoryPool<T> wraps ArrayPool for Memory<T>. Rent and return buffers. Critical in high-throughput server applications (ASP.NET Core, Dataflow). Always return rented buffers.
.Memory & Performance.WeakReference & Conditional Weak Tables[0]

WeakReference<T> (C# 7+) allows referencing an object without preventing GC. `TryGetTarget(out T target)` checks if alive. ConditionalWeakTable<TKey, TValue> attaches data to objects without extending their lifetime, using ephemeron semantics. Common: attaching metadata, caches, dep tables. Unlike dictionary, keys are compared by reference, and entries auto-remove when key is GC'd.
.Interop.P/Invoke (Platform Invoke)[0]

P/Invoke calls native functions from DLLs using DllImport. Specify CharSet, CallingConvention, EntryPoint. Marshal data between managed and unmanaged memory. Use LibraryImport (source-generated) in .NET 7+ for better performance.
.Interop.COM Interop[0]

COM interop enables calling COM components from .NET (and .NET components from COM). Use COM import attributes, RCW (Runtime Callable Wrapper). .NET 5+ improved COM activation. Common for Office automation, Windows shell extensions, and legacy COM libraries.
.Interop.Fixed Size Buffers[0]

Fixed-size buffers (fixed keyword) define inline arrays in structs for interop scenarios. Used in unsafe context. The buffer is embedded in the struct layout, matching native memory layouts. Commonly used with P/Invoke and binary protocol parsing.
.Interop.Marshal Class[0]

System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal provides methods for allocating/freeing unmanaged memory, converting between managed/unmanaged types, structure layout, COM interop, and size computations. Essential for low-level interop scenarios.
.Interop.WinRT Interop & COM[0]

WinRT (Windows Runtime) interop via C#/WinRT. Consume Windows APIs directly: `Windows.Storage.StorageFile`, `Windows.Graphics.Imaging`. For classic COM interop, use DllImport and COM interfaces with `[ComImport]` and `Guid`. Wrappers via `dynamic` and `IDispatch`. .NET provides built-in wrappers for common APIs. CsWinRT generates projections from .winmd files.
.Testing.xUnit.net Basics[0]

xUnit is .NET's most popular test framework. Use [Fact] for parameterless tests, [Theory] with [InlineData], [ClassData], or [MemberData] for parameterized tests. Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) is the standard structure. Use IClassFixture for shared context.
.Testing.NUnit Basics[0]

NUnit uses [Test], [TestCase], [SetUp], [TearDown], [OneTimeSetUp]. Supports assertions with Assert.That (constraint model), categories, retries, parallel execution. Classic assertions (AreEqual) also work but constraint model is preferred.
.Testing.Moq (Mocking)[0]

Moq creates mock objects for interfaces and classes. Setup method behavior, verify invocations, use Callback for side effects. Supports strict vs loose mocking (default: loose). Combine with It.Is<T>() for argument matching.
.Testing.FluentAssertions[0]

FluentAssertions provides readable, self-documenting assertions. Supports chaining, object graph comparison, collections, strings, timespans, exceptions, and more. Integrates with xUnit, NUnit, MSTest. Produces detailed failure messages.
.Testing.TDD with C#[0]

Test-Driven Development cycle: Red (write failing test), Green (write minimal code to pass), Refactor (improve code while tests pass). Tests drive API design. Use parameterized tests for edge cases. Keep tests fast, isolated, and deterministic.
.Testing.xUnit & Fluent Assertions[0]

xUnit.net is .NET's most popular test framework. `[Fact]` for parameterless tests, `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]`, `[ClassData]`, `[MemberData]` for parameterized. `ITestOutputHelper` for console output. FluentAssertions provides readable assertions: `result.Should().Be(42)`, `collection.Should().HaveCount(3).And.Contain(x => x > 0)`. Alternatives: Shouldly, NUnit.
..NET Ecosystem.NuGet Package Manager[0]

NuGet is the package manager for .NET. `dotnet add package` installs packages. `dotnet restore` resolves dependencies. PackageReference in .csproj stores versions. nuget.config controls sources. Use Central Package Management for multi-project solutions.
..NET Ecosystem.ASP.NET Core Minimal API[0]

ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs provide a concise way to build HTTP APIs with minimal ceremony. Use top-level statements, route handlers with dependency injection, and middleware. Perfect for microservices and simple endpoints.
..NET Ecosystem.Entity Framework Core[0]

EF Core is an object-relational mapper (ORM). Models map to database tables via DbContext. Supports migrations, LINQ queries, change tracking, eager/lazy/explicit loading, and providers for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, etc.
..NET Ecosystem.Blazor Basics[0]

Blazor builds interactive web UIs using C# instead of JavaScript. Blazor Server runs logic on the server via SignalR. Blazor WebAssembly runs compiled .NET in the browser. Blazor Hybrid embeds in native apps (MAUI, WPF). Components are .razor files.
..NET Ecosystem.Dependency Injection[0]

ASP.NET Core has built-in DI with three lifetimes: Singleton (one instance), Scoped (per request), Transient (new each time). Register services in Program.cs. The framework auto-injects into constructors of controllers, minimal APIs, and middleware.
..NET Ecosystem.Configuration & Options[0]

.NET supports configuration from JSON, environment variables, CLI args, and more via IConfiguration. Options pattern with IOptions<T> (reloadable), IOptionsSnapshot<T> (scoped, reloads per request), IOptionsMonitor<T> (singleton, observes changes). Strongly-typed settings with validation.
.Advanced.Source Generators[0]

C# 9+ source generators run at compile-time to emit C# source files. Create an IncrementalGenerator implementing IIncrementalGenerator. Access syntax trees, semantic models, and attributes. Used by System.Text.Json, Regex, and MediatR for compile-time code gen.
.Advanced.Compile-Time Code Generation with Roslyn[0]

Roslyn (the C# compiler platform) provides APIs for syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation, and compilation. Use CSharpSyntaxTree, SemanticModel, Compilation, and SyntaxGenerator to build or analyze code programmatically.
.Advanced.Native AOT Compilation[0]

Native AOT (Ahead-of-Time) compiles .NET directly to native code (no JIT/IL). Enables fast startup, small self-contained binaries, no runtime compilation. Limited to compatible APIs (no reflection by default). Enable with `<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>` in .csproj.
.Advanced.Function Pointers (delegate*)[0]

C# 9 function pointers (`delegate*<T>`) enable efficient native-like function pointer calls without delegate allocation. Used in unsafe contexts for interop and high-performance callbacks. More efficient than delegates (no object allocation).
.Advanced.Regex Source Generators[0]

C# 11+ Regex source generators ([GeneratedRegex]) compile regular expressions at build time. Eliminates runtime compilation (!), provides IntelliSense, and is AOT-compatible. RegexOptions regex options can be passed declaratively.
.Advanced.Raw String Literals[0]

C# 11 raw string literals use triple quotes `"""..."""` for multi-line strings. No escaping needed for quotes, backslashes. Indentation is determined by the closing `"""` position. Perfect for JSON, XML, SQL, regex embedded in code.
.Advanced.Interceptors (Experimental)[0]

Interceptors (C# 12 experimental) allow a source generator to replace a method call with a different implementation at compile time. Used for advanced AOP scenarios. Requires `[InterceptsLocation]` attribute. Still experimental, could change.
.Advanced.List Patterns[0]

C# 11 list patterns enable matching on arrays and lists in switch expressions. Supports slice patterns (`..`), discard (`_`), nested patterns. Useful for parsing, validation, and sequence matching without manual indexing.
.C# 12 & .NET 8 Features.Collection Expressions[0]

Collection expressions (C# 12) simplify collection creation: `int[] a = [1, 2, 3];`, `List<int> list = [1, 2, 3];`, `Span<int> span = [1, 2, 3];`. Spread operator `..` merges collections: `int[] both = [..first, ..second];`. Works with arrays, spans, `List<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`, and custom collection types via `[CollectionBuilder]`. Supports `ReadOnlySpan<T>` for zero-allocation.
.C# 12 & .NET 8 Features.Default Lambda Parameters[0]
C# 12 allows default parameter values in lambdas. Works with both lambda expressions and method group conversions. The default applies when the argument is omitted at the call site.
.C# 12 & .NET 8 Features.ref readonly Parameters[0]

C# 12 `ref readonly` parameters combine ref (pass by reference, avoid copy) with readonly (guarantee caller's value is not modified). Best for large readonly structs. The caller provides data without defensive copies.
.C# 12 & .NET 8 Features.Alias Any Type[0]
C# 12 global/using aliases can refer to any type, not just named types. Tuple types, array types, pointer types, nullable types — all can be aliased. Improves readability for complex type signatures.
.C# 12 & .NET 8 Features.params Collections[0]

C# 12 extends `params` to work with `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and `IEnumerable<T>` beyond just arrays. The compiler creates the collection efficiently with no allocation when using span overloads.
.C# 12 & .NET 8 Features.Primary Constructors[0]

Primary constructors (C# 12) for non-record classes/structs. Parameters are in scope for all members. Can initialize fields, properties. Useful for DI, simple initialization, reducing boilerplate. Parameters become captured by the class — compile to fields when accessed. Combine with `readonly` modifier. Record primary constructors existed since C# 9.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Small Methods (Fits in Your Head)[0]

Mark Seemann's core heuristic: methods should fit in your head — at most ~10–15 lines. Small methods reduce cognitive load, simplify testing, and force good naming. Extract until you can't extract anymore; each method does one thing at one level of abstraction.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Command-Query Separation[0]

CQS (from Bertrand Meyer, popularized by Seemann) says: a method should be a command (mutates state, returns void/Task) OR a query (returns a value, no side effects), never both. This makes code predictable, testable, and safe to compose.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Pure Functions & Determinism[0]

A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects (no I/O, no mutation). Pure functions are trivial to test, cache, parallelize, and reason about. Push side effects to the edges of your architecture.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Cyclomatic Complexity & Guard Clauses[0]

Cyclomatic complexity measures independent paths through code. Keep each method's complexity ≤ 4 (1 + number of decisions). Use guard clauses (early return) to flatten nesting. Extract conditional logic into well-named methods.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.API Surface & Information Hiding[0]

Minimize the public API surface of each type. Mark everything `private` by default, then promote only what external consumers need. Fewer public members = less coupling, easier refactoring, simpler testing. Apply the Interface Segregation Principle.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Property-Based Testing[0]

Property-Based Testing (from FsCheck for .NET) tests general properties/ invariants instead of specific examples. The framework generates random inputs to find edge cases. Properties like: roundtrip, idempotence, commutativity, and invariant preservation.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.SUT & Test Data Builders[0]

Test Data Builder pattern (from Growing Object-Oriented Software) constructs test objects with sensible defaults and explicit overrides. Avoids repetitive Arrange code, makes tests readable, and isolates test changes when constructors change.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Postel's Law & Defensive Coding[0]

Postel's Law: "Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept." Accept flexible inputs (handle edge cases gracefully) but produce strict, predictable outputs. Use null checks, validation, and normalization at boundaries.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Dependency Inversion & Composition Root[0]

Depend on abstractions, not concretions. Build a Composition Root (the entry point of the application) where all dependencies are wired together. This enables unit testing with mocks, delayed decisions about implementations, and parallel development.
.Software Engineering Heuristics.Parameter Objects & Immutability[0]

Replace long parameter lists (3+ parameters) with a parameter object. Using `record` types gives you immutability, value equality, and deconstruction for free. Parameter objects make call sites self-documenting and simplify method evolution.
css.json: Variables and data types in CSS.
Input and output operations in CSS.

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the visual presentation of HTML. Rules consist of a selector and a declaration block with properties and values. Apply via inline, internal (<style>), or external (.css file).
CSS selectors target elements: element (p), class (.my-class), id (#my-id), attribute ([type="text"]), universal (*). Combinators: descendant (div p), child (div > p), sibling (h2 + p).
Color formats: named (red), hex (#FF5733), RGB (rgb(255, 87, 51)), RGBA (rgba(255, 87, 51, 0.5)), HSL/HSLA. Units: px, em (relative to parent font), rem (relative to root), %, vw/vh, ch.

Typography properties: font-family, font-size, font-weight (100-900), font-style, text-align, text-decoration, text-transform, line-height, letter-spacing. Use web fonts via @font-face or Google Fonts.
Every element is a box: content (inner), padding (around content), border (edge), margin (outside). Use box-sizing: border-box to include padding/border in width.
CSS custom properties (variables) defined with --name, accessed with var(--name). They cascade and can be overridden, enabling easy theme systems.
CSS specificity determines which rule wins. Inline > ID > Class > Element. When equal, last rule wins. Use !important sparingly — it breaks the natural cascade.
Some CSS properties inherit from parent elements: color, font-family, line-height. Others like margin, padding, border do not. Control with inherit, initial, unset, revert.
The @layer rule defines cascade layers. Styles in later layers override earlier ones regardless of specificity. Use to organize resets, base styles, components, and utilities in predictable order.

Browsers apply default styles inconsistently. CSS resets remove all defaults (margin: 0, padding: 0). Normalize.css preserves useful defaults while fixing cross-browser differences. Choose based on project needs.
The display property controls rendering: block (full width, new line), inline (flows with text), inline-block (inline but accepts width/height), none (hidden, removed from flow). Modern: flex, grid.
Flexbox is a 1D layout model. Container: display: flex. Main axis: justify-content. Cross axis: align-items. Items wrap with flex-wrap, grow with flex-grow, order with order.
CSS Grid is a 2D layout system. Define columns with grid-template-columns, rows with grid-template-rows. Use grid-area with named template areas for complex layouts.
position values: static (default), relative (offset from normal), absolute (relative to positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to viewport), sticky (toggles between relative/fixed on scroll).
Media queries adapt layouts to screen sizes. Use @media (min-width: ...) for mobile-first approach. Common breakpoints: 576px (mobile), 768px (tablet), 992px (desktop), 1200px (wide).

Background properties: background-color, background-image, background-size, background-position, background-repeat. Gradients: linear-gradient() and radial-gradient(). Multiple backgrounds can be layered.
CSS animations use @keyframes to define sequences. The animation shorthand: name, duration, timing function, delay, iteration count, direction, fill mode.
Style lists with list-style-type, list-style-position, list-style-image. CSS counters (counter-reset, counter-increment) create numbered headings, table-of-contents, or custom list numbering.

Style form elements using CSS: inputs, textareas, selects, checkboxes, radio buttons, and buttons. Normalize browser defaults. Use :focus, :valid, :invalid, :disabled pseudo-classes for state styling.
The box-shadow property adds shadows: offset-x offset-y blur-radius spread-radius color. Multiple shadows can be layered. Use inset for inner shadows.
Text styling: text-shadow for shadows, text-overflow for ellipsis, word-break for breaking long words, white-space for spacing control, text-wrap for wrapping behavior.
CSS filter applies visual effects: blur(), brightness(), contrast(), grayscale(), sepia(), hue-rotate(), drop-shadow(). mix-blend-mode blends elements with their background.
clip-path clips elements to a shape: circle(), ellipse(), polygon(), inset(). shape-outside makes text wrap around a shape.
object-fit controls how replaced elements (images, videos) fit their container: fill, contain, cover, none, scale-down. object-position sets alignment within the box.
overflow controls content overflow: visible, hidden, scroll, auto. overflow-x/overflow-y for axis-specific. scroll-behavior: smooth for smooth scrolling. scroll-snap for snap points.
The cursor property changes the mouse cursor: pointer, grab, text, not-allowed, wait. pointer-events controls click/touch behavior: auto (default), none (disable), visiblePainted (SVG).

The resize property makes elements user-resizable: both, horizontal, vertical. field-sizing makes textareas/contenteditable auto-size. object-view-box crops replaced elements without changing the image.
Multi-column layout with column-count, column-width, column-gap, column-rule. Content flows automatically between columns. Useful for text-heavy layouts like newspapers.
Scalable CSS methodologies: BEM (Block Element Modifier) uses naming like .block__element--modifier. Prevents conflicts and improves maintainability by enforcing naming conventions.
CSS preprocessors extend CSS with variables, nesting, mixins, functions. SCSS features: $variables, @mixin/@include, & parent selector, built-in functions for colors and math.
The @layer rule controls cascade layer order. Later layers override earlier ones regardless of specificity. Useful for organizing resets, components, and utilities.
Container queries (@container) style elements based on container size rather than viewport. Define a containment context with container-type. Enables truly reusable components.
CSS nesting (native) lets you nest selectors like SCSS. The @scope rule limits styles to a subtree, providing better encapsulation without Shadow DOM.
Logical properties use flow-relative directions: margin-inline-start instead of margin-left, padding-block instead of padding-top/padding-bottom. Better for internationalization and RTL support.
Powerful CSS functions: calc() for math, min()/max()/clamp() for responsive values, attr() for HTML attributes, url() for resources, var() for variables.
content-visibility skips rendering of off-screen elements for performance. contain isolates layout/style/paint. content-visibility: auto automatically skips hidden content.
Modern CSS color functions: color-mix() blends colors, color() accesses wider gamuts (Display P3, sRGB), lch()/lab() for perceptually uniform colors, oklch()/oklab() for better gradients.
.CSS Advanced Topics.@property & Custom Properties Deep Dive[0]
The @property rule defines typed CSS custom properties with initial values and inheritance control. Enables animation of custom properties, validation, and better developer ergonomics.
.CSS Advanced Topics.Container Query Units & Style Queries[0]
Container query units: cqw (1% container width), cqh (1% height), cqi (1% inline size), cqb (1% block size), cqmin/cqmax. Style queries (@container style()) query computed style values.
View Transitions animate between page states or navigations. Use @view-transition navigation rule, view-transition-name on elements, and ::view-transition-* pseudo-elements for custom animations.
Beyond BEM: SMACSS (categorizes into base/layout/module/state/theme), ITCSS (layers by specificity), OOCSS (separates structure from skin, container from content). Choose what fits your project.
PostCSS is a tool for transforming CSS with JavaScript plugins. Autoprefixer automatically adds vendor prefixes (-webkit-, -moz-, etc.). Other plugins enable future CSS syntax today.
Utility-first CSS uses small, composable classes. Tailwind CSS provides .flex, .text-center, .p-4 etc. Encourages design consistency and reduces CSS file size. Trade-off: verbose HTML.
CSS Modules generate locally scoped class names. Imported like JS modules. Class names are hashed at build time to avoid conflicts. Works well with component frameworks like React, Vue, Svelte.
Advanced Grid: subgrid passes grid tracks to children. auto-fill/auto-fit for responsive grids without media queries. grid-auto-flow: dense fills gaps automatically.

CSS performance: minimize specificity chains, avoid expensive properties (box-shadow, border-radius), use will-change sparingly, avoid @import, reduce repaints/reflows, use GPU-accelerated properties (transform, opacity).

Browser DevTools: inspect computed styles, trace specificity, toggle pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus), edit live CSS, view box model diagram, debug animations with timeline. Use outline to visualize elements.

Print stylesheets optimize pages for paper: hide nav/sidebars/ads, use page-break-* properties, ensure link URLs print. Accessibility: respect prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme, prefers-contrast, forced-colors.

CSS Grid Layout is a two-dimensional layout system. Key properties: grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows define tracks. fr unit distributes available space. grid-template-areas provides visual layout mapping. auto-fit and auto-fill create responsive grids without media queries. minmax() sets flexible track sizes. gap controls gutter spacing. Grid placement functions: grid-column, grid-row, grid-area. Grid is best for page-level layouts and two-dimensional arrangements.

CSS Custom Properties (CSS variables) enable reusable values throughout a stylesheet. Declared with --name and accessed with var(--name, fallback). They cascade like regular CSS — set global variables on :root and override in specific scopes. CSS variables can be changed at runtime via JavaScript (element.style.setProperty('--color', 'red')) enabling dynamic theming. Use with calc() for computed values. Unlike preprocessor variables (Sass/Less), CSS variables cascade and can be updated dynamically.

CSS animations bring interfaces to life. @keyframes defines animation steps using percentage points or from/to. The animation shorthand: name, duration, timing function, delay, iteration count, direction, fill mode, play state. Timing functions: ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier(), steps(). animation-fill-mode: forwards retains the end state. animation-direction: alternate creates smooth back-and-forth animations. prefers-reduced-motion respects user accessibility settings.

CSS transform modifies element appearance: translate() (move), rotate() (turn), scale() (size), skew() (shear). transform-origin changes the pivot point. 3D transforms: translateZ(), rotateX(), rotateY(), perspective(). backface-visibility: hidden prevents reverse-side rendering. transition animates property changes smoothly with duration, timing function, and delay. Use will-change to hint at upcoming transforms for GPU acceleration. Hardware-accelerated properties: transform, opacity.

Container queries allow styling elements based on their container's size rather than the viewport. Define a containment context with container-type: inline-size and optionally name it with container-name. Use @container (min-width: 400px) to apply styles when the container reaches that width. Container queries are ideal for reusable component libraries where a component must adapt to various placement contexts. They work with cqw, cqi (container query units).

Block Element Modifier (BEM) is a naming convention that makes CSS more maintainable. Block: standalone component (.card). Element: part of a block (.card__title). Modifier: variant (.card--featured, .card__title--large). Benefits: prevents naming conflicts, increases readability, and creates a clear relationship between HTML and CSS. Each selector has the same specificity, making overrides predictable. Works well with preprocessors using & nesting.

CSS preprocessors extend CSS with features like variables, nesting, mixins, functions, and inheritance. Sass/SCSS is the most popular: $variables, @mixin/@include for reusable styles, @extend for inheritance, nesting for hierarchy, & parent selector, and built-in functions (darken, lighten, rgba). PostCSS is a tool for transforming CSS with plugins: Autoprefixer (adds vendor prefixes), PostCSS Preset Env (future CSS syntax), CSS Modules (local scoping). Modern browsers support many features (CSS variables, nesting via postcss-nesting) reducing preprocessor dependency. Consider native CSS vs preprocessed CSS based on team preferences and project needs.
curriculum.json: .angular.Getting Started.Components.exp

Components are the fundamental building blocks of Angular apps, each consisting of a TypeScript class, HTML template, and optional CSS styles. They control a view via a decorated class with @Component metadata.
.angular.Getting Started.Modules.exp

NgModules organize an Angular app into cohesive blocks of functionality by declaring components, importing dependencies, and providing services. Every app has a root module (AppModule) as the entry point.
.angular.Getting Started.Templates.exp
Angular templates extend HTML with custom syntax including interpolation ({{ }}), property binding ([ ]), event binding (( )), and structural directives (*ngIf, *ngFor) for dynamic views.
.angular.Services & DI.Dependency Injection.exp
Angular's dependency injection system provides dependencies to classes via constructor parameters. The injector hierarchy creates singleton or per-component instances of services automatically.
.angular.Services & DI.Services.exp
Services are singleton classes decorated with @Injectable that encapsulate business logic, data access, or cross-cutting concerns. They are the recommended way to share logic between components.
.angular.Services & DI.Providers.exp

Providers configure the injector with dependency recipes, controlling how services are created and scoped. They can be registered at module level, component level, or using providedIn: 'root' for tree-shaking.
.angular.Routing.Router.exp
Angular Router enables navigation between views in SPAs with URL-based routing, nested routes, lazy-loaded modules, and route parameters. It integrates with the browser's history API.
.angular.Routing.Lazy Loading.exp
Lazy loading loads feature modules on demand when the user navigates to their routes, reducing initial bundle size. Use loadChildren in route config to point to a module imported via dynamic import.
.angular.Routing.Guards.exp

Route guards control navigation using interfaces like CanActivate, CanDeactivate, and Resolve. They prevent unauthorized access, prompt for unsaved changes, and pre-fetch data before a route activates.
.angular.Forms.Template-driven.exp
Template-driven forms rely on directives in the template like ngModel for two-way data binding. They are simpler but less scalable than reactive forms, suitable for basic form use cases.
.angular.Forms.Reactive.exp
Reactive forms provide a model-driven approach with form control instances created programmatically, offering more predictability, testability, and advanced validation capabilities.
.angular.Forms.Validation.exp
Angular forms support built-in validators (required, minLength, pattern) and custom async validators. Validation state is exposed through CSS classes (ng-valid, ng-invalid) and component properties.
.angular.HTTP.HttpClient.exp
HttpClient is Angular's built-in HTTP client with typed request/response, interceptors, and automatic JSON parsing. Methods return Observables supporting RxJS operators for transformations.
.angular.HTTP.Interceptors.exp
Interceptors sit between the application and the backend, transforming outgoing requests or incoming responses. Common use cases include adding auth tokens, logging, and error handling.
.angular.HTTP.Error Handling.exp
