Error handling in HTTP requests is done via RxJS catchError operator, retrying failed requests, or displaying user-friendly error messages. Global error handling can be centralized in interceptors.
.angular.Advanced.Directives.exp

Angular offers three types of directives: components, structural directives (alter DOM layout), and attribute directives (change appearance or behavior). Custom directives encapsulate reusable DOM manipulation.
.angular.Advanced.Pipes.exp
Pipes transform data in templates for display, such as formatting dates, currencies, or filtering lists. Angular provides built-in pipes and you can create custom pure or impure pipes.
.angular.Advanced.Custom Decorators.exp
Decorators are TypeScript features used extensively in Angular for metadata. Custom decorators can extend component behavior, add logging, or transform class properties at design time.
.angular.Testing.Jasmine.exp
Jasmine is a behavior-driven development framework for testing JavaScript code with a clean, readable syntax. It provides describe/it blocks, matchers (toEqual, toContain), and spies.
.angular.Testing.Karma.exp
Karma is a test runner that executes tests in real browsers, providing fast feedback loops and reporting. It's the default test runner in Angular CLI projects via ng test.
.angular.Testing.TestBed.exp

TestBed is Angular's primary testing utility for configuring and creating component test environments. It manages module compilation, dependency injection, and provides ComponentFixture for interaction.
.angular.Performance.Change Detection.exp
Angular's default change detection checks every component in the tree when any data changes, ensuring consistency. It uses zone.js to patch browser APIs and trigger checks automatically.
.angular.Performance.OnPush.exp

OnPush change detection strategy reduces unnecessary checks by only running detection when input references change, events fire, or observables emit. It's essential for large lists and performance-critical views.
.angular.Performance.Code Splitting.exp
Angular supports code splitting through lazy-loaded modules and ES dynamic imports. The CLI generates separate chunks per lazy route, and the router loads them on demand when the user navigates.
.angular.Standalone Components.Standalone API.exp

Standalone components, directives, and pipes are self-contained without needing NgModules. Created with the standalone: true flag, they import dependencies directly and can be lazy-loaded via the router.
.angular.Standalone Components.Bootstrap Standalone.exp
Applications can bootstrap directly from a standalone component instead of NgModule. The main.ts calls bootstrapApplication with the root component and optional provider configuration.
.angular.Standalone Components.Routing Standalone.exp
Standalone components load lazily with loadComponent in the route config, eliminating the need for feature modules. Each route points directly to a component with its own imports.
.angular.Signals.Writable Signals.exp
Signals are reactive primitives that notify consumers when their value changes. Writable signals created with signal() expose get/set/update methods for synchronous state management.
.angular.Signals.Computed Signals.exp
Computed signals derive values from other signals with lazy evaluation and caching. They only recompute when dependent signals change, replacing manual ChangeDetectorRef calls.
.angular.Signals.Effects.exp
Effects run side effects automatically when their signal dependencies change. They are used for syncing state to localStorage, logging, or triggering imperative DOM operations.
.angular.Signals.Signal Inputs.exp
Signal-based inputs replace @Input with input() and input.required(), providing reactive input values without lifecycle hooks. They integrate natively with the change detection system.
.angular.CLI & Schematics.ng generate.exp
The Angular CLI generates components, directives, pipes, services, modules, and more using ng generate. Schematics customize generation with options for style, inline template, and routing.
.angular.CLI & Schematics.Custom Schematics.exp
Custom schematics automate project scaffolding by generating files, modifying existing code, and installing dependencies. They are published as npm packages and run with ng generate.
.angular.CLI & Schematics.Angular Builders.exp
Builders extend the Angular CLI build pipeline with custom build, test, or deploy logic. They replace Angular's default builder to support custom tooling like custom webpack configs.
.angular.Deferrable Views.@defer.exp
Deferrable views (introduced in Angular 17) lazy-load component dependencies with @defer blocks. They improve initial bundle size by deferring heavy components until a specified trigger.
.angular.Deferrable Views.Defer Triggers.exp
Defer triggers control when lazy content loads: on viewport (enters viewport), on interaction (user clicks), on immediate, on idle (browser idle), or on a custom timer.
.angular.Deferrable Views.Defer Dependencies.exp
Deferred components and their transitive dependencies are split into separate JavaScript chunks. Angular loads these chunks asynchronously when the trigger condition is met, reducing initial payload.
.angular.inject Function.inject().exp
The inject() function provides a programmatic alternative to constructor-based dependency injection. It can be called in the class body, making DI more flexible and reducing boilerplate.
.angular.inject Function.Injection Context.exp
inject() must be called within an injection context such as a constructor, class field initializer, or factory function. Outside these contexts it throws, ensuring predictable DI resolution.
.aws.AWS Fundamentals.AWS Account & Root User.exp

Create an AWS account at aws.amazon.com. Root user has full unrestricted access — enable MFA immediately. Never use root for daily tasks. Create IAM users and roles instead. Set up billing alerts. Use AWS Organizations to manage multiple accounts centrally. Enable CloudTrail in all regions.
.aws.AWS Fundamentals.IAM Users, Groups & Roles.exp

IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls access. Users are individuals. Groups organize users with shared permissions. Roles are assumed by services (EC2, Lambda) or federated users. Policies are JSON documents with Allow/Deny effects. Follow least privilege. Use managed policies when possible.
.aws.AWS Fundamentals.IAM Policies Deep.exp

IAM policies have: Version (2012-10-17), Statement list with Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (service:operation), Resource (ARN), and optional Condition (IP, time, MFA, tags). Use policy variables ${aws:username}. Managed policies vs inline. Permission boundaries limit max permissions. Service Control Policies (SCP) in Organizations.
.aws.AWS Fundamentals.AWS Organizations & SCPs.exp

AWS Organizations centrally manages multiple accounts. Root OU contains all accounts. Create OUs for structure (Production, Staging, Sandbox). Service Control Policies (SCPs) restrict max permissions across accounts. Consolidate billing for volume discounts. Use AWS SSO for user access across accounts.
.aws.AWS Fundamentals.Regions, AZs & Edge Locations.exp

AWS has 30+ regions worldwide (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1, etc.). Each region has 3-6 Availability Zones (AZs) — isolated data centers. Edge Locations are CDN endpoints (400+). Use multiple AZs for HA. Choose region based on latency, compliance, cost, and service availability. Some services are global (IAM, Route53, CloudFront).
.aws.Compute.EC2 Instances Deep.exp

EC2 provides virtual machines. Instance families: general (t3, m6i), compute (c6i), memory (r6i, x2gd), storage (i3, d2), GPU (p4, g5). Purchase options: On-Demand (pay per hour/sec), Reserved (1-3yr, up to 72% off), Spot (up to 90% off, interruptible), Dedicated Host. User data runs at boot. Placement groups control instance placement for low latency or HA.
.aws.Compute.EC2 Networking & Security Groups.exp

Security Groups are stateful firewalls attached to ENIs. Rules: allow only (no deny), evaluate all rules. NACLs are stateless firewalls at subnet level (allow/deny, rule numbers). Elastic IPs are static public IPs. ENIs are virtual network cards. VPC Flow Logs capture traffic metadata.
.aws.Compute.EC2 Auto Scaling.exp

Auto Scaling maintains desired instance count. Launch template specifies instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking (e.g., keep CPU at 50%), step scaling, scheduled scaling. Health checks replace unhealthy instances. Cooldown periods prevent rapid scaling. Lifecycle hooks run custom actions during scale events.
.aws.Compute.Elastic Load Balancing.exp

ALB (Application LB): HTTP/HTTPS, path-based routing, host-based routing, WebSockets. NLB (Network LB): TCP/UDP/TLS, ultra-low latency, static IP. Gateway LB: transparent inspection of traffic. Target groups route to instances, IPs, or Lambda. Sticky sessions via cookies. Health checks detect failures. Cross-zone load balancing distributes evenly.
.aws.Compute.AWS Lambda.exp

Lambda runs code without servers. Runtimes: Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, custom (provided.al2). Triggers: API Gateway, S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge, Kinesis. Max execution 15 min, max memory 10GB, max ephemeral storage 10GB. Concurrency limit per account (1000 default). Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity. Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm. Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations.
.aws.Compute.ECS, EKS & Fargate.exp

ECS runs Docker containers at scale. Launch types: Fargate (serverless, no EC2 to manage) and EC2 (control over instances). EKS is managed Kubernetes. ECR stores container images. Task definitions describe containers (CPU, memory, ports, env vars). Services maintain desired task count with load balancer integration.
.aws.Compute.Elastic Beanstalk.exp

Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS — upload code, AWS handles provisioning, load balancing, auto scaling, monitoring. Platforms: Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, PHP, Ruby, Go, Docker. Environments: Web tier (ALB + ASG) and Worker tier (SQS + background jobs). Customize with .ebextensions config files. Easy for MVPs and standard web apps.
.aws.Compute.EC2 Image Builder & AMIs.exp

EC2 Image Builder automates AMI creation. Pipeline steps: source image, build components (install packages), test components (validate), distribute to regions. Golden AMIs ensure consistent instances. Systems Manager Parameter Store tracks latest AMI IDs. Automate AMI refresh in Auto Scaling via lifecycle hooks.
.aws.Storage.S3 Deep Dive.exp

Amazon S3 is object storage with 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability. Storage classes: Standard (frequent access), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-cost optimization), Standard-IA (infrequent), One Zone-IA (lower cost, single AZ), Glacier Instant (archival, ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible (min retrieval), Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, 12hr retrieval). Versioning protects against deletes. Lifecycle policies transition between classes. S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda/SQS/SNS.
.aws.Storage.S3 Security & Encryption.exp

S3 security: Block Public Access (account/bucket level). Bucket policies (resource-based). IAM policies (identity-based). ACLs (legacy). Encryption: SSE-S3 (AES-256, AWS managed), SSE-KMS (KMS keys, audit trail), SSE-C (customer provided key), client-side encryption. Object Lock (WORM — write once read many). S3 Access Points simplify managing access for large datasets.
.aws.Storage.EBS & Instance Storage.exp

EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage for EC2. Volume types: gp3 (baseline 3000 IOPS, 125 MB/s, max 16000 IOPS), io2 (provisioned IOPS, 99.999% durability), st1 (throughput optimized, HDD), sc1 (cold HDD). Snapshots are incremental backups to S3. EBS Multi-attach for clustered workloads. EBS Fast Snapshot Restore for instant snapshot hydration. Instance Store is ephemeral (data lost on stop/terminate).
.aws.Storage.EFS & FSx.exp

EFS is managed NFS for Linux. Elastic — grows/shrinks automatically. Performance modes: General Purpose (default, latency-sensitive) and Max I/O (high-throughput, parallel). Throughput modes: Bursting and Provisioned. Lifecycle management moves files to EFS IA after N days. EFS Replication for cross-region DR. FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, AD integration) and FSx for Lustre (high-performance, HPC/AI).
.aws.Storage.CloudFront CDN.exp

CloudFront is a global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, Lambda Function URL, HTTP server. Behaviors route by path pattern. Price classes: All, 200 (most), NA+EU only. SSL/TLS termination via ACM. Geo-restriction (whitelist/blacklist countries). Lambda@Edge for custom logic. OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. Real-time logs to Kinesis. WAF integration for DDoS protection.
.aws.Databases.RDS Deep Dive.exp

RDS manages relational databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Multi-AZ: synchronous standby replica in another AZ for HA (failover is automatic). Read replicas: async replication for read scaling (up to 15). Automated backups with point-in-time recovery (up to 35 days). Manual snapshots persist beyond retention. Enhanced Monitoring (CloudWatch metrics per second). Performance Insights for query analysis. RDS Proxy for connection pooling.
.aws.Databases.Aurora.exp

Amazon Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible with cloud-native architecture. 6-way replication across 3 AZs — only 1/6 of data written (quorum). Auto-scaling storage from 10GB to 128TB. Aurora Serverless v2 scales to 0 ACUs (pay per second). Global Database: 1 primary region, up to 5 secondary regions with <1s replication. Backtrack: rewind DB to a specific time without restore. Parallel Query pushes analytics to storage layer.
.aws.Databases.DynamoDB.exp

DynamoDB is fully managed NoSQL key-value/document DB. Single-digit ms latency at any scale. Primary key: partition key (HASH) or composite (HASH + RANGE). Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, auto-scales) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, auto-scaling). DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Global Tables are multi-region, multi-writer (active-active). Streams capture changes for Lambda triggers or Kinesis. TTL auto-expires items.
.aws.Databases.ElastiCache & MemoryDB.exp

ElastiCache provides managed Redis and Memcached. Redis: multi-AZ, replication, persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets, streams, Lua scripting. Memcached: simple, multi-threaded, no persistence. Cluster Mode shards data across nodes (up to 500 shards). Global Datastore for cross-region replication. MemoryDB is Redis-compatible, durable (write-ahead log), for microservices requiring both speed and durability. Use cases: session store, caching, rate limiting, leaderboards, message queues.
.aws.Databases.Redshift & Data Analytics.exp

Redshift is cloud data warehouse (petabyte-scale). Columnar storage, massively parallel (MPP). Node types: DC (dense compute), DS/RA3 (managed storage). Distribution styles: KEY, ALL, EVEN. Sort keys define data order per block. Redshift Spectrum queries data directly in S3 without loading. Automatic workload management (WLM) prioritizes queries. Concurrency Scaling handles burst queries. Materialized views for pre-computed aggregates. Unload data to S3 for analysis.
.aws.Networking.VPC Design.exp

VPC is your isolated network in AWS. CIDR block defines IP range (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets divide the VPC (public for internet-facing, private for internal). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway (IGW) for public internet access. NAT Gateway for private subnets to reach internet (outbound only). VPC Peering connects VPCs within or across accounts. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-prem. Endpoints (Gateway: S3/DynamoDB; Interface: other services) provide private access without IGW.
.aws.Networking.Route53 DNS.exp

Route53 is a DNS service (authoritative + resolver). Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verify), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources — free, works at zone apex). Routing policies: Simple, Weighted, Latency, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multi-value. Health checks monitor endpoint health and route away from failures. Private hosted zones for internal DNS. DNSSEC for security.
.aws.Networking.AWS WAF & Shield.exp

AWS WAF is a web application firewall that protects HTTP endpoints. Rule groups: IP set, SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo-match, regex patterns. Managed rule groups from AWS (Core, SQL DB, Admin Protection, Known Bad Inputs). Shield Standard is free, protects against DDoS (L3/L4). Shield Advanced ($3k/mo) adds L7 DDoS protection, cost protection, DRT (DDoS Response Team). WAF integrates with CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync.
.aws.Networking.AWS KMS & Secrets Manager.exp

KMS manages encryption keys. Customer managed keys vs AWS managed keys. Automatic annual key rotation. Envelope encryption: generate a data key to encrypt data, encrypt the data key with a KMS key. Key policies control who can use/administer keys. Grant allows temporary access. Secrets Manager stores secrets (DB passwords, API keys) with automatic rotation via Lambda. Parameter Store (free) stores config data and secrets.
.aws.DevOps & Management.CloudFormation.exp

CloudFormation is IaC (Infrastructure as Code) on AWS. Templates written in YAML/JSON. Resources define AWS components. Parameters allow customization at deploy time. Outputs export values for cross-stack references. Change sets preview changes before applying. Nested stacks compose complex infrastructure. Drift detection checks if real-world resources match the template. StackSets deploy across accounts/regions via Organizations. DeletionPolicy controls resource retention on stack delete.
.aws.DevOps & Management.CI/CD with CodePipeline.exp

CodePipeline automates build-test-deploy. Source: CodeCommit, GitHub, Bitbucket, S3. Build: CodeBuild (managed build server, pay per minute). Deploy: CodeDeploy (EC2, Lambda, ECS), Elastic Beanstalk, CloudFormation. Stages run sequentially with manual approval gates. Artifacts stored in S3. CloudWatch Events trigger pipelines on source changes.
.aws.DevOps & Management.CloudWatch Monitoring.exp

CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms. Metrics: CPU, memory, disk, network, custom metrics. Alarms: threshold-based, composite (multiple conditions), anomaly detection. Logs: agent collects from EC2, streams to log groups. Logs Insights queries logs with SQL-like syntax. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors (IPs, endpoints). Synthetics (Canaries) monitor endpoints with Node.js scripts. ServiceLens traces requests across services (X-Ray integration). Dashboards visualize metrics in one place.
.aws.DevOps & Management.EventBridge & Step Functions.exp

EventBridge is a serverless event bus. Sources: AWS services, SaaS (Datadog, Zendesk), custom apps. Rules filter events and route to targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions). Pipes connects sources to targets with filtering and enrichment. Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows (visual state machine). Standard Workflows (up to 1-year duration) vs Express (up to 5-min, high volume). States: Task, Choice, Parallel, Map, Wait, Succeed, Fail. Error handling with retries and catch.
.aws.DevOps & Management.AWS Budgets & Cost Control.exp

AWS Budgets track spending and send alerts. Types: Cost budget, Usage budget, Savings Plans budget, Reservation budget. Budget actions can apply IAM policy or stop EC2 instances when threshold is exceeded. Cost Explorer visualizes spend. Compute Optimizer recommends right-sizing. Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker) offer discounts for commitment. Trusted Advisor checks cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits. Consolidated billing aggregates usage across accounts.
.aws.Advanced AWS.VPC Deep Dive.exp

VPC is the foundation of AWS networking. Subnets (public/private) segment IP ranges. Route tables direct traffic to IGW (public) or NATGW (private). NAT Gateway enables outbound internet for private subnets — costs ~$0.045/hr + data processed. VPC Peering connects VPCs directly (no transitive peering). Security Groups (stateful, allow-only) vs NACLs (stateless, allow/deny, rule numbers). Common mistake: forgetting NACL rules are stateless — must configure both inbound and outbound rules separately. VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata for analysis. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs/on-prem via a hub. Use VPC endpoints for private access to S3/DynamoDB without NAT/IGW.
.aws.Advanced AWS.Route53 & DNS.exp

Route53 is AWS's DNS service. Hosted zones contain DNS records for a domain. Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (cannot be used at zone apex), MX (mail), TXT (verification), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources, works at zone apex, free). Routing policies: Simple (single record), Weighted (A/B testing), Latency (best performance), Failover (active-passive DR), Geolocation (by user location), Geoproximity (by resource location). Health checks monitor endpoints. Common mistake: using CNAME at zone apex — use Alias instead. Enable DNSSEC for DNS spoofing protection.
.aws.Advanced AWS.CloudFront & CDN.exp

CloudFront is AWS's global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Distributions define content delivery configuration. Origins: S3 buckets, ALBs, EC2, custom HTTP servers. Behaviors route by URL path pattern. Lambda@Edge executes code at edge locations (viewer/origin request/response) — use for A/B testing, URL rewrites, authentication. Price classes: Price Class All (all edges), Price Class 200 (most, cheaper), Price Class 100 (US+Europe, cheapest). Invalidations clear edge caches (charged per path). OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. WAF integration for DDoS. Common mistake: caching sensitive data — set appropriate Cache-Control and Cookie/QueryString forwarding policies.
.aws.Advanced AWS.DynamoDB.exp

DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL with single-digit ms latency. Tables contain items (up to 400KB each). Primary key: Partition Key (HASH) alone or Composite (HASH + RANGE/Sort Key). GSIs (Global Secondary Indexes) have different partition/sort keys — eventually consistent, add after table creation. LSIs (Local Secondary Indexes) same partition key, different sort key — created only at table creation, strongly consistent. DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is an in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, best for variable traffic) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, cheaper for predictable traffic). Streams capture changes for 24h. TTL auto-expires items. Common mistake: scanning instead of querying — always Query with a partition key.
.aws.Advanced AWS.SQS & SNS.exp

SQS is fully managed message queuing. Standard queues: unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO queues: exactly-once processing, first-in-first-out, 3000 msg/s max (with batching). Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail after maxReceiveCount retries. Visibility timeout hides messages during processing — set longer than your processing time. Long polling reduces empty responses and costs. SNS is pub/sub messaging. Topics fan out messages to subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS). Fan-out pattern: SNS sends to multiple SQS queues for parallel processing. Message filtering with filter policies. Common mistake: forgetting to delete messages from SQS after processing (they reappear after visibility timeout!).
.aws.Advanced AWS.Step Functions & Workflows.exp

Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows as state machines. Standard Workflows: up to 1-year duration, exactly-once execution, billed per state transition. Express Workflows: up to 5-min duration, at-least-once, billed by execution time/memory. State types: Task (invoke Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SQS), Choice (if/else), Parallel (fan-out), Map (iterate array), Wait (delay), Succeed/Fail (terminate). Error handling: Retry (exponential backoff, maxAttempts) and Catch (redirect to fallback state). Timeouts prevent stuck executions. Heartbeats for long-running tasks. Common mistake: not setting appropriate timeouts — workflows can hang indefinitely.
.aws.Advanced AWS.CloudWatch & Monitoring.exp

CloudWatch is the single source of truth for AWS observability. Metrics: AWS service metrics (CPU, requests, latency) and custom metrics (up to 15-second granularity). Alarms: threshold-based, anomaly detection (ML-based), composite alarms (combine multiple conditions). Alarm actions trigger SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 stop/reboot. Logs Insights queries logs with a SQL-like query language. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors. Synthetics Canaries monitor endpoints. Dashboards combine metrics, logs, and alarms. Common mistake: not setting dimension combinations on custom metrics (each unique combination is a separate metric). Best practice: use structured JSON logging for easier Logs Insights queries. Set log retention to avoid accumulating costs.
.azure.Azure Fundamentals.Azure Account & Portal.exp

Create an Azure account at portal.azure.com. Free tier: $200 credit for 30 days + 55+ always-free services. Azure Portal is the web UI. Azure CLI for command-line management. PowerShell Az module for scripting. Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management layer. Every resource belongs to a resource group. Subscriptions group resource groups with billing boundaries. Management groups organize subscriptions hierarchically. Azure Blueprints for compliance.
.azure.Azure Fundamentals.Azure Regions & Availability.exp

Azure has 60+ regions worldwide, more than any other cloud provider. Region pairs (e.g., East US + West US) are 300+ miles apart for DR. Availability Sets (up to 3 fault domains + 5 update domains) for VMs. Availability Zones (3+ per region) are physically separate data centers within a region. Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads to a secondary region for disaster recovery. Proximity Placement Groups reduce VM-to-VM latency.
.azure.Azure Fundamentals.Azure Resource Manager & RBAC.exp

ARM manages all resources via declarative JSON/Bicep templates. Every resource has a unique ARM ID. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): roles are assignments of permissions at a scope (subscription, resource group, resource). Built-in roles: Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator. Custom roles define granular permissions. Managed Identities give Azure resources an identity in Entra ID without managing credentials. Azure Policy enforces rules across resources.
.azure.Azure Fundamentals.Azure Entra ID (formerly Active Directory).exp

Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service. Previously Azure AD. Tenants represent organizations. Users and Groups manage access. App registrations for OAuth2/OIDC authentication. Service principals are identities for applications. Managed identities for Azure resources (system-assigned or user-assigned). Conditional Access policies enforce MFA, device compliance, location. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) provides just-in-time admin access. Identity Protection detects compromised credentials.
.azure.Compute.Azure VMs Deep.exp

Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS compute. VM series: General purpose (B-series burstable, D-series balanced), Compute optimized (F-series), Memory optimized (E-series, M-series), Storage optimized (L-series), GPU (NC, ND, NV). Availability Sets distribute VMs across fault/update domains (99.95% SLA). Availability Zones provide 99.99% SLA. Azure Dedicated Host for compliance. VM Scale Sets automatically manage identical VMs with autoscaling. Proximity Placement Groups reduce inter-VM latency.
.azure.Compute.Azure App Service.exp

App Service is PaaS for web apps, REST APIs, and mobile backends. Supports .NET, Java, Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, Docker containers. Plans define pricing tier: Free/Shared (dev), Basic (custom domain, manual scale), Standard (auto-scale, staging slots), Premium (private endpoints, increased scale). Deployment Slots enable staging (swap with zero downtime). Auto-scale based on metrics or schedule. Built-in authentication (Entra ID, Google, Facebook). Hybrid Connections connect to on-prem resources. App Service Environment (ASE) is fully isolated, dedicated.
.azure.Compute.Azure Functions.exp

Azure Functions is serverless compute. Triggers: HTTP (API), Timer, Blob Storage, Queue Storage, Event Grid, Cosmos DB, Service Bus. Hosting plans: Consumption (pay per execution, auto-scale to zero), Premium (pre-warmed instances, VNet integration, unlimited execution), Dedicated (on App Service plan). Durable Functions for stateful workflows (function chaining, fan-out/fan-in, human interaction). Supports C#, JavaScript, Python, Java, PowerShell, TypeScript. Managed dependencies with PowerShell.
.azure.Compute.Azure Container Apps & AKS.exp

Azure Container Apps (ACA): serverless containers, auto-scaling (including scale to zero), HTTP ingress, revisions, Dapr integration, KEDA scaling. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS): managed Kubernetes, automated upgrades, node pools, Azure AD integration, Azure Policy for Gatekeeper, advanced networking (Calico/Cilium). Azure Container Instances (ACI): simple single-pod containers, fast startup, no orchestration. Azure Container Registry (ACR): private Docker registry, geo-replication, task automation.
.azure.Compute.Azure Batch & HPC.exp

Azure Batch runs large-scale parallel and HPC workloads. Creates and manages a pool of VMs, installs applications, schedules tasks. Auto-scale pool size based on queue depth. Low-priority VMs for up to 80% cost savings (can be preempted). Integration with Azure Storage for input/output. Azure CycleCloud for HPC cluster management. Useful for rendering, financial modeling, genomics, and Monte Carlo simulations.
.azure.Storage.Azure Blob Storage.exp

Azure Blob Storage is object storage for unstructured data. Access tiers: Hot (frequent, lowest access cost), Cool (infrequent, 30-day min), Cold (rare, 90-day min), Archive (offline, 180-day min, hours to retrieve). Storage types: Block blobs (general objects, up to 4.7TB), Append blobs (logs), Page blobs (VHDs, up to 8TB). Lifecycle management auto-tiers data. Immutable storage (WORM) for compliance. Soft delete protects against accidental deletion. Azure Files is managed SMB/NFS file shares. Static websites can be hosted directly from blob storage.
.azure.Storage.Azure Disk Storage.exp

Azure Managed Disks are block storage for VMs. Types: Ultra Disk (sub-ms latency, provisioned IOPS), Premium SSD v2 (high performance, cost-optimized), Premium SSD (production workloads), Standard SSD (dev/test), Standard HDD (backup, non-critical). Disk roles: OS disk (up to 4TB), data disks (up to 32TB per disk). Encryption at rest: SSE (platform-managed) or customer-managed keys (Azure Key Vault). Azure Disk Encryption via BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux). Shared disks (Windows Server Failover Cluster, Linux Pacemaker). Incremental snapshots for backup.
.azure.Storage.Azure Files & NetApp Files.exp

Azure Files provides fully managed SMB and NFS file shares. Accessible from Windows, Linux, macOS via standard file protocols. SMB Multichannel for performance. Azure File Sync caches shares on Windows Servers (hybrid). Identity-based auth (Entra ID DS or AD DS). Azure NetApp Files (ANF): enterprise-grade, high-performance NFS/SMB, on bare metal, sub-ms latency, up to 100GB/s throughput. Multiple service levels: Standard, Premium, Ultra. Cross-region replication for DR.
.azure.Storage.Azure CDN & Front Door.exp

Azure CDN is a global CDN with point-of-presence (POP) locations. Profiles: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (rules engine), Verizon (advanced HTTP), Akamai (real-time stats). Azure Front Door (AFD) is a modern cloud CDN with: global HTTP load balancing, TLS termination, web application firewall (WAF), URL rewrite/redirect, path-based routing, latency-based routing, caching acceleration. Front Door operates at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). WAF policies protect against SQL injection, XSS, bots, DDoS. Private link support for origin access.
.azure.Databases.Azure SQL Database.exp

Azure SQL Database is fully managed SQL Server (PaaS). Service tiers: General Purpose (serverless or provisioned, 5-99.99% HA), Business Critical (always-on, 99.995% HA), Hyperscale (up to 100TB, fast scaling). Elastic Pools share resources among multiple databases (cost-effective for many DBs with spiky usage). Geo-replication for DR (readable secondaries in other regions). Auto-failover groups for transparent failover. Azure SQL Managed Instance (SQL MI) is near-100% SQL Server compatible, with full network isolation. Advanced data security: vulnerability assessment, data discovery, threat detection.
.azure.Databases.Azure Database for MySQL & PostgreSQL.exp

Flexible Server (recommended) vs Single Server (legacy). Flexible Server features: zone-redundant HA, stop/start, burstable SKUs, private networking (VNet), up to 16TB storage, 35-day backup retention. Read replicas (up to 10). Azure Database for PostgreSQL: supports PostgreSQL 16+, pg_cron, pg_hint_plan, PostGIS, and other extensions. Built-in connection pooling with PgBouncer. Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL (formerly Hyperscale, Citus) distributes data across shards for multi-tenant apps. Azure Database Migration Service simplifies migration from on-prem.
.azure.Databases.Azure Cosmos DB.exp

Cosmos DB is globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database. APIs: NoSQL (native document), MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Cassandra, Gremlin (graph), Table (key-value). Single-digit ms latency at any scale. Multi-region writes (active-active) for 99.999% availability. Automatic and instant scaling (RU/s — Request Units per second). Analytical store for HTAP (hybrid transactional/analytical processing). Change Feed triggers Azure Functions. Point-in-time backup (continuous backup mode). Dedicated gateway for query routing. SLA-backed 99.999% read availability globally.
.azure.Databases.Azure Cache for Redis.exp

Azure Cache for Redis is managed Redis. Tiers: Basic (single node, dev/test, no SLA), Standard (replicated, 99.9% SLA), Premium (persistence, clustering, VNet, 99.95% SLA), Enterprise (Redis Enterprise, active geo-replication, modules: RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries, RedisBloom), Enterprise Flash (tiered storage, lower cost). Redis Cluster splits data across shards. Persistence: RDB (snapshots) or AOF (write-ahead log). Data eviction policies (LRU, TTL, LFU, random). Geo-replication for DR. Private endpoint for secure access.
.azure.Networking.Azure Virtual Network.exp

Azure VNet is your isolated network in Azure. Address space defined by CIDR. Subnets segment the VNet; each subnet can have a Network Security Group (NSG) with allow/deny rules. Azure Bastion provides RDP/SSH without public IPs. Service Endpoints connect PaaS services privately via Microsoft backbone. Private Link exposes services privately from your VNet (like your own service behind a private IP). VNet Peering connects VNets within same region (low latency). Global VNet Peering connects across regions. VPN Gateway connects on-premises via IPsec. ExpressRoute is dedicated private connection to Azure.
.azure.Networking.Azure Load Balancer & Traffic Manager.exp

Azure Load Balancer (L4): distributes TCP/UDP traffic across VMs. SKUs: Basic (no HA, no SLA) and Standard (99.99% SLA, availability zones, HA ports, outbound rules). Inbound NAT rules for direct VM access. Backend pools: VMs, VMSS, IP addresses. Health probes check endpoint health. Azure Application Gateway (L7): HTTP/HTTPS load balancer with WAF, URL-based routing, SSL termination, session affinity, rewrite rules. Traffic Manager: DNS-based traffic routing (performance, geographic, priority, weighted, multi-value). Azure DNS hosts domains.
.azure.Networking.Azure DNS & Private DNS.exp

Azure DNS hosts domains and provides name resolution. Authoritative DNS — no need to buy a separate DNS provider. Alias records map to Azure resources (free, zone apex support). Private DNS zones resolve names within VNets without public DNS. Auto-registration of VMs in Private DNS. Conditional forwarding for hybrid networks. Azure DDoS Protection (Basic: free, automatic; Standard: $3k/mo, advanced mitigation, analytics, DRT). Network Watcher monitors and diagnoses network issues (topology, IP flow verify, next hop, packet capture, VPN troubleshoot, connection monitor).
.azure.Networking.Azure Security Center & Defender.exp

Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Azure Security Center + Defender for Cloud) provides unified security management. Defender plans: Defender for Servers, Databases, Storage, Containers, Key Vault, App Service, SQL, DNS, Resource Manager. Key Vault stores secrets, keys, and certificates with HSM option. Access policies vs RBAC. Soft delete and purge protection. Azure Policy for compliance (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001). Sentinel is cloud-native SIEM (Microsoft's Splunk alternative). Secure Score measures security posture. Just-in-Time (JIT) VM access for temporary admin.
.azure.DevOps & Management.ARM & Bicep.exp

ARM templates (JSON) and Bicep (DSL, compiles to ARM) are Azure's IaC. Bicep is simpler: concise syntax, module support, intellisense, idempotent deployments. Resources reference each other via symbolic names. Modules decompose infrastructure into reusable files. Parameters, variables, outputs. Conditions and loops for conditional/count-based resources. Deployment scopes: resource group, subscription, management group. What-If shows changes before applying. Deployment stacks manage groups of resources as a single unit.
.azure.DevOps & Management.Azure DevOps Pipelines.exp

Azure DevOps provides CI/CD with Pipelines (build/test/deploy), Repos (Git), Boards (work tracking), Test Plans, Artifacts (package feeds). YAML pipelines define stages (sequential), jobs (parallel per stage), steps (tasks). Multi-stage: Build → Test → Deploy to staging → Approve → Deploy to production. Environments track deployments with approvals and checks. Service connections to Azure, GitHub, Docker, etc. Self-hosted agents run in your network. Variable groups and library for secrets. Integration with GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab.
.azure.DevOps & Management.Azure Monitor.exp

Azure Monitor collects and analyzes telemetry from Azure resources. Log Analytics workspaces store logs and metrics. Kusto Query Language (KQL) queries logs (like SQL for logs). Application Insights monitors live web apps (request rates, response times, failure rates, dependency tracking, distributed tracing, user behavior analytics). Smart detection highlights anomalies. Metrics Explorer visualizes numeric data. Alerts: metric, log, activity log, smart groups. Action groups send email, SMS, webhook, ITSM. Workbooks are interactive reports (parameterized, multi-visualization). Managed Grafana for dashboards.
.azure.DevOps & Management.Azure Automation & Logic Apps.exp

Azure Automation automates repetitive tasks: VM start/stop, patch management, configuration management. Runbooks (PowerShell, Python) execute on schedule or via webhook. Update Management assesses and installs OS updates. Change Tracking detects configuration changes. Desired State Configuration (DSC) enforces VM config state. Logic Apps are serverless workflows (visual designer, 400+ connectors). Triggers: HTTP, schedule, Azure services. Actions: condition, switch, parallel branches, loops. Enterprise integration: AS2, EDIFACT, X12, RosettaNet.
.azure.Advanced Azure.Azure DevOps.exp

Azure DevOps provides CI/CD with Pipelines (build/test/deploy), Repos (Git), Boards (work tracking), Test Plans, Artifacts (package feeds). YAML pipelines define stages (sequential), jobs (parallel per stage), steps (tasks). Multi-stage: Build to Test to Deploy with manual approval gates. Environments track deployments with approvals and checks. Service connections to Azure, GitHub, Docker. Self-hosted agents run in your network for custom dependencies. Variable groups and library for secrets. Common mistake: hardcoding secrets in pipelines — use Azure Key Vault integration or variable group secrets.
.azure.Advanced Azure.Azure Key Vault.exp

Key Vault stores secrets, encryption keys, and certificates. Soft delete (enabled by default) retains deleted items for retention period (90 days default). Purge protection prevents permanent deletion. Managed Identities (system-assigned or user-assigned) let Azure resources (VMs, App Services, Functions) authenticate to Key Vault without credentials. RBAC for Key Vault uses Azure RBAC (data plane) — preferred over access policies for modern setups. Key Vault Firewall restricts access by IP and VNet. Key rotation can be automated with Event Grid + Functions. Common mistake: storing secrets in code or config files instead of Key Vault. Enable diagnostics logs to audit secret access.
.azure.Advanced Azure.Azure Logic Apps.exp

Logic Apps are serverless workflows with a visual designer and 400+ connectors. Triggers: HTTP request, schedule (recurrence), Azure services (Blob created, Event Grid), SaaS (Salesforce, Slack). Actions: condition, switch, parallel branches, loops (forEach, until), compose/parse JSON. Managed connectors: Office 365, SharePoint, Dynamics 365, Service Bus, SQL Server. Integration Account for enterprise B2B (AS2, EDIFACT, X12, RosettaNet). Built-in connectors run natively for higher performance. Common mistake: not handling transient failures — configure retry policies on actions. Consumption plan (pay per action) vs Standard plan (dedicated, better performance, VNet integration).
.azure.Advanced Azure.Azure Event Grid.exp

Event Grid is a fully managed event routing service. Events are JSON payloads describing what happened. Topics: system topics (Azure service events like Blob Created, VM Deleted) and custom topics (your own events). Subscriptions: push to Event Handlers (Functions, Webhooks, Service Bus, Queue Storage, Hybrid Connections, Logic Apps). Event filtering by event type, subject prefix/suffix, or advanced filters (numeric ranges, boolean, string contains). Retry policy: exponential backoff (up to 30 days). Dead-letter destination for failed events. Common mistake: forgetting to validate webhook endpoints (Event Grid requires endpoint validation handshake). Up to 10M events/sec per region.
.azure.Advanced Azure.API Management.exp

API Management (APIM) publishes APIs to external and internal consumers. Products group APIs with access rules and rate limits. Subscriptions: product access keys for developers. Policies: XML-based transformation, validation, rate limiting, CORS, caching, IP filtering, JWT validation. Policy scopes: global, product, API, operation. Versioning: URL-based or header-based version schemes. Multiple deployment regions for low latency. Self-hosted gateway for on-prem/hybrid. Developer portal for API documentation and testing. Common mistake: exposing backend implementation details — use policies to transform requests/responses. Enable diagnostic logging for monitoring API usage and errors.
.backend.Internet & Fundamentals.How the Internet Works.exp

The internet is a global network of interconnected computers that communicate using standardized protocols. Data is broken into packets, routed through multiple nodes, and reassembled at the destination. Key concepts include IP addresses, DNS, TCP/IP, and the client-server model.
.backend.Internet & Fundamentals.What is HTTP.exp

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of data communication on the web. It's a request-response protocol where clients send requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to servers, which return status codes (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error) and response bodies.
.backend.Internet & Fundamentals.DNS & How It Works.exp

DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into machine-readable IP addresses (142.250.190.46). It's a hierarchical system with root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative nameservers. DNS resolution involves recursive queries that cache results for performance.
.backend.Internet & Fundamentals.What is Hosting.exp

Web hosting is a service that stores your website files on a server and makes them accessible via the internet. Types include shared hosting (multiple sites on one server), VPS (virtual private server), dedicated hosting (physical server for one client), and cloud hosting (scalable resources across multiple servers).
.backend.Internet & Fundamentals.Browsers & How They Work.exp

Browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) are user agents that fetch, render, and display web content. The browser engine parses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, constructs the DOM and CSSOM trees, performs layout calculations, and paints pixels to screen. Key components include the rendering engine, JavaScript engine (V8, SpiderMonkey), and networking stack.
.backend.Internet & Fundamentals.What is a Domain Name.exp

A domain name is a unique, human-readable address that identifies a website on the internet. Domain structure includes TLD (top-level domain like .com, .org), second-level domain (the name you choose), and subdomains (like www or blog). Domains are registered through registrars and must be renewed periodically.
.backend.Version Control Systems.Git Basics.exp

Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code during development. It allows multiple developers to work simultaneously, maintains a complete history of changes, and enables branching/merging. Key concepts: repositories, commits, branches, staging area, and remote tracking.
.backend.Version Control Systems.GitHub.exp

GitHub is a cloud-based platform for hosting Git repositories. It provides collaboration features like pull requests, code reviews, issue tracking, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, GitHub Pages for static hosting, and project management tools. It's the largest host of source code worldwide, owned by Microsoft.
.backend.Version Control Systems.GitLab.exp

GitLab is a DevOps platform that provides Git repository management, CI/CD pipelines, container registry, and project planning tools. It offers both cloud-hosted (GitLab.com) and self-managed (GitLab CE/EE) options. Key differentiators: built-in CI/CD with .gitlab-ci.yml, auto DevOps, and integrated monitoring.
.backend.Version Control Systems.Repo Hosting Services.exp

Beyond GitHub and GitLab, other repository hosting services include Bitbucket (Atlassian, integrates with Jira), SourceForge (one of the oldest), and self-hosted options like Gitea and Gogs. Each offers varying features for code review, access control, and integrations with CI/CD and project management tools.
.backend.Relational Databases.PostgreSQL.exp

PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source object-relational database known for reliability, feature robustness, and performance. It supports advanced data types, full-text search, JSON/JSONB, indexing (B-tree, Hash, GiST, GIN), transactions with ACID compliance, and extensibility through custom functions and extensions like PostGIS.
.backend.Relational Databases.MySQL.exp

MySQL is a widely-used open-source relational database management system, popular for web applications (especially with LAMP/LEMP stacks). It offers InnoDB (transactional, foreign keys) and MyISAM (full-text search) storage engines, replication support, and strong performance for read-heavy workloads.
.backend.Relational Databases.SQL & Querying.exp

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing relational databases. Core operations include SELECT (retrieve), INSERT (add), UPDATE (modify), DELETE (remove). Advanced features include JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL), subqueries, aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG), GROUP BY, HAVING, and window functions.
.backend.Relational Databases.Normalization.exp

Database normalization is the process of organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. Normal forms include 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependencies), 3NF (no transitive dependencies), and BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key). Denormalization is sometimes used for read performance optimization.
.backend.Relational Databases.ACID Transactions.exp

ACID is a set of properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably. Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data persists). Isolation levels range from Read Uncommitted (dirty reads) to Serializable (full isolation).
.backend.Relational Databases.Database Indexes.exp

Indexes are data structures (B-tree, Hash, GiST) that speed up data retrieval at the cost of slower writes and increased storage. A primary key automatically gets a unique index. Composite indexes (multiple columns) must follow leftmost prefix rule. Use EXPLAIN to analyze query plans and find missing indexes.
.backend.Relational Databases.Sharding & Scaling.exp

Database scaling strategies include vertical scaling (more powerful hardware) and horizontal scaling (distributing data across multiple servers). Sharding partitions data across databases based on a shard key (e.g., user_id hash). Other approaches include read replicas for read-heavy workloads, and connection pooling for managing many concurrent connections.
.backend.Relational Databases.Database Design & Modeling.exp

Database design involves creating an efficient schema that represents the problem domain. Start with an Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD), identify entities, attributes, and relationships (1:1, 1:M, M:N). Consider query patterns, access paths, and use cases. Tools like draw.io, dbdiagram.io, and MySQL Workbench help visualize schemas.
.backend.NoSQL Databases.MongoDB.exp

MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like BSON documents. It uses a sharded cluster architecture for horizontal scaling, replica sets for high availability, and the aggregation pipeline for data processing. Best suited for flexible schemas, rapid iteration, and hierarchical data.
.backend.NoSQL Databases.Redis.exp

Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, and message broker. It supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, and streams. Key features: sub-millisecond latency, pub/sub messaging, Lua scripting, persistence (RDB/AOF), and built-in replication. Ideal for caching, session storage, and real-time analytics.
.backend.NoSQL Databases.Cassandra.exp

Apache Cassandra is a distributed NoSQL database designed for high availability and linear scalability with no single point of failure. It uses a peer-to-peer architecture, tunable consistency levels, and the Cassandra Query Language (CQL). Best for write-heavy workloads, time-series data, and applications requiring multi-region deployment.
.backend.NoSQL Databases.Elasticsearch.exp

Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It provides near-real-time full-text search, structured search, aggregations, and analytics. Data is stored as JSON documents in indexes, which are sharded across nodes. Commonly used for log analysis (ELK stack), application search, and observability.
.backend.APIs & Web Services.REST APIs.exp

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to perform CRUD operations on resources identified by URLs. REST APIs should be stateless, use proper HTTP status codes, and support pagination, filtering, and versioning.
.backend.APIs & Web Services.GraphQL.exp

GraphQL is a query language for APIs developed by Meta. Clients request exactly the data they need, reducing over-fetching and under-fetching. A single endpoint (/graphql) handles all operations. Type system defines the schema, resolvers fetch data from various sources. Supports queries, mutations, and subscriptions for real-time data.
.backend.APIs & Web Services.gRPC.exp

gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework by Google that uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport. It supports bidirectional streaming, flow control, and multiplexing. Service definitions are written in .proto files, generating client and server code in multiple languages. Ideal for microservices communication.
.backend.APIs & Web Services.WebSockets.exp

WebSockets provide full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection, enabling real-time data exchange. Unlike HTTP request-response, the server can push data to clients. Used for chat apps, live notifications, collaborative editing, and gaming. Libraries like Socket.IO add fallback transports and room management.
.backend.APIs & Web Services.OpenAPI / Swagger.exp

OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a standard for describing REST APIs using a YAML or JSON specification. It defines endpoints, request/response schemas, authentication, and error codes. Tools like Swagger UI generate interactive documentation, and code generators create client SDKs and server stubs automatically.
.backend.Authentication & Authorization.JWT (JSON Web Tokens).exp

JWT is a compact, URL-safe token format for transmitting claims between parties. It consists of three parts: header (algorithm, type), payload (claims like user_id, role, exp), and signature (verified with a secret or key pair). JWTs are stateless — the server doesn't need to store session data, but they can't be revoked without a blocklist.
.backend.Authentication & Authorization.OAuth 2.0.exp

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that allows third-party apps to access user data without sharing passwords. It involves authorization server, resource server, and client. Grant types include Authorization Code (most common), Client Credentials (machine-to-machine), Implicit (legacy), and Refresh Token. Used by Google, GitHub, and Facebook login systems.
.backend.Authentication & Authorization.Basic Authentication.exp

Basic Authentication is the simplest HTTP authentication method. The client sends the username and password encoded in Base64 in the Authorization header. It's insecure over plain HTTP (easily decoded) and should only be used over HTTPS. Typically paired with session tokens or API keys for modern applications.
.backend.Authentication & Authorization.Session & Cookie Auth.exp

Session-based authentication uses server-side sessions identified by a cookie. When a user logs in, the server creates a session, stores it (in memory, Redis, or database), and sends the session ID as a cookie. The browser sends the cookie with each request. Provides easy revocation (delete the session) but requires server-side storage.
.backend.Authentication & Authorization.API Security Best Practices.exp

API security involves multiple layers: rate limiting (prevent abuse), input validation (sanitize all inputs), HTTPS everywhere, proper authentication/authorization (least privilege principle), CORS configuration, request size limits, SQL injection prevention (parameterized queries), XSS protection, CSRF tokens, and security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options).
.backend.Caching.Caching Strategies.exp

Caching stores frequently accessed data in a fast storage layer to reduce latency and database load. Common strategies include: Cache-Aside (application checks cache first), Read-Through (cache layer fetches from DB on miss), Write-Through (write to cache AND DB simultaneously), Write-Behind (async write to DB), and Cache Eviction policies (LRU, TTL, FIFO).
.backend.Caching.Redis as Cache.exp

Redis is the most popular caching solution due to its in-memory performance and rich data structures. Common caching patterns include: session storage, database query result caching, page caching (full HTML), rate limiting counters, leaderboards, and distributed locks. Redis Cluster provides automatic sharding for large-scale deployments.
.backend.Caching.Content Delivery Networks.exp

A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a distributed network of servers that delivers cached static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) from locations geographically closer to users. Leading providers include Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, and Akamai. CDNs reduce latency, offload origin servers, and provide DDoS protection. Dynamic content can also be accelerated through edge computing.
.backend.Caching.HTTP Caching.exp

HTTP caching allows browsers and proxies to store responses and reuse them. Cache-Control directives (max-age, no-cache, no-store, public, private) and ETags/Last-Modified headers control caching behavior. Conditional requests with If-None-Match (ETag) or If-Modified-Since allow servers to return 304 Not Modified instead of full responses, saving bandwidth.
.backend.Web Servers.Nginx.exp

Nginx is a high-performance web server, reverse proxy, load balancer, and HTTP cache. It uses an event-driven, asynchronous architecture that handles thousands of concurrent connections with low memory usage. Common use cases: serving static files, reverse proxying to application servers, SSL termination, rate limiting, and as a gateway for microservices.
.backend.Web Servers.Apache.exp

Apache HTTP Server is one of the oldest and most widely-used web servers. It uses a process-based (prefork) or threaded (worker/event) MPM architecture. Configuration is done through .htaccess files (per-directory) and httpd.conf. Supports modules for rewrites (mod_rewrite), SSL (mod_ssl), authentication, caching, and proxying.
.backend.Web Servers.Reverse Proxy.exp

A reverse proxy sits between clients and backend servers, forwarding requests and returning responses. Benefits include: load balancing across multiple servers, SSL termination (offloading encryption), caching static content, compression, rate limiting, and hiding backend server topology. Both Nginx and HAProxy are common reverse proxy solutions.
.backend.Testing.Unit Testing.exp

Unit testing validates individual components (functions, methods, classes) in isolation. Tests should be fast, deterministic, and independent. Follow the AAA pattern: Arrange (set up), Act (execute), Assert (verify). Mock external dependencies. Aim for high coverage on critical business logic. Use test runners like Jest, pytest, JUnit, or Go test.
.backend.Testing.Integration Testing.exp

Integration testing verifies that different components work together correctly — database queries, API endpoints, file I/O, and third-party service interactions. Unlike unit tests, integration tests use real (or containerized) dependencies. Test the boundary between your code and external systems. Use test databases and clean up data between tests.
.backend.Testing.API / E2E Testing.exp

End-to-end testing validates the entire system from the user's perspective. For backend APIs, this means sending real HTTP requests and verifying responses, status codes, headers, and side effects. Tools like Supertest (Node.js), pytest + requests (Python), REST Assured (Java), and Postman/Newman automate API testing.
.backend.Containers & Orchestration.Docker.exp

Docker packages applications and dependencies into lightweight, portable containers that run consistently across environments. Images are built from Dockerfiles using layered filesystems. Key concepts: Dockerfile (build instructions), images (read-only templates), containers (running instances), volumes (persistent data), networks (container communication), and Docker Compose (multi-container apps).
.backend.Containers & Orchestration.Docker Compose.exp

Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file. Each service specifies its image, ports, volumes, environment variables, and dependencies. Compose handles network creation, service discovery, and startup ordering. Essential for local development environments with multiple services (app + database + cache + queue).
.backend.Containers & Orchestration.Kubernetes Basics.exp

Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Key concepts: Pods (smallest deployable unit), Deployments (declarative updates), Services (networking abstraction), ConfigMaps/Secrets (configuration), and Ingress (external access). Kubectl is the command-line tool.
.backend.Message Brokers & Streaming.RabbitMQ.exp

RabbitMQ is a message broker implementing AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol). Producers send messages to exchanges, which route them to queues based on bindings and routing keys. Consumers process messages from queues. Supports multiple exchange types: direct, topic, fanout, and headers. Offers message durability, acknowledgments, and dead-letter queues for reliability.
.backend.Message Brokers & Streaming.Apache Kafka.exp

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant data pipelines. Topics are partitioned and replicated across brokers. Producers write events, consumers read from offsets. Unlike RabbitMQ, Kafka persists all messages for a configurable retention period. Used for event sourcing, log aggregation, stream processing, and data integration at scale.
.backend.Message Brokers & Streaming.Message Queue Patterns.exp

Common messaging patterns include: Work Queues (competing consumers distribute tasks), Pub/Sub (one-to-many broadcast), RPC (request-response over queue), Event Sourcing (storing events as authoritative state), CQRS (separate read/write models), Saga Pattern (distributed transactions via compensating actions), and Dead Letter Queues (failed message handling).
.backend.Monitoring & Observability.Logging.exp

Logging records application events for debugging, auditing, and monitoring. Structured logging (JSON format) enables machine parsing and search. Log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) control verbosity. Centralized logging with tools like ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Loki + Grafana aggregates logs from multiple services. Avoid logging sensitive data.
.backend.Monitoring & Observability.Metrics & Monitoring.exp

Metrics are numerical measurements of system health and performance collected over time. Key categories: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services, USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources. Common metrics: request latency (p50, p95, p99), error rates, throughput, CPU/memory usage, and database query times. Prometheus collects metrics; Grafana visualizes them.
.backend.Monitoring & Observability.Distributed Tracing.exp

Distributed tracing tracks requests as they flow through multiple services in a microservices architecture. Each request gets a trace ID, and each span represents a unit of work. Tools like Jaeger, Zipkin, and OpenTelemetry provide end-to-end visibility. Helpful for identifying latency bottlenecks, error propagation, and service dependencies.
.backend.Monitoring & Observability.Application Performance Monitoring.exp

APM tools provide comprehensive monitoring of application performance, including transaction traces, dependency maps, error tracking, and real-user monitoring. Popular solutions include Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, and open-source alternatives like SigNoz and Grafana Faro. APM helps identify slow queries, memory leaks, N+1 problems, and external service degradation.
.backend.CI/CD & DevOps.Continuous Integration.exp

CI automatically builds and tests every code change to detect integration issues early. Developers merge changes frequently (multiple times daily) into a shared branch. CI servers run automated tests, linting, type checking, and security scans. Failures are reported immediately. Tools include GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, and Travis CI.
.backend.CI/CD & DevOps.Continuous Deployment.exp

CD automatically deploys validated code changes to production (or staging) environments. The deployment pipeline includes building artifacts, running integration tests, deploying to staging, running smoke tests, and promoting to production with strategies like blue-green (two identical environments) or canary (gradual rollout). Rollbacks should be fast and reliable.
.backend.CI/CD & DevOps.Infrastructure as Code.exp

IaC manages infrastructure (servers, networks, databases) through machine-readable definition files, enabling version control, reproducibility, and automation. Tools include Terraform (multi-cloud provisioning), AWS CloudFormation, Pulumi (general-purpose languages), and Ansible (configuration management). IaC eliminates manual server configuration and drift between environments.
.backend.System Design & Architecture.Microservices.exp

Microservices architecture decomposes an application into small, independent services that communicate over a network. Each service owns its data (database-per-service), can be deployed independently, and is built around a business capability. Benefits include: independent scaling, technology diversity, and smaller codebases. Challenges include: distributed complexity, data consistency, and service discovery.
.backend.System Design & Architecture.Load Balancing.exp

Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to ensure reliability and performance. Types: DNS load balancing (round-robin), hardware load balancers (F5), software load balancers (HAProxy, Nginx), and cloud load balancers (AWS ALB/ELB, Google Cloud LB). Algorithms include round-robin, least connections, IP hash, and weighted distribution.
.backend.System Design & Architecture.Database Scaling.exp

Scaling databases involves read replicas (offload read queries to copies), connection pooling (manage DB connections efficiently), caching layers (Redis/Memcached), partitioning (vertical/horizontal), and sharding. Read replicas improve read throughput but introduce eventual consistency. Connection poolers like PgBouncer manage thousands of concurrent connections efficiently.
.backend.System Design & Architecture.Caching Architecture.exp

Multi-layer caching architecture: browser cache (private), CDN (edge cache), reverse proxy/load balancer (Nginx cache), application cache (in-memory), and database cache (buffer pool). Cache invalidation strategies include TTL-based (time to live), write-through (update cache and DB), write-behind (async), and event-driven invalidation (publish cache invalidation events).
.backend.AI in Backend Development.AI-Assisted Coding.exp

AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) use large language models to generate, refactor, and explain code. They integrate with IDEs and support context-aware completions, test generation, bug fixing, and code review. Best practices: provide clear context, review generated code, never blindly accept, and treat AI as a pair programmer, not a replacement.
.backend.AI in Backend Development.Building AI Features.exp

Backend developers integrate AI capabilities through API calls to LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) or self-hosted models (Llama, Mistral). Patterns include: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation — search documents + ask LLM), embeddings for semantic search, streaming responses for real-time chat, function calling for structured outputs, and AI agents for multi-step tasks.
.backend.AI in Backend Development.Prompt Engineering.exp

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing input prompts to get desired outputs from LLMs. Techniques include: few-shot prompting (providing examples), chain-of-thought (step-by-step reasoning), system prompts (setting behavior/role), structured output constraints (JSON mode), and temperature control (creativity vs precision). Key for building reliable AI-powered backend features.
.bootstrap.Getting Started.What is Bootstrap.exp

Bootstrap is the world's most popular front-end component library, providing a responsive grid system, pre-built UI components, and utility classes. It uses a mobile-first approach with 12-column grid, five responsive breakpoints (xs, sm, md, lg, xl), and Sass variables for customization. Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery dependency and uses vanilla JavaScript for interactive components.
.bootstrap.Getting Started.Grid System.exp

Bootstrap's grid uses flexbox with 12 columns across five breakpoints. Rows are wrappers for columns; columns specify width via col-{breakpoint}-{size}. Equal-width columns use col. Auto-layout with col-{breakpoint} adjusts per breakpoint. Nest rows inside columns. Offsets push columns right. Gutters control spacing via g-* classes.
.bootstrap.Getting Started.Breakpoints & Containers.exp

Bootstrap provides five breakpoints: xs (<576px), sm (≥576px), md (≥768px), lg (≥992px), xl (≥1200px), xxl (≥1400px). Containers center content horizontally: .container (max-width per breakpoint), .container-fluid (full width), .container-{breakpoint} (full width until breakpoint). Use d-* display utilities to show/hide elements per breakpoint.
.bootstrap.Layout.Columns & Gutters.exp

Columns use 12-unit system. Column classes: col-{breakpoint}-{size} or col-{size} without breakpoint. Use .row-cols-* to control number of columns per row on all breakpoints. Gutters: g-0 (no gap), g-1 through g-5 (increasing), gx-* (horizontal), gy-* (vertical). Column wrapping happens when more than 12 units are used in a row.
.bootstrap.Layout.Alignment & Ordering.exp

Flexbox alignment classes for rows and columns. Vertical: align-items-start/center/end, align-self-*. Horizontal: justify-content-start/center/end/around/between. Column ordering with order-{breakpoint}-{number}. First and last with order-first/order-last. Margin auto with me-auto/ms-auto centers in flex containers.
.bootstrap.Components.Buttons & Button Groups.exp

Bootstrap buttons use .btn with contextual classes: btn-primary, btn-secondary, btn-success, btn-danger, btn-warning, btn-info, btn-light, btn-dark, btn-link. Outline variants with btn-outline-*. Sizes: btn-lg, btn-sm. States: active, disabled. Button groups with .btn-group for horizontal grouping, .btn-group-vertical for vertical. Toolbars combine multiple groups.
.bootstrap.Components.Cards.exp

Cards are flexible content containers with optional header, body, footer. Build with .card, .card-body, .card-title, .card-text, .card-img-top. Card groups (.card-group) display as attached equal-width cards. Card decks (.card-deck deprecated — use row + cols instead). Horizontal cards with .row.g-0 > .col-md-4 + .col-md-8 inside card.
.bootstrap.Components.Navbar & Navigation.exp

Navbar is a responsive navigation header. Base: .navbar with .navbar-expand{-breakpoint}. Brand: .navbar-brand. Nav links: .navbar-nav with .nav-item and .nav-link. Toggler for mobile with data-bs-toggle=collapse. Supports dropdowns, forms, text, and color schemes (navbar-light/dark with bg-*). Sticky-top and fixed-top positions.
.bootstrap.Components.Modals & Alerts.exp

Modals are dialog boxes built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Structure: modal, modal-dialog, modal-content (header + body + footer). Trigger with data-bs-toggle=modal and data-bs-target. Sizes: modal-sm, modal-lg, modal-xl. Centered with modal-dialog-centered. Scrollable with modal-dialog-scrollable. Alerts: .alert with .alert-{color}. Dismissible with .alert-dismissible + data-bs-dismiss=alert.
.bootstrap.Components.List Group & Badges.exp

List groups display series of content. Base .list-group with .list-group-item. Active, disabled, links, buttons, flush (borderless), numbered variants. Badges: .badge with .bg-{color}, .rounded-pill for pill shape. Position badges with position-relative + position-absolute. Badges scale to parent font size.
.bootstrap.Components.Forms & Input Groups.exp

Form controls: .form-control (text, number, file, etc.), .form-select (dropdown), .form-check (checkboxes/radios), .form-range (sliders), .form-floating (floating labels). Input groups extend form controls with .input-group and .input-group-text. Validation with .is-valid/.is-invalid and .invalid-feedback/.valid-feedback. Layout with .row + .col-* and .form-label.
.bootstrap.Utilities.Spacing & Sizing.exp

Margin and padding use m{p}-{sides}-{size} notation. Sides: t (top), b (bottom), s (start/left), e (end/right), x (horizontal), y (vertical), blank (all). Sizes: 0 through 5 and auto. Responsive: {property}{sides}-{breakpoint}-{size}. Width: w-25/50/75/100, w-auto. Height: h-25/50/75/100, h-auto. Max-width: mw-100. Viewport: min-vw-100, min-vh-100.
.bootstrap.Utilities.Typography & Text.exp

Text alignment: text-start, text-center, text-end, text-{breakpoint}-{alignment}. Text transform: text-lowercase, text-uppercase, text-capitalize. Font weight: fw-bold, fw-semibold, fw-normal, fw-light. Font style: fst-italic. Text decoration: text-decoration-none, text-decoration-underline, text-decoration-line-through. Text truncation with text-truncate. Word break with text-break. Monospace with font-monospace.
.bootstrap.Utilities.Colors & Backgrounds.exp

Text colors: text-primary, text-secondary, text-success, text-danger, text-warning, text-info, text-light, text-dark, text-body, text-muted, text-white, text-black-50, text-white-50. Background colors: bg-primary, bg-secondary, bg-success, bg-danger, bg-warning, bg-info, bg-light, bg-dark, bg-body, bg-white, bg-transparent. Opacity: bg-opacity-10 through bg-opacity-75. Gradients: bg-gradient.
.bootstrap.Utilities.Display & Flex.exp

Display: d-{value} (none, inline, inline-block, block, grid, table, flex, inline-flex). Responsive: d-{breakpoint}-{value}. Flex utilities: flex-row/column, flex-wrap/nowrap, justify-content-*, align-items-*, align-self-*, flex-fill, flex-grow-*, flex-shrink-*. Gap: gap-0 through gap-5. Order: order-0 through order-5, order-first, order-last.
.bootstrap.Utilities.Borders & Shadows.exp

Borders: border, border-{side} (top/end/bottom/start), border-0, border-{side}-0. Border color: border-primary, border-secondary, etc. Border width: border-1 through border-5. Border radius: rounded, rounded-{size} (0/1/2/3/pill/circle), rounded-{side}-*. Shadows: shadow-none, shadow-sm, shadow, shadow-lg. Opacity: opacity-25/50/75/100. Overflow: overflow-auto/hidden/visible/scroll. Position: position-relative/absolute/fixed/sticky. Top/start/end/bottom: translate-middle.
.bootstrap.Content.Typography & Headings.exp

HTML headings h1-h6 with .h1-.h6 classes for non-heading elements. Display headings: display-1 through display-6 (larger, lighter). Lead paragraph: .lead. Inline text: <mark>, <small>, <s>, <u>, <strong>, <em>, <abbr>, <blockquote>, <code>, <kbd>, <pre>. Description list: <dl>, <dt>, <dd>.
.bootstrap.Content.Images & Figures.exp

Responsive images: .img-fluid (max-width:100% + height:auto). Thumbnail: .img-thumbnail. Image alignment: .float-start, .float-end, .mx-auto.d-block. Picture element support. Figures with <figure> + .figure, .figure-img, .figure-caption. Rounded corners: .rounded. Aspect ratios via ratio and ratio-{x}x{y} helpers for embedded content.
.bootstrap.Content.Tables.exp

Base .table. Variants: table-striped, table-hover, table-bordered, table-borderless, table-sm (compact). Contextual rows/headers: table-{active|primary|secondary|success|danger|warning|info|light|dark}. Responsive tables: wrap in .table-responsive (or .table-responsive-{breakpoint}). Table dark with .table-dark. Align top with align-middle/align-top.
.bootstrap.Forms.Form Controls & Inputs.exp

Form controls use .form-control on <input>, <textarea>, and <select>. Supported inputs: text, password, email, number, tel, url, search, date, time, datetime-local, month, week, color, file. Sizing with .form-control-lg, .form-control-sm. Readonly with readonly attribute. Disabled with disabled attribute. Plain text with .form-control-plaintext for displaying values as text.
.bootstrap.Forms.Select & Checks.exp

Custom select with .form-select. Sizing: form-select-lg, form-select-sm. Multiple select with multiple attribute. Checkboxes: .form-check-input wrapped in .form-check with .form-check-label. Radios same pattern. Inline with .form-check-inline. Switch type: .form-check-input type=checkbox role=switch. Disabled states supported on all.
.bootstrap.Forms.Validation.exp

Form validation uses .was-validated on <form> after submission or .needs-validation for custom validation. HTML5 validation constraints: required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, type, pattern. Visual feedback: .is-valid, .is-invalid, .valid-feedback, .invalid-feedback. Tooltip style: .valid-tooltip, .invalid-tooltip. Server-side validation by adding classes manually.
.bootstrap.Forms.Floating Labels.exp

Floating labels use .form-floating wrapper around form-control and label. Supports inputs and textareas. The label sits inside the input moving to a floating position on focus or when filled. Browser autofill is handled automatically. Works with selects and validation states. Ideal for streamlined forms.
.bootstrap.Customize.Sass Variables & Maps.exp

Bootstrap uses Sass variables and maps for customization. Key variable file: _variables.scss. Override before importing Bootstrap. Theme colors map: $theme-colors. Grid: $grid-breakpoints, $container-max-widths, $grid-columns. Spacing: $spacer with $spacers map. Utility API generates utility classes from Sass maps. Root variables via $prefix and CSS custom properties.
.bootstrap.Customize.CSS Custom Properties.exp

Bootstrap 5 sets many CSS custom properties on :root and components. Root: --bs-primary, --bs-body-color, --bs-border-radius, etc. Component-level: --bs-accordion-bg, --bs-modal-width. Override at runtime via CSS or JavaScript. Disable with $enable-css-variables: false. This enables dynamic theming without rebuilding Sass.
.bootstrap.Customize.Components & Theming.exp

Bootstrap offers multiple component Sass variants: accordion, alerts, badges, buttons, cards, carousel, dropdowns, forms, list group, modal, nav, navbar, offcanvas, pagination, popovers, progress, scrollspy, spinners, toasts, tooltips. Enable/disable components via $enable-* variables: $enable-button-pointers, $enable-caret, $enable-rounded, $enable-shadows, $enable-gradients, $enable-transitions, $enable-reduced-motion, $enable-smooth-scroll, $enable-grid-classes, $enable-container-classes, $enable-cssgrid, $enable-validation-icons.
.bootstrap.JavaScript.Modal & Offcanvas.exp

Modal via data-bs-toggle="modal" or JavaScript API: new bootstrap.Modal(element).show(). Methods: show, hide, toggle, dispose, handleUpdate. Events: show.bs.modal, shown.bs.modal, hide.bs.modal, hidden.bs.modal. Options: backdrop (true/static/false), keyboard, focus. Static backdrop prevents close on backdrop click. Offcanvas similar API: offcanvas-start/end/top/bottom.
.bootstrap.JavaScript.Tooltip & Popover.exp

Tooltips use Popper for positioning. Initialize with data-bs-toggle="tooltip" or JavaScript. Options: animation, container, delay, html, placement (top/bottom/left/right/auto), sanitize, selector, template, title, trigger (click/hover/focus/manual). Popovers extend tooltips with header + body content. Initialize: new bootstrap.Popover(element). Both need manual initialization for dynamically added elements.
.bootstrap.JavaScript.Collapse & Accordion.exp

Collapse toggles content visibility: data-bs-toggle="collapse", data-bs-target="#id". Accordion groups collapses with .accordion + .accordion-item structure. Accordion flush removes borders/background. Stay-open variant with data-bs-parent="#accordion" removed. Methods: show, hide, toggle. Events: show.bs.collapse, shown.bs.collapse, hide.bs.collapse, hidden.bs.collapse.
.bootstrap.JavaScript.Carousel & Toast.exp

Carousel cycles through images with previous/next controls and indicators. Base: .carousel.slide with .carousel-inner > .carousel-item. Options: interval, pause, wrap, keyboard, touch.
