Crossfade with .carousel-fade. Methods: cycle, pause, prev, next, dispose. Toasts: lightweight notification component with .toast. Auto-hide with data-bs-delay or options. Trigger manually via Bootstrap.Toast.
.bootstrap.JavaScript.ScrollSpy & Tabs.exp

ScrollSpy auto-activates nav links based on scroll position. Add data-bs-spy="scroll" to the scrollable element with data-bs-target="#navId". Works with nav, list-group, or simple links. Tab component toggles content panes: nav-tabs + tab-content with tab-pane. Active via show class. Fade with fade class. Methods: show, dispose. Events: show.bs.tab, shown.bs.tab.
.bootstrap.Helpers & Advanced.Sticky & Fixed Positioning.exp

Fixed top: .fixed-top (position:fixed + top:0). Fixed bottom: .fixed-bottom. Sticky top: .sticky-top (position:sticky + top:0). Sticky bottom: .sticky-bottom. Responsive sticky: .sticky-{breakpoint}-top. Z-index utilities: z-index utilities via z-* classes. Stacking context-aware. Sticky elements stay in flow until scroll threshold, unlike fixed elements removed from flow.
.bootstrap.Helpers & Advanced.Screen Readers & Accessibility.exp

Screen reader utilities: .visually-hidden (visually hide, still accessible), .visually-hidden-focusable (hide until focused). Focus ring with .focus-ring. Focus ring utilities: .focus-ring-{color}. Reduced motion: prefers-reduced-motion media query respected by Bootstrap. Color contrast ratios meet WCAG AA. ARIA attributes: role, aria-label, aria-hidden, aria-expanded, aria-controls.
.c.Getting Started.What is C.exp

C is a low-level, statically typed language developed by Dennis Ritchie in 1972. It provides direct memory access, minimal runtime, and is the foundation for most operating systems, embedded systems, and virtually every modern language.
.c.Getting Started.Hello World.exp
Every C program starts execution in `main()`. `#include <stdio.h>` brings in the standard I/O library. `printf()` prints formatted text. `return 0` signals success to the OS.
.c.Getting Started.C Syntax & Structure.exp

C programs consist of functions. `main()` is the entry point. Statements end with semicolons. Blocks are enclosed in braces. `#include` directives include header files. C is case-sensitive and whitespace-insensitive.
.c.Getting Started.Compilation Process.exp

C source code goes through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking. `gcc` (GNU C Compiler) is the standard compiler. Use `-o` to name the output, `-Wall` for warnings, `-g` for debug symbols.
.c.Getting Started.Data Types.exp

Basic types: `int`, `char`, `float`, `double`, `void`. Modifiers: `short`, `long`, `signed`, `unsigned`. `sizeof()` returns bytes. Type sizes vary by platform (int is usually 4 bytes, char is always 1).
.c.Getting Started.Comments.exp
C supports `//` single-line comments (C99+) and `/* */` multi-line comments. Comments are stripped by the preprocessor. Use comments to explain why, not what.
.c.Variables & Storage.Variables & Assignment.exp

Variables must be declared with a type before use. Naming rules: letters, digits, underscores; cannot start with digit. Convention uses snake_case. Uninitialized local variables contain garbage values.
.c.Variables & Storage.Constants & Literals.exp
Constants are fixed values that cannot be changed. Use `const` keyword or `#define` preprocessor. Integer, floating-point, character, and string literals. Suffixes: L (long), U (unsigned), F (float).
.c.Variables & Storage.Scope & Lifetime.exp
Scope determines where a variable is accessible. Block scope `{}`, file scope (global), function scope. Lifetime: automatic (stack) vs static (program duration). Variables shadow outer scopes.
.c.Variables & Storage.Storage Classes.exp
`auto` (default for locals), `register` (suggest CPU register), `static` (persists lifetime, limits scope), `extern` (declares variable defined elsewhere). `static` on globals limits to file.
.c.Variables & Storage.Type Qualifiers.exp
`const` makes variable read-only. `volatile` tells compiler value may change externally (hardware registers, signal handlers). `restrict` promises no other pointer aliases the same memory.
.c.Variables & Storage.Type Conversion.exp
Implicit conversion (type coercion) happens automatically: `int` -> `float` -> `double`. Explicit conversion (casting) uses `(type)` syntax. Promotion rules: values are promoted to the larger type.
.c.Variables & Storage.typedef.exp
`typedef` creates type aliases for cleaner code. Commonly used with structs, function pointers, and complex types. Doesn't create new types — just aliases.
.c.Operators.Arithmetic Operators.exp
Standard math: `+` addition, `-` subtraction, `*` multiplication, `/` division, `%` modulo (remainder). Integer division truncates toward zero. Mixing types causes implicit conversion.
.c.Operators.Relational & Logical Operators.exp
Relational: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Logical: `&&` (AND), `||` (OR), `!` (NOT). C treats 0 as false, non-zero as true. Short-circuit evaluation for && and ||.
.c.Operators.Bitwise Operators.exp
Manipulate individual bits: `&` AND, `|` OR, `^` XOR, `~` NOT, `<<` left shift, `>>` right shift. Used for flags, hardware control, and performance optimization.
.c.Operators.Assignment Operators.exp
Compound assignments: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`. More concise and can be more efficient than separate operation and assignment.
.c.Operators.sizeof, Ternary & Comma.exp
`sizeof` returns size in bytes (type or expression). Ternary `?:` is a compact if-else. Comma `,` evaluates both operands, returns the second. Useful in `for` loops.
.c.Operators.Operator Precedence.exp

Precedence determines evaluation order. Postfix > Unary > Multiplicative > Additive > Shift > Relational > Equality > Bitwise AND > XOR > OR > Logical AND > OR > Ternary > Assignment > Comma. Use parentheses to clarify.
.c.Control Flow.if / else if / else.exp
Conditional branching with `if`, `else if`, `else`. Conditions must be in parentheses. C treats 0 as false, non-zero as true. No boolean type in early C — use `<stdbool.h>` for `bool`.
.c.Control Flow.Switch Statement.exp

`switch` branches on integer/enum values. Each `case` must end with `break` to prevent fallthrough. `default` handles unmatched values. C23 allows `switch` on expression with multiple cases per label.
.c.Control Flow.Loops: for, while, do-while.exp
`for` when count is known (init; condition; increment). `while` when condition-based. `do-while` runs body at least once. All loops can be nested. Watch for infinite loops and off-by-one errors.
.c.Control Flow.break & continue.exp
`break` exits the innermost loop or switch immediately. `continue` skips rest of current iteration and goes to next. In nested loops, break only exits the innermost one.
.c.Control Flow.goto & Labels.exp
`goto` jumps to a labeled statement in the same function. Generally discouraged for structured flow, but useful for breaking out of deeply nested loops or centralized error cleanup.
.c.Control Flow.Infinite Loops & Pitfalls.exp
Common loop bugs: off-by-one (`<=` vs `<`), missing braces causing unintended body, using assignment `=` instead of comparison `==`, forgetting increment, and semicolon after `for` or `while`.
.c.Functions.Function Declaration & Definition.exp
Functions must be declared before use (prototype) or defined first. Return type, name, parameter list with types. `void` for no return value or no parameters. K&R style is obsolete.
.c.Functions.Pass by Value.exp
C passes arguments by value — functions receive copies. To modify variables in the caller, pass pointers. Arrays decay to pointers when passed. Structs are copied unless passed by pointer.
.c.Functions.Return Values.exp

Functions return a value matching their declared return type. No value needed for `void`. Returned value can be ignored by caller. Never return pointer to local variable — use `static` or dynamic allocation.
.c.Functions.Recursion.exp
A recursive function calls itself. Must have a base case to terminate. Stack memory is used for each call — deep recursion can cause stack overflow. Example: factorial, Fibonacci, tree traversal.
.c.Functions.Inline Functions.exp

`inline` suggests the compiler replace function calls with the body code to avoid call overhead (C99). Compiler may ignore. Static inline in headers is common. Modern compilers auto-inline better than programmers.
.c.Functions.Variadic Functions.exp
Functions with variable arguments use `<stdarg.h>`: `va_list`, `va_start()`, `va_arg()`, `va_end()`. At least one named parameter is required. No type safety — caller must provide correct types.
.c.Functions.main() Arguments.exp
`int main(int argc, char *argv[])` receives command-line arguments. `argc` is argument count (program name is argv[0]). `argv` is array of strings. `getopt()` for parsing flags.
.c.Pointers.Pointer Basics.exp

Pointers store memory addresses. `&` gets address of variable. `*` dereferences (accesses value at address). `NULL` is a safe pointer value. Always initialize pointers. Size is platform-dependent (4 or 8 bytes).
.c.Pointers.Pointer Arithmetic.exp

Incrementing a pointer moves to the next element of its type: `ptr + n` adds `n * sizeof(type)` bytes. Arrays and pointers are closely related. Subtraction gives the number of elements between two pointers.
.c.Pointers.Pointers & Arrays.exp

Array name decays to pointer to first element. `arr[i]` is equivalent to `*(arr + i)`. The `[]` operator works on pointers too. But `sizeof(arr)` differs from `sizeof(ptr)` — arrays remember their size at compile time.
.c.Pointers.Pointer to Pointer.exp
`int **pp` stores address of an `int*`. Used for dynamic 2D arrays, modifying pointer arguments in functions, and arrays of strings. Can be chained arbitrarily deep.
.c.Pointers.Void Pointers.exp

`void*` is a generic pointer that can hold any address. Must be cast to a specific type before dereferencing. Used in generic functions like `malloc()`, `qsort()`, `memcpy()`. No pointer arithmetic on void*.
.c.Pointers.Function Pointers.exp
Function pointers store addresses of functions. Used for callbacks, strategy patterns, and dynamic dispatch. Syntax: `returnType (*name)(params)`. `qsort()` takes a comparator function pointer.
.c.Pointers.Dynamic Memory Allocation.exp
`malloc()` allocates on heap, `free()` releases it. `calloc()` allocates and zero-initializes. `realloc()` resizes. Always check for NULL return. Free to avoid leaks. Include `<stdlib.h>`.
.c.Pointers.Memory Leaks & Debugging.exp

A memory leak occurs when allocated memory is never freed. Tools: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`), leak sanitizer. Common issues: forgetting to free, losing the pointer, double free, use-after-free.
.c.Arrays & Strings.One-Dimensional Arrays.exp
Contiguous memory blocks of the same type. Fixed size determined at compile time. Index from 0. No bounds checking — buffer overflows are dangerous and a common security vulnerability.
.c.Arrays & Strings.Multidimensional Arrays.exp
Arrays of arrays stored in row-major order. `int matrix[rows][cols]`. Access with `matrix[r][c]`. Can be passed to functions with all dimensions except first specified.
.c.Arrays & Strings.Array Initialization & Bounds.exp

Arrays can be initialized with `= {values}`. Designated initializers (C99): `int arr[5] = {[0]=1, [4]=5}`. C has no runtime bounds checking — accessing out of bounds causes undefined behavior: crashes or security holes.
.c.Arrays & Strings.Strings as char Arrays.exp
C strings are null-terminated char arrays (`\0` marks end). String literals are `char*` pointing to read-only memory. Always ensure buffer is large enough for the null terminator.
.c.Arrays & Strings.String Library.exp

`<string.h>` provides: `strlen()` (length), `strcpy()` (copy), `strncpy()` (bounded copy), `strcat()` (append), `strncat()` (bounded append), `strcmp()` (compare), `strchr()` (find char), `strstr()` (find substring). Always prefer bounded versions.
.c.Arrays & Strings.Array of Strings.exp
An array of strings is a 2D char array or array of char pointers. `char names[5][20]` — fixed size. `char *names[5]` — flexible, each string can differ in length. Both have different memory layouts.
.c.Arrays & Strings.Character Classification.exp

`<ctype.h>` provides: `isalpha()`, `isdigit()`, `isalnum()`, `isspace()`, `islower()`, `isupper()`, `tolower()`, `toupper()`. Functions work with `int` (EOF-safe). Very efficient — lookup-table based.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.Structs.exp
Structures group related data of different types. Define with `struct`. Access members with `.` (dot) operator. Use `->` with pointers to structs. Structs can be copied by assignment.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.Unions.exp

Unions store different types in the same memory location (size = largest member). Only one member can hold a value at a time. Useful for variant types, register access, and memory-efficient design. Type punning is common but can be undefined behavior.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.Bit Fields.exp

Bit fields pack multiple values into a single integer, specifying exact bits. Used in device drivers, network protocols, and embedded systems. Can't take address of a bit field. Order and alignment are implementation-defined.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.enum.exp

Enums define named integer constants (default: 0, 1, 2...). Can specify explicit values. Enums improve code readability and type safety (some compilers warn on switch missing cases). C23 allows `enum` with type specifier.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.Struct Padding & Alignment.exp

Compilers may add padding bytes between struct members for alignment. Reorder members from largest to smallest to minimize padding. `offsetof()` from `<stddef.h>` gets member offset. Packed structs with `__attribute__((packed))`.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.Flexible Array Members.exp

A struct can have an incomplete array as its last member (C99). Allows variable-length data without pointers. The struct is allocated with extra space for the array. Common in network protocols and variable-length records.
.c.Structures, Unions & Enums.Nested & Self-Referential Structs.exp

Structs can contain other structs as members. Self-referential structs (containing pointer to same type) are used for linked data structures: linked lists, trees, graphs. Forward declaration with `struct Name;`.
.c.File I/O.Opening & Closing Files.exp

`fopen()` opens a file: `r` read, `w` write (truncates), `a` append, `r+` read/write, `w+` read/write (truncates), `a+` read/append. `fclose()` closes. Always check return value for NULL. Binary mode: append `b` (e.g. `rb`, `wb`).
.c.File I/O.Reading & Writing Text.exp

Character: `fgetc()`, `fputc()`. Line: `fgets()` (safe, includes newline), `fputs()`. Block: `fread()`, `fwrite()`. `fgets()` reads at most n-1 chars and adds null terminator. `getline()` is POSIX, not standard C.
.c.File I/O.Formatted I/O.exp

`fprintf()` writes formatted output to a file. `fscanf()` reads formatted input from a file. Format specifiers: `%d` int, `%f` float, `%s` string, `%c` char, `%x` hex. `sscanf()` / `sprintf()` work with strings.
.c.File I/O.Binary I/O.exp

`fread()` and `fwrite()` read/write raw binary data. Parameters: pointer to data, size of each element, count, file pointer. Binary files are more compact and precise but not portable across endianness. Use `"rb"` / `"wb"` modes.
.c.File I/O.File Positioning.exp

`fseek(fp, offset, whence)` moves file position: `SEEK_SET` (beginning), `SEEK_CUR` (current), `SEEK_END` (end). `ftell()` returns current position. `rewind()` resets to beginning. `feof()` checks for end-of-file.
.c.File I/O.Error Handling.exp

File operations set `errno` on failure. `perror()` prints a descriptive error message to stderr. `strerror()` returns the error string. `ferror()` checks if a file stream has an error. Always check return values of I/O functions.
.c.Preprocessor.Macros (#define).exp
The preprocessor runs before compilation. `#define` creates macros (constants or function-like). Use parentheses to avoid precedence bugs. No type checking. Convention: UPPER_CASE names.
.c.Preprocessor.Conditional Compilation.exp
`#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#else`, `#elif`, `#endif` control which code gets compiled. Used for platform-specific code, debug builds, feature toggles. `defined()` operator works in `#if`.
.c.Preprocessor.Header Files & Guards.exp
Header files (`.h`) declare functions, macros, and types. Use include guards (`#ifndef`) to prevent double inclusion. `#pragma once` is a modern alternative (non-standard but widely supported).
.c.Preprocessor.#pragma & #error.exp

`#error` emits a compiler error with a custom message — stops compilation. `#pragma` provides compiler-specific instructions: `#pragma once` (header guard), `#pragma pack(push, 1)` (packing), `#pragma GCC optimize`. Non-standard.
.c.Preprocessor.Predefined Macros.exp

Standard predefined macros: `__FILE__` (current file), `__LINE__` (current line), `__DATE__` (compilation date), `__TIME__` (compilation time), `__STDC__` (1 if standard C), `__STDC_VERSION__` (C version: 199901L, 201112L, 202311L).
.c.Preprocessor.Stringification & Token Pasting.exp
`#` converts macro parameter to string literal. `##` concatenates two tokens into one. Useful for generating repetitive code patterns and creating type-generic macros.
.c.Preprocessor.Variadic Macros.exp
Macros with variable arguments using `__VA_ARGS__` (C99). Named variadic argument in C23 (`__VA_OPT__` for trailing comma handling). Useful for debug logging and generic printing.
.c.Standard Library.stdlib.h Utilities.exp

`atoi()` / `atol()` / `atof()` parse strings to numbers. `itoa()` is non-standard — use `sprintf()`. `rand()` / `srand()` for pseudo-random numbers. `qsort()` for sorting. `abs()` / `labs()` for absolute value. `div()` / `ldiv()` for quotient and remainder.
.c.Standard Library.math.h Functions.exp

Mathematical functions: `sqrt()`, `sin()`, `cos()`, `tan()`, `asin()`, `acos()`, `atan2()`, `pow()`, `exp()`, `log()`, `log10()`, `floor()`, `ceil()`, `fabs()`, `fmod()`. Link with `-lm`. Angles in radians.
.c.Standard Library.time.h Functions.exp

`time()` gets current time. `clock()` gets CPU time. `difftime()` calculates difference. `strftime()` formats time. `localtime()` / `gmtime()` convert to struct. `mktime()` converts back. `clock_gettime()` for nanosecond precision (POSIX).
.c.Standard Library.assert.h & setjmp.h.exp

`assert(expr)` aborts if expr is false (debug builds). Disable with `#define NDEBUG`. `setjmp()` / `longjmp()` provide non-local jumps (like try/catch). Save state with `jmp_buf`. Limited, use sparingly — complicates resource cleanup.
.c.Standard Library.signal.h Handling.exp

`signal()` sets a handler for OS signals: SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGTERM (termination), SIGSEGV (segfault), SIGFPE (divide by zero). Handler must be `void handler(int sig)`. Some signals (SIGKILL, SIGSTOP) cannot be caught.
.c.Standard Library.stddef.h & Limits.exp

`<stddef.h>`: `size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, `NULL`, `offsetof()`. `<limits.h>`: integer limits (INT_MIN, INT_MAX, LONG_MAX, CHAR_BIT). `<float.h>`: floating limits (FLT_MAX, DBL_EPSILON). `<stdint.h>`: fixed-width types (int32_t, uint64_t).
.c.Advanced Topics.Linked Lists.exp

A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node points to the next. Singly linked: `next` pointer. Doubly linked: `prev` and `next`. Operations: insert, delete, traverse, search. O(1) insert/delete given pointer, O(n) access by index.
.c.Advanced Topics.Debugging with GDB.exp

GDB is the GNU debugger. Compile with `-g` for debug symbols. Commands: `run`, `break`, `next`, `step`, `print`, `backtrace`, `watch`, `continue`. Set breakpoints on functions or lines. Inspect variables and memory.
.c.Advanced Topics.Memory Debugging (Valgrind).exp

Valgrind detects memory leaks, invalid accesses, and use-after-free. Run with `valgrind ./program`. Tools: `memcheck` (default), `callgrind` (profiling), `helgrind` (race conditions). Focus on errors = definitely lost bytes.
.c.Advanced Topics.Build Systems (Make).exp
Make automates compilation. Rules: `target: dependencies`, then tab-indented commands. Variables: `CC=gcc`, `CFLAGS=-Wall`. Automatic variables: `$@` (target), `$<` (first dep), `$^` (all deps).
.c.Advanced Topics.Multithreading (pthreads).exp

POSIX threads (`<pthreads.h>`) create concurrent execution. `pthread_create()`, `pthread_join()`, `pthread_mutex_lock/unlock()`, `pthread_cond_wait/signal()`. Data races cause undefined behavior. Always synchronize shared data.
.c.Advanced Topics.Network Programming (Sockets).exp

Berkeley sockets (`<sys/socket.h>`) for networking. Steps: `socket()`, `bind()`, `listen()`, `accept()` (server) or `connect()` (client). `send()` / `recv()` for data. Use `inet_pton()` for IP addresses. Compile with `-lsocket` on some systems.
.c.Advanced Topics.Atomics & _Generic (C11).exp

`<stdatomic.h>` (C11) provides portable atomic operations: `atomic_int`, `atomic_store()`, `atomic_load()`, `atomic_fetch_add()`, `atomic_compare_exchange_weak()`. `_Generic` (C11) enables type-generic macros like built-in overloads.
.c.C in Practice.Interactive I/O (getchar/putchar).exp

K&R-style character I/O with `getchar()` and `putchar()`. EOF is a macro (-1 on most systems). Ctrl+D (Unix) / Ctrl+Z (Windows) sends EOF. `getchar()` returns `int`, not `char`, to accommodate EOF. Classic book-copying program.
.c.C in Practice.Low-Level I/O (UNIX System Interface).exp

`<unistd.h>` provides `read()`, `write()`, `open()`, `close()`, `lseek()`. Lower-level than stdio — no buffering, direct file descriptors (ints). Used in systems programming, signal handlers, and performance-critical code. K&R Chapter 8 covers this.
.c.C in Practice.Storage Allocator (K&R Chapter 8).exp

K&R builds a `malloc()`-like allocator using a free list of headers. Each block has a header with size and pointer to next free block. `sbrk()` grows the program break. Real allocators are more sophisticated (thread caches, slab allocators, buddy system).
.c.C in Practice.Complex Declarations (Right-Left Rule).exp

Read C declarations spirally: start at identifier, go right, then left, then right again (spiral rule). `int *(*fp)(int)` is pointer-to-function taking int returning pointer-to-int. Practice with `signal()`: `void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int)`.
.c.C in Practice.Variable-Length Arrays (C99).exp

VLA syntax: `int arr[n]` where `n` is not a compile-time constant. Memory on stack (auto duration). `sizeof` on VLA computed at runtime. No VLA in file scope or structs. Support is optional in C11 (most compilers still provide it).
.c.C in Practice.Complex Numbers (C99).exp

`<complex.h>` provides `complex` type, `I` (imaginary unit), `creal()`, `cimag()`, `cabs()`, `carg()`, `conj()`, `csqrt()`, `cexp()`. Types: `float complex`, `double complex`, `long double complex`. Link with `-lm`.
.c.Defensive C.Defensive Programming.exp

From Learn C the Hard Way: always check return values, validate pointers before dereferencing, assert invariants in debug builds, and enable all compiler warnings. Use `const` for read-only parameters. Never trust user input or buffer sizes.
.c.Defensive C.Three Common Bugs.exp

Learn C the Hard Way drills these: 1) Off-by-one: loop runs one iteration too many/few. 2) Buffer overflow: writing past allocated space. 3) Use-after-free: accessing freed heap memory. Detect with `-fsanitize=address` and Valgrind.
.c.Defensive C.Safe String Handling.exp

C string functions are inherently unsafe. Prefer bounded versions: `strncpy()`, `strncat()`, `snprintf()` (always null-terminates). For POSIX: `strlcpy()` / `strlcat()`. Better yet, use a string struct with explicit length field.
.c.Defensive C.Pointer Pitfalls.exp

From Absolute Beginner's Guide: 1) Uninitialized pointers hold garbage — always init to NULL. 2) Dangling pointers reference freed memory — NULL after free. 3) Null dereference crashes. 4) Pointer arithmetic past bounds is UB. 5) Alignment violations on cast.
.c.Defensive C.Debugging Strategies.exp

Layer your approach: 1) Compiler warnings (`-Wall -Wextra`). 2) `assert()` to catch invariants. 3) `printf()` / `fprintf(stderr)` for tracing. 4) GDB for interactive debugging. 5) Valgrind for memory leaks. 6) AddressSanitizer for fast memory checking.
.c.Defensive C.Working with Multiple Files.exp

Split code across `.h` (declarations with include guards) and `.c` (definitions). `static` functions/variables are file-private. `extern` references names defined in other files. Compile all `.c` files and link them into one executable.
.cicd.CI/CD Fundamentals.What is CI/CD.exp

CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment. It is a method of frequently delivering apps to customers by introducing automation into the stages of app development. CI/CD bridges the gap between development and operations teams by automating build, test, and deployment processes.Continuous Integration ensures every code change is automatically built and tested, catching bugs early. Continuous Delivery extends CI by automatically deploying code to production-like environments for testing. Continuous Deployment takes it further — every change that passes all stages of the pipeline is automatically released to production.
.cicd.CI/CD Fundamentals.Pipeline Architecture.exp

A CI/CD pipeline is a series of automated steps that code goes through from commit to deployment. The typical stages are:
  • Source — code is pushed to version control (Git)
  • Build — code is compiled and dependencies are resolved
  • Test — automated tests (unit, integration, e2e) are run
  • Analyze — static analysis, linting, and security scanning
  • Package — artifacts (binaries, containers) are built and stored
  • Deploy — artifacts are deployed to staging or production
Each stage must pass before the next begins — this is called a gated pipeline. Modern pipelines run stages in parallel where possible for speed.
.cicd.CI/CD Fundamentals.Benefits of CI/CD.exp

Adopting CI/CD brings several key benefits:
  • Faster releases — automate manual steps to ship code multiple times a day
  • Reduced risk — catch bugs early with automated testing in every commit
  • Higher quality — consistent testing and code analysis standards
  • Developer productivity — less time spent on manual deployments and debugging
  • Auditability — every change is tracked, tested, and logged
  • Team confidence — automated validation means safer deployments
Companies practicing CI/CD deploy code 208x more frequently than those that don't (DORA State of DevOps report).
.cicd.Version Control & Git Integration.Git Hooks.exp

Git hooks are scripts that run automatically before or after Git events like commit, push, or merge. They are stored in the .git/hooks directory and can enforce policies locally before code reaches the remote repository.Common CI/CD use cases include:
  • pre-commit — run linters, format code, check for secrets
  • pre-push — run unit tests before pushing
  • commit-msg — enforce conventional commit format
  • post-merge — install new dependencies after pulling
Tools like Husky and lint-staged make managing hooks easier across teams.
.cicd.Version Control & Git Integration.Branching Strategies.exp

CI/CD pipelines work hand-in-hand with branching strategies. Common approaches include:
  • GitFlow — main, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches. Good for scheduled releases but complex.
  • GitHub Flow — single main branch with feature branches and pull requests. Simpler, ideal for continuous deployment.
  • Trunk-based Development — short-lived feature branches merged to main multiple times a day. Best for CI/CD with automated testing.
CI/CD pipelines typically trigger on push to specific branches (e.g., main) and on pull requests for validation before merge.
.cicd.Version Control & Git Integration.Pull Request Workflows.exp

Pull requests (PRs) are at the heart of modern CI/CD. A typical PR workflow:
  1. Developer creates a feature branch, commits changes, and pushes
  2. PR is opened, triggering a CI pipeline that runs tests and analysis
  3. PR checks report status (pass/fail) directly in the PR view
  4. Team reviews code; additional commits trigger re-runs
  5. Once approved and all checks pass, the PR is merged
  6. Merge triggers a CD pipeline to build and deploy
Tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Azure DevOps integrate PR checks natively with status badges and required checks.
.cicd.Continuous Integration.Build Automation.exp

Build automation is the process of automating the compilation of source code into executable artifacts. Every commit should produce a build to verify the code compiles correctly.Common build tools by language:
  • JavaScript/TypeScript — npm, yarn, pnpm, vite, webpack
  • Java — Maven, Gradle
  • Python — setuptools, poetry, pipenv
  • Go — go build
  • Rust — cargo build
  • C/C++ — CMake, Make, GCC
The build stage should be fast (under 5 minutes) to provide quick feedback. Cache dependencies between builds to speed up execution.
.cicd.Continuous Integration.Automated Testing.exp

Testing is the heart of CI. Every pipeline should run multiple levels of tests:
  • Unit tests — test individual functions and methods (fastest, most coverage)
  • Integration tests — test interactions between components (database, API, services)
  • End-to-end tests — test the full system from user perspective (slowest, least coverage)
The test pyramid suggests many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few e2e tests. Tests should be deterministic — always pass or fail the same way given the same code. Flaky tests undermine CI trust.
.cicd.Continuous Integration.Code Quality & Linting.exp

Automated code quality checks are essential in CI/CD. These include:
  • Linters — ESLint (JS/TS), Ruff/Flake8 (Python), Clippy (Rust), golangci-lint (Go)
  • Formatters — Prettier, Black, gofmt, rustfmt
  • Static analysis — SonarQube, CodeQL, Coverity
  • Type checking — TypeScript (tsc), mypy (Python), Flow
These checks should fail the pipeline if thresholds are not met (e.g., code coverage < 80%, lint errors, type errors). Many teams enforce formatting with pre-commit hooks and reserve CI for deeper analysis.
.cicd.CI/CD Tools.GitHub Actions.exp

GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform. Workflows are defined as YAML files in .github/workflows/. It offers deep GitHub integration, a large marketplace of pre-built actions, and supports Linux, macOS, Windows, and containers.Key concepts: workflows (automated processes), jobs (sets of steps), steps (individual tasks), runners (execution environments). GitHub provides free minutes for public repositories and paid minutes for private ones.
.cicd.CI/CD Tools.Jenkins.exp

Jenkins is the most widely used open-source automation server. It supports hundreds of plugins for building, deploying, and automating projects. Jenkins pipelines can be defined as code using Jenkinsfile with Declarative or Scripted pipeline syntax.Strengths: extreme flexibility, massive plugin ecosystem, mature community. Weaknesses: requires server management, UI can feel dated, plugin compatibility issues. Best for complex enterprise environments needing fine-grained control.
.cicd.CI/CD Tools.CircleCI.exp

CircleCI is a cloud-native CI/CD platform known for speed and reliability. Pipelines are configured in a .circleci/config.yml file. CircleCI supports parallelism, caching, and Orbs — reusable configuration packages that simplify complex pipelines.Key features: Docker layer caching, SSH debugging for troubleshooting, dynamic configuration via pipeline parameters, and optimized resource classes (CPU/RAM per job). CircleCI offers a generous free tier for individual developers and open-source projects.
.cicd.CI/CD Tools.Azure DevOps.exp

Azure DevOps is Microsoft's full DevSecOps platform providing a complete toolchain: Azure Pipelines (CI/CD), Azure Boards (work tracking), Azure Repos (Git repos), Azure Artifacts (package management), and Azure Test Plans (testing).Azure Pipelines supports any language, platform, and cloud. Key strengths: deep Azure integration, deployment groups for multi-machine rollouts, Kubernetes integration, and YAML or classic editor pipeline definitions. Free tier includes 1,800 minutes per month.
.cicd.GitLab CI/CD.GitLab CI/CD Overview.exp

GitLab CI/CD is GitLab's built-in continuous integration, delivery, and deployment system. Pipelines are defined declaratively in a .gitlab-ci.yml file at the repository root. GitLab CI/CD is deeply integrated into the GitLab platform, providing a unified experience for source control, CI/CD, container registry, package registry, and deployment.Key strengths: single application for the entire DevOps lifecycle, built-in auto-scaling runners, review apps for per-branch environments, and a generous free tier for both public and private repositories.
.cicd.GitLab CI/CD.GitLab CI Pipeline Configuration.exp

GitLab CI pipelines are defined in YAML with these core concepts:
  • Stages — groups of jobs that run in order (e.g., build, test, deploy). Jobs in the same stage run in parallel.
  • Jobs — define what to run (script, image, dependencies). Each job belongs to a stage.
  • Runners — agents that execute jobs. GitLab provides shared runners (Linux, Windows, macOS) and you can register your own.
  • Variables — environment variables for configuration. Can be set at project, group, or instance level.
  • Cache & Artifacts — cache speeds up dependency installs; artifacts pass build outputs between stages.
Example pipeline: lint → test → build → deploy. Jobs can run conditionally based on branch, tags, or changes to specific files.
.cicd.GitLab CI/CD.GitLab Auto DevOps.exp

Auto DevOps is GitLab's zero-configuration CI/CD pipeline. When enabled, GitLab automatically detects your application language and builds a complete pipeline including:
  • Code quality analysis (SonarQube)
  • SAST and Dependency Scanning
  • Container scanning and DAST
  • License compliance review
  • Automatic deployment to staging and production
  • Review Apps (temporary environments per merge request)
  • Performance testing and browser testing
Auto DevOps uses a Dockerfile or buildpack to build your app. It's ideal for teams new to CI/CD who want instant value without writing pipeline config.
.cicd.GitLab CI/CD.GitLab Runners & Scaling.exp

GitLab Runners are the agents that execute CI/CD jobs. Types include:
  • Shared runners — GitLab-hosted, available to all projects (Linux, Windows, macOS)
  • Group runners — available to all projects in a group
  • Project runners — dedicated to a single project
  • Specific runners — locked to specific projects or tags
Scaling strategies: use Docker autoscaling with Docker Machine or Kubernetes with the GitLab Runner Helm chart to spin up runners dynamically based on job demand. GitLab Runner supports executors including Docker, Kubernetes, SSH, and VirtualBox.
.cicd.Continuous Delivery & Deployment.Deployment Strategies.exp

Different deployment strategies balance risk, speed, and user impact:
  • Rolling Update — gradually replaces instances of the old version with the new one. Zero downtime, easy rollback.
  • Blue/Green — run two identical environments. Switch traffic from blue (current) to green (new) instantly. Instant rollback by switching back.
  • Canary — route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, then gradually increase. Real user validation with minimal risk.
  • Feature Flags — deploy code hidden behind toggles, then enable for specific users. Separates deployment from release.
Modern CD pipelines use a combination of these strategies depending on the application and risk tolerance.
.cicd.Continuous Delivery & Deployment.Rollback & Recovery.exp

Even the best pipelines can fail in production. CD systems must support fast, reliable rollback:
  • Automated rollback — if health checks fail after deployment, automatically revert to the last known-good version
  • Database rollbacks — use reversible migrations (up/down) to safely revert schema changes
  • Version pinning — always tag deployed versions (git tags, container tags) for easy identification
  • Audit trail — every deployment should log who deployed what, when, and the result
The golden rule: if it hurts, do it more often. Frequent, small deployments are easier to roll back than rare, large ones.
.cicd.Continuous Delivery & Deployment.Release Management.exp

Release management in CI/CD coordinates how changes move through environments:
  • Environment promotion — code flows: dev → staging → production, with gates at each stage
  • Semantic versioning — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.1.0) based on change impact
  • Changelogs — auto-generated from conventional commits
  • Release branches — for scheduled releases, create a release branch from main
  • Approval gates — manual approval steps before production deployment (compliance, QA sign-off)
Tools like Release Please, Semantic Release, and Changesets automate versioning and changelog generation.
.cicd.Infrastructure as Code CI/CD.Terraform in CI/CD.exp

Applying Infrastructure as Code (IaC) through CI/CD brings infrastructure changes under the same governance as application changes.Terraform CI/CD best practices:
  • Run terraform fmt and terraform validate in CI to check formatting and syntax
  • Use terraform plan in PRs to show infrastructure changes without applying them
  • Store state remotely (S3, Terraform Cloud) with state locking
  • Apply only after PR approval and plan review
  • Use workspaces or directories for environment separation
The terraform plan output in a PR comment is one of the most valuable CI/CD practices for infrastructure teams.
.cicd.Infrastructure as Code CI/CD.Configuration Management.exp

Configuration management tools maintain consistent system state across environments:
  • Ansible — agentless, push-based, YAML playbooks. Great for app deployment and server configuration.
  • Chef — Ruby-based DSL, pull-based with Chef Client and Server. Good for large-scale server fleets.
  • Puppet — declarative DSL, pull-based. Strong in enterprise environments.
In CI/CD, run config management as part of the deployment stage to ensure servers match the desired state after deployment.
.cicd.Infrastructure as Code CI/CD.Policy as Code.exp

Policy as Code (PaC) enforces rules automatically in the pipeline:
  • Open Policy Agent (OPA) — general-purpose policy engine. Enforce rules like "all S3 buckets must be encrypted" before apply.
  • Sentinel — HashiCorp's policy framework for Terraform and Vault.
  • Checkov — static analysis for IaC to find misconfigurations (open ports, hardcoded secrets).
  • Conftest — test configuration files against OPA policies in CI.
PaC shifts security left — catching policy violations before infrastructure is provisioned.
.cicd.Container CI/CD.Docker Build Pipelines.exp

Container-based CI/CD pipelines use Docker throughout the pipeline:
  • Build stage produces a Docker image with the application and all dependencies
  • Tag images with commit SHA, branch name, and semantic version
  • Push to a container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, GHCR)
  • Use multi-stage builds to minimize image size
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities (Trivy, Snyk, Docker Scout)
The same image built in CI is deployed everywhere — no "works on my machine" problems. Images are immutable and versioned.
.cicd.Container CI/CD.Kubernetes Deployments.exp

Deploying to Kubernetes from CI/CD involves:
  • Update the deployment manifest (YAML) with the new image tag
  • Use kubectl set image or patch the deployment
  • Apply with kubectl apply to trigger rolling update
  • Use Helm for templated releases — pass the image tag as a value
  • Monitor rollout with kubectl rollout status
Advanced setups use ArgoCD or Flux (GitOps) where the CD system watches a Git repository for manifest changes and synchronizes the cluster automatically.
.cicd.Container CI/CD.GitOps.exp

GitOps is a deployment model where the Git repository is the single source of truth for both application code and infrastructure. Changes are made via PRs, and an operator synchronizes the live environment to match the repository state.Key tools:
  • ArgoCD — Kubernetes-native CD tool. Syncs clusters to a Git repository with automatic or manual sync policies.
  • Flux — GitOps operator from Weaveworks. Supports multi-tenancy, image updates, and Kustomize/Helm.
Benefits: complete audit trail (every change is a Git commit), easy rollback (revert commit), and a single workflow for both dev and ops.
.cicd.Security in CI/CD.SAST & DAST.exp

Security testing should be integrated into every pipeline:
  • SAST (Static Application Security Testing) — analyzes source code for vulnerabilities without running it. Tools: SonarQube, CodeQL, Semgrep, Checkmarx. Runs early in the pipeline (build stage).
  • DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) — tests running applications for vulnerabilities. Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite. Runs against staging environments later in the pipeline.
SAST catches issues early (shift left), while DAST catches runtime vulnerabilities. Both should be gated — fail the pipeline on high-severity findings.
.cicd.Security in CI/CD.Secret Scanning.exp

Accidentally committing secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens) is one of the most common CI/CD security issues. Prevent and detect with:
  • Pre-commit hooks — tools like talisman, git-secrets, and detect-secrets scan before commits
  • CI scanning — GitHub Secret Scanning, GitLab Secret Detection, TruffleHog scan in the pipeline
  • Secret managers — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager
CI/CD configs should reference secrets from the CI platform's built-in secrets store (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, Jenkins credentials), never hardcode them.
.cicd.Security in CI/CD.SBOM & Supply Chain.exp

Software supply chain security is critical in 2026:
  • SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — a machine-readable inventory of all components in your software. Generated by tools like CycloneDX and Syft.
  • Dependency scanning — Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk automatically detect and update vulnerable dependencies
  • Artifact signing — sign container images and binaries with Cosign to verify authenticity
  • Attestations — create signed metadata about how and where artifacts were built
AI-generated code increases the importance of SBOM scanning. Every CI/CD pipeline should generate and verify SBOMs before deployment.
.cicd.Monitoring & Observability.Pipeline Metrics.exp

Track these key metrics to measure CI/CD pipeline health:
  • Pipeline duration — time from commit to deployment. Target: under 15 minutes total.
  • Build failure rate — percentage of builds that fail. Target: under 10%.
  • Deployment frequency — how often you deploy to production. Elite teams deploy multiple times per day.
  • Mean Time to Recover (MTTR) — time from detecting a failure to recovery. Target: under 1 hour.
  • Change failure rate — percentage of deployments causing incidents. Target: under 5%.
These are the DORA metrics — the industry standard for measuring DevOps and CI/CD performance.
.cicd.Monitoring & Observability.Pipeline Notifications.exp

Keep teams informed about pipeline status with automated notifications:
  • Slack/Discord — send messages on failure, success, or deployment events. Include links to the pipeline run.
  • Email — send summaries for failed pipelines or approval requests
  • Status badges — embed pipeline status (passing/failing) in README files
  • PR comments — post test results, coverage changes, and deployment URLs directly in PRs
Most CI/CD platforms have built-in notification integrations. Focus on actionable alerts — don't spam teams with every successful build.
.cicd.Monitoring & Observability.Incident Response.exp

When a CI/CD pipeline failure or production incident occurs, a structured response process is essential:
  1. Detect — automated monitoring and alerts detect the failure
  2. Stop the bleeding — rollback the deployment or block the pipeline
  3. Triage — determine severity, impact, and affected teams
  4. Investigate — review logs, metrics, and pipeline output to find root cause
  5. Remediate — fix the issue and push the fix through the same CI/CD pipeline
  6. Review — post-mortem to prevent recurrence
CI/CD pipelines themselves should be treated as critical infrastructure with their own monitoring, redundancy, and incident response plans.
.cloud.Cloud Fundamentals.What is Cloud Computing.exp
Cloud computing delivers computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet. Key benefits: pay-as-you-go, elastic scaling, reduced maintenance, global reach.
.cloud.Cloud Fundamentals.Deployment Models.exp

**Public cloud:** shared infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP). **Private cloud:** dedicated to one org. **Hybrid cloud:** mix of public and private. **Multi-cloud:** using multiple providers. **Community cloud:** shared by several orgs.
.cloud.Cloud Fundamentals.Cloud Providers Overview.exp

**AWS:** market leader, 200+ services. **Azure:** Microsoft ecosystem, enterprise focus. **GCP:** Google tools, data/AI strength. **DigitalOcean:** simple, developer-friendly. **Linode/Vultr:** budget options.
.cloud.Cloud Fundamentals.Regions & Availability Zones.exp

**Regions** are geographic areas (us-east-1, eu-west-2). **Availability Zones (AZs)** are isolated data centers within a region. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability. Choose regions close to users.
.cloud.Compute Services.Virtual Machines (EC2).exp
**AWS EC2** provides virtual servers. Choose instance types (general, compute, memory optimized). AMIs define OS/software. Security groups control traffic. Elastic IPs for static addresses.
.cloud.Compute Services.Serverless (Lambda).exp

**AWS Lambda** runs code without provisioning servers. Triggers: HTTP (API Gateway), S3 events, scheduled (CloudWatch), SQS. Supports Node.js, Python, Go, Java, C#, Ruby. Pay per execution + duration.
.cloud.Compute Services.Containers (ECS/EKS).exp
**ECS** (Elastic Container Service) runs Docker containers. **EKS** is managed Kubernetes. **Fargate** runs containers without managing servers. Use ECR for container image registry.
.cloud.Compute Services.App Engine (GCP).exp
**Google App Engine** is a PaaS that auto-scales apps. Standard environment (sandboxed, faster) vs Flexible (Docker, more features). Supports Go, Python, Java, Node.js, PHP, Ruby.
.cloud.Storage Services.Object Storage (S3).exp

**AWS S3** is object storage with 99.999999999% durability. Buckets hold objects. Storage classes: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier (archive). Versioning, lifecycle policies, static website hosting.
.cloud.Storage Services.Block Storage (EBS).exp
**EBS** provides block-level storage volumes for EC2. Types: gp3 (general), io2 (high-performance), st1 (throughput). Snapshots back up to S3. Can be encrypted. Attach to one instance at a time.
.cloud.Storage Services.CDN (CloudFront).exp

**CloudFront** is a CDN that caches content at edge locations. Origins: S3, HTTP server, ALB. Price classes determine edge coverage. Supports Lambda@Edge for custom logic at edge. SSL/TLS termination.
.cloud.Storage Services.File Storage (EFS).exp
**EFS** is a scalable, elastic NFS file system for Linux. Grows/shrinks automatically. Accessed by multiple EC2 instances simultaneously. Lifecycle management moves files to Infrequent Access tier.
.cloud.Cloud Databases.RDS (Relational).exp
**RDS** manages relational databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Features: Multi-AZ (HA), Read Replicas, automated backups, automated patching, encryption at rest.
.cloud.Cloud Databases.DynamoDB (NoSQL).exp
**DynamoDB** is a fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database. Single-digit millisecond performance. Auto-scaling, DAX (caching), Global Tables (multi-region), On-Demand capacity.
.cloud.Cloud Databases.MongoDB Atlas.exp
**MongoDB Atlas** is the official managed MongoDB service. Deploy across AWS/Azure/GCP. Features: auto-scaling, backups, BI Connector, Atlas Search, Serverless instances, global clusters.
.cloud.Cloud Databases.Firestore (GCP).exp
**Firestore** is a flexible, scalable NoSQL database for mobile/web apps. Real-time updates via listeners. Automatic multi-region replication. Strong consistency. Serverless — no provisioning needed.
.cloud.Cloud Databases.Cloud SQL.exp
**Cloud SQL** is GCP's managed relational database. Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server. Features: automatic replication, backups, failover, encryption, private network access. Up to 30TB storage.
.cloud.Cloud Databases.Cosmos DB (Azure).exp
**Cosmos DB** is Azure's globally distributed NoSQL database. Multi-model: document, key-value, graph, column-family. SLA-backed 99.999% availability. Single-digit ms latency anywhere in the world.
.cloud.Networking & Security.VPC (Virtual Private Cloud).exp
**VPC** is a logically isolated network in AWS. Subnets divide IP ranges (public/private). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway for public access. NAT Gateway for private subnets.
.cloud.Networking & Security.Load Balancers.exp

**ALB** (Application LB) routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic. **NLB** (Network LB) handles TCP/UDP. **ELB** (Classic) is legacy. Target groups route to instances. Health checks detect failures. Auto Scaling integrates with LBs.
.cloud.Networking & Security.IAM (Identity & Access).exp

**IAM** manages users, groups, roles, and policies. Policies are JSON documents defining permissions (Allow/Deny). Least privilege principle. Roles for EC2/Lambda to access services. MFA for extra security.
.cloud.Networking & Security.Security Best Practices.exp
Use IAM roles (not keys). Enable CloudTrail for auditing. Encrypt data at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). Security groups as firewalls. WAF for web attacks. Shield for DDoS. Regular security audits.
.cloud.DevOps & Deployment.CI/CD Pipelines.exp

Automate build, test, deploy with CI/CD. **AWS CodePipeline** + CodeBuild + CodeDeploy. **GitHub Actions** for simpler workflows. **GitLab CI** with built-in registry. Test in staging before production.
.cloud.DevOps & Deployment.Infrastructure as Code.exp
Manage cloud resources with code. **Terraform:** multi-cloud, declarative HCL. **CloudFormation:** AWS-native JSON/YAML. **Pulumi:** code in Python/TS/Go. Version control your infrastructure!
.cloud.DevOps & Deployment.Monitoring & Logging.exp

**CloudWatch:** metrics, logs, alarms. **X-Ray:** distributed tracing. **Prometheus + Grafana:** open-source monitoring. **ELK Stack:** Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana for log analysis. Set up alerts for critical metrics.
.cloud.DevOps & Deployment.Auto Scaling.exp

**Auto Scaling** adjusts compute capacity based on demand. Launch template defines instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking, step scaling, scheduled. Health checks replace unhealthy instances.
.cloud.Cloud Architecture.Microservices Architecture.exp

Microservices decompose an app into small, independent services. Each service has its own database, API, and deployment pipeline. API Gateways (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, GCP Apigee) route requests, handle auth, rate limiting. Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul) manages service-to-service communication with mTLS, traffic splitting, observability. Circuit breakers (Resilience4j, Hystrix) prevent cascading failures — fail fast and degrade gracefully. Common mistake: premature decomposition — start with a monolith, extract services when needed. Anti-pattern: shared databases between services (tight coupling). Use eventual consistency and saga patterns for distributed transactions.
.cloud.Cloud Architecture.Cloud Security Best Practices.exp

Shared Responsibility Model: provider secures the cloud (physical, network, hypervisor), you secure what's in the cloud (data, IAM, OS, app config). IAM least privilege: grant only required permissions — use service-specific roles, not admin. Encryption at rest: all cloud providers offer server-side encryption (SSE-S3, Azure SSE, GCP CSEK). Encryption in transit: enforce TLS 1.2+ everywhere, use HTTPS-only listeners. Secret management: store secrets in provider-native vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) — never in code or config files. Common mistake: over-permissive IAM policies (using wildcards). Enable CloudTrail/Audit Logs and set up anomaly alerts. Rotate keys and credentials regularly. Enable MFA for all human users.
.cloud.Cloud Architecture.Cost Optimization.exp

Right-sizing: match instance size to workload needs — analyze utilization metrics and downsize over-provisioned resources. Reserved instances / Committed use discounts: 1yr or 3yr commitment saves 30-70% for predictable workloads. Spot/Preemptible instances: 60-90% discount for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads (batch, ML training, CI/CD). Storage tiers: move infrequent data to cheaper tiers (S3 IA/Glacier, Azure Cool/Archive, GCP Nearline/Archive). Tagging strategy: tag all resources (Environment, Team, Project, Cost Center) for cost allocation and chargeback. Common mistake: leaving unused resources running (orphaned EBS volumes, idle load balancers, unattached IPs). Use budgets and alerts to track spending. Review and delete unused resources monthly.
.cloud.Cloud Architecture.High Availability & Disaster Recovery.exp

Multi-AZ: deploy across multiple availability zones in one region for resilience against AZ failure. Multi-region: deploy across geographic regions for region-level disaster recovery. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): max acceptable data loss (e.g., 1 hour = hourly backups). RTO (Recovery Time Objective): max acceptable downtime (e.g., 4 hours = time to restore). Backup strategies: automated snapshots, cross-region replication, point-in-time recovery. Failover patterns: Active-Passive (one region active, other on standby — Route53 failover), Active-Active (both regions serve traffic — Route53 latency routing, DynamoDB Global Tables, Cosmos DB multi-region writes). Common mistake: testing DR only once a year — automate DR drills. Use infrastructure as code to rebuild environments quickly.
.cloud.Cloud Architecture.Infrastructure as Code.exp

IaC manages cloud resources through code (declarative or imperative). Terraform: multi-cloud, state management (local or remote like S3/Terraform Cloud), HCL syntax, modules for reusability. CloudFormation: AWS-native, YAML/JSON, StackSets for multi-account, drift detection. Pulumi: code in TypeScript, Python, Go, C# — full programming language power (loops, functions, conditionals). State management: store state remotely (S3 + DynamoDB locking for Terraform, Pulumi Cloud, CloudFormation managed by AWS). Modular design: break infrastructure into reusable modules (vpc, compute, database) with versioning. Common mistake: storing state locally or not using state locking. Never manually modify resources outside of IaC (drift). Use pre-commit hooks for formatting. Validate templates before apply.
.cpp.Getting Started.What is C++.exp
C++ is a powerful, statically-typed systems programming language that extends C with object-oriented, generic, and functional features. It gives fine-grained control over memory and performance.
.cpp.Getting Started.C++ Versions.exp
Major standards: C++98 (original), C++11 (modern), C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23. Each adds features. Compile with -std=c++17, -std=c++20, etc. Always check compiler support.
.cpp.Getting Started.Compilers & Build.exp
Major compilers: GCC (g++), Clang, MSVC. Build systems: CMake (most common), Make, Ninja, Bazel. CMake generates build files for your platform.
.cpp.Getting Started.Project Structure.exp
Typical layout: src/ for .cpp, include/ for .hpp/.h, lib/ for dependencies, tests/ for unit tests. Use header guards (#pragma once) to prevent double inclusion.
.cpp.Getting Started.Namespaces.exp
Namespaces prevent name collisions. `std` is the standard library namespace. Nested namespaces (C++17): `namespace A::B::C {}`. Never `using namespace` in headers.
.cpp.Getting Started.Basic Syntax.exp
Semicolons terminate statements. Blocks use braces. `//` single-line, `/* */` multi-line comments. `std::cout` output, `std::cin` input. `#include` for headers.
.cpp.Variables & Types.Fundamental Types.exp
Integer: `int`, `short`, `long`, `long long`. `char`, `bool`, `float`, `double`, `void`. `signed`/`unsigned` variants. `sizeof` returns bytes.
.cpp.Variables & Types.auto & decltype.exp
`auto` deduces type from initializer (C++11). `decltype` yields the type of an expression. `auto&` deduces reference, `const auto&` deduces const reference.
.cpp.Variables & Types.Type Deduction Rules.exp
`auto` strips references and top-level const (unless you use `auto&` or `const auto&`). `decltype(auto)` preserves exact type (C++14). Template deduction follows similar rules.
.cpp.Variables & Types.nullptr & Fixed-Width Types.exp
`nullptr` (C++11) is the type-safe null pointer. `<cstdint>` provides `int32_t`, `uint64_t`, etc. with guaranteed sizes. `size_t` for sizes/indices.
.cpp.Variables & Types.const & constexpr.exp
`const` for runtime constants. `constexpr` (C++11) for compile-time constants. `constinit` (C++20) guarantees static initialization. `consteval` (C++20) produces compile-time only.
.cpp.Operators.Arithmetic & Logical.exp
`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (modulo). `++`, `--` (pre/post). `&&`, `||`, `!` short-circuit. Compound: `+=`, `-=`, etc. Integer division truncates toward zero.
.cpp.Operators.Bitwise & Shift.exp
`&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift). Useful for flags, bitfields, low-level protocols.
.cpp.Operators.Overloaded Operators Basics.exp
Operators can be overloaded for user types. `operator+`, `operator<<`, `operator[]`, `operator()`, etc. Keep semantics intuitive. Some cannot be overloaded (::, ., ?:, sizeof).
.cpp.Operators.User-Defined Literals.exp
Suffixes for literals (C++11). `operator""_suffix`. Common: `std::string` literal `s` (C++14), `std::chrono` literals. Must begin with underscore for user-defined.
.cpp.Control Flow.if / else.exp
Conditional branching. C++17 added `if constexpr` for compile-time branching in templates. C++17 init-statements: `if (init; cond)`.
.cpp.Control Flow.Switch.exp
Switch on integral/enum types. Each case needs `break` or `return`. `[[fallthrough]]` suppresses warnings. C++20 added init-statement for switch.
.cpp.Control Flow.Loops.exp
`for`, `while`, `do-while`. `break` exits, `continue` skips iteration. Classic for uses init;cond;incr pattern.
.cpp.Control Flow.Range-Based For.exp
Simplified iteration over containers (C++11). Works with arrays, STL containers, and anything with begin/end. Use `auto&` to avoid copies, `const auto&` for read-only.
.cpp.Control Flow.if constexpr.exp
Compile-time conditional (C++17). Unused branch is discarded, not compiled. Essential for template metaprogramming. Replaces SFINAE in many cases.
.cpp.Control Flow.Structured Bindings.exp
Decompose tuples, pairs, arrays, structs into individual variables (C++17). Works with `auto`, `auto&`, `const auto&`.
.cpp.Control Flow.Init-Statements.exp
Variables scoped to if/switch/for (C++17). Reduces scope, improves safety. Combined with structured bindings for powerful patterns.
.cpp.Functions.Declaration & Definition.exp
Declaration (prototype) tells compiler about name/return/params. Definition has the body. Default arguments go in declaration. `void` means no return.
.cpp.Functions.Overloading & Default Args.exp
Multiple functions with the same name but different parameters (overloading). Default arguments must be at the end. Resolved at compile time.
.cpp.Functions.Lambda Expressions.exp
Anonymous functions (C++11). `[]` capture by value, `[&]` by reference. Generic lambdas (C++14): `[](auto x)`. `mutable` allows modifying captured values.
.cpp.Functions.Trailing Return Type.exp
`auto func() -> type` (C++11). Useful when return type depends on parameter types. `decltype` in trailing return enables complex type computation.
.cpp.Functions.noexcept.exp
`noexcept` declares function won't throw. Optimizer can skip exception handling. `noexcept(condition)` for conditional noexcept. `noexcept` is part of function type.
.cpp.Functions.consteval / constinit.exp
`consteval` (C++20) forces compile-time evaluation (immediate function). `constinit` (C++20) guarantees static initialization order. Both complement constexpr.
.cpp.Functions.Function Try Blocks.exp
Function-level try block catches exceptions from constructor initializer lists and function bodies. Primarily useful in constructors for logging/re-throwing.
.cpp.Strings.std::string.exp
Dynamic, safe string from `<string>`. Methods: `length()`, `substr()`, `find()`, `rfind()`, `replace()`, `append()`, `insert()`, `erase()`. Concatenate with `+`.
.cpp.Strings.String Views.exp
`std::string_view` (C++17) is a non-owning reference to a string. Zero-copy. Perfect for function parameters. No null terminator guarantee.
.cpp.Strings.Raw String Literals.exp
Raw literals (C++11) preserve backslashes and newlines. `R"(text)"`. Delimiter optional: `R"delim(text)delim"`. Great for regex, file paths, JSON.
.cpp.Strings.String Conversion.exp
Convert between strings and numbers. `std::to_string()`, `std::stoi`, `stol`, `stod`, `stof`. `std::stringstream` for flexible formatting.
.cpp.Strings.UTF-8 Support.exp
C++11 added `u8"..."` for UTF-8 strings. C++20 made `char8_t` a distinct type. `<codecvt>` is deprecated. Use ICU or platform APIs for full Unicode support.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Classes & Objects.exp
Classes bundle data and methods. Access specifiers: `public`, `private`, `protected`. Constructors with initializer lists. `this` points to current instance.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Inheritance & Polymorphism.exp
Derived classes inherit from base. `virtual` functions enable dynamic dispatch. `override` keyword ensures correct override (C++11). Base class should have virtual destructor.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Virtual Destructors.exp
Base class must have virtual destructor to ensure derived destructors run when deleting through base pointer. `= default` for compiler-generated version.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Pure Virtual & Abstract Classes.exp
Pure virtual `= 0` makes class abstract (cannot instantiate). Derived classes must override. Interface-style classes have only pure virtual methods.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Virtual Inheritance.exp
Solves diamond problem where multiple bases share a common ancestor. `virtual` in inheritance specifier ensures only one copy of base subobject.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Copy & Swap Idiom.exp
Provide strong exception safety for copy-assignment. Implement copy constructor and destructor normally. Assignment operator takes by value (copy) then swaps.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Rule of Five.exp
If you define any of destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment, define all five. Or =default/=delete.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.Move Semantics.exp
Move transfers resources without copying (C++11). `std::move` casts to rvalue. Move constructor/assignment use `&&`. After move, source is in valid but unspecified state.
.cpp.Object-Oriented Programming.RAII.exp
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. Constructor acquires, destructor releases. Smart pointers, `std::fstream`, `std::lock_guard`, `std::thread` all follow RAII.
.cpp.STL Containers.std::vector.exp
Dynamic array with O(1) amortized push_back, O(n) insert/erase. Contiguous memory. Methods: `push_back`, `pop_back`, `emplace_back`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`.
.cpp.STL Containers.std::map & std::set.exp
Ordered associative containers (red-black tree). O(log n) lookup. `map<K,V>` key-value, `set<T>` unique values. Iterate in sorted order.
.cpp.STL Containers.std::unordered_map / set.exp
Hash-based containers (C++11). O(1) average lookup. Keys need hash function. No order guarantees. `reserve()` for pre-allocation.
.cpp.STL Containers.std::deque.exp
Double-ended queue. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Non-contiguous memory (chunks). Slightly slower than vector for index access.
.cpp.STL Containers.std::list & forward_list.exp
`std::list` doubly-linked, `std::forward_list` singly-linked (C++11). O(1) insert/erase anywhere with iterator. No random access. Higher per-element overhead.
.cpp.STL Containers.Container Adaptors.exp
`std::stack` (LIFO), `std::queue` (FIFO), `std::priority_queue` (max-heap). Built on underlying container (default deque or vector).
.cpp.STL Containers.std::array.exp
Fixed-size array wrapper (C++11). Stack-allocated. Knows its size. Safer than C arrays. `at()` for bounds checking. Compatible with STL algorithms.
.cpp.STL Algorithms.sort, find, transform.exp
Core algorithms from `<algorithm>`. `sort()`, `stable_sort()`, `find()`, `find_if()`, `transform()`, `for_each()`, `copy_if()`. Work on iterator pairs.
.cpp.STL Algorithms.lower_bound & binary_search.exp
Binary search on sorted ranges (O(log n)). `lower_bound` returns first >= value. `upper_bound` returns first > value. `binary_search` returns bool. `equal_range` returns both.
.cpp.STL Algorithms.partial_sort & nth_element.exp
`partial_sort` sorts first N elements, rest unsorted. `nth_element` places N-th element in correct position, partition around it. Both O(n log k) or O(n).
.cpp.STL Algorithms.accumulate & iota.exp
`std::accumulate` (<numeric>) sums/reduces a range. `std::iota` fills with incrementing values. `std::inner_product`, `std::adjacent_difference`, `std::partial_sum`.
.cpp.STL Algorithms.count_if & for_each.exp
`count_if` returns count matching predicate. `for_each` applies callable to each element. C++17: `for_each_n`. `all_of`, `any_of`, `none_of` for boolean checks.
.cpp.Templates.Function & Class Templates.exp
Templates parameterize types and values. `typename` or `class` for type params. Non-type params: `int N`. `auto` non-type params (C++17). Template specialization.
.cpp.Templates.Template Specialization.exp
Full specialization provides specific implementation for particular types. Partial specialization for some parameters. Used for type-specific optimization.
.cpp.Templates.Template Template Parameters.exp
Template parameter that is itself a template. Allows passing container templates. `template<typename> class Container`. Works with template template arguments.
.cpp.Templates.Variadic Templates.exp
Templates with variable number of arguments (C++11). `typename... Args`. Pack expansion with `...`. `sizeof...(Args)` for count. Recursive or fold-based processing.
.cpp.Templates.Fold Expressions.exp
Unary and binary folds over parameter packs (C++17). `(... op args)` unary right fold. `(args op ...)` unary left fold. `(init op ... op args)` binary fold.
.cpp.Templates.SFINAE & enable_if.exp
Substitution Failure Is Not An Error. `std::enable_if` controls template overload resolution. `<type_traits>` provides type predicates. Largely replaced by concepts in C++20.
.cpp.C++20 Features.Concepts.exp
Compile-time constraints on template parameters (C++20). Standard: `std::integral`, `std::floating_point`, `std::ranges::range`, `std::convertible_to`. Custom with `concept`.
.cpp.C++20 Features.Ranges Library.exp
Composable, lazy range algorithms (C++20). Pipe syntax `|` for composition. Views: `filter`, `transform`, `take`, `drop`, `reverse`, `join`. `std::views` namespace.
.cpp.C++20 Features.Coroutines.exp
Stackless coroutines (C++20). `co_await`, `co_yield`, `co_return`. Compiler generates state machine. Need library support (cppcoro, or custom promise/awaiter).
.cpp.C++20 Features.Modules.exp
Modern replacement for headers (C++20). `export module`, `import`. Faster compilation, no header guards, better encapsulation. Not all compilers fully support.
.cpp.C++20 Features.Spaceship Operator <=>.exp
Three-way comparison operator (C++20). Returns `std::strong_ordering`, `std::weak_ordering`, `std::partial_ordering`. `= default` generates all six comparison operators.
.cpp.C++20 Features.Views & Lazy Evaluation.exp
`std::views` provide lazy, composable transformations. No allocations. `std::span` is a non-owning view over contiguous memory (C++20). `std::string_view` for strings.
.cpp.C++23 Features.std::expected.exp
Error handling with either a value or an error (like Rust's Result). From `<expected>`. No exception overhead. Functional chaining with `and_then`, `or_else`, `transform`.
.cpp.C++23 Features.Deducing This.exp
Deduce the reference qualifier of `this` for member functions. Allows lambda-like syntax for member functions. Eliminates need for const/non-const overload pairs.
.cpp.C++23 Features.flat_map & flat_set.exp
Contiguous-storage associative containers. `std::flat_map<K,V>` sorted vector<pair>. Faster iteration, less memory, but O(n) insertion. From `<flat_map>`.
.cpp.C++23 Features.mdspan.exp
Multidimensional array view (C++23). Non-owning, layout-polymorphic. Supports strides, extents, subspan. From `<mdspan>`. Replaces manual index calculation.
.cpp.Smart Pointers.std::unique_ptr.exp
Exclusive ownership. Non-copyable, movable. `std::make_unique` (C++14). Custom deleter as template parameter. Automatic memory management with zero overhead.
.cpp.Smart Pointers.std::shared_ptr.exp
Reference-counted shared ownership. `std::make_shared` allocates control block and object together (one allocation). Thread-safe ref count.
.cpp.Smart Pointers.std::weak_ptr.exp
Non-owning reference to shared_ptr. Breaks circular references. Lock to get temporary shared_ptr. `expired()` checks if object still exists.
.cpp.Smart Pointers.enable_shared_from_this.exp
CRTP base class that lets object safely create shared_ptrs to itself. Requires object is already managed by shared_ptr. `shared_from_this()` method.
.cpp.Smart Pointers.Custom Deleters.exp
Smart pointers accept custom deleters (callable). For non-memory resources: file handles, sockets, C resources. Stored in control block (shared_ptr) or as part of unique_ptr type.
.cpp.Concurrency.std::thread.exp
OS thread wrapper. `join()` blocks until completion. `detach()` lets run independently (careful with dangling). `std::this_thread::sleep_for`, `get_id`.
.cpp.Concurrency.Mutex & Locks.exp
`std::mutex` protects shared data. `std::lock_guard` RAII lock. `std::unique_lock` more flexible (defer, try, timed). `std::shared_mutex` (C++17) reader-writer.
.cpp.Concurrency.Async & Futures.exp
`std::async` launches async tasks. `std::future<T>` gets result once. `std::promise<T>` manually sets value/exception. `std::packaged_task` wraps callable.
.cpp.Concurrency.std::jthread.exp
Joining thread (C++20). Automatically joins on destruction. Cooperative cancellation via `get_stop_token()`, `request_stop()`.
.cpp.Concurrency.std::latch & std::barrier.exp
`std::latch` (C++20) single-use countdown. `std::barrier` (C++20) reusable synchronization point. Both from `<latch>` and `<barrier>`.
.cpp.Concurrency.std::counting_semaphore.exp
Signaling mechanism (C++20). `std::counting_semaphore<max>` with `acquire()`, `release()`. Binary semaphore alias `std::binary_semaphore`. Good for producer-consumer.
.cpp.File I/O.std::fstream Basics.exp
File streams: `ifstream` (read), `ofstream` (write), `fstream` (read+write). RAII: closes in destructor. Open modes: `app`, `binary`, `in`, `out`, `trunc`.
.cpp.File I/O.std::filesystem.exp
Filesystem library (C++17). Path manipulation, directory iteration, file status. `std::filesystem::path`, `directory_iterator`, `file_status`. Cross-platform.
.cpp.File I/O.std::stringstream.exp
In-memory string I/O. `std::stringstream`, `std::istringstream`, `std::ostringstream`. Works with `<<` and `>>`. Useful for parsing and formatting.
.cpp.File I/O.Binary I/O.exp
Reading/writing raw bytes. `read()`, `write()` on streams. `reinterpret_cast` for type punning. Endianness and portability concerns.
.cpp.Error Handling.Exceptions.exp
Exception handling with `try`, `catch`, `throw`. Stack unwinding calls destructors. Catch by reference. `catch(...)` catches all. Re-throw with `throw;`.
.cpp.Error Handling.noexcept Specifier.exp
`noexcept` promises no exception. `noexcept(condition)` conditional. `noexcept` operator checks. Violation calls `std::terminate`. Optimizer can improve code.
.cpp.Error Handling.std::exception Hierarchy.exp
Standard exception classes from `<stdexcept>`. Base: `std::exception`. Derived: `logic_error`, `runtime_error`, `bad_alloc`, `bad_cast`, etc.
.cpp.Error Handling.Error Codes & std::error_code.exp
Lightweight error handling without exceptions. `<system_error>`: `std::error_code`, `std::error_category`. `std::errc` for standard POSIX errors.
.cpp.Build Systems.CMake Deep.exp
Modern CMake (3.x): targets, properties, generator expressions. `target_link_libraries`, `target_include_directories`, `INTERFACE/PUBLIC/PRIVATE`. FetchContent for dependencies.
.cpp.Build Systems.vcpkg.exp
C++ package manager by Microsoft. Manifest mode (`vcpkg.json`). Integrates with CMake via toolchain file. Ports for 2000+ libraries.
.cpp.Build Systems.Conan.exp
Decentralized C/C++ package manager. `conanfile.txt` or `conanfile.py`. Supports multiple generators (CMake, MSBuild, etc.). Profiles for configurations.
.cpp.Build Systems.Build Tools Overview.exp
Ninja (fast parallel builds), Make (classic), Bazel (monorepo), Meson (Python-based). C++20 modules require build system support.
.cpp.Frameworks.Qt Framework.exp
Cross-platform framework for GUI, networking, SQL, etc. Key modules: QtWidgets, QtCore, QtNetwork, QtQml, QtQuick. Signal-slot mechanism for communication.
.cpp.Frameworks.Boost Libraries.exp
Peer-reviewed, portable C++ library collection. Key: Boost.Asio (networking), Boost.Beast (HTTP/WebSocket), Boost.Filesystem, Boost.Test, Boost.PropertyTree, Boost.ProgramOptions.
.cpp.Frameworks.Unreal Engine C++.exp
UE uses C++ with reflection macros: `UCLASS`, `USTRUCT`, `UPROPERTY`, `UFUNCTION`. Gameplay classes, Actors, Components, GameplayAbilitySystem.
.cpp.Frameworks.Google Test & Benchmark.exp
Testing and benchmarking. GTest: `TEST`, `EXPECT_EQ`, `ASSERT_TRUE`. GMock for mocking. Google Benchmark for performance measurement.
.cpp.Utilities & Type Support.std::optional (C++17).exp

`std::optional<T>` holds a value or nothing. Avoids sentinel values (-1, nullptr, empty string). `has_value()`, `value()` (throws `std::bad_optional_access` on empty), `value_or(default)`. Monadic ops in C++23: `and_then`, `transform`, `or_else`.
.cpp.Utilities & Type Support.std::variant (C++17).exp

Type-safe union from `<variant>`. Holds one of several types at a time. `std::visit()` dispatches based on current type. `index()` returns which alternative is active. No undefined behavior unlike raw unions. `std::monostate` for empty variant.
.cpp.Utilities & Type Support.std::any (C++17).exp

Type-erased container (like `void*` but type-safe). From `<any>`. `any_cast<T>()` throws `std::bad_any_cast` on type mismatch. `has_value()`, `type()` for RTTI. Prefer `variant` when types are known at compile time.
.cpp.Utilities & Type Support.Type Traits & Metaprogramming.exp

`<type_traits>` provides compile-time queries: `is_integral`, `is_floating_point`, `is_pointer`, `is_same`, `remove_reference`, `decay`, `enable_if`. `static_assert` for compile-time checking. `if constexpr` (C++17) simplifies template code.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.Inline Variables (C++17).exp

C++17 extends `inline` to variables, allowing header-only definitions without ODR violations. Previously, static class members and global constants needed a `.cpp` definition. `inline constexpr` works too. All translation units share one address.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.[[nodiscard]] & [[maybe_unused]].exp

`[[nodiscard]]` (C++17) warns if return value is discarded. C++20 adds `[[nodiscard("reason")]]`. `[[maybe_unused]]` suppresses unused warnings. Essential for error-returning functions, RAII guards, and stub/hook points.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.std::clamp / std::gcd / std::lcm (C++17).exp

`std::clamp(v, lo, hi)` from `<algorithm>` constrains a value to [lo, hi]. `std::gcd` / `std::lcm` from `<numeric>` compute greatest common divisor and least common multiple. All are constexpr-friendly.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.Parallel STL Algorithms (C++17).exp

Execution policies from `<execution>`: `seq` (sequential), `par` (parallel threads), `par_unseq` (parallel + SIMD), `unseq` (C++20, vectorized single-thread). Apply to `sort`, `transform`, `for_each`, `reduce`, etc. Backend: Intel TBB or compiler-specific.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.Code Organization (PIMPL Idiom).exp

PIMPL (Pointer to Implementation) hides private members from the header, reducing recompilation dependencies. The header only has a forward-declared struct pointer (`Impl*` or `unique_ptr<Impl>`). The .cpp file defines the implementation struct.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.Design Patterns: Strategy & Observer.exp

Strategy: encapsulate algorithms behind a common interface, selected at runtime. Observer: one-to-many notification on state change. C++ supports both via virtual interfaces, `std::function`, and smart pointers for ownership management.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.Testing with Catch2 & GTest.exp

Catch2: header-only (v2) or compiled library (v3), BDD-style with SECTIONs. GTest: xUnit-style, `TEST()`, `EXPECT_EQ`, `ASSERT_TRUE`. Both support matchers, fixtures, and parameterized tests. Integrate with CMake: `enable_testing()` + `add_test()`.
.cpp.Modern C++ Practice.Performance Optimization.exp

From Professional C++: 1) Move semantics avoid deep copies. 2) Reserve vector capacity upfront. 3) Pass by const reference, not value. 4) CRTP avoids virtual dispatch in hot paths. 5) Profile first (Google Benchmark, perf). 6) Small-string optimization.
.cpp.Pointers & Memory.References.exp
A reference (`T&`) is an alias to an existing object. Cannot be null, must be initialized, cannot be rebound. Used for function parameters (pass by reference) and return values.
.cpp.Pointers & Memory.Raw Pointers.exp
Pointers hold memory addresses. Declared as `T*`. Dereference with `*`, get address with `&`. Can be null (`nullptr`). Support pointer arithmetic.
.cpp.Pointers & Memory.new & delete.exp
Dynamic memory allocation. `new` allocates + constructs, `delete` destructs + deallocates. Array forms: `new[]`, `delete[]`. Prefer smart pointers in modern C++.
.cpp.Pointers & Memory.Memory Leakage.exp
Memory allocated with `new` that is never `delete`d. Causes: lost pointers, exception before delete, circular shared_ptr. Tools: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer.
.cpp.Pointers & Memory.Memory Model.exp
C++ memory model defines how threads interact through memory. `std::memory_order` for atomics. Sequential consistency, acquire/release, relaxed.
.cpp.Pointers & Memory.Object Lifetime.exp
Objects are created (constructor), live, then destroyed (destructor). Storage durations: automatic (stack), static, thread, dynamic (heap).
.cpp.Type Casting.static_cast.exp
Compile-time cast between related types. Numeric conversions, upcasts/downcasts in class hierarchies, `void*` to typed pointer.
.cpp.Type Casting.dynamic_cast.exp
Runtime-checked cast for polymorphic types. Requires at least one virtual function. Returns null for pointers on failure.
.cpp.Type Casting.const_cast.exp
Adds or removes `const`/`volatile` qualification. Modifying a const object through const_cast is UB.
.cpp.Type Casting.reinterpret_cast.exp
Unsafe cast that reinterprets the bit pattern. No type checking. Used for serialization, hardware access.
.cpp.Type Casting.RTTI & typeid.exp
Run-Time Type Information. `typeid` returns `std::type_info`. `dynamic_cast` also uses RTTI. Disabled with `-fno-rtti`.
.cpp.Language Internals.Undefined Behavior.exp
