Backend services route to instance groups, serverless NEGs (Cloud Run, Functions), or zonal NEGs. Health checks: HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, SSL. Cloud CDN caches responses at edge. Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) controls access based on identity and context. Cloud Armor rules block or throttle traffic.
.gcp.Networking & Security.Cloud IAM & Security.exp

Cloud IAM with Conditions: allow access only if device is trusted, IP is from corporate network, MFA was used. Organization Policy Service: constraints on resources at org/folder/project level (e.g., disable public IPs, restrict regions). Cloud KMS: key management, HSM option, key rotation, CMEK for customer-managed encryption keys. Secret Manager: store API keys, passwords, certificates. Binary Authorization: enforce signed container images. VPC Service Controls: define security perimeters around Google-managed services. Security Command Center (Premium): vulnerability scanning, threat detection, compliance reporting.
.gcp.Networking & Security.Cloud Armor & DDoS Protection.exp

Google Cloud Armor provides WAF and DDoS protection. WAF rules: pre-configured rules (SQLi, XSS, LFI, RFI, RCE, scanners, protocol attacks), rate limiting, IP blacklist/whitelist, geo-based access control, custom expressions (CEL — Common Expression Language). Adaptive Protection uses ML to detect DDoS. DDoS: Google's global infrastructure inherently absorbs L3/L4 DDoS. Cloud Armor Managed Protection Plus adds L7 DDoS, bill protection, and DDoS response team. Cloud IDS (intrusion detection) monitors east-west traffic. Web Security Scanner finds CVEs in App Engine and Compute Engine.
.gcp.Data & AI.Cloud Pub/Sub.exp

Pub/Sub is fully managed async messaging. Topics (channels) and Subscriptions (pull, push, or BigQuery). At-least-once delivery. Message retention up to 7 days. Exactly-once processing with subscriber-side deduplication. Filtering by attributes. Ordering keys for message ordering within a partition. Schema registry for message schema validation. Snapshots for replaying messages. Seek to timestamp. Flow control: max outstanding messages. Dead letter topics for poison pills. Export subscriptions to Cloud Storage, BigQuery. Throughput: millions of msgs/sec.
.gcp.Data & AI.Dataflow & Dataproc.exp

Dataflow is serverless stream and batch processing (Apache Beam). Unified programming model for batch + streaming. Auto-scales workers. Exactly-once processing. Beam SDKs in Java, Python, Go. I/O connectors for Pub/Sub, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Spanner, Kafka. Streaming with exactly-once, event time, watermarks, triggers. FlexRS for batch with cost savings. Dataproc is managed Spark/Hadoop/Hive. 1-min cluster startup. Can use preemptible VMs. Cluster autoscaling. Spark SQL, MLlib, Structured Streaming. Pig, Hive, Tez, Presto, and 30+ Spark optimizations. Dataproc Serverless runs Spark without cluster management.
.gcp.Data & AI.Vertex AI.exp

Vertex AI is GCP's unified ML platform. AutoML: train models without code (tables, images, text, video). Custom training with pre-built or custom containers. Prediction: online (endpoint, <100ms) and batch. Model Registry: version models, deploy to endpoints, monitor. Feature Store: serving features for online/offline. Vertex AI Pipelines (Kubeflow Pipelines) orchestrate ML workflows. Model Evaluation: classification, regression, forecasting metrics. Generative AI: Model Garden (Gemini, Llama, Claude, Mistral), Vertex AI Studio (prompt design, tuning), Agent Builder (conversational AI agents). Embeddings API for vector search. Vertex AI Vector Search (Matching Engine, formerly) for similarity search.
.gcp.Data & AI.Cloud Composer & Workflows.exp

Cloud Composer is managed Apache Airflow. DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) define workflows as Python files. Operators for GCP services (BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, Kubernetes). Airflow Web UI for monitoring, triggers, logs. Scheduled triggers (cron) and event-based (Pub/Sub sensors). Works with any Airflow operator via KubernetesPodOperator. Workflows is serverless workflow orchestration (low-code YAML, parallel branches, subworkflows, HTTP calls, service account auth, 1yr execution timeout, event arc triggers). Cheaper and simpler than Composer for linear workflows.
.gcp.Advanced GCP.Cloud Build & CI/CD.exp

Cloud Build is a fully managed CI/CD platform. Build triggers auto-start builds on git push (Cloud Source Repos, GitHub, Bitbucket). cloudbuild.yaml defines build steps as containers. Steps run sequentially in isolated Docker containers. Substitutions: built-in ($PROJECT_ID, $BUILD_ID, $BRANCH_NAME, $SHORT_SHA) and custom. Artifacts can be pushed to Artifact Registry or Cloud Storage. Cloud Build supports Kaniko caching for faster Docker builds. Approvals for production deployments. Common mistake: running all steps sequentially instead of parallelizing independent tasks. Use step timeouts to prevent hung builds.
.gcp.Advanced GCP.Pub/Sub.exp

Pub/Sub is GCP's fully managed async messaging. Topics are named channels. Subscriptions: pull (consumer pulls messages), push (Pub/Sub sends to HTTP endpoint), BigQuery (direct to table), Cloud Storage (object writes). At-least-once delivery — consumers must handle duplicates. Exactly-once processing available via subscriber-side deduplication (message ID tracking). Dead-letter topics capture poison messages after maxDeliveryAttempts. Filtering by message attributes reduces irrelevant deliveries. Ordering keys maintain message order within a partition. Schema registry validates message structure. Seek to timestamp replays messages. Common mistake: not setting ackDeadline high enough for processing time. Use flow control to limit outstanding messages.
.gcp.Advanced GCP.Cloud Run Deep Dive.exp

Cloud Run is serverless containers with auto-scaling to zero. Revisions track deployments — each deploy creates a new revision. Traffic splitting: send % of traffic to specific revision (canary deployments, rollbacks). Min instances (0-~1000): 0 means scale to zero (cost-effective), >0 means keep instances warm (reduces cold starts). Max instances (default 100) caps concurrent instance count. Concurrency: how many requests one container handles simultaneously (default 80, max 250). VPC connector enables access to private VPC resources (Cloud SQL, Memorystore) without public IP. CPU allocation: only during request (default, cheaper) or always (needed for background threads). Cloud Run jobs for batch workloads. Common mistake: setting min instances too high for variable traffic wastes money. Use CPU always for apps with background processing.
.gcp.Advanced GCP.Secret Manager.exp

Secret Manager stores API keys, passwords, certificates, and other sensitive data. Secrets contain versions — each version stores the secret value. Access via IAM roles: Secret Manager Admin, Secret Manager Viewer, Secret Manager Secret Accessor. Automatic rotation: use Eventarc + Cloud Functions or Pub/Sub + Cloud Run. Replication: automatic (synced to multiple regions) or user-managed (choose regions). Common mistake: not enabling automatic replication for multi-region apps — secrets may not be available in all regions. Use CMEK (customer-managed encryption keys) for compliance. Version aliases: latest always points to the newest version. Integration with Cloud Run, GKE, Compute Engine, Cloud Functions.
.gcp.Advanced GCP.Cloud Deploy.exp

Cloud Deploy automates delivery to Cloud Run, GKE, and Anthos. Delivery pipelines define the deployment process. Targets represent environments (dev, staging, prod). Promotion strategies: automatic (promote to next target on success) or manual (require approval). Rollbacks can be automatic on failure or manual. Skaffold is the underlying engine — skaffold.yaml defines the app, manifests, and deployment strategy. Canary deployment: incremental traffic shifting (e.g., 25%, 50%, 100%). Verification phases test the deployment (e.g., Cloud Build CI, custom checks). Common mistake: not testing canary deployments with real traffic. Use Cloud Deploy's built-in verification capabilities.
.git.Git Basics.What is Git.exp
Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code, enabling collaboration and history management. GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting Git repositories.
.git.Git Basics.git init & clone.exp
Create a new local repository with git init, or copy an existing remote repository using git clone with HTTPS or SSH URLs.
.git.Git Basics.git add & commit.exp
Stage changes with git add and record them in history with git commit. The staging area lets you craft precise commits with meaningful messages.
.git.Git Basics.git status & log.exp
git status shows the current state of working directory and staging area. git log displays commit history with various formatting options.
.git.Git Basics.git diff.exp
Compare changes between working directory, staging area, and commits. Use diff to review changes before staging or committing.
.git.Git Basics.Config levels.exp
Git config has three levels: system (all users), global (your account), local (per-repo). Each level overrides the one above. Use --list to view all settings.
.git.Git Basics.Git Aliases.exp
Create shortcuts for frequent commands using git config alias. Aliases can chain commands and accept arguments for powerful shorthand.
.git.Git Basics.gitignore deep.exp
The .gitignore file uses glob patterns to exclude files. Negate patterns with !, ignore directories with trailing /, and use ** for nested patterns. Global gitignore applies to all repos.
.git.Git Basics.gitattributes.exp
The .gitattributes file controls how Git handles files per-path: line endings (CRLF vs LF), diff drivers, merge strategies, and language detection. Essential for cross-platform teams.
.git.Git Basics.Hook basics.exp
Git hooks are scripts in .git/hooks/ that trigger on actions like commit, push, or merge. Client hooks (pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg) and server hooks (pre-receive, post-receive) enforce policies.
.git.Git Basics.git worktree.exp
Worktrees let you check out multiple branches simultaneously in separate directories. Share the same repository but maintain independent working directories and index files.
.git.Branching & Merging.git branch.exp

Branches are lightweight pointers to commits. List, create, rename, and delete branches to isolate work on features or fixes.

Visual:
main  ●──●──●──●
            \
feature      ●──●──●
Each branch is just a pointer. Creating a branch doesn't copy files — it just creates a new label.
.git.Branching & Merging.git checkout & switch.exp
Switch between branches using checkout or the newer switch command. checkout can also restore files from history.
.git.Branching & Merging.git merge.exp

Integrate changes from one branch into another. Fast-forward merges apply commits directly; three-way merges create a merge commit.

Merge vs Rebase:
MERGE (preserves history)
main  ●──●──●──●──●
         \    /
feature   ●──●

REBASE (linear history)
main  ●──●──●──●──●
               /
feature       ●──●
Merge keeps ancestor relationships; rebase rewrites history for a clean line.
.git.Branching & Merging.Merge conflicts.exp
When parallel changes conflict, Git marks the file. Manually edit to resolve, then stage and commit the resolution.
.git.Branching & Merging.Merge strategies.exp
Git supports multiple merge strategies: recursive (default for two branches), octopus (multiple branches), ours (keep current), subtree. Pass -s to select strategy and -X for options.
.git.Branching & Merging.Squash merge.exp
Squash merging combines all commits from a feature branch into a single new commit on the target branch. Cleaner history but loses granular commit details.
.git.Branching & Merging.merge --squash vs squash merge.exp
merge --squash stages all changes without committing (you commit manually). GitHub's squash merge auto-commits. Both flatten history; use when granular commits lack individual value.
.git.Branching & Merging.git merge-tree.exp
merge-tree computes the three-way merge result without touching the index or working tree. Useful for previewing merge outcomes or scripting merge logic.
.git.Branching & Merging.Orphan branches.exp
Orphan branches share no commit history with the current branch. Useful for things like gh-pages, documentation, or starting a project in a subdirectory with separate history.
.git.Rebasing.git rebase.exp

Reapply commits from one branch onto another tip for a linear history. Use interactive rebase to squash, reorder, or edit commits.

Visual:
BEFORE:
main    A──B──C
         \
feature  D──E

AFTER rebase:
main    A──B──C
               \
feature        D'──E'
D' and E' are NEW commits (different hashes). The original D/E still exist until garbage collected. Rebase rewrites history — never rebase shared/pushed branches.
.git.Rebasing.Interactive rebase (fixup, reword, drop, exec).exp

Interactive rebase opens an editor where you choose actions per commit: pick (keep), reword (edit message), edit (amend content), squash (combine with previous), fixup (squash discarding message), drop (delete), exec (run command).
.git.Rebasing.Rebase strategies.exp
Rebase offers strategies like --rebase-merges (preserve merge commits), --strategy recursive, --strategy-option theirs for conflict resolution, and --ignore-date to reset timestamps.
.git.Rebasing.rebase --onto.exp
rebase --onto replays commits onto a different base than upstream. Extract a feature branch from the wrong parent, or move a sub-branch to start from a different point.
.git.Rebasing.Autosquash.exp
Autosquash automatically arranges fixup! and squash! commits during interactive rebase. Combined with git commit --fixup/--squash, it streamlines fixup workflows.
.git.Rebasing.When NOT to rebase.exp

Never rebase commits that exist on a shared/public branch. Rebase rewrites history — anyone who pulled your old branch will have divergent history. The bane of rebasing is the force push that breaks collaborators.
.git.Stashing & WIP.git stash.exp
Temporarily save uncommitted changes to clean your working directory. Apply, drop, or list stashes to manage WIP context switches.
.git.Stashing & WIP.Stash deep.exp
Stashes are stored as commits on the reflog of refs/stash. --include-untracked or --all captures untracked/ignored files. Stash show inspects contents without applying.
.git.Stashing & WIP.Partial stash.exp
Stash only specific files or hunks with --patch for interactive selection. You can also stash individual pathspecs using git stash push -- <path> since Git 2.13.
.git.Stashing & WIP.Stash across branches.exp
Stash is not branch-specific — you can stash on one branch and pop on another. Git auto-merges if changes apply cleanly; conflicts are handled manually.
.git.Stashing & WIP.Create branch from stash.exp
Turn a stash into a proper branch with git stash branch. This creates a new branch starting at the commit where the stash was originally created.
.git.Undoing & History.git reset & revert.exp
Reset moves branch pointers (soft, mixed, hard). Revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit, safe for shared history.
.git.Undoing & History.Reset modes deep (--soft, --mixed, --hard).exp

--soft: moves HEAD only (changes stay staged). --mixed (default): moves HEAD and unstages changes (working tree unchanged). --hard: moves HEAD, unstages, and discards working tree changes. --hard is DESTRUCTIVE.
.git.Undoing & History.git restore.exp
Restore is the modern alternative to checkout for restoring files. Restore working tree from index (default) or a specific commit. --staged un stages, --source <tree> picks from a commit.
.git.Undoing & History.git switch.exp
Switch is the modern alternative to checkout for branch operations. Cleaner semantics: switch branches, detach with --detach, create with -c, and return to previous with @{-1}.
.git.Undoing & History.Reflog deep.exp
The reflog is Git's safety net — it records every HEAD movement including resets, rebases, and merges. Entries expire in 90 days (30 for unreachable). Use it to recover from almost any mistake.
.git.Undoing & History.Orphan commits.exp
Orphan commits have no parent (root commits). The first commit in a repo is always an orphan. Create new root commits for independent history lines like gh-pages or separate documentation.
.git.Undoing & History.filter-branch vs filter-repo.exp

git filter-branch rewrites history en masse but is slow and dangerous. git filter-repo is the recommended replacement — faster, safer, and designed for large-scale history rewrites like purging secrets or splitting repos.
.git.Collaboration.git remote.exp
Remotes are references to remote repository URLs. Manage connections to push, pull, and fetch from collaboration sources.
.git.Collaboration.git push & pull.exp

Push local commits to a remote branch and pull (fetch + merge) remote changes into your current branch. Set upstream for convenience.

Push vs Pull vs Fetch:
LOCAL                     REMOTE
●──●──●  push ——————→  ●──●──●
●──●──●  ←————— pull   ●──●──●
●──●──●  ←—— fetch ——  ●──●──●
        (no merge)

PUSH  = upload + merge to remote
PULL  = fetch + merge (may conflict)
FETCH = download only (review first)
Always pull before push to avoid rejection. Use `git pull --rebase` for cleaner history.
.git.Collaboration.git fetch.exp

Download commits, files, and references from a remote without merging. Use fetch to review changes before integrating.

Fetch vs Pull:
FETCH: origin/main updated, main stays
main     ●──●──●──●
             \
origin/main  ●──●──●──●

PULL: origin/main updated AND merged
main     ●──●──●──●──●──●
                       (merge commit)
Fetch is safe — it never changes your working tree. Always fetch before push to check for remote changes.
.git.Collaboration.Pull Requests.exp
PRs propose changes from a fork or branch for review before merging. Include descriptions, reviewers, and link to issues for context.
.git.Collaboration.Pull request workflow.exp

The full PR lifecycle: fork/clone → branch → commit → push → open PR → request reviewers → address feedback → update branch → merge. Draft PRs signal work-in-progress.

PR Lifecycle:
Fork → Clone → Branch → Commit → Push → PR (Draft) → 
  ↓
Request Review → Address Feedback → Update Branch →
  ↓
Approve → Merge (Squash/Rebase/Merge) → Delete Branch
Use draft PRs for early feedback. Update the branch with more commits or rebase — avoid force pushes on shared PR branches.
.git.Collaboration.Code review.exp
Code review is the process of examining code changes before merging. Focus on correctness, style, design, and test coverage. Use inline comments, suggestion blocks, and review approval flows.
.git.Collaboration.Merge queue.exp
Merge queues group PRs and test them together before merging to main. Prevents semver conflicts where individual PRs pass CI but fail when combined. Available on GitHub with merge queues beta.
.git.Collaboration.PR & Issue templates.exp
Templates standardize PR and issue creation with YAML frontmatter or Markdown forms. Use checkboxes, dropdowns, and text areas to gather consistent information.
.git.Collaboration.GH CLI deep.exp
The gh CLI provides full GitHub workflow from the terminal: create PRs, manage issues, run workflows, review code, and manage releases. Use gh extension for custom functionality.
.git.Advanced Git.git cherry-pick.exp
Apply specific commits from one branch onto another. Useful for selective porting of changes without merging entire branches.
.git.Advanced Git.Sparse checkout.exp
Sparse checkout lets you work with only a subset of files in the working tree. Ideal for monorepos where you only need specific directories. Combined with cone mode for performance.
.git.Advanced Git.Shallow & deep clone.exp
Shallow clones (--depth 1) fetch only the latest commits — fast for CI. Deep clones fetch full history. --depth=N fetches N commits. --shallow-since filters by date.
.git.Advanced Git.Partial clone.exp

Partial clones defer downloading blob data until needed. --filter=blob:none skips all blobs at clone time — files are fetched on checkout. --filter=tree:0 skips trees too. Dramatically reduces clone time.
.git.Advanced Git.git bundle.exp
Bundle packs commits and refs into a single file for offline transport. Transfer via USB, email, or air-gapped networks. The receiver can pull or fetch from the bundle as if it were a remote.
.git.Advanced Git.git archive.exp
Export a snapshot of the repository as a tar or zip archive without the .git directory. Perfect for distribution, deployments, or sharing code without history.
.git.Advanced Git.git bisect run.exp
Bisect run automates git bisect by passing a script that exits 0 (good) or non-zero (bad). Git will binary-search the range and find the first bad commit automatically.
.git.Advanced Git.git blame & annotations.exp
git blame annotates each line with the commit, author, and date that last modified it. Useful for tracking when/why a change was made. -L limits to line range; -w ignores whitespace.
.git.Advanced Git.git grep.exp
git grep searches files in any revision, not just working tree. Faster than system grep by limiting to tracked files. Supports regex, line numbers, file names, and context.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.Blob objects.exp

Blobs store file content identified by SHA-1 hash. The blob hash is deterministic — same content always produces the same hash (content-addressable). Blobs don't store filenames — that's the tree's job.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.Tree objects.exp
Trees represent directory snapshots. A tree maps filenames → blob hashes (files) or sub-tree hashes (directories), plus permissions. Trees are also content-addressed by hash.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.Commit objects.exp
A commit is a snapshot pointer containing: tree hash (root directory), parent commit hash(es), author/committer info, timestamp, and message. The commit hash is what you see in git log.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.Packfiles.exp

Git stores objects in two forms: loose (individual files in .git/objects/) and packed (efficient deltas in .git/objects/pack/). Packfiles compress objects using delta encoding — storing only differences between versions.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.git gc.exp
Garbage collection packs loose objects into packfiles and prunes unreachable objects. Auto-runs on threshold (6700 loose objects). Manual gc optimizes repository size and performance.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.git fsck.exp
Filesystem check verifies repository integrity by scanning all objects and references. Detects dangling blobs, missing objects, and corruption. Run after hardware failures or suspicious behavior.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.git rev-parse.exp
rev-parse resolves any Git revision specifier to a SHA-1 hash. Parse branch names, tags, relative refs (HEAD~3), dates (@{yesterday}), or ranges. Essential for scripting and plumbing.
.git.Git Objects & Plumbing.git cat-file.exp
cat-file is the primary plumbing command to inspect Git objects. Pass type flag (-t), size (-s), pretty-print (-p), or check existence (-e). View any object by hash or revision.
.git.GitHub Actions.Actions (CI/CD).exp
GitHub Actions automates workflows (test, build, deploy) triggered by events like push, PR, or schedule. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/.
.git.GitHub Actions.Workflow syntax.exp

Workflow YAML defines triggers (on), jobs (parallel by default), steps (sequential), actions (reusable units), and expressions (${{ }}). Use if: conditionals, concurrency groups, and environment targets.
.git.GitHub Actions.Matrix builds.exp
Matrix strategies run the same job across multiple configurations (OS, version, environment). Use include to add variants, exclude to remove, and fail-fast to cancel all on failure.
.git.GitHub Actions.Reusable workflows.exp
Call a workflow from another workflow using the uses keyword with secrets and inputs. Reusable workflows reduce duplication across repos. They must be in a public repo or same org.
.git.GitHub Actions.Environment protection.exp
GitHub Environments add protection rules: required reviewers, wait timers, and deployment branch restrictions. Combined with secrets per-environment for secure deployments.
.git.GitHub Actions.Self-hosted runners.exp
Self-hosted runners run Actions on your own infrastructure. Register at repo/org/enterprise level. Use labels for routing. Ideal for custom hardware, internal networks, or cost savings at scale.
.git.GitHub Actions.OIDC.exp
OpenID Connect (OIDC) lets workflows authenticate to cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, HashiCorp) without storing long-lived secrets. Exchange a JWT token for temporary cloud credentials.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Issues & Projects.exp
GitHub Issues track bugs, features, and tasks. Projects organize issues into boards with columns for planning and tracking work.
.git.GitHub Advanced.GitHub Pages.exp
Host static websites directly from a repository. Configure source branch and folder in Settings, then access at username.github.io/repo.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Forks & Upstream.exp

Fork a repository to contribute without direct write access. Sync your fork by adding the original repo as an upstream remote.

Fork + Upstream Flow:
UPSTREAM (original/repo)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ fork (copy on GitHub)
ORIGIN (your/repo on GitHub)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ clone
LOCAL (your machine)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ add upstream remote
  ●──●──●──●  (sync from upstream)
Use `origin` for your fork, `upstream` for the original. Send PRs from your fork back to upstream.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Projects (Beta).exp
GitHub Projects provides spreadsheet-style project tracking with custom fields, views (table, board, roadmap), and automation. Link issues/PRs across repos in a single org-level project.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Discussions.exp
GitHub Discussions provide a forum-style space for Q&A, ideas, and announcements — separate from the issue tracker. Useful for community engagement, RFCs, and collective decision-making.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Codespaces.exp
GitHub Codespaces provides cloud-hosted development environments configured by a devcontainer.json file. Start, stop, and customize VSCode environments from any browser or VS Code.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Dependabot.exp
Dependabot automates dependency updates by scanning manifest files and opening PRs for out-of-date packages. Configure version strategies, schedule, and reviewers in dependabot.yml.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Secret scanning & code scanning.exp
Secret scanning detects exposed credentials (keys, tokens) in repos. Code scanning (CodeQL) finds vulnerabilities via static analysis. Both integrate into PR checks to prevent merging insecure code.
.git.GitHub Advanced.Branch protection rules.exp
Branch protection rules enforce workflows: require PRs, status checks, up-to-date branches, signed commits, or specific reviewers. Essential for main branch security and compliance.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.GitLab CI.exp
GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml with stages, jobs, and runners. Supports Kubernetes integration, auto DevOps, and built-in container registry. Jobs run in isolated environments.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.BitBucket Pipelines.exp
BitBucket Pipelines uses bitbucket-pipelines.yml for CI/CD with built-in Docker support and deployment environments. Integrates with Jira for traceable deployments.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.Gerrit.exp

Gerrit is a code review system for Git that uses a push-to-review workflow. Changes are pushed to refs/for/<branch> and must be reviewed and +2'ed before submission. Common in large-scale enterprise projects.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.Git LFS.exp
Git LFS (Large File Storage) replaces large files (binaries, assets, models) with text pointers in the repo while storing content on a remote server. Essential for game dev, ML, and design assets.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.Git submodules.exp
Embed one repository inside another as a submodule. Pins a specific commit so the parent repo tracks exact dependency versions.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.Submodules vs subtrees.exp

Submodules reference external repos as pointers; subtrees merge external code directly into your repo. Subtrees give you full control (no external dependency), submodules keep history separate. Choose subtrees for stability, submodules for active external development.
.git.GitOps & Platforms.Monorepo strategies.exp
Monorepos store multiple projects in a single repository. Strategies: Nx/Turborepo for JS, Bazel for polyglot, Gradle for JVM, and Pants for Python. Tooling handles selective builds and tests.
.git.Best Practices.Gitignore.exp
The .gitignore file specifies intentionally untracked files (build artifacts, dependencies, env files) that Git should ignore.
.git.Best Practices.Commit Messages.exp
Write clear, conventional commit messages. Use imperative mood, capitalize first word, and include scope/tag for automatic changelogs.
.git.Best Practices.Branch Strategies.exp
Common branching models: Git Flow (develop/release/hotfix), GitHub Flow (feature branches -> main), and trunk-based development for CI/CD.
.git.Best Practices.Signing Commits.exp
Sign commits with GPG or SSH keys to verify authorship. GitHub marks signed commits as Verified for trust and authenticity.
.git.Best Practices.Squashing Commits.exp
Combine multiple commits into one for cleaner history. Use squash during merge on GitHub or interactive rebase locally.
.git.Best Practices.Conventional commits.exp

Conventional Commits specification standardizes commit messages: type(scope): description. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert. Enables automatic versioning and changelog generation.
.git.Best Practices.Semantic versioning with tags.exp
Semantic versioning (semver): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR = breaking changes, MINOR = features, PATCH = fixes. Tag releases with annotated tags and push them to trigger deployment workflows.
.git.Best Practices.Trivial merges.exp

Trivial merges (fast-forward only) keep linear history without merge commits. Use when feature branches have a single commit or no divergent history. Configure branch settings to require linear history.
.git.Best Practices.Clean history.exp

A clean Git history is readable, searchable, and bisectable. Guidelines: one logical change per commit, write descriptive messages, squash WIP/fixup commits, rebase before merging, avoid merge commits in feature branches.
.git.Best Practices.Code review checklist.exp

A systematic code review checklist covers: correctness (edge cases, error handling), security (input validation, auth), performance (N+1 queries, memory), style (project conventions), testing (coverage, meaningful tests), and documentation (API, README).
.git.Best Practices.CI gates.exp

CI gates are automated checks that block merging if they fail. Common gates: lint, type check, unit tests, integration tests, build, security scan, coverage threshold. Combine with branch protection to enforce.
.go.Getting Started.What is Go.exp

Go is a compiled, statically-typed language designed for simplicity, concurrency, and fast execution. Built by Google for systems programming and microservices. Common mistake: assuming Go is like Java/C# — Go has no classes, no inheritance, no exceptions, and no generics (pre-1.18). Best practice: embrace Go's simplicity — prefer composition over inheritance, use explicit error returns instead of exceptions, and leverage goroutines for concurrency.
.go.Getting Started.Go Syntax.exp

Go syntax emphasizes clarity and brevity. Uses curly braces for blocks and semicolons are optional. Comments use // or /* */. Common mistake: placing the opening brace on a new line — Go requires the opening brace on the same line as the declaration (enforced by gofmt). Best practice: run gofmt or go fmt on all code to enforce canonical formatting; use meaningful names even for short variables.
.go.Getting Started.Your First Program.exp

Every Go program starts with a package declaration and a main() function for executables. The package must be 'main' for a runnable binary. Common mistake: using 'print' or 'println' for serious output — prefer fmt.Println for formatted output to stdout. Best practice: structure all real programs with package main, a main() function, and use imports for standard library packages rather than built-in print.
.go.Getting Started.Go Playground.exp
The Go Playground (go.dev/play) lets you write, run, and share Go code in your browser. Great for experimentation and sharing bug repros.
.go.Getting Started.go run vs go build.exp
go run compiles and runs a program without producing a binary. go build produces a standalone executable in the current directory.
.go.Getting Started.GOPATH & Module Basics.exp
GOPATH was the original workspace location. Modern Go uses modules (go mod) instead. GOPATH is still used for global binary installs via go install.
.go.Variables & Types.Variable Declaration.exp

Declare variables using var, const, or short declaration (:=). Types can be explicit or inferred. Common mistake: using := outside a function — it only works inside function bodies; package-level declarations require var or const. Best practice: use := for local variables with clear initialization; use var for zero-value declarations (var x int); use const for compile-time constants. Scope and shadowing: inner scopes can redeclare a name from an outer scope — the inner declaration shadows the outer one. Always check that you haven't accidentally shadowed a package-level variable inside a function using :=.
.go.Variables & Types.Primitive Types.exp

Go includes bool, string, int, uint, float32, float64, complex64, and more. Integer types have fixed sizes (int8, int16, int32, int64). Rune is an alias for int32 representing a Unicode code point. Complex numbers (complex64, complex128) are first-class with real+imag syntax. String literals come in two forms: raw (backtick-quoted, no escapes) and interpreted (double-quoted, supports \n, \t, etc.). Common mistake: confusing int and int64 — int is platform-dependent (32 or 64 bit); int64 is always 64 bit. Use int unless you need a specific size.
.go.Variables & Types.Type Conversion.exp
Explicitly convert between compatible types using T(value) syntax. Go does NOT do implicit type conversion.
.go.Variables & Types.Constants.exp

Constants are immutable values that must be known at compile time. Use const keyword with iota for enumerated constants. iota resets to 0 in each const block and increments by 1 for each line. Common mistake: thinking constants can be computed at runtime — they must be determinable at compile time, so function calls or runtime expressions don't work. Best practice: use iota for sequential numeric enums; use typed constants (const X type = val) for type safety; use untyped constants for flexibility in expressions.
.go.Variables & Types.Zero Values.exp
Variables declared without an explicit initial value are assigned a zero value: 0 for numbers, false for bool, "" for strings, nil for pointers/slices/maps/channels/interfaces.
.go.Variables & Types.Short Declaration (:=).exp
Use := inside functions for type-inferred variable declaration and assignment. Cannot use at package level. At least one variable on left must be new.
.go.Variables & Types.Type Inference.exp
Go infers types from the right-hand side of := or var declarations. Untyped numeric constants get default types (int, float64, complex128) when needed.
.go.Operators.Arithmetic Operators.exp
Standard math: +, -, *, /, %. Go supports ++ and -- but only as statements, not expressions.
.go.Operators.Comparison Operators.exp
Compare values using ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=. Return boolean results. Valid for comparable types.
.go.Operators.Logical Operators.exp
Combine booleans with &&, ||, and !. Short-circuit evaluation is supported: && stops on first false, || stops on first true.
.go.Operators.Bitwise Operators.exp
Manipulate bits using &, |, ^, <<, >>, and &^ (AND NOT, a.k.a. bit clear).
.go.Operators.Increment/Decrement Statements.exp
++ and -- are statements, not expressions. They cannot be used in assignments or comparisons. Only postfix notation is allowed.
.go.Operators.Operator Precedence.exp
Go operator precedence from highest to lowest: *, /, %, <<, >>, &, &^; then +, -, |, ^; then ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=; then &&; then ||. Use parentheses to clarify.
.go.Control Flow.If & Else.exp
Standard conditional branching. Parentheses are optional; braces are required. If can include a short statement before the condition.
.go.Control Flow.Switch Statement.exp
Multi-way branching on a single expression. Cases don't fall through by default. Use fallthrough keyword explicitly when needed.
.go.Control Flow.For Loop.exp
Go has only one loop construct. Use for with init, condition, and post, or as while/infinite loop.
.go.Control Flow.Break & Continue.exp
Exit loops early with break or skip to next iteration with continue. Labels let you break/continue outer loops.
.go.Control Flow.Label Statements.exp
Labels mark a position in code for break, continue, or goto. Use them to exit or continue outer loops from nested inner loops.
.go.Control Flow.Type Switch.exp
A switch that asserts the dynamic type of an interface value. Each case specifies a type. Useful with interface{} or any.
.go.Control Flow.Defer.exp
Defer postpones a function call until the surrounding function returns. Deferred calls are executed in LIFO order. Arguments are evaluated immediately.
.go.Control Flow.Goto.exp

Goto jumps to a labeled statement within the same function. Cannot jump over variable declarations or into blocks. Use sparingly — goto is widely discouraged in idiomatic Go. Prefer structured control flow (for, if/else, switch) over goto. The only acceptable uses are breaking out of deeply nested loops or error cleanup in generated code.
.go.Functions.Function Declaration.exp
Define functions with func keyword. Specify parameter types and return types explicitly.
.go.Functions.Multiple Return Values.exp
Functions can return multiple values. Commonly used for (result, error) pattern.
.go.Functions.Named Return Values.exp
Name return values for cleaner code. They act as variables initialized to zero values. A bare return returns the current values of named returns.
.go.Functions.Variadic Functions.exp
Accept variable number of arguments using ... syntax. Creates a slice of the arguments. Only the last parameter can be variadic.
.go.Functions.Anonymous Functions & Closures.exp
Functions without a name assigned to variables or passed directly. Closures capture surrounding variables by reference, not by value.
.go.Functions.init Functions.exp
init() runs automatically when a package is initialized, before main(). Multiple init() calls in a file run in order; across files they run in lexical order. No parameters or return values.
.go.Functions.Function Values.exp
Functions are first-class values in Go. They can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions (higher-order functions).
.go.Collections.Arrays.exp
Fixed-size sequences with homogeneous elements. Size is part of the type ([3]int != [4]int). Passed by value (copied) when assigned or passed to functions.
.go.Collections.Slices.exp
Dynamic-length views backed by an underlying array. Slice expression [low:high] creates a view into an existing array or slice without copying data.
.go.Collections.Slice Internals.exp
A slice is a descriptor: pointer to underlying array, length, capacity. Append grows by doubling the capacity up to 1024, then ~25% growth. Slicing beyond len but within cap reuses the backing array.
.go.Collections.Maps.exp
Unordered key-value collections built on hash tables. Keys must be comparable types (== works). Maps are reference types; zero value is nil.
.go.Collections.Range Loops.exp
Iterate with range over slices, maps, strings, channels. For slices: returns index, value. For maps: returns key, value. For strings: returns byte index, rune.
.go.Collections.make vs new.exp
make(T, args) creates slices, maps, and channels (initialized, ready to use). new(T) allocates zero value and returns *T. make returns T (not *T).
.go.Pointers & References.Pointer Basics.exp

Pointers hold memory addresses. Use & to get a variable's address and * to dereference (read or write through the pointer). Zero value is nil. Go has automatic memory management with garbage collection — allocated memory is freed when no references remain. Unlike C/C++, you don't manually free memory. The GC runs concurrently with a short STW pause. Escape analysis determines whether values live on the stack or heap: if a pointer escapes the function scope, the value is heap-allocated.
.go.Pointers & References.Pointers to Structs.exp
Access struct fields through pointers using dot notation. Go automatically dereferences struct pointers for field access.
.go.Pointers & References.Pointers as Parameters.exp
Go is pass-by-value. Use pointers to allow a function to modify its caller's data, or to avoid copying large structs.
.go.Pointers & References.new() Function.exp
new(T) allocates zero-value storage for T and returns *T. It never returns nil. Equivalent to &T{} for structs. Use when you need a pointer to a zero-valued instance.
.go.Pointers & References.Pointer vs Value Receiver.exp
Use pointer receiver (*T) when the method modifies the receiver, or when the struct is large. Use value receiver (T) for small, immutable types. Pointer receiver avoids copying on each call.
.go.Structs & Composition.Struct Definition.exp
Group related fields into a struct type. Exported fields start with uppercase letter for visibility across packages.
.go.Structs & Composition.Struct Tags.exp
Struct tags are metadata strings attached to fields, commonly used by encoding/json, validation libraries, and ORMs. Tags appear after the field type in backticks.
.go.Structs & Composition.Anonymous (Embedded) Fields.exp
Embed types without a field name. Their methods and fields are promoted to the embedding struct. Not inheritance, but composition.
.go.Structs & Composition.Struct Methods.exp
Attach methods to types using receiver syntax. Methods are functions with a receiver parameter between func and method name.
.go.Structs & Composition.Pointer Receivers.exp
Pointer receiver allows modification of the struct. Value receiver works on a copy. Consistency: if any method has pointer receiver, all should.
.go.Structs & Composition.Struct Comparison.exp
Structs with only comparable fields (no slices, maps, or functions) can be compared with == and used as map keys.
.go.Structs & Composition.Constructor Functions.exp
Go has no constructors. Use factory functions (NewXxx or New) that return a pointer to a struct, optionally performing validation or initialization.
.go.Interfaces.Interface Definition.exp

Define interfaces as a set of method signatures. Any type implementing all methods implicitly satisfies the interface. Interfaces are satisfied implicitly. Methods vs functions: a method is a function with a receiver parameter (func (t Type) MethodName()). Methods can only be defined on types within the same package. Functions are standalone (func Name()). Use methods when behavior depends on receiver state; use functions for stateless operations. Prefer methods for types that model domain concepts.
.go.Interfaces.Implicit Implementation.exp
Go uses structural typing. A type satisfies an interface simply by implementing its methods. No explicit declaration like 'implements' is needed.
.go.Interfaces.Type Assertions.exp
Extract the concrete value from an interface using value.(Type). The two-value form prevents panics: val, ok := x.(Type).
.go.Interfaces.Empty Interface (any).exp
interface{} (or 'any' in Go 1.18+) accepts values of any type. Used before generics for containers. Now used when truly any type is needed.
.go.Interfaces.Interface Composition.exp
Combine interfaces by embedding them in a new interface. A type must implement all embedded interfaces' methods to satisfy the composed interface.
.go.Interfaces.Interface Values & Nil.exp
An interface value is a (type, value) pair. An interface is nil only when both the type and value are nil. A nil pointer inside a non-nil interface is not nil!
.go.Interfaces.Best Practices (Accept interfaces, return structs).exp
Accept interfaces to allow flexibility from callers; return concrete types so callers can access fields and methods without type assertions.
.go.Error Handling.Error Interface.exp
Errors are values implementing the built-in error interface: Error() string. Functions return nil to indicate success.
.go.Error Handling.Error Checking.exp

Idiomatic Go checks errors immediately. Use guard clauses for early returns. Handle errors once — don't ignore or handle them multiple times. For debugging, use stack traces: when a panic occurs, Go prints the full goroutine stack. Use debug.PrintStack() or runtime/debug.Stack() to capture stacks without panicking. The errors package can also include stack information with libraries like pkg/errors or fmt.Errorf+%w for error chains.
.go.Error Handling.Custom Error Types.exp
Create custom error types by implementing the Error() string method. Custom types carry additional context for callers to inspect.
.go.Error Handling.Sentinel Errors.exp
Sentinel errors are predefined error variables (convention: names start with Err) used as sentinel values for specific failure conditions. Compare with == or use errors.Is.
.go.Error Handling.Error Wrapping.exp
Use fmt.Errorf with %w to wrap errors, preserving the original error for errors.Is and errors.As. %W (uppercase) is NOT valid; use lowercase %w.
.go.Error Handling.errors.Is and errors.As.exp
errors.Is(err, target) checks if any error in the chain matches target. errors.As(err, targetType) finds the first error of a given type. Both work through wrapping layers.
.go.Error Handling.Panic & Recover.exp
Panic stops normal execution and unwinds the stack. Recover catches a panic inside a deferred function. Only use panics for truly exceptional, unrecoverable situations.
.go.Concurrency.Goroutines.exp
Lightweight concurrent execution managed by the Go runtime (not OS threads). Launch with go keyword. Goroutines share the same address space; use channels or sync primitives for coordination.
.go.Concurrency.Channels.exp
Typed conduits for goroutine communication. Use ch := make(chan T) to create. Send: ch <- v. Receive: v := <-ch. Block until both ends are ready.
.go.Concurrency.Buffered Channels.exp
Channels with capacity: make(chan T, cap). Send blocks only when buffer is full; receive blocks only when buffer is empty. Reduces synchronization points.
.go.Concurrency.Range & Close.exp
Sender closes a channel with close(ch). Receiver can range over the channel, receiving values until the channel is closed. Detect closed channels with v, ok := <-ch.
.go.Concurrency.Select Statement.exp
Wait on multiple channel operations simultaneously. Select blocks until one case is ready. Use default for non-blocking operations. Use nil channels to disable cases.
.go.Concurrency.WaitGroup.exp
sync.WaitGroup blocks until all goroutines finish. Add(n) increments the counter, Done() decrements, Wait() blocks until counter reaches 0. Typically Add is called before starting goroutines.
.go.Concurrency.sync.Once.exp
sync.Once ensures a function is executed exactly once, even across multiple goroutines. Used for lazy initialization, singleton setup, and one-time configuration.
.go.Concurrency.Mutex & RWMutex.exp
sync.Mutex provides mutual exclusion. Lock/Unlock protects critical sections. sync.RWMutex allows multiple readers or one writer. RLock/RUnlock for read-only access.
.go.Concurrency.Worker Pools.exp
Fixed number of goroutines processing jobs from a channel. Controls concurrency, limits resource usage. Use a buffered channel for jobs and close it to signal completion.
.go.Concurrency.Fan-in / Fan-out.exp
Fan-out: multiple goroutines read from one channel (distributes work). Fan-in: multiple goroutines write to one channel (multiplexing results). Use a merge function with sync.WaitGroup.
.go.Packages & Imports.Package Declaration.exp
Every Go file belongs to a package. Executables use 'package main', libraries use any descriptive name. One directory = one package.
.go.Packages & Imports.Importing Packages.exp

Use import for dependencies. Standard library packages have short paths; remote packages use full module paths. go mod tidy manages required versions. Key tooling commands: go doc shows documentation for any package/symbol (go doc fmt.Println), go clean removes built artifacts (go clean -cache), go version prints the Go version. Use go doc for quick reference without leaving the terminal.
.go.Packages & Imports.Exported Names.exp
Capitalized names are exported (public), lowercase are unexported (package-private). Exported names are accessible across packages; unexported only within the same package.
.go.Packages & Imports.Package Initialization (init).exp
init() runs when a package is imported. Multiple init()s across a package run in file name order. init() functions cannot be called directly. They run before main().
.go.Packages & Imports.Internal Packages.exp
Packages under an 'internal/' directory are only importable by code rooted at the internal's parent. Enforces encapsulation boundaries within a module.
.go.Packages & Imports.Blank Imports.exp
Import a package solely for its side effects (init() execution) using _. The dot alias '.' imports all exported names into the current namespace.
.go.Packages & Imports.Import Cycles.exp
Go does not allow import cycles. A cannot import B if B imports A (directly or indirectly). Break cycles by extracting shared types into a third package, or using interfaces.
.go.File I/O.Reading Files (os.ReadFile).exp
os.ReadFile (Go 1.16+) reads a file into memory. Replaces deprecated ioutil.ReadFile. Use for small files. For large files, use bufio.Scanner or io.Copy with limited buffer.
.go.File I/O.Writing Files (os.WriteFile).exp
os.WriteFile writes data to a file, creating or truncating it. The third argument is file permissions (Unix mode). Replaces deprecated ioutil.WriteFile.
.go.File I/O.Buffered I/O (bufio).exp
bufio provides buffered reading and writing for efficiency. bufio.Scanner reads line-by-line (default) or via SplitFunc. bufio.Writer buffers writes to reduce syscalls.
.go.File I/O.io.ReadAll.exp
io.ReadAll reads from an io.Reader until EOF, returning the full byte slice. Replaces ioutil.ReadAll. Works with any reader: files, HTTP bodies, strings, etc.
.go.File I/O.io.Copy.exp
io.Copy copies from an io.Reader to an io.Writer until EOF. Efficiently streams data without loading everything into memory. Returns bytes copied and any error.
.go.File I/O.File Permissions & ioutil Deprecation.exp
ioutil is deprecated since Go 1.16. Replace ioutil.ReadFile with os.ReadFile, ioutil.WriteFile with os.WriteFile, ioutil.ReadAll with io.ReadAll, ioutil.TempFile with os.CreateTemp.
.go.File I/O.Directory Operations.exp
Read directories with os.ReadDir (returns sorted []os.DirEntry). Walk directory trees with filepath.Walk or filepath.WalkDir. Create dirs with os.MkdirAll.
.go.Testing.Test Functions.exp
Write tests in *_test.go files. Test functions follow func TestXxx(t *testing.T). Use t.Error/t.Fatal for failures. Run with go test.
.go.Testing.Table-Driven Tests.exp
Define test cases as a slice of structs. Iterate over them for clean, DRY tests that cover many inputs. Each case can include a name for clear failure output.
.go.Testing.Subtests.exp
Run subtests with t.Run(name, fn) for hierarchical test organization. Subtests share setup/teardown and can be run selectively with go test -run pattern.
.go.Testing.Test Helpers.exp
Helper functions in tests reduce boilerplate. Call t.Helper() to mark a function as a test helper so failure line numbers point to the caller, not the helper.
.go.Testing.Test Coverage.exp
Go has built-in coverage. Run go test -cover to see percentage. go test -coverprofile=coverage.out generates a profile. Use go tool cover -html=coverage.out for visual report.
.go.Testing.Fuzzing.exp
Go 1.18+ fuzzing randomly generates inputs to find bugs. Fuzz test: func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F). Seed with f.Add(), then f.Fuzz(targetFn).
.go.Testing.Benchmarks.exp
Measure performance with BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B). b.N is adjusted by the framework for stable timing. Use b.ResetTimer() and b.ReportAllocs() for accurate measurements.
.go.Standard Library.fmt Package.exp
Formatted I/O with Print, Printf, Println, Sprintf, Fprintf. Verbs: %v (value), %+v (with fields), %T (type), %d (int), %s (string), %#v (Go-syntax).
.go.Standard Library.strings & strconv Packages.exp
strings: Contains, Split, Join, ToUpper, ToLower, Trim, Replace, Builder (efficient string building). strconv: Atoi, Itoa, ParseBool, FormatFloat, ParseInt.
.go.Standard Library.io Package.exp
Core I/O interfaces: io.Reader, io.Writer, io.Closer, io.Seeker. Utility functions: io.Copy, io.ReadAll, io.MultiReader, io.TeeReader, io.LimitReader.
.go.Standard Library.encoding/json Package.exp
Marshal/Unmarshal Go values to/from JSON. Struct tags control field names, omitempty skips zero values. Use json.NewDecoder for streaming JSON (files, HTTP).
.go.Standard Library.flag Package.exp
Parse command-line flags with flag package. Supports -flag, -flag=x, --flag (double dash works). Types: String, Int, Bool, Duration, Float64, or custom flag.Value.
.go.Standard Library.log Package.exp
Simple logging to stderr with timestamps. log.Printf, log.Fatalf (calls os.Exit(1)), log.Panicf (calls panic). Use log.New for custom output, flags, and prefix.
.go.Standard Library.os/exec Package.exp
Run external commands. exec.Command(name, args...). cmd.Output() returns stdout, cmd.CombinedOutput() returns both. Pipe stdin/stdout/stderr for interactive commands.
.go.Standard Library.time Package.exp
Time and duration with nanosecond precision. Parse (reference time: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006 = 1 2 3 4 5 6 -7). Timer/Ticker for events. Sleep for pauses.
.go.Standard Library.context Package.exp
Context propagates deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values. Create with context.Background() or context.TODO(). Derive with WithCancel, WithTimeout, WithDeadline, WithValue.
.go.Standard Library.sync Package.exp
Synchronization primitives: Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, Once, Cond, Pool, Map (concurrent-safe map). sync.Map is optimized for read-heavy or append-only patterns.
.go.Modules & Tooling.Go Modules.exp

Go modules define a project's dependencies and versioning. go.mod declares the module path and requirements. go.sum contains checksums for reproducibility. Cross-compilation is built-in: set GOOS and GOARCH env vars to target different platforms (GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build). Common targets: linux/amd64, darwin/amd64, darwin/arm64, windows/amd64. Use go tool dist list to see all supported targets. Cross-compilation doesn't require additional toolchains — Go includes all targets in the standard distribution.
.go.Modules & Tooling.Workspace Mode.exp
Go 1.18+ workspace mode (go.work) lets you work on multiple modules simultaneously. Useful for local development across interdependent modules. go work init creates the file.
.go.Modules & Tooling.Build Tags.exp
Build tags (or build constraints) conditionally compile files. Placed at top of file: //go:build tag. Multiple tags combine with &&, ||, and !. Use for platform-specific code or feature flags.
.go.Modules & Tooling.go generate.exp
go generate scans //go:generate directives to run tools automatically. Commonly used for code generation: protobufs, stringers, mocks, and embed. Run with go generate ./....
.go.Modules & Tooling.go tooling (vet, fmt, fix).exp
go vet detects suspicious constructs (e.g., unreachable code, wrong Printf verbs). go fmt automatically formats code to canonical style. go fix updates old API usage to newer versions.
.go.Modules & Tooling.Dependency Management (go get).exp
go get manages module dependencies. Latest compatible version: go get pkg@latest. Specific version: go get pkg@v1.2.3. Upgrade minor: go get -u ./.... Remove unused: go mod tidy.
.go.Modules & Tooling.Generics.exp
Go 1.18+ supports type parameters for functions and types. Use constraints (interface with type sets) to restrict acceptable types. 'any' is a shortcut for interface{}. Comparable constraint for ==.
.go.Networking.HTTP Server (net/http).exp
Build HTTP servers with http.HandleFunc or http.Handler interface. http.ListenAndServe starts the server. Default mux is http.DefaultServeMux.
.go.Networking.HTTP Client.exp
http.Client with Get, Post, Do methods. Respect context cancellation, always close response body, set timeouts to avoid hanging connections.
.go.Networking.Routing & ServeMux (Go 1.22+).exp
Go 1.22 enhanced the default mux with method-based routing and path parameters using {param} and {param...} patterns.
.go.Networking.Middleware Pattern.exp
Middleware wraps http.Handler to add cross-cutting concerns: logging, auth, recovery, rate limiting, CORS. Use a function that takes and returns http.Handler.
.go.Networking.Templates (html/template).exp
html/template generates safe HTML output with automatic context-aware escaping. Use template.ParseFiles or template.New(). Execute with a data struct and func map.
.go.Networking.TLS & HTTPS.exp
Use http.ListenAndServeTLS to serve HTTPS. Generate self-signed certs with crypto/tls or use Let's Encrypt via autocert. Always serve HTTPS in production.
.go.Networking.TCP & UDP Sockets.exp
Low-level networking with net.Dial (TCP/UDP) and net.Listen. Build custom protocols. Use bufio for line-based protocols. Always set deadlines.
.go.Database & SQL.database/sql Interface.exp
database/sql provides a generic SQL interface. Open a database with sql.Open (driver name + DSN). Use sql.DB for connection pooling. Run queries with Query, QueryRow, Exec.
.go.Database & SQL.Querying (Query & QueryRow).exp
Query returns *sql.Rows (cursor). Iterate with rows.Next() and rows.Scan(). QueryRow returns at most one row, returns sql.ErrNoRows if none. Always close rows.
.go.Database & SQL.Prepared Statements.exp
Prepare statements with db.Prepare for repeated execution. Prevents SQL injection and improves performance. Use $1, $2 (PostgreSQL) or ? (MySQL/SQLite) placeholders.
.go.Database & SQL.Transactions.exp
Use db.Begin() to start a transaction. tx.Exec, tx.Query within the transaction. Commit or Rollback. Ensures atomicity — all operations succeed or none do.
.go.Database & SQL.Connection Pooling.exp
sql.DB manages a connection pool. Configure with SetMaxOpenConns (max concurrent), SetMaxIdleConns (idle pool), SetConnMaxLifetime (connection age), SetConnMaxIdleTime.
.go.Database & SQL.Migrations (golang-migrate).exp
Manage schema changes with migration tools like golang-migrate/migrate. Migration files: 001_create_users.up.sql and 001_create_users.down.sql. Run up/down programmatically via CLI.
.go.Database & SQL.Database Drivers.exp
Register database drivers via blank imports. Common drivers: lib/pq (PostgreSQL), go-sql-driver/mysql (MySQL), mattn/go-sqlite3 (SQLite), mongo-driver (MongoDB).
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.Go Design Philosophy.exp

Learning Go emphasizes simplicity: no inheritance, no generics (until 1.18), no exceptions. Go favors composition over inheritance, explicit error handling, and readability over cleverness. Bodner calls this 'the boring language that gets things done'. The key insight: Go is designed for large teams maintaining code over years.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.nil & Zero Values Mental Model.exp

Know Go teaches the nil mental model: nil is a value, not an error. Nil slices have len=0 and can append to. Nil maps return zero values but panic on write. Nil interfaces have dynamic type nil (not just value nil). A nil pointer inside an interface makes it non-nil! Book insight: always think about what zero value means for your types.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.slog Structured Logging (Go 1.21+).exp

slog provides structured, leveled logging with key-value pairs. Levels: Debug, Info, Warn, Error. Use slog.New with JSONHandler or TextHandler. slog.Group for nested keys. slog.Attr for reusable attributes. The book recommendation: always use structured logging for production.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.errors.Join & Error Handling (Go 1.20+).exp

errors.Join combines multiple errors into one. Useful for batch validation and deferred cleanup. Know Go emphasizes thinking of errors as values that can be combined. Also new: fmt.Errorf with multiple %w (Go 1.20+ can wrap multiple errors).
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.maps & slices Packages (Go 1.21+).exp
Standard library packages for generic operations on maps and slices. No more hand-rolling Contains, DeleteFunc, Filter, etc. These are type-safe and efficient.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.Range over Iterators & func (Go 1.23+).exp

Go 1.23 adds range-over-iterator support. Any function with func(yield func(K, V) bool) can be ranged. The iter package provides Seq and Seq2 types. Libraries can expose iterators instead of requiring callbacks.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.Embedding (//go:embed).exp

go:embed embeds files into the binary at compile time. Supports files, directories, and globs. Embed as []byte, string, or embed.FS. Know Go recommends embed for static assets over reading files at runtime.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.Race Detector & Data Races.exp

The Go race detector catches concurrent unsafe access. Run with -race flag. Learning Go: if two goroutines access the same variable without synchronization, it's a race. Know Go says 'always run tests with -race before shipping'. The detector has ~false negative rate but no false positives.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.Profiling & pprof.exp

Go's built-in profiler: CPU, memory, goroutine, mutex, block profiles. Learning Go: always profile before optimizing. Use net/http/pprof for web apps, runtime/pprof for CLIs. The book's advice: 'measure, don't guess'.
.go.Learning Go & Best Practices.sync/atomic (Go 1.19+ Typed API).exp

Go 1.19+ added typed atomic values: atomic.Int64, atomic.Value, etc. Learning Go recommends them over sync.Mutex for simple counters and flags. The zero value is ready to use, no initialization needed.
.go.Ecosystem & Frameworks.CLI Applications (Cobra).exp

Build powerful CLI applications with Cobra (spf13/cobra), the framework behind kubectl, gh, and hugo. Cobra handles commands, flags, subcommands, and help generation. Commands are structured as a tree with Run functions. Use PersistentFlags for flags shared across subcommands and LocalFlags for command-specific ones. Best practice: organize commands in a cmd/ directory; use Viper (spf13/viper) with Cobra for config file support.
.go.Ecosystem & Frameworks.Web Frameworks (Gin, Echo).exp

While net/http suffices for many cases, frameworks like Gin (gin-gonic/gin) and Echo (labstack/echo) add routing with parameters, middleware chaining, request binding/validation, and grouped routes. Gin uses a radix tree router for high performance. Echo has built-in middleware for CORS, logging, recovery, and CSRF. Common mistake: adding a framework when the standard library would suffice — start with net/http and add a framework only when you need advanced routing or middleware. Best practice: use Gin for REST APIs with JSON; use Echo if you prefer a more minimalist API.
.go.Ecosystem & Frameworks.gRPC & Protocol Buffers.exp

gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for serialization. Define services in .proto files, generate Go code with protoc. Supports four service types: unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Common mistake: using gRPC for browser clients without gRPC-Web — browsers don't support HTTP/2 trailers directly. Best practice: use gRPC for internal microservices communication; use REST/JSON for external/public APIs; always set deadlines on gRPC calls to prevent hanging.
.go.Ecosystem & Frameworks.Logging Libraries (Zap, Zerolog).exp

For high-performance structured logging, Zap (uber-go/zap) and Zerolog (rs/zerolog) offer zero-allocation logging paths. Zap claims to be 10x faster than the standard log package in its SugaredLogger mode and 100x faster in its Logger mode. Zerolog uses a chained API. Both support leveled logging (Debug, Info, Warn, Error), structured fields, and JSON output. Best practice: use slog (standard library, Go 1.21+) for most applications; reach for Zap or Zerolog when profiling shows logging is a bottleneck.
.go.Ecosystem & Frameworks.Linters & Code Quality.exp

Maintain code quality with automated tools. golangci-lint runs multiple linters in parallel (staticcheck, revive, govet, errcheck, ineffassign, and 30+ more). staticcheck is a curated set of advanced vet checks. govulncheck scans dependencies for known CVEs. Best practice: run golangci-lint in CI for every PR; use golangci-lint run --fix to auto-fix issues; run govulncheck ./... before deploying to catch vulnerable dependencies.
.go.Advanced Go.Reflection.exp

The reflect package allows inspecting and manipulating types and values at runtime. Use reflect.TypeOf to get type information, reflect.ValueOf to get the value. Common use cases: serialization (encoding/json uses reflection), testing frameworks, and generic utilities. Common mistake: overusing reflection — it's slow, breaks type safety, and makes code hard to understand. Best practice: avoid reflection unless absolutely necessary; prefer type assertions, interfaces, or code generation (go generate) over reflect.
.go.Advanced Go.CGO Basics.exp

CGO lets Go call C code directly. Use import "C" with special comments (// #include ...) above it. CGO requires a C compiler and adds build complexity. Common use cases: linking with native libraries (SDL, OpenSSL), performance-critical sections, and system calls not exposed by Go. Common mistake: using CGO when a pure Go alternative exists — prefer cgo-free builds (CGO_ENABLED=0) for simpler cross-compilation. Best practice: isolate CGO code behind a pure Go interface; use //go:build cgo build tags for conditional compilation.
.go.Advanced Go.Escape Analysis.exp

Escape analysis is the compiler's optimization that determines whether a value can be allocated on the stack (fast, no GC overhead) or must be on the heap (GC-managed). A value escapes if its pointer is returned, stored in a global, or passed to a function that stores it. Use go build -gcflags='-m' to see escape analysis decisions. Common mistake: assuming small values stay on the stack — if a pointer escapes, even an int goes to the heap. Best practice: prefer value receivers over pointer receivers for small structs; avoid returning pointers to local variables when possible; use -gcflags='-m' to check your assumptions.
.go.Advanced Go.unsafe Package.exp

The unsafe package provides low-level primitives for bypassing Go's type safety. unsafe.Pointer converts between arbitrary pointer types. uintptr is an integer type for pointer arithmetic. Common use cases: efficient serialization, interacting with C libraries via CGO, and performance-critical hot paths. Common mistake: using unsafe for ordinary code — it breaks the memory safety guarantees that make Go reliable. Best practice: avoid unsafe in application code; if you must use it, keep it confined to a small, well-tested package with a safe public API; never use uintptr after the referenced object is garbage collected.
.go.Deployment & DevOps.Docker Multi-stage Builds.exp

Use multi-stage Docker builds to create minimal Go images. Stage 1: build the binary with golang:alpine. Stage 2: copy the binary to scratch or distroless (no OS, ~5MB image). Key benefits: tiny attack surface, fast deployment, no build tools in production. Common mistake: using ubuntu or full golang images in production — adds 300MB+ of unnecessary weight. Best practice: use scratch for pure Go binaries; use gcr.io/distroless/base if you need libc (CGO); use alpine:3.x if you need a shell and common tools; always set CGO_ENABLED=0 for static linking.
.go.Deployment & DevOps.Kubernetes Deployment.exp

Deploy Go services to Kubernetes with Deployments (replicas, rolling updates) and Services (networking). Use liveness probes to restart unhealthy pods and readiness probes to route traffic only when ready. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration. Common practice: expose metrics via Prometheus on a separate port, use healthz/readyz endpoints for probes, and set resource limits. Best practice: use client-go for in-cluster Go clients; always set context.WithTimeout for database and HTTP calls within pods; use the --restart=Never flag for one-shot jobs.
.godot.Getting Started.Hello Godot.exp

Godot uses a scene-based architecture. Every game is built with nodes arranged in a tree. The main script extends Node or one of its subclasses like Node2D, Sprite2D, or CharacterBody2D. GDScript is Godot's primary scripting language — it's Python-like and deeply integrated with the engine.

To start, create a scene with a Node2D root, attach a GDScript, and use the _ready() function for initialization. Run your scene to see the output.
.godot.Nodes & Scenes.Scene Tree.exp

Every Godot game is a tree of nodes. A scene is a collection of nodes organized hierarchically. Nodes can be added, removed, and rearranged at runtime. The SceneTree manages all active nodes and handles processing, rendering, and input.
.godot.GDScript Deep.Types & Syntax.exp

GDScript is dynamically typed with optional static typing. Use : Type to declare types. The @export annotation exposes variables in the inspector. @onready defers initialization until the node is ready. Match statements provide powerful pattern matching. Lambda functions with func syntax are first-class citizens.
.godot.Physics.PhysicsBody & Collisions.exp

Godot provides three physics body types: StaticBody (non-moving obstacles), RigidBody (full physics simulation), and CharacterBody (kinematic movement with custom logic). Use move_and_slide() for CharacterBody movement with automatic collision resolution. Collision layers and masks control which objects interact.
.godot.Signals & Groups.Event System.exp

Signals are Godot's built-in event system. They are type-safe and can be connected in the editor or via code. Custom signals are declared with the signal keyword. Groups tag nodes for bulk operations — call methods on all group members or get all nodes in a group. Use CONNECT_ONE_SHOT for one-time connections and CONNECT_DEFERRED for safe cross-frame calls.
.godot.Tilemaps & TileSets.TileSet & TileMapLayer.exp

The TileMapLayer node creates grid-based levels. A TileSet resource defines tiles with physics layers, navigation polygons, and terrain definitions for auto-tiling. You can add custom data per tile. Use terrain bits for automatic tile connection (like biome blending). Animated and random tiles add visual variety without code.
.godot.Shaders.CanvasItem & Spatial.exp

Godot supports three shader types: canvas_item (2D nodes), spatial (3D nodes), and particles (particle systems). Shaders use a GLSL-like language with Godot-specific uniforms and built-ins. VisualShader provides a node-based editor for creating shaders without code. Use uniforms to expose parameters to the inspector.
.godot.Input Handling.Input Map & Actions.exp

Godot's Input Map in Project Settings defines named actions bound to keys, buttons, or controller axes. Use Input.get_action_strength() for analog input (trigger pressure, joystick). The _input(event) callback processes individual events, while _process() or _physics_process() polling handles continuous input. Action names enable easy rebinding.
.godot.Animation.AnimationPlayer & AnimationTree.exp

The AnimationPlayer node animates any node property via keyframes. AnimationTree adds state machine blending with parameters. Blend spaces (1D/2D) blend between animations based on a parameter like speed or direction. Root motion allows animations to drive character movement. Use AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback to control state transitions.
.godot.Audio.Audio & Buses.exp

Godot uses an audio bus system for routing and effects. AudioStreamPlayer plays 2D sounds, AudioStreamPlayer2D/3D provides positional audio. The Audio bus layout allows adding effects like reverb, EQ, compression, and distortion per bus. Use AudioServer for global control. Stream players support OGG, MP3, and WAV formats.
.godot.Resources.Resource System.exp

Resources are reusable data containers saved as .tres (text) or .res (binary). They store game data like item definitions, stats, dialogue trees, and level configs. Create custom resources by extending the Resource class. Resources are cached by default — use preload() or load() to access them. Use .duplicate() for unique runtime instances.
.godot.Editor Plugins.@tool & EditorPlugin.exp

Scripts with the @tool annotation run in the editor, enabling live preview and custom tools. Use EditorPlugin to add docks, buttons, menu items, and inspector plugins. Create custom gizmos for in-editor manipulation. Build importers, exporters, and level editors that extend Godot's functionality without modifying the engine itself.
.godot.GDExtension.C++ Bindings.exp

GDExtension (Godot 4) allows writing C++ libraries that dynamically link without recompiling the engine. Ideal for performance-critical systems like custom physics, pathfinding, or audio processing. Classes registered via GDExtension are fully accessible from GDScript. Replaces the GDNative system from Godot 3. Uses the godot-cpp bindings library for C++ API access.
.godot.XR & Render.OpenXR + Render Modes.exp

Godot 4 offers three renderers: forward_plus (desktop, many lights, SSAO, glow), mobile (faster, simpler, for mobile), and gl_compatibility (OpenGL fallback). XR support via OpenXR — use XROrigin3D, XRCamera3D, and XRController3D. Supports hand tracking, passthrough AR, and standalone headsets.
.godot.2D Sprites & Viewports.Sprites, Layers & Effects.exp

Sprite2D displays textures with properties like centered, flip, offset, and modulate. AnimatedSprite2D plays sprite sheet animations via the SpriteFrames resource. CanvasLayer separates rendering layers for parallax or UI. Viewport renders to a texture for mini-maps, security cameras, or in-game screens. Light2D adds 2D dynamic lighting with shadow caster occlusion.
.godot.3D World & Lighting.3D Nodes & Environment.exp

Godot 4 uses Node3D as the base for all 3D nodes. MeshInstance3D renders meshes with materials. Lighting includes DirectionalLight3D (sun), OmniLight3D (point), and SpotLight3D (cone). WorldEnvironment controls sky, ambient light, fog, and tonemapping. VoxelGI and SDFGI provide real-time global illumination.
.godot.UI & Themes.Control Nodes & Theming.exp

Godot's UI system uses Control nodes: Button, Label, TextureRect, Panel, Container (HBox, VBox, Grid, Margin). Theme resources define colors, fonts, icons, and styles across all UI elements. Use Theme.duplicate() for runtime theme variants. StyleBoxFlat, StyleBoxTexture, and StyleBoxLine style individual elements.
.godot.Networking & Multiplayer.Multiplayer API.exp

Godot's high-level multiplayer system syncs game state across the network. MultiplayerSpawner auto-spawns scenes on all peers. MultiplayerSynchronizer replicates properties. Use the @rpc annotation for remote procedure calls with modes: authority, any_peer, call_local, reliable, unreliable. ENetMultiplayerPeer handles low-level connection.
.godot.Save & File Systems.File I/O & Save Games.exp

Godot provides FileAccess for binary and text file operations. ConfigFile manages INI-style configs with sections and keys. ResourceSaver and ResourceLoader persist/.res and .tres resources. Use OS.get_user_data_dir() for cross-platform save paths. ZIPPacker/ZIPReader handle compressed archives.
.godot.Performance Optimization.Profiling & Optimization.exp

Godot's Debugger has a Profiler tab (Script, Visual, Servers) and a Monitors tab (FPS, physics time, draw calls). Use Engine.get_frames_per_second() for runtime FPS. Key optimizations: sprite atlasing, MultiMesh instancing, object pooling, disabling off-screen nodes with VisibleOnScreenNotifier2D, and reducing draw calls via batching. Use Performance singleton for custom metrics.
.godot.Procedural Generation.Procedural Content.exp

Godot's FastNoiseLite provides Perlin, Simplex, Cellular, and Value noise for procedural generation. Use NoiseTexture2D to generate texture-based noise. SurfaceTool builds custom meshes programmatically. Combine with ArrayMesh for complex procedural geometry. Generate terrain heightmaps, cave systems, and infinite worlds using chunk-based loading.
.godot.Export & Deployment.Export Templates & Platforms.exp

Godot exports to Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, and Web. Configure export presets in Project > Export. Install export templates via Editor > Manage Export Templates. Set application name, version, icon, and orientation per platform. Use OS.get_name() for platform detection. For mobile: configure AAB/APK signing, permissions, and screen sizes.
.graphql.Getting Started.Schema.exp

A GraphQL schema defines the shape of available data and operations using the Schema Definition Language (SDL). It acts as a contract between client and server, specifying types, queries, and mutations.
.graphql.Getting Started.Queries.exp
Queries are read-only operations that request specific fields from the server. Clients specify exactly which fields they need, eliminating over- and under-fetching common in REST APIs.
.graphql.Getting Started.Mutations.exp
Mutations are write operations that create, update, or delete data. They follow the same field-selection pattern as queries but guarantee sequential execution and can return the modified state.
.graphql.Type System.Scalars.exp
GraphQL's built-in scalar types are Int, Float, String, Boolean, and ID. Custom scalars (Date, JSON, URL) can be defined for domain-specific data with custom validation and serialization logic.
.graphql.Type System.Objects.exp

Object types represent complex data structures with named fields, each returning a specific type. Fields can be required (`!`), have default values, and accept arguments for filtering or transformation.
.graphql.Type System.Enums.exp
Enums define a fixed set of allowed values, providing type safety and self-documentation. They are ideal for status fields, categories, roles, and any field with a constrained set of options.
.graphql.Type System.Interfaces.exp
Interfaces define common fields that multiple object types must implement. They enable polymorphic queries where a field can return different object types sharing the same base interface.
.graphql.Queries.Fields.exp

Clients specify exactly which fields to retrieve, enabling efficient data fetching. Fields can be nested to traverse relationships, and aliases allow requesting the same field with different arguments.
.graphql.Queries.Arguments.exp
Every field can accept arguments for filtering, sorting, or formatting. Arguments are strongly typed and can be required or optional with default values, enabling precise data retrieval.
.graphql.Queries.Aliases.exp

Aliases let you rename the result of a field to avoid naming conflicts when requesting the same field multiple times. They are essential for comparing data or fetching multiple resources in one query.
.graphql.Queries.Fragments.exp

Fragments are reusable units of field selections that reduce duplication in queries. They can spread across multiple query operations and support conditional inclusion with `... on Type` for union/interface types.
.graphql.Mutations.Input Types.exp
