Input types encapsulate mutation arguments as structured objects, enabling complex nested data inputs. They are defined with the `input` keyword and support required fields, defaults, and nested input types.
.graphql.Mutations.Return Types.exp

Mutations return modified or created objects to allow clients to update their local state immediately. Returning the full object is a best practice, and error information can be included via union types.
.graphql.Mutations.Error Handling.exp
GraphQL returns errors in a standardized `errors` array alongside partial data. Structured error handling with error codes, field-level validation, and union types provides better client diagnostics.
.graphql.Resolvers.Root Resolver.exp
Root resolvers are functions that resolve each field in the Query and Mutation types. They receive four arguments: parent, args, context, and info, and can perform any async operation.
.graphql.Resolvers.DataLoader.exp
DataLoader batches and caches database queries to solve the N+1 problem in GraphQL. It coalesces individual requests within a single event-loop tick into a single batched query.
.graphql.Resolvers.Batching.exp

Batching extends DataLoader to group multiple similar operations. It's especially useful for external API calls, database queries, and compute-intensive operations where combining requests improves performance.
.graphql.Subscriptions.WebSocket.exp
GraphQL subscriptions enable real-time communication over WebSockets. The `graphql-ws` library handles the WebSocket protocol, allowing clients to subscribe to events and receive push updates.
.graphql.Subscriptions.Event-based.exp
Subscriptions use an async iterator pattern with a publish-subscribe mechanism. Events are triggered by mutations or external sources, and the PubSub system broadcasts data to all active subscribers.
.graphql.Subscriptions.Real-time.exp

Real-time features like live chat, notifications, collaborative editing, and live dashboards are powered by subscriptions. Filtering, authentication, and connection management are critical for production use.
.graphql.Apollo.Apollo Server.exp

Apollo Server is a production-ready GraphQL server that integrates with Express, Fastify, Lambda, and other frameworks. It provides schema stitching, caching, error handling, and Apollo Studio integration out of the box.
.graphql.Apollo.Apollo Client.exp
Apollo Client manages GraphQL state on the client side, handling caching, loading states, optimistic updates, and error handling. It works with React, Vue, Angular, and plain JavaScript applications.
.graphql.Apollo.Cache.exp

Apollo's InMemoryCache normalizes data by type and ID, allowing automatic deduplication and cache updates after mutations. Policies like `cache-first`, `network-only`, and `cache-and-network` control fetch behavior for optimal UX.
.graphql.Best Practices.N+1 Problem.exp

The N+1 problem occurs when resolving related fields triggers one query per parent item. DataLoader batches these into single queries, while inspecting query plans and using JOIN-based resolvers provide further optimization.
.graphql.Best Practices.Security.exp

GraphQL security involves query depth limiting, complexity analysis, rate limiting, authentication, authorization, and persistent whitelisted queries. These prevent malicious queries from overloading the server.
.graphql.Best Practices.Pagination.exp

Cursor-based pagination is the GraphQL standard using `after`/`before` with `first`/`last` arguments. It provides consistent results even when data changes, unlike offset-based pagination which can skip or duplicate items.
.java.Java Basics.What is Java.exp

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed for platform independence via the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Its 'write once, run anywhere' philosophy means compiled Java bytecode runs on any device with a JVM. Java was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems and first released in 1995. It is statically typed, garbage-collected, and has a vast ecosystem of libraries and frameworks. Java is one of the most popular languages for enterprise software, Android development, and large-scale distributed systems.
.java.Java Basics.JDK vs JRE vs JVM.exp

The Java ecosystem has three key components. JVM (Java Virtual Machine) executes Java bytecode — it's the runtime engine. JRE (Java Runtime Environment) includes the JVM plus core libraries needed to run Java applications. JDK (Java Development Kit) includes the JRE plus development tools like compiler (javac), debugger (jdb), and archiver (jar). To develop Java, you need the JDK. To only run Java programs, the JRE suffices. Modern practice: always install the JDK. Java 11+ offers a single JDK download that includes everything.
.java.Java Basics.Basic Syntax.exp

Java syntax is C-family: classes, methods, statements end with semicolons, blocks use curly braces. Every Java application must have a main method with the exact signature 'public static void main(String[] args)'. File names must match the public class name. Java is case-sensitive. The entry point is always the main method. A Java source file can have at most one public class, and the file must be named after it.
.java.Java Basics.Comments.exp

Java has three comment styles. Single-line comments start with // and extend to the end of the line. Multi-line comments are enclosed between /* and */. Javadoc comments /** ... */ are a special multi-line format processed by the javadoc tool to generate API documentation. Javadoc is widely used in the Java ecosystem and supports tags like @param, @return, and @see. Writing clear Javadoc is considered a professional best practice.
.java.Java Basics.Data Types.exp

Java has 8 primitive types and reference types. Primitives: byte (8-bit), short (16), int (32), long (64), float (32-bit IEEE 754), double (64), char (16-bit Unicode), boolean. Reference types include classes, interfaces, arrays, and enums. Primitives store values directly in memory; reference types store references (pointers) to objects. The default value for numeric primitives is 0, for boolean it's false, and for reference types it's null. Java does not have unsigned primitives (except char).
.java.Java Basics.Variables & Scope.exp

Java variables must be declared with a type before use. Scope determines where a variable is accessible: local variables (inside methods/blocks), instance variables (inside class, outside methods — belong to object), and static variables (class-level, shared across all instances). Local variables must be initialized before use. Instance and static variables get default values. Block-scoped variables (declared inside {}) are only visible within that block.
.java.Java Basics.Type Casting.exp

Type casting converts a value from one type to another. Widening (implicit) converts smaller to larger types automatically — int to long for example. Narrowing (explicit) requires a cast operator because data may be lost — long to int with (int). Primitive casting can lose precision for floating-point to integer. Reference casting works up and down the inheritance hierarchy: upcasting (subclass → superclass) is automatic; downcasting requires explicit cast and may throw ClassCastException.
.java.Java Basics.Operators.exp

Java provides a full set of operators. Arithmetic: + - * / %. Relational: == != < > <= >=. Logical: && || !. Bitwise: & | ^ ~ << >> >>>. Assignment: = += -= etc. Increment/decrement: ++ -- (prefix/postfix). Ternary: ? : . Operator precedence matters — use parentheses for clarity. The + operator is overloaded: adds numbers or concatenates strings. Integer division truncates toward zero. The remainder % can be negative if the dividend is negative.
.java.Java Basics.Conditionals.exp

Java has if-else and switch statements. if-else chains evaluate boolean expressions. Switch works with int, char, String (Java 7+), and enums. Java 14+ introduced switch expressions with arrow syntax, which don't fall through and can return values. Switch expressions must be exhaustive (cover all cases). Pattern matching for switch (preview in Java 17+, stable in Java 21) allows type-based matching. Always handle the default case in switch, even if just for safety.
.java.Java Basics.Loops.exp

Java supports for, enhanced for-each, while, and do-while loops. The classic for loop has initialization, condition, and update. The enhanced for-each iterates over arrays and Iterables cleanly. The while loop runs while a condition is true. The do-while loop runs at least once then checks the condition. Break exits the loop entirely; continue skips to the next iteration. Labels (outer:) can control which loop break/continue applies to in nested loops.
.java.Java Basics.Arrays.exp

Arrays in Java are fixed-size, zero-indexed containers for elements of the same type. They are objects, created with new or with array literal syntax. The length property gives the number of elements. Arrays can be multidimensional. The java.util.Arrays class provides utility methods: sort, binarySearch, fill, copyOf, toString, deepEquals. Arrays are covariant (String[] is a subtype of Object[]), which can cause runtime ArrayStoreException. For dynamic sizing, use ArrayList instead.
.java.Java Basics.Strings.exp

String is immutable in Java — once created, its value cannot change. String literals are interned (stored in a pool) and reused. String concatenation with + creates new strings; for repeated concatenation, use StringBuilder (unsynchronized) or StringBuffer (synchronized). Key methods: length, charAt, substring, indexOf, replace, split, trim, toLowerCase, toUpperCase, equals, equalsIgnoreCase, compareTo. Use equals() for value comparison, == for reference comparison.
.java.Java Basics.Exception Handling.exp

Java uses try-catch-finally for exception handling. Exceptions are objects representing abnormal conditions. Checked exceptions (extends Exception) must be declared or caught — the compiler enforces this. Unchecked exceptions (extends RuntimeException) don't require handling. Use try-with-resources (Java 7+) to auto-close resources like streams. The finally block always executes. Multi-catch (Java 7+) lets you catch multiple exception types in one block. Custom exceptions extend Exception or RuntimeException.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Classes & Objects.exp

A class is a blueprint for objects. It defines fields (state) and methods (behavior). An object is an instance of a class, created with the new keyword followed by a constructor. The constructor initializes the object's state. Java supports method overloading (multiple methods with same name but different parameters). The this keyword refers to the current instance. Classes can have static members that belong to the class itself, not instances.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Constructors.exp

Constructors initialize objects. They have the same name as the class and no return type. If no constructor is defined, Java provides a default no-arg constructor. You can overload constructors. The this() call invokes another constructor in the same class (must be the first statement). A private constructor prevents external instantiation (used in singletons and utility classes). Records (Java 16+) automatically generate canonical constructors.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Access Modifiers.exp

Access modifiers control visibility. public: accessible from anywhere. protected: accessible within the same package and subclasses. default (package-private): accessible only within the same package (no modifier). private: accessible only within the same class. Apply to classes, methods, and fields. A top-level class can be public or package-private. Inner classes can have all four. Good encapsulation: make fields private, provide public getters/setters if needed. Protected methods are part of the API for subclass implementers.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Static Keyword.exp

The static keyword makes a member belong to the class rather than instances. Static fields are shared across all instances — only one copy exists. Static methods can be called without an instance and cannot access instance members directly. Static initialization blocks run once when the class is first loaded. Static imports (import static) bring static members into scope without qualifying them. Static nested classes behave like top-level classes but are enclosed for packaging. Common uses: utility methods, constants, counters.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Inheritance.exp

Inheritance allows a class to derive fields and methods from a parent class using the extends keyword. Java supports single class inheritance (one parent per class) but multiple interface inheritance. The super keyword accesses parent class members. All classes implicitly extend Object. Method overriding allows a subclass to provide a specific implementation of a parent method — the @Override annotation is recommended. Constructors are not inherited; the subclass constructor must call super(). Final classes cannot be subclassed.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Encapsulation.exp

Encapsulation hides internal state and requires all interaction through methods. Achieve by marking fields private and providing public getters/setters. This protects data integrity by allowing validation in setters, enables changing implementation without affecting callers, and makes code more maintainable. JavaBeans convention uses getX() for getters and setX() for setters. For boolean fields, the getter is often isX(). Immutable objects take encapsulation further — no setters, all fields final, defensive copying in constructors.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Polymorphism.exp

Polymorphism means 'many forms'. It allows objects of different types to respond to the same method call in their own way. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading (same name, different parameters). Runtime polymorphism is method overriding — the JVM decides at runtime which method to call based on the actual object type, not the reference type. This is the foundation of the Strategy and Template Method patterns. Polymorphism enables programming to interfaces rather than implementations.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Abstraction.exp

Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential features. Abstract classes (declared with abstract) can have both abstract methods (no body, must be overridden) and concrete methods. They can have constructors and fields. Interfaces (declared with interface) originally had only abstract methods, but Java 8+ added default and static methods. An abstract class models 'is-a' relationships with shared state; interfaces model 'can-do' capabilities. Java doesn't support multiple class inheritance, but a class can implement multiple interfaces.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Interfaces.exp

Interfaces define contracts that implementing classes must fulfill. Before Java 8, interfaces had only abstract methods and constants. Java 8 added default methods (with body) and static methods. Java 9 added private methods. Functional interfaces (with a single abstract method) enable lambda expressions. Common interfaces: Runnable, Comparator, Callable, Consumer, Function, Predicate, Supplier. Default methods allow interfaces to evolve without breaking existing implementations. Use @FunctionalInterface to mark single-abstract-method interfaces.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Enums.exp

Enums (enum keyword) define a fixed set of named constants. They are implicitly final subclasses of java.lang.Enum. Enums can have fields, constructors, methods, and implement interfaces. Each constant can have its own body with overridden methods. Enums provide type safety (no invalid values), built-in methods like values() and valueOf(), and switch compatibility. Use enums instead of int constants or String constants for fixed sets like days, colors, status codes, or configuration options.
.java.Object-Oriented Programming.Records.exp

Records (Java 16+) are transparent carriers for immutable data. They automatically generate a canonical constructor, accessor methods (componentName()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). All fields are private final. Records cannot extend other classes (they implicitly extend java.lang.Record) but can implement interfaces. Compact constructors allow validation without explicit field assignment. Use records for DTOs, value objects, and any data carrier where boilerplate would otherwise make code verbose.
.java.Functional Programming.Lambda Expressions.exp

Lambda expressions (Java 8+) provide a concise way to represent anonymous functions. Syntax: (parameters) -> expression or { body }. They can only be used with functional interfaces (interfaces with one abstract method). Parameters can be explicitly typed or inferred. Single parameter parentheses are optional. The lambda body can be a single expression (no return needed) or a block. Lambdas can capture effectively final variables from the enclosing scope. They enable functional-style programming and make code more expressive.
.java.Functional Programming.Functional Interfaces.exp

Functional interfaces have exactly one abstract method. Java provides built-in functional interfaces in java.util.function: Function<T,R> (maps T→R), Consumer<T> (accepts T, returns void), Supplier<T> (supplies T), Predicate<T> (tests T, returns boolean), UnaryOperator<T> (T→T), BinaryOperator<T> (T,T→T). Primitive variants avoid boxing: IntFunction, LongConsumer, DoublePredicate, etc. @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended — it causes compile error if the interface doesn't meet the contract.
.java.Functional Programming.Method References.exp

Method references are shorthand for lambdas that call an existing method. Four kinds: Class::staticMethod, object::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod (first parameter becomes the receiver), and Class::new (constructor reference). Method references make code more readable by naming the method explicitly. They work wherever functional interfaces are expected. Static method reference: Math::max. Instance method reference: list::add. Instance method of arbitrary object: String::length. Constructor reference: ArrayList::new.
.java.Functional Programming.Stream API.exp

The Stream API (Java 8+) processes sequences of elements declaratively. Streams don't store data; they pipeline operations. Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, peek) return a new stream. Terminal operations (collect, forEach, reduce, count, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch, findFirst, findAny) produce a result or side effect. Streams are lazy — intermediate operations execute only when a terminal operation is invoked. Streams cannot be reused. Common collectors: toList(), toSet(), toMap(), groupingBy(), joining().
.java.Functional Programming.Optional.exp

Optional<T> (Java 8+) is a container that may or may not hold a value, designed to reduce null pointer exceptions. It forces callers to handle the absent case explicitly. Common creation: Optional.of(value) (non-null), Optional.ofNullable(value), Optional.empty(). Key methods: isPresent(), ifPresent(consumer), orElse(default), orElseGet(supplier), orElseThrow(exceptionSupplier), map(), flatMap(), filter(), isEmpty() (Java 11+). Optional is not serializable and should not be used for fields, method parameters, or collection elements.
.java.Collections Framework.List Interface.exp

List is an ordered, indexed collection that allows duplicates. Implementations: ArrayList (resizable array — fast random access, slow insertion/deletion in middle), LinkedList (doubly-linked — fast insertion/deletion at ends, slow random access), Vector (legacy synchronized array), CopyOnWriteArrayList (thread-safe, copy-on-write). Key methods: add, get, set, remove, indexOf, contains, size, isEmpty, clear, subList, sort. Lists support iteration with for-each, iterator, listIterator, and streams. Use List.of() (Java 9+) for immutable lists.
.java.Collections Framework.Set Interface.exp

Set is a collection with no duplicate elements. Implementations: HashSet (hash table — O(1) operations, no ordering guarantee), LinkedHashSet (hash + linked list — insertion order), TreeSet (red-black tree — sorted order, O(log n)), EnumSet (bit vector — extremely fast for enums). Key methods: add, remove, contains, size, isEmpty, addAll, retainAll, removeAll. Sets rely on equals() and hashCode() for element comparison. TreeSet requires Comparable or a Comparator. CopyOnWriteArraySet provides thread safety.
.java.Collections Framework.Map Interface.exp

Map stores key-value pairs. Implementations: HashMap (hash table — O(1) operations, no ordering), LinkedHashMap (insertion or access order), TreeMap (sorted by keys, O(log n)), EnumMap (keys are enum type, extremely fast), WeakHashMap, IdentityHashMap, ConcurrentHashMap (thread-safe). Key methods: put, get, getOrDefault, remove, containsKey, containsValue, keySet, values, entrySet, putIfAbsent, replace, merge, compute, forEach. Null keys: HashMap allows one null key; TreeMap does not (NPE).
.java.Collections Framework.Queue & Deque.exp

Queue follows FIFO (first-in-first-out). Deque supports insertion/removal at both ends. Key implementations: LinkedList (Queue/Deque), ArrayDeque (fast, no capacity limit, preferred over Stack), PriorityQueue (heap-based priority ordering), ConcurrentLinkedDeque (thread-safe). Queue methods: offer/add (insert), poll/remove (retrieve and remove), peek/element (retrieve without remove). Deque adds: addFirst, addLast, offerFirst, offerLast, pollFirst, pollLast, peekFirst, peekLast. ArrayDeque is faster than Stack and LinkedList for queue/deque operations.
.java.Collections Framework.Collections Utility.exp

java.util.Collections provides static utility methods for collections. Key methods: sort, binarySearch, reverse, shuffle, rotate, fill, copy, swap, min, max, frequency, disjoint, singletonList, unmodifiableList, synchronizedList, checkedList. Use Collections.emptyList/set/map for immutable empty collections. Collections.unmodifiableXxx creates read-only views. Collections.synchronizedXxx wraps collections for thread safety (though ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList are preferred). Collections.checkedXxx provides type safety at runtime.
.java.Generics.Generic Classes.exp

Generics (Java 5+) enable type-safe programming by parameterizing types. A generic class uses type parameters in angle brackets. The compiler enforces type consistency, eliminating casts and preventing ClassCastException at runtime. Type parameters are conventionally single uppercase letters: E (element), K (key), V (value), T (type), N (number), S/U (other types). The diamond operator <> (Java 7+) infers type arguments. Raw types (without <>) should never be used — they bypass type checking. Generic information is erased at runtime (type erasure).
.java.Generics.Generic Methods.exp

Generic methods introduce their own type parameters, independent of the class's type parameters. The type parameter is declared before the return type in angle brackets. Type inference determines the type from arguments. Generic methods enable algorithms that work with multiple types while maintaining type safety. They're commonly used in utility classes for sorting, searching, or transforming collections. Bounded type parameters (<T extends Comparable<T>>) restrict types to those with specific capabilities.
.java.Generics.Wildcards.exp

Wildcards (?) represent unknown types in generics. Unbounded wildcards <?> accept any type. Upper-bounded wildcards <? extends T> accept T or any subtype. Lower-bounded wildcards <? super T> accept T or any supertype. Wildcards enable flexibility when the exact type parameter is unknown. The PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) principle guides usage: use extends when reading values (producer), use super when writing values (consumer). Wildcards cannot appear in type parameter definitions, only in usage contexts.
.java.Generics.Type Erasure.exp

Type erasure removes generic type information at compile time, replacing type parameters with their bounds (or Object if unbounded). This enables backward compatibility with pre-generics code. The compiler adds casts where needed and generates bridge methods for polymorphism. Erasure means you cannot use instanceof with parameterized types, create arrays of parameterized types, or use primitive type parameters. Understanding erasure is essential for advanced patterns and troubleshooting ClassCastException from raw type interop. Reflection cannot retrieve generic type arguments at runtime (with some exceptions for field declarations).
.java.I/O & File Handling.Stream I/O.exp

Java I/O uses streams for sequential data input/output. Byte streams (InputStream, OutputStream) handle binary data. Character streams (Reader, Writer) handle text with encoding support. Key classes: FileInputStream/FileOutputStream for files, BufferedInputStream/BufferedOutputStream for buffering, InputStreamReader/OutputStreamWriter for character conversion, BufferedReader/PrintWriter for line-oriented text. Always close streams in finally blocks or use try-with-resources (Java 7+). The decorator pattern layers streams for added functionality (buffering, filtering, compression).
.java.I/O & File Handling.NIO (New I/O).exp

Java NIO (New I/O, Java 1.4+; NIO.2, Java 7+) provides non-blocking I/O, channels, buffers, selectors, and file system API. The java.nio.file package (Java 7+) includes high-level file operations: Path, Files, FileSystem, FileVisitor. Key Files methods: readAllLines, write, copy, move, delete, createDirectories, walk, find, lines (lazy stream), probeContentType. Path represents a file system path. Files.lines() returns a Stream<String> for efficient large file processing. PathMatcher handles glob patterns.
.java.I/O & File Handling.Serialization.exp

Serialization converts an object into a byte stream for storage or transmission. Implement Serializable (marker interface — no methods). Use ObjectOutputStream for writing and ObjectInputStream for reading. The transient keyword excludes fields from serialization. serialVersionUID ensures class version compatibility — always declare it explicitly. Externalizable provides custom serialization logic. Java's built-in serialization is considered slow and has security risks — prefer JSON, Protocol Buffers, or similar for new projects. Records are serializable by default.
.java.Concurrency.Threads & Runnable.exp

Java provides built-in threading via the Thread class and the Runnable interface. Extending Thread is simpler but limits inheritance. Implementing Runnable is more flexible and follows composition over inheritance. The run() method contains the thread's work; start() launches a new thread. Thread states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED. Use Thread.sleep(millis) for pauses. Interrupt a thread with interrupt() and check with isInterrupted() or InterruptedException. For simple tasks, use virtual threads (Java 21+) or ExecutorService instead.
.java.Concurrency.Synchronization.exp

Synchronization prevents thread interference and memory consistency errors. The synchronized keyword creates a mutual exclusion lock (intrinsic lock or monitor). Synchronized instance methods lock on 'this'. Static synchronized methods lock on the Class object. Synchronized blocks allow specifying the lock object for finer granularity. Volatile guarantees visibility of writes across threads (but not atomicity). Locks are reentrant — a thread can acquire a lock it already holds. Deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other's locks indefinitely — avoid by consistent lock ordering.
.java.Concurrency.ExecutorService.exp

ExecutorService (Java 5+) manages a pool of threads and decouples task submission from execution. Factory methods in Executors: newFixedThreadPool(n), newCachedThreadPool(), newSingleThreadExecutor(), newScheduledThreadPool(). Submit tasks via execute(Runnable) or submit(Callable<T>) which returns Future<T>. shutdown() gracefully stops accepting tasks; shutdownNow() attempts to stop running tasks. ScheduledExecutorService supports delayed and periodic execution. For CPU-bound tasks, pool size ≈ availableProcessors. For I/O-bound, a larger pool is appropriate.
.java.Concurrency.CompletableFuture.exp

CompletableFuture (Java 8+) represents a future result that can be manually completed and supports functional composition. Factory methods: supplyAsync (returns value), runAsync (no return). Composition: thenApply (transform), thenAccept (consume), thenRun (run after), thenCompose (flatMap for futures), thenCombine (merge two), allOf (wait for all), anyOf (wait for first). Async variants accept an Executor. exceptionally/ handle for error recovery. thenApply vs thenCompose: apply wraps value, compose returns new CompletableFuture. CompletableFuture enables declarative asynchronous programming without blocking.
.java.Concurrency.Virtual Threads.exp

Virtual threads (Java 21+, preview in Java 19-20) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the OS. Millions of virtual threads can run on a small number of OS threads. They are ideal for I/O-bound workloads where threads spend time waiting. Create with Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) or Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Virtual threads use carrier threads (platform threads) from a ForkJoinPool. They cannot be prioritized or daemon-set. Pinning occurs when virtual threads block in synchronized blocks or native methods — avoid synchronized in favor of ReentrantLock.
.java.Build Tools.Maven Basics.exp

Maven is a build automation and project management tool using XML (pom.xml) for configuration. It follows convention over configuration: standard directory layout (src/main/java, src/test/java). Key concepts: coordinates (groupId:artifactId:version), dependencies, plugins, profiles, lifecycle phases (compile, test, package, install, deploy). The pom.xml defines the project. Maven downloads dependencies from repositories (Maven Central). Common commands: mvn clean, compile, test, package, install. Maven ensures reproducible builds across environments.
.java.Build Tools.Gradle Basics.exp

Gradle is a build automation tool using Groovy or Kotlin DSL. It uses a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks, supporting incremental builds, caching, and parallel execution. build.gradle (Groovy) or build.gradle.kts (Kotlin) defines the build. Key concepts: plugins, dependencies, tasks, configurations. Gradle Wrapper (gradlew) ensures consistent versions across environments. Benefits over Maven: faster builds (incremental, caching), more concise syntax, flexibility with custom tasks. Gradle is the default for Android development.
.java.Database Access.JDBC.exp

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is the standard API for connecting Java applications to relational databases. Steps: load driver (auto-loaded in JDBC 4+), get Connection, create Statement/PreparedStatement, execute query, process ResultSet, close resources. PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection by parameterizing queries. Connection pooling (HikariCP) is essential for production. Transaction management: setAutoCommit(false), commit(), rollback(). JDBC is low-level and verbose — most projects use JPA, Spring Data, or jOOQ for higher-level abstraction.
.java.Database Access.JPA & Hibernate.exp

JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is the standard ORM specification for Java. Hibernate is the most popular JPA implementation. Key annotations: @Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue, @Column, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @JoinColumn, @JoinTable. EntityManager manages persistence operations: persist, find, merge, remove, createQuery. JPQL queries entities with object-oriented syntax. Spring Data JPA (on Spring Boot) further simplifies with repository interfaces (JpaRepository) that auto-implement CRUD methods.
.java.Testing.JUnit 5.exp

JUnit 5 (Jupiter) is the standard testing framework for Java. Key annotations: @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll (static), @Disabled, @DisplayName, @Tag, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest, @Nested. Assertions: assertEquals, assertTrue, assertFalse, assertNull, assertThrows, assertAll (grouped assertions). assertAll executes all assertions even if some fail. Assumptions.assumeTrue skips tests conditionally. Lifecycle methods: @BeforeEach runs before each test, @BeforeAll runs once before all tests. Test methods must not be private or static.
.java.Testing.Mockito.exp

Mockito is a mocking framework for unit tests. It creates mock objects that simulate real dependencies. Key features: @Mock annotation creates mocks, @InjectMocks injects mocks into the tested object, @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) for JUnit 5. Methods: when().thenReturn() stubs behavior, doThrow() for exceptions, verify() checks method calls, ArgumentCaptor captures arguments, spy() wraps a real object with partial mocking. Good practices: mock external dependencies (database, network, filesystem); don't mock value objects. Prefer Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) style: given/when/then.
.java.Web Frameworks.Spring Boot Basics.exp

Spring Boot is a framework that simplifies Spring application setup with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and production-ready features. @SpringBootApplication combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. Dependency injection uses @Autowired or constructor injection. Key starters: spring-boot-starter-web (REST APIs), spring-boot-starter-data-jpa (database), spring-boot-starter-test (testing). Properties in application.yml or application.properties. Spring Boot Actuator provides health checks and metrics. Embedded Tomcat runs the application without external server.
.java.Web Frameworks.Servlets & JSP.exp

Servlets are Java classes that handle HTTP requests and responses in a web container (Tomcat, Jetty). HttpServlet provides doGet, doPost, doPut, doDelete methods. Lifecycle: init(), service(), destroy(). Servlet 3.0+ supports annotations (@WebServlet) instead of web.xml. JSP (JavaServer Pages) embeds Java in HTML using <% %> scriptlets, ${EL} expressions, and JSTL tags. Modern applications prefer Spring Boot and REST APIs over raw servlets, but understanding servlets is fundamental for Java web concepts.
.java.Logging.SLF4J & Logback.exp

SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is a logging abstraction. Logback is the most popular SLF4J implementation. Levels: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR. Configure via logback.xml. Logback features: rolling file appenders, conditional logging, MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) for contextual data. Parameterized logging with {} avoids string concatenation overhead. Best practices: use slf4j-api in libraries (not logback directly), use appropriate levels, log meaningful messages with context. Avoid logging in tight loops. MDC is great for request tracing (correlation IDs).
.java.Java Platform Features.Modules (Project Jigsaw).exp

The Java module system (Project Jigsaw, Java 9+) enables strong encapsulation and explicit dependencies. A module-info.java declares module name, exports (which packages are accessible), requires (dependencies), opens (for reflection), provides/uses (service loader). Benefits: reliable configuration (no classpath hell), strong encapsulation (internal packages hidden), scalable (smaller runtimes with jlink). The java.base module is implicitly required. Migration: unnamed modules (classpath) can access named modules' exported packages but not vice versa. Use jdeps to analyze dependencies.
.java.Java Platform Features.Date & Time API.exp

The java.time package (Java 8+) replaces the flawed java.util.Date and Calendar. Key classes: LocalDate (date only), LocalTime (time only), LocalDateTime (date+time, no zone), ZonedDateTime (date+time+zone), Instant (machine timestamp), Duration (time-based amount), Period (date-based amount), DateTimeFormatter (format/parse). All classes are immutable and thread-safe. Parse/format with DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(). TemporalAdjusters provide common date adjustments (firstDayOfMonth, nextMonday). Duration.between() measures elapsed time. Unlike old Date, months are 1-12 and years are proper (not 1900-based).
.java.Java Platform Features.Annotations.exp

Annotations provide metadata about code. Built-in: @Override, @Deprecated, @SuppressWarnings, @FunctionalInterface. Meta-annotations on custom annotations: @Retention (SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME), @Target (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, etc.), @Documented, @Inherited, @Repeatable. RUNTIME retention allows reflection-based processing. Spring, Hibernate, JUnit, and Jackson heavily use annotations. Custom annotations enable declarative programming. Annotation processors (javac) generate code at compile time (Lombok uses this). Processing runtime annotations via reflection or the AnnotatedElement interface.
.java.Java Platform Features.Newer Language Features.exp

Java continues to evolve rapidly. Key newer features: Text Blocks (Java 13/15) for multi-line strings with """ """ delimiters. Pattern Matching for instanceof (Java 16+) eliminates casts. Switch Expressions with -> (Java 14+) and Pattern Matching for switch (Java 21+). Sealed Classes (Java 17+) restrict subclassing — the permits clause lists allowed subtypes. Record Patterns (Java 21+) destructure records in pattern matching. String Templates (preview in Java 21+). SequencedCollection (Java 21+) adds first/last access to ordered collections.
.js.Fundamentals.What is JavaScript.exp

JavaScript is a high-level, interpreted language that runs in browsers and on servers (Node.js). It has good parts (functions as first-class citizens, objects, closures) and bad parts (global variables, type coercion quirks). Crockford's 'The Good Parts' advises avoiding the bad parts by using strict mode, === over ==, and minimizing global scope. A key insight from Eloquent JavaScript: think of JavaScript as a language where functions are values that can be passed around, making it deeply rooted in functional programming patterns alongside its imperative style.
.js.Fundamentals.Syntax & Comments.exp

JavaScript syntax is C-like with semicolons, blocks, and case-sensitivity. Crockford recommends always using semicolons — automatic semicolon insertion (ASI) can break code when lines start with ( or [. Comments should explain WHY, not WHAT. Eloquent JavaScript emphasizes clean formatting: consistent indentation (2 spaces), meaningful names, and breaking complex expressions into smaller named pieces.
.js.Fundamentals.Strict Mode.exp
Use 'use strict' to enable a safer, more predictable subset of JavaScript behavior and avoid common silent errors.
.js.Fundamentals.Statements & Blocks.exp
Learn how statement groups and block scope work with braces, and why grouping code carefully helps avoid bugs.
.js.Variables & Types.var let const.exp

The Good Parts advises never using var — it leaks scope and causes subtle bugs. Use const by default, let only when reassignment is needed. const doesn't mean immutable, only that the binding can't change.
.js.Variables & Types.Primitive Types.exp
JavaScript has 7 primitive types. Primitives are immutable (you can't change them — operations return new values). typeof null returns 'object' (a JS bug from day one).
.js.Variables & Types.Reference Types.exp

Objects, arrays, and functions are reference types: variables hold a pointer to the value in memory. Assigning or passing copies the reference, not the value — mutating one affects the other. Use spread or structuredClone() for copies.
.js.Variables & Types.Truthy & Falsy.exp

Every value coerces to boolean in conditionals. Crockford calls JavaScript's falsy rules 'a land of false promises' — learn them exactly to avoid bugs. Only 7 falsy values exist: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. The tricky one: empty arrays [] and objects {} are truthy. Eloquent JavaScript shows a practical pattern: use explicit Boolean() or !! for clarity, and avoid relying on coercion in complex conditions.
.js.Variables & Types.Type Conversion.exp
JavaScript is weakly typed — it converts types automatically. This is convenient but dangerous. The Good Parts: always use === and explicit conversion.
.js.Variables & Types.Template Literals.exp
Template literals use backticks (`) instead of quotes. Embed expressions with ${}. They support multi-line without \n.
.js.Variables & Types.null vs undefined.exp
undefined means a variable was declared but not assigned. null is intentionally empty — you assign it explicitly. They are different types.
.js.Variables & Types.Symbol & BigInt.exp
Symbol creates unique, immutable identifiers for object properties. BigInt represents integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER using n suffix.
.js.Operators.Arithmetic Operators.exp

Standard math: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), % (remainder/modulo), ** (exponentiation). Prefix/postfix ++ and -- increment/decrement by 1. Common mistake: + also does string concatenation — if either operand is a string, both are coerced to strings. Best practice: use parentheses to clarify operator precedence; avoid relying on ++ inside expressions.
.js.Operators.Comparison Operators.exp

Compare values and return a boolean. Relational: >, <, >=, <=. Equality: === (strict, no coercion) and == (loose, coerces types). Common mistake: using == allows type coercion (e.g., 5 == '5' is true), which causes subtle bugs. Best practice: always use === and !==; use Object.is() for NaN comparisons (Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true, unlike NaN === NaN which is false).
.js.Operators.Logical Operators.exp

&& (AND) returns the first falsy operand or the last truthy one. || (OR) returns the first truthy operand or the last falsy one. ! (NOT) inverts truthiness and always returns boolean. Common mistake: && and || short-circuit — if the left operand determines the result, the right operand is never evaluated. This means side effects in the right operand may not run. Best practice: use || for default values and && for conditional execution, but beware that 0, '', and false are falsy so defaults may not work as expected — use ?? for null/undefined only.
.js.Operators.Assignment Operators.exp

Compound assignment combines an operation with assignment: +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, **=, &&=, ||=, ??= (ES2021). They update the variable in place. Common mistake: ??= only assigns if the current value is null or undefined — unlike ||= which assigns for any falsy value. Best practice: prefer compound assignment for clarity when updating a variable relative to its current value.
.js.Operators.Ternary Operator.exp

The conditional (ternary) operator takes three operands: condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse. It's an expression, not a statement — it returns a value that can be assigned or used inline. Common mistake: nesting ternaries makes code unreadable — use if/else for more than one condition. Best practice: use ternaries for simple yes/no branches; keep them on one line for readability.
.js.Operators.Spread & Rest.exp

Spread (...) expands iterables (arrays, strings, objects) into individual elements. Rest (...) collects remaining elements into an array or object. Common mistake: spread creates a shallow copy — nested objects are still referenced, not cloned. Best practice: use spread for immutable updates (copying arrays/objects) and rest for flexible function parameters and destructuring.
.js.Control Flow.If Else.exp

Branch execution based on boolean conditions. The condition is coerced to boolean — any truthy value passes. Common mistake: assigning (=) instead of comparing (==) in conditions — 'if (x = 5)' assigns 5 (truthy) and always runs. Best practice: use curly braces even for single statements; prefer === over == for comparisons; use early returns (guard clauses) to reduce nesting.
.js.Control Flow.Else If.exp
else if chains additional conditions after if. Each condition is evaluated in order — the first true match runs and the rest are skipped. Use else if when exactly one branch should execute.
.js.Control Flow.Switch Statement.exp

Multi-way branching comparing the same expression to multiple values using strict equality (===). Use break to prevent fall-through to the next case. Common mistake: forgetting break causes execution to fall through to the next case (sometimes intentional). Best practice: always include break (or return); use default for unmatched values; consider if/else for ranges (switch is for discrete values only).
.js.Control Flow.for Loops.exp

Three types: for (init; condition; increment) — classic counted loop. for...of iterates over values of iterables (arrays, strings, Map, Set). for...in iterates over enumerable property keys of objects. Common mistake: using for...in for arrays (iterates keys as strings, includes inherited properties). Best practice: use for...of for arrays, for...in for objects, and classic for when you need the index.
.js.Control Flow.while & do while.exp

while checks the condition before each iteration — may run zero times. do...while checks after — always runs at least once. Common mistake: forgetting to update the loop variable causes infinite loops (hangs the browser). Best practice: prefer for loops when you know the iteration count; use while for condition-controlled loops (reading input, waiting for a state change).
.js.Control Flow.break & continue.exp

break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next. With labeled statements, break and continue can control outer loops from inside nested ones. Common mistake: using break in forEach() callback — it doesn't work (forEach doesn't respect break). Best practice: use labeled breaks sparingly (they can make control flow hard to follow); prefer extracting to a function with early return.
.js.Control Flow.Nested Loops.exp

A loop inside another loop. Each outer iteration triggers a full inner loop run. Complexity is O(n*m) — a 100×100 grid runs 10,000 iterations. Use labeled break/continue to control outer loops from inside. Common mistake: quadratic complexity on large datasets can freeze the browser. Best practice: consider flatMap(), combined data structures, or early termination when possible.
.js.Control Flow.Error Handling.exp

try/catch/finally handles runtime exceptions. try runs the risky code; catch receives the error object; finally always runs (even after return). Common mistake: catching and ignoring errors silently — always log or re-throw. Best practice: catch specific error types when possible; use finally for cleanup (closing files, clearing state); throw custom Error objects (not strings or numbers) for stack traces.
.js.Functions.Function Declarations.exp

Functions are the fundamental building block of JavaScript. Eloquent JavaScript calls them 'values that contain behavior'. Function declarations are hoisted (moved to top), which Crockford considers useful for organizing code top-down. A function always returns something — undefined if no explicit return. The Good Parts says: 'functions are the best part of JavaScript' — they create scope, enable modularity, and are the only way to create private variables. Every function has access to the scope in which it was defined (closure), making them powerful tools for encapsulation.
.js.Functions.Function Expressions.exp

A function expression assigns a function to a variable. Unlike declarations, function expressions are NOT hoisted — you can't call them before the definition line. Named function expressions have a name property for debugging but the name is only visible inside the function scope. Common mistake: expecting function expressions to be hoisted like declarations. Best practice: use const for function expressions to prevent reassignment; use named expressions for better stack traces in recursion and debugging.
.js.Functions.Arrow Functions.exp

Arrow functions provide shorter syntax: (params) => expression. Key differences from regular functions: they inherit this from the enclosing scope (lexical this), cannot be used as constructors (no new), and don't have arguments object. Common mistake: using arrow functions for object methods — this won't refer to the object. Best practice: use arrow functions for callbacks, array methods (map/filter/reduce), and when you want lexical this; use regular functions for object methods, constructors, and when you need dynamic this.
.js.Functions.Default Parameters.exp

Default parameter values are used when the argument is undefined (not when it's null or other falsy values). Defaults can be expressions or even function calls — they're evaluated at call time, not definition time. Common mistake: thinking defaults trigger on null — they only trigger on undefined. Best practice: put default parameters after required ones so calling code can skip them; avoid complex default expressions that hide bugs.
.js.Functions.Rest Parameters.exp

Rest parameters (...) collect remaining arguments into a real array (unlike the array-like arguments object). Must be the last parameter. Common mistake: confusing rest with the arguments object — arguments is array-like (no .map/.filter) and includes ALL parameters, not just the extras. Best practice: prefer rest over arguments for clarity; use rest in destructuring to capture remaining items.
.js.Functions.Closures.exp

A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has returned. This is JavaScript’s most powerful pattern — it enables data privacy (module pattern), function factories, event handlers with state, and memoization. Common mistake: closures capture variables by reference, not by value — loop closures all see the final value unless you use let or an IIFE. Best practice: use closures for encapsulation (hide implementation details); be mindful of memory if the closure retains large objects.
.js.Objects & Classes.Objects.exp

Objects are the foundation of JavaScript — almost everything is an object or can behave like one. Crockford calls objects 'containers of properties, where each property has a name and a value'. Objects are passed by reference, making them efficient but also dangerous when mutated in place. Eloquent JavaScript describes objects as 'octopuses with any number of tentacles' — they can hold any type. The Good Parts recommends object literals as the simplest and safest way to create objects, avoiding new Object() and similar verbose forms.
.js.Objects & Classes.This Keyword.exp

this is one of JavaScript's most misunderstood features. Crockford calls this 'a source of enormous confusion'. Its value depends entirely on HOW a function is called: method call → the object, plain call → undefined (strict) or global (sloppy), constructor call (new) → the new instance, call/apply/bind → explicitly set. Eloquent JavaScript calls this 'the function's context'. Arrow functions avoid the confusion by inheriting this from the enclosing scope — Crockford recommends using them for callbacks. The Good Parts says: 'this is always bound to the global object in inner functions' — capture it with a variable (that = this) or use arrow functions.
.js.Objects & Classes.Prototypes.exp

Prototypal inheritance is JavaScript's native inheritance model. Crockford explains: 'a prototype is an object from which other objects inherit properties'. Unlike classical inheritance (classes inherit from classes), objects inherit directly from objects. Object.create() creates a new object with a specified prototype. The Good Parts advocates for prototypal over classical inheritance — it's simpler and more flexible. Eloquent JavaScript describes the prototype chain as 'a series of objects linked together' ending at Object.prototype. When you access a property, JavaScript walks the chain until found. Favor composition over inheritance in large systems.
.js.Objects & Classes.Classes.exp

Class syntax (ES2015) is sugar over prototypes: class defines a constructor, methods go on the prototype, and static methods go on the constructor itself. Supports extends for inheritance and super for parent calls. Common mistake: thinking classes are a new inheritance model — they're still prototypal underneath. Best practice: use class syntax over manual prototype manipulation for readability; prefer composition over deep inheritance chains.
.js.Objects & Classes.Inheritance.exp

extends creates a subclass that inherits from a parent class. super() calls the parent constructor; super.method() calls a parent method. Subclasses can override methods and access parent implementations. Common mistake: forgetting to call super() in the subclass constructor — causes ReferenceError. Best practice: keep inheritance shallow (1-2 levels max); prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) for code reuse.
.js.Objects & Classes.Getters & Setters.exp

Getters (get) and setters (set) let you define properties that call functions when accessed or assigned. They look like normal property access but can run validation, computation, or logging. Common mistake: getters should not have side effects (callers expect property-like behavior). Best practice: use getters for computed properties and setters for validation; avoid expensive operations in getters since callers don't expect function-call overhead.
.js.Arrays & Collections.Arrays.exp

Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Arrays are objects — typeof [] returns 'object'. The length property is auto-updated but can be set manually (truncates or creates empty slots). Common mistake: using for...in on arrays (iterates keys as strings and includes inherited properties). Best practice: use array literal [] over new Array(); use for...of, forEach, or array methods (map/filter) for iteration.
.js.Arrays & Collections.Array Methods.exp

Eloquent JavaScript calls array methods like map, filter, and reduce 'higher-order functions' — functions that operate on other functions. They enable a declarative style: you describe WHAT you want, not HOW. This is more readable and less error-prone than manual for loops. map transforms each element, filter selects elements, reduce combines elements into a single value, find locates the first match, some checks if any element matches, every checks if all match. The Good Parts cautions against mutating arrays while iterating — use map/filter to create new arrays instead.
.js.Arrays & Collections.Destructuring.exp

Unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables. Supports nested destructuring, default values, and rest patterns. Common mistake: trying to destructure null or undefined — throws TypeError. Best practice: provide defaults for safe destructuring; use renaming (object: { oldName: newName }) to avoid naming conflicts.
.js.Arrays & Collections.Map & Set.exp

Map stores key-value pairs where keys can be any type (objects, functions, primitives) — unlike objects which only accept strings/symbols. Map preserves insertion order and has O(1) lookup. Set stores unique values of any type. Common mistake: using objects as maps — object keys are always strings; Map keys preserve type (number key 1 !== string key '1'). Best practice: use Map over plain objects for dynamic key collections; use Set for deduplication and fast membership checks.
.js.Arrays & Collections.WeakMap & WeakSet.exp

WeakMap holds 'weak' references to object keys — if no other reference to the key exists, the entry is garbage collected. WeakSet similarly holds weak references to objects. Not iterable and no .size property because the contents could change anytime due to GC. Common mistake: expecting WeakMap/WeakSet to be iterable or have .size — they don't by design. Best practice: use WeakMap for private data (closure alternative), caching associated with DOM elements, or preventing memory leaks from long-lived references.
.js.Arrays & Collections.Iterators & Generators.exp

Iterators are objects with a next() method that returns { value, done }. Any object with [Symbol.iterator] is iterable (works with for...of, spread, destructuring). Generators (function*) simplify iterator creation — they pause at each yield and resume on the next call. Common mistake: generators are single-use iterables — you can't restart them; create a new generator each time. Best practice: use generators for lazy sequences, infinite streams, and async iteration (async function*).
.js.DOM & Browser APIs.DOM Manipulation.exp

The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's API for HTML. Select elements with querySelector (single) or querySelectorAll (NodeList). Modify content via textContent, innerHTML, or classList. Common mistake: using innerHTML when textContent is safer (innerHTML parses HTML and can introduce XSS). Best practice: cache DOM references in variables (querying the DOM is slow); use classList.add/remove/toggle instead of className string manipulation; prefer textContent over innerHTML for text-only changes.
.js.DOM & Browser APIs.Events.exp

Events signal user interaction (click, keydown, submit, scroll). addEventListener(type, handler) attaches a handler. Events flow through three phases: capture (outer to inner), target, and bubble (inner to outer). Common mistake: using inline event handlers (onclick=) — they create global functions and only allow one handler per event. Best practice: use addEventListener over onclick; use event delegation (listen on parent) for dynamic child elements; call removeEventListener to prevent memory leaks.
.js.DOM & Browser APIs.Forms & Validation.exp

Handle form submission, read input values, and validate before sending. The submit event fires on the form element (not the button). Access fields via the elements collection or by id. Use e.preventDefault() to stop submission and validate first. Common mistake: listening for click on the submit button instead of submit on the form — the form can also be submitted via Enter key. Best practice: validate on submit (not on every keystroke for performance); use the Constraint Validation API (required, minlength, pattern attributes) for basic checks.
.js.DOM & Browser APIs.Fetch API.exp

fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object. The Response must be parsed (.json(), .text()) before data is available. fetch only rejects on network errors — HTTP errors (404, 500) still resolve. Common mistake: forgetting that fetch doesn't reject on HTTP error status — check response.ok. Best practice: always handle network errors with .catch(); use AbortController to cancel in-flight requests; set appropriate Content-Type headers for POST/PUT.
.js.DOM & Browser APIs.Local Storage.exp

localStorage persists data across browser sessions (no expiration). sessionStorage persists only for the current tab session — cleared when the tab closes. Both store strings only — objects must be serialized with JSON.stringify/parse. Storage limit is ~5-10MB per origin. Common mistake: storing objects directly — they become '[object Object]'; always use JSON.stringify. Best practice: wrap localStorage access in try/catch (private browsing may throw); use JSON for structured data; clear unused keys to stay under quota.
.js.DOM & Browser APIs.Timers.exp

setTimeout runs a function once after a delay; setInterval runs repeatedly at the interval. Both return an ID passed to clearTimeout/clearInterval to cancel. Common mistake: assuming setInterval runs at exact intervals — if the callback takes longer than the interval, calls stack up. Best practice: use recursive setTimeout instead of setInterval for precise timing; always clear timers in cleanup code to prevent memory leaks; use requestAnimationFrame for visual animations (more efficient than setTimeout).
.js.Async JavaScript.Promises.exp

A Promise represents a value that may be available now, later, or never. States: pending (initial), fulfilled (resolved), or rejected (error). .then() handles fulfillment, .catch() handles rejection, .finally() runs regardless. Promises are microtasks — they resolve before macrotasks like setTimeout. Common mistake: not returning the promise from .then() breaks the chain — the next .then() receives undefined. Best practice: always return promises from chains; handle rejection at the end of the chain (not per-link); use Promise.all for parallel work.
.js.Async JavaScript.Async/Await.exp

async functions always return a Promise. await pauses execution until the awaited promise settles — but only within the async function (the caller continues). Common mistake: calling async functions without awaiting them — they still run but you lose the return value and error handling. Best practice: wrap await calls in try/catch for error handling; use Promise.all for independent parallel async operations (sequential await is slower); top-level await works in ES modules.
.js.Async JavaScript.Fetch & HTTP.exp

fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise<Response>. Always check response.ok — fetch only rejects on network errors, not HTTP errors. GET is default; POST/PUT/PATCH require method and body. Common mistake: not checking response.ok — a 404 resolves successfully. Best practice: always check .ok and throw for non-2xx; use AbortController for timeout/cancellation; set Content-Type for requests with body.
.js.Async JavaScript.Event Loop.exp

The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model — single-threaded but non-blocking. Eloquent JavaScript explains: 'when a program needs to wait, it schedules a callback and continues running other code'. The call stack runs synchronously; async callbacks go to the task queue. Promises and async/await use the microtask queue (higher priority than macrotasks like setTimeout). This means promise callbacks run BEFORE timer callbacks, even zero-delay timers. Crockford says: 'understanding the event loop is essential — everything in JavaScript happens in a single thread, and if you block it, the whole page freezes'.
.js.Async JavaScript.Web Workers.exp

Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread — they can't access the DOM, window, or parent scope. Communicate with the main thread via postMessage() and onmessage. Workers are great for CPU-intensive tasks (image processing, data parsing, encryption). Common mistake: trying to access DOM or window inside a worker — not available. Best practice: use workers for expensive computations that would block the UI; use structuredClone or Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) for efficient data passing; terminate workers when done to free resources.
.js.Async JavaScript.Async Iteration.exp

Async iteration (for await...of) consumes async iterables with [Symbol.asyncIterator] that returns promises from next(). async function* defines an async generator. Useful for streaming data (paginated APIs, WebSocket messages, file chunks). Common mistake: using for...of instead of for await...of on async iterables — for...of doesn't await promises. Best practice: use async generators for streaming scenarios; handle errors inside the loop with try/catch.
.js.Modern JavaScript.ES Modules.exp
Share code with import/export syntax, and run modules in modern browsers or bundlers.
.js.Modern JavaScript.Spread Syntax.exp
Expand iterable values into arrays or function calls, and merge object properties effortlessly.
.js.Modern JavaScript.Optional Chaining.exp

Optional chaining (?.) short-circuits to undefined if the value before ?. is null or undefined — without throwing. Works with property access (?.), method calls (?.()), and dynamic access (?.[]). Common mistake: thinking ?. prevents 'undefined is not a function' for methods that don't exist — it does, but only when the object itself is null/undefined. Best practice: combine ?. with ?? for safe deep access chains; don't overuse — if a value should always exist, let it throw (fail fast).
.js.Modern JavaScript.Nullish Coalescing.exp

?? returns the right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined. Unlike || which returns the right operand for ANY falsy value (0, '', false). Common mistake: using || for defaults when 0 or '' are valid values — || treats them as absent. Best practice: use ?? for default values when the left side could be a valid falsy value (empty string, zero, false); use || for truly absent values (when undefined/null and falsy should both get the default).
.js.Modern JavaScript.Dynamic Import.exp

import() is a function-like expression that dynamically loads a module at runtime. It returns a Promise resolving to the module namespace object. Enables code splitting (load only what's needed), lazy loading (load on user interaction), and conditional imports (platform detection). Common mistake: dynamic imports are NOT hoisted — they execute when reached. Best practice: use dynamic imports for large libraries not needed on initial load (charts, editors, heavy utilities); combine with top-level await in module scripts.
.js.Modern JavaScript.Promise Combinators.exp

Promise.all waits for ALL promises — rejects fast if ANY rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for ALL to settle (resolve or reject) — never rejects, returns results with status. Promise.race returns the first settled promise. Promise.any returns the first fulfilled promise — rejects only if ALL reject. Common mistake: using Promise.all when one failure shouldn't fail the whole batch — use allSettled. Best practice: use all for dependent parallel work (must all succeed), allSettled for independent results, race for timeouts, any for fastest success.
.js.Frameworks & Tools.React.exp

React is a component-based UI library. Components return JSX (JavaScript XML) describing what to render. Props pass data from parent to child; state manages component-local data that triggers re-renders. Common mistake: mutating state directly (this.state.x = 5) instead of using setState or the state setter. Best practice: prefer functional components with hooks (useState, useEffect) over class components; keep components small and focused; lift shared state to the closest common ancestor.
.js.Frameworks & Tools.Vue.exp

Vue is a progressive framework with reactive templates and a component system. Options API uses data(), methods, computed, and watch. Composition API (setup) provides better code organization. Common mistake: using normal variables in data() instead of reactive ref() or reactive() — Vue can only track reactive objects. Best practice: prefer the Composition API for complex logic reuse; use computed for derived state instead of methods in templates; use v-bind:key in v-for for efficient re-rendering.
.js.Frameworks & Tools.Express.exp

Express is a minimalist Node.js web framework. Define routes with app.get/post/put/delete. Middleware functions (app.use) process requests in order — they can modify req/res, end the request, or call next(). Common mistake: forgetting to call next() in middleware — the request hangs. Best practice: structure routes with express.Router() for modularity; use error-handling middleware (4 args) for centralized errors; parse bodies with express.json() middleware.
.js.Frameworks & Tools.Next.js.exp

Next.js is a React framework for production with file-based routing (pages/ or app/), SSR/SSG, and API routes. Pages/ directory: each file becomes a route. App Router (app/) uses layouts, loading states, and server components. Common mistake: fetching data in client components when server components would be more efficient. Best practice: use server components for initial data fetching (rendered on server, smaller JS bundle); use getStaticProps (Pages Router) for SSG; leverage Suspense boundaries for streaming.
.js.Frameworks & Tools.NestJS.exp

NestJS is a progressive Node.js framework built with TypeScript that uses decorators for controllers, providers, modules, and middleware. It supports Express or Fastify under the hood. Common mistake: forgetting to register providers in module decorators — unregistered providers cause runtime injection errors. Best practice: use modules to organize features; keep controllers thin (delegate logic to services); leverage dependency injection for testability.
.js.Frameworks & Tools.Vite.exp

Vite is a fast build tool that uses native ES modules for dev (instant HMR) and Rollup for production builds. Supports JS, TS, JSX, CSS, and assets out of the box. Common mistake: thinking Vite only works for frontend frameworks — it works with vanilla JS and library development too. Best practice: use vite.config.js for custom configuration (aliases, plugins, proxy); leverage HMR for fast iteration.
.js.Built-in Objects.JSON.exp

JSON.parse converts JSON strings to objects; JSON.stringify serializes objects to JSON strings. Essential for data exchange and API communication. Common mistake: JSON.parse throws on invalid JSON — always wrap in try/catch or use a safe parser. Best practice: use JSON.stringify's replacer and space arguments for controlled serialization; avoid storing undefined, BigInt, or circular references — they're silently dropped or throw.
.js.Built-in Objects.Math & Number.exp

Math provides constants and methods for math operations: random, floor, round, ceil, max, min, abs, pow, sqrt, sin, cos, PI, E. Number offers parseInt, parseFloat, isNaN, isFinite, isInteger, and EPSILON. Common mistake: using Math.floor for rounding — use Math.round for standard rounding and Math.trunc for integer truncation. Best practice: use Number.isNaN over global isNaN (global coerces, Number.isNaN doesn't); use Math.max/Math.min with spread for arrays; avoid floating-point equality checks — use epsilon comparison.
.js.Built-in Objects.Date & Time.exp

Date handles date/time operations: creation, formatting, arithmetic, and timezone handling. Months are zero-indexed (0 = January). Date objects are mutable — all set methods mutate in place. Common mistake: date parsing with strings is unreliable across browsers — use Date.parse cautiously or a date library. Best practice: use toISOString() for storage/serialization; use Intl.DateTimeFormat for localized display; use timestamps (Date.now()) for calculations to avoid month-index confusion.
.js.Built-in Objects.String Methods.exp

Strings have built-in methods for manipulation: slice, substring, split, replace/replaceAll, toUpperCase/toLowerCase, trim, includes, startsWith, endsWith, repeat, padStart/padEnd, match, matchAll, and charAt. Strings are immutable — all methods return a new string. Common mistake: confusing slice (accepts negative indices) with substring (treats negative as 0). Best practice: use replaceAll (ES2021) over replace with global regex for simpler replacement; use template literals for concatenation; use includes over indexOf for readability.
.js.Built-in Objects.Proxy & Reflect.exp
Proxy wraps an object to intercept operations (get, set, delete, etc.) via traps. Reflect provides methods that mirror the default proxy behavior for forwarding.
.js.Built-in Objects.Intl API.exp
Intl provides locale-aware formatting for dates, numbers, currencies, and collation. Intl.DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, and ListFormat are the most common.
.js.Built-in Objects.TypedArrays (ArrayBuffer).exp
TypedArrays provide views over raw binary data in an ArrayBuffer. Types include Int8Array, Uint8Array, Float64Array, and more for performance-critical work.
.js.Built-in Objects.structuredClone & Deep Copy.exp
structuredClone creates a deep copy of an object, handling circular references and types like Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and Blob.
.js.Hoisting & Scopes.Hoisting Explained.exp

Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code execution. var declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined — accessing them before declaration returns undefined, not ReferenceError. let and const are hoisted but NOT initialized — they exist in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from block start until declaration, so accessing them throws ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted entirely (body included), so they can be called before their definition. Function expressions are NOT hoisted — use them only after the assignment line.
.js.Hoisting & Scopes.Global Scope.exp

The global scope is the outermost scope. In browsers, window is the global object; in Node.js, it's global. Variables declared with var at the top level become properties of the global object. let, const, and class at the top level do NOT become global object properties — they exist in the global scope but are not properties of window/global. Relying on global variables is considered bad practice — they create naming conflicts and make code hard to reason about. The Good Parts: minimize global scope by using IIFEs or modules.
.js.Hoisting & Scopes.Lexical Scoping.exp

Lexical (static) scoping means a variable's scope is determined by its position in the source code, not by how functions are called at runtime. Inner functions can access variables from outer scopes, but not vice versa. This is the foundation of closures — a function remembers the scope in which it was defined. JavaScript has no dynamic scoping — this is not scope, it's context (determined by call pattern). Understanding lexical scope helps predict which variables are accessible at any point in the code.
.js.Equality Comparisons.Object.is.exp

Object.is (ES6) compares two values for equality. It behaves like === except for two edge cases: Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true (NaN === NaN is false), and Object.is(0, -0) returns false (0 === -0 is true). Use Object.is when you need NaN equivalence or need to distinguish signed zeros. For most cases, === is sufficient and more readable. Object.is does NOT perform deep object comparison — references must match. It's available on all modern platforms and polyfillable for older ones.
.js.Equality Comparisons.SameValueZero.exp

SameValueZero is an equality algorithm used by Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes. It behaves like Object.is but treats -0 and 0 as equal. This means NaN is considered equal to itself (unlike ===) but -0 equals 0 (unlike Object.is). It's not directly callable in user code but is used internally by Set.has(), Map.has(), and includes(). Understanding it helps explain why Set.has(NaN) returns true but indexOf(NaN) returns -1.
.js.Async Details.The Event Loop.exp

The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model: single-threaded, non-blocking, and asynchronous by necessity. The call stack runs synchronous code. When an async operation completes, its callback is queued. Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) go to the task queue. Microtasks (Promise.then, async/await, queueMicrotask) go to the microtask queue. After each macrotask, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue before processing the next macrotask. This means promise callbacks run before setTimeout callbacks, even zero-delay ones. Blocking the call stack with long synchronous work freezes the page.
.js.Async Details.Microtasks vs Macrotasks.exp

Microtasks include Promise.then/catch/finally, MutationObserver, and queueMicrotask. Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, and UI rendering (browser). After every macrotask, the event loop processes all pending microtasks before the next macrotask or render. This is why Promise-based code runs before timer callbacks. queueMicrotask() explicitly schedules a microtask. Microtasks can starve the event loop if they continuously enqueue more microtasks — causing the page to become unresponsive despite no single long task.
.js.Async Details.Callbacks.exp

A callback is a function passed to another function for later execution. They are the foundation of async JavaScript — used in setTimeout, event handlers, fs.readFile, and fetch. Callback-based code suffers from 'callback hell' (pyramid of doom) when nested. Modern alternatives: Promises and async/await. The error-first callback pattern (Node.js convention) passes error as the first argument: callback(err, result). Always handle errors in callbacks — unhandled errors silently disappear.
.js.Modules.ES Modules (ESM).exp

ES Modules (ES6) use import and export statements. Each module has its own scope — no global leakage. Named exports export multiple values with specific names. Default export exports a single main value per module. Dynamic import() (ES2020) loads modules on demand (returns a Promise). ESM is static — imports are hoisted and resolved before execution, enabling tree-shaking. Modules are strict by default. Use type='module' on script tags in browsers, or 'type': 'module' in package.json for Node.js.
.js.Modules.CommonJS (CJS).exp

CommonJS is Node.js's original module system using require() and module.exports. require() loads modules synchronously — fine for servers but not browsers. module.exports can be any value. exports is a shorthand reference to module.exports — reassigning exports breaks the reference. Node.js supports both CJS (file.js or .cjs) and ESM (.mjs or type='module' package.json). Use require() for dynamic conditional imports. CJS modules are not tree-shakeable because exports are determined at runtime.
.js.Memory Management.Memory Lifecycle.exp

JavaScript manages memory automatically via garbage collection. The lifecycle: (1) Allocate — memory is reserved when you create values (objects, arrays, closures, DOM nodes); (2) Use — references point to the allocated memory as your code runs; (3) Release — when a value is no longer reachable, its memory becomes eligible for garbage collection. Reachability means the value can be accessed from a root (global object, current call stack, active closures). Values can become unreachable when all references go out of scope, are reassigned, or set to null.
.js.Memory Management.Garbage Collection.exp

Modern JavaScript engines use generational garbage collection. Young generation: new objects are allocated here — collected frequently (minor GC) since most objects die young. Old generation: objects that survive multiple GC cycles are promoted here — collected less often (major GC). The mark-and-sweep algorithm: starting from roots (global object, stack, DOM), the GC marks all reachable objects, then sweeps (frees) unmarked objects. Common memory leaks: detached DOM elements (referenced in JS but removed from DOM), forgotten timers holding references, global variable accumulation, and closures retaining large unnecessary data.
.js.Using Browser DevTools.Console Debugging.exp

Browser DevTools console is essential for debugging. console.log() prints values. console.error() and console.warn() print with severity icons and stack traces. console.table() renders arrays/objects as sortable tables. console.time()/timeEnd() measures execution. console.group()/groupEnd() nests logs. console.count() counts calls. console.trace() prints the call stack. Using debugger; statement pauses execution. For real debugging, use Sources panel breakpoints — they're more precise than console.log scatterguns.
.js.Using Browser DevTools.Performance Debugging.exp

Performance debugging identifies slow code. Use the Performance panel to record activity: look for long tasks (>50ms block main thread), forced reflow (reading layout properties after DOM mutations), and layout thrash (alternating reads/writes in loops). Lighthouse audits performance. Use performance.now() for precise timing. The Network panel shows request timing and waterfall. Avoid: forcing layout with offsetWidth/Height in loops, heavy synchronous work on the main thread, and excessive DOM manipulations without batching.
.js.Using Browser DevTools.Debugging Memory Leaks.exp

Memory leaks cause page slowdown and crashes. Use the Memory panel to take heap snapshots — compare 'before' and 'after' to see retained objects.
