Atlas provides automated backups with configurable retention (1-35 days for M10+). Serverless and M0 have continuous backups. Restore via UI, API, or CLI. Supports point-in-time recovery (PITR) within the retention window.
.mongodb.Backup & Recovery.Ops Manager & On-Premise Backups.exp

Ops Manager (Enterprise) provides automated backup, monitoring, and DB management for on-premise MongoDB. Supports continuous block-level backups with incremental snapshots, queryable backups, and point-in-time recovery.
.mongodb.Backup & Recovery.Continuous Backups & PITR.exp

Continuous backups apply oplog entries on top of snapshots for point-in-time recovery within a window. Trade-off: higher storage cost vs granular recovery. PITR allows restoring to any second within the window.
.mongodb.Backup & Recovery.Backup Strategy & Best Practices.exp

Combine snapshot backups (mongodump/Atlas snapshots) with oplog-based continuous backup for PITR. Automate with cron/Ops Manager/Atlas. Test restores regularly. Store backups in different region. Consider compliance retention.
.mysql.Getting Started.What is MySQL.exp

MySQL is the world's most popular open-source relational database. It uses SQL for querying and is commonly used with LAMP/LEMP stacks. Known for speed, reliability, and ease of use. Owned by Oracle, with MariaDB as a popular fork.
.mysql.Getting Started.Installing MySQL.exp

Install via package manager, official APT/YUM repos, Docker, or use XAMPP/MAMP for local dev. The mysql service must be running. Check status with systemctl. First-run setup: mysql_secure_installation.
.mysql.Getting Started.Connecting with mysql CLI.exp
The mysql CLI connects to a MySQL server. Options: -h host, -P port, -u user, -p password prompt. Use -e for inline queries. \q or exit to quit. Use \u db_name to switch databases.
.mysql.Getting Started.MySQL Data Types.exp

MySQL supports many data types: INT, BIGINT, VARCHAR, CHAR, TEXT, DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP, FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, JSON, ENUM, SET, BLOB. Choose types carefully — VARCHAR(255) for short strings, TEXT for long, DECIMAL for money.
.mysql.Data Definition.CREATE TABLE.exp

CREATE TABLE defines a new table. Specify columns with names and types, then constraints. ENGINE=InnoDB is default (supports transactions, FK). ENGINE=MyISAM is older (full-text search, no transactions). CHARACTER SET and COLLATE control encoding.
.mysql.Data Definition.ALTER TABLE.exp

ALTER TABLE modifies an existing table: ADD, DROP, MODIFY, CHANGE columns, or rename table. Use ALTER to add/drop indexes, constraints, and change storage settings. Be careful with large tables — ALTER can lock the table.
.mysql.Data Definition.DROP & TRUNCATE.exp

DROP TABLE removes the table entirely (data + structure). TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure — faster than DELETE for whole-table removal, but can't be rolled back in some engines. Use with extreme caution.
.mysql.Data Definition.Constraints.exp

Constraints enforce data integrity: PRIMARY KEY (unique identifier), FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity), UNIQUE (no duplicates), NOT NULL (required), CHECK (value validation), DEFAULT (fallback value). InnoDB supports FK constraints.
.mysql.CRUD Operations.SELECT.exp

SELECT retrieves rows. Use * for all columns, or list specific ones. WHERE filters, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT restricts rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates. AS renames columns. Use EXPLAIN to check query performance.
.mysql.CRUD Operations.INSERT.exp

INSERT adds rows. INSERT INTO ... VALUES for single row, INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...), for multiple. INSERT ... SET is an alternative syntax. LAST_INSERT_ID() returns the auto-generated id. Use ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for upsert.
.mysql.CRUD Operations.UPDATE.exp

UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE to avoid updating all rows. LIMIT restricts how many rows to update. Use JOIN in UPDATE to update based on values in other tables. Check affected rows with ROW_COUNT().
.mysql.CRUD Operations.DELETE.exp
DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE or all rows are deleted. Use JOIN to delete from multiple tables. TRUNCATE is faster for clearing all rows. Check what you'll delete first with SELECT COUNT(*).
.mysql.CRUD Operations.WHERE Clause.exp

WHERE filters rows. Operators: =, !=, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL. Combine with AND, OR, NOT. Use parentheses for complex logic. LIKE uses % (any chars) and _ (single char). IN matches any value in a list.
.mysql.CRUD Operations.ORDER BY & LIMIT.exp
ORDER BY sorts results (ASC ascending, DESC descending). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET skips rows (for pagination). For large pagination, use WHERE instead of OFFSET for better performance.
.mysql.Joins & Relationships.INNER JOIN.exp
INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables. Use table aliases for readability. Always prefix columns with table name/alias in JOIN queries. INNER JOIN is the most common join type.
.mysql.Joins & Relationships.LEFT & RIGHT JOIN.exp
LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where right doesn't match. RIGHT JOIN is the opposite (rarely used — prefer LEFT JOIN). Useful for finding missing relationships.
.mysql.Joins & Relationships.CROSS JOIN & SELF JOIN.exp

CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product (every row of A × every row of B). SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using aliases. Used for hierarchies (employees/managers), date ranges, and adjacency lists.
.mysql.Joins & Relationships.UNION & UNION ALL.exp

UNION combines results from multiple SELECT queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL is faster but keeps duplicates. All SELECTs must have the same number of columns with compatible types. Column names come from the first query.
.mysql.Aggregation & Grouping.GROUP BY & HAVING.exp

GROUP BY groups rows by column values. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) compute per-group stats. HAVING filters groups (like WHERE for groups). SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY or aggregate functions.
.mysql.Aggregation & Grouping.Aggregate Functions.exp

COUNT(*): row count. COUNT(col): non-null count. SUM(col): total. AVG(col): average. MIN(col): minimum. MAX(col): maximum. GROUP_CONCAT(col): concatenates values into a string. DISTINCT inside aggregates: COUNT(DISTINCT col).
.mysql.Aggregation & Grouping.ROLLUP & GROUPING.exp
WITH ROLLUP adds subtotal and grand total rows to GROUP BY results. GROUPING() distinguishes subtotal rows from regular rows. Useful for summary reports and dashboards.
.mysql.Functions & Expressions.String Functions.exp

MySQL has powerful string functions: CONCAT (join strings), SUBSTRING (extract part), LENGTH (byte count), CHAR_LENGTH (character count), UPPER/LOWER (case), TRIM (remove spaces), REPLACE (find/replace), LOCATE (position of substring).
.mysql.Functions & Expressions.Date & Time Functions.exp

Key functions: NOW() (current datetime), CURDATE() (date), CURTIME() (time). DATE_FORMAT for custom formatting. DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB for arithmetic. DATEDIFF for difference. EXTRACT for parts (YEAR, MONTH, DAY).
.mysql.Functions & Expressions.Conditional Expressions.exp

IF(condition, true_val, false_val) — simple ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END — multi-way branching. IFNULL(val, default) — coalesce null. COALESCE(val1, val2, ..., default) — first non-null.
.mysql.Indexes & Performance.Index Basics.exp

Indexes speed up SELECT queries at the cost of slower INSERT/UPDATE. CREATE INDEX on frequently queried columns. PRIMARY KEY is a clustered index. UNIQUE index enforces uniqueness. Use EXPLAIN to check if queries use indexes.
.mysql.Indexes & Performance.EXPLAIN Query Analysis.exp

EXPLAIN shows how MySQL executes a query. Key fields: type (ALL=full scan, ref/eq_ref=index lookup), possible_keys (indexes MySQL could use), key (index actually used), rows (estimated rows examined), Extra (Using index=covered, Using filesort=bad).
.mysql.Indexes & Performance.Slow Query Log.exp

Enable the slow query log to find performance issues. Set long_query_time (default 10s). Log queries that don't use indexes with log_queries_not_using_indexes. Analyze with mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest.
.mysql.Advanced.Transactions.exp

Transactions group operations as atomic units: all succeed or all roll back. START TRANSACTION / BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT creates rollback points. InnoDB supports transactions (MyISAM does not).
.mysql.Advanced.Stored Procedures.exp

Stored procedures are reusable SQL blocks stored on the server. DELIMITER changes the statement delimiter. IN, OUT, INOUT parameters. Variables with DECLARE. Handlers for error handling. Reduces network traffic for complex operations.
.mysql.Advanced.Views.exp

Views are saved SQL queries that act like virtual tables. Simplify complex queries, add security layers (restrict columns), and provide abstraction. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents inserts/updates that don't match the view condition.
.mysql.Advanced.Triggers.exp

Triggers automatically execute SQL when a table event occurs (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). BEFORE/AFTER timing. FOR EACH ROW per-row trigger. OLD/ NEW refer to row values. Useful for auditing, validation, and derived data.
.mysql.Advanced.JSON in MySQL.exp

MySQL has native JSON data type and functions: JSON_EXTRACT (or -> operator), JSON_UNQUOTE (or ->>), JSON_ARRAY, JSON_OBJECT, JSON_SET, JSON_KEYS, JSON_CONTAINS. Index JSON fields with generated columns.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.AWS RDS for MySQL.exp

Amazon RDS for MySQL is a managed MySQL service on AWS. Automates backups, patching, failover, and scaling. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Multi-AZ for HA with synchronous standby replica. Read replicas for read scaling. Storage auto-scaling up to 64TB. Encryption at rest with KMS. Performance Insights for query monitoring.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.AWS Aurora MySQL.exp

Amazon Aurora MySQL is AWS's cloud-native MySQL-compatible engine. Up to 5x faster than standard MySQL. Auto-scaling storage up to 128TB. 6-way replication across 3 AZs with 1/6th data written (quorum). Aurora Serverless v2 scales to zero. Global Database for cross-region replication. Backtrack rewinds DB without restore. Built-in connection pooling with RDS Proxy.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.Google Cloud SQL for MySQL.exp

Cloud SQL is GCP's fully managed MySQL service. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Automated backups with point-in-time recovery. High availability with regional failover across zones. Read replicas (including cross-region). Cloud SQL Proxy for secure IAM-based auth without public IP. Integrates with Vertex AI for in-database ML predictions. 30TB max storage. Private networking via VPC.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.Azure Database for MySQL.exp

Azure Database for MySQL is Microsoft's managed offering. Flexible Server mode: zone-redundant HA, stop/start, burstable SKUs. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Automated backups with 35-day retention. Azure Private Link for VNet integration. Azure Defender for threat detection. Read replicas (up to 10) within region and cross-region. Flexible Server supports up to 16TB storage.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.Oracle HeatWave MySQL.exp

Oracle HeatWave is MySQL on OCI with an integrated in-memory query accelerator. HeatWave engine runs analytics directly on MySQL data — no ETL. Up to 6.5x faster than Aurora at half the cost. Built-in ML: HeatWave AutoML trains models inside the database. Lakehouse: query object storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob, OCI) directly from MySQL. Consistent pricing across all global regions. Automatic in-memory caching of InnoDB buffer pool.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.PlanetScale.exp

PlanetScale is a serverless MySQL-compatible platform built on Vitess (YouTube's MySQL sharding layer). Git-like database branching: create schema branches, test changes, deploy via deploy requests with zero-downtime. Automatic horizontal scaling via Vitess sharding. Deploy requests for schema change review. Non-blocking schema migrations using gh-ost. Point-in-time recovery. Global read replicas. Connect via standard MySQL protocol. Foreign keys limited (Vitess constraint). Free $5/mo starter plan.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.DigitalOcean & Aiven.exp

DigitalOcean Managed Databases: simple managed MySQL with automated backups, HA failover, monitoring. Starts at $15/mo (1 vCPU, 1GB). Aiven: multi-cloud MySQL on AWS/Azure/GCP, with BYOC option. Free tier available. PlanetScale, Aiven, and DigitalOcean offer managed MySQL outside the big 3 clouds, often simpler pricing and less lock-in.
.mysql.MySQL Cloud.Migration to Cloud MySQL.exp

Strategies: dump-and-restore (mysqldump to cloud), logical replication, or physical migration (AWS DMS, GCP Database Migration Service, Azure DMS). For minimal downtime use CDC-based replication. Validate character sets, timezone, sql_mode differences. Plan for network latency — co-locate app and DB in same region. Use connection pooling (ProxySQL, RDS Proxy) for serverless apps.
.mysql.Advanced SQL.Stored Procedures.exp

Stored procedures are reusable SQL blocks stored on the server. Use DELIMITER to change the statement delimiter. IN parameters pass values in, OUT returns values, INOUT does both. Variables declared with DECLARE. DECLARE ... HANDLER for error handling. A common mistake is forgetting to reset DELIMITER back to ;. Procedures reduce network traffic by executing logic server-side.
.mysql.Advanced SQL.Triggers.exp

Triggers execute automatically on table events: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. BEFORE triggers validate or modify data before the operation, AFTER triggers run after. OLD refers to pre-change values (UPDATE/DELETE), NEW refers to post-change values (INSERT/UPDATE). A common mistake is creating recursive triggers (a trigger on Table A that updates Table A again). Use triggers sparingly — they're invisible to applications and can make debugging hard.
.mysql.Advanced SQL.Views.exp

Views are saved SELECT queries that behave like virtual tables. They simplify complex joins, restrict column access (security), and provide schema abstraction. Updatable views must map directly to a single table's columns. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents INSERT/UPDATE that would make rows disappear from the view. Views do not improve performance — they're just stored queries, not materialized (unlike materialized views in PostgreSQL).
.mysql.Advanced SQL.Indexing Strategies.exp

MySQL supports BTREE (default, for =, >, <, BETWEEN, LIKE without leading %) and HASH (MEMORY engine only, for = only). Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule: index on (a, b, c) helps queries on a, a+b, a+b+c, but not b or c alone. Use EXPLAIN to verify index usage. Common mistakes: over-indexing (slows writes), indexing low-cardinality columns (e.g., gender), and not covering highly selective columns first.
.mysql.Advanced SQL.Transactions & Isolation.exp

START TRANSACTION begins a transaction. COMMIT saves changes permanently. ROLLBACK undoes all changes since START TRANSACTION. SAVEPOINT creates a named rollback point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes to that point. Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads), READ COMMITTED (default in most DBs, no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (default in MySQL/InnoDB, no non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (fully isolated, slowest). Higher isolation = less concurrency. A common mistake is forgetting that DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) implicitly commit the current transaction.
.mysql.Administration.User Management.exp

CREATE USER creates a new user with a host (e.g., 'user'@'localhost'). GRANT assigns privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALL PRIVILEGES. REVOKE removes privileges. FLUSH PRIVILEGES reloads the grant tables (not needed if using GRANT/REVOKE directly, but needed after manual INSERT/UPDATE on mysql.user). Common mistake: creating 'user'@'%' (any host) when only localhost is needed — a security risk. Always use strong passwords. SHOW GRANTS to inspect current privileges.
.mysql.Administration.Backup & Restore.exp

mysqldump is the primary backup tool. Use --single-transaction for InnoDB consistency without locking. --routines, --triggers, --events include them. --all-databases or --databases for specific DBs. mysqlimport bulk-loads data from text files. SELECT INTO OUTFILE exports query results to a file on the server. Common mistake: forgetting --single-transaction on a live InnoDB DB (causes table locks). For large DBs, use Percona XtraBackup for physical/hot backups — mysqldump is too slow for >50GB.
.next.Getting Started.Pages.exp

The Pages Router is the original routing system in Next.js. Pages in the pages directory automatically become routes based on their file name, with index.js mapping to the root and nested folders creating nested paths.
.next.Getting Started.Routing.exp
Next.js supports dynamic routes using bracket syntax like [id].js. Links are created using the next/link component for client-side navigation with prefetching.
.next.Getting Started.App Router.exp
The App Router (app directory) is the modern routing system using React Server Components by default. Routes are defined by folders with page.js files, and layouts can be nested via layout.js.
.next.Data Fetching.getServerSideProps.exp

getServerSideProps runs on every request on the server, fetching data before rendering the page. It is used when you need fresh data on each request or access to request-time information like cookies.
.next.Data Fetching.getStaticProps.exp
getStaticProps runs at build time to fetch data for static generation. The generated HTML is reused for each request, making it ideal for content that changes infrequently.
.next.Data Fetching.Server Actions.exp

Server Actions allow running server-side code directly from client components. They are functions defined with 'use server' that can be called via form actions or programmatically, handling mutations without building API routes.
.next.Rendering.SSR.exp

Server-Side Rendering generates HTML on each request, delivering fully rendered pages to the client. This improves SEO and initial load performance at the cost of slower response times compared to static generation.
.next.Rendering.SSG.exp

Static Site Generation pre-renders pages at build time into HTML and JSON files. These static files are served by CDN with near-instant load times, ideal for marketing pages, blogs, and documentation.
.next.Rendering.ISR.exp

Incremental Static Regeneration allows updating static content after build without rebuilding the entire site. Pages are served from cache and regenerated in the background when the revalidation window expires.
.next.Rendering.CSR.exp
Client-Side Rendering fetches data and renders content in the browser after the initial page load. This is useful for highly interactive, user-specific dashboards where SEO is not critical.
.next.Styling.CSS Modules.exp
CSS Modules scope styles locally to the component by generating unique class names. Files named *.module.css are automatically supported, preventing style conflicts across components.
.next.Styling.Tailwind.exp
Next.js integrates with Tailwind CSS out of the box. Tailwind's utility classes enable rapid styling directly in JSX, with purging of unused styles in production builds.
.next.Styling.CSS-in-JS.exp
CSS-in-JS libraries like styled-components and Emotion work with Next.js but require configuration. The app router requires using a registry to collect styles during server-side rendering.
.next.API Routes.REST.exp
Next.js API routes let you build REST endpoints inside the pages/api directory. Each file exports functions matching HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) that receive req and res objects.
.next.API Routes.Middleware.exp
Middleware runs before every request and can modify headers, redirect users, or rewrite URLs. It is defined as middleware.ts in the root of the project and executes on the Edge runtime.
.next.API Routes.Edge Functions.exp
Edge Functions run on the Vercel Edge Network using the Edge Runtime. They provide low-latency, globally distributed execution for API routes, middleware, and server rendering.
.next.Authentication.NextAuth.exp
NextAuth.js (now Auth.js) provides a complete authentication solution for Next.js. It supports OAuth providers, email magic links, and credentials with minimal setup using the app router.
.next.Authentication.JWT.exp
JSON Web Tokens are commonly used for stateless authentication in Next.js. Tokens are signed server-side and verified on each request, often stored in httpOnly cookies for security.
.next.Authentication.Session Management.exp
Session management in Next.js can use database-backed sessions or JWT-based sessions via NextAuth. The session is accessed via useSession on the client or getServerSession on the server.
.next.Performance.Image Optimization.exp
The next/image component automatically optimizes images with lazy loading, responsive sizes, and WebP/AVIF format conversion. Images are served via the built-in image optimizer API.
.next.Performance.Fonts.exp
next/font automatically optimizes and self-hosts Google Fonts and custom fonts, eliminating external requests. It supports variable fonts and subsetting for reduced bundle size.
.next.Performance.Bundle Analysis.exp
Next.js provides built-in bundle analysis through @next/bundle-analyzer. It generates visual reports showing the size of each JavaScript bundle and its dependencies to identify optimization targets.
.next.Deployment.Vercel.exp
Vercel is the official deployment platform for Next.js, offering zero-config deploys from Git, automatic HTTPS, edge functions, and preview deployments for every pull request.
.next.Deployment.Docker.exp
Next.js apps can be containerized with Docker for deployment on any container orchestration platform. A multi-stage Dockerfile optimizes for build speed and image size.
.next.Deployment.Self-hosted.exp
Next.js supports self-hosting on any Node.js server using the standalone output mode. The standalone folder includes only production dependencies, minimizing deployment size.
.next.App Router Advanced.Route Groups.exp
Route groups organize routes without affecting URL paths by wrapping folder names in parentheses. They are useful for separating marketing, admin, and auth sections with different layouts.
.next.App Router Advanced.Parallel Routes.exp
Parallel routes render multiple pages simultaneously in the same layout using named slots. Each slot has its own loading and error states, enabling complex dashboard and feed layouts.
.next.App Router Advanced.Intercepting Routes.exp
Intercepting routes overlay content from another route within the current layout using (..) syntax. They are commonly used for modal previews that render as full pages on hard refresh.
.next.Metadata & SEO.Static Metadata.exp
The metadata object export defines page-level SEO data including title, description, Open Graph, and Twitter cards. It supports static values and template-based title generation.
.next.Metadata & SEO.Dynamic Metadata.exp
Dynamic metadata is generated with the generateMetadata function that receives route params and search params, enabling SEO data based on fetched content.
.next.Metadata & SEO.Metadata API.exp
Next.js provides a comprehensive Metadata API covering Open Graph, Twitter cards, JSON-LD structured data, manifest, icons, robots, sitemaps, and alternate language links.
.next.Build & Tooling.Turbopack.exp
Turbopack is Next.js's Rust-based incremental bundler replacing webpack in development. It provides near-instant HMR, sub-second cold starts, and incremental computation for large projects.
.next.Build & Tooling.Partial Prerendering.exp
Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering on the same page. Static shell content is served instantly while dynamic holes stream in after rendering on the server.
.next.Build & Tooling.Instrumentation.exp
Instrumentation hooks allow running code on server startup. The register() function in instrumentation.ts is useful for OpenTelemetry tracing, metrics setup, and infrastructure initialization.
.node.Getting Started.REPL.exp

The Node.js REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop) provides an interactive shell to execute JavaScript expressions in real time. It's useful for quick prototyping, debugging, and testing code snippets without creating a file.
.node.Getting Started.Modules.exp
Node.js uses the CommonJS module system by default, where each file is treated as a separate module. Modules are loaded using `require()` and exports are defined via `module.exports` or `exports`.
.node.Getting Started.NPM.exp
NPM is the default package manager for Node.js, used to install, manage, and publish packages. It reads `package.json` to resolve dependencies and supports semantic versioning for version control.
.node.Getting Started.ES Modules.exp
Node.js supports ES modules (import/export) alongside CommonJS. Use .mjs extension or set "type": "module" in package.json. ES modules support top-level await and static analysis for tree-shaking.
.node.Getting Started.Global Objects.exp
Node.js provides global objects like __dirname, __filename, process, Buffer, and console that are available without importing. Each module has its own __dirname and __filename scoped to that file.
.node.File System.fs module.exp
The `fs` module provides both synchronous and asynchronous methods to interact with the file system. The promise-based API (`fs/promises`) is preferred for modern async code.
.node.File System.Path.exp
The `path` module provides utilities for working with file and directory paths. It handles path normalization, joining segments, and extracting file extension or directory components.
.node.File System.Streams.exp
Streams allow processing data piece by piece without loading entire files into memory. They are ideal for handling large files or real-time data like video and HTTP responses.
.node.File System.File Watching.exp
Node can watch files or directories for changes using fs.watch or fs.watchFile. Useful for live reload, build tools, and monitoring config file changes without restarting the process.
.node.Async Programming.Callbacks.exp
Callbacks are functions passed as arguments to be executed after an async operation completes. They form the foundation of async programming in Node but can lead to deeply nested 'callback hell'.
.node.Async Programming.Promises.exp

Promises represent the eventual completion or failure of an async operation, providing a cleaner chaining mechanism than callbacks. A promise exists in one of three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected.
.node.Async Programming.async/await.exp

async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises that makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code. Functions declared with `async` always return a Promise, and `await` pauses execution until the Promise settles.
.node.Async Programming.Event Loop.exp

The event loop is the core mechanism that enables Node's non-blocking I/O. It processes callbacks through phases: timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, and close callbacks, all in a single thread.
.node.HTTP.HTTP Module.exp
The `http` module allows creating HTTP servers and clients without external dependencies. It handles low-level networking, request parsing, and response writing with a stream-based API.
.node.HTTP.Server.exp
Building an HTTP server involves handling requests and sending responses. Each request receives an IncomingMessage object and a ServerResponse object for controlling the response data and headers.
.node.HTTP.Request Handling.exp

Node.js processes requests via event emitters on the request stream. You can listen for 'data' and 'end' events to read request bodies, parse headers via `req.headers`, and inspect the URL and method.
.node.NPM.Package Management.exp
NPM manages project dependencies defined in `package.json`. The `node_modules` folder stores installed packages, and `package-lock.json` ensures reproducible installs across environments.
.node.NPM.Scripts.exp
The `scripts` field in `package.json` defines aliases for commands that can be run via `npm run`. Pre/post hooks allow automatic script chaining, and scripts have access to `node_modules/.bin`.
.node.NPM.Publishing.exp
Publishing packages to the npm registry requires an npm account, a unique package name, and proper versioning via `npm version`. Packages should include a README, license, and main entry point.
.node.NPM.Workspaces.exp
NPM workspaces allow managing multiple packages in a single monorepo. Dependencies are hoisted to the root node_modules, and scripts can run across all workspaces concurrently.
.node.NPM.NPX.exp
NPX runs npm packages without installing them globally. It's useful for one-off commands like scaffolding tools, linters, or any CLI tool that you don't need permanently.
.node.Buffers & Streams.Buffer.exp

Buffer provides a way to work with binary data directly in Node.js. It is a fixed-size chunk of memory allocated outside the V8 heap, useful for handling raw data from files, networks, or crypto operations.
.node.Buffers & Streams.Readable/Writable.exp
Streams are classified into Readable, Writable, Duplex, and Transform types. Readable streams produce data that can be consumed via `data` events or piped to Writable streams.
.node.Buffers & Streams.Transform.exp
Transform streams are Duplex streams that can modify data during read/write operations. They are commonly used for compression, encryption, and data format conversion.
.node.Buffers & Streams.Pipeline & Finished.exp
stream.pipeline handles piping streams with automatic cleanup and error propagation. stream.finished provides a callback when a stream is no longer readable or writable.
.node.Child Processes.spawn.exp
spawn launches a new process with streaming I/O. It returns a ChildProcess object with stdin, stdout, and stderr streams, ideal for long-running processes with large output.
.node.Child Processes.exec.exp
exec spawns a shell and runs a command, buffering the output. It's simpler than spawn for short commands but has a 1MB output buffer limit and higher risk of shell injection.
.node.Child Processes.fork.exp
fork creates a new Node.js process with an IPC channel for message passing. It is designed for offloading CPU-intensive work to separate processes while keeping communication easy.
.node.Child Processes.execFile.exp
execFile is similar to exec but spawns the command directly without a shell, making it more secure. It is suitable for running binary executables with arguments and no shell interpretation.
.node.Events & Emitters.EventEmitter.exp
EventEmitter is a core Node.js pattern for handling asynchronous events. Objects emit named events that trigger registered listener functions, enabling decoupled communication between components.
.node.Events & Emitters.Custom Events.exp
Custom events allow building event-driven architectures. Use event names as constants to avoid typos, and leverage EventEmitter for pub/sub patterns throughout your application.
.node.Events & Emitters.Max Listeners.exp
EventEmitter warns about memory leaks when more than 10 listeners are attached. Use setMaxListeners to increase the limit, but first investigate if listeners are being properly removed.
.node.Errors & Debugging.Error Handling.exp
Node.js uses the standard Error class and supports custom error types. Unhandled promise rejections and uncaught exceptions should be caught globally to prevent process crashes.
.node.Errors & Debugging.Debugger.exp

Node.js includes a built-in debugger accessible via `--inspect` flag, which opens a Chrome DevTools-compatible interface. The `debugger` statement creates breakpoints, and `node inspect` provides a CLI debugger.
.node.Errors & Debugging.Process.exp

The `process` object provides information about the current Node.js process, including environment variables, command-line arguments, memory usage, and exit control. It is available globally everywhere.
.node.Errors & Debugging.Profiling.exp
Node.js built-in profiler and V8 inspector help identify performance bottlenecks. Use --prof for CPU profiling and the inspector for flame graphs and heap snapshots.
.node.Errors & Debugging.Console Methods.exp
The console module provides debugging utilities beyond console.log: console.table for arrays, console.time for timing, console.trace for stack traces, and console.group for nested output.
.node.Testing.Assert.exp
Node's built-in assert module provides basic assertion testing. While minimal, it is useful for simple checks and can be used with the built-in test runner.
.node.Testing.Jest.exp
Jest is the most popular testing framework for Node.js with zero-config setup, built-in mocking, code coverage, snapshot testing, and watch mode.
.node.Testing.Mocha & Chai.exp
Mocha is a flexible test framework paired with Chai for assertions. It supports BDD/TDD interfaces, async testing, and extensive plugin ecosystems.
.node.Testing.Node Test Runner.exp
Node 18+ includes a built-in test runner (node:test) with assertion library (node:assert). It supports mocking, code coverage, and runs tests in parallel without external dependencies.
.node.Process Management.PM2.exp
PM2 is a production process manager for Node.js with load balancing, auto-restart, log management, monitoring dashboard, and zero-downtime deployments.
.node.Process Management.Environment Variables.exp
Environment variables configure Node.js apps across environments without code changes. Use dotenv for local development and process.env for runtime access.
.node.Process Management.Graceful Shutdown.exp
Production Node.js apps must handle SIGTERM gracefully, closing connections and completing in-flight requests before exiting.
.node.Security.Helmet.exp
Helmet secures Express apps by setting HTTP headers: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, and more.
.node.Security.Input Validation.exp
Validate and sanitize all user input to prevent injection attacks. Use libraries like Joi, Zod, or express-validator for schema validation.
.node.Security.CORS.exp
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing must be configured to control which domains can access your API. Restrict origins, methods, and headers to the minimum needed.
.node.Advanced.Worker Threads.exp
Worker threads enable true multi-threading in Node.js for CPU-intensive tasks. Each worker runs in its own V8 context with isolated memory, communicating via message passing.
.node.Advanced.Cluster.exp
The cluster module allows forking multiple Node.js processes to share server load across CPU cores. The master process distributes incoming connections to worker processes via round-robin scheduling.
.node.Advanced.Performance Hooks.exp
The perf_hooks module provides performance measurement APIs similar to the Web Performance API. Use PerformanceObserver to collect timing data for monitoring and optimization.
.nuxt.Getting Started.Project Setup.exp
Nuxt 3 projects are created using the nuxi CLI. The scaffolding tool asks about desired features like package manager, UI framework, and modules, generating a ready-to-develop project structure.
.nuxt.Getting Started.Pages.exp
The pages directory in Nuxt automatically generates routes based on file structure. Each .vue file becomes a route, with index.vue as the root and dynamic routes using brackets like [id].vue.
.nuxt.Getting Started.Routing.exp
Nuxt provides <NuxtLink> for client-side navigation and <NuxtPage> for rendering matched routes. Route middleware can be defined to protect pages or redirect users based on conditions.
.nuxt.Data Fetching.useFetch.exp
useFetch is the simplest way to fetch data in Nuxt 3. It automatically deduplicates requests, handles caching, and provides reactive refs for data, pending state, and error handling.
.nuxt.Data Fetching.useAsyncData.exp
useAsyncData provides more control over data fetching than useFetch. It accepts a custom fetcher function and supports keys for caching, refresh intervals, and lazy loading options.
.nuxt.Data Fetching.Server Routes.exp
Server routes in the server/api directory handle backend logic with h3 event handlers. They support all HTTP methods and can access request body, query parameters, and cookies directly.
.nuxt.Rendering.Universal.exp
Universal rendering is Nuxt's default mode, combining server-side rendering with client-side hydration. The server renders HTML on first request, then Vue takes over for SPA-like navigation.
.nuxt.Rendering.SPA.exp
Single Page Application mode disables server-side rendering entirely. All rendering happens client-side, with the server only serving a minimal HTML shell. Useful for fully client-driven apps.
.nuxt.Rendering.Static Generation.exp
Static generation pre-renders all pages at build time using nuxt generate. The output is a fully static site deployable on any static hosting provider like Netlify or Vercel.
.nuxt.Modules.Auth.exp
The @sidebase/nuxt-auth module provides a complete authentication system for Nuxt 3. It supports multiple auth providers, session management, and middleware protection out of the box.
.nuxt.Modules.Content.exp
Nuxt Content is a file-based CMS that reads Markdown, JSON, and YAML files from the content directory. It provides a queryable MongoDB-like API and automatic rendering of content files.
.nuxt.Modules.Tailwind.exp
The Nuxt Tailwind module integrates Tailwind CSS with zero configuration. It auto-imports the config, enables HMR for styles, and purges unused classes in production builds.
.nuxt.Modules.SEO.exp
Nuxt provides built-in SEO tools through useHead composable and the @nuxtjs/seo module. It manages meta tags, Open Graph, structured data, and sitemaps for better search visibility.
.nuxt.State Management.useState.exp
useState is Nuxt's built-in reactive state composable that works across server and client. It creates a singleton ref that persists across component re-renders and is serialized during SSR.
.nuxt.State Management.Pinia.exp
Pinia is the recommended state management library for Nuxt 3. It provides a intuitive API with full TypeScript support, devtools integration, and automatic SSR hydration.
.nuxt.State Management.Store Patterns.exp
Nuxt stores follow the composition API pattern with defineStore. Stores can be organized by domain feature and accessed anywhere in the app via the generated composable function.
.nuxt.Auth & Middleware.Route Middleware.exp
Route middleware in Nuxt runs before entering a route and can redirect or cancel navigation. Middleware files are placed in the middleware directory and can be applied globally or per-route.
.nuxt.Auth & Middleware.Auth Module.exp
The nuxt-auth module provides session-based authentication with built-in login pages, OAuth support, and credential-based auth. It automatically handles token refresh and session persistence.
.nuxt.Deployment.Vercel.exp
Deploying Nuxt to Vercel requires the Vercel preset. Vercel automatically detects the framework, optimizes serverless functions, and provides edge network distribution.
.nuxt.Deployment.Netlify.exp
Nuxt deploys to Netlify using the Netlify preset, generating edge functions for server routes. Netlify provides automatic HTTPS, deploy previews, and form handling.
.nuxt.Deployment.Node Server.exp
The Node server preset runs Nuxt as a standalone Node.js application. This is ideal for self-hosting on VPS, Docker containers, or traditional server environments.
.nuxt.Advanced.Auto-imports.exp

Nuxt automatically imports composables, components, and utilities from predefined directories. Components in components/, composables in composables/, and utils in utils/ are auto-imported without explicit imports.
.nuxt.Advanced.Layers.exp
Nuxt layers allow extending a base Nuxt project from external sources or local directories. Layers can override components, pages, composables, and configuration, enabling modular architectures.
.nuxt.Advanced.Modules Dev.exp
Creating custom Nuxt modules allows packaging reusable functionality. Modules can modify the Nuxt configuration, add hooks, register components, and integrate with the build pipeline.
.nuxt.Nuxt DevTools.Overview.exp
Nuxt DevTools provides an in-app panel with page inspection, component tree, state editor, timeline, and module management. It is available in development with zero configuration.
.nuxt.Nuxt DevTools.Pages & Components.exp
The DevTools Pages tab displays all auto-detected routes with their middleware, layout, and data dependencies. The Components tab shows the live component tree with state inspection.
.nuxt.Nuxt DevTools.Timeline & Analysis.exp
The Timeline tab records async operations, navigation events, and rendering performance. It helps identify slow API calls, excessive reactivity, and rendering bottlenecks.
.nuxt.Assets & Media.Nuxt Image.exp
Nuxt Image (@nuxt/image) provides automatic image optimization with responsive sizes, format conversion to WebP/AVIF, lazy loading, and CDN provider integrations (Cloudinary, Imgix, etc).
.nuxt.Assets & Media.Public Assets.exp
Assets in the public/ directory are served at the root URL without processing. Assets in assets/ are processed by Vite (version-hashed, minified) and imported via ~/assets path.
.nuxt.Assets & Media.Fonts.exp
Nuxt Fonts (@nuxt/fonts) automatically optimizes Google Fonts and custom fonts with self-hosting, subsetting, and fallback generation to eliminate CLS from font swaps.
.nuxt.Server & Nitro.Nitro Engine.exp
Nitro is Nuxt's server engine powering API routes, middleware, and SSR. It supports multiple deployment presets (Node, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare) and auto-detects the target environment.
.nuxt.Server & Nitro.Hybrid Rendering.exp
Hybrid rendering lets you define different rendering strategies per route: SSR, SSG, SPA, or ISR. Route rules control caching, prerendering, and rendering modes granularly.
.nuxt.Server & Nitro.Server Storage.exp
Nitro's server storage provides a unified key-value API across filesystem, Redis, Cloudflare KV, and other drivers. It handles session storage, cache, and file uploads without extra dependencies.
.pg.Getting Started.PostgreSQL History & Overview.exp

PostgreSQL began as POSTGRES at UC Berkeley in 1986, led by Michael Stonebraker. It evolved into PostgreSQL (Post-GreSQL) in 1996, emphasizing SQL compliance and extensibility. Today it is the world's most advanced open-source relational database, known for ACID compliance, MVCC, extensibility, and a vibrant community.
.pg.Getting Started.Installation & Configuration.exp

PostgreSQL can be installed via package managers (apt, yum, brew), Docker, or compiled from source. The main configuration file is postgresql.conf, controlling memory, logging, connections, and replication settings. After install, the postgres service must be started.
.pg.Getting Started.psql Basics.exp

psql is the official interactive terminal for PostgreSQL. Connect to a database, run SQL queries, and use backslash meta-commands. Essential commands: \c to connect, \dt list tables, \d describe, \l list databases, \du list roles.
.pg.Getting Started.pgAdmin GUI.exp

pgAdmin is a popular web-based GUI for PostgreSQL. It provides visual query building, schema browsing, dashboard monitoring, and server management. The server runs as a Python/Flask app and can be accessed via browser.
.pg.Getting Started.Connection Strings & Service File.exp

PostgreSQL supports libpq connection strings (postgresql://user:pass@host:port/db) and a pg_service.conf file that stores named connection parameters for reuse. Environment variables (PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD) also configure connections.
.pg.Getting Started..pgpass & Authentication.exp

The .pgpass file stores passwords for non-interactive connections. Format: hostname:port:database:username:password. File must have 0600 permissions. psql and other libpq clients read it automatically when no password is provided.
.pg.Getting Started.psql Meta-Commands Deep Dive.exp

psql offers 100+ backslash meta-commands. \g executes the query buffer, \i includes a file, \o redirects output, \x toggles expanded display, \e opens an external editor, \timing shows query duration, \watch repeats a query, and \copy performs server-side data transfer.
.pg.Data Definition.CREATE TABLE Deep Dive.exp

CREATE TABLE defines a new relation with named columns, data types, and optional constraints. Supports storage parameters (FILLFACTOR, autovacuum), WITH OIDs (deprecated), ON COMMIT behavior for temp tables, and tablespace assignment. Columns can have defaults, nullability, and compression.
.pg.Data Definition.Column Constraints.exp

Constraints enforce data integrity at the column level: NOT NULL prevents nulls, UNIQUE ensures no duplicates, DEFAULT supplies a fallback value, CHECK validates a boolean expression, and REFERENCES (foreign key) links to another table's column. Multiple constraints can stack.
.pg.Data Definition.Table Constraints & EXCLUDE.exp

Table-level constraints span multiple columns: PRIMARY KEY (composite), UNIQUE (composite), FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, and EXCLUDE. EXCLUDE ensures no two rows satisfy a condition using GiST operators, useful for calendar bookings, IP allocation, and overlapping ranges.
.pg.Data Definition.Sequences & SERIAL.exp

Sequences generate unique numeric values. SERIAL is shorthand for creating an INTEGER column with an auto-incrementing sequence. Sequences support CACHE, CYCLE, MINVALUE, MAXVALUE, and can be manipulated via nextval(), currval(), setval(), and ALTER SEQUENCE.
.pg.Data Definition.IDENTITY Columns.exp

GENERATED AS IDENTITY (SQL standard) replaces SERIAL. Supports BY DEFAULT (allows manual override) or ALWAYS (prevents manual override). Offers better schema introspection, no orphan sequences, and proper dependency tracking. Preferred over SERIAL in modern PostgreSQL.
.pg.Data Definition.GENERATED Columns.exp

Generated columns compute values from other columns. STORED means the value is computed on write and stored physically. VIRTUAL is not yet supported in PostgreSQL. Useful for derived data like full_name from first and last name, or price with tax.
.pg.Data Definition.Table Inheritance.exp

PostgreSQL supports table inheritance where a child table inherits all columns from a parent. Queries on the parent include child rows by default (use ONLY to exclude children). Useful for partitioning and code reuse, though modern partitioning is preferred over traditional inheritance.
.pg.Data Definition.Table Partitioning.exp

Partitioning splits large tables into smaller physical pieces while preserving a single logical view. Methods: RANGE (by date/id range), LIST (by discrete values), HASH (by hash of key). Partitions can be sub-partitioned, and partition pruning dramatically improves query performance.
.pg.Data Definition.Temporary Tables.exp

Temporary tables (prefixed with TEMP or TEMPORARY) exist only for the duration of a session or transaction. They are visible only to the creating session, stored in a temporary schema, and can have ON COMMIT DROP or ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS behavior. Useful for intermediate results.
.pg.Data Definition.UNLOGGED Tables.exp

UNLOGGED tables skip WAL (Write-Ahead Log) generation, making writes ~10x faster. They are NOT crash-safe — truncated or lost after an unclean shutdown. Ideal for ephemeral or cache data that can be rebuilt. Cannot be replicated via streaming replication.
.pg.Data Types.Numeric Types.exp

PostgreSQL offers SMALLINT (2 bytes), INTEGER (4 bytes), BIGINT (8 bytes), NUMERIC(p,s) for exact precision, REAL (4-byte float), DOUBLE PRECISION (8-byte float), and MONEY for currency. NUMERIC is preferred for financial calculations requiring exact decimal storage without rounding errors.
.pg.Data Types.Character Types.exp

CHAR(n) is a fixed-length string (blank-padded), VARCHAR(n) is variable-length with a limit, and TEXT is unlimited. PostgreSQL treats all three similarly internally — there is no performance penalty for TEXT over VARCHAR. Use CHECK if you need length constraints beyond the type itself.
.pg.Data Types.Binary Data (BYTEA).exp

BYTEA stores binary strings (byte arrays). Supports hex format (\x...) and escape format. Use encode()/decode() for conversion to/from hex, base64. BYTEA is limited to 1 GB per value. For large objects >1 GB, use the large object API (lo_creat, lo_import, lo_export).
.pg.Data Types.Date/Time Types.exp

PostgreSQL has DATE (no time), TIME (no date, with/without timezone), TIMESTAMP (date+time, with/without timezone), TIMESTAMPTZ (with timezone), and INTERVAL (duration). TIMESTAMPTZ stores internally as UTC and converts to session timezone on display. Use AT TIME ZONE for conversions.
.pg.Data Types.Boolean & UUID.exp

BOOLEAN stores TRUE, FALSE, or NULL. Accepts 'yes'/'no', '1'/'0', 't'/'f' as input. UUID stores Universally Unique Identifiers (128-bit). The uuid-ossp or pgcrypto extension provides generation functions (gen_random_uuid()). UUIDs are ideal for distributed system primary keys.
.pg.Data Types.Arrays & Composite Types.exp

Arrays store multiple values of the same type in a single column. Use array constructors or ARRAY[...] syntax. Supports multi-dimensional arrays and rich operators (@>, <@, &&). Composite types bundle multiple fields into one column, created via CREATE TYPE or inferred from table row types.
.pg.Data Types.Range Types.exp

Range types represent intervals: int4range, int8range, numrange, tsrange, tstzrange, daterange. Operators include && (overlap), @> (contains), <@ (contained by), -|- (adjacent). GiST indexes on ranges enable fast exclusion constraints and overlap queries for scheduling, geofencing, and log analysis.
.pg.Data Types.JSON & JSONB Deep Dive.exp

JSON stores text as-is (preserving whitespace, order, duplicates). JSONB stores a decomposed binary format (efficient indexing, no duplicates, no key order). JSONB supports GIN indexes for containment (@>), existence (?), and key/value queries. Operators: -> (json), ->> (text), #> (path), #>> (path text).
.pg.Data Types.hstore Key-Value Store.exp

hstore stores sets of key-value pairs within a single column (both keys and values are strings). Requires the hstore extension. Useful for semi-structured attributes when the schema is not fixed. Operators: -> (value by key), ? (key exists), @> (contains pair), || (concatenate).
.pg.Data Types.Network Address Types.exp

PostgreSQL provides inet (IPv4/IPv6 addresses), cidr (network blocks), and macaddr (MAC addresses). Built-in operators test containment (<<=, <<), sort, and compare. The ip4r extension (not built-in) adds indexed range operations for advanced network queries.
.pg.Data Types.Geometric Types.exp

PostgreSQL supports geometric data types: point (x,y), line, lseg (line segment), box, path (open/closed), polygon, and circle. Operators test containment (@>), intersection (?-\||), distance (<->). GiST indexes accelerate geometric queries. Useful for GIS-like applications without PostGIS overhead.
.pg.Data Types.Domain & Custom Types.exp

CREATE DOMAIN creates a reusable type based on an existing type with constraints (CHECK, NOT NULL, DEFAULT). CREATE TYPE creates a custom composite or enum type (or base type via C extension). Domains are great for business-level validation like us_zip_code, email, or positive_numeric.
.pg.Querying.SELECT Deep Dive.exp

SELECT defines the projection, FROM specifies the source, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY groups for aggregation, HAVING filters groups, ORDER BY sorts results, and LIMIT/OFFSET paginates. Execution order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> WINDOW -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
.pg.Querying.JOIN Types.exp

INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches. RIGHT JOIN is the symmetric opposite. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matching where possible. CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product of all row combinations.
.pg.Querying.LATERAL & Self Joins.exp

LATERAL allows a subquery in FROM to reference columns from preceding FROM items. Essential for top-N-per-group queries and calling set-returning functions per row. Self JOIN joins a table to itself (using aliases) to query hierarchical data like org charts or threaded comments.
.pg.Querying.Set Operations.exp

UNION combines results of two queries, deduplicating rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates. INTERSECT returns rows present in both queries. EXCEPT returns rows from the first query not present in the second. All set operations require matching column counts and compatible data types.
.pg.Querying.Recursive CTE.exp

WITH RECURSIVE lets a CTE reference itself. The anchor member runs first (non-recursive), then the recursive member repeatedly joins the CTE's output until no new rows are produced. Essential for tree traversal (org charts, category hierarchies), graph queries, and generating series.
.pg.Querying.Correlated Subqueries.exp

A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query and is re-evaluated for every row. Used in WHERE (with EXISTS, IN, comparisons), SELECT (as a scalar subquery), and HAVING clauses. Can be slower than JOINs on large datasets, but is expressive for row-by-row comparisons.
.pg.Querying.ANY, ALL, EXISTS.exp

ANY compares a value to any element in a subquery result (equivalent to IN but more flexible with operators like > ANY). ALL requires the comparison to hold for every element. EXISTS returns TRUE if the subquery has any rows. These are powerful for semi-join and anti-join patterns.
.pg.Querying.FILTER Clause for Aggregates.exp

The FILTER clause lets aggregate functions conditionally include rows without a subquery or CASE. Multiple aggregates can use different filters on the same column set. More readable and often faster than CASE-based conditional aggregation. Compatible with GROUP BY.
.pg.Querying.GROUPING SETS, CUBE, ROLLUP.exp

GROUPING SETS produces multiple grouping levels in a single query. ROLLUP generates hierarchical subtotals (e.g., by year, then month, then day). CUBE produces all possible grouping combinations. The GROUPING() function identifies which level a row belongs to, preventing ambiguity with actual NULLs.
.pg.Querying.Window Functions Deep Dive.exp

Window functions compute values across sets of rows related to the current row without collapsing them. RANK() and DENSE_RANK() assign rankings with or without gaps. NTILE(n) divides rows into n buckets. LAG()/LEAD() access adjacent rows. FIRST_VALUE()/LAST_VALUE() get window endpoints. Frame clauses (ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS BETWEEN) define the sliding window.
.pg.Modifying Data.INSERT ON CONFLICT (UPSERT).exp

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT handles unique/primary key violations gracefully. DO NOTHING skips the insert silently. DO UPDATE SET ... acts as an UPDATE when a conflict occurs (the UPSERT pattern). The EXCLUDED pseudo-table references the values that would have been inserted. Conflict targets can be constraint names or columns.
.pg.Modifying Data.RETURNING Clause.exp

The RETURNING clause returns values from inserted, updated, or deleted rows — similar to OUTPUT in SQL Server. Supports * or specific expressions. Works with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE. Essential for getting auto-generated keys (SERIAL, IDENTITY) without a separate SELECT.
.pg.Modifying Data.MERGE (PostgreSQL 15+).exp

MERGE (also called upsert) conditionally inserts, updates, or deletes rows in a target table based on a source of rows. WHEN MATCHED/WHEN NOT MATCHED branches control the action. More expressive than INSERT ON CONFLICT for complex synchronization scenarios like data warehouse merges.
.pg.Modifying Data.UPDATE with FROM.exp

UPDATE ... FROM extends standard SQL to allow joining additional tables in the UPDATE statement. Useful for updating values based on matches in another table or aggregated values. The joined table(s) appear after FROM, with conditions in WHERE to control which rows update.
.pg.Modifying Data.DELETE with USING.exp

DELETE ... USING (PostgreSQL-specific) allows joining additional tables to determine which rows to delete. Similar to UPDATE FROM syntax. Useful for bulk deletes based on conditions in related tables, like purging orphaned records or cleaning up by business rules from a reference table.
.pg.Modifying Data.COPY for Bulk Loading.exp

COPY is the fastest way to import/export data. COPY (server-side) requires file system access on the server. \copy (psql meta-command) works client-side. Supports CSV, TEXT, and BINARY formats. HEADER skips the first line. DELIMITER specifies column separator. NULL specifies the null string.
.pg.Modifying Data.Foreign Data Wrappers.exp

Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW) let PostgreSQL query external data sources as if they were local tables. postgres_fdw connects to remote PostgreSQL databases. mysql_fdw, mongo_fdw handle other databases. file_fdw reads flat files. CREATE FOREIGN TABLE defines the structure. IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA bulk-imports remote tables.
.pg.Indexing.B-Tree Index Deep Dive.exp

B-Tree (balanced tree) is the default and most common index type. Supports =, <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, and pattern matching (if left-anchored). Also handles ORDER BY and MIN/MAX efficiently. Multiple NULLs are stored together (at the front or back depending on sort order).
.pg.Indexing.Hash Index.exp

Hash indexes store 32-bit hash codes of indexed values. Only support equality comparisons (=). In PostgreSQL 10+, hash indexes are WAL-logged and crash-safe. Use them when you only need equality lookups on large, random values where B-Tree would be deeper. Generally smaller than B-Tree for simple equality.
.pg.Indexing.GiST Index.exp

GiST (Generalized Search Tree) is a balanced tree structure supporting custom operator classes. Used for geometric data (@@, ~=, &&), full-text search (tsvector), range type overlap (&&), and trigram similarity (pg_trgm). Supports nearest-neighbor search (ORDER BY <-> LIMIT n).
.pg.Indexing.GIN Index.exp

GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes composite values like elements within arrays, JSONB documents, tsvectors, and hstore. Excellent for containment (@>), existence (?), and full-text search queries. GIN builds fast but is slower to update. GIN can be FASTUPDATE-enabled for better write performance.
.pg.Indexing.SP-GiST & BRIN Indexes.exp

SP-GiST (Space-Partitioned GiST) supports partitioned search trees (quadtrees, kd-trees) for point data, network addresses, and text. BRIN (Block Range Index) summarizes min/max values per block range. BRIN is orders of magnitude smaller than B-Tree and ideal for append-only, naturally-ordered data like time-series logs.
.pg.Indexing.Bloom Filter Index.exp

The bloom extension provides Bloom filter indexes — a probabilistic data structure that tests set membership with a tunable false-positive rate. Ideal for multi-column equality queries on many columns where creating individual indexes is impractical. Supports only = queries and can have false positives.
.pg.Indexing.Partial & Expression Indexes.exp

Partial indexes index only rows satisfying a WHERE clause — smaller and faster than full indexes. Expression indexes index the result of a function or expression rather than a raw column. Essential for case-insensitive lookups, computed columns, and conditional indexing of only relevant rows.
.pg.Indexing.Covering Indexes & Index-Only Scans.exp

A covering index includes all columns needed by a query, allowing index-only scans that never touch the heap (table). PostgreSQL supports INCLUDE to add non-key columns to a unique or primary key index. This allows a query to be satisfied entirely from the index, dramatically reducing I/O.
.pg.Indexing.Concurrent & Conditional Index Operations.exp

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds an index without locking the table against writes (uses extra CPU and I/O). DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY removes without blocking. REINDEX rebuilds indexes (CONCURRENTLY mode in v12+). Indexes can be marked UNUSABLE (but not yet supported in vanilla PostgreSQL — use INVALID).
.pg.Performance.EXPLAIN Deep Dive.exp

EXPLAIN shows the query plan (sequential scan, index scan, join type, etc.) with estimated costs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows actual timing and rows. Additional options: BUFFERS (shared/local hit/read/dirtied), TIMING (enable/disable per-node timing), FORMAT JSON, and SETTINGS (showing planner parameters). Parallel plans show Workers Launched and worker timing.
.pg.Performance.VACUUM Deep Dive.exp

VACUUM reclaims storage occupied by dead tuples and updates visibility maps. VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table (exclusive lock, shrinks disk). VACUUM (without FULL) marks space for reuse but doesn't return it to the OS. VERBOSE shows detailed per-table activity. FREEZE aggressively marks tuples as frozen for anti-wraparound.
.pg.Performance.ANALYZE & Statistics.exp

ANALYZE collects table statistics (column distributions, correlation, null fractions, most-common values) used by the query planner. Run standalone or as VACUUM ANALYZE. pg_stats (system view) exposes histogram buckets, n_distinct, and correlation. Accurate statistics are critical for optimal query plans.
.pg.Performance.Autovacuum Tuning.exp

Autovacuum automatically runs VACUUM and ANALYZE based on dead tuple thresholds. Key parameters: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (triggers when dead tuples > threshold + scale * total), autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit (I/O throttling), and autovacuum_naptime. Per-table overrides via storage parameters.
.pg.Performance.pg_stat_statements.exp

pg_stat_statements tracks execution statistics for all SQL queries: calls, total_time, min/max/mean time, rows, shared hit/read/dirtied, and temp file I/O. Essential for identifying slow queries, high-frequency queries, and I/O patterns. Requires shared_preload_libraries and creating the extension.
.pg.Performance.Query Tuning & Join Strategies.exp

PostgreSQL uses three join strategies: Nested Loop (good for small inner sets), Hash Join (good for large, unindexed joins), and Merge Join (good for sorted inputs). The planner chooses based on row estimates and cost parameters. Enable/disable via SET enable_hashjoin = off for debugging. Key practice: ensure proper indexes align with join and filter columns.
.pg.Performance.Memory Settings.exp

shared_buffers (typically 25% of RAM) is PostgreSQL's cache within its own memory. effective_cache_size estimates OS-level file system cache (helps planner decide index vs sequential scan). work_mem per-operation sort/hash memory (too high risks OOM, too low causes temp file spills). maintenance_work_mem for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX. wal_buffers for WAL throughput.
.pg.Performance.Parallel Query Execution.exp

PostgreSQL can parallelize sequential scans, joins, aggregates, and some window functions across worker processes. Controlled by max_parallel_workers_per_gather, parallel_tuple_cost, and parallel_setup_cost. Tables can set parallel_workers storage parameter. Parallelism benefits large scans but has overhead for small queries.
.pg.Functions & Triggers.PL/pgSQL Variables & Cursors.exp

PL/pgSQL is PostgreSQL's native procedural language. DECLARE defines variables (with DEFAULT or NOT NULL). %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchor types to columns or table rows. Cursors iterate through query result sets row by row — declare, open, fetch, close. FOR loops implicitly handle cursors.
.pg.Functions & Triggers.PL/pgSQL Exception Handling.exp

PL/pgSQL provides structured exception handling with BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END blocks. Caught exceptions can specify SQLSTATE or condition names (e.g., division_by_zero, unique_violation, foreign_key_violation). GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS retrieves error details. Note: exception blocks force a subtransaction, which has overhead.
.pg.Functions & Triggers.SQL Functions.exp

SQL functions (LANGUAGE sql) are simple, fast, and can be inlined by the planner. Support RETURNS scalar, SETOF record/table, or single row. Can be used in FROM clauses when marked RETURNS TABLE. SQL functions have no variables, no procedural logic — just a single query (or multiple with the last one returned).
.pg.Functions & Triggers.Triggers (BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF).exp

Triggers fire functions automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE. BEFORE triggers run before the operation (can modify the NEW row or prevent action). AFTER triggers run after the operation (see final values). INSTEAD OF triggers on views intercept operations entirely. FOR EACH ROW fires per row; FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once.
.pg.Functions & Triggers.Column-Specific & Event Triggers.exp

Column-specific triggers fire only when specified columns are mentioned in UPDATE. Use UPDATE OF col1, col2 in the trigger definition. Event triggers (CREATE EVENT TRIGGER) fire on DDL events (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) at the database level, allowing logging or prevention of schema changes.
.pg.Functions & Triggers.Trigger Functions (TG_OP, TG_TABLE_NAME).exp

Trigger functions receive automatic special variables: TG_OP (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE), TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_TABLE_SCHEMA, TG_WHEN (BEFORE/AFTER), TG_LEVEL (ROW/STATEMENT), TG_RELID, TG_NAME. OLD and NEW represent row states. A generic audit trigger uses these to log all table changes dynamically.
.pg.Functions & Triggers.DO Blocks.exp

DO blocks execute anonymous PL/pgSQL (or other procedural language) code without creating a persistent function. Useful for one-off scripts, migrations, data cleanups, and administrative tasks. Can declare variables, use cursors, handle exceptions — same as a full function but nameless and immediate.
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.Stored Procedures (CALL).exp

Stored procedures (CREATE PROCEDURE) differ from functions: they support transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside the procedure), have no return value, and are invoked with CALL. Introduced in PostgreSQL 11. Useful for ETL pipelines, multi-step operations requiring intermediate commits, and administrative tasks.
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.PostGIS Extension.exp

PostGIS is the gold standard for spatial databases. It adds geometry, geography, and raster types, spatial indexes (GiST on geometry), and hundreds of functions (ST_Distance, ST_Intersects, ST_Within). Enables GIS queries, map rendering, and geospatial analytics. Requires CREATE EXTENSION postgis; then add a geometry column.
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.pg_stat_statements & uuid-ossp.exp

pg_stat_statements provides query execution statistics (see Performance section). uuid-ossp generates UUIDs via OSSP library (uuid_generate_v1mc, uuid_generate_v4) or use pgcrypto's gen_random_uuid() instead, which doesn't need uuid-ossp. Both extensions are simple to enable and essential for distributed IDs.
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.pgcrypto & citext.exp

pgcrypto provides cryptographic functions: digest(), hmac(), crypt() for password hashing, pgp_sym_encrypt()/pgp_pub_encrypt() for encryption, and gen_random_uuid()/gen_random_bytes(). citext provides a case-insensitive character string type that behaves like TEXT but comparisons are case-insensitive — ideal for email fields or usernames.
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.Fuzzy String Matching.exp

pg_trgm (trigram) and fuzzystrmatch (Levenshtein, Metaphone, Soundex, Double Metaphone) provide fuzzy text matching. pg_trgm creates a GIN or GiST index of 3-character substrings for fast similarity searches using %, <-> (distance), and word_similarity. Essential for search-as-you-type, deduplication, and spell correction.
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.unaccent & Full-Text Extensions.exp

unaccent removes diacritical marks (accents) from text, enabling accent-insensitive search. Typically combined with full-text search and an immutable function wrapping to_tsvector for GIN indexes. Also useful with citext and pg_trgm. Essential for internationalized applications (French, Spanish, German, etc.).
.pg.Procedures & Extensions.TimescaleDB & pg_plan_advsr.exp

TimescaleDB is a time-series extension adding hypertables (automatic partitioning by time), continuous aggregates, compression, and retention policies. pg_plan_advsr (plan advisor) analyzes slow queries and suggests index or rewriting improvements. Other notable extensions: pg_partman (partition management), pgaudit (audit logging), and hypopg (hypothetical indexes).
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.MVCC Internals.exp

Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) allows readers never to block writers and vice versa. Each row has xmin (creating transaction ID) and xmax (deleting/expiring transaction ID). A snapshot captures active transactions at a point in time. Visibility rules determine which row versions are visible. Old versions (dead tuples) are cleaned by VACUUM.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.Isolation Levels.exp

PostgreSQL supports four ANSI isolation levels, but only three distinct behaviors: Read Committed (default — sees committed data at each statement start), Repeatable Read (sees snapshot from first statement in transaction, retry on serialization failure), Serializable (detects true serialization conflicts with SSI). Higher levels reduce concurrency but increase consistency.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).exp

SSI is PostgreSQL's Serializable implementation. Unlike Repeatable Read, SSI detects read-write conflicts that could cause serialization anomalies (e.g., write skew). Uses predicate locks (not row locks) to track read dependencies. SSI provides true serializability at the cost of more serialization failures requiring retry logic.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.Deadlock Detection.exp

PostgreSQL automatically detects deadlocks (cycles in lock wait graph). When detected, one session is aborted with ERROR: deadlock detected. The deadlock_timeout setting (default 1s) controls how often the deadlock check runs. Shorter timeouts detect deadlocks faster but use more CPU. Application code should retry on deadlock errors.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.Advisory Locks.exp

Advisory locks are application-level locks managed by PostgreSQL. Session-level (pg_advisory_lock) blocks until released. Transaction-level (pg_advisory_xact_lock) auto-releases on commit/rollback. Try variants (pg_try_advisory_lock) return false immediately instead of blocking. Keyed by a single bigint or two integers. Useful for distributed job queues and rate limiting.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.SKIP LOCKED & NOWAIT.exp

SKIP LOCKED (PostgreSQL 9.5+) skips rows locked by other transactions — ideal for work queues where multiple workers select jobs. NOWAIT fails immediately if a row is locked, instead of waiting. Both used with FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE. SKIP LOCKED eliminates busy-waiting and lock contention in high-concurrency job processing.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.Row Locking.exp

PostgreSQL provides row-level locking clauses on SELECT: FOR UPDATE (write lock, blocks other FOR UPDATE/FOR NO KEY UPDATE/FOR SHARE/FOR KEY SHARE), FOR NO KEY UPDATE (weaker write lock), FOR SHARE (read lock, blocks FOR UPDATE/FOR NO KEY UPDATE but not FOR SHARE), FOR KEY SHARE (weakest, blocks only FOR UPDATE). These are the foundation of pessimistic locking.
.pg.Transactions & Concurrency.Predicate Locking.exp

Predicate locks prevent phantom reads in SERIALIZABLE isolation. Instead of row locks, PostgreSQL acquires predicate locks on index pages or whole tables that represent a query's read range. If two transactions read overlapping ranges and one writes, SSI detects the conflict. SiLockEntry view shows predicate lock state.
.pg.Security.Roles Deep Dive.exp

Roles can be LOGIN (for user authentication), SUPERUSER (full access, needed for extension creation and system config), CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS. INHERIT means parent role's privileges are inherited. Roles can be organized in hierarchies (GRANT role TO role). Groups are just roles without LOGIN. ALTER ROLE sets per-role configuration.
.pg.Security.GRANT / REVOKE Privileges.exp

GRANT assigns privileges (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, CREATE, CONNECT, TEMPORARY, EXECUTE, USAGE, ALL) on databases, schemas, tables, columns, sequences, functions, and procedural languages. GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA grants future tables are NOT included (use default privileges). REVOKE removes privileges. Default privileges for future objects via ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES.
.pg.Security.Row-Level Security (RLS).exp

Row-Level Security (RLS) restricts which rows a user can see or modify based on a policy expression. Enable RLS on a table (ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY), then create policies. WITH CHECK controls INSERT/UPDATE new rows. USING controls SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE visibility. BYPASSRLS role attribute exempts superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS.
.pg.Security.Column-Level Security.exp

Column-level security restricts which columns a user can access. Implemented via column-level GRANT (GRANT SELECT(col1, col2) ON table TO role). Unprivileged columns appear as NULL in SELECT * or are rejected entirely depending on context. Often combined with views for fine-grained access control beyond simple column grants.
.pg.Security.TLS / SSL Configuration.exp

PostgreSQL supports TLS/SSL for encrypted connections. Configure ssl = on in postgresql.conf, provide server certificate (server.crt) and private key (server.key), and optional CA (root.crt) for client certificate authentication. sslmode=require in client connection strings enforces TLS. For production, prefer verify-full sslmode with proper CA verification.
.pg.Security.pg_hba.conf Deep Dive.exp

pg_hba.conf controls client authentication: local (Unix socket), host (TCP/IP with or without SSL), hostssl, hostnossl. Authentication methods: trust (no password, dev only), password (plaintext), md5, scram-sha-256, cert (client certificate), ldap, pam, peer (OS user), and reject. Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins.
.pg.Security.Password Profiles & SCRAM-SHA-256.exp

PostgreSQL 10+ uses SCRAM-SHA-256 as the default password hashing mechanism (md5 still available for legacy). It's a challenge-response protocol that never sends the password in plaintext. Password expiration (valid until), password_encryption parameter, and account locking (via pg_hba.conf reject rules) provide profile-like management. Extensions like pg_password_history add rotation enforcement.
.pg.Backup & Replication.pg_dump / pg_restore.exp

pg_dump creates logical backups of a single database (plain SQL, custom, directory, or tar format). pg_dumpall backs up all databases plus global objects (roles, tablespaces). pg_restore restores from custom/directory/tar formats with parallel jobs (-j) and selective restore (-t, -n). Plain format can be restored via psql. Essential for schema migrations and data export.
.pg.Backup & Replication.pg_basebackup.exp

pg_basebackup creates a binary (physical) backup of the entire PostgreSQL cluster. Required for setting up streaming replication and Point-in-Time Recovery. Produces a consistent copy using WAL archiving. Supports compression (gzip, lz4, zstd), progress output, and parallel transfer with --wal-method=stream. The -X stream option includes WAL in the backup.
.pg.Backup & Replication.Continuous Archiving & WAL.exp

WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records every change to the database. Continuous archiving copies WAL segments to a safe location for PITR. Configure archive_mode, archive_command (e.g., cp to NFS or S3), and restore_command. WAL segments are 16 MB each. WAL compression (wal_compression) reduces storage. Monitor via pg_stat_archiver.
.pg.Backup & Replication.Streaming Replication.exp

Streaming replication sends WAL data from primary to standby in real time. Standby runs in recovery mode, applying WAL continuously. Hot standby allows read-only queries on standby. Configuration: wal_level >= replica, max_wal_senders >= number of replicas, primary_conninfo on standby. pg_stat_replication shows replication lag.
.pg.Backup & Replication.Synchronous Replication.exp

Synchronous replication guarantees that commits on primary are confirmed by at least one standby before reporting success. Set synchronous_standby_names to specify which standbys are synchronous (FIRST, ANY). sync_state = sync in pg_stat_replication. Provides zero-data-loss but increases commit latency. Use for critical financial or compliance workloads.
.pg.Backup & Replication.Logical Replication.exp

Logical replication publishes individual table changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) via a publication on the publisher, subscribed to on the subscriber. Unlike streaming replication, it allows selective replication (specific tables), major version upgrades, and bidirectional replication. Uses pgoutput plugin. Built on top of WAL decoding.
.pg.Backup & Replication.Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) & pg_rewind.exp

PITR restores a database to any point in time after a base backup, by replaying WAL up to the target time (recovery_target_time), transaction ID (recovery_target_xid), or named restore point. Configure recovery.conf (PG12+) or postgresql.conf recovery parameters (PG12+). pg_rewind syncs a stale replica with the new primary after a failover, enabling fast rejoin.
.pg.Advanced Topics.LISTEN / NOTIFY Pub-Sub.exp

LISTEN subscribes to a notification channel. NOTIFY sends an asynchronous message (up to 8000 bytes payload) to all sessions listening on that channel. pg_notify(text, text) function sends from SQL. Used for cache invalidation, triggering application workers, and real-time UI updates without polling.
.pg.Advanced Topics.COPY Protocol Deep Dive.exp

The COPY protocol (\copy in psql, PQputCopyData in libpq) streams data between client and server. PostgreSQL 14+ supports COPY ... FROM PROGRAM (superuser only, dangerous), COPY ... WHERE for row filtering on import, and COPY ... ON_ERROR for error handling (ignore, stop). The \copy meta-command routes through the client, not the server.
.pg.Advanced Topics.Custom Aggregate Functions.exp

PostgreSQL allows creating custom aggregate functions with CREATE AGGREGATE. Define an sfunc (state transition function), stype (state type), and optionally a finalfunc (final calculation), initcond (initial condition), and combinefunc (for parallel/partial aggregation). Useful for rolling averages, statistical aggregations, or custom JSON accumulation.
.pg.Advanced Topics.Procedural Languages (PL/Python, PL/V8).exp

PostgreSQL supports multiple procedural languages via extensions. PL/Python (plpython3u) allows writing functions in Python with access to numpy, pandas, etc. PL/V8 (plv8) runs JavaScript inside PostgreSQL. PL/Tcl and PL/Perl are also available. These are powerful for data science, complex string processing, and integrating external libraries directly in SQL.
.pg.Advanced Topics.FDW Deep Dive (file_fdw, postgres_fdw).exp

file_fdw queries CSV, text, or program output as foreign tables. Great for ad-hoc data analysis without loading data into the database. postgres_fdw connects to remote PostgreSQL, supports INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (pushdown). IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA bulk-creates foreign tables. Options include fetch_size, use_remote_estimate, and async_capable for parallel remote scans.
.pg.Advanced Topics.Table Sampling & Parallel Query Details.exp

TABLESAMPLE (BERNOULLI, SYSTEM) returns a random sample of rows. SYSTEM is faster (uses physical pages), BERNOULLI is more accurate (row-level). Percent specifies approximate sample size. REPEATABLE(seed) gives reproducible samples. For parallel queries, max_parallel_workers_per_gather controls workers per query, parallel_tuple_cost offsets overhead, and gather nodes merge worker results.
.pg.Mastering PostgreSQL 15.date_bin Time Bucketing.exp

`date_bin` (PostgreSQL 14+) buckets timestamps into fixed intervals. Essential for time-series aggregation: bin timestamps into 5-minute, hourly, or daily buckets. The function aligns to a specified origin. Much cleaner than manual arithmetic with EXTRACT and FLOOR. Used with GROUP BY for time-series rollups.
.pg.Mastering PostgreSQL 15.WAL & Checkpoint Tuning.exp
