Jest is a delightful JavaScript testing framework with zero configuration, built-in assertions, mocking, and code coverage. It's the default test runner in Create React App.
.react.Testing.React Testing Library.exp
React Testing Library builds on top of DOM Testing Library and encourages testing components from the user's perspective. It queries rendered output rather than testing implementation details.
.react.Testing.Cypress.exp
Cypress is an end-to-end testing framework that runs in the browser, providing real-time reloads, time travel debugging, and automatic waiting. It's ideal for integration and E2E tests.
.react.Performance.Code Splitting.exp
Code splitting breaks your bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial load time. React.lazy and Suspense make code splitting declarative and easy to implement.
.react.Performance.Lazy Loading.exp
Lazy loading defers loading of non-critical resources until they are needed. Combined with Suspense, it shows a fallback UI while the lazy component loads asynchronously.
.react.Performance.Memoization.exp
React.memo is a higher-order component that prevents re-rendering when props haven't changed. useCallback memorizes callback functions to maintain referential equality across renders.
.react.State Management.Redux.exp

Redux is a predictable state container with a single store, immutable updates via pure reducers, and actions dispatched to trigger state changes. The Redux Toolkit simplifies boilerplate significantly.
.react.State Management.Zustand.exp
Zustand is a minimal state management library with a hook-based API, no boilerplate, and support for middleware. It's ideal for projects that need simple global state without Redux overhead.
.react.State Management.Context API.exp
Context API provides a built-in way to share values across the component tree without prop drilling. It's best suited for low-frequency updates like theme, locale, or auth state.
.react.Concurrent React.useTransition.exp
useTransition marks state updates as non-urgent transitions, keeping the UI responsive during expensive re-renders. The isPending flag shows a loading state without blocking user input.
.react.Concurrent React.useDeferredValue.exp
useDeferredValue lets you defer re-rendering a non-urgent part of the tree. The deferred value lags behind the real value, allowing urgent updates (like input typing) to stay responsive.
.react.Server Components.RSC Basics.exp
React Server Components run exclusively on the server, never sent to the client. They reduce bundle size by keeping heavy dependencies server-side and can directly access databases and file systems.
.react.Server Components.Server Actions.exp
Server Actions are async functions that run on the server, invoked from client components. Use 'use server' to mark them, enabling direct mutations without building API routes.
.react.Error Handling.Error Boundaries.exp
Error Boundaries catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree, displaying a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. Class components with componentDidCatch are required.
.react.Error Handling.Error Recovery.exp
Use key props to reset error boundaries. Changing the key unmounts and remounts the component tree, clearing the error state without a full page refresh.
.react.Advanced Patterns.Portals.exp
Portals render children into a DOM node outside the parent component's hierarchy, useful for modals, tooltips, and dropdowns that need to escape overflow or z-index clipping.
.react.Advanced Patterns.TypeScript with React.exp
TypeScript with React provides type safety for props, state, hooks, and event handlers. Use generic types for useState, useRef, and forwardRef for stricter typing.
.redis.Getting Started.Installation.exp
Redis can be installed via package managers, compiled from source, or run via Docker. The default configuration listens on port 6379 and stores data in memory with optional persistence to disk.
.redis.Getting Started.Data Types.exp
Redis supports Strings, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Hashes, Bitmaps, HyperLogLogs, Streams, and Geospatial indexes. Each type has optimized commands for specific use cases and data access patterns.
.redis.Getting Started.CLI.exp

The `redis-cli` command-line interface connects to Redis servers for interactive or scripted use. It supports command execution, monitoring, slow log analysis, and server administration with built-in help.
.redis.Strings & Numbers.SET/GET.exp

Strings are the most fundamental Redis data type, capable of storing text, numbers, or binary data up to 512MB. SET stores a key-value pair, GET retrieves it, and commands like `SETNX` help with distributed locks.
.redis.Strings & Numbers.INCR.exp

Redis provides atomic increment/decrement operations that are essential for counters, rate limiting, and real-time analytics. Commands like `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`, and `INCRBYFLOAT` operate on string values holding numbers.
.redis.Strings & Numbers.Expiry.exp
TTL (Time To Live) automatically removes keys after a specified duration. `EXPIRE`, `TTL`, and `PERSIST` manage key lifetimes. Expiry is crucial for caching, temporary tokens, and session management.
.redis.Lists & Sets.LPUSH/LPOP.exp
Lists are ordered sequences of strings, efficient for queue and stack implementations. LPUSH adds to the left, RPUSH adds to the right; LPOP and RPOP remove and return elements from either end.
.redis.Lists & Sets.SADD.exp

Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. SADD adds members, SREM removes them, SMEMBERS returns all members, and SISMEMBER checks existence. Sets are ideal for tagging, deduplication, and relations.
.redis.Lists & Sets.Union/Intersect.exp
Set operations enable powerful data analysis: SUNION combines sets, SINTER finds common elements, and SDIFF finds differences. These are used for recommendations, permissions, and social features.
.redis.Hashes & Sorted Sets.HSET.exp
Hashes store field-value pairs within a single key, ideal for representing objects. They provide memory-efficient storage with commands for individual field CRUD, bulk operations, and field counting.
.redis.Hashes & Sorted Sets.ZADD.exp

Sorted Sets associate each member with a numeric score, maintaining order by score. ZADD adds or updates members, ZRANGE retrieves by rank, and ZRANK gets position. Perfect for leaderboards and priority queues.
.redis.Hashes & Sorted Sets.Ranking.exp

Sorted Sets excel at real-time leaderboards with atomic score updates, range queries, and pagination. Combined with aggregation commands like ZCOUNT and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, they handle ranking systems efficiently.
.redis.Persistence.RDB.exp
RDB (Redis Database) performs point-in-time snapshots at configurable intervals. It creates compact single-file backups, ideal for disaster recovery, but may lose data written between snapshots.
.redis.Persistence.AOF.exp

Append-Only File (AOF) logs every write operation for durability. It provides finer-grained persistence than RDB with fsync policies (every write, every second, or OS-controlled) and can be rewritten to compact.
.redis.Persistence.Backup/Restore.exp

Redis backup involves copying RDB/AOF files, or using `redis-cli --rdb` for live snapshots. Restore requires stopping the server, placing the backup file correctly, and restarting. SLAVEOF enables replication-based recovery.
.redis.Pub/Sub.Channels.exp

Pub/Sub implements the publish-subscribe messaging pattern where publishers send messages to channels without knowledge of subscribers. SUBSCRIBE listens on channels, PUBLISH sends messages, and UNSUBSCRIBE stops listening.
.redis.Pub/Sub.Pattern Subscribe.exp

PSUBSCRIBE enables subscription to channels matching a glob-style pattern. This allows listening to multiple related channels (e.g., `user:*`, `orders:*`) with a single subscription for efficient message routing.
.redis.Pub/Sub.Messaging.exp

Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no message persistence; subscribers only receive messages sent after subscription. For reliable messaging, use Redis Streams which support consumer groups, acknowledgment, and message history.
.redis.Clustering.Sentinel.exp

Redis Sentinel provides high availability through automatic failover, monitoring, notifications, and service discovery. A Sentinel cluster monitors master/replica instances and promotes a replica when the master fails.
.redis.Clustering.Cluster Mode.exp

Redis Cluster automatically shards data across multiple nodes using hash slots (0-16383). Each node handles a subset of slots, providing horizontal scalability and automatic rebalancing when nodes are added or removed.
.redis.Clustering.Sharding.exp

Hash slots distribute keys deterministically: `HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384`. Client-side sharding is also possible for simpler setups, but Redis Cluster handles routing transparently with MOVED redirections.
.redis.Use Cases.Caching.exp

Redis caching improves application performance by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Common patterns include cache-aside (lazy loading), write-through, and TTL-based expiry with automatic cache invalidation.
.redis.Use Cases.Rate Limiting.exp

Redis enables efficient distributed rate limiting using INCR with TTL. The sliding window algorithm tracks request counts per time window, and the token bucket algorithm offers more flexible rate control.
.redis.Use Cases.Session Store.exp

Redis is an ideal session store for distributed applications because of its speed, built-in TTL, and atomic operations. `connect-redis` or `ioredis-session` replace the default in-memory session store for persistence across restarts.
.redis.Use Cases.Queues.exp
Redis Lists provide the foundation for lightweight job queues. `LPUSH` + `BRPOP` implement reliable FIFO queues with blocking pops. Bull and Kue are popular Node.js queue libraries built on Redis.
.remix.Getting Started.Routing.exp
Remix uses a file-based routing system in the app/routes directory. Each file represents a route segment, with dot and folder conventions creating nested URL structures automatically.
.remix.Getting Started.Nested Routes.exp
Nested routes in Remix allow multiple components to render on the same URL. The parent route's layout wraps child routes through the <Outlet /> component, enabling complex UI hierarchies.
.remix.Getting Started.Layouts.exp
Layout routes use the special app/root.tsx file and route-specific layout.tsx files. Layouts wrap child routes and persist across navigation, preventing full page re-renders.
.remix.Data Loading.loader.exp
Loaders are server-side functions that fetch data before rendering a route. They run on every request, returning data that becomes available to the component via the useLoaderData hook.
.remix.Data Loading.useLoaderData.exp
useLoaderData returns the typed data from the nearest route loader. It provides type safety when used with TypeScript and the typeof loader generic pattern.
.remix.Data Loading.params.exp
Params give access to dynamic segments from the URL pattern. They are available in loaders and actions via the params argument, matching the bracket syntax in the route filename.
.remix.Mutations.action.exp
Actions handle form submissions and data mutations on the server. They run on POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE requests and can return data, redirects, or errors to the client.
.remix.Mutations.Form.exp
The <Form> component submits data without JavaScript by default. When JS loads, it progressively enhances to use fetch, providing optimistic UI and pending states without full page reloads.
.remix.Mutations.useFetcher.exp
useFetcher allows submitting actions or loading data without navigational transitions. It is ideal for non-blocking interactions like add-to-cart buttons or inline search suggestions.
.remix.Web Standards.Request/Response.exp
Remix embraces Web Fetch API standards. Loaders and actions receive native Request objects and return Response objects, making routes portable across server environments.
.remix.Web Standards.Headers.exp
Headers in Remix can be set at the route level for caching, security, and content negotiation. The headers export controls both document and resource route responses.
.remix.Web Standards.Cookies.exp
Remix provides a cookies API that integrates with the Web Fetch standard. Cookies are created, read, and written using the cookie utilities from @remix-run/node.
.remix.Error Handling.ErrorBoundary.exp
ErrorBoundary catches unexpected rendering errors in a route. When an error is thrown, Remix renders the closest ErrorBoundary instead of the default component, showing a fallback UI.
.remix.Error Handling.CatchBoundary.exp
CatchBoundary handles expected error responses from loaders and actions. It receives the thrown Response object, allowing different UI for 404, 403, and other status codes.
.remix.CSS & Styling.Links.exp
Remix manages CSS through the links export, which adds link tags to the document head. This enables route-level CSS loading and automatic cleanup when navigating away.
.remix.CSS & Styling.Route Styles.exp
Route styles in Remix support both traditional CSS files and CSS-in-JS solutions. CSS files can be imported in links functions, with automatic scoping via CSS Modules.
.remix.CSS & Styling.Tailwind.exp
Remix supports Tailwind CSS through the conventional PostCSS setup. The @tailwind directives are processed during build, generating optimized CSS with unused class purging.
.remix.Deployment.Fly.io.exp
Fly.io is the recommended deployment target for Remix, offering global edge regions and effortless scaling. Remix apps deploy as Docker containers running close to users worldwide.
.remix.Deployment.Vercel.exp
Vercel supports Remix via the @remix-run/vercel adapter. It automatically optimizes serverless functions and delivers assets through Vercel's edge network.
.remix.Deployment.Netlify.exp
Netlify deploys Remix apps using the Netlify adapter, providing serverless functions for the Remix server and global CDN for static assets via Netlify Edge.
.remix.Deployment.Cloudflare.exp
The Cloudflare Workers adapter runs Remix on Cloudflare's edge network. It uses Workers KV for sessions and Durable Objects for real-time state.
.remix.Advanced.Resource Routes.exp
Resource Routes return non-HTML content such as JSON, images, PDFs, or sitemaps. They handle requests without rendering a component, functioning as pure API endpoints within the routes system.
.remix.Advanced.WebSockets.exp
Real-time features in Remix are achieved through WebSocket integrations. While Remix does not include WebSockets natively, it pairs well with libraries like Socket.io or PartyKit.
.remix.Advanced.Caching.exp
Remix leverages HTTP caching extensively. The headers export allows setting Cache-Control headers per route, and loaders can implement conditional requests with ETags for efficient revalidation.
.remix.Vite Plugin.Remix Vite Plugin.exp
Remix now ships as a Vite plugin for faster builds, HMR, and streamlined configuration. The vite.config replaces remix.config with a familiar Vite API and automatic React Fast Refresh.
.remix.Vite Plugin.Plugin Configuration.exp
The Remix Vite plugin accepts options for server entry, routes directory, future flags, and build output. It integrates with other Vite plugins like Tailwind and MDX for a unified build pipeline.
.remix.Vite Plugin.HMR & Fast Refresh.exp
Vite-powered HMR updates Remix route components in milliseconds without losing page state. React Fast Refresh preserves component state across edits, dramatically improving the dev feedback loop.
.remix.Session Management.createCookieSessionStorage.exp
Cookie session storage encodes session data directly in encrypted cookies, suitable for small payloads. It requires no database and is the simplest session strategy for Remix apps.
.remix.Session Management.createSessionStorage.exp
createSessionStorage allows custom backing stores (database, Redis) for larger session data while using a cookie only for the session ID. This scales beyond cookie size limits.
.remix.Session Management.Flash Messages.exp
Flash messages are one-time session values that are cleared after being read, ideal for success or error notifications after form submissions. They use the session's flash method.
.remix.Type Inference.Typed Loader Data.exp
useLoaderData infers the return type of the route's loader using typeof loader. This provides end-to-end type safety from the server to the client without manual type definitions.
.remix.Type Inference.Typed Actions.exp
useActionData provides type-safe access to action return values. Combine with typeof action for compile-time checking of error messages, form data, and mutation results.
.remix.Type Inference.serialize Type.exp
Remix's SerializeFrom type unwraps Promise and Response types from loaders, providing a cleaner type for client-side hooks when the loader uses async patterns.
.rnative.Getting Started.JSX.exp
JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML and is compiled to React.createElement calls. It allows writing UI components declaratively in React Native.
.rnative.Getting Started.Components.exp
Components are reusable building blocks in React Native, defined as functions returning JSX. They accept props and manage their own state using hooks.
.rnative.Getting Started.StyleSheet.exp
StyleSheet provides a way to define styles with performance benefits through abstraction. It validates and optimizes style objects, and styles are only sent to native once.
.rnative.Getting Started.Expo CLI.exp
Expo is the recommended framework for building React Native apps. It provides managed workflows, over-the-air updates, and access to native APIs without Xcode or Android Studio.
.rnative.Core Components.View.exp
View is the fundamental container component supporting flexbox layout, styling, touch handling, and accessibility. It maps to UIView on iOS and View on Android.
.rnative.Core Components.Text.exp
Text is the only component that renders text in React Native. It supports nesting, styling, and event handling like onPress.
.rnative.Core Components.Image.exp
Image displays images from local assets, network URLs, or data URIs. It requires explicit dimensions when loading from network sources.
.rnative.Core Components.ScrollView.exp
ScrollView is a scrolling container for multiple components and views. It loads all content upfront and is best for smaller amounts of content.
.rnative.Core Components.Pressable.exp
Pressable is the modern touch handling component that provides feedback for different press states. Use instead of TouchableOpacity for more control.
.rnative.Core Components.Modal & StatusBar.exp
Modal presents content on top of the app, useful for alerts and forms. StatusBar controls the device status bar appearance per screen.
.rnative.Navigation.React Navigation.exp
React Navigation is the standard navigation library for React Native apps, providing stack, tab, and drawer navigators with native transitions.
.rnative.Navigation.Stack.exp
Stack navigator manages a navigation stack where screens are pushed and popped. It provides native-like transitions and header customization.
.rnative.Navigation.Tab.exp
Tab navigator provides bottom or top tab navigation with icons and labels. Each tab maintains its own navigation state for independent back stacks.
.rnative.Navigation.Drawer.exp
Drawer navigator creates a side menu that slides in from the left, supporting nested navigators and custom drawer content.
.rnative.Navigation.Expo Router.exp
Expo Router provides file-based routing similar to Next.js. Files in the app/ directory automatically become routes with support for layout files and deep linking.
.rnative.New Architecture.Fabric.exp
Fabric is the new rendering system that uses JSI (JavaScript Interface) instead of the Bridge. It enables synchronous communication and better performance for UI updates.
.rnative.New Architecture.TurboModules.exp
TurboModules replace the old Native Modules system, allowing lazy loading of native modules and efficient type-safe communication via JSI.
.rnative.New Architecture.JSI.exp
JavaScript Interface (JSI) enables direct, synchronous communication between JavaScript and native code without the Bridge. It eliminates the serialization overhead of the old architecture.
.rnative.State & Data.useState.exp
useState is a React hook that adds local state to functional components, returning a state variable and a setter function.
.rnative.State & Data.AsyncStorage.exp
AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value storage system for persisting data across app restarts on both iOS and Android.
.rnative.State & Data.Zustand.exp
Zustand is a minimal state management library with a hook-based API. It works well in React Native for global state without boilerplate.
.rnative.State & Data.MMKV Storage.exp
MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage by Tencent. It's significantly faster than AsyncStorage and ideal for performance-critical persistence.
.rnative.Animations.Animated API.exp
React Native's built-in Animated API provides declarative animations using Animated.Value and timing/spring configurations. It drives animations natively on the UI thread.
.rnative.Animations.Reanimated.exp
Reanimated provides gesture-driven animations that run entirely on the UI thread using worklets. It enables smooth 60fps animations for complex interactions.
.rnative.Animations.Gesture Handler.exp
Gesture Handler replaces PanResponder with native gesture processing. It supports pan, pinch, rotation, tap, long press, and custom gesture compositions.
.rnative.Networking.fetch.exp
The Fetch API provides a native way to make HTTP requests in React Native. It returns promises and supports JSON, text, and binary responses.
.rnative.Networking.Axios.exp
Axios is a promise-based HTTP client with interceptors, automatic JSON parsing, and request cancellation. It provides a cleaner API than fetch.
.rnative.Networking.React Query.exp
React Query (TanStack Query) manages server state with automatic caching, refetching, pagination, and optimistic updates.
.rnative.Networking.WebSocket.exp
WebSocket enables full-duplex real-time communication over a persistent TCP connection, ideal for chat apps, live updates, and gaming.
.rnative.Device APIs.Camera.exp
React Native Camera provides device camera access with support for photos, videos, barcode scanning, and custom camera UI.
.rnative.Device APIs.Location.exp
Geolocation APIs provide device location through GPS or network positioning, supporting high-accuracy and background location tracking.
.rnative.Device APIs.Push Notifications.exp
Push notifications allow sending alerts to user devices even when the app is closed. Firebase Cloud Messaging is the standard solution.
.rnative.Performance.FlatList.exp
FlatList efficiently renders large lists by virtualizing rows, recycling components, and rendering only visible items. It supports headers, footers, and pull-to-refresh.
.rnative.Performance.Optimization.exp
React Native optimization includes using PureComponent, useMemo, avoiding inline functions in render, and minimizing re-renders with React.memo.
.rnative.Performance.Hermes.exp
Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine optimized for React Native, reducing app startup time, memory usage, and APK/IPA size.
.rnative.Performance.InteractionManager.exp
InteractionManager schedules tasks to run after animations or navigation transitions complete, preventing dropped frames during critical UI updates.
.rnative.Advanced.Skia.exp
React Native Skia provides a high-performance 2D graphics canvas for custom drawing, image manipulation, and complex animations using the Skia graphics library.
.rnative.Advanced.CodePush.exp
CodePush enables over-the-air JavaScript bundle updates without going through the App Store review process, allowing instant bug fixes and small feature updates.
.rnative.Advanced.AppState.exp
AppState tracks whether the app is in foreground, background, or inactive state. Use it to pause/resume timers, network requests, and animations.
.rnative.Deployment.iOS.exp
iOS deployment requires an Apple Developer account, Xcode configuration, and provisioning profiles. The app is archived and uploaded via Xcode or Transporter.
.rnative.Deployment.Android.exp
Android deployment generates a signed APK or AAB using keystore credentials. The build is created with Gradle and uploaded to the Play Console.
.rnative.Deployment.EAS Build.exp
Expo Application Services (EAS) Build compiles and signs your app in the cloud without requiring Xcode or Android Studio installed locally.
.rust.Getting Started.What is Rust.exp
Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, speed, and concurrency. It guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector through its ownership system and zero-cost abstractions.
.rust.Getting Started.Rust Syntax Basics.exp

Rust uses `fn` for functions, `let` for variables, and macros with `!`. Semicolons end expressions, blocks use curly braces. `main` is the program entry point. Statements vs expressions distinction is key.
.rust.Getting Started.Variables & Mutability.exp
Variables are immutable by default. Use `mut` to make them mutable. `const` for compile-time constants. Shadowing redeclares a variable with `let`, allowing type changes.
.rust.Getting Started.Scalar Types.exp
Four scalar types: integers (i8-u128, i64, usize), floats (f32, f64), bool, char. Integer overflow wraps in release, panics in debug. Underscores improve readability: `1_000_000`.
.rust.Getting Started.rustup & Toolchains.exp
rustup manages Rust toolchains. Switch between stable, beta, nightly. `rustup target add` for cross-compilation. `rustup component add` for tools. `rustup show` displays active toolchain.
.rust.Getting Started.Cargo Basics.exp
Cargo is Rust's build system and package manager. `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`, `cargo check`, `cargo clean`. Cargo.toml defines metadata and dependencies.
.rust.Getting Started.rustfmt.exp
rustfmt auto-formats code according to style guidelines. `cargo fmt` formats the whole project. `rustfmt --check` verifies formatting in CI. Configure with `rustfmt.toml`.
.rust.Getting Started.Clippy.exp
Clippy is Rust's linter with 550+ rules. `cargo clippy` catches common mistakes, non-idiomatic code, and performance pitfalls. `#[allow(clippy::...)]` silences specific lints.
.rust.Getting Started.rust-analyzer.exp
rust-analyzer provides IDE support: code completion, goto-definition, type hints, inlay hints, rename, diagnostics. LSP server used by VS Code, Neovim, Emacs, and Zed.
.rust.Control Flow.if / else if / else.exp
Conditions must be `bool` — no truthy/falsy coercion. `if` is an expression, assignable with `let`. All arms must return the same type. Blocks evaluate to their last expression.
.rust.Control Flow.Loops (loop, while, for).exp
`loop` repeats forever until `break`. `while` loops on a condition. `for` iterates over iterators. `for (0..n)` is range syntax. Use `continue` to skip to next iteration.
.rust.Control Flow.Pattern Matching (match).exp
`match` is Rust's powerful pattern matching. Arms must be exhaustive. Patterns can bind, match ranges (`..=`), use `|` for alternatives, and guards with `if`.
.rust.Control Flow.if let.exp
`if let` combines `match` for a single pattern, ignoring others. Useful with `Option`, `Result`, and enums. Reduces boilerplate when only one arm matters.
.rust.Control Flow.while let.exp
`while let` repeatedly matches a pattern until it fails. Common with iterators, `Option`-producing functions, and mutable borrow patterns.
.rust.Control Flow.Labeled Break & Continue.exp
Loop labels (`'label`) disambiguate nested loops. `break 'label` exits the named loop. `continue 'label` skips to the next iteration of the named loop.
.rust.Control Flow.Loop Returning Values.exp
`loop` can return a value with `break value`. `break` with no value returns `()`. Useful for retry logic or initializing values from fallible operations.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Ownership Rules.exp
Each value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. Ownership can be moved. This guarantees memory safety without GC.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Move Semantics.exp
Assigning or passing a value moves ownership unless the type implements `Copy`. Stack-only types (integers, bools, floats, chars, tuples of Copy types) are copied.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Borrowing & References.exp
References borrow values without taking ownership. `&T` (immutable, shared). `&mut T` (mutable, exclusive). References must never outlive their referent.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Borrow Rules Deep.exp
At any time: either one mutable reference, or any number of immutable references. References must always be valid. The borrow checker enforces this at compile time.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Split Borrows.exp
Rust allows borrowing different fields of a struct simultaneously. The borrow checker tracks borrows at the field level, enabling mutable access to disjoint fields.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL).exp
NLL makes the borrow checker smarter: borrows end when they're last used, not at the end of the scope. This reduces friction with the borrow checker significantly.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Slices.exp
Slices are dynamically-sized views into contiguous sequences. `&str` is a string slice. `&[T]` is an array slice. They are fat pointers (ptr + length) and never own data.
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.Interior Mutability.exp
Interior mutability allows mutating data through shared references. Provided by `Cell<T>` (Copy types, no threads), `RefCell<T>` (runtime borrow checking, no threads), and `Mutex<T>` (thread-safe).
.rust.Ownership & Borrowing.RefCell & Borrow Checking at Runtime.exp
RefCell enforces borrow rules at runtime — panics on violation. `borrow()` returns `Ref<T>`, `borrow_mut()` returns `RefMut<T>`. Useful when the compiler can't verify correctness.
.rust.Functions.Function Declaration.exp
Functions use `fn` with snake_case naming. Parameters require type annotations. Return type is `-> Type`. The last expression in a block is implicitly returned. Early return with `return`.
.rust.Functions.Methods & Associated Functions.exp
Methods are functions defined in `impl` blocks with a `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` parameter. Associated functions (like constructors) don't take `self` and are called with `::`.
.rust.Functions.Closures.exp
Closures are anonymous functions that capture their environment. `||` syntax. Traits: `Fn` (immutable capture), `FnMut` (mutable capture), `FnOnce` (consume capture). Each closure has a unique type.
.rust.Functions.Diverging Functions & Never Type.exp
`!` (never type) indicates a function that never returns. `panic!()`, `loop {}`, `todo!()`, `unreachable!()` all diverge. Used in match arms that must match any type.
.rust.Functions.Function Pointers.exp
`fn(T) -> U` is a function pointer type, not a closure. Cannot capture environment. Useful for callbacks and FFI. Coerces from closures that don't capture.
.rust.Functions.Where Clauses.exp
`where` clauses specify trait bounds after the function signature. More readable for complex generics. Same semantics as inline bounds. Required for some complex bound patterns.
.rust.Functions.Higher-Order Functions.exp
Functions can take closures as parameters using generic bounds. Iterator adapters like `map`, `filter`, `fold` enable functional pipelines. Combinators compose nicely.
.rust.Compound Types.Tuples.exp
Tuples group values of different types. Fixed length. Destructure with pattern matching or index syntax `.0`, `.1`. Unit tuple `()` is the empty tuple, representing absence of value.
.rust.Compound Types.Arrays.exp
Arrays have fixed length `[T; N]`. Stored on stack. Bounds-checked at runtime. Slices `&[T]` borrow array elements. `[0; 100]` creates an array filled with the same value.
.rust.Compound Types.Vectors.exp
`Vec<T>` is a growable heap-allocated array. Use `vec![]` macro. Amortized O(1) push. `Vec::with_capacity(n)` pre-allocates. `drain`, `retain`, `splice` are powerful methods.
.rust.Compound Types.Strings (&str vs String).exp
`&str` is a borrowed string slice (UTF-8). `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer. `&str` to `String` via `.to_string()` or `String::from()`. Strings are not `Index` due to UTF-8.
.rust.Compound Types.Structs.exp
Structs define custom data with named fields. Use `impl` blocks for methods. Field init shorthand when variable matches field name. Struct update syntax `..other` fills remaining fields.
.rust.Compound Types.Tuple Structs.exp
Tuple structs have unnamed fields accessed by position. Newtype pattern wraps a single type. Good for type safety without field name overhead. `struct Wrapper(T)`.
.rust.Compound Types.Unit Structs.exp
Unit structs have no fields — act as markers or flags. Zero size. Useful for implementing traits without data, or as phantom types with `PhantomData`.
.rust.Compound Types.Enums.exp
Enums define sum types with variants. Variants can hold data (tuple or struct). `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` are the most common enums. `match` enforces exhaustive handling.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Generics.exp
Generics abstract over types, enabling code reuse. Monomorphization generates specialized code per concrete type at compile time. Type parameters are declared with `<T>`.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Traits.exp
Traits define shared behavior (like interfaces). Types implement traits with `impl Trait for Type`. Traits can provide default method implementations. Must be in scope to use methods.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Derive Macros.exp
`#[derive(...)]` auto-implements common traits: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default, PartialOrd, Ord. Saves boilerplate and ensures correctness.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Supertraits.exp
Supertraits express that one trait extends another. `trait A: B` means types implementing A must also implement B. Used with `where Self: SuperTrait` for method access.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Trait Objects & dyn Trait.exp

Trait objects enable dynamic dispatch via vtable. `dyn Trait` is unsized — must be behind a pointer (`&dyn Trait`, `Box<dyn Trait>`). Objects must be object-safe (no generic methods, no Self by value).
.rust.Traits & Generics.impl Trait Syntax.exp
`impl Trait` in argument position is like a generic. In return position, it returns an opaque type implementing Trait. Cannot return multiple types. Useful for returning closures/iterators.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Associated Types.exp
Associated types define placeholder types within a trait. One implementation per type — unlike generics which allow multiple impls. Used extensively in Iterator, Deref, and operator traits.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Blanket Implementations.exp
Blanket impls implement a trait for all types satisfying bounds. `impl<T: Display> ToString for T {}` is a blanket impl. They allow adding methods to all types meeting criteria.
.rust.Traits & Generics.Trait Bounds & where Clauses.exp
Trait bounds constrain generics. Multiple bounds: `T: Clone + Debug`. `where` clauses improve readability. `impl Trait` as shorthand. `?Sized` opts out of the implicit Sized bound.
.rust.Error Handling.Result & Option.exp
`Result<T, E>` for recoverable errors. `Option<T>` for nullable values. `?` operator propagates errors. `unwrap()` and `expect()` extract values or panic. `ok_or()` converts Option to Result.
.rust.Error Handling.The ? Operator.exp
`?` unwraps `Result` or `Option`, returning early on error/None. Converts error types via `From` trait. Only works in functions returning Result, Option, or types implementing `FromResidual`.
.rust.Error Handling.Panic & Unrecoverable Errors.exp
`panic!()` unwinds the stack (or aborts with `panic = "abort"`). Use for unrecoverable states. `unwrap`, `expect`, `unreachable!()`, `todo!()`, `unimplemented!()` all panic on use.
.rust.Error Handling.Custom Error Types.exp
Implement `std::error::Error` for custom errors. Requires `Display` + `Debug`. `source()` method for error chaining. `Box<dyn Error>` for type-erased error handling.
.rust.Error Handling.thiserror Crate.exp
thiserror derives `std::error::Error` with minimal boilerplate. Supports `#[error("...")]` for Display, `#[source]` for error chaining, and `#[from]` for automatic From impls.
.rust.Error Handling.anyhow / eyre Crates.exp

anyhow provides `Result<T, anyhow::Error>` for application-level error handling. `bail!()` and `ensure!()` macros. Context method `.context()`. eyre is a similar alternative with better error reports.
.rust.Error Handling.Error Chaining.exp
Errors chain via `source()` or `.context()`. The `?` operator auto-converts via `From`. Libraries define specific error types; apps use anyhow/eyre. `Error::source` iterates the chain.
.rust.Error Handling.Result Combinators.exp
`map`, `map_err`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `ok`, `err`, `transpose` — these combinators transform Results without explicit match.
.rust.Collections.Vec.exp

`Vec<T>` is the primary sequence type — growable, heap-allocated, contiguous. Amortized O(1) push/pop. O(n) insert/remove. `with_capacity` pre-allocates. `drain`, `splice`, `retain` for advanced operations.
.rust.Collections.VecDeque.exp
`VecDeque<T>` is a double-ended queue with O(1) push/pop at both ends. Ring buffer internally. Use for queue/sliding window patterns. `make_contiguous()` for slice access.
.rust.Collections.HashMap & HashSet.exp
`HashMap<K, V>` stores key-value pairs with O(1) average lookup. `HashSet<T>` is a set of unique values. Both require keys to implement `Hash + Eq`. `entry()` API handles insert-or-update.
.rust.Collections.BTreeMap & BTreeSet.exp
`BTreeMap` / `BTreeSet` maintain sorted order with O(log n) operations. Keys must implement `Ord`. Use when order matters or for range queries. `range()` returns entries within bounds.
.rust.Collections.BinaryHeap.exp
`BinaryHeap<T>` is a max-heap priority queue. O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop. Use `Reverse<T>` for min-heap. `into_sorted_vec()` drains in order.
.rust.Collections.LinkedList.exp
`LinkedList<T>` is a doubly-linked list. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Split/append operations. Generally slower than Vec/VecDeque due to cache behavior. Use for heavy splitting.
.rust.Collections.Iterators Deep.exp
Iterators are lazy. Adapters: `map`, `filter`, `flat_map`, `flatten`, `take`, `skip`, `zip`, `enumerate`, `chain`, `cycle`. Consumers: `collect`, `sum`, `fold`, `reduce`, `any`, `all`, `find`.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Box<T> (Heap Allocation).exp
`Box<T>` allocates on the heap. Used for recursive types (linked lists), trait objects (`Box<dyn Trait>`), and large data moved infrequently. Derefs to `&T` / `&mut T`.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Rc<T> (Reference Counting).exp
`Rc<T>` enables shared ownership within a single thread. `Rc::clone()` increments reference count. `strong_count` / `weak_count`. `Weak<T>` prevents cycles. Use `Arc` for threads.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Arc<T> (Atomic RC).exp
`Arc<T>` is `Rc` + atomic reference counting — thread-safe. `Arc::clone()` is atomic. Pair with `Mutex<T>` for mutable shared state. `Arc<[T]>` for shared slices.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Cell<T> & RefCell<T>.exp
`Cell<T>` provides interior mutability for Copy types (no borrow checking — just copy in/out). `RefCell<T>` provides interior mutability for any type, checking borrows at runtime.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Cow (Clone-on-Write).exp
`Cow<'a, B>` abstracts borrowed vs owned data. `Cow::Borrowed(&str)` / `Cow::Owned(String)`. Call `.to_mut()` to get mutable access, cloning if borrowed. Ideal for read-mostly APIs.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Pin<T>.exp
`Pin<T>` ensures a value is never moved again. Required for self-referential structs and async generators. `Pin<&mut T>` / `Pin<Box<T>>`. Unsafe to construct. Foundation of async Rust.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Drop Order.exp
Variables drop in reverse declaration order. Struct fields drop in declaration order. `std::mem::forget` skips Drop. `ManuallyDrop` controls Drop. Nested values: outer drops first, then inner.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Mutex, RwLock, Condvar.exp
`Mutex<T>` guards shared data across threads. `RwLock<T>` allows concurrent reads / exclusive writes. `Condvar` blocks threads until a condition is met. `PoisonError` on panic.
.rust.Advanced Rust.Channels (mpsc).exp
`std::sync::mpsc` provides multi-producer, single-consumer channels. `Sender` clones for multiple producers. `Receiver` has `recv`, `try_recv`, `iter`. `crossbeam` offers multi-consumer variants.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Modules & Paths.exp
`mod` declares a module. Files and directories mirror modules. `pub` controls visibility. `super` / `crate` / `self` keywords for paths. `pub(crate)` restricts to crate.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Re-exports.exp
`pub use` re-exports items at a different path, making them part of the public API. Useful for flattening module hierarchies and renaming. `pub(crate) use` for internal re-exports.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Nested Modules & File System.exp
Modules can be nested inline or in files. `mod foo;` looks for `foo.rs` or `foo/mod.rs`. `mod foo { ... }` for inline. The 2018 edition uses the `foo.rs` convention.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Cargo.toml & Crate Types.exp
Crate types: `bin` (binary), `lib` (library), `cdylib` (C-compatible dynamic lib), `staticlib`, `proc-macro`. `edition` field selects Rust edition. `[profile.*]` for optimization settings.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Dependencies & Features.exp
Dependencies from crates.io, git, or path. `features` enable conditional compilation. `default-features = false` to opt out. `[target.'cfg(...)'.dependencies]` for platform-specific deps.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Workspaces.exp
Workspaces manage multiple crates in one project. Shared `target/` and `Cargo.lock`. Members listed in `[workspace]`. `cargo build -p specific-crate` to build a single member.
.rust.Modules & Cargo.Conditional Compilation.exp
`#[cfg()]` gates code on target, feature, or OS. `cfg!()` is a runtime boolean. `#[cfg_attr(...)]` conditionally applies attributes. `cfg(test)` gates test-only code.
.rust.Lifetimes.Basic Lifetime Annotations.exp
Lifetimes (`'a`) annotate how long references are valid. Prevent dangling references. The borrow checker validates lifetimes at compile time. Elision rules handle common patterns automatically.
.rust.Lifetimes.Lifetime Elision Rules.exp

Three elision rules: 1) each input reference gets its own lifetime. 2) with one input lifetime, output gets that lifetime. 3) with `&self`/`&mut self`, output gets self's lifetime. These cover 95%+ of cases.
.rust.Lifetimes.'static Lifetime.exp
`'static` references live for the entire program. String literals have type `&'static str`. `Box::leak` produces `&'static mut`. Const items are effectively static.
.rust.Lifetimes.Lifetime Bounds & Subtyping.exp
`'a: 'b` means 'a outlives 'b (is a subtype of 'b). Required when one lifetime must strictly outlive another. Common in structs and complex function signatures.
.rust.Lifetimes.Higher-Ranked Trait Bounds (HRTB).exp
HRTBs with `for<'a>` express that a bound must hold for all lifetimes. `Fn(&i32)` is sugar for `for<'a> Fn(&'a i32)`. Required for trait objects and closure bounds.
.rust.Lifetimes.Variance.exp
Variance describes how lifetimes compose: `&'a T` is covariant in 'a, `&'a mut T` is invariant in 'a, `fn(T) -> U` is contravariant in T. `Cell<T>` makes T invariant. Important for type safety.
.rust.Lifetimes.Lifetime Coercion.exp
Rust coerces shorter lifetimes to longer ones when safe. `&'a T` coerces to `&'b T` if `'a: 'b`. String `&str` to `&str` with shorter lifetime. Occurs implicitly at coercion sites.
.rust.Lifetimes.NLL Deep.exp
NLL (Non-Lexical Lifetimes) allows borrows to end before the scope ends. Two-phase borrows let reborrowing during method calls. The borrow checker uses a location-aware analysis.
.rust.Async Rust.async/await Basics.exp
`async fn` returns a `Future`. `.await` polls the future to completion. Futures are lazy — they do nothing until awaited or polled. An executor is required to drive futures.
.rust.Async Rust.Tokio Runtime Deep.exp
Tokio provides a multi-threaded (work-stealing) or single-threaded runtime. `#[tokio::main]` attribute sets up the runtime. Key components: reactor (I/O events), scheduler (tasks), timers.
.rust.Async Rust.Async Traits.exp
Async traits require nightly or workarounds. `async-trait` crate desugars to `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`. Upcoming native async traits in Rust will remove this overhead.
.rust.Async Rust.select! & join! Macros.exp
`tokio::select!` waits on multiple futures, completing when the first finishes. `futures::join!` awaits multiple futures concurrently. `try_join!` returns on first error.
.rust.Async Rust.join_all / FuturesUnordered.exp
`futures::future::join_all` awaits a collection of futures, returning all results. `FuturesUnordered` polls a set of futures, yielding results as they complete — ideal for dynamic workloads.
.rust.Async Rust.Async Streams.exp
`Stream` trait is the async version of `Iterator`. `StreamExt` provides `next()`, `map`, `filter`, `fold`. `tokio_stream` and `futures` libraries. `async-stream` macro creates streams.
.rust.Async Rust.Pin Projection.exp

Pin projection allows safely accessing fields of a pinned struct using `pin_project` or `pin_utils`. Critical for self-referential async state machines. `#[pin_project]` attribute handles the unsafe parts.
.rust.Async Rust.Async Sync Primitives.exp
Tokio provides async-aware synchronisation: `Mutex` (hold across .await), `RwLock`, `Semaphore`, `Barrier`, `Notify`, `watch`, `broadcast` channels. Never hold a std::sync::Mutex across .await.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.Raw Pointers.exp

`*const T` and `*mut T` are raw pointers with no safety guarantees. Can be null, dangling, or aliased. Dereferencing requires `unsafe`. Create from references with `as *const T`. Used for FFI and perf.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.Unsafe Functions & Blocks.exp
`unsafe fn` marks an unsafe function that callers must wrap in `unsafe {}`. `unsafe` blocks opt into: deref raw pointers, call unsafe fns, access mutable statics, implement unsafe traits.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.Calling C (FFI).exp
`extern "C"` declares functions from C libraries. `#[link(name = "...")]` links native libs. `#[no_mangle]` prevents name mangling. `unsafe` to call. `libc` crate provides C type aliases.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.#[repr(C)] & repr Attributes.exp
`#[repr(C)]` lays out struct fields like C (no reordering). `#[repr(transparent)]` wraps a single field with same layout. `#[repr(packed)]` removes padding. `#[repr(align(n))]` sets alignment.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.no_std & Global Allocator.exp
`#![no_std]` removes the standard library for embedded/kernel targets. Use `core` and `alloc` crates. `#[global_allocator]` replaces the default allocator. `alloc_error_handler` for OOM.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.#[link] & extern Blocks.exp
`#[link(name = "foo", kind = "static")]` links native libraries. `extern "C"` (or "system", "stdcall") blocks declare foreign functions. `#[link_name = "actual_name"]` overrides the symbol name.
.rust.Unsafe & FFI.Exposing Rust to C (cdylib).exp
`#[no_mangle]` with `extern "C"` exposes Rust functions to C. `CString` creates null-terminated strings. `Cargo.toml` needs `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]`. FFI-safe types only.
.rust.Patterns & Idioms.Builder Pattern.exp
Builder pattern constructs complex objects with many optional parameters. Methods return `&mut Self` or `Self` for chaining. `build()` consumes the builder and produces the final value.
.rust.Patterns & Idioms.RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization).exp
RAII ties resource lifetime to scope. Files, locks, and memory are released in `Drop`. `MutexGuard`, `File`, `Box` all use RAII. Cannot forget to release — the compiler handles it.
.rust.Patterns & Idioms.Newtype Pattern.exp
Wrap a single type in a tuple struct for type safety and trait impls. Zero-cost abstraction — the wrapper is optimized away. Used for units, IDs, and implementing external traits on external types.
.rust.Patterns & Idioms.Deref Pattern & Deref Coercion.exp
Implementing `Deref<Target=U>` allows smart pointers to behave like references. `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, `Arc<T>` all deref to their inner type. `DerefMut` for mutable deref. Chains `.` auto-derefs.
.rust.Patterns & Idioms.Drop Order in Composed Types.exp
Struct fields drop in declaration order. Tuple fields drop in index order. Slices/vectors drop elements front-to-back. Closures drop their captures when the closure drops.
.rust.Patterns & Idioms.Typestate Pattern.exp

Typestate encoding uses the type system to enforce state transitions. Methods consume the current state and return the next. Invalid transitions are compile-time errors. Common in builders and protocols.
.rust.Testing.Unit Tests.exp
Unit tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file. Test functions are annotated with `#[test]`. Assert with `assert!`, `assert_eq!`, `assert_ne!`. `#[should_panic]` for expected panics.
.rust.Testing.Integration Tests.exp
Integration tests live in `tests/` directory at crate root. Each file is a separate crate. They test the public API only. `cargo test --test integration_test_name` runs a specific file.
.rust.Testing.Doc Tests.exp
Doc tests are code blocks in `///` or `//!` docs. Run with `cargo test`. Code blocks with ` ``` ` are compiled and run. ` ```ignore ` skips compilation. ` ```no_run ` compiles but doesn't run.
.rust.Testing.Test Organization & Attributes.exp

`#[cfg(test)]` only compiles test modules. `#[test]` marks a test. `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]`. `#[ignore]` skips a test. `#[bench]` for benchmarks (nightly). `cargo test -- --nocapture` for stdout.
.rust.Testing.Benchmarks.exp
`cargo bench` runs benchmark functions with `#[bench]` (nightly). Or use the `criterion` crate (stable). Criterion measures time, generates reports, and detects performance regressions.
.rust.Testing.Property Testing with proptest.exp
proptest generates many random inputs to verify properties. `proptest!` macro defines strategies. `#[proptest]` is an alternative. Checks invariants hold for all inputs. Finds edge cases.
.rust.Testing.Mocking & Test Doubles.exp
Mock objects simulate dependencies. `mockall` crate generates mock types from trait definitions. `#[automock]` for single methods. Use with dependency injection for isolated tests.
.rust.Macros.Declarative Macros (macro_rules!).exp
`macro_rules!` matches patterns and generates code. Metavariables: `$expr`, `$ty`, `$ident`, `$stmt`, `$pat`, `$tt`. Repetition with `$()*`, `$()+`, `$()?`. Hygiene prevents name collisions.
.rust.Macros.Macro Patterns & Designators.exp
Designators: `block`, `expr`, `ident`, `item`, `lifetime`, `literal`, `meta`, `pat`, `path`, `stmt`, `tt`, `ty`, `vis`. `tt` (token tree) is the most flexible — matches any single token group.
.rust.Macros.Procedural Macros (proc-macro).exp
Procedural macros operate on the token stream. Three kinds: `#[derive]`, attribute-like `#[...]`, function-like `name!()`. Defined in proc-macro crates. `proc_macro::TokenStream` as input/output.
.rust.Macros.Derive Macros.exp
Derive macros automatically implement traits. Custom derive macros use `#[proc_macro_derive(Name)]`. Generate impl blocks. The `syn` crate parses token streams. `quote` crate generates output tokens.
.rust.Macros.Attribute Macros.exp
Attribute macros customize items they annotate. `#[proc_macro_attribute]` receives the attribute arguments and the annotated item tokens. Used for `#[tokio::main]`, `#[async_trait]`, etc.
.rust.Macros.Debugging Macros.exp
`cargo expand` (cargo-expand) shows macro expansion output. `log_syntax!()` prints tokens during expansion. `trace_macros!()` logs all macro invocations. `stringify!()` converts to string.
.spring.Getting Started.What is Spring.exp

Spring is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications. Spring Boot simplifies Spring development with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter dependencies. Key modules: Spring Core (DI/IoC), Spring MVC (web), Spring Data (databases), Spring Security (auth), Spring Cloud (microservices). Spring Boot's opinionated defaults reduce boilerplate while remaining configurable. Convention over configuration with auto-configuration classes. Starter POMs bundle related dependencies.
.spring.Getting Started.Project Structure.exp

Spring Boot projects follow a layered architecture. Typical structure: controller (REST endpoints), service (business logic), repository (data access), model/entity (domain objects), dto (data transfer objects), config (configuration classes), exception (custom exceptions), util (utilities). Resources folder contains application.yml, static files, and templates. The @SpringBootApplication main class is typically at the root package. Package structure by feature or by layer.
.spring.Getting Started.Configuration.exp

Spring Boot externalizes configuration via application.properties or application.yml. YAML is more readable for hierarchical config. Profile-specific files: application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml. Active profiles via spring.profiles.active. Custom properties with @ConfigurationProperties (type-safe). @Value for simple injection. Environment variables override properties. Random values with ${random.int}. Command-line args override file properties. Spring Cloud Config for centralized config.
.spring.Dependency Injection.Spring IoC.exp

Inversion of Control (IoC) is Spring's core - the container manages object creation and wiring. Annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController register beans. @Autowired injects dependencies (by type). @Primary resolves conflicts when multiple beans of same type. @Qualifier specifies exact bean. @Bean for explicit declaration in @Configuration classes. @Scope controls bean lifecycle (singleton, prototype, request, session). @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy for lifecycle callbacks.
.spring.Spring MVC.REST Controllers.exp

@RestController combines @Controller + @ResponseBody for REST APIs. Request mapping annotations: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping. Extract data with: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @RequestHeader. @Valid for request validation. ResponseEntity for full HTTP response control. @ExceptionHandler for controller-level exception handling. @InitBinder for custom data binding.
.spring.Spring MVC.Exception Handling.exp

Global exception handling with @ControllerAdvice. @ExceptionHandler for specific exceptions. Custom error response DTO for consistent API errors. HTTP status code mapping: 400 (bad request), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict), 500 (internal error). Field-level validation errors with MethodArgumentNotValidException. ResponseEntityExceptionHandler provides default Spring exceptions.
.spring.Data Access (JPA).JPA Entities.exp

Spring Data JPA simplifies database access. Entities are POJOs with @Entity annotation. @Table customizes table name. @Id + @GeneratedValue for primary keys. @Column for column customization. Relationships: @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany. @JoinColumn for foreign key. Cascade types: ALL, PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE. Fetch types: LAZY (default for collections), EAGER. @Embeddable for value objects. @Enumerated for enums. @PrePersist/@PreUpdate for lifecycle callbacks.
.spring.Data Access (JPA).Spring Data Repositories.exp

Spring Data JPA generates implementations at runtime. Extend JpaRepository<T, ID> for full CRUD. Custom query methods via method naming: findBy, findByFieldNameContaining, findByFieldNameBetween, countBy, existsBy. @Query for custom JPQL/SQL. @Modifying + @Transactional for update/delete. Specifications for dynamic queries. Projections for partial data. @EntityGraph for eager fetching. Pageable for pagination.
.spring.REST APIs.Building REST APIs.exp

Spring Boot makes building REST APIs straightforward. Use @RestController with request mappings. Content negotiation via produces/consumes. HATEOAS with links for discoverability. Versioning via URL, header, or content type. CORS with @CrossOrigin or global config. HTTP method support: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove). @Valid for request body validation. DTOs to decouple API from entities.
.spring.REST APIs.API Documentation.exp

Springdoc OpenAPI generates API documentation automatically. Add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui dependency. Access at /swagger-ui.html and /v3/api-docs. Customize with @OpenAPIDefinition, @Info, @Tag, @Operation, @ApiResponse. Group APIs with GroupedOpenApi. Spring Boot 3.x uses springdoc v2. Configuration via application.yml. OAuth2 security scheme definition. Request/response examples with @Schema.
.spring.Security.Spring Security.exp

Spring Security provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common attacks. Add spring-boot-starter-security dependency. Core concepts: SecurityFilterChain (filter pipeline), AuthenticationManager (auth processing), UserDetailsService (user lookup), PasswordEncoder (password hashing). @EnableMethodSecurity for method-level security with @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured. CSRF protection (enabled by default for non-REST, disable for REST APIs with stateless JWT). CORS, headers, and exception handling configured in SecurityFilterChain bean.
.spring.Security.JWT Authentication.exp

JWT (JSON Web Token) is commonly used for stateless REST API authentication. Flow: User logs in with credentials, server validates and returns JWT token, client sends token in Authorization header on subsequent requests, server validates token on each request. Use io.jsonwebtoken (jjwt) library. JWT contains claims (sub, iat, exp, roles). Access tokens (short-lived) and refresh tokens (long-lived) pattern. Blacklist for token revocation.
.spring.Testing.Spring Boot Testing.exp

Spring Boot provides comprehensive testing support. @SpringBootTest for integration tests. @WebMvcTest for controller layer (loads only web beans). @DataJpaTest for repository layer (in-memory DB). @MockBean for mocking dependencies. TestRestTemplate or MockMvc for HTTP testing. @TestContainers for real database integration tests. AssertJ for fluent assertions. Test slices reduce startup time by loading only relevant beans.
.spring.Boot Features.Actuator & Monitoring.exp

Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready monitoring and management endpoints. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency. Key endpoints: /health (app health), /info (app info), /metrics (metrics), /env (environment), /loggers (logging levels), /httptrace (HTTP trace), /beans (all beans), /mappings (route mappings). Custom health indicators, metrics with Micrometer, and info contributors. Expose via HTTP or JMX. Integrate with Prometheus/Grafana for monitoring.
.spring.Boot Features.Profiles & Logging.exp

Spring profiles activate different configurations per environment. Use @Profile on beans or profile-specific YAML/properties files. Set active profiles via spring.profiles.active. Logging with Logback (default). Configure levels per package: logging.level.com.example=DEBUG. Logback-spring.xml for advanced config. Logstash encoder for JSON logging (ELK stack). Distributed tracing with Micrometer Tracing + Zipkin. Structured logging for better observability.
.spring.Microservices.Spring Cloud.exp

Spring Cloud provides tools for building microservices. Service discovery with Netflix Eureka or Consul. API Gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway. Load balancing with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer. Circuit breakers with Resilience4j. Distributed configuration with Spring Cloud Config. Distributed tracing with Micrometer + Zipkin. Event-driven communication with Spring Cloud Stream. Feign/WebClient for inter-service HTTP calls. Centralized logging with ELK stack.
.spring.Reactive.WebFlux.exp

Spring WebFlux provides reactive programming support for non-blocking, event-driven applications. Built on Project Reactor (Mono and Flux types). Reactive MongoDB, Cassandra, R2DBC for databases. WebClient for non-blocking HTTP calls. Reactive WebSockets. Functional endpoints with RouterFunctions. Backpressure handling. Better scalability for I/O-bound applications with fewer threads. Netty is the default embedded server for WebFlux.
.sqlite.Getting Started.What is SQLite.exp

SQLite is a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration SQL database engine. It's the most widely deployed database in the world — embedded in browsers, phones, IoT devices. The entire database is a single file. No separate server process needed.
.sqlite.Getting Started.Installing SQLite.exp
SQLite comes pre-installed on macOS and most Linux distros. On Windows, download from sqlite.org. Or use a package manager: apt, brew, or compile from source. The sqlite3 CLI tool is all you need.
.sqlite.Getting Started.SQLite CLI Basics.exp
The sqlite3 CLI is the main interface. Dot-commands start with . (not SQL). Key commands: .tables, .schema, .databases, .import, .output, .mode, .dump, .quit. SQL statements end with ;.
.sqlite.Getting Started.SQLite Data Types.exp

SQLite uses dynamic typing: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB. Type affinity (flexible): INTEGER affinity for whole numbers, REAL for floats, TEXT for strings, BLOB for binary. BOOLEAN stored as INTEGER 0/1. No separate DATE type — use TEXT, INTEGER (Unix), or REAL (Julian).
.sqlite.Getting Started.SQLite Limitations.exp

No concurrent writes (single writer, shared lock). No user management/authentication. 64-bit ROWID limit (~9 quintillion rows). 140TB max DB size (pragma page_size * max_pages). Limited ALTER TABLE (DROP COLUMN was added in 3.35, but no MODIFY COLUMN).
.sqlite.Data Definition.CREATE TABLE.exp

CREATE TABLE defines a table. Column constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK. SQLite auto-creates INTEGER PRIMARY KEY as ROWID alias (auto-increment). WITHOUT ROWID tables use the PRIMARY KEY as the B-tree key.
.sqlite.Data Definition.ALTER TABLE.exp

SQLite supports limited ALTER TABLE: RENAME TABLE, RENAME COLUMN (3.25+), ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN (3.35+). Cannot MODIFY, ALTER, or ADD CONSTRAINT after creation. Workaround: create new table, copy data, drop old, rename.
.sqlite.Data Definition.DROP & TRUNCATE.exp
DROP TABLE removes the table entirely. SQLite has no TRUNCATE TABLE — use DELETE FROM without WHERE. For large tables, DROP and recreate with same schema, or use DELETE and VACUUM to reclaim space.
.sqlite.Data Definition.Constraints & Foreign Keys.exp

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON enables FK enforcement (off by default!). Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY. ON DELETE/UPDATE: CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT, NO ACTION.
.sqlite.CRUD Operations.SELECT.exp
SELECT retrieves rows. Support for WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING. SQLite's LIMIT/OFFSET syntax is standard. Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to check optimization.
.sqlite.CRUD Operations.INSERT.exp

INSERT adds rows. Standard VALUES syntax. Multi-row INSERT supported (3.20+). INSERT OR REPLACE / INSERT OR ROLLBACK / INSERT OR ABORT / INSERT OR FAIL / INSERT OR IGNORE for conflict handling. last_insert_rowid() returns the auto-generated id.
.sqlite.CRUD Operations.UPDATE.exp
UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports UPDATE FROM (joins in UPDATE) since 3.33. No LIMIT in UPDATE — use a subquery or WHERE with ROWID.
.sqlite.CRUD Operations.DELETE.exp
DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports DELETE FROM JOIN USING (since 3.35) and RETURNING clause (3.35+) to return deleted rows.
.sqlite.CRUD Operations.WHERE & Filtering.exp
Standard WHERE operators: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, GLOB, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL. LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII. GLOB uses Unix wildcards (*, ?). Combine with AND, OR.
.sqlite.CRUD Operations.ORDER BY & LIMIT.exp

ORDER BY sorts results. NULLs sort first by default (change with NULLS FIRST/LAST). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET for pagination. For efficient pagination, use WHERE on indexed column instead of OFFSET.
.sqlite.Functions & Expressions.String Functions.exp
SQLite has practical string functions: || for concatenation, LENGTH, UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTR, REPLACE, TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM, INSTR (find substring), LIKE/GLOB, || for concatenation. No CONCAT() — use ||.
.sqlite.Functions & Expressions.Date & Time Functions.exp

SQLite has no date/time storage type. Use TEXT (ISO-8601), INTEGER (Unix timestamp), or REAL (Julian day). Functions: date(), time(), datetime(), strftime(), julianday(). strftime uses C-style format strings.
.sqlite.Functions & Expressions.Conditional & Math Functions.exp

IIF(condition, true_val, false_val) — ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END for multi-way. IFNULL(val, default) replaces NULL. COALESCE returns first non-null. Math: ABS, ROUND, RANDOM, TOTAL, AVG, COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX.
.sqlite.Advanced Features.Transactions.exp

SQLite has full ACID transactions. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT for nested transactions (savepoints). IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE transaction types control locking. WAL mode allows concurrent reads during a write.
.sqlite.Advanced Features.Views & Triggers.exp

Views: saved queries acting as virtual tables. CREATE VIEW, DROP VIEW. Triggers: automatic SQL execution on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. BEFORE/AFTER and INSTEAD OF (for views). FOR EACH ROW (only option — no FOR EACH STATEMENT).
.sqlite.Advanced Features.Indexes & Performance.exp

CREATE INDEX speeds up queries. Types: single-column, composite, UNIQUE, partial (WHERE clause), DESC. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows query execution. ANALYZE collects statistics for better query planning. Use WHERE clause indexes.
.sqlite.Advanced Features.Full-Text Search (FTS5).exp
SQLite's FTS5 extension provides full-text search. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE using fts5. MATCH for searching. Supports stemming, ranking (bm25), prefix queries, and content tables (external content).
.sqlite.Advanced Features.JSON Support.exp

SQLite has JSON functions: json_extract, json_set, json_remove, json_array, json_object, json_each (table function), json_type. The -> and ->> operators work like MySQL. Use json_valid to check JSON validity.
.sqlite.Advanced Features.WAL Mode & Concurrency.exp

WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) allows concurrent readers during a write. PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL. Better performance for many reads + occasional writes. Checkpoint moves WAL content to main DB. PRAGMA synchronous controls durability vs speed.
.sqlite.Advanced Features.VACUUM & Maintenance.exp

VACUUM rebuilds the database file, reclaiming space and defragmenting. AUTO_VACUUM is incremental but less effective. PRAGMA auto_vacuum = 1 enables incremental vacuum. PRAGMA integrity_check verifies database health.
.sqlite.SQLite Ecosystem.SQLite with Python.exp
Python's sqlite3 module is part of the standard library. No external dependencies. Connection, cursor, execute, commit, close pattern. Use ? placeholders for parameterized queries (never f-strings!).
.sqlite.SQLite Ecosystem.SQLite with Node.js.exp
Use better-sqlite3 (synchronous, fast) or sql.js (WASM, browser-compatible). better-sqlite3: prepare, run, get, all, iterate. No async — synchronous is fine for SQLite's speed.
.sqlite.SQLite Ecosystem.SQLite with Go.exp
Use mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO) or modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go). Standard database/sql interface. Placeholder: ?. WAL mode for concurrency.
.sqlite.SQLite Ecosystem.SQLite in Browsers.exp
sql.js compiles SQLite to WebAssembly for in-browser use. Also: OPFS (Origin Private File System) with SQLite WASM builds from sqlite.org. Great for offline-first apps, demos, and tools.
.sqlite.SQLite Ecosystem.CLI Tips & Tricks.exp
The sqlite3 CLI is powerful: .mode for output (column, csv, json, html), .headers on/off, .output file, .import for CSV loading, .dump for backup, .read for script execution, .timer for timing.
.sqlite.Advanced SQLite.Window Functions.exp

Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them like GROUP BY. ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique number, RANK() allows ties with gaps, DENSE_RANK() allows ties without gaps. LEAD() accesses the next row's value, LAG() accesses the previous row's value. OVER() defines the window; PARTITION BY splits into groups, ORDER BY orders within each group. SQLite has supported window functions since version 3.25. A common mistake is forgetting ORDER BY inside OVER for functions that depend on order (like ROW_NUMBER).
.sqlite.Advanced SQLite.CTEs & Recursive Queries.exp

CTEs (Common Table Expressions) use WITH to define a named subquery that can be referenced multiple times. WITH RECURSIVE allows self-referencing CTEs for traversing hierarchical or graph data. The recursive CTE has two parts: the anchor (initial rows, no recursion) and the recursive member (references the CTE itself). Must use UNION ALL. SQLite limits recursion depth with PRAGMA recursive_triggers and an internal max depth of 1000 (configurable). Common mistake: forgetting the UNION ALL between anchor and recursive members.
.sqlite.Advanced SQLite.Full-Text Search (FTS5).exp

FTS5 is SQLite's full-text search extension. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE USING fts5 creates the search index. MATCH performs the search. Supports prefix queries (*), phrase queries ("in double quotes"), and NEAR proximity searches. The bm25() function ranks results. FTS5 can use an external content table (content=) to avoid duplicating data. Use snippet() to get highlighted excerpts. Common mistake: forgetting that FTS5 is an extension that may not be available in all builds (check with PRAGMA compile_options).
.sqlite.Advanced SQLite.Triggers.exp

Triggers in SQLite run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. BEFORE and AFTER control timing. INSTEAD OF triggers are used on views (since views aren't directly updatable). FOR EACH ROW is the only option (no FOR EACH STATEMENT). OLD.column and NEW.column access row values. Use RAISE(ABORT, 'message') to cancel an operation. Common mistake: triggers that recursively fire (Table A trigger updates Table A, firing the trigger again) — SQLite stops at recursion depth limit.
.sqlite.Advanced SQLite.Views & Indexes.exp

Views encapsulate complex queries as virtual tables. Indexes speed up lookups at the cost of write speed. Partial indexes index only rows matching a WHERE condition — saves space and improves speed for filtered queries. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether indexes are being used. The WITH clause can be used inside views. Common mistake: assuming a view with ORDER BY guarantees order (it doesn't — wrap in SELECT ... FROM (view) ORDER BY). Always use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to verify index usage.
.sqlite.SQLite Internals.WAL Mode & Journaling.exp

SQLite has two journaling modes: DELETE (default) and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging). DELETE mode: changes go to a rollback journal, readers and writers block each other. WAL mode: changes are appended to a separate WAL file, readers can read the old DB while a write is in progress — much better concurrency. Checkpoints merge the WAL into the main DB (automatic or manual). WAL is faster for most workloads. Trade-off: WAL requires more file descriptors and is slightly worse for very large transactions. PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL is safe with WAL and faster than FULL. Common mistake: not setting WAL mode in applications with concurrent reads.
.sqlite.SQLite Internals.JSON Support.exp

SQLite has robust JSON support since 3.9.0. json_extract() extracts values, json_set() updates values, json_remove() deletes keys. The -> and ->> operators (3.38+) provide shorthand: -> returns JSON, ->> returns SQL text/integer/real. json_each() expands a JSON array into rows (table function). json_group_array() aggregates values into a JSON array. json_group_object() aggregates into a JSON object. Common mistake: assuming JSON values in TEXT columns are validated — SQLite does not validate JSON on insert unless you use a CHECK(json_valid(data)) constraint.
.svelte.Getting Started.Reactivity.exp

Svelte's reactivity is compiler-driven: assignments to variables automatically trigger DOM updates without a virtual DOM or manual state management. The compiler instruments variable assignments to invalidate dependencies.
.svelte.Getting Started.Templates.exp

Svelte templates extend HTML with {expression} bindings, {#if} blocks, {#each} loops, and {#await} for promises. The template syntax is concise and compiles to highly optimized imperative DOM operations.
.svelte.Getting Started.Logic.exp
Svelte provides logic blocks ({#if}, {:else if}, {:else}) and loops ({#each}, {:else}) within templates. Loops support destructuring and index tracking without special directives.
.svelte.Components.Props.exp
Props in Svelte are declared with the export keyword inside a component script, allowing parent components to pass data. Props can have default values and are reactive when reassigned.
.svelte.Components.Slots.exp
Slots allow parent components to inject content into a child's layout. Named slots and slot props enable flexible component composition and scoped content distribution.
.svelte.Components.Events.exp
Svelte uses the createEventDispatcher helper to forward custom events from child to parent components. DOM events are bound directly with on: directives like on:click.
.svelte.Stores.Writable.exp
Writable stores are the most basic store type, providing set, update, and subscribe methods. They allow cross-component state sharing without prop drilling and auto-subscribe in Svelte templates.
.svelte.Stores.Derived.exp
Derived stores compute values from one or more dependent stores, updating automatically when their sources change. They support transformations and can produce derived writable stores.
.svelte.Stores.Custom Stores.exp
Custom stores encapsulate logic by wrapping the store primitives and exposing a controlled API. They hide implementation details while providing the same subscribe contract for template binding.
.svelte.Lifecycle.onMount.exp
onMount is the most commonly used lifecycle function, executing after the component is first rendered. It's ideal for data fetching, DOM measurements, and cleanup via returned teardown functions.
.svelte.Lifecycle.beforeUpdate.exp
beforeUpdate runs before the DOM is updated after state changes, making it useful for reading the DOM before Svelte patches it. It's the counterpart to afterUpdate.
.svelte.Lifecycle.afterUpdate.exp
afterUpdate runs after the DOM has been updated following state changes, suitable for DOM measurements or scrolling to newly rendered elements. It fires after every component update.
.svelte.Lifecycle.onDestroy.exp
onDestroy registers a callback that runs when a component is unmounted, making it the right place for cleanup like clearing timers, unsubscribing from stores, or canceling network requests.
.svelte.Motion.Tweened.exp
Tweened stores smoothly interpolate numeric values over time, creating animated transitions between states. They support configurable easing functions and interpolation durations.
.svelte.Motion.Spring.exp
Spring stores simulate physics-based animations using stiffness, damping, and mass parameters. They create natural-feeling motion that responds dynamically to changing target values.
.svelte.Motion.Transitions.exp

Svelte's built-in transitions (fade, slide, scale, fly) and custom transition functions provide declarative enter/exit animations. They work with the transition: directive and support in/out modifiers.
.svelte.Motion.Animations.exp
Svelte's animate: directive enables FLIP-based animations for list reordering, automatically calculating position changes and animating elements to their new positions smoothly.
.svelte.Advanced.Actions.exp

Actions are Svelte's approach to integrating with DOM elements imperatively, similar to use:action. They receive the element and optional parameters, returning lifecycle methods like destroy for cleanup.
.svelte.Advanced.Context API.exp
The context API allows passing data to a component and all its descendants without prop drilling. setContext and getContext are scoped to the component tree, not globally like stores.
.svelte.Advanced.Special Elements.exp
Svelte provides special elements like <svelte:body>, <svelte:head>, <svelte:window>, and <svelte:options> for declaring side effects and configuration directly in templates.
.svelte.SvelteKit Basics.Routing.exp
SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where each +page.svelte file in src/routes creates a route. Dynamic parameters are captured with [bracket] notation in directory names.
.svelte.SvelteKit Basics.Endpoints.exp
Endpoints are server-only API routes defined as +server.js files exporting request handlers. They handle GET, POST, PUT, DELETE requests and return JSON or other responses.
.svelte.SvelteKit Basics.SSR.exp
SvelteKit renders pages server-side by default, generating HTML on the server for fast initial loads and SEO. SSR can be disabled per route or globally for fully client-rendered apps.
.svelte.Testing.Vitest.exp
Vitest integrates seamlessly with SvelteKit projects for fast unit and integration testing with Vite-powered HMR, Jest-compatible API, and native ESM support.
.svelte.Testing.Playwright.exp
Playwright is the recommended E2E testing framework for SvelteKit, providing cross-browser automation, network interception, and component testing across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.
.svelte.Svelte 5 Runes.$state.exp
Svelte 5 introduces runes, explicit reactivity markers prefixed with $. $state replaces let-based reactivity and works outside .svelte files, making .svelte.ts files possible for shared state.
.svelte.Svelte 5 Runes.$derived.exp
$derived computes values from $state dependencies and updates automatically. Unlike the store-based derived, it works in any .svelte or .svelte.ts file with no setup wrapper.
.svelte.Svelte 5 Runes.$effect.exp
$effect runs a callback whenever its reactive dependencies change, consolidating lifecycle and reactivity into one primitive. The returned teardown function handles cleanup on re-run or destroy.
.svelte.Svelte 5 Runes.$props.exp
$props replaces the export let pattern for component props in Svelte 5. It accepts a default object and returns reactive bindings that update when the parent re-renders.
.svelte.Svelte 5 Runes.$bindable.exp
$bindable marks a prop as eligible for two-way binding using bind: in the parent. It provides a default value and enables the parent-child sync pattern without manual event dispatching.
.svelte.Snippets.Snippet Blocks.exp
Snippets are reusable template fragments defined with {#snippet name} and rendered with {@render name}. They accept parameters and can be passed between components as first-class template values.
.svelte.Snippets.Snippet Props.exp
Snippets passed as props allow parent components to inject template content into children, replacing slot-based composition with a more explicit and type-safe pattern.
.svelte.Snippets.Children Snippet.exp
The implicit children snippet captures default content between component tags. It provides a cleaner alternative to the default slot for wrapping content in layout components.
.sveltekit.Getting Started.Project Setup.exp
Create a new SvelteKit project with the CLI, choosing from demo app, skeleton project, or minimal setup. The project includes Vite, TypeScript, ESLint, and Prettier out of the box.
.sveltekit.Getting Started.Routing.exp
SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where files in src/routes map to URL paths. +page.svelte files define pages, +layout.svelte wraps nested routes, and dynamic params use [bracket] directories.
.sveltekit.Getting Started.Layouts.exp
Layout components wrap child routes with shared UI like headers and footers. Nested layouts inherit from parent layouts, and +layout.js can run data loading for an entire route segment.
.sveltekit.Data Loading.load.exp
