The load function runs before a page or layout renders, fetching data on the server during SSR and on the client during client-side navigation. It returns data passed to the page as $page.data.
.sveltekit.Data Loading.Page Data.exp
Page data from load is available in +page.svelte via $page.data. Data is typed automatically when using TypeScript, and re-fetched reactively when load dependencies change via depends().
.sveltekit.Data Loading.Layout Data.exp
Layout load functions in +layout.js combine data for all child routes using merge strategies, accessible from any child page or layout. This is ideal for fetching shared resources like user profiles.
.sveltekit.Endpoints.GET.exp
GET handlers in +server.js return data from the server, typically JSON. They receive request event with params, url, fetch, and locals, making them ideal for API routes.
.sveltekit.Endpoints.POST.exp
POST handlers accept request bodies for creating resources, validating input, and returning appropriate status codes. They're used for REST APIs and can handle multipart uploads.
.sveltekit.Endpoints.API Routes.exp
API routes in SvelteKit are server-only endpoints defined alongside pages, sharing the same filesystem routing. They can use server-side secrets and databases without exposing them to the client.
.sveltekit.Endpoints.Form Actions.exp
Form actions handle POST form submissions with progressive enhancement, running on the server to mutate data and return validation errors or success responses without JavaScript required.
.sveltekit.SSR & SSG.Rendering Modes.exp
SvelteKit supports SSR (default), prerendering (SSG), and CSR modes configurable per route or globally. SSR renders on the server on each request, SSG pre-builds static HTML at build time.
.sveltekit.SSR & SSG.Prerendering.exp
Prerendering generates static HTML files at build time for routes that don't need server data, suitable for marketing pages and blogs. Prerendered routes can be served from CDN with zero server cost.
.sveltekit.SSR & SSG.CSR.exp
Client-side rendering skips server rendering entirely, loading the page as a shell and fetching data on the client. Useful for authenticated dashboard pages or apps that need minimal server load.
.sveltekit.Auth.Session Management.exp

SvelteKit sessions can be managed with cookies, JWTs, or server-side stores accessible via the event.locals object in hooks. Authentication libraries like Lucia or Auth.js integrate seamlessly with the hooks pattern.
.sveltekit.Auth.Cookies.exp
SvelteKit provides a cookies API in server contexts for reading, setting, and deleting cookies with configurable options for path, maxAge, secure, httpOnly, and sameSite.
.sveltekit.Auth.OAuth.exp

OAuth authentication flows are handled server-side using endpoints or form actions, redirecting users to providers and exchanging authorization codes for tokens. Libraries like Lucia provide OAuth adapters.
.sveltekit.Deployment.Adapters.exp
Adapters configure SvelteKit for deployment on various platforms by transforming the build output. Each adapter optimizes for the target platform's capabilities and constraints.
.sveltekit.Deployment.Vercel.exp
The Vercel adapter deploys SvelteKit apps to Vercel's serverless edge network with automatic CDN caching, ISR, and serverless function support for dynamic routes.
.sveltekit.Deployment.Netlify.exp
The Netlify adapter deploys to Netlify's platform with serverless functions, split testing, and form handling. It supports on-demand builders for incremental static regeneration.
.sveltekit.Deployment.Node.exp
The Node adapter creates a standalone Node.js server for traditional hosting environments. It produces a single output with middleware support, ready for PM2 or Docker deployment.
.sveltekit.Advanced.Hooks.exp
Hooks are server-side middleware that intercept every request in handle, or module-level functions like handleError and handleFetch. They enable session management, redirects, and error tracking.
.sveltekit.Advanced.Params.exp

Params matchers validate and transform dynamic route parameters before load runs, preventing invalid requests from reaching data loading logic. Built-in matchers include int, uuid, and custom matchers.
.sveltekit.Advanced.Error Handling.exp
SvelteKit provides structured error handling with error/is-error utility, custom error pages (+error.svelte), and the handleError hook for logging and monitoring integration.
.sveltekit.View Transitions.Client Navigation.exp
SvelteKit integrates with the View Transition API for smooth page transitions on client-side navigation. The onNavigate lifecycle runs before navigation, enabling transition setup.
.sveltekit.View Transitions.Cross-document Transitions.exp
Cross-document view transitions work across full page loads by defining @view-transition CSS rules. SvelteKit handles the JavaScript enhancement for seamless cross-page animations.
.sveltekit.View Transitions.Element-level Transitions.exp
Individual elements can have their own view-transition-name for independent animation. Paired with the View Transition API, elements morph smoothly between pages without layout shifts.
.sveltekit.Environment & Config.$env/static/private.exp
$env/static/private provides build-time environment variables accessible only on the server. These are inlined at build time and reserved for secrets like API keys and database URLs.
.sveltekit.Environment & Config.$env/static/public.exp
$env/static/public exposes build-time environment variables prefixed with PUBLIC_ to both client and server code. These are safe for the browser and inlined during build.
.sveltekit.Environment & Config.$env/dynamic.exp
$env/dynamic/private and $env/dynamic/public load environment variables at runtime instead of build time. Dynamic env vars are useful when the same build deploys to multiple environments.
.sveltekit.Link Options.data-sveltekit-preload-data.exp
Link options control prefetching behavior. data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover" starts loading data when the user hovers over a link, reducing perceived navigation time.
.sveltekit.Link Options.data-sveltekit-reload.exp
data-sveltekit-reload forces a full page navigation instead of client-side routing, useful when the target page uses different global CSS or needs a clean JavaScript context.
.sveltekit.Link Options.data-sveltekit-keepfocus.exp
data-sveltekit-keepfocus preserves the currently focused element across navigation, improving accessibility for keyboard users on single-page applications.
.swift.Getting Started.What is Swift.exp

Swift is Apple's modern programming language for iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and beyond. It combines the performance of compiled languages with the expressiveness of scripting languages. Open-sourced in 2015.
.swift.Getting Started.Swift Syntax.exp
Swift uses `var` for mutable variables, `let` for constants. No semicolons needed. Parentheses around conditions are optional. Braces are required for all control flow.
.swift.Getting Started.Variables & Constants.exp
`let` declares constants (immutable binding). `var` declares variables (mutable). Type inference is common, but types can be annotated explicitly. Swift is type-safe with no implicit conversions.
.swift.Getting Started.Basic Types.exp
Swift's fundamental types: Int, Double, Float, Bool, String, Character. Collection types: Array, Set, Dictionary. All types are strongly inferred and strictly checked at compile time.
.swift.Getting Started.Xcode & Playgrounds.exp
Xcode is the official IDE for Swift development. Playgrounds provide interactive coding environments with live results, timeline views, and inline visualization of values.
.swift.Getting Started.Swift Versions.exp
Swift evolves rapidly. Swift 5.9 introduced macros and parameter packs. Swift 5.10 completed actor isolation. Swift 6 enhances concurrency safety and enables strict concurrency checking by default.
.swift.Getting Started.Swift REPL & Format.exp
Swift has an interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop) for quick experimentation. `swift format` auto-formats code. `swiftc` compiles directly. Run with `swift` in terminal.
.swift.Variables & Types.Type Inference.exp
Swift infers types from literal values and expressions. The compiler deduces the type without explicit annotations. Inference works across function returns, closures, and complex expressions.
.swift.Variables & Types.Type Safety.exp
Swift is a type-safe language. Every value has a known type at compile time. Type mismatches produce compiler errors, preventing runtime type errors. No implicit type conversions.
.swift.Variables & Types.Tuples.exp
Tuples group multiple values into a single compound value. Values can be accessed by position (.0, .1) or by name. Tuples are value types useful for returning multiple values.
.swift.Variables & Types.Type Aliases.exp
`typealias` creates an alternative name for an existing type. Improves code readability and abstracts complex types like closures or generic types.
.swift.Variables & Types.Numeric Types.exp
Swift offers Int (signed), UInt (unsigned), Int8/16/32/64, Float (32-bit), Double (64-bit), and CGFloat. Use `.random(in:)` for randomization. Overflow trapping prevents silent truncation.
.swift.Variables & Types.Booleans & Characters.exp
Bool has `true` and `false`. Character is a single Unicode grapheme cluster. `String` is a collection of Characters. Use toggle() to flip a Bool value.
.swift.Variables & Types.Any & AnyObject.exp
`Any` can represent any type (including functions and optionals). `AnyObject` represents any class instance. Avoid using these in favor of generics and protocol types for type safety.
.swift.Control Flow.if / else.exp
`if` and `else` work as expected. Conditions must be Bool expressions (no truthiness). Swift supports `if let` for optional binding and `if case` for pattern matching.
.swift.Control Flow.switch.exp
`switch` supports pattern matching, ranges, tuples, value binding, and where clauses. No implicit fallthrough — use `fallthrough` explicitly. Must be exhaustive with `default` or all cases covered.
.swift.Control Flow.for-in & while.exp
`for-in` iterates over sequences, ranges, and collections. `while` loops on a condition. `repeat-while` guarantees at least one execution. Use `break` and `continue` for flow control.
.swift.Control Flow.if case & guard let.exp
`if case` pattern-matches without a full switch. `guard let` unwraps optionals with early exit, reducing nested `if-let` blocks. `guard` must transfer control (return, break, throw).
.swift.Control Flow.for where.exp
`for where` filters loop iterations inline. Combines iteration with condition without nesting an `if` inside the loop body.
.swift.Control Flow.Labeled Statements.exp
Labels identify loops and switch statements for precise `break` and `continue` control. Useful for breaking out of nested loops.
.swift.Control Flow.Availability Check.exp
`#available` checks API availability at runtime. `@available` marks declarations with minimum platform versions. Guard against using unavailable APIs on older OS versions.
.swift.Control Flow.#warning & #error.exp
`#warning` emits a compiler warning. `#error` emits a compiler error, preventing compilation. Useful for TODOs, reminders, and blocking incomplete code from shipping.
.swift.Functions.Function Declaration.exp
Functions use `func` keyword. Parameters have argument labels (external) and parameter names (internal). `_` omits the external label. Return type with `->`. Functions are first-class types.
.swift.Functions.Closures.exp
Closures are anonymous function literals. Syntax: `{ (params) -> ReturnType in body }`. Trailing closure syntax omits parameter labels. Shorthand: `$0`, `$1`. Closures capture surrounding context.
.swift.Functions.inout Parameters.exp
`inout` parameters allow functions to modify variables passed as arguments. Use `&` prefix when calling. The parameter is copied-in, modified, and copied-out (copy-in copy-out).
.swift.Functions.@discardableResult.exp
`@discardableResult` suppresses the unused-result compiler warning. Use when a function performs work through side effects and the result is optional to consume.
.swift.Functions.autoclosure.exp
`@autoclosure` wraps an expression in a closure automatically, delaying evaluation until called. Useful for short-circuiting, lazy evaluation, and assertion-style APIs.
.swift.Functions.Operator Functions.exp
Custom types can implement operators as static functions. Precedence groups define evaluation order. Define both prefix/postfix/infix and assignment variants.
.swift.Functions.Variadic Parameters.exp
Variadic parameters accept zero or more values of the same type. Use `...` after the type. Inside the function, the parameter is an array. Only one variadic per function.
.swift.Functions.Nested Functions.exp
Functions can be defined inside other functions. Nested functions capture variables from the enclosing scope (closures). Useful for helper logic that is only relevant within a single function.
.swift.Optionals.Optional Basics.exp
Optionals represent values that may be nil. `Type?` is syntactic sugar for `Optional<T>`. Unwrap with `!` (force), `if let`, `guard let`, or nil-coalescing `??`.
.swift.Optionals.Optional Chaining.exp
Optional chaining (`?.`) safely accesses properties and methods on optional values. Returns nil if any link in the chain is nil. Can be chained multiple levels deep.
.swift.Optionals.map & flatMap on Optionals.exp
Optionals conform to map/flatMap. `map` transforms an optional's value if non-nil, preserving nil. `flatMap` flattens nested optionals. Chains transformations without unwrapping.
.swift.Optionals.Implicitly Unwrapped Optionals.exp
IUOs (`Type!`) automatically force-unwrap when accessed. Used for properties that start nil but are set before use (e.g., IBOutlets). Safer to use regular optionals in new code.
.swift.Optionals.Nil Coalescing Deep.exp
`??` unwraps an optional with a default value. `??` can chain multiple fallbacks. Combine with ternary and `?:` for concise optional handling.
.swift.Optionals.Optional Pattern Matching.exp
Optionals integrate with switch-case pattern matching. Match `.some` and `.none` directly, or use optional pattern `let x?`. Works with `if case` and `for case`.
.swift.Collections.Arrays.exp
Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Type-safe and grow dynamically. Methods: append, insert, remove, map, filter, reduce, sort, forEach, first, last.
.swift.Collections.Sets.exp
Unordered collections of unique values. `Set<Element>`. Efficient membership testing with `contains`. Set operations: union, intersection, subtracting, symmetricDifference.
.swift.Collections.Dictionaries.exp
Key-value collections with hashable keys. `[Key: Value]`. Access and modify with subscript. `updateValue(_:forKey:)` returns optional old value. Use `default` subscript for safe access.
.swift.Collections.Slice.exp
Array slices are lightweight views into portions of an array. They share memory with the original. Use Array(slice) to create a new array. Preserves indices of the original.
.swift.Collections.Lazy Sequences.exp
`lazy` defers computation until elements are accessed. Avoids creating intermediate arrays. Chain multiple transformations efficiently with lazy evaluation.
.swift.Collections.anySatisfy & allSatisfy.exp
`allSatisfy` checks if every element meets a condition. `contains(where:)` checks if any element matches. `first(where:)` finds the first match.
.swift.Collections.reduce into.exp
`reduce(into:)` accumulates into a mutable result (usually a collection). More efficient than `reduce` for building arrays/dictionaries since it avoids copying.
.swift.Collections.zip & sequence.exp
`zip(_:_:)` pairs elements from two sequences into tuples (stops at shortest). `sequence(first:next:)` and `sequence(state:next:)` generate infinite/lazy sequences.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Structs Deep.exp
Structs are value types. They receive automatic memberwise initializers. Properties can have observers (willSet, didSet). Mutating methods can modify self. Copy on write for performance.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Classes Deep.exp
Classes are reference types. Support inheritance, deinitializers, and multiple references to the same instance. ARC manages memory. Use `===` for identity comparison.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Properties & Observers.exp
Stored properties hold values. Computed properties calculate on access. Property observers willSet/didSet watch changes. lazy properties initialize on first access.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Mutating Methods.exp
Value types cannot modify their properties in methods by default. Mark methods `mutating` to allow self-modification. Mutating methods can reassign self entirely.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Static Subscript.exp
Types can have static subscripts, enabling type-level subscript access. Useful for registry patterns, default values, and lookup tables.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Subclass Deep.exp
Classes support single inheritance. Override methods with `override` keyword. `final` prevents overriding. `super` accesses parent. `required` init ensures subclasses implement it.
.swift.Structs & Classes.Convenience & Required Init.exp
`convenience init` calls another init (delegating). `required init` forces subclasses to implement it. `failable init?` returns nil. `designated init` is the primary initializer.
.swift.Structs & Classes.@objc & Dynamic.exp
`@objc` exposes Swift declarations to Objective-C runtime. Required for target-action patterns, KVO, and some UIKit APIs. `dynamic` enables method swizzling via ObjC dispatch.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Protocols.exp
Protocols define blueprints of methods, properties, and requirements. Structs, classes, and enums can adopt protocols. Protocols can have default implementations via extensions.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Extensions.exp
Extensions add functionality to existing types. Add computed properties, methods, initializers, subscripts, and protocol conformance. Cannot override existing or add stored properties.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Protocol Composition.exp
Protocol composition combines multiple protocols into a single requirement using `&`. A type must conform to all composed protocols. Use with type annotations and generic constraints.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Associated Types Deep.exp
Associated types (`associatedtype`) define placeholder types within protocols. Concrete types are resolved by the conforming type. Use `where` clauses for additional constraints.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Conditional Conformance.exp
Types can conform to protocols only under certain conditions using `extension: where`. Enables powerful composability like Array: Equatable only when Element: Equatable.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Opaque Types.exp
`some` keyword hides the concrete return type while preserving protocol conformance. The compiler knows the concrete type. Enables abstraction without generics at the call site.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Existential Types.exp
`any` keyword creates an existential box for protocol types. Unlike `some` (opaque), `any` can hold any conforming type at runtime with a performance cost of the existential container.
.swift.Protocols & Extensions.Default Implementations.exp
Protocol extensions provide default method implementations. Conforming types can override or use the default. Combine with constrained extensions for conditional defaults.
.swift.Enums.Enum Basics.exp
Enums define a common type for a group of related values. Can have methods, computed properties, and initializers. Cases are first-class values.
.swift.Enums.Associated Values.exp
Enum cases can carry associated values of any type. Each case can have different associated types. Enables tagged unions and the Result pattern.
.swift.Enums.Indirect Enums.exp
`indirect` enables recursive enums where a case references the enum itself. Required for recursive data structures like lists and trees. Mark individual cases or the whole enum.
.swift.Enums.CaseIterable.exp
`CaseIterable` protocol auto-generates an array of all enum cases. Access via `AllCases`. Works for enums without associated values. Useful for menus, pickers, and iteration.
.swift.Enums.@unknown default.exp
`@unknown default` handles future enum cases without breaking exhaustive switches. The compiler warns if all known cases are not covered. Use alongside explicit cases.
.swift.Enums.Raw Values.exp
Enums can have raw values of String, Character, Int, or floating-point types. Raw values are unique per case. Auto-increment for Int if unspecified. Access with `.rawValue`.
.swift.Error Handling.do / try / catch.exp
Errors are thrown with `throw` from `Error` conforming types. `try` calls throwing functions. `do/catch` handles errors. Catch specific cases before generic. `defer` runs cleanup on scope exit.
.swift.Error Handling.try? & try! Deep.exp
`try?` converts throwing expressions to optional (nil on error). `try!` disables error propagation, crashing on failure. Use `try?` for optional handling, `try!` only when guaranteed.
.swift.Error Handling.Result Type.exp
`Result<Success, Failure>` captures either a success value or error as a value. Useful for async callbacks, composeable error handling, and mapping over errors.
.swift.Error Handling.Throwing Properties.exp
Properties can throw errors by delegating to throwing functions in their getter. Computed properties marked with `get throws` (Swift 5.9+).
.swift.Error Handling.Throwing Subscripts.exp
Subscripts can throw errors (Swift 5.9+). Access elements with `try` when the subscript can fail. Useful for safe collection access beyond bounds.
.swift.Error Handling.rethrowing.exp
`rethrows` indicates a function only throws if its closure parameter throws. The function itself never throws directly. Enables higher-order functions that preserve throw behavior.
.swift.Error Handling.Defer.exp
`defer` schedules code to execute when the current scope exits, regardless of errors or early returns. Multiple defers execute in reverse order (stack-like).
.swift.Error Handling.Custom Errors.exp
Custom error types conform to the `Error` protocol (or `Swift.LocalizedError`). Use enums with associated values for structured error information.
.swift.Generics.Generic Functions.exp
Generic functions work with any type. Type parameters (`<T>`) represent placeholders. Type constraints (`where T: Equatable`) restrict allowed types. Swift infers type parameters at call sites.
.swift.Generics.Generic Types.exp
Generic types like `Array<T>` work with any element type. Define custom generic structs, classes, and enums with type parameters. Methods can add their own generic parameters.
.swift.Generics.Generic Where Clauses.exp
`where` clauses add constraints to generic parameters and associated types. Specify conformance, inheritance, and equality relationships between types.
.swift.Generics.Constrained Extensions.exp
Extensions on generic types can be constrained with `where` clauses. Methods and properties inside constrained extensions are only available when the constraints are met.
.swift.Generics.Phantom Types.exp
Phantom types are generic parameters not used in the struct's stored properties. They add type-level state without runtime overhead. Enforce invariants at compile time.
.swift.Generics.Type Erasure.exp
Type erasure wraps a concrete generic type into an abstract type, hiding the generic parameter. Common patterns: AnySequence, AnyPublisher. Implement via a box/wrapper class.
.swift.Advanced Swift.KeyPaths.exp
Key paths (`\Type.property`) provide type-safe references to properties. `WritableKeyPath` for mutable access. Useful for functional programming, sorting, and binding.
.swift.Advanced Swift.Dynamic Member Lookup.exp
`@dynamicMemberLookup` enables dot-syntax access to arbitrary properties via a `subscript(dynamicMember:)` method. Useful for JSON handling, scripting, and DSLs.
.swift.Advanced Swift.Result Builders.exp
Result builders (formerly function builders) construct complex values from a block of statements. Power SwiftUI's DSL, AttributedStringBuilder, and custom DSLs.
.swift.Advanced Swift.@propertyWrapper Deep.exp
Property wrappers encapsulate getter/setter logic. Custom wrappers use `@propertyWrapper` with `wrappedValue`. `projectedValue` provides additional API via `$` prefix.
.swift.Advanced Swift.Codable & JSON Deep.exp
`Codable` (Encodable & Decodable) auto-generates serialization. Custom keys with `CodingKeys` enum. Custom encoding/decoding via `encode(to:)` and `init(from:)`.
.swift.Advanced Swift.Regex.exp
Swift 5.7+ introduces native regex literals `/pattern/`. `Regex<Output>` type with type-safe captures. Use `firstMatch`, `wholeMatch`, and `matches` for matching.
.swift.Advanced Swift.Opaque vs Existential.exp
`some` (opaque) preserves concrete type identity at compile time. `any` (existential) boxes the type at runtime. Some types work for return values; any types work for heterogeneous collections.
.swift.Advanced Swift.Opaque Parameter Types.exp
Swift 5.7+ allows `some` in function parameter position (like `some View`). Equivalent to a generic parameter with a protocol constraint but written more concisely.
.swift.Concurrency.async/await.exp
Swift's structured concurrency uses async functions and await calls. async functions can suspend and resume, freeing the thread. Building block for all modern Swift concurrency.
.swift.Concurrency.Actors Deep.exp
Actors protect mutable state with actor isolation. Only one task accesses actor state at a time. `nonisolated` for methods that don't access actor state. `isolated` parameters for cross-actor calls.
.swift.Concurrency.Task Groups.exp
Task groups create structured concurrency trees. Tasks added run in parallel. Group collects all results before returning. `withThrowingTaskGroup` for throwing tasks.
.swift.Concurrency.async let.exp
`async let` launches a child task that runs concurrently with the current task. All async let bindings must be awaited before the enclosing scope exits.
.swift.Concurrency.MainActor.exp
`@MainActor` ensures code runs on the main actor (main thread). Mark types, functions, or closures. `await` required when calling from non-main context.
.swift.Concurrency.Global Actors.exp
Global actors provide shared concurrency isolation across types. Define with `@globalActor`. All properties/methods of an actor-isolated type share the same executor.
.swift.Concurrency.Sendable.exp
`Sendable` protocol guarantees a type is safe to share across concurrency domains. Value types are implicitly Sendable. Classes must be final with immutable state or use actor isolation.
.swift.Concurrency.AsyncSequence Deep.exp
AsyncSequence provides asynchronous iteration over values over time. `AsyncStream` creates custom async sequences. `AsyncAlgorithms` package adds zip, merge, combineLatest.
.swift.Concurrency.Task Local Values.exp
Task-local values propagate through the async task hierarchy. Scoped to specific task trees. Useful for logging context, request IDs, and configuration that follows async flow.
.swift.Memory.ARC Deep.exp
Automatic Reference Counting manages memory for class instances. Each strong reference increments the count. Deallocation happens at zero. `deinit` for cleanup. Retain cycles prevent deallocation.
.swift.Memory.Strong Reference Cycles.exp
Strong reference cycles (retain cycles) occur when two instances hold strong references to each other. Memory is never reclaimed. Use `weak` or `unowned` to break cycles.
.swift.Memory.unowned vs weak Deep.exp

`weak` references auto-nil when object deallocates, always optional. `unowned` assumes object lives at least as long, non-optional (crash on access after dealloc). Use weak for optional relationship, unowned for guaranteed co-lifetime.
.swift.Memory.Closure Capture Lists.exp
Closures capture references strongly by default. Capture lists `[weak self]` or `[unowned self]` break retain cycles with closures. Use weak for escaping closures to avoid cycles.
.swift.Memory.@NSCopying.exp
`@NSCopying` copies the property value on assignment using the NSCopying protocol. Ensures the instance holds its own copy rather than sharing mutable reference.
.swift.Memory.Memory Layout.exp
`MemoryLayout` provides the size, alignment, and stride of any type. Useful for understanding struct packing, interop with C, and performance optimization.
.swift.Swift Package Manager.Package.swift.exp
SPM uses Package.swift manifest. Define targets, dependencies, products in a declarative Swift DSL. `// swift-tools-version: 5.9` declares the manifest version.
.swift.Swift Package Manager.Package Structure.exp
Standard SPM layout: Sources/PackageName/*.swift, Tests/PackageNameTests/*.swift, Package.swift at root. Resources in Sources/PackageName/Resources/. Use `.target(name:resources:)` to declare.
.swift.Swift Package Manager.Binary Targets.exp
Binary targets distribute pre-compiled frameworks (e.g., Firebase, Sentry). Reference remote .xcframework URLs or local paths. SPM downloads and links the binary.
.swift.Swift Package Manager.SPM Plugins.exp
Swift Package Manager plugins extend build processes. Build Tool Plugins run before compilation (code gen, linting). Command Plugins run on-demand (formatting, documentation).
.swift.Swift Package Manager.Macro Targets.exp
Swift macros generate code at compile time. SPM 5.9+ supports macro targets. Macros reduce boilerplate and can introspect code at compile time.
.swift.Swift Package Manager.Build Settings.exp
SPM supports Swift compiler flags, linker flags, C settings, and preprocessor macros per target and configuration. Conditionally apply with `.when(platforms:, configuration:)`.
.swift.Swift Package Manager.SPM Commands.exp
Key SPM commands: `swift build`, `swift test`, `swift run`, `swift package generate-xcodeproj`, `swift package --version`. Resolution info with `swift package show-dependencies`.
.swift.Protocol-Oriented Programming.POP Principles.exp

Protocol-Oriented Programming is a core Swift paradigm (from The Swift Programming Language): start with a protocol, provide default implementations via extensions, use protocol inheritance and composition. Prefer protocols over superclasses for flexibility.
.swift.Protocol-Oriented Programming.Protocol Inheritance & Composition.exp
Protocols can inherit from multiple protocols (unlike classes). Protocol composition `&` combines requirements. Use `AnyObject` protocol for class-only protocols. From The Swift Programming Language.
.swift.Protocol-Oriented Programming.Protocol Extensions & Defaults.exp

Protocol extensions provide default implementations, computed properties, and methods. Constrained extensions (`where`) add capabilities only when specific conditions are met. This powers Swift's standard library.
.swift.Protocol-Oriented Programming.Empty Protocols (Marker).exp
Empty protocols mark types with a semantic property without requiring methods. `Sendable`, `Codable`, `Hashable` are examples. Combined with constrained extensions and generics.
.swift.Protocol-Oriented Programming.Self Requirements.exp
Protocols can use `Self` to reference the conforming type. `Equatable` uses Self for ==. `Identifiable` uses Self for ID. Useful for type-safe comparison, copying, and factory patterns.
.swift.Swift in Practice.Access Control.exp

Swift's access levels: `open` (subclassable outside module), `public` (visible outside module), `internal` (default, module-wide), `fileprivate` (file scope), `private` (declaration scope). Use the most restrictive level possible.
.swift.Swift in Practice.URLSession & Networking.exp
Swift's URLSession provides async HTTP networking. `data(from:)` for GET requests, `upload(for:from:)` for POST. Combine with Codable for type-safe JSON parsing. From Hacking with Swift.
.swift.Swift in Practice.Custom ViewModifier & Animation.exp
Custom `ViewModifier` encapsulates reusable view styling. Combine with `withAnimation` for animated transitions. From Hacking with Swift's practical SwiftUI patterns.
.swift.Swift in Practice.Date & Time Handling.exp
Swift provides `Date`, `DateFormatter`, `Calendar`, `DateComponents`, and `DateInterval`. Use `RelativeDateTimeFormatter` for human-readable relative dates. From Hacking with Swift.
.swift.Swift in Practice.SwiftUI Preferences & Custom Layout.exp
Preferences pass data from child to parent views in SwiftUI. `PreferenceKey` aggregates values. `GeometryReader` for layout calculations. From Hacking with Swift's advanced SwiftUI coverage.
.swift.Swift in Practice.UIKit Integration with SwiftUI.exp
SwiftUI can wrap UIKit views via `UIViewRepresentable` and `UIViewControllerRepresentable`. Bridge UIKit delegates, data sources, and target-action patterns. From Hacking with Swift.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.View Protocol.exp
SwiftUI views conform to the `View` protocol. The `body` computed property describes the view hierarchy. Views are lightweight value types describing UI.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.Modifiers.exp
Modifiers configure views. Each modifier returns a new view. Order matters. Common modifiers: .padding(), .font(), .foregroundColor(), .frame(), .background(), .clipShape(), .shadow().
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.@State.exp
`@State` creates mutable state within a view. SwiftUI automatically updates the view when state changes. Use `private` access. State is owned by the view's storage.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.@Binding.exp
`@Binding` creates a two-way connection to a source of truth owned by a parent view. Use `$` prefix to pass binding. Child views read/write through the binding.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.@Observable.exp
SwiftUI 6+ uses `@Observable` macro for observable objects (replacing `ObservableObject`). SwiftUI tracks property reads and only updates views when observed properties change.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.@Environment.exp
`@Environment` reads values from the view's environment. System environments: colorScheme, locale, managedObjectContext, dismiss. Custom environments via `.environment()` modifier.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.StateObject & ObservedObject.exp
`@StateObject` creates and owns a reference-type observable object. `@ObservedObject` observes an object owned elsewhere. `@StateObject` ensures the object lives across view recreation.
.swift.SwiftUI Basics.Lists & Navigation.exp
`List` renders scrollable rows. `NavigationStack` enables push navigation. `NavigationLink` links to detail views. Use `\.self` for identifiable data or custom Identifiable conformance.
.tailwind.Getting Started.Utility-First.exp
Tailwind's utility-first approach uses small, composable classes for styling directly in HTML. Instead of writing custom CSS, you combine utilities like flex, text-center, and p-4 to build designs.
.tailwind.Getting Started.Setup.exp
Tailwind is installed via npm and configured through tailwind.config.js. The PostCSS plugin processes the CSS directives, scanning your source files for class usage to generate the final stylesheet.
.tailwind.Getting Started.Configuration.exp
The tailwind.config.js file controls content paths, theme extensions, variants, and plugins. Custom values can extend the default theme without overriding the complete design system.
.tailwind.Layout.Flexbox.exp
Tailwind provides comprehensive flexbox utilities including flex-direction, justify-content, align-items, and flex-wrap. Responsive variants allow different flex behaviors at each breakpoint.
.tailwind.Layout.Grid.exp
Tailwind's grid utilities enable CSS Grid layouts with grid-cols, grid-rows, and gap classes. Items can span multiple columns or rows using col-span and row-span utilities.
.tailwind.Layout.Spacing.exp
Spacing in Tailwind uses a consistent scale for margin, padding, and gap classes. The scale ranges from 0 to 96, with values like p-4 (1rem), mx-auto (auto margins), and gap-8 (2rem).
.tailwind.Layout.Sizing.exp
Width and height utilities follow the spacing scale plus fractional and viewport values. Classes like w-full, h-screen, max-w-7xl, and min-h-screen handle common sizing needs.
.tailwind.Typography.Font.exp
Tailwind provides font-family, font-size, font-weight, and font-style utilities. Classes like font-sans, text-lg, font-bold, and italic compose to create typographic styles.
.tailwind.Typography.Text.exp
Text utilities cover alignment, decoration, transform, and overflow. Truncation, line-clamping, and text wrapping classes handle common text layout challenges.
.tailwind.Typography.Alignment.exp
Tailwind's text alignment and vertical alignment classes work alongside flex and grid for precise text positioning. Text can be aligned left, center, right, or justified.
.tailwind.Typography.Lists.exp
List style utilities control markers, position, and indentation. Tailwind provides list-none, list-disc, list-decimal, and list-inside/list-outside for ordered and unordered lists.
.tailwind.Colors.Custom Colors.exp
Custom colors are added through the theme.extend.colors configuration. Tailwind generates shades from 50 to 900 automatically, or you can define exact hex values for each shade.
.tailwind.Colors.Color Palette.exp

Tailwind's default palette includes eight color families (gray, red, yellow, green, blue, indigo, purple, pink) each with 11 shades. Colors are applied via bg-*, text-*, border-*, and ring-* utilities.
.tailwind.Colors.Dark Mode.exp
Dark mode is enabled via the darkMode config option. The dark: prefix applies styles only when dark mode is active, either via class strategy or media query.
.tailwind.Responsive.Breakpoints.exp
Tailwind uses five default breakpoints: sm (640px), md (768px), lg (1024px), xl (1280px), and 2xl (1536px). Breakpoint prefixes conditionally apply styles at specific viewport widths.
.tailwind.Responsive.Mobile-First.exp
Tailwind follows a mobile-first approach where unprefixed utilities apply to all screen sizes. Larger screen overrides use breakpoint prefixes like md: or lg: to modify the base styles.
.tailwind.Responsive.Responsive Patterns.exp
Common responsive patterns include stacking on mobile and side-by-side on desktop, hiding/showing elements per breakpoint, and adjusting spacing or typography across viewports.
.tailwind.Components.Buttons.exp
Tailwind buttons combine padding, colors, borders, and hover states. Focus rings ensure accessibility, and disabled states convey inactive buttons with reduced opacity.
.tailwind.Components.Cards.exp
Cards are built with rounded corners, shadows, padding, and dividers. Tailwind's utility classes compose to create consistent card components with header, body, and footer sections.
.tailwind.Components.Modals.exp
Modals use fixed positioning, backdrop overlays, and z-index utilities. Transitions and transforms create smooth open/close animations using Tailwind's transition utilities.
.tailwind.Components.Forms.exp
Form elements are styled with consistent padding, borders, and focus states. Tailwind provides form-specific classes for inputs, selects, textareas, checkboxes, and radio buttons.
.tailwind.Advanced.Custom Plugins.exp
Tailwind plugins allow adding new utilities, components, or base styles programmatically. Plugins use the addUtilities, addComponents, addBase, and matchUtilities API functions.
.tailwind.Advanced.Directives.exp
Tailwind's CSS directives (@tailwind, @apply, @layer, @config) control how styles are generated and applied. @apply inlines utility classes into custom CSS, while @layer organizes styles.
.tailwind.Advanced.Functions.exp
Tailwind provides theme(), screen(), and other CSS functions. theme() accesses design tokens from the config, while screen() generates media query strings for custom CSS.
.tailwind.Optimization.PurgeCSS.exp
Tailwind automatically removes unused CSS in production by scanning content files. The content array in config specifies the paths to scan, resulting in dramatically smaller CSS bundles.
.tailwind.Optimization.JIT Mode.exp
Just-in-Time mode (now default in v3) generates styles on-demand as you author HTML. This eliminates unused CSS entirely, enables arbitrary values like top-[117px], and speeds up builds.
.tailwind.Optimization.Bundle Size.exp
Tailwind's production builds typically result in CSS files under 10KB after purging. The built-in minification and tree-shaking ensure only the utilities you actually use end up in the final bundle.
.terraform.Getting Started.HCL Syntax.exp
HCL is Terraform's declarative language for defining infrastructure. Blocks define resources, providers, and variables in a human-readable format.
.terraform.Getting Started.Terraform Init/Plan/Apply.exp
The core workflow is init (download providers), plan (preview changes), and apply (execute changes). Destroy tears down managed resources.
.terraform.Getting Started.Providers.exp
Providers are plugins that interact with cloud APIs. Terraform downloads provider binaries during init based on the required_providers block.
.terraform.Getting Started.Files & Layout.exp
Terraform configurations follow a standard file layout. main.tf for resources, variables.tf for inputs, outputs.tf for results, and terraform.tfvars for values.
.terraform.Resources & Data.Resource Blocks.exp
Resources are the primary objects Terraform manages, with a type and local name. Arguments configure the resource, and attributes are exported for reference.
.terraform.Resources & Data.Data Sources.exp
Data sources fetch or compute information from providers without creating resources. They import existing infrastructure attributes for use in config.
.terraform.Resources & Data.Dependencies.exp
Terraform automatically creates implicit dependencies from resource references. Explicit depends_on forces ordering when implicit references are insufficient.
.terraform.Variables & Expressions.Input Variables.exp
Input variables parameterize configurations for reuse across environments. They support type constraints, defaults, and validation blocks.
.terraform.Variables & Expressions.Outputs.exp
Outputs expose resource attributes for use in other configurations or display after apply. They are essential for sharing data between modules.
.terraform.Variables & Expressions.Locals.exp
Local values assign names to expressions for reuse. They reduce duplication and improve readability without being user-configurable.
.terraform.Variables & Expressions.Dynamic Blocks.exp
Dynamic blocks generate nested configuration blocks from collections. They reduce duplication when creating multiple similar blocks.
.terraform.Variables & Expressions.for_each & count.exp
for_each creates multiple resources from a map or set of strings. count creates resources from a numeric index. for_each is preferred when keys matter.
.terraform.Variables & Expressions.Splat & Conditionals.exp
Splat expressions extract attributes from resource lists. Conditionals enable if-then-else logic inline in resource configurations.
.terraform.State.Local State.exp
Terraform state maps real-world resources to configuration, storing IDs, attributes, and metadata in a JSON state file.
.terraform.State.Remote State.exp
Remote state stores state files in shared backends like S3, Azure Storage, or Terraform Cloud, enabling team collaboration and locking.
.terraform.State.State Locking.exp
State locking prevents concurrent modifications to state files. DynamoDB (for S3) or native backend locking ensures consistency.
.terraform.State.State Migration.exp
State can be migrated between backends using terraform init -migrate-state. This is needed when switching from local to remote state.
.terraform.Modules.Root Module.exp
The root module is the directory containing main.tf where terraform is executed. It can call child modules to organize infrastructure.
.terraform.Modules.Child Modules.exp
Child modules are reusable configurations called with source argument, accepting input variables and exposing outputs for composition.
.terraform.Modules.Module Registry.exp
The Terraform Registry hosts thousands of pre-built public modules for AWS, Azure, GCP, and other providers, versioned with semantic tags.
.terraform.Modules.Module Composition.exp
Multiple modules can be composed together, passing outputs from one module as inputs to another for building complete infrastructure stacks.
.terraform.CI/CD & Automation.Terraform Cloud.exp
Terraform Cloud provides remote state storage, VCS integration, plan/apply workflows, cost estimation, and Sentinel policy enforcement.
.terraform.CI/CD & Automation.CI/CD Integration.exp
Terraform in CI/CD requires a backend for state storage, environment-specific variable files, and approval gates for production applies.
.terraform.CI/CD & Automation.Testing.exp
Terraform testing includes syntax validation, plan validation with custom rules, and integration testing with Terratest.
.terraform.Provisioners.file.exp
The file provisioner copies files or directories to the remote resource using SSH or WinRM after resource creation.
.terraform.Provisioners.remote-exec.exp
remote-exec runs inline scripts or scripts from files on the remote resource. It is commonly used for initial software installation.
.terraform.Provisioners.local-exec.exp
local-exec runs commands on the machine executing Terraform, useful for triggering external tools or registration scripts.
.terraform.Provisioners.Best Practices.exp
Provisioners are a last resort. Prefer user_data scripts, configuration management tools, or pre-baked AMIs for idempotent and reliable setup.
.terraform.Workspaces.Workspace Strategy.exp
Workspaces manage multiple environment states within the same configuration. Each workspace has its own state file for environment isolation.
.terraform.Workspaces.Environment Separation.exp
Environments use workspace names in naming conventions, variable overrides, and module configuration to isolate infrastructure.
.terraform.Advanced.Sensitive Values.exp
Sensitive variables and outputs mask values in logs and CLI output. Terraform still stores sensitive values in state plaintext, so state must be secured.
.terraform.Advanced.Moved Blocks.exp
Moved blocks refactor resource addresses without destroying and recreating resources. They map old addresses to new ones in state.
.terraform.Advanced.Import.exp
terraform import brings existing infrastructure under Terraform management by mapping real-world resources to configuration.
.ts.Fundamentals.What is TypeScript.exp

TypeScript is JavaScript with types — not a new language. Baumgartner in 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons' emphasizes: 'TypeScript is about describing the shape of data, not about strict rules'. It adds a compile-time type system on top of JS that's erased at runtime. The key insight: TypeScript's type system is structural (shapes match if they have the same properties) NOT nominal (like Java/C# where names matter). This means you can pass an object matching an interface without explicitly implementing it — it 'fits' the shape. Think of types as documentation that the compiler enforces.
.ts.Fundamentals.Type Annotations.exp

Annotations tell TypeScript what type you expect. Baumgartner advises: 'let TypeScript infer where it can, annotate where it needs to'. Inference works for initialization (let x = 5 → number) and return types. Annotate function parameters always (they can't be inferred from the caller) and complex return types for documentation. A key lesson from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': annotating too much is as problematic as annotating too little — let inference work, but be explicit at module boundaries (exports, API contracts).
.ts.Fundamentals.Basic Types.exp

TypeScript's basic types mirror JavaScript: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, void, never, any, bigint, symbol. void means the function returns nothing useful (actually returns undefined). never means the function never returns (always throws or infinite loop). Common mistake: assuming null/undefined are assignable to every type — with strictNullChecks, they must be explicitly unioned. Best practice: enable strictNullChecks; use void for callback return types that may be ignored; use never for exhaustive checks in switch statements.
.ts.Fundamentals.unknown vs any.exp

any disables type checking entirely — it's an escape hatch that should be avoided. unknown is the type-safe counterpart: you must narrow it via typeof, instanceof, or type guards before use. Common mistake: using any instead of unknown when the type truly isn't known.
.ts.Fundamentals.Enums.exp

Enums define named constants. Numeric enums auto-increment from 0 and have reverse mappings (value → name). String enums require explicit values and have no reverse mapping. const enum is inlined at compile time (zero runtime cost) but can't be used with isolatedModules or bundlers. Common mistake: assuming enums are just strings — numeric enums have bidirectional mappings which adds runtime code. Best practice: prefer string enums for readability and serialization; use const enum for performance-critical numeric constants; consider union of string literals as a simpler alternative.
.ts.Fundamentals.Type Inference.exp

TypeScript infers types from values when no annotation is given. Inference works for variable initialization, return values, and generic calls. A common mistake is assuming inference is always correct — complex scenarios may need explicit annotations for clarity.
.ts.Fundamentals.Literal Types.exp

Literal types restrict a variable to an exact string, number, or boolean value. Combine with union types for constrained options. A common mistake is thinking any string matching the literal format is assignable — the value must be exactly the literal.
.ts.Fundamentals.Strict Mode.exp

Enable strict: true in tsconfig to activate all strict checks: noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, and alwaysStrict. A common mistake is starting a project without strict mode and adding it later — much harder to migrate.
.ts.Type System.Union Types.exp

Unions express 'either this type OR that type'. Baumgartner says: 'union types are TypeScript's most powerful feature — they model reality where data comes in multiple shapes'. The best part: TypeScript forces you to NARROW the type before using type-specific operations. This eliminates entire categories of runtime errors. Narrowing happens through typeof, instanceof, in, discriminated property checks, or custom type guards. A key insight from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': always use discriminated unions (a common literal property like kind) for clear, exhaustive type narrowing — they're the backbone of TypeScript error handling patterns.
.ts.Type System.Intersection Types.exp

Intersection types combine multiple types into one, requiring all properties from each type. Use & to merge object types. A common mistake is intersecting primitives (like string & number), which results in never.
.ts.Type System.Type Aliases.exp

Type aliases name a type for reuse. Baumgartner: 'use type for unions, intersections, and tuples; use interface for object shapes you might extend'. type can represent anything (primitives, unions, tuples, objects); interface is restricted to objects. The key difference: interfaces can be declaration-merged (reopened and extended), types cannot. A lesson from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': prefer interface for public API contracts (they're more discoverable in editor tooltips and error messages), use type for complex type expressions.
.ts.Type System.Interfaces.exp

Interfaces define the shape of objects. Baumgartner in 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons' highlights: 'interfaces are open — they can be extended via declaration merging'. This makes them ideal for library types that users might want to augment. Interfaces also extend cleanly (extends), can be implemented in classes, and produce better error messages. A critical insight: interfaces evaluate lazily (they don't resolve all members immediately), while type aliases evaluate eagerly. This matters for recursive types — interfaces handle them naturally, types need explicit indirection.
.ts.Type System.Structural Typing.exp

TypeScript uses structural (duck) typing: type compatibility is determined by shape, not name. Two types with identical members are interchangeable. A common mistake is expecting nominal typing behavior where type names should differ.
.ts.Type System.Type Assertions.exp

Type assertions (as) tell TypeScript you know more about a type than it does. They do not perform runtime checks. A common mistake is using assertions to silence errors instead of fixing the real type issue. Prefer 'as' over angle-bracket syntax in JSX.
.ts.Type System.Branded Types.exp

Branded types add a phantom property to simulate nominal typing. This prevents mixing structurally compatible types like UserId and OrderId. A common mistake is forgetting that brands are compile-time only — they have no runtime effect.
.ts.Type System.satisfies Operator.exp

The satisfies operator validates that a value matches a type without widening the inferred type. This preserves the narrowest type for autocomplete and type-checking. A common mistake is using a type annotation instead, which widens the type.
.ts.Type Guards & Narrowing.typeof Type Guards.exp

typeof narrows primitive types in conditional blocks. TypeScript understands typeof returning 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'symbol', 'bigint', 'undefined', 'object', and 'function'. A common mistake is checking typeof null which returns 'object' — use value === null instead.
.ts.Type Guards & Narrowing.instanceof Type Guards.exp

instanceof narrows types based on constructor/prototype chain. Works with classes and built-in constructors like Date, Error, RegExp. A common mistake is using instanceof with interfaces — they are compile-time only and erased at runtime.
.ts.Type Guards & Narrowing.Equality Narrowing.exp

Equality checks (===, !==) narrow types by excluding mismatched values. Switch statements and strict equality against literal types narrow to the matching branch. A common mistake is using == instead of === which allows type coercion.
.ts.Type Guards & Narrowing.Truthiness Narrowing.exp

Truthiness checks (if, &&, ||, !) narrow types by excluding falsy values: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN. A common mistake is forgetting that empty string '' and 0 are falsy — use ?? for null/undefined only.
.ts.Type Guards & Narrowing.Type Predicates.exp

Type predicates (parameterName is Type) are custom type guard return types. They tell TypeScript what a value is when the function returns true. A common mistake is writing a predicate that doesn't actually check — TypeScript trusts your predicate blindly.
.ts.Type Guards & Narrowing.Discriminated Unions.exp

Discriminated unions use a common literal property (the discriminant) to narrow each variant. TypeScript understands switch/case and if/else checks on the discriminant. A common mistake is not using a literal type as the discriminant.
.ts.Functions.Function Types.exp

Function types describe callable signatures: parameter types and return type. Use type aliases or inline syntax. A common mistake is forgetting that callbacks can have optional parameters and void return types are assignable from any return value.
.ts.Functions.Optional & Default Parameters.exp

Mark parameters as optional with ? or provide default values. Optional params must follow required ones. Default parameters are always optional and infer their type from the default value. A common mistake is mixing up order — optional params can't precede required ones.
.ts.Functions.Generic Functions.exp

Generics preserve type information through functions. Baumgartner: 'generics are about describing relationships between types'. The classic example: Array<T> — the type parameter T flows from creation through every method. TypeScript infers T from arguments 90% of the time. Constrain T with extends when you need specific capabilities (like T extends HasLength). A key insight from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': 'generics are contagious' — once you add a type parameter to a function, every function that wraps it likely needs one too. Use multiple type parameters for complex relationships.
.ts.Functions.Function Overloads.exp

Overloads declare multiple call signatures for a single implementation. The implementation signature must be compatible with all overloads but is not callable directly. A common mistake is having an implementation signature that can't satisfy all overloads.
.ts.Functions.Rest Parameters.exp

Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an array. Type them as an array type. TypeScript also supports typed tuples for rest parameters in variadic patterns. A common mistake is thinking rest must be the last parameter — it must be the only last parameter.
.ts.Functions.this Parameters.exp

TypeScript uses a fake first parameter named 'this' to type the function's context. This catches errors where 'this' is used incorrectly, common in callbacks and event handlers. A common mistake is forgetting to bind 'this' or using arrow functions when a dynamic 'this' is needed.
.ts.Functions.Async Functions.exp

Async functions always return Promise<T> where T is the resolved type. Annotate the return type as Promise<T> for clarity. A common mistake is forgetting that async functions wrap the returned value in Promise — you must await or .then() to get the value.
.ts.Functions.void & never Return Types.exp

void means the function completes normally but returns nothing meaningful (actually returns undefined). never means the function never completes — it always throws or loops forever. A common mistake is assigning void to something expecting a value, or thinking never is the same as void.
.ts.Functions.Nested Loops.exp

Nested loops in TypeScript work like JavaScript but benefit from type safety — the compiler tracks array element types, ensures indices are valid numbers, and catches out-of-bounds when using array types with literal index access. Use for...of with destructuring for cleaner 2D iteration. Prefer flat() and flatMap() for transforming nested structures over manual nested loops when possible.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Classes.exp

TypeScript classes add type annotations to fields, constructors, and methods. Fields must be declared with types or initialized. A common mistake is forgetting to initialize a field or declare it — the strictPropertyInitialization check will catch this.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Inheritance.exp

Use extends to create subclasses. Call super() before accessing this in the constructor. A common mistake is forgetting super() entirely or calling super() after accessing this. Use the override keyword to explicitly mark method overrides.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Access Modifiers.exp

public (default), private, and protected control member visibility. private prevents access outside the class; protected allows access in subclasses. A common mistake is relying on these for runtime security — they are compile-time only and erased at runtime.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Abstract Classes.exp

Abstract classes define shared behavior with abstract methods that subclasses must implement. They cannot be instantiated directly. A common mistake is trying to use new on an abstract class or forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a subclass.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Interfaces with Classes.exp

Classes can implement interfaces to guarantee a shape. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Unlike extends, implements doesn't inherit implementation, only enforces shape. A common mistake is thinking implements provides default implementations — it only enforces type contracts.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Static Members.exp

Static properties and methods belong to the class, not instances. Access them via ClassName.property. A common mistake is trying to access static members through an instance or using this inside a static method to access instance members.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Parameter Properties.exp

Parameter properties combine declaration and assignment in one step. Prefix a constructor parameter with public, private, protected, or readonly to auto-create the field. A common mistake is forgetting that the access modifier is required — without it, it's just a regular parameter, not a property.
.ts.Classes & OOP.Mixins.exp

Mixins compose behavior from multiple classes using constructor type patterns. TypeScript doesn't support multiple inheritance, but mixins provide a composable alternative. A common mistake is not properly typing the constructor return type or forgetting to call super in a mixin.
.ts.Generics.Generic Types.exp

Generic types parameterize types with type variables, enabling reusable, type-safe containers. Type variables are placeholders for actual types determined at use. A common mistake is not providing enough type parameters or omitting them entirely when inference fails.
.ts.Generics.Constraints.exp

Use extends to constrain type parameters to types with specific properties. This allows the generic implementation to safely access those properties. A common mistake is not constraining when you need to call methods on the generic value.
.ts.Generics.Utility Types.exp

TypeScript provides built-in utility types: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Record<K,T>, Pick<T,K>, Omit<T,K>, Exclude<T,U>, Extract<T,U>, NonNullable<T>, and more. They reduce boilerplate for common type transformations.
.ts.Generics.Generic Classes.exp

Generic classes maintain type parameters across all members and methods. The type parameter is fixed at construction time. A common mistake is not specifying the type parameter when creating an instance, causing inference from the constructor args.
.ts.Generics.Conditional Types.exp

Conditional types select between types based on a condition. Baumgartner calls them 'TypeScript's if/else at the type level'. The structure T extends U ? X : Y. A critical behavior: they DISTRIBUTE over unions — if T is string | number, the conditional applies to each member separately and the results are unioned. The infer keyword captures a type from within a larger type. A lesson from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': 'conditional types are the foundation of all advanced TypeScript patterns' — they power ReturnType, Extract, Exclude, and NonNullable. Use them to build type transformations that adapt to the input type.
.ts.Generics.Mapped Types.exp

Mapped types transform each property of a type using { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }. Add modifiers like ? and readonly to create variations. A common mistake is forgetting that mapped types preserve modifiers by default — use -? and -readonly to remove them.
.ts.Generics.Template Literal Types.exp

Template literal types construct string types at the type level using embedded type placeholders. Combined with union types, they generate all possible combinations. A common mistake is thinking they work at runtime — they are purely compile-time constructs.
.ts.Generics.infer Keyword.exp

The infer keyword introduces a type variable within a conditional type's extends clause, capturing a type from a larger structure. It powers most advanced utility types like ReturnType. A common mistake is using infer outside a conditional type — it's only valid in the extends clause.
.ts.Utility Types.Partial<T>.exp

Partial<T> makes all properties of T optional. Useful for update operations where you only supply changed fields. A common mistake is applying Partial to deeply nested objects — it only affects the top level.
.ts.Utility Types.Required<T>.exp

Required<T> makes all properties of T required (removes optionality). Useful for transforming optional configs into full required types. A common mistake is forgetting Required does not affect nested optional properties.
.ts.Utility Types.Readonly<T>.exp

Readonly<T> makes all properties of T readonly. Useful for immutable objects and configs. A common mistake is thinking Readonly prevents deep mutation — use as const or DeepReadonly for nested immutability.
.ts.Utility Types.Record<K,T>.exp

Record<K,T> creates an object type with keys K and values T. K is usually a union of string literals. A common mistake is using Record<string, T> when you know the specific keys — prefer a mapped type for better autocomplete.
.ts.Utility Types.Pick<T,K>.exp

Pick<T,K> creates a type with only the specified keys K from T. Useful for creating lightweight view types from full data types. A common mistake is picking keys that don't exist on T — TypeScript catches this at compile time.
.ts.Utility Types.Omit<T,K>.exp

Omit<T,K> creates a type without the specified keys K from T. The inverse of Pick. Useful for excluding sensitive fields. A common mistake is using Omit when you want to exclude by value type rather than key name.
.ts.Utility Types.Exclude<T,U>.exp

Exclude<T,U> removes types from T that are assignable to U. Works with union types. A common mistake is using Exclude for object properties when you should use Omit — Exclude works on union members, not object keys.
.ts.Utility Types.Extract<T,U>.exp

Extract<T,U> extracts types from T that are assignable to U. The opposite of Exclude. Useful for filtering union types to a subset. A common mistake is expecting Extract to filter object properties — use Pick instead.
.ts.Utility Types.NonNullable<T>.exp
NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined from T. Useful for cleaning up after validation. A common mistake is using NonNullable on object types expecting it to remove null properties from fields.
.ts.Utility Types.ReturnType<T>.exp

ReturnType<T> extracts the return type of a function type T. Uses conditional types with infer internally. A common mistake is passing a function value instead of a type — use typeof to get the type first.
.ts.Utility Types.Parameters<T>.exp
Parameters<T> extracts the parameter types of a function type T as a tuple. Useful for forwarding argument types to wrappers. A common mistake is forgetting Parameters returns a tuple, not a union.
.ts.Utility Types.Awaited<T>.exp
Awaited<T> unwraps Promise types recursively. Useful for getting the resolved type of async functions. A common mistake is using Awaited on non-Promise types — it passes them through unchanged.
.ts.Advanced Types.Conditional Types.exp

Advanced conditional types enable type-level branching and filtering. They distribute over unions unless wrapped with brackets. Use them for building utilities like Exclude and Extract. A common mistake is assuming conditionals work at runtime — they are purely compile-time.
.ts.Advanced Types.Mapped Types.exp

Advanced mapped types iterate over object keys with keyof. Use the as clause for key remapping and combine with conditional types to filter keys. A common mistake is not accounting for readonly and optional modifiers that are preserved by default.
.ts.Advanced Types.Indexed Access Types.exp

Indexed access types (T[K]) retrieve the type of a property at key K. Use T[keyof T] for all values or T[number] for array elements. A common mistake is using a key that doesn't exist on the type, which produces a compile-time error.
.ts.Advanced Types.Type Guards.exp

Type guards narrow types in conditional blocks using x is T predicates. Use typeof, instanceof, or custom functions. A common mistake is writing guards that are too broad or forgetting that in operator also acts as a type guard in TS 5.5+.
.ts.Advanced Types.Variadic Tuple Types.exp

Variadic tuple types use spread in tuple positions to capture variable-length patterns. They enable strongly typed concatenation, partial application, and parameter forwarding. A common mistake is forgetting that spreads in tuples create new tuple types.
.ts.Advanced Types.Recursive Types.exp

Recursive types reference themselves to model nested structures like JSON, trees, or linked lists. TypeScript supports recursive type aliases but has depth limits to prevent infinite expansion. A common mistake is creating infinitely recursive types without a base case.
.ts.Advanced Types.Discriminated Unions.exp

Discriminated unions are TypeScript's most important pattern for modeling state. Baumgartner: 'they make impossible states impossible'. A discriminated union has a common literal property (the discriminant, like kind or status) that tells TypeScript which variant is active. Inside a switch on the discriminant, TypeScript narrows the type to the specific variant. This eliminates entire classes of runtime errors (wrong property access, missing cases). 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons' emphasizes: 'model your data as discriminated unions, not optional fields' — instead of optional error/loading/data fields, use a single union with { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success', data: T } | { status: 'error', error: string }.
.ts.Advanced Types.keyof & typeof Operators.exp

keyof T produces a union of the keys of T. typeof x extracts the type of a value at compile time. Combine them for dynamic property access patterns. A common mistake is using typeof at runtime instead of compile-time — typeof at runtime is JavaScript's typeof.
.ts.Modules & Tooling.ESM Imports.exp

TypeScript supports ES module import/export syntax. Use import type for type-only imports to avoid runtime overhead. A common mistake is mixing default and named imports incorrectly, or forgetting that type-only imports are erased at compile time.
.ts.Modules & Tooling.Namespaces.exp

Namespaces group related code under a global namespace. They are legacy constructs — prefer ES modules for new code. Still useful for ambient declarations and library definitions. A common mistake is mixing namespace and module imports.
.ts.Modules & Tooling.Decorators.exp

Decorators modify classes, methods, properties, or parameters. They are experimental in TypeScript (enable experimentalDecorators). Use them for metaprogramming, logging, and dependency injection. A common mistake is forgetting that decorator evaluation order matters.
.ts.Modules & Tooling.tsconfig.exp

tsconfig.json configures the TypeScript compiler. Key options: target, module, strict, outDir, rootDir, and lib. A common mistake is not including files in the project or using conflicting module and moduleResolution settings.
.ts.Modules & Tooling.Declaration Files.exp

Declaration files (.d.ts) describe JavaScript module shapes without implementation. Use declare module for third-party libs and declare global for augmenting globals. A common mistake is writing implementation code in .d.ts files — they should only contain type declarations.
.ts.Modules & Tooling.Triple-Slash Directives.exp

Triple-slash directives are single-line comments referencing other files. Used in declaration files for legacy reference management. Types, path, and lib directives exist. A common mistake is using these in modern projects — prefer ESM imports instead.
.ts.Asynchronous TypeScript.Promise Types.exp

Promise<T> represents an asynchronous value. The type parameter T is the resolved type. A common mistake is treating Promise<T> as T — you must await or .then() to unwrap the value. Promise<void> is common for fire-and-forget async operations.
.ts.Asynchronous TypeScript.Async/Await.exp

Async functions always return Promise<T>. Await unwraps the promise inside an async function. TypeScript tracks types through await. A common mistake is forgetting to await a promise or wrapping an already-async function in another Promise unnecessarily.
.ts.Asynchronous TypeScript.Async Iterators.exp

Async iterators (AsyncIterable<T>) produce values asynchronously. Use for await...of to consume them. Useful for streaming data, paginated APIs, and event streams. A common mistake is using for...of (sync) on an async iterable, which causes a runtime error.
.ts.Asynchronous TypeScript.Typed Event Emitters.exp

Typed event emitters use generics to map event names to payload types. This provides type-safe on/emit patterns. A common mistake is not typing the event map, resulting in any-typed event data throughout the codebase.
.ts.Asynchronous TypeScript.Promise Combinators.exp

Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.allSettled, and Promise.any have typed return values. TypeScript infers tuples/unions from the input array. A common mistake is assuming Promise.all returns a loose array — it returns a tuple when given a tuple literal.
.ts.Asynchronous TypeScript.Error Handling in Async Code.exp

Async errors require try/catch. In strict mode, caught errors are typed as unknown — you must narrow them. A common mistake is assuming the error is always an Error instance or not handling non-Error throws like strings or objects.
.ts.Modern Patterns.Template Literal Types.exp

Template literal types construct string types at compile time using embedded type expressions. Combined with unions, they generate all possible string combinations automatically. A common mistake is assuming these can be used at runtime — they're erased during compilation.
.ts.Modern Patterns.satisfies Operator.exp

satisfies validates a value's type while preserving the narrowest inferred type for autocomplete. Unlike type annotations, it doesn't widen. A common mistake is using a type annotation instead of satisfies, which loses the specific types of individual properties.
.ts.Modern Patterns.Assertion Functions.exp

Assertion functions use the asserts return type to narrow types after a call. They throw if the assertion fails, making subsequent code safe. A common mistake is writing assertion functions without the asserts keyword, which prevents TypeScript from narrowing.
.ts.Modern Patterns.Branded Types.exp

Branded types add a unique phantom property to create distinguishable types from structurally identical ones. This prevents mixing values like emails and phone numbers. A common mistake is forgetting to cast at the boundary — brands are not automatically applied.
.ts.Modern Patterns.Nominal Typing.exp

TypeScript uses structural typing by default. To simulate nominal typing (type identity matters), use brands, enum discriminants, or intersection with unique class types. A common mistake is expecting structural typing to catch nominal mismatches automatically.
.ts.Modern Patterns.Covariance & Contravariance.exp

Covariance preserves assignment direction (Dog[] is Animal[]). Contravariance reverses it (function parameters). TypeScript is covariant for most types but checks function parameters bivariantly by default — strictFunctionTypes fixes this. A common mistake is expecting array invariance.
.ts.DOM & TypeScript.Typed DOM APIs.exp

TypeScript includes DOM type definitions. Use specific element types (HTMLInputElement, HTMLCanvasElement) instead of generic Element for type-safe property access. A common mistake is using querySelector without the generic parameter, resulting in an Element type.
.ts.DOM & TypeScript.Event Typing.exp

DOM events have specific types (MouseEvent, KeyboardEvent, FocusEvent, SubmitEvent) with typed properties. Use addEventListener's generic for proper typing. A common mistake is typing all events as Event, losing access to event-specific properties like clientX or key.
.ts.DOM & TypeScript.Form Typing.exp

Type form access with HTMLFormElement and HTMLInputElement. FormData provides key-value access. A common mistake is forgetting to check if a form element exists before accessing it, or not casting data.get() results.
.ts.DOM & TypeScript.Fetch Typing.exp

The fetch API returns Promise<Response>. Parse the body with json(), text(), etc. Type the parsed data, not the fetch call. A common mistake is not checking res.ok or assuming JSON parsing always succeeds.
.ts.Error Handling.Typed Error Classes.exp

Create custom Error subclasses with typed properties. Set the name property for proper instanceof checks. A common mistake is forgetting to set error.name — without it, instanceof may work inconsistently across inheritance chains.
.ts.Error Handling.Try/Catch with unknown.exp

In strict mode, catch variables are unknown, not any. Narrow them with instanceof, typeof, or custom guards. A common mistake is accessing err.message without checking — TypeScript will error with 'Object is of type unknown'.
.ts.Error Handling.Result Types.exp

Result types model success/failure without exceptions using a discriminated union. This forces callers to handle both paths explicitly. A common mistake is using exceptions for expected failure modes instead of modeling them in the type system.
.ts.Error Handling.Definite Assignment Assertions.exp

Use the ! assertion (!:) to tell TypeScript that a variable is definitely assigned, even when the compiler can't prove it. Common in class properties initialized in constructor helpers or lifecycle methods. A common mistake is overusing it to silence warnings instead of restructuring code.
.ts.Error Handling.Null Checks.exp

With strictNullChecks, null and undefined are distinct types. Use optional chaining (?.), nullish coalescing (??), and type guards to handle nullable values safely. A common mistake is using || instead of ?? for defaults — || treats empty string and 0 as falsy.
.ts.Ecosystem.Formatting (Prettier).exp

Prettier is the standard TypeScript formatter handling semicolons, quotes, trailing commas, and indentation. Integrate with editor format-on-save and CI checks. A common mistake is Prettier conflicting with ESLint — use eslint-config-prettier to disable formatting rules in ESLint.
.ts.Ecosystem.Linting (ESLint).exp

ESLint with @typescript-eslint catches TypeScript-specific issues like unused variables, unsafe assertions, and promise handling errors. A common mistake is disabling strict rules like no-explicit-any — prefer incremental fixing.
.ts.Ecosystem.DefinitelyTyped & @types.exp

DefinitelyTyped is the community repository of TypeScript type definitions. Install with @types/package-name. Most popular libraries now include bundled types. A common mistake is installing @types for a package that already ships its own types.
.ts.Ecosystem.Build Tools.exp

Modern TypeScript projects often skip tsc for building and use bundlers instead. Vite, tsup, and SWC are popular choices. Use tsc --noEmit for type-checking only and a bundler for output. A common mistake is using tsc for both checking and bundling.
.ts.Configuration & Build.Strict Compiler Options.exp

Beyond strict: true, individual strict flags include noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, and alwaysStrict. Additional safety: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes.
.ts.Configuration & Build.Module Resolution.exp

moduleResolution controls how TypeScript resolves imports: classic, node, node16, nodenext, or bundler. bundler is best for modern bundlers like Vite and esbuild. A common mistake is using node with ESNext module output, causing resolution mismatches.
.ts.Configuration & Build.Path Aliases.exp

Path aliases allow cleaner imports by mapping directories to short prefixes. Configure in tsconfig paths and sync with your bundler. A common mistake is setting baseUrl but forgetting to configure the bundler's resolve alias to match.
.ts.Configuration & Build.Project References.exp

Project references split a codebase into independently buildable sub-projects. Each has a tsconfig with composite: true. Improves build performance via incremental compilation and enforces module boundaries. A common mistake is circular references between projects.
.ts.Configuration & Build.Build Modes.exp

Use tsc -b for build mode with project references. It builds all referenced projects in dependency order with incremental compilation. --clean removes build artifacts. A common mistake is running plain tsc instead of tsc -b in a monorepo with references.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.LLM API Integration.exp

Call OpenAI/Claude from Node.js with full type safety. Use zod for response validation, handle streaming with AsyncIterable, manage rate limits with p-limit. Common mistake: not validating LLM responses at runtime — JSON parse can fail; always use a schema-based parser.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.LangChain.js.exp
