LangChain.js brings chains, agents, and retrieval to Node.js/TypeScript with full type safety. Supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, local models, vector stores, and tool integration. Common mistake: not typing chain inputs/outputs — use RunnableWithMessageHistory for typed conversations.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Vercel AI SDK.exp

Vercel AI SDK provides React/Vue/Svelte hooks for streaming LLM responses, tool calling, and structured generation. Framework-agnostic core with React/Vue/Svelte adapters. Handles streaming, abort controllers, error boundaries. Common mistake: using it only with Vercel — it works with any Node.js framework (Express, Fastify).
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Embeddings & Vector Search in JS.exp

Generate embeddings from JS (OpenAI, Transformers.js) and search them in vector databases. Chroma.js for local use, pgvector for Postgres, Pinecone for managed. Use worker_threads to avoid blocking the event loop for embedding generation. Common mistake: recomputing embeddings on every query — cache results.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Transformers.js.exp

Run Hugging Face models directly in the browser or Node.js with Transformers.js. No GPU, no Python — pure ONNX runtime in JS. Supports text classification, embeddings, token generation, image classification, speech-to-text. Common mistake: downloading full model weights on every page load — use IndexedDB caching via quantized models.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Browser ML (WebGPU/WebNN).exp

Run ML models in the browser with hardware acceleration. TensorFlow.js for training/inference; ONNX Runtime for cross-framework model deployment; MediaPipe for vision/audio pipelines; WebGPU for GPU compute. Common mistake: assuming all devices support WebGPU — always provide WebGL fallback.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Structured LLM Output with Zod.exp

Combine Zod schemas with LLM calls for type-safe, validated structured output. Zod's discriminated unions power conditional LLM responses; refine/transform validate complex business rules. Integrates with OpenAI structured outputs, Vercel AI SDK tool calls, LangChain withStructuredOutput. Common mistake: making schemas too strict — LLMs need room for variation.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Streaming & Real-time AI.exp

Stream LLM responses over Server-Sent Events or WebSocket for real-time UX. AbortController for cancellation, backpressure handling, reconnection logic. Use ReadableStream for Node.js-to-browser streaming. Common mistake: buffering entire response before sending — defeats purpose of streaming.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.AI-Powered Search.exp

Build semantic search with embeddings + vector DB. Hybrid search combines keyword (BM25) with semantic (vector) for best results. Rerank results with cross-encoders. Use Result type pattern for type-safe search responses. Common mistake: ignoring keyword search — pure semantic search misses exact matches.
.ts.AI & LLMs in TypeScript.Building AI Agents in TypeScript.exp

Build AI agents with tool-use, memory, and planning in TypeScript. Use the ReAct pattern (Thought → Action → Observation), maintain conversation history, and execute tools safely. TypeScript's discriminated unions model agent state perfectly. Common mistake: infinite loops — always cap iterations and depth.
.unity.Getting Started.Hello Unity.exp

Unity uses a component-based architecture. Game objects are empty containers that get behavior from attached components. Scripts are written in C# and inherit from MonoBehaviour. The Start() method runs once at initialization, and Update() runs every frame.

Create a C# script, attach it to a GameObject, and use Start() to print to the console. Press Play to see your output in the Console window.
.unity.GameObjects & Components.Working with Components.exp

Everything in Unity is a GameObject with components. Transform is the only required component (position, rotation, scale). You can add components like Rigidbody (physics), Collider (collision detection), Renderer (visuals), and custom scripts. Use GetComponent<T>() to access components at runtime.
.unity.Physics.Colliders & Rigidbodies.exp

Unity's physics system uses Rigidbody components for physics-driven movement and Colliders for shape definition. Use Physics.Raycast() for line-of-sight and shooting. Colliders can be triggers (no physical response) for detection zones. Physics Materials control friction and bounciness. Joints connect Rigidbodies together (Hinge, Fixed, Spring, Configurable).
.unity.Prefabs.Prefab System.exp

Prefabs are reusable GameObject templates. Create a GameObject, drag it to the Project window to make a prefab. Nested prefabs contain other prefabs. Prefab variants inherit from a base prefab with overrides. Use Instantiate() to spawn prefabs at runtime. The Prefab Mode allows editing the prefab in isolation without affecting scene instances.
.unity.Shaders.Shader Graph.exp

Shader Graph is Unity's node-based shader editor for creating shaders without code. Supports Universal RP and HDRP. PBR Graph (physically-based) vs Unlit Graph. Master Stack controls final output: Vertex, Fragment, Surface options. Use Sub Graphs for reusable node groups. Keywords enable multi-compile shader variants. Blackboard properties expose parameters to the inspector.
.unity.UI Toolkit.UXML & USS.exp

UI Toolkit is Unity's web-inspired UI system. UXML defines layout structure (like HTML), USS provides styling (like CSS). Runtime UI for in-game HUD and menus, Editor UI for tool windows. Data binding connects UI elements to C# data sources. The UI Builder window enables visual editing. Event system supports propagation, pooling, and custom events.
.unity.Animation.Mecanim & Animator.exp

Mecanim is Unity's animation system. The Animator Controller defines a state machine with states (idle, walk, run) and transitions. Blend Trees blend multiple animations by parameter (speed, direction). Avatar masks enable layered animation (upper body shooting while walking). Apply Root Motion for animation-driven movement. Animation Events trigger code at specific frames.
.unity.Scriptable Objects.Data Architecture.exp

ScriptableObjects are data containers that avoid MonoBehaviour overhead. Use them for game events, item definitions, dialogue trees, level configs, and audio settings. Create assets at runtime with CreateInstance(). Use [CreateAssetMenu] for easy asset creation. They enable data-driven architecture — designers can tweak values without touching code.
.unity.Unity Gaming Services.UGS.exp

Unity Gaming Services is Unity's cloud platform providing Authentication, Cloud Save, Lobby, Relay (P2P), Economy, Analytics, and Cloud Code. Players can sign in anonymously or with external providers. Cloud Save persists player progress. Lobby + Relay enables multiplayer without custom backend. All services integrate through the Unity Gaming Services SDK.
.unity.Multi-Scene Workflows.Scene Management.exp

Multi-scene workflows split a game into additive scenes: persistent managers, UI layer, gameplay levels. Use LoadSceneMode.Additive to load without unloading. SceneManager.sceneLoaded event tracks loading. DontDestroyOnLoad keeps objects across scenes. Addressables provide async scene loading with dependency management and remote content delivery.
.unity.Editor Tools.Custom Editors.exp

Unity Editor can be extended with Custom Editors (replace inspector UI), PropertyDrawers (custom field rendering), EditorWindows (standalone tool windows), Gizmos (in-scene visualization), and MenuItems. Use IMGUI or UI Toolkit for editor UI. SerializedObject and SerializedProperty provide safe data access with Undo support.
.unity.NavMesh AI.Navigation.exp

Unity's AI Navigation system bakes a NavMesh from scene geometry. NavMeshAgent handles pathfinding and movement. OffMeshLinks connect disconnected areas (jumps, ladders). NavMeshObstacle dynamically affects the navmesh. The system uses RVO (Reciprocal Velocity Obstacles) for agent avoidance. Bake settings control agent radius, height, slope, and step offset.
.unity.VFX Graph.Visual Effects.exp

VFX Graph is Unity's GPU-accelerated particle system with node-based graph editing. Supports millions of particles with minimal CPU overhead. Use events to trigger particle bursts, exposed properties for runtime control, and custom blocks with Shader Graph integration. Capacities set maximum concurrent particles. Output updates: Lit Quad, Mesh, Line, Trail, Ribbon.
.unity.DOTS & Jobs.ECS & Burst Compiler.exp

Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack (DOTS) includes Entities (archetypes), Components (struct data only), and Systems (logic). The Burst Compiler translates C# to highly optimized native code via LLVM. The Jobs System provides safe multithreading with dependency management. Together they enable processing thousands of entities at high performance with no GC allocations.
.unity.2D Game Development.Sprites & 2D World.exp

Unity's 2D features include SpriteRenderer for rendering sprites, SpriteShape for terrain/rails, and SpriteMask for visibility. Sorting Layers and Order in Layer control draw order. 2D physics uses Rigidbody2D, Collider2D variants (Box, Circle, Polygon, Edge), and PhysicsMaterial2D. CompositeCollider2D merges colliders on a single body.
.unity.Lighting & Reflections.Lighting & Probes.exp

Unity lighting includes Directional (sun), Point (bulb), Spot (cone), and Area (rectangle) lights. Real-time vs baked lighting. Lightmapping: bake indirect lighting into lightmaps with Progressive Lightmapper. Reflection Probes capture environment reflections on metallic/glossy surfaces. Light Probe Groups provide indirect lighting on dynamic objects. Emission on materials contributes to baked lighting.
.unity.Audio Systems.AudioSources & Mixers.exp

Unity's audio system uses AudioSource to play AudioClip assets. AudioMixer provides bus routing with groups (Master, Music, SFX, Voice) and effects (reverb, EQ, compression). Spatial Blend controls 2D vs 3D positioning. 3D audio uses distance attenuation curves and Doppler effect. AudioReverbZone creates realistic environment transitions.
.unity.Cinemachine.Intelligent Cameras.exp

Cinemachine provides modular camera system with virtual cameras. CinemachineVirtualCamera defines camera behavior: FramingTransposer (follow), FreeLook (3rd person orbit), BlendList (cutscene sequences). Priority system blends between cameras. Noise (Perlin) adds screen shake. Dolly tracks animate cameras along paths. Aim components: Composer, GroupComposer, HardLookAt.
.unity.Object Pooling & Optimization.Performance & Pooling.exp

Object pooling prevents GC spikes by reusing objects instead of instantiate/destroy. The Profiler window shows CPU/GPU/Rendering/Memory usage. Frame Debugger: Window > Analysis > Frame Debugger to inspect draw calls. Key optimizations: reduce draw calls (static batching, GPU instancing), LOD groups, occlusion culling, texture atlasing, and reducing material count.
.unity.Localization.Multi-Language Support.exp

Unity's Localization package manages multiple languages via String Tables and Asset Tables. Use LocalizeStringEvent for UI text and LocalizeSpriteEvent for images. Locale selection at runtime via LocalizationSettings.SelectedLocale. Smart Strings with placeholders ({0}, {count}) handle pluralization. Font fallback ensures CJK and special character support.
.unity.Terrain & Environment.Terrain Engine.exp

Unity's Terrain system creates large outdoor environments. Paint heightmaps, textures (albedo, normal), trees, and details (grass, bushes). Terrain layers blend textures based on height and angle. Wind Zones animate vegetation. Tree Creator generates procedural trees. Use Terrain Settings for pixel error, base map distance, and detail object density.
.unity.AR Foundation.Augmented Reality.exp

AR Foundation provides a cross-platform AR framework for iOS (ARKit) and Android (ARCore). Key components: ARSession (manages AR lifecycle), ARPlaneManager (detects surfaces), ARPointCloudManager (feature points), ARAnchorManager (world anchors), and ARRaycastManager (hit testing). Place virtual objects on detected planes with ARPlacementInteractable.
.unreal.Getting Started.Hello Unreal.exp

Unreal Engine uses C++ and Blueprints for game logic. The primary gameplay class is AActor, which represents any object that can be placed in the world. The BeginPlay() method runs when the actor enters play, and Tick() runs every frame.

Create a C++ class inheriting from AActor, override BeginPlay(), and use UE_LOG to print to the Output Log. Compile and place your actor in the level to see the output.
.unreal.Actors & Components.Actor Lifecycle.exp

AActor is the base class for all gameplay objects in Unreal. Actors have a lifecycle: construction, BeginPlay, Tick, and EndPlay. Actors can contain components (USceneComponent, UStaticMeshComponent, etc.) for modular behavior. UPROPERTY() and UFUNCTION() macros expose members to Blueprints and the engine's reflection system.
.unreal.Blueprints.Blueprint vs C++.exp

Blueprints provide visual scripting for rapid iteration — ideal for designers and prototyping. C++ excels at performance-critical systems, engine extensions, and complex algorithms. Best practice: implement base classes in C++ with BlueprintNativeEvent functions, then let designers extend them in Blueprints. Use UPROPERTY(BlueprintReadWrite) and UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable/BlueprintImplementableEvent) to bridge both worlds.
.unreal.Chaos Physics.Collision & Destruction.exp

UE5's Chaos Physics replaces PhysX as the default physics engine. It supports destructible meshes via Voronoi fracturing, cloth simulation, and vehicle dynamics with modular suspension/engine/transmission. Use UPhysicsAsset for per-bone collision. Chaos handles large-scale destruction with breakable constraints and clustered particle systems.
.unreal.UMG UI.Widgets & HUD.exp

Unreal Motion Graphics (UMG) is the UI system for HUDs, menus, and in-game interfaces. Widget Blueprints combine a visual designer with event graphs. Key containers: Canvas Panel (absolute positioning), Horizontal/Vertical Box, Overlay, Grid Panel. Use BindWidget in C++ for type-safe access to widget elements. Widget animations create transitions without Tick(). Retainer Box caches widget rendering for performance.
.unreal.Materials.Material Editor.exp

Unreal's Material Editor is a node-based graph for creating shaders. Material Instances inherit from parent materials with parameter overrides — use them to create variants without recompiling. Material Functions encapsulate reusable node networks. Key nodes: TextureSample, Lerp, Multiply, Fresnel, Panner, Time. Use Material Parameter Collections for global material parameters accessible from Blueprints.
.unreal.World Partition.Large World Streaming.exp

UE5's World Partition replaces level streaming for open worlds. One File Per Actor (OFPA) stores each actor in its own package. The world is divided into streaming cells loaded/unloaded based on player proximity. HLOD (Hierarchical Level of Detail) generates proxy meshes for distant objects. World Partition works with Landscape, foliage, and PCG-generated content.
.unreal.MetaSounds.Procedural Audio.exp

MetaSounds is UE5's high-performance audio system using a node-based graph for real-time sound synthesis and processing. Build sounds from oscillators, envelopes, filters, delays, and convolution reverb. Parameters are controllable from Blueprints/C++ at audio rate. Replaces legacy Sound Cues with fully deterministic, CPU-efficient audio. Supports multi-channel output, sidechain compression, and dynamic music systems.
.unreal.Animation Blueprints.AnimBP & State Machines.exp

Animation Blueprints control per-bone animation blending. The AnimGraph uses state machines, blend spaces, aim offsets, and layered blending per bone. Cached poses save performance by reusing evaluated poses. Sub-anim instances handle weapon/ability-specific animations. Root motion extraction drives character movement from animations. Use NativeUpdateAnimation() in C++ for efficient parameter updates.
.unreal.Smart Objects & State Tree.Interactive World Objects.exp

Smart Objects define interactive behaviors for world objects (sitting, leaning, opening). Combined with State Tree — a hierarchical behavior system with state transitions, conditions, and tasks. State Tree is lightweight, data-driven AI designed for smart interactions. Smart Object definitions include slots, interaction ranges, and behavior filters. State Tree replaces older behavior tree systems for character-scene interactions.
.unreal.PCG Framework.Procedural Content Generation.exp

UE5's Procedural Content Generation framework uses a graph-based node system to generate content at runtime or in-editor. Nodes include terrain spawning, scattering, noise filtering, density mapping, and collision checks. PCG integrates with World Partition and Landscape for open-world generation. Custom C++ nodes extend the graph. Generate foliage, rocks, buildings, and entire biomes procedurally.
.unreal.Mass Entity System.ECS & Crowd AI.exp

UE5's Mass framework is a data-oriented ECS system for simulating thousands of AI agents efficiently. Fragments store data (position, velocity, AI state), Processors implement logic, and Archetypes define composition. Mass includes built-in LOD (full simulation → simplified → off-screen), crowd avoidance, movement, and sensory systems. Use Mass for crowds, wildlife, traffic, and ambient NPCs.
.unreal.Enhanced Input.Input System.exp

UE5's Enhanced Input System replaces legacy Action/Axis mappings. UInputAction defines actions with modifiers (dead zone, chorded, negate) and triggers (pressed, held, double-tap, tap, release). UInputMappingContext organizes context-sensitive bindings with priority layering. Use Player Mappable Keys for user rebinding. Supports gamepad, keyboard, mouse, and touch.
.unreal.Niagara VFX.VFX System.exp

Niagara is UE5's next-gen visual effects system. Emitters define particle behavior through Spawn, Update, and Render stages. Modules add forces, noise, collisions, and scaling. GPU particles handle massive counts (100K+) efficiently. Data Interfaces connect to external data (mesh, audio, AI). Use Niagara for fire, explosions, weather, magic spells, and environmental effects. System assets combine multiple emitters.
.unreal.Landscapes & Foliage.Terrain & Vegetation.exp

UE5's Landscape tool sculpts vast terrains with heightmaps, layers, and erosion simulation. Use landscape brushes: sculpt, paint, smooth, and noise. Foliage system paints instanced vegetation (grass, trees, rocks) across landscapes. Procedural Foliage Spawner volumes auto-populate areas based on density, slope, and collision rules. Nanite supports millions of foliage instances with minimal overhead.
.unreal.Sequencer & Cinematics.Sequencer & Cutscenes.exp

Sequencer is UE's cinematic editor for in-game cutscenes and cinematics. Key components: Level Sequence (tracks actors, cameras, audio, events), Camera Cut Track (switches cameras), Take Recorder (record in-editor performances). Supports animation tracks, sub-sequences, and event tracks triggering Blueprints. Cinematic Camera actors with film presets and depth of field.
.unreal.AI Behavior Trees.AI & Behavior Trees.exp

Unreal's AI system centers on Behavior Trees — hierarchical task graphs with Sequence, Selector, Condition, Task, and Decorator nodes. Blackboard stores shared AI data (target, location, state). Environment Query System (EQS) finds tactical positions. AI Perception Component handles sight, hearing, and damage detection. Use AAIController to run behavior trees on pawns.
.unreal.Sound Cues & Audio Mixing.Legacy Audio & Attenuation.exp

Alongside MetaSounds, UE supports Sound Cues (wave player, delay, mixer, modulator). USoundAttenuation sets distance falloff, reverb send, and occlusion. USoundConcurrency limits overlapping instances. UAudioVolume changes audio settings in world regions. Audio Mixing: master/submix buses, EQ, compression, and reverb effects on audio submixes.
.unreal.Optimization & Profiling.Unreal Insights & Optimization.exp

Unreal Insights is UE5's central profiling tool. Use console commands: stat fps, stat unit, stat game, stat rhi. ProfileGPU shows per-draw-call cost. Key optimizations: Nanite for high-poly meshes, Virtual Shadow Maps, Lumen scalability settings, HLOD merging, texture streaming pool, and PSO caching. Use -trace launch args for Unreal Insights capture.
.unreal.Packaging & Deployment.Project Packaging.exp

Package your UE project via File > Package Project. Target platforms: Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS, and consoles (Xbox, PS5, Switch). Configure project settings: maps, default game mode, input, packaging (cook everything vs. by the book). Handle platform-specific SDKs (Steamworks, Epic Online Services). Create installer with NSIS or platform store submission packages.
.unreal.Control Rig & IK.Procedural Animation.exp

Control Rig is UE5's procedural animation system that runs within the animation blueprint. Full-body IK using FABRIK solver, aim constraints, multi-priority IK, and spring dynamics. Control Rig graphs operate in the editor for rigging and at runtime for dynamic corrections. Sequencer integration for cinematic rigging. Python scripting for automation and batch rigging operations.
.unreal.Gameplay Ability System.GAS Framework.exp

The Gameplay Ability System (GAS) is a robust framework for abilities, buffs, cooldowns, and attributes. Core components: UAbilitySystemComponent (attach to characters), UGameplayAbility (skill definitions), UGameplayEffect (temporary/permanent stat changes), UAttributeSet (character stats). Uses FGameplayTag for blocking, stacking, and categorization. Widely used in AAA shooters and RPGs.
.vite.Getting Started.Project Setup.exp
Vite scaffolds projects using create-vite with templates for vanilla JS/TS, React, Vue, Svelte, Lit, and more. The setup process installs dependencies and configures the build tool in seconds.
.vite.Getting Started.CLI Commands.exp
Vite provides three primary CLI commands: vite (dev server), vite build (production build), and vite preview (preview production build). Flags like --port, --host, and --mode customize behavior.
.vite.Getting Started.Dev Server.exp

Vite's dev server uses native ES modules and esbuild pre-bundling for instant startup. Hot Module Replacement updates modules without full page reloads, preserving application state during development.
.vite.Configuration.vite.config.js.exp
Vite is configured via vite.config.js using the defineConfig helper for type hints. The config file supports conditional configurations based on mode, environment, and build targets.
.vite.Configuration.Plugins.exp
Plugins extend Vite's functionality using a Rollup-compatible plugin API. They can transform code, inject styles, optimize assets, and hook into the build lifecycle at various stages.
.vite.Configuration.Resolve.exp
The resolve config controls module resolution, including aliases, extensions, and main fields. Path aliases simplify imports by mapping @/ to the src directory.
.vite.CSS & Assets.PostCSS.exp
Vite includes PostCSS support out of the box. A postcss.config.js file is automatically detected, enabling features like Tailwind CSS, Autoprefixer, and custom CSS transformations.
.vite.CSS & Assets.CSS Modules.exp
CSS Modules are supported natively for files ending in .module.css. Class names are locally scoped by default, and the generated module object maps original class names to hashed versions.
.vite.CSS & Assets.Static Assets.exp
Vite handles static assets (images, fonts, SVGs) as ES module imports. Assets smaller than a configurable threshold are inlined as base64 data URLs, while larger files are emitted as separate files.
.vite.Build.Production Build.exp
The vite build command produces optimized assets for production. It bundles with Rollup, minifies with esbuild or terser, applies code splitting, and generates hashed filenames for caching.
.vite.Build.Code Splitting.exp
Vite automatically splits code into separate chunks for dynamic imports. Manual chunking can be configured in the build.rollupOptions to separate vendor libraries from application code.
.vite.Build.Chunking.exp
Advanced chunking strategies control how modules are grouped into output files. Vite supports async chunk loading, CSS code splitting, and granular control over chunk file names.
.vite.Environment Variables.Mode.exp
Vite modes (development, production, custom) determine which .env files are loaded. Custom modes like staging or test use .env.staging or .env.test files for environment-specific configuration.
.vite.Environment Variables..env Files.exp
Vite loads environment variables from .env files with specific priority: .env.[mode].local > .env.[mode] > .env.local > .env. Only variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to client code.
.vite.Environment Variables.Import.meta.env.exp
Environment variables are accessed via import.meta.env in client code. Vite also provides built-in variables like import.meta.env.MODE, import.meta.env.PROD, and import.meta.env.DEV.
.vite.Plugins.Official.exp
Vite's official plugins include @vitejs/plugin-react (with Fast Refresh), @vitejs/plugin-vue, @vitejs/plugin-svelte, and @vitejs/plugin-legacy for legacy browser support.
.vite.Plugins.Community.exp
The community ecosystem includes plugins for PWA (vite-plugin-pwa), SVG (vite-plugin-svg), compression (vite-plugin-compression), and more. Most popular frameworks have dedicated Vite plugins.
.vite.Plugins.Custom Plugins.exp
Custom Vite plugins follow the Rollup plugin convention with additional Vite-specific hooks. Plugins use the name, apply, enforce, and various transform/build hooks to modify behavior.
.vite.SSR.Server-Side Rendering.exp
Vite provides SSR support with built-in APIs for development and production. The SSR build produces a server entry point that can render Vue/React components on the server.
.vite.SSR.SSR Build.exp
The SSR build generates a separate bundle optimized for Node.js execution. It disables CSS extraction and produces ESM or CJS output depending on the configured format.
.vite.Migration.Webpack to Vite.exp

Migrating from Webpack involves replacing loaders with Vite plugins, converting CommonJS to ESM, and adapting custom Webpack configurations to Vite's simpler config format. Most Webpack loaders have Vite equivalents.
.vite.Migration.CRA to Vite.exp
Migrating from Create React App to Vite requires installing Vite, moving index.html to the root, replacing react-scripts with Vite scripts, and updating env variables from REACT_APP_ to VITE_.
.vite.Advanced Features.Environment API.exp
Vite 6's Environment API provides a programmatic interface for configuring multiple environments (client, server, edge) within the same config, each with its own plugins and resolve options.
.vite.Advanced Features.Library Mode.exp
Library mode builds your code as a reusable library instead of an app. Vite outputs ESM, CJS, and UMD formats with externalized dependencies and TypeScript declaration generation.
.vite.Advanced Features.Web Workers.exp
Vite supports web workers with a simple ?worker import suffix, automatically bundling worker scripts into separate chunks. Inline workers are bundled into the main file.
.vite.Advanced Features.WebAssembly.exp
Vite supports importing .wasm files directly as ES modules, initializing WebAssembly modules with automatic compilation and providing exported functions for use in application code.
.vite.Advanced Features.Glob Imports.exp
Glob imports with import.meta.glob load multiple modules from the filesystem dynamically, supporting eager loading, pattern matching, and import assertions for Markdown or JSON files.
.vue.Getting Started.Template Syntax.exp
Vue uses an HTML-based template syntax that binds the DOM to component instance data using directives like v-bind, v-if, and v-for. Templates are compiled into optimized render functions.
.vue.Getting Started.Reactivity.exp
Vue's reactivity system tracks dependencies and automatically updates the DOM when data changes. It uses Proxy objects in Vue 3 to intercept property access and mutations.
.vue.Getting Started.Instance.exp
Every Vue component is backed by a component instance holding data, computed properties, methods, and lifecycle hooks. A root instance is created via createApp to mount the application.
.vue.Components.Props.exp
Props are custom attributes registered on a component that allow parent-to-child data flow. Vue validates prop types at runtime in development mode to catch bugs early.
.vue.Components.Slots.exp
Slots allow parents to inject content into a child component's layout, enabling flexible composition. Named slots and scoped slots provide even more control over content distribution.
.vue.Components.Emits.exp
Emits define custom events a component can fire to communicate upward to its parent. Using defineEmits with TypeScript gives type safety for event payloads.
.vue.Composition API.ref.exp
ref creates a reactive reference to any value, wrapping it in an object with a .value property. Accessing .value triggers dependency tracking for Vue's reactivity system.
.vue.Composition API.reactive.exp
reactive returns a deeply reactive proxy of an object, working directly with property access without .value. It's best suited for plain objects or arrays with nested data.
.vue.Composition API.computed.exp
computed creates derived state that updates automatically when its dependencies change. Computed values are lazily evaluated and cached until their reactive sources change.
.vue.Composition API.watch.exp
watch observes one or more reactive sources and calls a callback when values change, providing old and new values. Use watchEffect for running side effects automatically.
.vue.Routing.Vue Router.exp
Vue Router is the official routing library for Vue, enabling SPA navigation with nested routes, dynamic segments, and route-level code splitting. It integrates deeply with Vue's reactivity.
.vue.Routing.Navigation Guards.exp
Navigation guards protect routes from unauthorized access, handle async data fetching before navigation, or cancel navigation conditionally. They can be global, per-route, or in-component.
.vue.State.Pinia.exp

Pinia is the recommended state management library for Vue 3 with a modular architecture, full TypeScript support, and a simple API similar to Composition API. Each store is an object with state, getters, and actions.
.vue.State.State Management.exp
Vue's state management pattern involves lifting shared state into centralized stores, avoiding prop drilling across deeply nested components. Stores are singleton modules accessible from anywhere.
.vue.State.Persistence.exp
State persistence saves store data to localStorage or sessionStorage so it survives page reloads. Plugins like pinia-plugin-persistedstate automate serialization and hydration.
.vue.Forms.v-model.exp
v-model provides two-way data binding on form inputs, select elements, and textareas. Vue 3's v-model can bind to multiple values and has customizable modifiers like .lazy and .trim.
.vue.Forms.Validation.exp
Form validation in Vue can be manual with computed properties or use libraries like VeeValidate and Vuelidate. These provide declarative rules, error messages, and async validation.
.vue.Forms.Form Libraries.exp

Libraries like FormKit or VeeValidate provide form building, validation, and submission handling with minimal boilerplate. They integrate with any UI component library and handle complex nested forms.
.vue.Advanced.Transitions.exp
Vue's transition system automatically applies CSS classes when elements enter or leave the DOM. It supports JavaScript hooks, custom transition classes, and reusable transition components.
.vue.Advanced.Teleport.exp
Teleport allows rendering a component's template fragment outside its parent DOM hierarchy, useful for modals, tooltips, and toasts that need to break out of overflow containers.
.vue.Advanced.Suspense.exp
Suspense manages async dependencies in the component tree, showing fallback content while nested async components resolve. It works with async setup(), dynamic imports, and async components.
.vue.Testing.Vitest.exp
Vitest is a blazing-fast unit test framework powered by Vite, compatible with Jest API and offering native ESM support, HMR, and parallel execution out of the box.
.vue.Testing.Vue Test Utils.exp
Vue Test Utils is the official testing utility library for Vue components, providing mount, shallowMount, and utilities for stubbing, mocking, and asserting component behavior.
.vue.Testing.Cypress.exp
Cypress provides component testing and E2E testing for Vue apps with an interactive runner, automatic waiting, and network stubbing. It mounts components directly in the browser.
.vue.Composables.useMouse.exp

Composables are functions that leverage the Composition API to encapsulate reusable stateful logic. A useMouse composable tracks mouse position with reactive coordinates that any component can consume.
.vue.Composables.useLocalStorage.exp
Composables can wrap browser APIs like localStorage with reactive deserialization. The composable pattern allows sharing state across components without Pinia when the scope is small.
.vue.Composables.Composable Contracts.exp
Well-designed composables follow predictable naming (useXxx), return a plain object or single ref, accept options via a single reactive object, and provide cleanup via onUnmounted.
.vue.TypeScript.Typed Props.exp
defineProps with TypeScript generics provides full type safety for component props. The generic syntax is the recommended approach over the runtime declaration for strict typing.
.vue.TypeScript.Typed Emits.exp
defineEmits with TypeScript validates event payloads at compile time. The call signature syntax maps event names to their payload types for complete type coverage.
.vue.TypeScript.Typed Refs.exp
Type parameters for ref, reactive, and computed enable strict type checking. Template refs use InstanceType to access the component type for direct method calls.
.vue.Ecosystem.VueUse.exp
VueUse is a collection of over 200 composable utilities for common patterns like geolocation, clipboard, dark mode, media queries, and fetch with reactive state management.
.vue.Ecosystem.Vue DevTools.exp
Vue DevTools is a browser extension providing component inspection, state editing, timeline profiling, route visualization, and Pinia store debugging with time-travel capabilities.
.vue.Ecosystem.VitePress.exp
VitePress is a Vue-powered static site generator for documentation. It uses markdown content with Vue components, automatic search, and a default theme optimized for technical docs.
.webpack.Getting Started.Entry.exp
The entry point tells Webpack where to start resolving dependencies. It's the root module that Webpack uses to build the dependency graph. Multiple entry points are supported for multi-page apps.
.webpack.Getting Started.Output.exp
Output configuration tells Webpack where to emit the bundled files and how to name them. The path and filename properties are required. Content hashes enable long-term caching.
.webpack.Getting Started.Loaders.exp
Loaders allow Webpack to process files other than JavaScript by transforming them into valid modules. They are defined in the module.rules array and process right-to-left through a chain.
.webpack.Getting Started.Plugins.exp
Plugins extend Webpack's capabilities by performing optimizations, asset management, and environment injection. They are added to the plugins array and hook into the compilation lifecycle.
.webpack.Getting Started.Mode.exp

Webpack supports three modes: development, production, and none. Production mode enables optimizations like minification and tree-shaking. Development mode enables fast incremental builds and source maps.
.webpack.Getting Started.Webpack 5 Features.exp
Webpack 5 introduced built-in asset modules (replacing file-loader/url-loader), module federation, persistent caching, and better code splitting. Many older loaders are no longer needed.
.webpack.Loaders.Babel.exp
Babel transpiles modern ES6+ JavaScript into backwards-compatible versions. The @babel/preset-env preset handles syntax transformation based on target browsers.
.webpack.Loaders.CSS/SASS.exp
CSS and SASS loaders transform stylesheets into JavaScript modules. The chain of loaders processes right-to-left, typically sass-loader -> css-loader -> style-loader.
.webpack.Loaders.TypeScript.exp
TypeScript is compiled via ts-loader or babel-loader with @babel/preset-typescript. ForkTsCheckerWebpackPlugin runs type checking in a separate process for faster builds.
.webpack.Loaders.Images & Fonts.exp
Webpack 5 asset modules handle images, fonts, and other media files. The 'asset' type automatically inlines small files as base64 and emits larger ones as separate files.
.webpack.Plugins.HtmlWebpack.exp
HtmlWebpackPlugin simplifies creation of HTML files that automatically include all Webpack bundles. It supports templating, minification, and cache-busting.
.webpack.Plugins.MiniCssExtract.exp
MiniCssExtractPlugin extracts CSS into separate files instead of inlining them in JavaScript. This improves caching and parallel loading. Use it in production for better performance.
.webpack.Plugins.DefinePlugin.exp
DefinePlugin creates global constants at compile time, useful for injecting environment variables. Values are evaluated as code expressions, so strings need JSON.stringify.
.webpack.Plugins.ProgressPlugin.exp
ProgressPlugin reports build progress to the console during compilation. It's useful in CI environments and for monitoring slow builds during development.
.webpack.Optimization.Code Splitting.exp
Code splitting breaks bundles into smaller chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial load time. SplitChunksPlugin handles shared module extraction automatically.
.webpack.Optimization.Tree Shaking.exp
Tree shaking eliminates dead code by analyzing ES module import/export statements. It requires 'sideEffects': false in package.json and production mode to work correctly.
.webpack.Optimization.Minification.exp
TerserWebpackPlugin minifies JavaScript by removing whitespace, renaming variables, and eliminating dead code. It runs automatically in production mode but can be customized.
.webpack.Optimization.Persistent Caching.exp
Webpack 5 persistent caching stores compilation results to disk, dramatically speeding up subsequent builds. Set cache.type to 'filesystem' and provide a version or name.
.webpack.Optimization.Bundle Analysis.exp
Bundle analysis tools visualize the composition of output bundles, helping identify large dependencies and opportunities for code splitting.
.webpack.Configuration.Dev/Prod.exp
Separate Webpack configs for development and production allow different optimizations. A common config merged via webpack-merge avoids duplication across environments.
.webpack.Configuration.Multiple Configs.exp
Webpack supports exporting an array of configurations for building multiple bundles in a single run, useful for libraries or multi-page applications.
.webpack.Configuration.Env Variables.exp
Environment variables can be passed via CLI using --env and accessed in the config function. DefinePlugin injects them into application code at compile time.
.webpack.Dev Server.HMR.exp
Hot Module Replacement updates modules in the browser without a full page reload. It preserves application state during development for a faster feedback loop.
.webpack.Dev Server.Proxy.exp
Dev server proxy forwards API requests to a backend server during development, avoiding CORS issues. It supports path rewriting, HTTPS, and WebSocket proxying.
.webpack.Dev Server.Live Reload.exp
Live reload automatically refreshes the browser when files change. It is enabled by default in webpack-dev-server and works with watch mode for rapid development iteration.
.webpack.Module Federation.Host Config.exp
Module Federation allows multiple separate Webpack builds to share code and components at runtime. The host application consumes remotes and can share dependencies as singletons.
.webpack.Module Federation.Remote Config.exp
The remote application exposes components via ModuleFederationPlugin. It specifies which modules are exposed and what dependencies are shared with the host.
.webpack.Module Federation.Shared Dependencies.exp
Shared dependencies prevent multiple instances of the same library from loading. The singleton option ensures only one instance exists, and eager loads critical dependencies.
.webpack.Advanced.Custom Loaders.exp
Custom loaders transform source files by implementing a function that receives the source and returns the modified output. Loaders run in a pipeline from right to left.
.webpack.Advanced.Custom Plugins.exp
Custom plugins hook into Webpack's compilation lifecycle using the apply method and tap into compiler hooks for custom behavior.
.webpack.Advanced.Web Workers.exp
Webpack supports Web Workers out of the box. Worker files can be bundled separately and instantiated with the standard Worker constructor.
.webpack.Advanced.PWA Support.exp
Webpack can generate service workers and manifest files for Progressive Web Apps using WorkboxPlugin. It precaches static assets and enables offline functionality.
.webpack.Performance.Caching.exp
Webpack uses content hashes in filenames to enable long-term caching. The [contenthash] placeholder generates unique hashes based on file contents, so only changed files get new URLs.
.webpack.Performance.Long-term Caching.exp
Long-term caching strategies separate vendor code from application code so vendors change less frequently. Module IDs should be deterministic for stable chunk hashes.
.zig.Getting Started.Install Zig.exp
Zig can be installed via zigup, zigenv, package managers, or pre-built binaries from ziglang.org/download. The Zig compiler produces native binaries for cross-compilation out of the box.
.zig.Getting Started.zig init-exe.exp
The `zig init-exe` command scaffolds a new executable project with a src/main.zig and build.zig. Use `zig init-lib` for library projects.
.zig.Getting Started.Hello World.exp
Zig's hello world uses `std.debug.print` for output. The `@import` built-in brings in the standard library. `!void` indicates the function may return an error.
.zig.Getting Started.build.zig Explained.exp
The build.zig file is Zig code that defines how to build your project. It uses the standard Build API to configure executable, library, test, and run steps with cross-compilation targets.
.zig.Getting Started.Zig Version Manager.exp
Zig is pre-1.0 and evolves rapidly. Use `zigup` or `zigenv` to manage multiple Zig versions. Each Zig version may have subtle language or standard library changes.
.zig.Types.Integer Types.exp
Zig provides signed (i) and unsigned (u) integers from 2 to 65535 bits: u8, i32, u64, i128, u256, etc. Arbitrary bit-widths like u7 or i13 are supported with optimal machine code generation.
.zig.Types.Floats.exp
Floating point types: f16 (half), f32 (float), f64 (double), f80 (x86 extended), f128 (quad). Literals use decimal or scientific notation with optional type suffix.
.zig.Types.Bool & Void.exp
`bool` has `true` and `false` values. `void` is the empty type used for functions returning nothing or as a tag for inferred error sets. `anyopaque` replaces C's void pointer.
.zig.Types.anytype.exp
`anytype` as a function parameter accepts any type at compile time, enabling duck-typed generics. Each call site monomorphizes the function for the concrete type.
.zig.Types.Type Coercion.exp
Zig performs safe implicit coercions: widening integers (u8 -> u16), optional to error union, pointer to const pointer, single-item to slice. Narrowing requires @intCast or @floatCast.
.zig.Types.enum & union.exp
Enums define named constants with explicit or inferred integer tag values. Tagged unions combine a tag with variant payloads in a type-safe way without hidden fields.
.zig.Variables & Constants.const vs var.exp
`const` declares an immutable binding; the value cannot be reassigned but may still be mutable via pointers. `var` declares a mutable binding. Both require explicit or inferred types.
.zig.Variables & Constants.Comptime Constants.exp
`comptime` variables are evaluated at compile time. `comptime var` creates a compile-time mutable variable. Comptime blocks can execute arbitrary Zig during compilation.
.zig.Variables & Constants.Shadowing.exp
Zig allows variable shadowing in nested scopes. An inner declaration with the same name temporarily hides the outer one. Shadowing is lexical and confined to the block.
.zig.Variables & Constants.Undefined & Default Values.exp
`undefined` leaves a variable uninitialized (use with caution). Types like integers, floats, bools have no default. Struct fields can have default values. `@memset` zeroes memory.
.zig.Variables & Constants.Anonymous Bindings.exp
Use `_` as a variable name to discard values. This suppresses unused-variable warnings and is required when you intentionally ignore a return value or loop index.
.zig.Control Flow.if Expressions.exp
`if` is an expression that returns a value. All branches must return the same type. Supports optional and error union capture syntax for concise unwrapping.
.zig.Control Flow.while with continue expressions.exp
`while` loops can have a continue expression executed at the end of each iteration (before the condition check). Supports break/continue and optional capture.
.zig.Control Flow.for with Ranges.exp
`for` iterates over arrays, slices, and ranges. Range syntax `0..n` creates an exclusive range. Supports multiple objects in parallel, element pointers, and index capture.
.zig.Control Flow.Labeled break & continue.exp
Loops can be labeled with `:label` syntax. `break :label` exits the named outer loop. `continue :label` skips to the next iteration of the named loop. Useful for nested loops.
.zig.Control Flow.switch Expressions.exp
switch is an expression that must be exhaustive. Supports ranges (...), multiple cases, enums, integers, and value capture with `=>` syntax for concise branches.
.zig.Control Flow.Inline Loops.exp
`inline for` and `inline while` unroll loops at compile time. Required when iterating over comptime-known tuples or when the loop body must be comptime-evaluable.
.zig.Functions.Function Basics.exp
Functions are defined with `fn`. Parameters are immutable constants. Return type follows the parameter list. Functions can be public (`pub`) or private. `!T` indicates an error-returning function.
.zig.Functions.Function Pointers.exp
Functions have types like `*const fn(params) return_type`. Function pointers enable callbacks, dynamic dispatch, and polymorphism. Use `&function` to create a pointer.
.zig.Functions.Inline Functions.exp
`inline fn` forces the function body to be inlined at every call site. Useful for comptime-only operations or when function call overhead must be eliminated.
.zig.Functions.Calling Conventions.exp

`callconv(.C)` uses the C ABI for FFI. `callconv(.Inline)` forces inlining. `callconv(.Async)` enables async frames. `.Unspecified` lets the compiler decide. Default is `.Inline` except for pub functions.
.zig.Functions.Error Return Traces.exp
Zig tracks error return traces that show the call chain when an error is returned (not thrown). This is a debugging aid with zero overhead when no error occurs. Disable with `-fno-return-traces`.
.zig.Functions.Nested Functions.exp
Functions can be nested inside other functions. Nested functions capture their enclosing scope's constants and types. They are not closures (no runtime captures).
.zig.Arrays, Slices & Strings.Multi-dimensional Arrays.exp
Zig supports multi-dimensional arrays with `[rows][cols]T` syntax. They are stored in row-major order. Access with `arr[row][col]`. Can be iterated with nested for loops.
.zig.Arrays, Slices & Strings.Sentinel Arrays.exp
Sentinel-terminated arrays `[N:s]T` and slices `[:s]T` guarantee a terminating value at the end. `[:0]u8` is common for C strings. The sentinel counts as part of the array but not the length.
.zig.Arrays, Slices & Strings.String Literals.exp
String literals are `*const [N:0]u8` (pointer to sentinel array). They coerce to `[]const u8`. Multiline strings use `\\` continuation. Raw strings use `c"..."` syntax for C strings.
.zig.Arrays, Slices & Strings.Format Strings.exp
`std.fmt.format` and `std.debug.print` use format strings. Specifiers: `{d}` (decimal), `{s}` (string), `{x}` (hex), `{b}` (binary), `{e}` (scientific), `{any}` (debug). Pad with `{d:5}` or `{x:08}`.
.zig.Arrays, Slices & Strings.Slice Operations.exp
Slices support runtime range syntax `[start..end]`, `[start..]` (to end), `[0..len]`. `@as` can coerce arrays to slices. Slices have `.len` and `.ptr` fields. Bounds-checked at runtime.
.zig.Arrays, Slices & Strings.Array Concatenation & Multiplication.exp
The `++` operator concatenates arrays at compile time. The `**` operator repeats an array. Both produce new comptime-known arrays. For runtime, use `std.mem.concat`.
.zig.Pointers & Memory.Many-item Pointers.exp
`[*]T` is a pointer to an unknown number of T elements (many-item pointer). No length information. Often used for C interop. Index with `ptr[i]`. Must know bounds externally.
.zig.Pointers & Memory.Pointer Alignment.exp
Pointers carry alignment information in their type. `*align(N) T` specifies alignment. `@alignCast` changes alignment (unsafe). Misaligned access can crash on some architectures.
.zig.Pointers & Memory.Slice Pointers.exp
`[]const T` is a slice (fat pointer: ptr + len). Slices are the preferred way to work with contiguous memory. Syntax `arr[start..end]` creates a slice. `@as` coerces arrays to slices.
.zig.Pointers & Memory.Allocator Types.exp

Zig provides several allocators: `page_allocator` (syscall per alloc), `arena_allocator` (arena free), `GeneralPurposeAllocator` (heap), `FixedBufferAllocator` (pre-allocated buffer), `StackFallbackAllocator`.
.zig.Pointers & Memory.Memory Leak Detection.exp
GeneralPurposeAllocator can detect memory leaks on deinit. Enable leak detection with `.{ .enable_memory_limit = true }` or check `deinit()` return value which indicates leaks.
.zig.Pointers & Memory.Comptime Pointer Handling.exp
Pointers to comptime-known values can be created and manipulated at compile time. `@ptrFromInt` converts an integer to a pointer. `@intFromPtr` gets the address. Use with caution.
.zig.Error Handling.Error Sets.exp
Error sets are declared with `error{...}` syntax. They define a set of named error values. Errors are values, not exceptions — they have no stack trace overhead until returned.
.zig.Error Handling.Error Union Inference.exp
`!T` is shorthand for an inferred error set. The compiler determines which errors a function can return by analyzing all `try`/`return error.` expressions within it. No explicit set needed.
.zig.Error Handling.Merge Error Sets.exp
The `||` operator merges two error sets. Useful when combining multiple error-returning functions. `anyerror` is the global error set that all errors coerce to.
.zig.Error Handling.catch / unreachable.exp
`catch` handles errors from error unions. `catch |err| { ... }` captures the error. `catch unreachable` asserts the operation will not fail (panics on error). `catch 0` provides a default value.
.zig.Error Handling.try Keyword.exp
`try` unwraps an error union. On success, it yields the payload value. On error, it returns the error from the enclosing function. Syntactic sugar for `catch |e| return e`.
.zig.Error Handling.Global Error Set.exp
`anyerror` is the global error set containing every possible error. It's the supertype of all error sets. Use for error-agnostic code or when the exact error set is unknown at compile time.
.zig.Optionals.orelse & Unwrap.exp
`orelse` provides a default value when an optional is null. `x orelse default` unwraps if present, otherwise returns `default`. Can also use `orelse return`, `orelse unreachable`.
.zig.Optionals.if Capture.exp
`if (optional) |value| { ... } else { ... }` captures the unwrapped value in the true branch. The captured value is a const binding. Use `if (x) |*ptr|` for mutable capture.
.zig.Optionals.Payload Capturing.exp
Optionals can be used with `while` loops to iterate until null. `while (iter.next()) |val| { ... }` captures the payload. Also works with error unions: `while (try iter.next()) |val|`.
.zig.Optionals.Optional Pointers.exp
Optional pointers `?*T` are size-optimized: null is represented as address 0, so no extra tag byte. This makes `?*T` the same size as `*T`. Useful for linked lists and trees.
.zig.Comptime.Compile-time Parameters.exp

Function parameters prefixed with `comptime` are evaluated at compile time. Common uses: generic type parameters (`comptime T: type`), comptime integers for array sizes, and comptime booleans for conditional compilation.
.zig.Comptime.Compile-time Variables.exp
`comptime var` declares a mutable variable evaluated at compile time. `comptime` blocks execute arbitrary Zig at build time. Useful for generating lookup tables, assertions, and precomputed values.
.zig.Comptime.@compileLog.exp
`@compileLog(...)` prints values at compile time, useful for debugging comptime code. It outputs to stderr during compilation. Does not generate runtime code.
.zig.Comptime.@field.exp
`@field(lhs, field_name)` accesses a field or method by comptime string name. Enables dynamic field access at compile time. Pairs with `@hasField` for safe access.
.zig.Comptime.@hasDecl & @hasField.exp
`@hasDecl(comptime T, name)` checks if a declaration (type, fn, const) exists. `@hasField(comptime T, name)` checks if a struct/union has a field. Both return comptime `bool`.
.zig.Comptime.Compile-time Reflection.exp
`@typeInfo` returns a tagged union describing any type's structure (fields, decls, layout). `@Type` creates a type from `@typeInfo` data. `@typeName` returns the string name of a type.
.zig.Structs & Unions.packed Structs.exp
`packed struct` lays out fields at the bit level with no padding. Fields use bit-level packing. Use `u1`, `u4`, `u7` etc. for precise bit widths. Field order is guaranteed.
.zig.Structs & Unions.extern Structs.exp
`extern struct` follows the C ABI layout for FFI compatibility. Has platform-specific padding and alignment. Use for interfacing with C libraries and binary protocols.
.zig.Structs & Unions.Zero-bit Types.exp

Types with zero size include `void`, `comptime_int`, `comptime_float`, and empty structs `struct{}`. They occupy no memory but participate in type checking. Arrays of zero-bit types also have zero size.
.zig.Structs & Unions.Field Alignment.exp
Struct fields can specify alignment with `align(N)`. Also use `packed` for bit-level or `extern` for C-style alignment. Use `@alignOf(T)` to query a type's alignment requirement.
.zig.Structs & Unions.Default Field Values.exp
Struct fields can have default values. When constructing with `Struct{ ... }`, omitted fields use their defaults. `undefined` can also be used as a field value to leave it uninitialized.
.zig.Structs & Unions.Anonymous Structs & Unions.exp

Anonymous structs and union literals can be created inline. Struct literals use `.{ .field = val }`. Tuple-like structs use `.{ val1, val2 }`. Anonymous unions use `@as(union(Tag), .{ .variant = val })`.
.zig.Standard Library.ArrayList.exp
`std.ArrayList(T)` is a dynamically-growing array of contiguous elements. Supports append, insert, remove, pop, and iteration. Uses an allocator for memory management.
.zig.Standard Library.AutoHashMap.exp
`std.AutoHashMap(K, V)` is a hash map with automatic key hashing. Uses `std.hash_map` internally. Supports put, get, remove, contains, and key-value iteration with an allocator.
.zig.Standard Library.BufMap.exp
`std.BufMap` is a string-to-string hash map. Keys and values are `[]const u8`. Convenient for configuration parsing, environment variables, and text-based key-value stores.
.zig.Standard Library.BufferedWriter.exp

`std.io.BufferedWriter` wraps a writer with an internal buffer, reducing system calls. Use `.writer()` to access the buffered writer. Flush with `.flush()` when done. Essential for file and network I/O performance.
.zig.Standard Library.File I/O.exp
`std.fs` provides filesystem operations: open, create, delete, rename, read, write. Use `cwd()` (current directory), `openFile`, `createFile`, `readToEndAlloc`, `writeAll`. Errors are explicit.
.zig.Standard Library.Formatting.exp
`std.fmt.format` is the core formatting function. `std.fmt.allocPrint` allocates a formatted string. `std.fmt.bufPrint` formats into a buffer. Custom formatters for user types via `format` method.
.zig.Advanced.Async / Await Deep Dive.exp
Zig's async functions use cooperative multitasking with no hidden runtime. `suspend` yields control. `resume` continues a suspended frame. Async frames are explicit values. Works with any event loop.
.zig.Advanced.@cImport in Depth.exp
`@cImport` parses C headers at compile time. `@cInclude`, `@cDefine`, `@cUndef`, `@cIncludeOptions` control the C preprocessor. Translate C types to Zig: `*c_void`, `c_int`, `c_char`, etc.
.zig.Advanced.Inline Assembly.exp

`asm` blocks embed architecture-specific assembly. Use `volatile` to prevent optimization. Output and input constraints use a declarative syntax. Useful for performance-critical or hardware-specific code.
.zig.Advanced.Vectorization.exp

Zig has built-in vector types: `@Vector(len, T)` for SIMD. Vectors support element-wise arithmetic and built-in reduction operations. The compiler auto-vectorizes where possible. Use `@shuffle`, `@reduce`.
.zig.Advanced.@export & Section Attributes.exp
`@export` makes a declaration available to the linker with a specific name, linkage, and section. Use for shared library exports, interrupt handlers, or placing code/data in custom linker sections.
.zig.Advanced.Build System Advanced.exp

The build system supports conditional compilation with `comptime` options, custom build steps, dependency management via `build.zig.zon`, cross-compilation to any target, and custom run/test configurations.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).Testing with zig test.exp

Zig has a built-in test framework. Write tests with `test` blocks. Run with `zig test src/main.zig`. The testing allocator catches memory leaks. `std.testing` provides expect, expectEqual, expectError, and allocator for leak detection.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).build.zig.zon Package Manager.exp
Zig's package manager uses `build.zig.zon` to declare dependencies with URL and hash verification. Use `zig fetch --save` to add packages. Dependencies expose modules importable in build.zig.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).Cross-Compilation.exp

Zig cross-compiles out of the box — no SDK needed. Specify `-target` with triple: `arch-os-abi`. Supports x86_64-linux, aarch64-macos, wasm32-freestanding, and hundreds more. Build.zig uses `b.standardTargetOptions(.{})` for configurable targets.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).WebAssembly with Zig.exp
Zig is a first-class Wasm language. Target wasm32-freestanding for WASI or wasm32-emscripten for browser. Zig outputs small .wasm files with no runtime overhead. Export functions with `export fn`.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).C Interop Deep Dive.exp

Zig has first-class C interop. `@cImport` parses C headers. Types: `c_int`, `c_uint`, `c_long`, `c_char`, `*anyopaque` for `void*`. Call Zig from C with `export fn` and `callconv(.C)`. Translate C headers automatically with `zig translate-c`.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).Zig fmt & Code Style.exp
`zig fmt` auto-formats code to canonical style: 4-space indent, opening brace on same line. Style guide: camelCase for functions/vars, PascalCase for types. Use `zig fmt --check` in CI.
.zig.Zig in Practice (ziglang.org/learn).Debugging Zig Programs.exp

Use `std.debug.print` for logging, `@breakpoint()` for debugger breakpoints, `std.debug.assert` for invariants. Build with `-Doptimize=Debug` (default) for full debug info. Error Return Trace shows the call chain on errors. Use LLDB or GDB for step debugging.
.asm.Number Systems and Data Representation.Binary Numbers[0]

Computers use binary (base-2) with digits 0 and 1. Each position represents a power of 2. A byte is 8 bits (0-255). A nibble is 4 bits. Binary addition: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1. The LSB is bit 0, MSB is bit 7. Binary is the foundation of all machine-level operations.
.asm.Number Systems and Data Representation.Hexadecimal System[0]

Hexadecimal (base-16) uses digits 0-9 and A-F. Each hex digit represents 4 bits (a nibble). Hex is the standard notation for assembly: addresses, opcodes, and data. Two hex digits = one byte. Prefix: 0x (C/ASM) or h (MASM). Converting hex to binary is trivial: F=1111, A=1010, etc.
.asm.Number Systems and Data Representation.Two's Complement[0]

Signed integers use two's complement. The MSB is the sign bit (0=positive, 1=negative). To negate: invert all bits and add 1. Range for N bits: -2^(N-1) to 2^(N-1)-1. For 8 bits: -128 to +127. The CPU doesn't distinguish signed vs unsigned — the same ADD instruction works for both; the programmer interprets the result.
.asm.Number Systems and Data Representation.Boolean Logic[0]

Boolean algebra operates on true (1) and false (0). AND: both must be 1. OR: at least one is 1. XOR: exactly one is 1. NOT: invert. NAND, NOR are complements. De Morgan's laws: NOT(A AND B) = NOT(A) OR NOT(B). Truth tables define all combinations. Assembly provides AND, OR, XOR, NOT, TEST instructions.
.asm.Number Systems and Data Representation.Bit Shifting[0]

SHL/SHR shift bits left/right by a count. Each left shift multiplies by 2; each right shift divides by 2 (unsigned). SAR preserves the sign bit. ROL/ROR rotate bits through a circle. RCL/RCR rotate through the carry flag. Shift counts can be an immediate or CL register.
.asm.Number Systems and Data Representation.ASCII and BCD Numbers[0]

ASCII digits: '0'=0x30 through '9'=0x39. To convert ASCII to binary: subtract 0x30. To convert binary to ASCII: add 0x30. Unpacked BCD stores one decimal digit per byte (0x00-0x09). Packed BCD stores two digits per byte (high/low nibble). DAA adjusts after ADD for packed BCD. DAS adjusts after SUB. AAA/AAS/AAM/AAD are legacy ASCII adjust instructions.
.asm.Getting Started with Assembly.Environment Setup[0]

NASM is the assembler of choice for x86-64 Linux. Install: `sudo apt install nasm` (Debian/Ubuntu), `sudo yum install nasm` (RHEL/Fedora), `brew install nasm` (macOS), or download from nasm.us (Windows). Assemble: `nasm -f elf64 prog.asm -o prog.o`. Link: `ld -o prog prog.o`. Run: `./prog`. For libc programs: `gcc -no-pie -o prog prog.o`. Debug: `nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf prog.asm`. Use make or shell scripts for multi-file projects.
.asm.Getting Started with Assembly.Basic NASM Syntax[0]

NASM syntax: `[label:] instruction [operands] [; comment]`. Labels mark positions and are symbolic addresses. Local labels start with a dot (`.loop`) and are scoped to the preceding global label. Sections: `.data` (initialized data), `.bss` (uninitialized), `.text` (code). Directives: `global` exports symbols, `extern` imports, `equ` defines constants, `times` repeats. The entry point is `_start` for standalone or `main` for programs linking with libc.
.asm.Getting Started with Assembly.Memory Segments[0]

An ELF binary has segments loaded by the OS. `.text` — executable code, read-only, mapped with RX permissions. `.data` — initialized global/static variables, mapped RW. `.bss` — uninitialized data, zero-filled at load time, mapped RW (occupies no disk space). The stack — temporary data (local vars, return addresses), grows downward from high addresses. The heap — dynamically allocated memory via brk/sbrk or mmap, grows upward from low addresses.
.asm.Getting Started with Assembly.Variables[0]

Variables are named memory locations declared with DB (byte), DW (word), DD (dword), DQ (qword), or DT (10 bytes). Initialize with a value or comma-separated list for arrays. Use TIMES for repeating patterns. Access with `mov reg, [var_name]` for load, `mov [var_name], reg` for store. NASM doesn't have typed variables — the assembler just associates a name with an address; you must use the correct instruction size.
.asm.Getting Started with Assembly.Constants[0]

NASM constants are evaluated at assembly time, not runtime. `EQU` assigns a name to a value (cannot be redefined). `%assign` defines a numeric constant that can be redefined. `%define` is a textual macro replacement (like C's #define). Constants improve readability and maintainability — use them for syscall numbers, buffer sizes, flags, and masks. They consume no memory and have no runtime overhead.
.asm.x64 Architecture and Registers.CPU Architecture Overview[0]

The x86-64 CPU has: ALU (arithmetic logic unit), control unit, registers (fast on-chip storage), cache (L1/L2/L3), MMU (memory management unit), FPU (floating-point), and SIMD units. Execution pipeline: fetch decode execute memory access write-back. Long mode (64-bit) allows 64-bit addressing, 16 general-purpose registers, and SSE/AVX.
.asm.x64 Architecture and Registers.General Purpose Registers[0]

x86-64 has 16 GPRs: RAX (accumulator), RBX (base), RCX (counter), RDX (data), RSI (source index), RDI (dest index), RBP (base pointer), RSP (stack pointer), R8-R15 (extended). Sub-registers: RAX EAX (32) AX (16) AH/AL (8). In 64-bit mode, writing to a 32-bit subregister zero-extends to 64 bits.
.asm.x64 Architecture and Registers.Special Purpose Registers[0]

RIP (instruction pointer) points to the next instruction. RFLAGS stores condition flags: CF (carry), PF (parity), AF (adjust), ZF (zero), SF (sign), OF (overflow), IF (interrupt), DF (direction). Control registers CR0-CR4 manage system state. Segment registers (CS, DS, ES, FS, GS, SS) are largely vestigial in 64-bit mode.
.asm.x64 Architecture and Registers.Stack and Calling Conventions[0]

The stack grows downward (RSP decreases on push). PUSH decrements RSP then stores; POP loads then increments RSP. The System V AMD64 ABI: first 6 args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9; return value in RAX. RSP must be 16-byte aligned before CALL. CALL pushes return address; RET pops it. The red zone (128 bytes below RSP) is scratch space.
.asm.x64 Architecture and Registers.Memory Addressing Modes[0]

x86-64 addressing: [base + index*scale + displacement]. Scale can be 1, 2, 4, 8. Modes: register (mov rax, rbx), immediate (mov rax, 42), direct (mov rax, [addr]), register indirect (mov rax, [rbx]), base+displacement (mov rax, [rbx+8]), indexed (mov rax, [array+rbx*8]), RIP-relative (mov rax, [rel msg]). 64-bit uses RIP-relative by default for data access.
.asm.NASM Assembly Basics.Hello World[0]

NASM syntax: label: instruction operands ; comment. Sections: .data (initialized data), .bss (uninitialized data), .text (code). The `_start` label is the ELF entry point. Use `nasm -f elf64 file.asm && ld -o file file.o`. System calls use `syscall` with the syscall number in RAX and arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8, R9.
.asm.NASM Assembly Basics.Data Types and Directives[0]

NASM data directives: DB (byte), DW (word = 2 bytes), DD (dword = 4), DQ (qword = 8), DT (10 bytes), DO (16), DY (32), DZ (64). TIMES repeats data. EQU defines constants. $ is the current address. RESB/RESW/RESD/RESQ reserve space in .bss.
.asm.NASM Assembly Basics.Moving Data[0]

MOV copies data between registers, memory, and immediates. MOV cannot do memory-to-memory directly. MOVZX (zero-extend) and MOVSX (sign-extend) for smaller to larger sizes. XCHG swaps values. LEA loads effective address without accessing memory. CMOVcc (conditional move) avoids branches.
.asm.NASM Assembly Basics.Arithmetic Instructions[0]

ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV for arithmetic. ADD/SUB work on any operand size. MUL unsigned: RAX = RAX * rm. IMUL for signed. DIV unsigned: RAX / rm  quotient=RAX, remainder=RDX. IDIV for signed. ADC/SBB include carry. INC/DEC increment/decrement. NEG negates.
.asm.NASM Assembly Basics.Control Flow and Branching[0]

Unconditional: JMP. Conditional: JE, JNE, JG, JL, JGE, JLE, JA, JB, JAE, JBE, JO, JS, JC, JP. Based on RFLAGS set by CMP or arithmetic. CMP subtracts operands, sets flags, discards result. TEST performs AND, sets flags, discards result. Jcc checks specific flags.
.asm.NASM Assembly Basics.Loops[0]

The LOOP instruction decrements RCX and jumps to a label if RCX != 0. LOOPE/LOOPZ (loop while equal) also checks ZF=1. LOOPNE/LOOPNZ (loop while not equal) also checks ZF=0. For more control, implement loops manually with a counter register, CMP, and conditional jump. Nested loops require saving/restoring the outer loop counter.
.asm.Procedures and the Stack.CALL and RET[0]

CALL pushes the return address (RIP) onto the stack then jumps to the target. RET pops the return address and jumps back. Near calls (within same segment) are standard in 64-bit. CALL can be direct (call label) or indirect (call rax, call [table+rcx*8]). RET can take an immediate to pop extra bytes.
.asm.Procedures and the Stack.Passing Arguments[0]

System V AMD64 ABI: integer args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 (left to right). Additional args on the stack. Return value in RAX. Callee-saved: RBX, RBP, R12-R15. Caller-saved: RAX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, R8-R11. Stack must be 16-byte aligned before CALL.
.asm.Procedures and the Stack.Stack Frames[0]

A stack frame is created with `push rbp; mov rbp, rsp`. Local variables are allocated by subtracting from RSP: `sub rsp, 32`. RBP provides a stable reference: parameters at positive offsets [rbp+16+], locals at negative offsets [rbp-8]. Leave instruction: `mov rsp, rbp; pop rbp`.
.asm.Procedures and the Stack.Recursion[0]

A recursive procedure calls itself. Each call creates a new stack frame with its own parameters, local variables, and return address. Must have a base case to terminate and a recursive case that progresses toward the base. Deep recursion can overflow the stack (default ulimit ~8MB). Use the stack to save state across calls. Factorial and Fibonacci are classic examples.
.asm.Procedures and the Stack.Macros[0]

NASM macros: %define (single-line) and %macro (multi-line). %define can have parameters: `%define mulby2(x) x*2`. Multi-line: `%macro name paramcount` ... `%endmacro`. %rotate cycles through parameters. %assign for numeric macros. Conditional assembly: %if, %elif, %else, %endif.
.asm.Procedures and the Stack.Multi-File Programs[0]

Large programs split into multiple .asm files and link together. Use `extern` to declare symbols from other files, `global` to make symbols visible. Assemble each file separately, link together. `nasm -f elf64 util.asm -o util.o && nasm -f elf64 main.asm -o main.o && ld -o prog main.o util.o`. Avoid name collisions with LOCAL labels (.label).
.asm.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Flag Register[0]

RFLAGS is 64-bit but only lower 32 bits are used. Key flags: CF (carry), PF (parity), AF (adjust), ZF (zero), SF (sign), OF (overflow), DF (direction), IF (interrupt). LAHF/SAHF transfer flags to/from AH.
.asm.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Comparison and TEST[0]
CMP = SUB that only sets flags. Used before conditional jumps for signed (JG, JL, JGE, JLE, JE, JNE) and unsigned (JA, JB, JAE, JBE). TEST = AND that only sets flags. Used for bit testing.
.asm.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Conditional Moves[0]
CMOVcc combines comparison and move: CMOVZ, CMOVNZ, CMOVG, CMOVL, CMOVGE, CMOVLE, CMOVA, CMOVB. Avoids branch mispredictions. SETcc sets a byte to 0/1 based on condition.
.asm.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Logical Instructions[0]
AND, OR, XOR, NOT, NEG, TEST. AND for bit masking. OR sets bits. XOR toggles. XOR same register is idiomatic zero. AND with 1 checks parity. NOT flips all bits.
.asm.Condition Codes and Logical Operations.Bit Manipulation[0]

BT (bit test), BTC (bit test and complement), BTR (bit test and reset), BTS (bit test and set). BSF/BSR (bit scan forward/reverse). POPCNT counts set bits. LZCNT/TZCNT (leading/trailing zero count). SHLD/SHRD (double precision shifts).
.asm.Strings and Data Structures.String Instructions[0]

String instructions use RSI (source) and RDI (dest). MOVSB/MOVSW/MOVSD/MOVSQ (move). LODSB/LODSW/LODSD/LODSQ (load from [RSI]). STOSB/STOSW/STOSD/STOSQ (store to [RDI]). CMPSB/CMPSW/CMPSD/CMPSQ (compare). SCASB/SCASW/SCASD/SCASQ (scan). REP repeats RCX times. REPE/REPNE repeats while equal/not equal.
.asm.Strings and Data Structures.Arrays and Addressing[0]

Arrays are contiguous memory. Element access: base + index * element_size. Word: `mov ax, [array + rbx*2]`. Dword: `mov eax, [array + rcx*4]`. Qword: `mov rax, [array + rdx*8]`. LEA calculates addresses. Multidimensional arrays use row-major ordering.
.asm.Strings and Data Structures.Structures and Records[0]

Structures group related data. NASM uses STRUC/ENDSTRUC with RESB/RESW/RESD/RESQ for fields. Initialize with ISTRUC/IEND. Field access with `[struc_variable + field_name]`. Alignment: naturally align fields. PADDING between fields maintains alignment.
.asm.Strings and Data Structures.Buffers and I/O[0]

Buffers are memory blocks for data transfer. .bss reserves uninitialized space with RESB. For file I/O, use sys_open (rax=2), sys_read (0), sys_write (1), sys_close (3). sys_open returns fd in RAX (-1 on error). Buffered I/O: read chunks into buffer, process, write output.
.asm.Strings and Data Structures.String Comparison and Search[0]

String compare: CMPSB/CMPSW/CMPSD with REPE/REPNE prefix. REPE CMPSB compares until mismatch or RCX=0. String search: SCASB scans for a byte. REPNE SCASB finds a byte. For null-terminated strings use `repne scasb` to find length.
.asm.Floating Point and SIMD.x87 Floating Point[0]

The legacy x87 FPU uses a stack of 8 registers (ST0-ST7). Instructions: FLD (load), FST/FSTP (store/pop), FADD, FSUB, FMUL, FDIV, FCHS, FSQRT, FCOM (compare), FTST (compare with 0). x87 is mostly superseded by SSE but still used in legacy code.
.asm.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Scalar Operations[0]

SSE provides XMM0-XMM15 (128-bit) registers. Scalar: ADDSD (add scalar double), SUBSD, MULSD, DIVSD, SQRTSD. MOVSD moves scalar double. CVTSI2SD converts integer to double, CVTSD2SI converts double to integer. UCOMISD compares scalars.
.asm.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Packed Operations[0]

SSE processes multiple elements at once: packed add/sub/mul/div on 2 doubles or 4 floats. ADDPS (packed single), ADDPD (packed double). SUBPS, MULPS, DIVPS. Also: MAXPS, MINPS, SQRTPS. HADDPS (horizontal add) sums adjacent pairs. MOVAPS/MOVUPS for aligned/unaligned moves.
.asm.Floating Point and SIMD.AVX and Advanced SIMD[0]

AVX extends XMM to 256-bit YMM registers (YMM0-YMM15). Three-operand syntax: `vaddps ymm0, ymm1, ymm2`. Non-destructive sources. AVX2 adds gather, FMA. AVX-512 extends to 512-bit ZMM. VZEROUPPER clears upper bits when mixing SSE and AVX.
.asm.Floating Point and SIMD.SSE Integer and Conversion[0]

SSE2 adds 128-bit integer ops in XMM: PADDB/W/D/Q, PSUBB/W/D/Q, PMULLW/D. PCMPEQB/W/D (compare equal). PCMPGTB/W/D. PAND, POR, PXOR, PANDN. PACKSSWB/PACKUSDW (pack with saturation). PMOVMSKB creates integer mask from byte MSBs.
.asm.Interfacing with C and Linux.Linux System Calls[0]

Linux syscalls: RAX = syscall number, RDI/RSI/RDX/R10/R8/R9 = args, syscall invokes the kernel. Return in RAX. Common: 0=read, 1=write, 2=open, 3=close, 9=mmap, 12=brk, 60=exit. Syscall numbers differ between x86 and x64. See /usr/include/asm/unistd_64.h.
.asm.Interfacing with C and Linux.Calling C Library Functions[0]

Link with gcc instead of ld to use libc: `nasm -f elf64 prog.asm && gcc -no-pie -o prog prog.o`. Libc provides printf, malloc, fopen, etc. The C runtime expects `main` instead of `_start`. RSP must be 16-byte aligned before CALL.
.asm.Interfacing with C and Linux.Command Line Arguments[0]

When linked with libc and using `main`, argc is in RDI, argv is in RSI. argc = argument count (program name counts as 1). argv = array of char* pointers, null-terminated. Environment variables (envp) are in RDX.
.asm.Interfacing with C and Linux.File I/O with syscalls[0]

File operations: open (returns fd), read/write, close, lseek. sys_open: path in RDI, flags in RSI, mode in RDX. Flags: O_RDONLY=0, O_WRONLY=1, O_RDWR=2, O_CREAT=0x40, O_TRUNC=0x200, O_APPEND=0x400. Always check return values: negative = error.
.asm.Interfacing with C and Linux.Memory Management[0]

sys_brk (12) allocates heap memory. Call with RDI=0 to get current break, then RDI=new_break to allocate. More flexible: sys_mmap (9) maps anonymous memory. mmap args: addr=0, length, prot=3 (PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE), flags=0x22 (MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS), fd=-1, offset=0. munmap (11) frees.
.asm.Interfacing with C and Linux.Debugging with GDB[0]

Assemble with debug symbols: `nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf prog.asm`. GDB commands: break, run, stepi, nexti, info registers, x/Nx addr (examine memory), disas (disassemble), backtrace. Use layout reg for register view, layout asm for disassembly.
.asm.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Performance Optimization[0]

x64 optimization: minimize memory access (load once, reuse), align code/data to cache lines (64 bytes), avoid branch mispredictions (use CMOV, bit manipulation), use SIMD for parallel processing, unroll loops carefully, prefer register args over stack, avoid partial register stalls (use movzx not mov+and), use LEA for arithmetic when possible.
.asm.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Inline Assembly (GCC)[0]

GCC inline assembly: `asm("instructions" : outputs : inputs : clobbers)`. Extended asm: `asm volatile("add %1, %0" : "+r"(a) : "r"(b))`. AT&T syntax (src,dst) vs Intel (dst,src). Use `-masm=intel` for Intel syntax. Constraints: r=register, m=memory, i=immediate.
.asm.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Interrupts and Exception Handling[0]

x86-64 has an IDT (Interrupt Descriptor Table). Linux exceptions: #DE (divide error, vector 0), #DB (debug, 1), #BP (breakpoint, 3), #GP (general protection, 13), #PF (page fault, 14). The `int` instruction triggers software interrupts (syscall is preferred on x64).
.asm.Advanced Topics and Optimization.PIC and Position-Independent Code[0]

Position-independent code (PIC) is required for shared libraries. Use `lea rax, [rel symbol]` instead of `mov rax, symbol`. NASM's `default rel` sets RIP-relative addressing as default. For shared libraries: `nasm -f elf64 -dPIC lib.asm && gcc -shared -o lib.so lib.o`. GOT and PLT enable dynamic linking.
.asm.Advanced Topics and Optimization.Multithreading and Atomic Ops[0]

Atomic operations prevent race conditions. LOCK prefix: `lock inc dword [counter]`, `lock xadd`, `lock cmpxchg`, `lock bts`. CMPXCHG (compare and exchange) is the core of lock-free programming. MFENCE/LFENCE/SFENCE for memory ordering. POSIX threads (pthreads) can be called from assembly via libc. Thread-local storage (TLS) uses the FS segment register in x86-64.
.bash.Getting Started.What is Bash[0]

Bash (Bourne Again SHell) is a Unix shell and command language written by Brian Fox for the GNU Project. It's the default shell on most Linux distributions and macOS. Bash interprets commands, runs programs, and supports scripting with variables, control flow, and functions.
.bash.Getting Started.Terminal vs Shell[0]

A terminal (or terminal emulator) is the graphical window where you type commands. A shell (like Bash) is the program inside that terminal that interprets your commands. The terminal sends your keystrokes to the shell, and the shell sends output back to the terminal.
.bash.Getting Started.Navigating the Filesystem[0]

pwd prints your current directory. ls lists directory contents. cd changes directory. Use absolute paths (starting with /) or relative paths. ~ is your home directory, . is current directory, .. is parent directory.
.bash.Getting Started.man & Help[0]
