man displays the system manual for any command. Use q to quit, / to search, n/N for next/prev match. Most commands also support --help or -h for a quick usage summary. info provides more detailed documentation.
.bash.Getting Started.Basic Commands Overview[0]

Essential commands: echo (print text), date (show date/time), whoami (current user), id (user info), uname (system info), uptime (system uptime), cal (calendar), clear (clear terminal), history (command history), hostname (system hostname).
.bash.File Operations.Creating & Deleting Files[0]

touch creates empty files or updates timestamps. rm removes files. Use -i for confirmation, -f to force, -r for directories. Be careful — rm -rf is powerful and dangerous. mkdir creates directories, rmdir removes empty directories.
.bash.File Operations.Copying & Moving[0]

cp copies files and directories. mv moves or renames files. Both accept -i (interactive), -v (verbose), -u (update newer). For directories, cp needs -r (recursive). mv always works on directories without extra flags.
.bash.File Operations.Linking Files[0]

ln creates links. Hard links are multiple directory entries pointing to the same inode — deleting one doesn't affect others. Soft links (symlinks) are pointers to another path — they break if the target is moved or deleted. Symbolic links can cross filesystems.
.bash.File Operations.Finding Files[0]

find searches the filesystem by name, type, size, date, and more. locate uses a prebuilt database for faster searches but may be stale. which shows the path of an executable. whereis finds binary, source, and man pages.
.bash.File Operations.File Attributes & stat[0]

stat displays detailed file metadata: size, blocks, permissions, timestamps (access, modify, change), and inode number. file detects the file type by examining magic bytes. du estimates file/directory size usage.
.bash.Viewing & Editing Files.cat & less[0]

cat concatenates and displays files. Use it for small files or joining files. less is a pager for viewing large files with scroll, search, and navigation. less is better than cat for files longer than one screen. Use q to quit less.
.bash.Viewing & Editing Files.head & tail[0]

head shows the first N lines (default 10) of a file. tail shows the last N lines. tail -f follows a file as it grows — essential for monitoring logs. Both support -n for line count and -c for byte count.
.bash.Viewing & Editing Files.nano & vim Basics[0]

nano is a beginner-friendly terminal text editor with on-screen shortcuts. vim is a powerful modal editor with multiple modes: Normal (navigation), Insert (editing), Visual (selection), and Command (ex commands). Learn vim for speed; use nano for simplicity.
.bash.Viewing & Editing Files.Viewing Binary & Special Files[0]

hexdump (hd), xxd, and od display binary file contents in hexadecimal, octal, or ASCII. strings extracts printable strings from binary files. Use these for debugging binary formats or examining executables.
.bash.Text Processing.grep — Search Text[0]

grep searches files for patterns using regular expressions. Common options: -i (ignore case), -r (recursive), -v (invert match), -n (line numbers), -l (filename only), -c (count matches), -E (extended regex), -o (only matching).
.bash.Text Processing.sed — Stream Editor[0]

sed processes and transforms text non-interactively. Most common: s/old/new/g (substitute), /pattern/d (delete), -n 'p' (print). sed supports in-place editing with -i. It works line-by-line by default.
.bash.Text Processing.awk — Text Processing[0]

awk is a powerful text-processing language for field-based data. Default field separator is whitespace. $0 is the whole line, $1, $2, etc. are fields. Supports patterns, actions, and built-in variables (NF, NR, FS, OFS).
.bash.Text Processing.cut, sort, uniq[0]

cut extracts columns by delimiter (-d, -f). sort sorts lines alphabetically or numerically (-n), reverse (-r), unique (-u). uniq removes adjacent duplicates (use sort first). wc counts lines/words/characters.
.bash.Text Processing.tr & diff[0]
tr translates or deletes characters (from stdin only). Usage: tr 'set1' 'set2'. diff compares files line by line. comm compares sorted files for common/unique lines.
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.Understanding Permissions[0]

Linux file permissions: r (read=4), w (write=2), x (execute=1). Three tiers: owner (u), group (g), others (o). ls -l shows permissions as -rwxr-xr--. The first character indicates file type (-=file, d=dir, l=symlink).
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.chmod — Change Permissions[0]
chmod changes file permissions using symbolic (u+x, g-w, o=r) or octal (755, 644) modes. Common settings: 755 (rwxr-xr-x) for directories/executables, 644 (rw-r--r--) for files. Use -R for recursive.
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.chown & chgrp[0]
chown changes file owner and group. chgrp changes group only. Syntax: chown user:group file. Use -R for recursive. Only root can change ownership; a user can chgrp to groups they belong to.
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.chown & chgrp[1]

# Change owner
sudo chown alice file.txt
sudo chown alice:admin file.txt
sudo chown :admin file.txt         # change group only

# Recursive
sudo chown -R alice:users /home/alice

# chgrp
chgrp developers project/
chgrp -R developers shared/
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.chown & chgrp[2]
chown
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.umask & Default Permissions[0]

umask sets default permissions for new files and directories. It subtracts from the base permissions (666 for files, 777 for dirs). Common: umask 022 = 644/755, umask 077 = 600/700. Set it in .bashrc.
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.sudo & Root Access[0]

sudo executes a command as another user (default root). sudo -i opens a root shell. visudo edits /etc/sudoers safely. /etc/sudoers.d/ contains drop-in configs. The sudoers file controls who can run what commands.
.bash.Permissions & Ownership.Special Permissions[0]

SUID (setuid, 4xxx) runs a program with the file owner's privileges. SGID (setgid, 2xxx) runs with group privileges — on directories, new files inherit the group. Sticky bit (1xxx, chmod +t) prevents non-owners from deleting files in shared directories (/tmp).
.bash.Process Management.Viewing Processes[0]

ps lists running processes. Common: ps aux (all users, detailed), ps ef (full-format), ps -eo (custom format). top shows real-time process info. htop is an interactive alternative (install separately). Uptime shows system load averages.
.bash.Process Management.Managing Processes[0]
kill sends signals to processes. Common signals: SIGTERM (15, graceful), SIGKILL (9, force), SIGHUP (1, reload). killall kills by name. pkill kills by pattern. pgrep finds PIDs by name.
.bash.Process Management.Background & Foreground Jobs[0]

Appending & runs a command in the background. Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job. bg resumes a suspended job in the background. fg brings a job to the foreground. jobs lists background jobs. disown detaches a job from the shell.
.bash.Process Management.Systemd & Services[0]

systemctl manages systemd services. Common: start, stop, restart, enable, disable, status. service is the legacy command. systemd units are defined in .service files in /etc/systemd/system/ and /lib/systemd/system/.
.bash.I/O Redirection & Pipes.Standard Streams[0]

Three standard streams: stdin (0, input), stdout (1, output), stderr (2, errors). By default, stdin comes from keyboard, stdout/stderr go to terminal. Redirection changes where these streams point. < redirects stdin, > redirects stdout.
.bash.I/O Redirection & Pipes.Pipes[0]

Pipes (|) connect stdout of one command to stdin of another. This creates powerful command chains called pipelines. Each command runs in parallel. The exit status of a pipeline is that of the last command (pipefail option changes this).
.bash.I/O Redirection & Pipes.Here Documents & Strings[0]

Here documents (<< EOF) pass multi-line input to a command until a delimiter. Here strings (<<<) pass a single string as stdin. These are especially useful in scripts for providing inline input to commands.
.bash.I/O Redirection & Pipes.Process Substitution[0]
Process substitution <(command) or >(command) treats command output as a file. Useful for diffing command outputs or passing multiple inputs. Available in bash but not POSIX sh.
.bash.I/O Redirection & Pipes.tee & xargs[0]

tee reads stdin and writes to both stdout and files (like a T-pipe). Useful for logging while still seeing output. xargs reads items from stdin and executes a command with them. Essential for batch operations.
.bash.Shell Scripting Basics.Shebang & Execution[0]

The shebang (#!) on the first line tells the kernel which interpreter to use. Make scripts executable with chmod +x. Run with ./script.sh or bash script.sh. Arguments are $1, $2, ..., $0 is the script name.
.bash.Shell Scripting Basics.Variables[0]

Variables are assigned with name=value (no spaces). Read with $name or ${name}. Always quote variables ("$var") to prevent word splitting and globbing. Use readonly to make variables immutable, unset to remove them.
.bash.Shell Scripting Basics.Expansions & Substitutions[0]

Bash supports several expansions: brace ({a,b,c}), tilde (~), parameter ($var, ${var:-default}), command ($(cmd)), and arithmetic ($((expr))). Expansion happens in a specific order before the command executes.
.bash.Shell Scripting Basics.Quoting[0]

Single quotes preserve every character literally. Double quotes preserve most but allow $, ``, \, and ! expansion. Backslash escapes the next character. ANSI-C quoting ($'...') interprets escape sequences like \n, \t.
.bash.Shell Scripting Basics.Exit Codes[0]

Every command returns an exit code (0 = success, 1-255 = failure). $? contains the exit code of the last command. Use && (run if success) and || (run if failure) for chaining. exit terminates a script with a code.
.bash.Control Flow.if/elif/else[0]

if executes commands based on the exit status of a test command. test or [ ] evaluates conditions: numeric (-eq, -ne, -lt, -gt), string (=, !=, -z, -n), file (-f, -d, -e, -r, -w, -x). Use [[ ]] for extended bash tests with &&, ||, =~.
.bash.Control Flow.for Loops[0]
for iterates over a list of words, array elements, or command output. Use for ((expr; cond; incr)) for C-style loops. Use continue to skip iteration, break to exit early.
.bash.Control Flow.while & until Loops[0]

while runs as long as the test command succeeds. until runs as long as the test command fails. Use read for line-by-line processing. Use break to exit, continue to skip iteration. watch out for infinite loops!
.bash.Control Flow.case Statement[0]
case matches a value against patterns (like switch). Patterns can use *, ?, [...], and | for alternation. Each case ends with ;;. Use *) for default. esac ends the statement.
.bash.Control Flow.select Menu[0]

select creates an interactive menu from a list of items. The user picks a number, and the selected item is stored in the variable. Combined with case for menu-driven scripts. Break out with Ctrl+D or an empty input.
.bash.Functions & Advanced Scripting.Defining Functions[0]

Functions group commands for reuse. Define with function name { } or name() { }. Use local for function-scoped variables. Functions return with return (0-255) or set an exit code. Declare -f lists defined functions.
.bash.Functions & Advanced Scripting.Arrays[0]

Bash supports indexed arrays (declare -a) and associative arrays (declare -A). Accessed with ${array[index]}. ${array[@]} expands all elements. ${#array[@]} gives length. Useful for lists and lookups.
.bash.Functions & Advanced Scripting.Argument Parsing with getopts[0]

getopts parses command-line flags and options in scripts. Each option character can have a colon suffix to require an argument. OPTIND tracks the next argument index. Use a while loop with case for processing.
.bash.Functions & Advanced Scripting.Error Handling & Trap[0]

trap catches signals and executes commands. Common: trap 'cleanup' EXIT, trap 'handler' INT (Ctrl+C). set -e exits on error, set -u errors on undefined variables, set -o pipefail catches pipeline errors. Combined: set -euo pipefail.
.bash.Functions & Advanced Scripting.Debugging Scripts[0]

bash -x script.sh prints each command before execution (xtrace). set -x enables within a script. PS4 customizes the trace prompt. bash -n script.sh checks syntax without running. bash -v prints input lines.
.bash.Networking & Transfer.curl — HTTP Requests[0]

curl transfers data using various protocols (HTTP, FTP, etc.). Common: curl URL (fetch), curl -o file (save), curl -O (save with filename), curl -I (headers only), curl -d (POST data), curl -H (custom header).
.bash.Networking & Transfer.wget — Download Tool[0]
wget is a non-interactive downloader supporting recursive downloads, resuming, and mirroring. Unlike curl, wget is designed for downloads and works well with -r (recursive), -c (resume), -m (mirror).
.bash.Networking & Transfer.ssh — Remote Access[0]

SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote access. ssh user@host connects to a remote machine. Key-based auth with ssh-keygen + ssh-copy-id is more secure than passwords. ~/.ssh/config simplifies connections.
.bash.Networking & Transfer.scp & rsync[0]

scp securely copies files over SSH. rsync is a powerful sync tool that transfers only differences, supports compression (-z), archive mode (-a), and deletion (-delete). rsync is better for large or repeated transfers.
.bash.Networking & Transfer.Network Diagnostics[0]
ping tests host reachability. netstat (or ss) shows network connections, ports, and routing tables. ss is the modern replacement for netstat. dig/nslookup queries DNS. traceroute traces network path.
.bash.Shell Configuration.Bash Startup Files[0]

.bashrc runs for interactive non-login shells. .bash_profile (or .profile) runs for login shells. .bash_logout runs on logout. On macOS, Terminal opens login shells (use .bash_profile). On Linux, terminals typically use .bashrc.
.bash.Shell Configuration.Aliases[0]
Aliases create shorthand commands. List all aliases with alias (bare). Remove with unalias. Aliases don't accept arguments (use functions instead). Put aliases in .bashrc for persistence.
.bash.Shell Configuration.Environment Variables[0]

Environment variables are inherited by child processes. Set with export VAR=value. PATH controls where the shell looks for executables. Common: HOME, USER, SHELL, EDITOR, LANG, PATH, PS1. Add to .bashrc for persistence.
.bash.Shell Configuration.PS1 Prompt Customization[0]
PS1 defines the primary prompt. Use escape sequences: \u (user), \h (host), \w (working dir), \W (basename), \d (date), \t (time), \n (newline), \$ (# for root, $ otherwise). Set in .bashrc.
.bash.Shell Configuration.Command Completion[0]

Bash programmable completion completes commands, filenames, and arguments. Complete with Tab (double Tab to show all). bash-completion package adds completion for git, ssh, apt, and hundreds of commands.
.bash.Job Scheduling & Automation.cron — Scheduled Jobs[0]

cron runs commands at scheduled times. crontab -e edits your user's crontab. Format: minute hour day month weekday command. Use */n for every n, commas for lists, hyphens for ranges. Cron output is emailed by default.
.bash.Job Scheduling & Automation.at — One-Time Jobs[0]
at schedules a command for a specific time (one-time). Use at now + 5 minutes, at 2 PM tomorrow, etc. atq lists pending jobs, atrm removes a job. Commands are read from stdin or piped.
.bash.Job Scheduling & Automation.Writing Robust Scripts[0]

Robust scripts handle errors, use strict mode, validate arguments, and log output. Always quote variables, check command success, provide usage messages, and clean up temp files. set -euo pipefail is essential.
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Shell Injection & Prevention[0]

Shell injection occurs when user-controlled input is interpreted as code. Always quote variables ("$var"), use printf instead of echo for untrusted data, avoid eval entirely, and use $() instead of backticks for command substitution. Validate inputs against whitelists, not blacklists.
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Safe Temp Files[0]

Always use mktemp for temporary files — it creates files in a safe location with a random name, preventing race conditions and symlink attacks. Clean up with trap. Never use hardcoded paths in /tmp or patterns based on $$ (predictable).
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Input Validation[0]
Validate all external input before using it. Use [[ =~ ]] for regex matching, check exit codes, validate types and ranges. Prefer whitelist (allow known-good) over blacklist (block known-bad).
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Secrets Management[0]

Never hardcode passwords, API keys, or tokens in scripts. Use environment variables, read -s for interactive input, restrict file permissions on sensitive files, and consider dedicated secret management tools like pass or vault.
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Defensive Patterns[0]

Production scripts need strict error handling. Always use set -euo pipefail to fail on errors, unset variables, and pipeline failures. Set IFS safely to prevent word splitting on spaces. Use fail-fast design and provide context in error messages.
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Filesystem Security[0]

Be aware of filesystem security risks: world-writable files can be modified by anyone, symlink attacks can trick privileged scripts into writing to unexpected locations, and rm -rf patterns need careful handling.
.bash.Bash Security & Hardening.Auditing & Compliance[0]
Track script execution for forensics and compliance. Use logger for syslog integration, log command traces with bash -x, maintain audit trails of who ran what and when.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Testing Scripts[0]

Treat bash scripts like production code: use static analysis with ShellCheck, write unit tests with bats or shunit2, and verify syntax with bash -n. ShellCheck catches bugs like missing quotes, unused variables, and common antipatterns.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Profiling & Performance[0]

Bash scripts can be slow due to subprocess spawning. Use built-in operations instead of external commands, measure with time and PS4 traces, and avoid expensive patterns like $(cat file) (use < file or $(<file)).
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Parallel Execution[0]

Run tasks in parallel to speed up batch jobs. Use xargs -P for parallel command execution, GNU parallel for more control, and background + wait for ad-hoc parallelism. Use flock to prevent concurrent access to shared resources.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Structured Logging[0]
Good logging is essential for debugging and monitoring. Use timestamped log entries with severity levels, write to dedicated log files, integrate with syslog, and implement log rotation.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Interactive & TUI Scripts[0]
Bash can create interactive terminal interfaces using built-in read/select and tools like whiptail and dialog. Build menus, progress bars, input forms, and file pickers for user-friendly scripts.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Bash Portability[0]

Not all systems use bash — some use dash (Debian/Ubuntu /bin/sh), busybox ash, or zsh. Write portable scripts by avoiding bashisms, using POSIX sh syntax, and testing with dash. Use command -v for feature detection instead of assuming paths.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Config File Parsing[0]
Parse configuration files without sourcing them (sourcing is dangerous with untrusted files). Parse .env files, INI-style configs, and use jq/yq for JSON and YAML.
.bash.Advanced Scripting Techniques.Math & Data Processing[0]
Bash built-in arithmetic ($(( ))) handles integers. For floating point, use bc or awk. For structured data, use jq. For statistics on arrays, use built-in operations.
.bash.DevOps & Tooling with Bash.Git Automation[0]
Bash scripts can automate git workflows: batch operations, branch management, hook scripts, and CI pipeline glue. Git hooks (.git/hooks/) are bash scripts triggered by git events.
.bash.DevOps & Tooling with Bash.Docker & Containers[0]
Script Docker workflows: build images, manage containers, run health checks, and orchestrate multi-container operations. Useful for dev environments, CI/CD, and deployment automation.
.bash.DevOps & Tooling with Bash.API Interaction[0]
Interact with REST APIs using curl. Parse JSON responses with jq, handle errors, implement pagination, and respect rate limits. Essential for cloud tooling and web service automation.
.bash.DevOps & Tooling with Bash.Database Interaction[0]
Run database queries from bash scripts for automation: backups, migrations, reporting, and data import. Use non-interactive mode with environment variables for credentials.
.bash.DevOps & Tooling with Bash.Cloud CLI Automation[0]
Cloud provider CLIs (aws, gcloud, az) are built for scripting. Automate resource provisioning, configuration, and monitoring with bash wrappers and jq output parsing.
.bash.DevOps & Tooling with Bash.System Monitoring[0]
Build custom monitoring scripts for system health checks, disk usage alerts, service availability monitoring, and notification integration.
.php.Getting Started.What is PHP[0]

PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely-used open-source scripting language designed for web development. PHP code is executed on the server, generating HTML that is sent to the client. It can be embedded directly into HTML and works seamlessly with databases.
.php.Getting Started.PHP Syntax[0]

PHP code is enclosed in <?php ... ?> tags. Statements end with semicolons. PHP can be embedded anywhere in HTML. Variables start with $. Whitespace is ignored. The closing ?> is optional at the end of a file (recommended to omit to prevent accidental output).
.php.Getting Started.Variables[0]

PHP variables start with $ followed by a letter or underscore. They are dynamically typed and case-sensitive. Variables can be assigned by value or by reference (&). Variable variables ($$var) allow dynamic variable names.
.php.Getting Started.Data Types[0]

PHP supports: string, int, float, bool, array, object, null, resource. Use var_dump() to inspect type and value. gettype() returns the type name. Type juggling happens automatically; use strict comparison (===, !==) to avoid surprises.
.php.Getting Started.Constants & Magic Constants[0]

define() defines runtime constants. const keyword defines compile-time constants (must be in top-level scope). Magic constants like __FILE__, __DIR__, __LINE__, __CLASS__, __METHOD__ change based on where they're used.
.php.Getting Started.PHP Tags & Output[0]
Multiple ways to output: echo (language construct), print (returns 1), printf (formatted), var_dump (debug info). Short echo tag <?= is shorthand for <?php echo. Always available in PHP 5.4+.
.php.Control Flow.if/else/elseif[0]

Standard conditional execution. elseif (one word) is the recommended form over else if (two words, requires braces). Use switch for many conditions on the same variable. Match (PHP 8+) is a stricter switch without loose comparison.
.php.Control Flow.switch & match[0]

switch compares loosely (==). Use break to prevent fall-through; default for no match. match (PHP 8+) compares strictly (===), returns a value, and doesn't require break. match throws UnhandledMatchError on no match.
.php.Control Flow.for & foreach[0]

for loops use counter (init; condition; increment). foreach is the preferred way to iterate arrays: foreach($arr as $value) or foreach($arr as $key => $value). Use break to exit, continue to skip iteration.
.php.Control Flow.while & do-while[0]
while runs before checking condition (may run 0 times). do-while runs at least once. Use with caution to avoid infinite loops. Common for reading data until exhausted.
.php.Control Flow.Alternative Syntax[0]
PHP provides alternative syntax for control structures using colons and endif/endwhile/endfor/endforeach/endswitch. This is commonly used in templates to mix PHP with HTML cleanly.
.php.Functions.Defining Functions[0]

Functions are defined with the function keyword. They can have typed parameters and return types (PHP 7+). Default parameter values are supported. Use return to return a value; functions without return return null.
.php.Functions.Variable Scope[0]

Variables defined outside functions are global — use global keyword to access them inside functions. Static variables persist between calls. Function parameters are local. The $GLOBALS superglobal provides access to all global variables.
.php.Functions.Type Declarations[0]

PHP 7+ supports scalar type declarations: int, float, string, bool, void, iterable, mixed (PHP 8+), never (PHP 8.1+). Nullable types use ? prefix (e.g., ?string). Union types (PHP 8+) use | (e.g., int|string). Strict mode enabled with declare(strict_types=1).
.php.Functions.Anonymous Functions & Closures[0]

Anonymous functions (closures) can be assigned to variables or passed as arguments. Use function ($arg) use ($var) { ... } to import variables from the outer scope. Arrow functions (PHP 7.4+) provide shorter syntax with fn($arg) => expr.
.php.Functions.Variable Functions & Callbacks[0]
If a variable name has parentheses appended, PHP looks for a function with that name. call_user_func() and call_user_func_array() call callbacks. Useful for dynamic dispatch and event handling.
.php.Arrays & Data Structures.Indexed Arrays[0]

PHP arrays are ordered maps. Indexed arrays use numeric keys starting from 0. Create with array() or short syntax []. Access with $arr[index]. Count elements with count(). Manipulate with array_push, array_pop, array_shift, array_unshift.
.php.Arrays & Data Structures.Associative Arrays[0]

Associative arrays use string keys. Useful for key-value mappings and structured data. Access with $arr['key'] or $arr[$key]. Check key existence with isset() or array_key_exists(). Merge arrays with array_merge().
.php.Arrays & Data Structures.Multidimensional Arrays[0]
Arrays can contain other arrays for nested data structures. Access with multiple indices ($arr[0]['name']). Useful for representing complex data like tables, matrices, or nested records.
.php.Arrays & Data Structures.Array Functions[0]

PHP has a rich set of array functions: array_map (transform), array_filter (filter), array_reduce (aggregate), array_merge (combine), array_diff (difference), array_intersect (common), array_keys (get keys), array_values (get values), sort functions (sort, rsort, asort, ksort, usort).
.php.Arrays & Data Structures.SPL Data Structures[0]

SPL (Standard PHP Library) provides built-in data structures: SplStack, SplQueue, SplHeap, SplPriorityQueue, SplFixedArray, SplObjectStorage. These are more memory-efficient than plain arrays for specific use cases.
.php.OOP.Classes & Objects[0]

Classes define blueprints for objects. new creates instances. $this refers to the current instance. Properties and methods can be public, protected, or private. Constructor __construct() initializes properties. Type declarations work on properties (PHP 7.4+) and promoted properties (PHP 8+).
.php.OOP.Inheritance[0]

extends creates a child class that inherits parent methods and properties. Use parent:: to call parent methods. Override methods by redefining them. final keyword prevents overriding. abstract classes define base functionality with abstract methods.
.php.OOP.Interfaces & Traits[0]

Interfaces define contracts with method signatures. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Traits enable horizontal code reuse — they're like partial classes. Use traits with the use keyword inside a class.
.php.OOP.Namespaces[0]

Namespaces organize code and prevent naming conflicts. Declare with namespace at file top. Import with use keyword. Aliases with use ... as .... Fully qualified names start with \ (global namespace). Follow PSR-4 for autoloading.
.php.OOP.Static Methods & Properties[0]

Static members belong to the class, not instances. Accessed with :: (Scope Resolution Operator). self:: refers to the current class, static:: refers to the called class (late static binding). parent:: accesses parent class.
.php.File Handling.Reading Files[0]

file_get_contents() reads entire file as string. file() reads into array by lines. fopen() with fread()/fgets() provides streaming access. feof() checks end-of-file. Always close with fclose(). Use file_exists() and is_readable() to check first.
.php.File Handling.Writing Files[0]

file_put_contents() writes string to file (replaces). Use FILE_APPEND flag to append. fopen() with w (write), a (append), x (create exclusive) modes. flock() for file locking. fwrite() for streaming writes.
.php.File Handling.File Info & Directories[0]

File functions: basename(), dirname(), pathinfo(), filesize(), filemtime(), filetype(). Directory functions: mkdir(), rmdir(), scandir(), glob(). Recursive directory iteration with RecursiveDirectoryIterator.
.php.File Handling.File Uploads[0]

Files are uploaded via POST forms with enctype="multipart/form-data". Access via $_FILES superglobal. Use move_uploaded_file() to store. Validate file type, size, and errors. Beware of security: validate extensions, limit size, scan for malware.
.php.Forms & User Input.GET & POST[0]

$_GET contains URL query parameters. $_POST contains POST body. $_REQUEST combines both (avoid for security). $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] tells the HTTP method. Use htmlspecialchars() or htmlentities() to prevent XSS when outputting user data.
.php.Forms & User Input.Input Validation[0]

Validate input: filter_var() with FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL, FILTER_VALIDATE_URL, etc. Check string length with strlen(), patterns with preg_match(). Use filter_input() to access and filter in one step. Sanitize with FILTER_SANITIZE_*.
.php.Forms & User Input.Sessions[0]

Sessions store user data across requests. session_start() begins or resumes a session. Store in $_SESSION array. Cookie with session ID is sent to client. Regenerate session ID after login with session_regenerate_id() to prevent fixation.
.php.Forms & User Input.Cookies[0]

setcookie() sends a cookie to the browser. $_COOKIE reads incoming cookies. Set path, domain, secure, httponly, and samesite for security. Cookies are stored client-side and sent with every request to the domain.
.php.Databases.PDO Connection[0]

PDO (PHP Data Objects) provides a consistent interface for multiple database types. Connect with DSN string. PDO supports prepared statements, transactions, and error handling. Use try/catch for connection errors.
.php.Databases.Prepared Statements[0]

Prepared statements prevent SQL injection by separating SQL from data. Use named (:name) or positional (?) placeholders. prepare() returns a PDOStatement. execute() binds and runs. Fetch results with fetch(), fetchAll(), or fetchColumn().
.php.Databases.CRUD Operations[0]

Create (INSERT), Read (SELECT), Update (UPDATE), Delete (DELETE). Use transactions for multiple related operations. beginTransaction(), commit(), rollback(). Always use prepared statements for any user-influenced data.
.php.Databases.MySQLi[0]

MySQLi is a MySQL-only alternative to PDO. Supports both procedural and OOP styles. Use prepared statements with $mysqli->prepare(). Procedural functions (mysqli_connect, mysqli_query) are also available.
.php.Error Handling.Exceptions[0]

PHP uses try/catch blocks for exception handling. throw new Exception('message') raises an exception. Multiple catch blocks for different exception types. finally block runs regardless of whether an exception occurred (PHP 5.5+).
.php.Error Handling.Error Reporting[0]

error_reporting() sets which errors are reported. Use E_ALL for development. display_errors controls output. log_errors saves to file. set_error_handler() catches non-exception errors. trigger_error() manually triggers errors.
.php.Error Handling.Custom Exception Classes[0]

Create custom exceptions by extending Exception. Use different exception classes for different error types. Catch specific exceptions before general ones. SPL exceptions (InvalidArgumentException, RuntimeException, LogicException) cover common cases.
.php.Modern PHP & Ecosystem.Composer & Autoloading[0]

Composer is the dependency manager for PHP. composer.json defines dependencies. composer install/downloads packages into vendor/. PSR-4 autoloading maps namespaces to directories. require 'vendor/autoload.php' loads everything.
.php.Modern PHP & Ecosystem.PSR Standards[0]

PSR (PHP Standards Recommendations) define coding standards: PSR-1 (basic coding), PSR-4 (autoloading), PSR-7 (HTTP messages), PSR-12 (extended coding style). Following PSR standards ensures interoperability between PHP packages.
.php.Modern PHP & Ecosystem.PHP 8 Features[0]

PHP 8 introduced: named arguments, attributes (annotations), constructor property promotion, union types, match expression, nullsafe operator (?->), str_contains(), str_starts_with(), str_ends_with(), readonly properties (8.1), enums (8.1), fibers (8.1).
cypress.json: Introduction to cypress and its ecosystem.
Cypress is an open-source end-to-end testing framework installed via npm. It includes its own test runner, assertion library, and browser control with automatic waiting.
Cypress tests use Mocha-style describe/it blocks. Tests run in a real browser with automatic waiting, DOM snapshotting, and time-travel debugging.
Cypress bundles Chai assertions with should and expect syntax. Assertions automatically retry until the element meets the condition or times out.
Cypress is configured via cypress.config.js. The config file controls browsers, timeouts, baseUrl, video recording, and plugins for extending functionality.
cy.get selects elements by CSS selectors, returning a jQuery-wrapped element. It supports chaining and built-in retry-ability.
cy.find scopes the selection to descendants of a previously yielded element. It is ideal for navigating within a specific container.
cy.contains selects elements by their text content, which is more resilient to DOM structure changes than CSS selectors.
Use data-* attributes like data-cy for robust selectors that resist CSS and text changes. Avoid brittle selectors tied to implementation details.
cy.click simulates a mouse click on a DOM element. It supports options like multiple clicks, position offsets, and force-clicking hidden elements.
cy.type simulates keyboard input into form fields character by character. It supports special keys via curly braces like {enter}.
cy.select picks an option from a <select> element by value, text, or index. It supports multiple selection when the multiple attribute is present.
cy.trigger simulates hover events since Cypress lacks a native hover command. It shows hidden menus and tooltips.
cy.intercept spies on and modifies HTTP requests at the network level. It can stub responses, wait for requests, and assert on request details.
Request stubbing returns static data instead of hitting the real server, making tests fast, deterministic, and independent of backend availability.
cy.wait pauses test execution until a specific aliased network request completes. It can also wait for a specified amount of time.
Stubbing replaces server responses entirely, useful for testing edge cases, loading states, and error handling without a real server.
Test API endpoints directly with cy.request. It bypasses the UI and allows testing backend logic, authentication, and data shapes.
Fixtures are external data files (JSON, images, etc.) stored in cypress/fixtures. They provide realistic test data that can be reused across tests.
Custom commands wrap reusable logic into chainable Cypress commands via Cypress.Commands.add, improving test readability and reducing duplication.
Custom commands can be strongly typed using TypeScript. Augment the Cypress namespace for autocomplete and type safety.
Test data factories generate consistent, repeatable data for tests. Using beforeEach hooks ensures a clean state before each test run.
Cypress automatically captures screenshots on test failure. Manual screenshots can be taken with cy.screenshot for visual documentation.
Cypress records video of the entire test run. Videos are stored in cypress/videos and can be configured or disabled in cypress.config.js.
Cypress runs headlessly in CI with cypress run. The Cypress GitHub Action or Docker image provides browsers and dependencies.
Use cypress-axe for automated accessibility checks. It scans the DOM for WCAG violations and integrates directly into your test assertions.
Component testing mounts individual components in isolation using cy.mount. It requires the @cypress/react or @cypress/vue adapter.
Props are passed directly to the mounted component to test different states and configurations without needing the full application.
Event callbacks can be verified using Cypress spies. cy.spy wraps a function and tracks whether it was called with expected arguments.
Page Objects encapsulate page-specific selectors and actions into reusable classes, reducing test duplication and insulating tests from UI changes.
Real-world E2E tests simulate complete user journeys like signup, purchase, or search. They test critical business flows from start to finish.
cy.origin enables testing across multiple domains, useful for OAuth flows, payment gateways, and third-party integrations.
Cypress debugging tools include cy.pause to halt execution, cy.debug to log the current subject, and browser DevTools for interactive inspection.
Cypress Dashboard records test runs, provides parallelization, flaky test detection, and video/screenshot history. Connect via project ID.
Split test files across multiple CI machines to reduce test suite duration. Requires Cypress Dashboard for orchestration.
Cypress Cloud automatically detects flaky tests by analyzing test history. It provides flakiness scores and auto-retries for unreliable tests.

Cypress Component Testing mounts individual components in isolation, ideal for developing UI libraries or complex widgets. Custom commands (Cypress.Commands.add) encapsulate reusable logic like login flows, API mocking patterns, and assertion helpers. Overwrite existing commands for centralized behavior. Fixtures provide test data in JSON format. cy.intercept() handles API mocking at the network level. Interceptors can modify responses, simulate delays, and verify request payloads. Custom commands should return the chain for chaining support.

Cypress integrates with CI/CD via cypress run (headless) or cypress run --headed. Parallelization splits tests across machines for faster CI. cypress-parallel or native parallelization (Dashboard) speeds up suites. Cypress Dashboard records test runs, screenshots, videos, and flake analysis. cypress cache manages binary versions. Cypress.Cloud provides test analytics. Retry-ability (retries config) handles flaky tests. Record key: CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY. Grouping: --group flag for multi-machine runs.
debugging.json: .Console & DevTools.Console API Methods.exp

The Console API provides a suite of methods for debugging directly in the browser's developer console. These tools let you log structured data, measure performance, trace execution, and group related output.Key methods include console.log() for general logging, console.table() for tabular data, console.group()/console.groupEnd() for nesting output, console.time()/console.timeEnd() for performance measurement, console.assert() for conditional logging, console.trace() for stack traces, and console.dir() for interactive object inspection.
.Console & DevTools.Browser DevTools Panels.exp

Modern browser DevTools consist of specialized panels: Elements (DOM/CSS inspection), Console (JS execution), Sources (debugger with breakpoints), Network (HTTP requests), Memory (heap snapshots), Performance (profiling and flame charts), Application (storage, service workers), and Security (certificate inspection).Open DevTools with F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I. Each panel specializes in a different aspect of debugging and should be used depending on the type of issue being investigated.
.Console & DevTools.Line Breakpoints.exp

Line breakpoints pause script execution at a specific line, allowing variable inspection and call stack analysis. Click the line number gutter in the Sources panel to set one. A blue arrow indicates an active breakpoint.Breakpoints survive page reloads as long as DevTools is open. They can be disabled temporarily (uncheck) or removed entirely (right-click > Remove breakpoint). Use the Breakpoints pane to manage all breakpoints at once.
.Console & DevTools.Conditional Breakpoints.exp

Conditional breakpoints pause only when a condition evaluates to true. Right-click the gutter and select Add conditional breakpoint. They are shown with an orange arrow and are extremely useful for debugging specific iterations or edge cases without stopping on every call.The condition is any valid JavaScript expression. You can also use logpoints (right-click > Add logpoint) which log to the console without pausing — perfect for adding temporary logging without editing source code.
.Console & DevTools.DOM & Event Breakpoints.exp

DOM Change breakpoints pause on DOM modifications: subtree modifications (children added/removed), attribute modifications (class/style), and node removal. Set them by right-clicking an element in the Elements panel.XHR/Fetch breakpoints pause when a network request matches a URL pattern. Add them in Sources > XHR/Fetch Breakpoints by clicking + and entering a URL substring.Event Listener Breakpoints pause when a specific event fires. Check event types in Sources > Event Listener Breakpoints — useful for debugging event handler chains and third-party scripts.
.Console & DevTools.Exception Breakpoints & debugger.exp

Exception breakpoints pause on errors. Click the stop sign icon in Sources: once pauses on uncaught exceptions (yellow), again (blue) pauses on ALL exceptions including caught ones.The debugger; statement acts as a programmatic breakpoint. When DevTools is open, execution pauses at that line. Wrap it in conditionals for targeted debugging — but remove them before production (ESLint rule: no-debugger).
.Debugging Workflow.Call Stack Navigation.exp

Call stack navigation controls are essential for stepping through code execution:
  • Step Over (F10) — execute line, stay in current function
  • Step Into (F11) — go into called functions
  • Step Out (Shift+F11) — exit current function
  • Resume (F8) — continue to next breakpoint
  • Drop Frame — rewinds to function start (restart current function execution)
The Call Stack pane shows the chain of function calls leading to the current breakpoint. Each entry is clickable — clicking it jumps to that frame and shows its scope variables.
.Debugging Workflow.Scope & Watch Expressions.exp

The Scope pane displays variables at each level: Local, Closure, Script, Module, Global, and Block scopes. Use it to inspect values, detect variable shadowing, and understand closure behavior.Watch Expressions evaluate JS expressions each time execution pauses. Add them in the Watch pane (Sources panel, right side below Scope) by clicking +. Examples: item.price > 50 ? 'Expensive' : 'Cheap', total.toFixed(2).Live Expressions in the Console panel (eye icon) continuously evaluate expressions in real-time, like document.title or window.innerWidth.
.Debugging Workflow.Async Stack Traces.exp

Async stack traces preserve the calling chain across async operations. Chrome DevTools traces promise chains, async/await calls, and setTimeout/setInterval callbacks. This is crucial for debugging asynchronous code where the traditional call stack would be lost.Understanding the event loop order is essential: synchronous code runs first, then microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask), then macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval). Set breakpoints to observe execution order.
.Network & Storage.Network Panel Inspection.exp

The Network panel shows headers, payload, cookies, timing, and initiator for every request. The Initiator tab links to the source code that triggered the request. Use filters (by type, URL, status code) to isolate specific requests.Key features: Preserve log keeps requests across page reloads, Disable cache simulates first-load experience, and Throttling emulates slow network conditions (Slow 3G, Fast 3G, offline).
.Network & Storage.Storage & Application Inspection.exp

The Application panel shows all browser storage: LocalStorage, SessionStorage, Cookies, IndexedDB, Cache Storage, and more. You can view, edit, and delete entries directly — useful for debugging authentication state, cached data, and offline capabilities.For Service Workers, the Application panel allows inspecting registered workers, simulating offline mode (Offline checkbox), and triggering updates. The Clear Site Data button is handy for resetting all storage during debugging.
.Network & Storage.Memory Profiling.exp

Memory debugging involves three key tools in DevTools:
  • Heap Snapshots — capture memory state at a point in time. Compare two snapshots to find memory leaks by filtering for Detached elements.
  • Allocation Timelines — show where memory is allocated over time. Blue bars represent new allocations, sawtooth patterns indicate garbage collection.
  • CPU Profiling — shows where execution time is spent. Record in the Performance panel. Look for long tasks (red bars > 50ms that block the main thread).
Key metrics: Shallow size (object itself) vs Retained size (object + all referenced objects).
.Python Debugging.print() & f-strings.exp

Python's print() is the simplest debugging tool. Modern f-strings (Python 3.6+) support inline variable printing with f"{var=}" syntax (Python 3.8+), format specifiers like :.2f for precision, and custom __str__/__repr__ for object representation.Use pprint for pretty-printing complex data structures. For real-time output, print to stderr with file=sys.stderr, flush=True. In production, prefer the logging module.
.Python Debugging.pdb & breakpoint().exp

Python's built-in pdb module provides a full interactive debugger. The breakpoint() function (Python 3.7+) drops into the debugger at that line. IPython's ipdb offers tab completion and syntax highlighting.Key pdb commands: l (list source), n (next), s (step into), c (continue), p (print expression), pp (pretty-print), w (where/show stack), u/d (up/down stack). Set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 to disable all breakpoints globally.Post-mortem debugging (pdb.pm()) lets you inspect state after an exception — enter the debugger at the exact crash frame.
.Python Debugging.Logging Module.exp

Python's logging module provides hierarchical loggers, multiple handlers (Stream, File, Rotating, Syslog, SMTP), formatters, and configurable levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL).Configure via basicConfig() or dictConfig. Loggers follow a hierarchy — child loggers propagate to parents. Debug logger setup by inspecting logger.handlers, logger.getEffectiveLevel(), and logger.propagate.Use third-party logger level control: logging.getLogger("urllib3").setLevel(logging.WARNING) to suppress verbose libraries.
.Python Debugging.Exception Hooks & Tracebacks.exp

Python's exception handling uses try/except/else/finally blocks. The sys.excepthook intercepts uncaught exceptions globally for logging. The traceback module provides utilities for extracting, formatting, and printing stack traces.The inspect module gives deeper introspection: inspect.stack() shows call frames, inspect.getsource() retrieves source code, and inspect.signature() shows function parameters. Use gc.get_referrers() to find what holds references to objects.
.Python Debugging.IDE & Remote Debugging.exp

Modern IDEs provide visual debugging for Python. VS Code and PyCharm offer breakpoints, variable inspection, watch expressions, and step-through controls.For remote debugging, use debugpy: call debugpy.listen() to start the debug server, then attach from your IDE. For testing, use pytest --pdb to enter the debugger on test failure. Jupyter supports %debug for post-mortem inspection after errors.
.Advanced Debugging.Source Maps.exp

Source maps map compiled JavaScript back to original TypeScript source code. Enable with sourceMap: true in tsconfig.json. Chrome DevTools automatically loads .map files to show TS code in the Sources panel.For production, upload source maps to error tracking services (Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog) so stack traces point back to original source. Use sentry-cli, datadog-ci, or bugsnag-sourcemaps for upload. Always strip source maps from production static assets to avoid exposing source code.
.Advanced Debugging.Workspace Overrides & Pretty-Printing.exp

Workspace Overrides let you edit files directly in Sources and persist changes across page reloads. Enable in Sources > Filesystem > Add folder to workspace. Edits are saved to a local folder and take effect on every reload — no server changes needed.Pretty-printing ({ } button in Sources panel) reformats minified code into readable JS. The Blackbox feature hides framework/lib scripts from stack traces. Use //# sourceURL=name.js for naming eval'd code in the Sources panel.
.Advanced Debugging.REPL & Node.js Remote Debugging.exp

Node.js debugging with --inspect flags enables Chrome DevTools connection. Use --inspect-brk to pause on first line. Connect via chrome://inspect and click "Open dedicated DevTools for Node".The Node.js REPL provides an interactive debugging environment with commands: .help, .break (exit multi-line), .save (save session), .load (load file), .editor (multi-line editing). The repl module lets you create custom REPLs with defined commands.
.Advanced Debugging.Memory Leak Patterns.exp

Memory leaks occur when objects are retained unintentionally. Common patterns:
  • Uncleared intervals/timers — always save the interval ID and clear on unmount
  • Detached DOM references — removing elements from DOM but keeping JS references
  • Accidental globals — undeclared variables (x = 5 without let/const)
  • Closures retaining large data — closures capture the entire outer scope
  • Forgotten event listeners — listeners on removed elements prevent GC
Use Chrome DevTools Memory panel > Heap snapshots to identify leaks. Compare two snapshots and filter by "Detached" to find retained DOM elements.
.Production Debugging.Error Tracking & Monitoring.exp

Production error tracking tools (Sentry, LogRocket, Datadog RUM) capture errors with context: browser, device, user actions, and network state. Integrate via SDK for real-time monitoring with source map support.Set up global error handlers: window.onerror for runtime errors and unhandledrejection for promise rejections. These provide a safety net for errors that slip through try/catch blocks.
.Production Debugging.Network Mocking & Blocking.exp

The Network panel in DevTools supports request blocking, mocking, and offline simulation. Right-click a request > Block request URL to simulate API failures. Use the Network conditions panel to emulate offline mode, custom latency, and specific user agents.For browser extensions debugging, use chrome://extensions (Chrome) or about:debugging (Firefox). Enable developer mode to inspect background scripts, content scripts, and popup pages. Manifest V3 extensions use Service Workers — inspect them in Application > Service Workers.
.Production Debugging.Go Debugging.exp

Delve is the standard debugger for Go programs. Key commands: break (set breakpoint), continue (resume), next (step over), step (step into), print (evaluate expression), goroutines (list all goroutines).Go's built-in race detector (go run -race) finds concurrent access bugs. The pprof tool provides CPU, heap, goroutine, and block profiling via net/http/pprof. Use go tool trace for execution trace visualization.
django.json: Introduction to Django and its ecosystem.

Django is a high-level Python web framework that encourages rapid development with a clean, pragmatic design. It follows the 'batteries-included' philosophy, providing ORM, admin panel, authentication, forms, templates, and more out of the box. Django uses the MTV (Model-Template-View) architectural pattern, which is similar to MVC but with different naming. It emphasizes DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles and security by default.

A Django project consists of a project directory and one or more apps. The project contains settings, root URL configuration, and WSGI/ASGI configuration. Apps are reusable modules that contain models, views, templates, and static files. The manage.py script is a command-line utility for administrative tasks. key files: settings.py (configuration), urls.py (URL routing), wsgi.py (deployment entry), asgi.py (async deployment entry). Each app has its own migrations, admin, tests, and apps configuration.

Django settings control every aspect of the framework. Key settings: INSTALLED_APPS (list of enabled apps), MIDDLEWARE (request/response processing pipeline), DATABASES (database configuration), TEMPLATES (template engine config), STATIC_URL/STATIC_ROOT (static files), MEDIA_URL/MEDIA_ROOT (user uploads). Use python-decouple or django-environ for environment variables. SECRET_KEY must be kept secret. DEBUG=False in production. ALLOWED_HOSTS restricts domain names.
Working with data and APIs in Django.

Django's test framework extends Python's unittest. Use TestCase for database-backed tests. Client simulates browser requests. Factory Boy creates test data. pytest-django is a popular alternative. Key assertions: assertEqual, assertContains, assertTemplateUsed, assertRedirects, assertQuerysetEqual. Tests live in tests.py per app or a tests/ directory. Run with python manage.py test. Use --keepdb to preserve test database between runs.

Models are Python classes that define the structure of your database tables. Each model maps to a single database table, and each attribute maps to a database column. Django automatically creates the table schema, manages relationships (ForeignKey, ManyToManyField, OneToOneField), and provides a powerful QuerySet API. Common field types: CharField, IntegerField, BooleanField, DateField, DateTimeField, TextField, EmailField, URLField, FileField, ImageField. Field options: null, blank, default, unique, choices, verbose_name, help_text.

Migrations are Django's way of propagating model changes to the database schema. They're Python files that describe database operations. Key commands: makemigrations (creates migration files), migrate (applies migrations), sqlmigrate (shows SQL), showmigrations (lists migrations). Migrations track dependencies and can be merged. Always create migrations after changing models. Use --name for custom migration names. For data migrations, create empty migration and use RunPython.

QuerySets are lazy database lookups that allow chaining filters. They are evaluated only when iterated, sliced, or converted to list. Key methods: all(), filter(), exclude(), get(), create(), update(), delete(), order_by(), values(), values_list(), select_related(), prefetch_related(), annotate(), aggregate(), distinct(), count(), exists(), first(), last(), latest(), earliest(). Field lookups: exact, iexact, contains, icontains, in, gt, gte, lt, lte, startswith, endswith, range, date, year, month, day, isnull, regex, iregex.

Django supports three relationship types: ForeignKey (many-to-one), ManyToManyField (many-to-many), and OneToOneField (one-to-one). ForeignKey requires on_delete option (CASCADE, PROTECT, SET_NULL, SET_DEFAULT, SET(), DO_NOTHING, RESTRICT). related_name defines reverse relation name (default: modelname_set). ManyToManyField can use through for intermediary models with extra fields. OneToOneField extends another model (like inheritance). Generic Foreign Keys allow relations to any model.

Function-based views (FBVs) are simple Python functions that take an HttpRequest and return an HttpResponse. They are the most straightforward way to handle requests. The function receives the request object and optional URL parameters. Returns HttpResponse, render(), redirect(), or JsonResponse. Can be decorated with @login_required, @require_http_methods, @csrf_exempt, etc. Simple and explicit but can become repetitive for CRUD operations.

Class-based views (CBVs) organize view logic into reusable classes. Django provides generic CBVs: ListView, DetailView, CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView, FormView, TemplateView, RedirectView. CBVs use attributes and methods for configuration: model, template_name, context_object_name, form_class, success_url, paginate_by. Override methods: get_queryset(), get_context_data(), form_valid(), get_success_url(). Mixins allow combining reusable behavior. CBVs reduce boilerplate for CRUD but have a steeper learning curve.

URL configuration maps URL patterns to views using django.urls.path() and re_path(). Each URL pattern has a route, view, optional kwargs, and a unique name. Include() allows nesting app URL configs. path converters: str, int, slug, uuid, path. Custom path converters can be defined. Use namespacing with app_name and include with namespace. The {% url %} template tag reverses URL names. For complex patterns, use re_path() with regex. Always name your URLs for maintainability.

Django template language uses {{ variables }} and {% tags %}. Variables can be attributes, dictionary keys, or list indices. Filters transform variables: date, default, length, upper, lower, title, pluralize, slugify, truncatechars, safe, escape, join. Tags control logic: {% if %}, {% for %}, {% block %}, {% extends %}, {% include %}, {% url %}, {% load %}, {% static %}. Template inheritance with {% extends %} and {% block %} is the most powerful feature. Context processors make variables available in all templates.

Static files (CSS, JS, images) are managed via django.contrib.staticfiles. In development, use runserver. In production, use collectstatic to gather files. Configure STATIC_URL, STATICFILES_DIRS (additional directories), STATIC_ROOT (production destination). Use {% load static %} and {% static 'path' %} in templates. For user uploads, use MEDIA_URL and MEDIA_ROOT with ImageField/FileField. Whitenoise is a popular package for serving static files in production.

Django forms handle HTML form generation, validation, and processing. Form classes define fields with validation rules. Forms can be bound (with data) or unbound. Common fields: CharField, EmailField, IntegerField, BooleanField, DateField, ChoiceField, MultipleChoiceField, FileField, ImageField. Validators: built-in (required, min_length, max_length, min_value, max_value), regex, custom. Widgets control HTML rendering: TextInput, Textarea, Select, CheckboxInput, RadioSelect, FileInput. Form rendering: form.as_p, form.as_table, form.as_ul, or manual field-by-field.

Form processing follows a pattern: GET renders empty form, POST validates and processes. Check request.method, instantiate form with request.POST (and request.FILES for uploads), call form.is_valid(), access cleaned_data, redirect on success or re-render with errors. ModelForm.save() creates or updates a model instance. Use commit=False for pre-save processing. FormSets manage multiple forms of the same type. Inline form sets handle related model forms.

Django's built-in authentication system handles users, groups, permissions, and sessions. The User model provides username, password, email, first_name, last_name. Extend via OneToOneField (Profile model) or AbstractUser (custom user model). Key views: LoginView, LogoutView, PasswordChangeView, PasswordResetView. Decorators: @login_required, @permission_required, @user_passes_test. Mixins: LoginRequiredMixin, PermissionRequiredMixin, UserPassesTestMixin. django.contrib.auth.urls provides all auth URL patterns.

Django's permission system assigns permissions to users and groups. Each model gets three default permissions: add_, change_, delete_, and optionally view_. Groups bundle permissions for role-based access. Check permissions with user.has_perm(), @permission_required, or PermissionRequiredMixin. Custom permissions can be defined in model Meta. The admin interface provides group and permission management. Object-level permissions require third-party packages like django-guardian.

Django's admin interface provides automatic CRUD for models. Register models with admin.site.register() or use @admin.register() decorator. Customize with ModelAdmin options: list_display, list_filter, search_fields, list_editable, list_per_page, ordering, date_hierarchy, readonly_fields, fieldsets, exclude, inlines. Enhance with actions, custom templates, and widget overrides. Admin has built-in authentication, permissions, and history tracking.

Django REST Framework (DRF) is a powerful toolkit for building Web APIs. Install with pip install djangorestframework. Core concepts: Serializers (convert complex types to/from JSON), Views (APIView, ViewSets), Routers (auto-generate URL patterns), Authentication & Permissions. DRF provides browsable API, content negotiation, throttling, filtering, and versioning. Use ModelSerializer for model-based serializers, ReadOnlyModelViewSet for read-only endpoints.

ViewSets combine logic for multiple actions (list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update, destroy) into a single class. ModelViewSet provides all CRUD operations. Routers automatically generate URL patterns from ViewSets. DefaultRouter creates API root view. Custom actions with @action decorator. Filter backends: DjangoFilterBackend, SearchFilter, OrderingFilter. Override get_queryset, perform_create, get_serializer_class for customization.

Django deployment requires a production-ready web server (Gunicorn, uWSGI), reverse proxy (Nginx, Apache), and database (PostgreSQL). Environment variables for secrets. Use django-environ or python-decouple. Disable DEBUG, configure ALLOWED_HOSTS, use secure cookies, enable HTTPS. Static files served via Whitenoise or CDN. Media files served via Nginx or cloud storage (S3, GCS). Database connection pooling with pgbouncer. Caching with Redis/Memcached. Celery for async tasks. Sentry for error tracking.
dk.json: .Getting Started.What is Docker[0]
Containerization platform that packages applications with their complete dependencies into isolated units called containers.
.Getting Started.Containers vs Images[0]
Images are read-only blueprints; containers are runnable, isolated instances created from those blueprints.
.Getting Started.Docker Architecture[0]
Docker uses a client-server architecture with a CLI communicating via REST API to a daemon (dockerd) that manages images, containers, networks, and volumes.
.Getting Started.Docker Desktop[0]
Desktop application for macOS, Windows, and Linux that includes Docker Engine, Docker CLI, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and a GUI management dashboard.
.Getting Started.WSL2 Backend[0]
On Windows, Docker Desktop can run the Linux kernel inside a lightweight WSL2 VM for native Linux container performance without Hyper-V.
.Getting Started.Daemon Configuration[0]
Dockerd behavior is configured via daemon.json, controlling storage driver, log driver, registry mirrors, insecure registries, and resource limits.
.Getting Started.docker info[0]
Display system-wide information about the Docker installation, including OS, storage driver, CPUs, memory, and running container counts.
.Getting Started.Lifecycle Management[0]
Create, launch, stop, and clean up container runtimes explicitly through Docker commands.
.Getting Started.Listing & Inspecting[0]
List running containers with docker ps, all containers with -a, and view detailed metadata with docker inspect.
.Images & Dockerfiles.Dockerfile Basics[0]
Instruction set for creating container images. Each instruction creates a layer in the final image.
.Images & Dockerfiles.FROM Variants[0]
Choose base images wisely: alpine (5MB), slim (Debian minimal), distroless (language runtime only), or scratch (empty) for different size and security trade-offs.
.Images & Dockerfiles.RUN Layers[0]
Each RUN instruction creates a new layer. Chain commands with && and clean up in the same layer to reduce image size.
.Images & Dockerfiles.COPY vs ADD[0]
COPY copies files from context into the image. ADD does the same plus supports remote URLs and auto-extracting tar archives. Prefer COPY unless you need ADD's extras.
.Images & Dockerfiles.ARG vs ENV[0]
ARG defines build-time variables (not in final image unless persisted). ENV defines runtime environment variables that persist in the final image.
.Images & Dockerfiles.WORKDIR[0]
Sets the working directory for all subsequent Dockerfile instructions (RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, ADD). Creates the directory if it does not exist.
.Images & Dockerfiles.USER[0]
Switch to a non-root user for better security. Always create a dedicated user; never run containers as root unless absolutely necessary.
.Images & Dockerfiles.EXPOSE[0]
Documents which ports the container listens on at runtime. It is documentation only — does not publish the port. Use -p or -P at runtime to publish.
.Images & Dockerfiles.LABEL[0]
Add metadata as key-value pairs to the image. Used for versioning, maintainer info, and organization. Use with --filter for image queries.
.Images & Dockerfiles.SHELL[0]
Override the default shell (Linux: /bin/sh, Windows: cmd) used by RUN instructions. Useful for Windows containers or custom shells.
.Images & Dockerfiles.HEALTHCHECK[0]
Tells Docker how to test if the container is working. Docker checks the command periodically; exits with 0 = healthy, 1 = unhealthy.
.Images & Dockerfiles.Multi-Stage Build[0]
Use multiple FROM statements to chain build environments. Copy only required artifacts to the final stage, drastically reducing image size.
.Images & Dockerfiles.BuildKit[0]
Modern Docker build backend (enabled by default in newer versions) with parallel builds, secrets mounting, SSH mounts, and better caching.
.Images & Dockerfiles.Buildx[0]
Extended build capabilities built on BuildKit. Enables multi-architecture builds, simultaneous builds for linux/amd64, linux/arm64, etc.
.Images & Dockerfiles.Cache Mounts[0]
Persist package manager caches across builds using BuildKit cache mounts, speeding up repeated RUN instructions significantly.
.Images & Dockerfiles..dockerignore[0]
Prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the Docker daemon during builds, reducing context size and improving build speed.
.Container Management.docker run deep[0]
The primary command to create and start containers. Supports --name, --rm (auto-remove on exit), --restart, -d (detach), --network, and many more flags.
.Container Management.Interactive Mode[0]
Run containers interactively with -it (--interactive + --tty) for shell access, debugging, or one-off commands.
.Container Management.Detachment[0]
Run containers in the background with -d flag. Re-attach with docker attach, or follow logs with docker logs -f.
.Container Management.Resource Limits[0]
Constrain container CPU, memory, and disk I/O using --memory, --cpus, --memory-swap, and --blkio-weight flags.
.Container Management.Logging Drivers[0]
Configure how containers send logs. Drivers: json-file (default), syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, gcplogs, and local (efficient).
.Container Management.Restart Policies[0]
Control automatic container restarts: no (never), always, on-failure[:max-retries], unless-stopped (also restarts after daemon restart).
.Container Management.stop vs kill[0]
docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful shutdown, 10s timeout), then SIGKILL. docker kill sends any signal (default SIGKILL) immediately.
.Container Management.update[0]
Dynamically update container resource constraints, restart policy, and other configuration on a running container without recreating it.
.Container Management.rename[0]
Rename a running or stopped container without affecting its internal state, IP, or volumes.
.Container Management.wait[0]
Block the shell until a container stops, then return its exit code. Useful for scripting and CI pipelines.
.Container Management.Port Mapping Deep[0]
Map container ports to the host with -p (specific) or -P (random ephemeral ports). Supports IPv4/IPv6, multiple protocols, and ranges.
.Container Management.Environment Variables[0]
Pass configuration via -e flags, --env-file, or ENV instructions in Dockerfile. Variables are isolated per container.
.Networking.Port Forwarding[0]
Map isolated internal container ports onto host interfaces, enabling external access to containerized services.
.Networking.DNS Resolution[0]
Containers on user-defined bridges resolve each other by container name or network alias. Docker embeds a DNS server at 127.0.0.11.
.Networking.Network Drivers Deep[0]
bridge (default, NAT), host (no isolation), overlay (multi-host), macvlan (MAC per container), ipvlan (IP per container), none (isolated).
.Networking.User-Defined Bridge[0]
Create custom bridge networks for automatic DNS resolution, network isolation between groups, and attach/detach containers dynamically.
.Networking.Host Network[0]
Remove network isolation to run directly on the host's network stack. No port mapping needed; container sees host interfaces.
.Networking.Macvlan[0]
Assign a real MAC address to each container, making them appear as physical devices on the network. Useful for legacy apps that require direct network access.
.Networking.Ipvlan[0]
Assign IP addresses to containers sharing the host's MAC address. L2 mode (same subnet) and L3 mode (routing between subnets) supported.
.Networking.Network Aliases[0]
Give a container multiple DNS names within a network. Useful for running multiple variants of the same service.
.Networking.Container Networking Model[0]
Docker's CNM defines Sandbox (namespace), Endpoint (veth pair), and Network (bridge/overlay) as core primitives for container networking.
.Networking.Overlay Networks[0]
Multi-host networks that span across Docker swarm nodes, enabling container communication across different hosts securely over VXLAN.
.Storage.Named Volumes[0]
Persistent data directories managed by Docker, isolated from container lifecycle. Survive container removal and can be shared across containers.
.Storage.Bind Mounts[0]
Mount a host file or directory into a container at a specific path. Changes are reflected instantly on both sides.
.Storage.tmpfs Mounts[0]
Mount a temporary filesystem stored in memory (RAM), not on disk. Data is lost when the container stops. Ideal for secrets or cache.
.Storage.Storage Drivers[0]
Manage image layers and container writable layers. overlay2 (default, modern), aufs (legacy), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfs.
.Storage.Volume Drivers[0]
Plugins that extend Docker volumes to remote storage systems: NFS, SSHFS, S3, Azure File, Google Cloud, REX-Ray, Portworx.
.Storage.Backup & Restore Volumes[0]
Back up volume data using a temporary container that mounts the volume and creates a tar archive.
.Storage.Bind Mount Deep[0]
Bind mounts can be read-only, create missing host paths automatically, and support SELinux relabeling with :Z or :z suffixes.
.Storage.Permissions[0]
Container processes run as root by default, creating files owned by root on bind-mounted directories. Use --user or USER to match host UID/GID.
.Compose.Compose File Structure[0]
YAML file defining services, networks, and volumes for multi-container applications. Version 3 targets Swarm; version 2 targets single-engine.
.Compose.Profiles[0]
Selectively start services with --profile. Services only start when their profile is activated, enabling different environments (dev, test, staging).
.Compose.Extends[0]
Inherit and override service definitions from another Compose file or within the same file, reducing duplication across environments.
.Compose.depends_on Deep[0]
Control startup order between services. Supports condition: service_started, service_healthy (requires healthcheck), or service_completed_successfully.
.Compose.Healthcheck in Compose[0]
Define container health checks in Compose. Automatically used by depends_on condition: service_healthy and by Swarm for rolling updates.
.Compose.env_file[0]
Load environment variables from one or more files. Supports multiple env_file entries; values are available to the container at runtime.
.Compose.Secrets in Compose[0]
Manage sensitive data (passwords, API keys, certificates) using Docker secrets. Mounted as files at /run/secrets/ inside the container.
.Compose.Configs in Compose[0]
Manage non-sensitive configuration files (config files, nginx conf, etc.) similar to secrets. Mounted at the specified target path.
.Compose.Deploy Section[0]
Swarm-only deployment configuration: replicas, update config, rollback config, restart_policy, placement constraints, resources, and endpoint mode.
.Compose.Compose Watch[0]
Automatically update running containers when source files change (Compose 2.22+). Supports sync, rebuild, and restart actions.
.Swarm.Swarm Init[0]
Initialize a Docker Swarm cluster, transforming the host into a manager node. Swarm manages services across multiple hosts.
.Swarm.Node Types[0]
Managers run the control plane and Raft consensus (odd count recommended). Workers run only tasks. Nodes can be promoted or demoted.
.Swarm.Raft Consensus[0]
Swarm uses the Raft algorithm to maintain a consistent cluster state across manager nodes. Requires at least 3 managers for high availability.
.Swarm.Service Replication[0]
Deploy replicated services across Swarm nodes with --replicas. Docker schedules tasks evenly across available nodes.
.Swarm.Rolling Updates[0]
Update services incrementally with controlled parallelism and delay. Supports automatic rollback on failure and health check gate.
.Swarm.Secrets Deep[0]
Encrypted secrets stored in the Swarm Raft store. Only granted services can access them. Mounted as tmpfs files at /run/secrets/.
.Swarm.Configs in Swarm[0]
Similar to secrets but for non-sensitive config files. Configs are stored in the Swarm Raft store and mounted into containers.
.Swarm.docker stack[0]
Deploy a complete Compose application to Swarm as a stack. Stack name prefixes all service names for isolation.
.Swarm.Swarm Mode Networking[0]
Swarm uses ingress overlay network for routing mesh, and can attach services to custom overlay networks for multi-host communication.
.Swarm.Routing Mesh[0]
Swarm's routing mesh allows any node in the cluster to accept traffic on published ports and route it to a container on any other node.
.Security.Seccomp Profiles[0]
Linux syscall filter (Secure Computing Mode) that restricts which system calls a container can make. Docker ships a default seccomp profile allowing ~300 of ~450 syscalls.
.Security.AppArmor[0]
Mandatory Access Control (MAC) system that confines programs to a limited set of resources. Docker generates and loads an AppArmor profile for containers by default.
.Security.Linux Capabilities[0]
Fine-grained privileges for container processes. Drop all capabilities with --cap-drop=all, then add only required ones. Avoid --privileged.
.Security.Read-Only Root[0]
Mount the container's root filesystem as read-only. Writable paths use tmpfs or volume mounts. Prevents attackers from modifying the filesystem.
.Security.User Namespaces[0]
Map container root (UID 0) to a non-privileged host UID, so root inside the container has no special privileges on the host. Enabled via daemon.json.
.Security.Content Trust[0]
Verify image publisher identity and image integrity using digital signatures (Docker Notary). Only signed images can be pulled or run.
.Security.Image Scanning[0]
Scan container images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in OS packages and application dependencies. Use docker scout or third-party tools.
.Security.Secrets Management[0]
Never bake secrets into images. Use Docker secrets (Swarm), --secret (BuildKit build), --env-file, or dedicated tools like Vault.
.Security.gVisor[0]
Container sandbox runtime (runsc) that adds a kernel between the container and the host OS, intercepting syscalls for stronger isolation.
.Security.Security Best Practices[0]
Defense-in-depth: run non-root, read-only root, drop capabilities, enable content trust, scan images, use secrets, and avoid --privileged.
.Monitoring & Logging.docker events[0]
Stream real-time events from the Docker daemon: container start/stop/destroy, image pull, volume mount, network connect, etc.
.Monitoring & Logging.Prometheus Metrics[0]
Docker daemon exposes native Prometheus metrics at /metrics endpoint. Configure in daemon.json for cluster-level monitoring with Prometheus + Grafana.
.Monitoring & Logging.ELK Stack with Docker[0]
Centralized logging with Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana. Containers send logs via the gelf log driver to Logstash or directly to Elasticsearch.
.Monitoring & Logging.cAdvisor[0]
Google's cAdvisor (container advisor) exposes real-time resource usage and performance metrics per container. Often paired with Prometheus.
.Monitoring & Logging.Resource Monitoring Deep[0]
docker stats shows live CPU, memory, network, and disk I/O per container. Pair with --no-stream for a single snapshot.
.Monitoring & Logging.Logging Drivers[0]
Containers can use different log drivers: json-file (default), local (efficient compression), none (no logs), syslog, journald, fluentd, awslogs, gelf, gcplogs.
.Monitoring & Logging.Telemetry Logs[0]
View container STDOUT/STDERR output with docker logs. Supports tailing, timestamps, since/until filtering, and following.
.CI/CD.Docker in Docker[0]
Run Docker inside a Docker container (dinD) for CI pipelines that need to build and push images. Use --privileged or mount /var/run/docker.sock.
.CI/CD.Caching Strategies[0]
Speed up CI builds by caching layers. Use --cache-from to pull a previously built image and use its layers as cache. Combine with BuildKit.
.CI/CD.Multi-Arch Builds[0]
Build images for multiple architectures (amd64, arm64, arm/v7) simultaneously using docker buildx. Use --platform flag and push manifest lists.
.CI/CD.GitHub Actions with Docker[0]
Build and push Docker images in GitHub Actions workflows. Use docker/login-action, docker/setup-buildx-action, and docker/build-push-action.
.CI/CD.Docker Layer Caching[0]
Preserve Docker image layers across CI runs. Use GitHub Actions cache or registry cache mounts to avoid rebuilding unchanged layers.
.CI/CD.Build Cache Optimization[0]
Structure Dockerfiles for maximum cache reuse: install dependencies before copying source, use cache mounts for package managers.
.Docker Desktop.Kubernetes Integration[0]
Docker Desktop includes a single-node Kubernetes cluster. Enable in Settings > Kubernetes. Use kubectl directly or via the Docker Desktop UI.
.Docker Desktop.Dev Environments[0]
Create reproducible development environments from Git repositories. Docker Desktop clones, builds, and runs the project without installing tools locally.
.Docker Desktop.Extensions[0]
Extend Docker Desktop functionality with marketplace extensions: disk usage analyzers, secret managers, database GUIs, Prometheus/Grafana, and more.
.Docker Desktop.Resource Settings[0]
Configure CPU, memory, swap, and disk image size for Docker Desktop's VM. Adjust based on workload needs (default: 2 CPUs, 8GB RAM, 64GB disk).
.Best Practices.Image Size Optimization[0]
Minimize image size: use alpine or distroless, multi-stage builds, chain RUN commands, clean package manager caches, and omit debug tools.
.Best Practices.Security Scanning[0]
Regularly scan images for vulnerabilities. Integrate scanning into CI/CD. Use docker scout, Trivy, Grype, or Snyk to detect and fix CVEs.
.Best Practices.Dockerfile Linter (Hadolint)[0]
Static analysis for Dockerfiles. Checks for best practice violations, security issues, and common mistakes. Integrates with IDEs and CI.
.Best Practices..dockerignore Deep[0]
Exclude unnecessary files from build context to speed builds, reduce image size, and avoid cache invalidation from irrelevant file changes.
