Optimize by: deferring non-critical CSS/JS, inlining critical CSS in <head>, using <link rel="preload"> for important resources, and minimizing render-blocking resources. First Contentful Paint (FCP) and Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measure perceived load speed.

SEO metadata helps search engines understand and rank your content. Essential meta tags: <title> (unique per page, 50-60 chars), <meta name="description"> (150-160 chars), Open Graph tags (Facebook, LinkedIn: og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url), Twitter Cards (twitter:card, twitter:site). Structured data using JSON-LD (Schema.org) enhances search results with rich snippets (reviews, recipes, events, FAQs, breadcrumbs). Use Google's Rich Results Test to validate structured data.

The <template> element holds HTML that is not rendered until cloned into the DOM via JavaScript. The <slot> element is used inside web components for content projection — it acts as a placeholder where the parent's light DOM content is inserted. Named slots (slot="name") allow multiple insertion points. Templates are the foundation of reusable web components and are supported in all modern browsers.

Input and output operations in HTML/CSS.

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language for creating web pages. It uses tags to structure content. HTML documents form the backbone of every website. An HTML document starts with a DOCTYPE declaration, followed by <html>, <head>, and <body> elements.

Every HTML document has a standard structure. The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration defines the document type. The <html> element wraps all content. Inside <head> we put metadata. Inside <body> we put visible content.

HTML provides six levels of headings (<h1> to <h6>) to structure content hierarchically. <h1> is most important, <h6> the least. Paragraphs use <p>. Use <br> for line breaks and <hr> for thematic breaks.

Use <strong> for importance, <em> for emphasis, <mark> for highlighted text, <small> for fine print, <del> for deleted text, and <ins> for inserted text. Use <sub> for subscript and <sup> for superscript.
HTML comments: <!-- comment -->. Attributes provide element metadata: id (unique), class (CSS class), style (inline CSS), title (tooltip). Use data-* attributes for custom data.
Links use the <a> tag with href. Use target="_blank" for new tabs. Links can target external pages, internal sections (#id), emails (mailto:), and phones (tel:).
The <img> tag embeds images. Required attributes: src (path) and alt (accessibility text). Optional: width, height, loading="lazy". Wrap in <figure>/<figcaption> for captions.
Three list types: unordered <ul>, ordered <ol>, and description <dl>. List items use <li>. Nested lists go inside <li> elements.
Tables use <table>, <tr> (row), <th> (header), <td> (data). Group with <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>. Merge cells with colspan and rowspan.
Forms collect user input. The <form> element wraps controls. Common input types: text, password, email, number, checkbox, radio, file, date. Always pair with <label>.

HTML elements are either block-level (start on a new line, take full width) or inline (flow within text). Common block: <div>, <p>, <h1>-<h6>, <section>. Common inline: <span>, <a>, <strong>, <img>. CSS display can change this behavior.
Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <footer>. This improves accessibility, SEO, and code readability.
Embed media with <audio> and <video>. Use <source> for multiple formats. The controls attribute shows playback UI. Use <track> for subtitles. Supported: MP3, MP4, WebM, OGG.
The <iframe> tag embeds another HTML page. Use sandbox for security, loading="lazy" for deferred loading, and always set title for accessibility.
SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is embeddable directly in HTML. Elements: <circle>, <rect>, <path>, <text>, <g>. SVG scales infinitely without quality loss.
The <canvas> element provides a drawable region manipulated via JavaScript. Supports 2D graphics, charts, animations, and game rendering. Unlike SVG, canvas is pixel-based.
Custom data-* attributes store extra info on elements. Access via JavaScript element.dataset. Useful for storing state or configuration without non-standard attributes.
The <picture> element provides responsive images with multiple <source> elements using media queries. Works with srcset for resolution switching.
Use <object> and <embed> for embedding PDFs, plugins, or legacy content. <param> passes parameters. Modern practice prefers native HTML or iframes.
MathML marks up mathematical notation using <math> and child elements like <mi>, <mo>, <mfrac>, <msqrt>. Natively supported in modern browsers.
HTML5 validation attributes: required (mandatory), minlength/maxlength (text length), min/max (range), pattern (regex). CSS pseudo-classes :valid/:invalid style states.
ARIA attributes supplement HTML semantics: role, aria-label, aria-hidden, aria-expanded, aria-current. Always use semantic HTML first — ARIA augments, not replaces.
Meta tags control search snippets. Key tags: description, robots, og:title (Open Graph), twitter:card. JSON-LD structured data enables rich search results.
HTML5 interactive elements: <details>/<summary> for disclosure widgets, <dialog> for modals. These provide built-in interactivity without JavaScript.

Hidden inputs (<input type="hidden">) store data not visible to users. Use for CSRF tokens, session IDs, and form state. Security measures: validate server-side, use CSRF tokens, set proper enctype, never trust hidden values.
Advanced form attributes: novalidate skips validation, enctype="multipart/form-data" for files, form attribute lets inputs live outside <form>.
Web Storage API: localStorage (persists across sessions) and sessionStorage (cleared on tab close). Both store key-value pairs as strings. ~5MB per origin.
Geolocation API accesses user location via navigator.geolocation. getCurrentPosition() for one-time, watchPosition() for tracking. Handle permission denial gracefully.
Drag and Drop API: Set draggable="true" on elements. Events: dragstart, dragover, drop. Use dataTransfer to pass data between drag source and target.
Web Workers run JS in background threads. Communicate via postMessage() / onmessage. Cannot access DOM, window, or parent. Great for CPU-intensive tasks.
Server-Sent Events (SSE) push updates from server to client over HTTP. Use EventSource to subscribe. Simpler than WebSockets for unidirectional data flow.
WebSockets provide full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection. Events: open, message, close, error. Ideal for real-time apps like chat and games.
Fetch API provides promise-based HTTP requests. fetch(url, options) returns a Response promise. Use response.json(), response.text(), or response.blob().
File API reads local files via <input type="file"> and FileReader. Blob represents binary data. Use URL.createObjectURL() for file previews.
IndexedDB is a browser-based NoSQL database. Stores structured objects with indexes for fast queries. Asynchronous API. Use for complex client-side storage beyond localStorage.
History API manipulates browser session history. pushState() adds entries, replaceState() modifies current. Listen for popstate events. Essential for SPAs.
Web Components let you create reusable custom elements. Use customElements.define(), Shadow DOM for encapsulation, <template> for markup, and <slot> for composition.
Service Workers act as proxy between browser and network. Enable offline support, caching, push notifications, and background sync. They run in a separate thread and cannot access DOM.
Proper landmark elements: exactly one <main>, one <h1>. Use <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <footer> for page regions.
Microdata adds machine-readable semantics via itemscope, itemtype, itemprop. Schema.org provides vocabulary. Enables rich search results like stars, prices, and recipes.
Optimize HTML delivery: use defer for scripts, rel="preload" for critical assets, rel="preconnect" for third-party origins, inline critical CSS. Reduce DOM size and render-blocking resources.
Lazy loading defers off-screen resources. Use loading="lazy" on images/iframes. Resource hints: preload (critical), prefetch (future), preconnect (early connection).
WCAG principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust (POUR). Target WCAG 2.1 AA minimum. Use skip links, proper heading hierarchy, sufficient color contrast, keyboard navigation.
On-page SEO: descriptive title tags (50-60 chars), unique meta descriptions (150-160 chars), heading hierarchy, image alt text, canonical URLs, clean URL structure with hyphens.
Mobile-first starts with smallest screens and enhances. Essential: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">. Use relative units and touch targets of min 44x44px.
Security: use rel="noopener noreferrer" on external links, sandbox on iframes, Content Security Policy headers. Sanitize user input. Beware of XSS, clickjacking, form hijacking.
Internationalization: use lang attribute on <html>, dir="rtl" for right-to-left, hreflang for alternate language versions, UTF-8 encoding.
Always validate HTML using the W3C Validator. Common issues: unclosed tags, duplicate IDs, improper nesting, missing alt attributes, deprecated elements like <center> or <font>.

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the visual presentation of HTML. Rules consist of a selector and a declaration block with properties and values. Apply via inline, internal (<style>), or external (.css file).
CSS selectors target elements: element (p), class (.my-class), id (#my-id), attribute ([type="text"]), universal (*). Combinators: descendant (div p), child (div > p), sibling (h2 + p).
Color formats: named (red), hex (#FF5733), RGB (rgb(255, 87, 51)), RGBA (rgba(255, 87, 51, 0.5)), HSL/HSLA. Units: px, em (relative to parent font), rem (relative to root), %, vw/vh, ch.

Typography properties: font-family, font-size, font-weight (100-900), font-style, text-align, text-decoration, text-transform, line-height, letter-spacing. Use web fonts via @font-face or Google Fonts.
Every element is a box: content (inner), padding (around content), border (edge), margin (outside). Use box-sizing: border-box to include padding/border in width.
CSS custom properties (variables) defined with --name, accessed with var(--name). They cascade and can be overridden, enabling easy theme systems.
CSS specificity determines which rule wins. Inline > ID > Class > Element. When equal, last rule wins. Use !important sparingly — it breaks the natural cascade.
Some CSS properties inherit from parent elements: color, font-family, line-height. Others like margin, padding, border do not. Control with inherit, initial, unset, revert.
The @layer rule defines cascade layers. Styles in later layers override earlier ones regardless of specificity. Use to organize resets, base styles, components, and utilities in predictable order.

Browsers apply default styles inconsistently. CSS resets remove all defaults (margin: 0, padding: 0). Normalize.css preserves useful defaults while fixing cross-browser differences. Choose based on project needs.
The display property controls rendering: block (full width, new line), inline (flows with text), inline-block (inline but accepts width/height), none (hidden, removed from flow). Modern: flex, grid.
Flexbox is a 1D layout model. Container: display: flex. Main axis: justify-content. Cross axis: align-items. Items wrap with flex-wrap, grow with flex-grow, order with order.
CSS Grid is a 2D layout system. Define columns with grid-template-columns, rows with grid-template-rows. Use grid-area with named template areas for complex layouts.
position values: static (default), relative (offset from normal), absolute (relative to positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to viewport), sticky (toggles between relative/fixed on scroll).
Media queries adapt layouts to screen sizes. Use @media (min-width: ...) for mobile-first approach. Common breakpoints: 576px (mobile), 768px (tablet), 992px (desktop), 1200px (wide).

Background properties: background-color, background-image, background-size, background-position, background-repeat. Gradients: linear-gradient() and radial-gradient(). Multiple backgrounds can be layered.
CSS animations use @keyframes to define sequences. The animation shorthand: name, duration, timing function, delay, iteration count, direction, fill mode.
Style lists with list-style-type, list-style-position, list-style-image. CSS counters (counter-reset, counter-increment) create numbered headings, table-of-contents, or custom list numbering.

Style form elements using CSS: inputs, textareas, selects, checkboxes, radio buttons, and buttons. Normalize browser defaults. Use :focus, :valid, :invalid, :disabled pseudo-classes for state styling.
The box-shadow property adds shadows: offset-x offset-y blur-radius spread-radius color. Multiple shadows can be layered. Use inset for inner shadows.
Text styling: text-shadow for shadows, text-overflow for ellipsis, word-break for breaking long words, white-space for spacing control, text-wrap for wrapping behavior.
CSS filter applies visual effects: blur(), brightness(), contrast(), grayscale(), sepia(), hue-rotate(), drop-shadow(). mix-blend-mode blends elements with their background.
clip-path clips elements to a shape: circle(), ellipse(), polygon(), inset(). shape-outside makes text wrap around a shape.
object-fit controls how replaced elements (images, videos) fit their container: fill, contain, cover, none, scale-down. object-position sets alignment within the box.
overflow controls content overflow: visible, hidden, scroll, auto. overflow-x/overflow-y for axis-specific. scroll-behavior: smooth for smooth scrolling. scroll-snap for snap points.
The cursor property changes the mouse cursor: pointer, grab, text, not-allowed, wait. pointer-events controls click/touch behavior: auto (default), none (disable), visiblePainted (SVG).

The resize property makes elements user-resizable: both, horizontal, vertical. field-sizing makes textareas/contenteditable auto-size. object-view-box crops replaced elements without changing the image.
Multi-column layout with column-count, column-width, column-gap, column-rule. Content flows automatically between columns. Useful for text-heavy layouts like newspapers.
Scalable CSS methodologies: BEM (Block Element Modifier) uses naming like .block__element--modifier. Prevents conflicts and improves maintainability by enforcing naming conventions.
CSS preprocessors extend CSS with variables, nesting, mixins, functions. SCSS features: $variables, @mixin/@include, & parent selector, built-in functions for colors and math.
The @layer rule controls cascade layer order. Later layers override earlier ones regardless of specificity. Useful for organizing resets, components, and utilities.
Container queries (@container) style elements based on container size rather than viewport. Define a containment context with container-type. Enables truly reusable components.
CSS nesting (native) lets you nest selectors like SCSS. The @scope rule limits styles to a subtree, providing better encapsulation without Shadow DOM.
Logical properties use flow-relative directions: margin-inline-start instead of margin-left, padding-block instead of padding-top/padding-bottom. Better for internationalization and RTL support.
Powerful CSS functions: calc() for math, min()/max()/clamp() for responsive values, attr() for HTML attributes, url() for resources, var() for variables.
content-visibility skips rendering of off-screen elements for performance. contain isolates layout/style/paint. content-visibility: auto automatically skips hidden content.
Modern CSS color functions: color-mix() blends colors, color() accesses wider gamuts (Display P3, sRGB), lch()/lab() for perceptually uniform colors, oklch()/oklab() for better gradients.

The @property rule defines typed CSS custom properties with initial values and inheritance control. Enables animation of custom properties, validation, and better developer ergonomics.
.CSS Advanced Topics.Container Query Units & Style Queries[0]
Container query units: cqw (1% container width), cqh (1% height), cqi (1% inline size), cqb (1% block size), cqmin/cqmax. Style queries (@container style()) query computed style values.
View Transitions animate between page states or navigations. Use @view-transition navigation rule, view-transition-name on elements, and ::view-transition-* pseudo-elements for custom animations.
Beyond BEM: SMACSS (categorizes into base/layout/module/state/theme), ITCSS (layers by specificity), OOCSS (separates structure from skin, container from content). Choose what fits your project.
PostCSS is a tool for transforming CSS with JavaScript plugins. Autoprefixer automatically adds vendor prefixes (-webkit-, -moz-, etc.). Other plugins enable future CSS syntax today.
Utility-first CSS uses small, composable classes. Tailwind CSS provides .flex, .text-center, .p-4 etc. Encourages design consistency and reduces CSS file size. Trade-off: verbose HTML.
CSS Modules generate locally scoped class names. Imported like JS modules. Class names are hashed at build time to avoid conflicts. Works well with component frameworks like React, Vue, Svelte.
Advanced Grid: subgrid passes grid tracks to children. auto-fill/auto-fit for responsive grids without media queries. grid-auto-flow: dense fills gaps automatically.

CSS performance: minimize specificity chains, avoid expensive properties (box-shadow, border-radius), use will-change sparingly, avoid @import, reduce repaints/reflows, use GPU-accelerated properties (transform, opacity).

Browser DevTools: inspect computed styles, trace specificity, toggle pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus), edit live CSS, view box model diagram, debug animations with timeline. Use outline to visualize elements.

Print stylesheets optimize pages for paper: hide nav/sidebars/ads, use page-break-* properties, ensure link URLs print. Accessibility: respect prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme, prefers-contrast, forced-colors.

A class is a blueprint for objects. It defines fields (state) and methods (behavior). An object is an instance of a class, created with the new keyword followed by a constructor. The constructor initializes the object's state. Java supports method overloading (multiple methods with same name but different parameters). The this keyword refers to the current instance. Classes can have static members that belong to the class itself, not instances.

Inheritance allows a class to derive fields and methods from a parent class using the extends keyword. Java supports single class inheritance (one parent per class) but multiple interface inheritance. The super keyword accesses parent class members. All classes implicitly extend Object. Method overriding allows a subclass to provide a specific implementation of a parent method — the @Override annotation is recommended. Constructors are not inherited; the subclass constructor must call super(). Final classes cannot be subclassed.

Interfaces define contracts that implementing classes must fulfill. Before Java 8, interfaces had only abstract methods and constants. Java 8 added default methods (with body) and static methods. Java 9 added private methods. Functional interfaces (with a single abstract method) enable lambda expressions. Common interfaces: Runnable, Comparator, Callable, Consumer, Function, Predicate, Supplier. Default methods allow interfaces to evolve without breaking existing implementations. Use @FunctionalInterface to mark single-abstract-method interfaces.

Constructors initialize objects. They have the same name as the class and no return type. If no constructor is defined, Java provides a default no-arg constructor. You can overload constructors. The this() call invokes another constructor in the same class (must be the first statement). A private constructor prevents external instantiation (used in singletons and utility classes). Records (Java 16+) automatically generate canonical constructors.

Access modifiers control visibility. public: accessible from anywhere. protected: accessible within the same package and subclasses. default (package-private): accessible only within the same package (no modifier). private: accessible only within the same class. Apply to classes, methods, and fields. A top-level class can be public or package-private. Inner classes can have all four. Good encapsulation: make fields private, provide public getters/setters if needed. Protected methods are part of the API for subclass implementers.

The static keyword makes a member belong to the class rather than instances. Static fields are shared across all instances — only one copy exists. Static methods can be called without an instance and cannot access instance members directly. Static initialization blocks run once when the class is first loaded. Static imports (import static) bring static members into scope without qualifying them. Static nested classes behave like top-level classes but are enclosed for packaging. Common uses: utility methods, constants, counters.

Encapsulation hides internal state and requires all interaction through methods. Achieve by marking fields private and providing public getters/setters. This protects data integrity by allowing validation in setters, enables changing implementation without affecting callers, and makes code more maintainable. JavaBeans convention uses getX() for getters and setX() for setters. For boolean fields, the getter is often isX(). Immutable objects take encapsulation further — no setters, all fields final, defensive copying in constructors.

Polymorphism means 'many forms'. It allows objects of different types to respond to the same method call in their own way. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading (same name, different parameters). Runtime polymorphism is method overriding — the JVM decides at runtime which method to call based on the actual object type, not the reference type. This is the foundation of the Strategy and Template Method patterns. Polymorphism enables programming to interfaces rather than implementations.

Anonymous classes are one-use classes defined inline with new Interface/Class() { ... }. They can implement interfaces or extend classes, have fields, and override methods. Before Java 8, they were essential for event listeners and comparators. Lambdas (Java 8+) replaced them for functional interfaces. Anonymous classes can access effectively-final local variables and enclosing instance members. They create a .class file per usage while lambdas use invokedynamic. Use anonymous classes when implementing interfaces with multiple methods.

Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential features. Abstract classes (declared with abstract) can have both abstract methods (no body, must be overridden) and concrete methods. They can have constructors and fields. Interfaces (declared with interface) originally had only abstract methods, but Java 8+ added default and static methods. An abstract class models 'is-a' relationships with shared state; interfaces model 'can-do' capabilities. Java doesn't support multiple class inheritance, but a class can implement multiple interfaces.

Enums (enum keyword) define a fixed set of named constants. They are implicitly final subclasses of java.lang.Enum. Enums can have fields, constructors, methods, and implement interfaces. Each constant can have its own body with overridden methods. Enums provide type safety (no invalid values), built-in methods like values() and valueOf(), and switch compatibility. Use enums instead of int constants or String constants for fixed sets like days, colors, status codes, or configuration options.

Java supports four kinds of nested classes. Static nested classes: behave like top-level classes but are packaged inside another class for namespace grouping. Inner classes (non-static): have access to enclosing instance's fields/methods. Local classes: defined inside a method, visible only within the block. Anonymous classes: one-use classes defined inline with new Interface/Class() { ... }. Anonymous classes are often replaced by lambdas (functional interfaces). Inner classes hold a reference to the enclosing instance — can cause memory leaks.

Every class inherits from Object. Three critical overridable methods: equals (value equality), hashCode (hash-based collections), toString (string representation). Contract: if a.equals(b), a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Always override hashCode when overriding equals. Use Objects.hash() for simple hash codes. toString should include all significant fields for debugging. Records (Java 16+) auto-generate all three. Use Objects.equals for null-safe equality checks. IDE templates generate correct implementations reliably.

Favor composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a). Composition uses interfaces and delegation instead of deep class hierarchies. Benefits: more flexible (change behavior at runtime), looser coupling, easier testing (mock dependencies), no fragile base class problem. Implement: declare an interface, implement with a class, pass dependencies via constructor. The Decorator pattern uses composition. Inheritance is appropriate for true is-a relationships with shared behavior and template method pattern.

Records (Java 16+) are transparent carriers for immutable data. They automatically generate a canonical constructor, accessor methods (componentName()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). All fields are private final. Records cannot extend other classes (they implicitly extend java.lang.Record) but can implement interfaces. Compact constructors allow validation without explicit field assignment. Use records for DTOs, value objects, and any data carrier where boilerplate would otherwise make code verbose.
Input and output operations in Java.

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed for platform independence via the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Its 'write once, run anywhere' philosophy means compiled Java bytecode runs on any device with a JVM. Java was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems and first released in 1995. It is statically typed, garbage-collected, and has a vast ecosystem of libraries and frameworks. Java is one of the most popular languages for enterprise software, Android development, and large-scale distributed systems.

The Java ecosystem has three key components. JVM (Java Virtual Machine) executes Java bytecode — it's the runtime engine. JRE (Java Runtime Environment) includes the JVM plus core libraries needed to run Java applications. JDK (Java Development Kit) includes the JRE plus development tools like compiler (javac), debugger (jdb), and archiver (jar). To develop Java, you need the JDK. To only run Java programs, the JRE suffices. Modern practice: always install the JDK. Java 11+ offers a single JDK download that includes everything.

Java syntax is C-family: classes, methods, statements end with semicolons, blocks use curly braces. Every Java application must have a main method with the exact signature 'public static void main(String[] args)'. File names must match the public class name. Java is case-sensitive. The entry point is always the main method. A Java source file can have at most one public class, and the file must be named after it.

Java has three comment styles. Single-line comments start with // and extend to the end of the line. Multi-line comments are enclosed between /* and */. Javadoc comments /** ... */ are a special multi-line format processed by the javadoc tool to generate API documentation. Javadoc is widely used in the Java ecosystem and supports tags like @param, @return, and @see. Writing clear Javadoc is considered a professional best practice.

var (Java 10+) infers the type of a local variable from its initializer. It reduces boilerplate for obvious types (e.g., var list = new ArrayList<String>()). var can only be used for local variables, for-each loop variables, and try-with-resources. It cannot be used for fields, method parameters, or return types. var requires an initializer and cannot be null without explicit type. Overuse harms readability — use var when the right-hand side clearly indicates the type.

Autoboxing automatically converts primitives to their wrapper types (int → Integer, boolean → Boolean, etc.). Unboxing converts wrappers back to primitives. This happens in assignments, method arguments, arithmetic, and collections. Wrappers are immutable. Beware: null wrapper unboxing throws NullPointerException. Equality: == on wrappers compares references, not values (use .equals()). Integer caching: values -128 to 127 are cached. Performance: autoboxing in loops creates many objects — avoid in hot paths.

Java has 8 primitive types and reference types. Primitives: byte (8-bit), short (16), int (32), long (64), float (32-bit IEEE 754), double (64), char (16-bit Unicode), boolean. Reference types include classes, interfaces, arrays, and enums. Primitives store values directly in memory; reference types store references (pointers) to objects. The default value for numeric primitives is 0, for boolean it's false, and for reference types it's null. Java does not have unsigned primitives (except char).

Java variables must be declared with a type before use. Scope determines where a variable is accessible: local variables (inside methods/blocks), instance variables (inside class, outside methods — belong to object), and static variables (class-level, shared across all instances). Local variables must be initialized before use. Instance and static variables get default values. Block-scoped variables (declared inside {}) are only visible within that block.

Type casting converts a value from one type to another. Widening (implicit) converts smaller to larger types automatically — int to long for example. Narrowing (explicit) requires a cast operator because data may be lost — long to int with (int). Primitive casting can lose precision for floating-point to integer. Reference casting works up and down the inheritance hierarchy: upcasting (subclass → superclass) is automatic; downcasting requires explicit cast and may throw ClassCastException.

Java provides a full set of operators. Arithmetic: + - * / %. Relational: == != < > <= >=. Logical: && || !. Bitwise: & | ^ ~ << >> >>>. Assignment: = += -= etc. Increment/decrement: ++ -- (prefix/postfix). Ternary: ? : . Operator precedence matters — use parentheses for clarity. The + operator is overloaded: adds numbers or concatenates strings. Integer division truncates toward zero. The remainder % can be negative if the dividend is negative.

Java has if-else and switch statements. if-else chains evaluate boolean expressions. Switch works with int, char, String (Java 7+), and enums. Java 14+ introduced switch expressions with arrow syntax, which don't fall through and can return values. Switch expressions must be exhaustive (cover all cases). Pattern matching for switch (preview in Java 17+, stable in Java 21) allows type-based matching. Always handle the default case in switch, even if just for safety.

Java supports for, enhanced for-each, while, and do-while loops. The classic for loop has initialization, condition, and update. The enhanced for-each iterates over arrays and Iterables cleanly. The while loop runs while a condition is true. The do-while loop runs at least once then checks the condition. Break exits the loop entirely; continue skips to the next iteration. Labels (outer:) can control which loop break/continue applies to in nested loops.

Arrays in Java are fixed-size, zero-indexed containers for elements of the same type. They are objects, created with new or with array literal syntax. The length property gives the number of elements. Arrays can be multidimensional. The java.util.Arrays class provides utility methods: sort, binarySearch, fill, copyOf, toString, deepEquals. Arrays are covariant (String[] is a subtype of Object[]), which can cause runtime ArrayStoreException. For dynamic sizing, use ArrayList instead.

The string pool (intern pool) stores unique String literals to save memory. String literals are automatically interned. new String("text") creates a new object on the heap (not pooled). intern() returns the canonical representation from the pool. The pool is garbage-collected. All compile-time constant expressions are interned. In Java 7+, the pool moved from PermGen to the heap. Use intern() sparingly — it can cause performance issues with many unique strings. Deduplication via G1 GC is automatic.

String is immutable in Java — once created, its value cannot change. String literals are interned (stored in a pool) and reused. String concatenation with + creates new strings; for repeated concatenation, use StringBuilder (unsynchronized) or StringBuffer (synchronized). Key methods: length, charAt, substring, indexOf, replace, split, trim, toLowerCase, toUpperCase, equals, equalsIgnoreCase, compareTo. Use equals() for value comparison, == for reference comparison.

Try-with-resources (Java 7+) automatically closes resources implementing AutoCloseable. Multiple resources separated by semicolons. Resources are closed in reverse order of declaration. Suppressed exceptions: if both try block and close() throw, the close exception is suppressed (accessible via getSuppressed()). Custom resources implement AutoCloseable (close throws Exception) or Closeable (close throws IOException). Use try-with-resources for files, streams, database connections, and any Closeable resource.

Java uses try-catch-finally for exception handling. Exceptions are objects representing abnormal conditions. Checked exceptions (extends Exception) must be declared or caught — the compiler enforces this. Unchecked exceptions (extends RuntimeException) don't require handling. Use try-with-resources (Java 7+) to auto-close resources like streams. The finally block always executes. Multi-catch (Java 7+) lets you catch multiple exception types in one block. Custom exceptions extend Exception or RuntimeException.

Effective exception handling follows guidelines: catch specific exceptions, not Throwable or Exception. Don't swallow exceptions with empty catch blocks. Use finally or try-with-resources for cleanup. Throw early, catch late — throw where detected, catch at appropriate abstraction boundary. Wrap low-level exceptions in domain-specific exceptions (exception translation). Log exceptions where caught, not where thrown. Preserve the original exception as cause when wrapping. Avoid exception control flow — don't use exceptions for normal program logic. Prefer unchecked exceptions for programming errors (IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException). Fail-fast: validate inputs early with Objects.requireNonNull() and input validation.

Lambda expressions (Java 8+) provide a concise way to represent anonymous functions. Syntax: (parameters) -> expression or { body }. They can only be used with functional interfaces (interfaces with one abstract method). Parameters can be explicitly typed or inferred. Single parameter parentheses are optional. The lambda body can be a single expression (no return needed) or a block. Lambdas can capture effectively final variables from the enclosing scope. They enable functional-style programming and make code more expressive.

Primitive streams (IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream) avoid boxing overhead. They provide range(), rangeClosed(), sum(), average(), summaryStatistics(), mapToObj(), boxed(). Primitive optionals (OptionalInt, OptionalLong, OptionalDouble) avoid boxing for optional values. Stream.toList() collects to a List but doesn't guarantee mutability. Use .collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new)) for mutable lists. Parallel streams use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() by default.

Functional interfaces have exactly one abstract method. Java provides built-in functional interfaces in java.util.function: Function<T,R> (maps T→R), Consumer<T> (accepts T, returns void), Supplier<T> (supplies T), Predicate<T> (tests T, returns boolean), UnaryOperator<T> (T→T), BinaryOperator<T> (T,T→T). Primitive variants avoid boxing: IntFunction, LongConsumer, DoublePredicate, etc. @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended — it causes compile error if the interface doesn't meet the contract.

Method references are shorthand for lambdas that call an existing method. Four kinds: Class::staticMethod, object::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod (first parameter becomes the receiver), and Class::new (constructor reference). Method references make code more readable by naming the method explicitly. They work wherever functional interfaces are expected. Static method reference: Math::max. Instance method reference: list::add. Instance method of arbitrary object: String::length. Constructor reference: ArrayList::new.

The Stream API (Java 8+) processes sequences of elements declaratively. Streams don't store data; they pipeline operations. Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, peek) return a new stream. Terminal operations (collect, forEach, reduce, count, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch, findFirst, findAny) produce a result or side effect. Streams are lazy — intermediate operations execute only when a terminal operation is invoked. Streams cannot be reused. Common collectors: toList(), toSet(), toMap(), groupingBy(), joining().

Collectors (java.util.stream.Collectors) accumulate stream elements into containers. Common collectors: toList(), toSet(), toMap(), toCollection(), joining(), counting(), summarizingDouble(), partitioningBy(), groupingBy(). toMap handles key collisions with a merge function. groupingBy(classifier, downstream) enables nested grouping. downstream can be another collector (counting, mapping, filtering, flatMapping, collectingAndThen). teeing (Java 12+) merges two independent collectors. Custom collectors via Collector.of() for specialized accumulations.

Optional<T> (Java 8+) is a container that may or may not hold a value, designed to reduce null pointer exceptions. It forces callers to handle the absent case explicitly. Common creation: Optional.of(value) (non-null), Optional.ofNullable(value), Optional.empty(). Key methods: isPresent(), ifPresent(consumer), orElse(default), orElseGet(supplier), orElseThrow(exceptionSupplier), map(), flatMap(), filter(), isEmpty() (Java 11+). Optional is not serializable and should not be used for fields, method parameters, or collection elements.

List is an ordered, indexed collection that allows duplicates. Implementations: ArrayList (resizable array — fast random access, slow insertion/deletion in middle), LinkedList (doubly-linked — fast insertion/deletion at ends, slow random access), Vector (legacy synchronized array), CopyOnWriteArrayList (thread-safe, copy-on-write). Key methods: add, get, set, remove, indexOf, contains, size, isEmpty, clear, subList, sort. Lists support iteration with for-each, iterator, listIterator, and streams. Use List.of() (Java 9+) for immutable lists.

Set is a collection with no duplicate elements. Implementations: HashSet (hash table — O(1) operations, no ordering guarantee), LinkedHashSet (hash + linked list — insertion order), TreeSet (red-black tree — sorted order, O(log n)), EnumSet (bit vector — extremely fast for enums). Key methods: add, remove, contains, size, isEmpty, addAll, retainAll, removeAll. Sets rely on equals() and hashCode() for element comparison. TreeSet requires Comparable or a Comparator. CopyOnWriteArraySet provides thread safety.

Map stores key-value pairs. Implementations: HashMap (hash table — O(1) operations, no ordering), LinkedHashMap (insertion or access order), TreeMap (sorted by keys, O(log n)), EnumMap (keys are enum type, extremely fast), WeakHashMap, IdentityHashMap, ConcurrentHashMap (thread-safe). Key methods: put, get, getOrDefault, remove, containsKey, containsValue, keySet, values, entrySet, putIfAbsent, replace, merge, compute, forEach. Null keys: HashMap allows one null key; TreeMap does not (NPE).

Queue follows FIFO (first-in-first-out). Deque supports insertion/removal at both ends. Key implementations: LinkedList (Queue/Deque), ArrayDeque (fast, no capacity limit, preferred over Stack), PriorityQueue (heap-based priority ordering), ConcurrentLinkedDeque (thread-safe). Queue methods: offer/add (insert), poll/remove (retrieve and remove), peek/element (retrieve without remove). Deque adds: addFirst, addLast, offerFirst, offerLast, pollFirst, pollLast, peekFirst, peekLast. ArrayDeque is faster than Stack and LinkedList for queue/deque operations.

Java provides both unmodifiable views (Collections.unmodifiableXxx()) and immutable collections (List.of(), Set.of(), Map.of() Java 9+, List.copyOf() Java 10+). Unmodifiable wrappers delegate to the backing collection — if the backing collection changes, the view changes. Immutable collections guarantee no changes: of() factories reject nulls, copyOf() copies defensively. Immutable collections are memory-efficient (no capacity overhead) and thread-safe without synchronization. Stream.toList() (Java 16+) returns an immutable list. Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size, modifiable list backed by the array.

ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array — O(1) random access, O(n) insertion/deletion at middle, amortized O(1) append. LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list — O(n) random access, O(1) insertion/deletion at ends, O(1) removal with ListIterator. Memory: ArrayList is more compact (contiguous array). LinkedList has per-node overhead. Use ArrayList for most cases — its predictable performance and cache-friendliness win. Use LinkedList only when frequent head insertion/deletion or when implementing a queue/deque (ArrayDeque is preferred).

Java provides multiple sorting approaches. Comparable (natural order) via compareTo. Comparator (custom order) via compare or factory methods. Arrays.sort() and Collections.sort() use TimSort (O(n log n)). List.sort() (Java 8+) sorts in-place. Stream.sorted() returns a new stream. Comparator factory methods: comparing, thenComparing, reversed, naturalOrder, nullsFirst, nullsLast. For primitives, Arrays.sort uses Dual-Pivot Quicksort.

java.util.Collections provides static utility methods for collections. Key methods: sort, binarySearch, reverse, shuffle, rotate, fill, copy, swap, min, max, frequency, disjoint, singletonList, unmodifiableList, synchronizedList, checkedList. Use Collections.emptyList/set/map for immutable empty collections. Collections.unmodifiableXxx creates read-only views. Collections.synchronizedXxx wraps collections for thread safety (though ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList are preferred). Collections.checkedXxx provides type safety at runtime.

Generics (Java 5+) enable type-safe programming by parameterizing types. A generic class uses type parameters in angle brackets. The compiler enforces type consistency, eliminating casts and preventing ClassCastException at runtime. Type parameters are conventionally single uppercase letters: E (element), K (key), V (value), T (type), N (number), S/U (other types). The diamond operator <> (Java 7+) infers type arguments. Raw types (without <>) should never be used — they bypass type checking. Generic information is erased at runtime (type erasure).

Generic methods introduce their own type parameters, independent of the class's type parameters. The type parameter is declared before the return type in angle brackets. Type inference determines the type from arguments. Generic methods enable algorithms that work with multiple types while maintaining type safety. They're commonly used in utility classes for sorting, searching, or transforming collections. Bounded type parameters (<T extends Comparable<T>>) restrict types to those with specific capabilities.

Wildcards (?) represent unknown types in generics. Unbounded wildcards <?> accept any type. Upper-bounded wildcards <? extends T> accept T or any subtype. Lower-bounded wildcards <? super T> accept T or any supertype. Wildcards enable flexibility when the exact type parameter is unknown. The PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) principle guides usage: use extends when reading values (producer), use super when writing values (consumer). Wildcards cannot appear in type parameter definitions, only in usage contexts.

Java infers generic types from context in method calls (diamond operator, Java 7+), lambda parameters, and method return types. The compiler uses target-type inference: it looks at the expected type (assignment target, method parameter) to determine type parameters. Type inference can fail with ambiguous targets — provide explicit type witnesses (ClassName.<Type>method()) or cast. Java 8+ significantly improved inference with lambda expressions and method references. Java 10+ var uses local variable type inference.

Type erasure removes generic type information at compile time, replacing type parameters with their bounds (or Object if unbounded). This enables backward compatibility with pre-generics code. The compiler adds casts where needed and generates bridge methods for polymorphism. Erasure means you cannot use instanceof with parameterized types, create arrays of parameterized types, or use primitive type parameters. Understanding erasure is essential for advanced patterns and troubleshooting ClassCastException from raw type interop. Reflection cannot retrieve generic type arguments at runtime (with some exceptions for field declarations).

RandomAccessFile supports reading/writing at arbitrary positions in a file. It implements DataInput/DataOutput for typed I/O. The mode parameter: "r" (read), "rw" (read/write), "rws"/"rwd" (synchronous writes). seek(position) moves the file pointer. MappedByteBuffer (via FileChannel.map()) memory-maps a file region for extremely fast access. Memory-mapped files are ideal for large files, databases, and shared memory. Prefer NIO channels and mapped buffers for performance-critical file I/O.

Java I/O uses streams for sequential data input/output. Byte streams (InputStream, OutputStream) handle binary data. Character streams (Reader, Writer) handle text with encoding support. Key classes: FileInputStream/FileOutputStream for files, BufferedInputStream/BufferedOutputStream for buffering, InputStreamReader/OutputStreamWriter for character conversion, BufferedReader/PrintWriter for line-oriented text. Always close streams in finally blocks or use try-with-resources (Java 7+). The decorator pattern layers streams for added functionality (buffering, filtering, compression).

Java NIO (New I/O, Java 1.4+; NIO.2, Java 7+) provides non-blocking I/O, channels, buffers, selectors, and file system API. The java.nio.file package (Java 7+) includes high-level file operations: Path, Files, FileSystem, FileVisitor. Key Files methods: readAllLines, write, copy, move, delete, createDirectories, walk, find, lines (lazy stream), probeContentType. Path represents a file system path. Files.lines() returns a Stream<String> for efficient large file processing. PathMatcher handles glob patterns.

java.util.zip provides GZIP and ZIP compression. GZIP compresses single streams (common in HTTP, file transfer). ZIP handles multiple files with a directory structure. Use GZIPOutputStream/GZIPInputStream for compression. ZipOutputStream/ZipInputStream for archives. Deflater/Inflater for raw compression. Compress before storing or transmitting large data. Use buffered streams for performance. Compression level (0-9): 0 = no compression, 9 = maximum. Default is -1 (platform-specific).

Serialization converts an object into a byte stream for storage or transmission. Implement Serializable (marker interface — no methods). Use ObjectOutputStream for writing and ObjectInputStream for reading. The transient keyword excludes fields from serialization. serialVersionUID ensures class version compatibility — always declare it explicitly. Externalizable provides custom serialization logic. Java's built-in serialization is considered slow and has security risks — prefer JSON, Protocol Buffers, or similar for new projects. Records are serializable by default.

Java provides built-in threading via the Thread class and the Runnable interface. Extending Thread is simpler but limits inheritance. Implementing Runnable is more flexible and follows composition over inheritance. The run() method contains the thread's work; start() launches a new thread. Thread states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED. Use Thread.sleep(millis) for pauses. Interrupt a thread with interrupt() and check with isInterrupted() or InterruptedException. For simple tasks, use virtual threads (Java 21+) or ExecutorService instead.

Synchronization prevents thread interference and memory consistency errors. The synchronized keyword creates a mutual exclusion lock (intrinsic lock or monitor). Synchronized instance methods lock on 'this'. Static synchronized methods lock on the Class object. Synchronized blocks allow specifying the lock object for finer granularity. Volatile guarantees visibility of writes across threads (but not atomicity). Locks are reentrant — a thread can acquire a lock it already holds. Deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other's locks indefinitely — avoid by consistent lock ordering.

ExecutorService (Java 5+) manages a pool of threads and decouples task submission from execution. Factory methods in Executors: newFixedThreadPool(n), newCachedThreadPool(), newSingleThreadExecutor(), newScheduledThreadPool(). Submit tasks via execute(Runnable) or submit(Callable<T>) which returns Future<T>. shutdown() gracefully stops accepting tasks; shutdownNow() attempts to stop running tasks. ScheduledExecutorService supports delayed and periodic execution. For CPU-bound tasks, pool size ≈ availableProcessors. For I/O-bound, a larger pool is appropriate.

CompletableFuture (Java 8+) represents a future result that can be manually completed and supports functional composition. Factory methods: supplyAsync (returns value), runAsync (no return). Composition: thenApply (transform), thenAccept (consume), thenRun (run after), thenCompose (flatMap for futures), thenCombine (merge two), allOf (wait for all), anyOf (wait for first). Async variants accept an Executor. exceptionally/ handle for error recovery. thenApply vs thenCompose: apply wraps value, compose returns new CompletableFuture. CompletableFuture enables declarative asynchronous programming without blocking.

java.util.concurrent.atomic provides lock-free, thread-safe atomic operations on single variables. Classes: AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference, LongAdder (high-contention counter), AtomicIntegerArray, AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater. Methods: get, set, compareAndSet, getAndIncrement, updateAndGet. java.util.concurrent.locks provides Lock, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock. ReentrantLock offers tryLock (non-blocking attempt), fair ordering, and Condition. Prefer atomic classes for simple counters/flags, ReentrantLock for complex synchronization.

ForkJoinPool (Java 7+) is a work-stealing thread pool designed for divide-and-conquer tasks. The common pool (ForkJoinPool.commonPool()) is shared across all parallel streams and CompletableFuture. RecursiveAction (no result) and RecursiveTask<V> (result) model fork/join tasks. Parallel streams use the common pool by default. ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker allows threads to block without starving the pool. The pool size defaults to Runtime.availableProcessors() - 1. Custom pools isolate parallel workloads from the common pool.

Virtual threads (Java 21+, preview in Java 19-20) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the OS. Millions of virtual threads can run on a small number of OS threads. They are ideal for I/O-bound workloads where threads spend time waiting. Create with Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) or Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Virtual threads use carrier threads (platform threads) from a ForkJoinPool. They cannot be prioritized or daemon-set. Pinning occurs when virtual threads block in synchronized blocks or native methods — avoid synchronized in favor of ReentrantLock.

Maven is a build automation and project management tool using XML (pom.xml) for configuration. It follows convention over configuration: standard directory layout (src/main/java, src/test/java). Key concepts: coordinates (groupId:artifactId:version), dependencies, plugins, profiles, lifecycle phases (compile, test, package, install, deploy). The pom.xml defines the project. Maven downloads dependencies from repositories (Maven Central). Common commands: mvn clean, compile, test, package, install. Maven ensures reproducible builds across environments.

Maven's build lifecycle has three built-in lifecycles: default (main build), clean (cleanup), site (documentation). The default lifecycle phases: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy. Plugins bind to lifecycle phases — maven-compiler-plugin (compile), maven-surefire-plugin (test), maven-jar-plugin (package), maven-install-plugin (install). Plugin configuration in pom.xml under <build><plugins>. Profiles (mvn -P profile-name) enable environment-specific config. Multi-module projects with <modules> parent POM.

Gradle is a build automation tool using Groovy or Kotlin DSL. It uses a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks, supporting incremental builds, caching, and parallel execution. build.gradle (Groovy) or build.gradle.kts (Kotlin) defines the build. Key concepts: plugins, dependencies, tasks, configurations. Gradle Wrapper (gradlew) ensures consistent versions across environments. Benefits over Maven: faster builds (incremental, caching), more concise syntax, flexibility with custom tasks. Gradle is the default for Android development.

Large Java projects benefit from multi-module builds and performance tuning. Gradle features: build caching (reuses outputs from previous builds), parallel execution (--parallel), configuration on demand, incremental compilation, Gradle Build Cache Server. Maven features: -T for parallel builds, multi-threaded resolver, incremental compilation. Common patterns: modular projects (api, impl, test modules), dependency locking (gradle.lockfile / maven-lockfile), version catalogs (libs.versions.toml), convention plugins (shared build logic), composite builds for multi-repo development. Profile builds to find bottlenecks.

Flyway is a database migration tool using versioned SQL scripts. Migration files follow naming: V<version>__<description>.sql (e.g., V1__create_users.sql, V2__add_email.sql). Flyway tracks applied migrations in a schema_history table. Commands: migrate, clean, info, validate, baseline, repair. Spring Boot auto-configures Flyway if present on classpath. Make migrations idempotent and never modify committed migration files. Use generated (repeatable) migrations for views/functions.

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is the standard API for connecting Java applications to relational databases. Steps: load driver (auto-loaded in JDBC 4+), get Connection, create Statement/PreparedStatement, execute query, process ResultSet, close resources. PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection by parameterizing queries. Connection pooling (HikariCP) is essential for production. Transaction management: setAutoCommit(false), commit(), rollback(). JDBC is low-level and verbose — most projects use JPA, Spring Data, or jOOQ for higher-level abstraction.

Connection pooling reuses database connections to avoid the overhead of establishing new connections. HikariCP is the fastest and most popular pool. Configure: maximumPoolSize (10-20 for moderate apps), minimumIdle, connectionTimeout (30s), idleTimeout, maxLifetime. Always use a pool in production — raw DriverManager connections are too slow. Spring Boot auto-configures HikariCP. Monitor pool health with metrics (HikariConfigMetrics). Connection timeout vs socket timeout: connection timeout is pool wait; socket timeout is database response wait.

JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is the standard ORM specification for Java. Hibernate is the most popular JPA implementation. Key annotations: @Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue, @Column, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @JoinColumn, @JoinTable. EntityManager manages persistence operations: persist, find, merge, remove, createQuery. JPQL queries entities with object-oriented syntax. Spring Data JPA (on Spring Boot) further simplifies with repository interfaces (JpaRepository) that auto-implement CRUD methods.

JUnit 5 (Jupiter) is the standard testing framework for Java. Key annotations: @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll (static), @Disabled, @DisplayName, @Tag, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest, @Nested. Assertions: assertEquals, assertTrue, assertFalse, assertNull, assertThrows, assertAll (grouped assertions). assertAll executes all assertions even if some fail. Assumptions.assumeTrue skips tests conditionally. Lifecycle methods: @BeforeEach runs before each test, @BeforeAll runs once before all tests. Test methods must not be private or static.

Integration tests verify component interactions (database, network, files). Tools: Testcontainers for throwaway Docker containers (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka), Spring Boot @SpringBootTest for application context loading, REST Assured / WebTestClient for HTTP endpoints, @DataJpaTest for JPA slice tests, @WebMvcTest for controller layer. Use @Testcontainers (JUnit 5 extension) to manage container lifecycle. H2 in-memory database works for quick tests but differs from production DB. @DirtiesContext restarts the Spring context after dirty tests. WireMock mocks external HTTP APIs. Stratify: pure unit tests are fast, integration tests are slower, end-to-end tests are slowest.

Parameterized tests (JUnit 5) run the same test logic with different inputs. @ParameterizedTest replaces @Test. @ValueSource (primitive/string), @CsvSource (inline CSV), @CsvFileSource (CSV file), @MethodSource (factory method), @EnumSource, @NullSource, @EmptySource, @NullAndEmptySource. ArgumentsAccessor for accessing arguments programmatically. Custom ArgumentProvider for complex types. Use @DisplayName with {index}, {arguments}, or named placeholders for descriptive test names.

Mockito is a mocking framework for unit tests. It creates mock objects that simulate real dependencies. Key features: @Mock annotation creates mocks, @InjectMocks injects mocks into the tested object, @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) for JUnit 5. Methods: when().thenReturn() stubs behavior, doThrow() for exceptions, verify() checks method calls, ArgumentCaptor captures arguments, spy() wraps a real object with partial mocking. Good practices: mock external dependencies (database, network, filesystem); don't mock value objects. Prefer Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) style: given/when/then.

Spring Boot is a framework that simplifies Spring application setup with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and production-ready features. @SpringBootApplication combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. Dependency injection uses @Autowired or constructor injection. Key starters: spring-boot-starter-web (REST APIs), spring-boot-starter-data-jpa (database), spring-boot-starter-test (testing). Properties in application.yml or application.properties. Spring Boot Actuator provides health checks and metrics. Embedded Tomcat runs the application without external server.

REST API best practices in Java: use @RestController, consistent error responses via @ControllerAdvice, DTOs for request/response, validation with @Valid and Jakarta Bean Validation, pagination with Pageable (Spring), HATEOAS for discoverability. Content negotiation with produces/consumes. Version APIs via URL (/api/v1/) or Accept header. Use ResponseEntity for fine-grained response control (status, headers). Handle idempotency for PUT/DELETE. Use @ExceptionHandler or @ControllerAdvice for centralized error handling.

Servlets are Java classes that handle HTTP requests and responses in a web container (Tomcat, Jetty). HttpServlet provides doGet, doPost, doPut, doDelete methods. Lifecycle: init(), service(), destroy(). Servlet 3.0+ supports annotations (@WebServlet) instead of web.xml. JSP (JavaServer Pages) embeds Java in HTML using <% %> scriptlets, ${EL} expressions, and JSTL tags. Modern applications prefer Spring Boot and REST APIs over raw servlets, but understanding servlets is fundamental for Java web concepts.

Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC) allows enriching log output with contextual data (request IDs, user IDs, session IDs). MDC is a thread-local map — put(key, value) adds context; clear() removes it. Use a servlet filter or Spring interceptor to populate MDC per request. Structured logging outputs JSON instead of plain text, making it parseable by log aggregation tools (ELK, Splunk). Logstash encoder for Logback outputs JSON directly. Combine MDC with structured logging for full observability.

SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is a logging abstraction. Logback is the most popular SLF4J implementation. Levels: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR. Configure via logback.xml. Logback features: rolling file appenders, conditional logging, MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) for contextual data. Parameterized logging with {} avoids string concatenation overhead. Best practices: use slf4j-api in libraries (not logback directly), use appropriate levels, log meaningful messages with context. Avoid logging in tight loops. MDC is great for request tracing (correlation IDs).

String is immutable — each concatenation creates a new object. StringBuilder (unsynchronized, faster) and StringBuffer (synchronized, thread-safe) provide mutable character sequences for efficient string building. Use StringBuilder in single-threaded contexts, StringBuffer when multiple threads access it. Key methods: append, insert, delete, replace, reverse, substring, length, setLength, trimToSize. Capacity management: ensureCapacity() pre-allocates. For simple concatenation in a single statement, the compiler optimizes + to StringBuilder anyway.

Java's regex support (java.util.regex) centers on Pattern (compiled regex) and Matcher (stateful engine). Pattern.compile(regex) creates a Pattern. Flags: CASE_INSENSITIVE, MULTILINE, DOTALL, UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS. Matcher methods: matches (full match), find (partial match), group (matched text), start/end (positions), replaceAll/replaceFirst (replace), split (split). Groups capture with parentheses: group(0) is entire match, group(1) is first capture. Backreferences in regex. Performance: compile Pattern once and reuse.

StringJoiner joins strings with a delimiter (with optional prefix/suffix). String.join() for simple delimited joining. java.util.Formatter and String.format() for printf-style formatting. MessageFormat for locale-sensitive formatting. DecimalFormat for number formatting. String.formatted() (Java 15+) is a convenience instance method. Indent and transform (Java 12+) for line-by-line string manipulation.

The java.util.function package (Java 8+) provides 43 functional interfaces for lambda expressions and method references. Core interfaces: Supplier<T> (get), Consumer<T> (accept), BiConsumer<T,U> (accept), Function<T,R> (apply), BiFunction<T,U,R> (apply), UnaryOperator<T> (apply), BinaryOperator<T> (apply), Predicate<T> (test), BiPredicate<T,U> (test). Primitive variants: IntFunction, LongConsumer, DoublePredicate, ToIntFunction, ObjIntConsumer. Common combinators: andThen, compose for Functions; and, or, negate for Predicates.

Beyond basic LocalDate/LocalTime, java.time provides: YearMonth, MonthDay, Year for partial dates. OffsetTime/OffsetDateTime for fixed-offset zones. ZonedDateTime for full timezone rules (DST-aware). ZoneId for timezone identifiers. Duration (seconds/nanos) and Period (years/months/days). Instant for machine timestamps. TemporalAdjusters for calendar calculations. DateTimeFormatter for parsing/formatting with locale support. Clock for alternate time sources (testing). All classes are immutable and thread-safe.

Beyond basic Collections methods, advanced utilities: checkedList/checkedSet/checkedMap for type-safe views at runtime. newSetFromMap creates a Set from a Map (useful for ConcurrentHashMap-backed sets). disjoint checks if two collections have no elements in common. frequency counts occurrences. nCopies creates a list with repeated elements. enumeration/asEnumeration bridges legacy and modern APIs. rotate shifts elements. indexOfSubList/lastIndexOfSubList finds sublist positions. CopyOnWriteArrayList and ConcurrentHashMap live in java.util.concurrent.

JAR (Java Archive) packages compiled .class files, resources, and metadata into a single file. Manifest (META-INF/MANIFEST.MF) specifies: Main-Class (executable JAR), Class-Path (dependencies), Multi-Release (multi-version JARs). Create JARs with jar CLI or build tools. An executable JAR runs with java -jar. uber-JAR (fat JAR) bundles dependencies. jlink creates custom runtime images with only needed modules for smaller deployment.

The Java module system (Project Jigsaw, Java 9+) enables strong encapsulation and explicit dependencies. A module-info.java declares module name, exports (which packages are accessible), requires (dependencies), opens (for reflection), provides/uses (service loader). Benefits: reliable configuration (no classpath hell), strong encapsulation (internal packages hidden), scalable (smaller runtimes with jlink). The java.base module is implicitly required. Migration: unnamed modules (classpath) can access named modules' exported packages but not vice versa. Use jdeps to analyze dependencies.

The java.time package (Java 8+) replaces the flawed java.util.Date and Calendar. Key classes: LocalDate (date only), LocalTime (time only), LocalDateTime (date+time, no zone), ZonedDateTime (date+time+zone), Instant (machine timestamp), Duration (time-based amount), Period (date-based amount), DateTimeFormatter (format/parse). All classes are immutable and thread-safe. Parse/format with DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(). TemporalAdjusters provide common date adjustments (firstDayOfMonth, nextMonday). Duration.between() measures elapsed time. Unlike old Date, months are 1-12 and years are proper (not 1900-based).

Annotations provide metadata about code. Built-in: @Override, @Deprecated, @SuppressWarnings, @FunctionalInterface. Meta-annotations on custom annotations: @Retention (SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME), @Target (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, etc.), @Documented, @Inherited, @Repeatable. RUNTIME retention allows reflection-based processing. Spring, Hibernate, JUnit, and Jackson heavily use annotations. Custom annotations enable declarative programming. Annotation processors (javac) generate code at compile time (Lombok uses this). Processing runtime annotations via reflection or the AnnotatedElement interface.

The Vector API (JEP 426, incubated since Java 16, preview in 20+) expresses vector computations that compile to SIMD instructions (AVX, NEON) on supported hardware. Types: FloatVector, IntVector, LongVector, DoubleVector. Operate on vectors of species (VectorSpecies, e.g., FloatVector.SPECIES_256 = 8 floats). Operations: add, sub, mul, div, fma, reduceLanes (sum, max, min), blend, lanewise. Performance: loop unrolling + SIMD without JIT auto-vectorization uncertainty. Falls back to scalar loops on unsupported hardware. Requires --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector.

The Foreign Function & Memory API (FFM API, Java 22+) replaces JNI with a safe, pure-Java mechanism for calling native code and accessing off-heap memory. MemorySegment represents a contiguous region of off-heap memory. Arena manages segment lifecycle (implicit/confined/shared). Linker.nativeLinker() creates native method handles downcallHandle. SymbolLookup finds native symbols. MemoryLayout describes the layout of C structs. The FFM API is more ergonomic and safer than JNI, with cleaner resource management and no native code generation.

Java continues to evolve rapidly. Key newer features: Text Blocks (Java 13/15) for multi-line strings with """ """ delimiters. Pattern Matching for instanceof (Java 16+) eliminates casts. Switch Expressions with -> (Java 14+) and Pattern Matching for switch (Java 21+). Sealed Classes (Java 17+) restrict subclassing — the permits clause lists allowed subtypes. Record Patterns (Java 21+) destructure records in pattern matching. String Templates (preview in Java 21+). SequencedCollection (Java 21+) adds first/last access to ordered collections.
js.json: Variables are containers for storing data values.
JavaScript has dynamic types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, object, symbol, bigint.
Operators perform operations on variables and values.
Control flow statements control the execution order of code.
Loops repeat code execution based on conditions.
Functions are reusable blocks of code.
Comments explain code and are ignored during execution.
Use 'use strict' to enable a safer, more predictable subset of JavaScript behavior and avoid common silent errors.
What happens when you assign to an undeclared variable in strict mode?
In strict mode, assigning to an undeclared variable throws a ReferenceError instead of creating a global variable. This prevents accidental globals.

Add a declaration keyword (let or const) before the variable.

JavaScript is a high-level, interpreted language that runs in browsers and on servers (Node.js). It has good parts (functions as first-class citizens, objects, closures) and bad parts (global variables, type coercion quirks). Crockford's 'The Good Parts' advises avoiding the bad parts by using strict mode, === over ==, and minimizing global scope. A key insight from Eloquent JavaScript: think of JavaScript as a language where functions are values that can be passed around, making it deeply rooted in functional programming patterns alongside its imperative style.
Prints output to the browser console
console.log() prints its arguments to the browser's developer console. It's the most common way to debug JavaScript.

JavaScript syntax is C-like with semicolons, blocks, and case-sensitivity. Crockford recommends always using semicolons — automatic semicolon insertion (ASI) can break code when lines start with ( or [. Comments should explain WHY, not WHAT. Eloquent JavaScript emphasizes clean formatting: consistent indentation (2 spaces), meaningful names, and breaking complex expressions into smaller named pieces.
Learn how statement groups and block scope work with braces, and why grouping code carefully helps avoid bugs.

JavaScript engines: V8 (Chrome, Node.js, Deno), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari), Chakra (Edge legacy). All implement ECMAScript spec. Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation: Ignition (interpreter) + TurboFan (optimizing compiler) in V8. Engines add hooks via the host environment (browser APIs, Node.js APIs). The ECMAScript spec defines the language; engines may extend it.
Strings have built-in methods for manipulation.
Numbers have built-in methods and properties.
The Math object provides mathematical constants and functions.
JavaScript can convert between types implicitly or explicitly.

Eloquent JavaScript calls array methods like map, filter, and reduce 'higher-order functions' — functions that operate on other functions. They enable a declarative style: you describe WHAT you want, not HOW. This is more readable and less error-prone than manual for loops. map transforms each element, filter selects elements, reduce combines elements into a single value, find locates the first match, some checks if any element matches, every checks if all match. The Good Parts cautions against mutating arrays while iterating — use map/filter to create new arrays instead.
Arrays can be iterated with forEach, map, filter, reduce.
Sets store unique values of any type.
Maps store key-value pairs with any type keys.

Unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables. Supports nested destructuring, default values, and rest patterns. Common mistake: trying to destructure null or undefined — throws TypeError. Best practice: provide defaults for safe destructuring; use renaming (object: { oldName: newName }) to avoid naming conflicts.
The spread operator expands iterables into elements.
JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify() convert between JSON and objects.

Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Arrays are objects — typeof [] returns 'object'. The length property is auto-updated but can be set manually (truncates or creates empty slots). Common mistake: using for...in on arrays (iterates keys as strings and includes inherited properties). Best practice: use array literal [] over new Array(); use for...of, forEach, or array methods (map/filter) for iteration.

Map stores key-value pairs where keys can be any type (objects, functions, primitives) — unlike objects which only accept strings/symbols. Map preserves insertion order and has O(1) lookup. Set stores unique values of any type. Common mistake: using objects as maps — object keys are always strings; Map keys preserve type (number key 1 !== string key '1'). Best practice: use Map over plain objects for dynamic key collections; use Set for deduplication and fast membership checks.

WeakMap holds 'weak' references to object keys — if no other reference to the key exists, the entry is garbage collected. WeakSet similarly holds weak references to objects. Not iterable and no .size property because the contents could change anytime due to GC. Common mistake: expecting WeakMap/WeakSet to be iterable or have .size — they don't by design. Best practice: use WeakMap for private data (closure alternative), caching associated with DOM elements, or preventing memory leaks from long-lived references.

Iterators are objects with a next() method that returns { value, done }. Any object with [Symbol.iterator] is iterable (works with for...of, spread, destructuring). Generators (function*) simplify iterator creation — they pause at each yield and resume on the next call. Common mistake: generators are single-use iterables — you can't restart them; create a new generator each time. Best practice: use generators for lazy sequences, infinite streams, and async iteration (async function*).
Objects are collections of key-value pairs.
ES6 classes provide a cleaner syntax for OOP.
Getters and setters control property access.
The "this" keyword refers to the current execution context.
These methods explicitly set the value of "this".
Static methods belong to the class itself, not instances.
Private fields are accessible only within the class.
Arrow functions provide a concise function syntax.
A closure is a function with access to its outer scope.
Functions that take or return other functions.
A function that calls itself to solve problems.
Function parameters can have default values.
Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an array.
Immediately Invoked Function Expressions run immediately.
Functions passed as arguments to other functions.
Promises represent eventual completion of async operations.
Async/await provides cleaner syntax for promises.
Try/catch blocks handle errors in async code.
The event loop handles async operations in JS.
Microtasks have higher priority than macrotasks.
The Fetch API makes HTTP requests.
Web Workers run scripts in background threads.
Service Workers act as network proxies for offline support.

The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's API for HTML. Select elements with querySelector (single) or querySelectorAll (NodeList). Modify content via textContent, innerHTML, or classList. Common mistake: using innerHTML when textContent is safer (innerHTML parses HTML and can introduce XSS). Best practice: cache DOM references in variables (querying the DOM is slow); use classList.add/remove/toggle instead of className string manipulation; prefer textContent over innerHTML for text-only changes.

Events signal user interaction (click, keydown, submit, scroll). addEventListener(type, handler) attaches a handler. Events flow through three phases: capture (outer to inner), target, and bubble (inner to outer). Common mistake: using inline event handlers (onclick=) — they create global functions and only allow one handler per event. Best practice: use addEventListener over onclick; use event delegation (listen on parent) for dynamic child elements; call removeEventListener to prevent memory leaks.
Events propagate from child to parent elements.
Handling events on multiple children via a parent.
Persistent key-value storage in the browser.
Drawing 2D graphics with the Canvas API.

Handle form submission, read input values, and validate before sending. The submit event fires on the form element (not the button). Access fields via the elements collection or by id. Use e.preventDefault() to stop submission and validate first. Common mistake: listening for click on the submit button instead of submit on the form — the form can also be submitted via Enter key. Best practice: validate on submit (not on every keystroke for performance); use the Constraint Validation API (required, minlength, pattern attributes) for basic checks.

fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object. The Response must be parsed (.json(), .text()) before data is available. fetch only rejects on network errors — HTTP errors (404, 500) still resolve. Common mistake: forgetting that fetch doesn't reject on HTTP error status — check response.ok. Best practice: always handle network errors with .catch(); use AbortController to cancel in-flight requests; set appropriate Content-Type headers for POST/PUT.

localStorage persists data across browser sessions (no expiration). sessionStorage persists only for the current tab session — cleared when the tab closes. Both store strings only — objects must be serialized with JSON.stringify/parse. Storage limit is ~5-10MB per origin. Common mistake: storing objects directly — they become '[object Object]'; always use JSON.stringify. Best practice: wrap localStorage access in try/catch (private browsing may throw); use JSON for structured data; clear unused keys to stay under quota.

setTimeout runs a function once after a delay; setInterval runs repeatedly at the interval. Both return an ID passed to clearTimeout/clearInterval to cancel. Common mistake: assuming setInterval runs at exact intervals — if the callback takes longer than the interval, calls stack up. Best practice: use recursive setTimeout instead of setInterval for precise timing; always clear timers in cleanup code to prevent memory leaks; use requestAnimationFrame for visual animations (more efficient than setTimeout).

Modern Web APIs: File API (read files via FileReader), Drag & Drop (dragstart/dragover/drop events), Clipboard API (navigator.clipboard read/write), Geolocation, Web Storage, Web Workers. FileReader.readAsText/DataURL for preview. Clipboard.writeText/readText for copy/paste. Check API support with feature detection before use.
Maps compiled code back to source code.
React concept adapted: catching render errors.
Using and managing packages from npm.
Tools that bundle JS files for production.
Tools that convert modern JS to older syntax.
Tools that analyze code for potential errors.
Tools for writing and running tests.
Weak references for garbage collection sensitive caching.
Delaying function execution until after a pause.
Splitting code into chunks loaded on demand.
