The Good Parts advises never using var — it leaks scope and causes subtle bugs. Use const by default, let only when reassignment is needed. const doesn't mean immutable, only that the binding can't change.
JavaScript has 7 primitive types. Primitives are immutable (you can't change them — operations return new values). typeof null returns 'object' (a JS bug from day one).

Objects, arrays, and functions are reference types: variables hold a pointer to the value in memory. Assigning or passing copies the reference, not the value — mutating one affects the other. Use spread or structuredClone() for copies.

Every value coerces to boolean in conditionals. Crockford calls JavaScript's falsy rules 'a land of false promises' — learn them exactly to avoid bugs. Only 7 falsy values exist: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. The tricky one: empty arrays [] and objects {} are truthy. Eloquent JavaScript shows a practical pattern: use explicit Boolean() or !! for clarity, and avoid relying on coercion in complex conditions.
JavaScript is weakly typed — it converts types automatically. This is convenient but dangerous. The Good Parts: always use === and explicit conversion.
Template literals use backticks (`) instead of quotes. Embed expressions with ${}. They support multi-line without \n.
undefined means a variable was declared but not assigned. null is intentionally empty — you assign it explicitly. They are different types.
Symbol creates unique, immutable identifiers for object properties. BigInt represents integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER using n suffix.

Standard math: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), % (remainder/modulo), ** (exponentiation). Prefix/postfix ++ and -- increment/decrement by 1. Common mistake: + also does string concatenation — if either operand is a string, both are coerced to strings. Best practice: use parentheses to clarify operator precedence; avoid relying on ++ inside expressions.

Compare values and return a boolean. Relational: >, <, >=, <=. Equality: === (strict, no coercion) and == (loose, coerces types). Common mistake: using == allows type coercion (e.g., 5 == '5' is true), which causes subtle bugs. Best practice: always use === and !==; use Object.is() for NaN comparisons (Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true, unlike NaN === NaN which is false).

&& (AND) returns the first falsy operand or the last truthy one. || (OR) returns the first truthy operand or the last falsy one. ! (NOT) inverts truthiness and always returns boolean. Common mistake: && and || short-circuit — if the left operand determines the result, the right operand is never evaluated. This means side effects in the right operand may not run. Best practice: use || for default values and && for conditional execution, but beware that 0, '', and false are falsy so defaults may not work as expected — use ?? for null/undefined only.

Compound assignment combines an operation with assignment: +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, **=, &&=, ||=, ??= (ES2021). They update the variable in place. Common mistake: ??= only assigns if the current value is null or undefined — unlike ||= which assigns for any falsy value. Best practice: prefer compound assignment for clarity when updating a variable relative to its current value.

The conditional (ternary) operator takes three operands: condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse. It's an expression, not a statement — it returns a value that can be assigned or used inline. Common mistake: nesting ternaries makes code unreadable — use if/else for more than one condition. Best practice: use ternaries for simple yes/no branches; keep them on one line for readability.

Spread (...) expands iterables (arrays, strings, objects) into individual elements. Rest (...) collects remaining elements into an array or object. Common mistake: spread creates a shallow copy — nested objects are still referenced, not cloned. Best practice: use spread for immutable updates (copying arrays/objects) and rest for flexible function parameters and destructuring.

Branch execution based on boolean conditions. The condition is coerced to boolean — any truthy value passes. Common mistake: assigning (=) instead of comparing (==) in conditions — 'if (x = 5)' assigns 5 (truthy) and always runs. Best practice: use curly braces even for single statements; prefer === over == for comparisons; use early returns (guard clauses) to reduce nesting.
else if chains additional conditions after if. Each condition is evaluated in order — the first true match runs and the rest are skipped. Use else if when exactly one branch should execute.

Multi-way branching comparing the same expression to multiple values using strict equality (===). Use break to prevent fall-through to the next case. Common mistake: forgetting break causes execution to fall through to the next case (sometimes intentional). Best practice: always include break (or return); use default for unmatched values; consider if/else for ranges (switch is for discrete values only).

Three types: for (init; condition; increment) — classic counted loop. for...of iterates over values of iterables (arrays, strings, Map, Set). for...in iterates over enumerable property keys of objects. Common mistake: using for...in for arrays (iterates keys as strings, includes inherited properties). Best practice: use for...of for arrays, for...in for objects, and classic for when you need the index.

while checks the condition before each iteration — may run zero times. do...while checks after — always runs at least once. Common mistake: forgetting to update the loop variable causes infinite loops (hangs the browser). Best practice: prefer for loops when you know the iteration count; use while for condition-controlled loops (reading input, waiting for a state change).

break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next. With labeled statements, break and continue can control outer loops from inside nested ones. Common mistake: using break in forEach() callback — it doesn't work (forEach doesn't respect break). Best practice: use labeled breaks sparingly (they can make control flow hard to follow); prefer extracting to a function with early return.

A loop inside another loop. Each outer iteration triggers a full inner loop run. Complexity is O(n*m) — a 100×100 grid runs 10,000 iterations. Use labeled break/continue to control outer loops from inside. Common mistake: quadratic complexity on large datasets can freeze the browser. Best practice: consider flatMap(), combined data structures, or early termination when possible.

try/catch/finally handles runtime exceptions. try runs the risky code; catch receives the error object; finally always runs (even after return). Common mistake: catching and ignoring errors silently — always log or re-throw. Best practice: catch specific error types when possible; use finally for cleanup (closing files, clearing state); throw custom Error objects (not strings or numbers) for stack traces.

Functions are the fundamental building block of JavaScript. Eloquent JavaScript calls them 'values that contain behavior'. Function declarations are hoisted (moved to top), which Crockford considers useful for organizing code top-down. A function always returns something — undefined if no explicit return. The Good Parts says: 'functions are the best part of JavaScript' — they create scope, enable modularity, and are the only way to create private variables. Every function has access to the scope in which it was defined (closure), making them powerful tools for encapsulation.

A function expression assigns a function to a variable. Unlike declarations, function expressions are NOT hoisted — you can't call them before the definition line. Named function expressions have a name property for debugging but the name is only visible inside the function scope. Common mistake: expecting function expressions to be hoisted like declarations. Best practice: use const for function expressions to prevent reassignment; use named expressions for better stack traces in recursion and debugging.

Arrow functions provide shorter syntax: (params) => expression. Key differences from regular functions: they inherit this from the enclosing scope (lexical this), cannot be used as constructors (no new), and don't have arguments object. Common mistake: using arrow functions for object methods — this won't refer to the object. Best practice: use arrow functions for callbacks, array methods (map/filter/reduce), and when you want lexical this; use regular functions for object methods, constructors, and when you need dynamic this.

Default parameter values are used when the argument is undefined (not when it's null or other falsy values). Defaults can be expressions or even function calls — they're evaluated at call time, not definition time. Common mistake: thinking defaults trigger on null — they only trigger on undefined. Best practice: put default parameters after required ones so calling code can skip them; avoid complex default expressions that hide bugs.

Rest parameters (...) collect remaining arguments into a real array (unlike the array-like arguments object). Must be the last parameter. Common mistake: confusing rest with the arguments object — arguments is array-like (no .map/.filter) and includes ALL parameters, not just the extras. Best practice: prefer rest over arguments for clarity; use rest in destructuring to capture remaining items.

A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has returned. This is JavaScript’s most powerful pattern — it enables data privacy (module pattern), function factories, event handlers with state, and memoization. Common mistake: closures capture variables by reference, not by value — loop closures all see the final value unless you use let or an IIFE. Best practice: use closures for encapsulation (hide implementation details); be mindful of memory if the closure retains large objects.

Objects are the foundation of JavaScript — almost everything is an object or can behave like one. Crockford calls objects 'containers of properties, where each property has a name and a value'. Objects are passed by reference, making them efficient but also dangerous when mutated in place. Eloquent JavaScript describes objects as 'octopuses with any number of tentacles' — they can hold any type. The Good Parts recommends object literals as the simplest and safest way to create objects, avoiding new Object() and similar verbose forms.

this is one of JavaScript's most misunderstood features. Crockford calls this 'a source of enormous confusion'. Its value depends entirely on HOW a function is called: method call → the object, plain call → undefined (strict) or global (sloppy), constructor call (new) → the new instance, call/apply/bind → explicitly set. Eloquent JavaScript calls this 'the function's context'. Arrow functions avoid the confusion by inheriting this from the enclosing scope — Crockford recommends using them for callbacks. The Good Parts says: 'this is always bound to the global object in inner functions' — capture it with a variable (that = this) or use arrow functions.

Prototypal inheritance is JavaScript's native inheritance model. Crockford explains: 'a prototype is an object from which other objects inherit properties'. Unlike classical inheritance (classes inherit from classes), objects inherit directly from objects. Object.create() creates a new object with a specified prototype. The Good Parts advocates for prototypal over classical inheritance — it's simpler and more flexible. Eloquent JavaScript describes the prototype chain as 'a series of objects linked together' ending at Object.prototype. When you access a property, JavaScript walks the chain until found. Favor composition over inheritance in large systems.

Class syntax (ES2015) is sugar over prototypes: class defines a constructor, methods go on the prototype, and static methods go on the constructor itself. Supports extends for inheritance and super for parent calls. Common mistake: thinking classes are a new inheritance model — they're still prototypal underneath. Best practice: use class syntax over manual prototype manipulation for readability; prefer composition over deep inheritance chains.

extends creates a subclass that inherits from a parent class. super() calls the parent constructor; super.method() calls a parent method. Subclasses can override methods and access parent implementations. Common mistake: forgetting to call super() in the subclass constructor — causes ReferenceError. Best practice: keep inheritance shallow (1-2 levels max); prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) for code reuse.

Getters (get) and setters (set) let you define properties that call functions when accessed or assigned. They look like normal property access but can run validation, computation, or logging. Common mistake: getters should not have side effects (callers expect property-like behavior). Best practice: use getters for computed properties and setters for validation; avoid expensive operations in getters since callers don't expect function-call overhead.

A Promise represents a value that may be available now, later, or never. States: pending (initial), fulfilled (resolved), or rejected (error). .then() handles fulfillment, .catch() handles rejection, .finally() runs regardless. Promises are microtasks — they resolve before macrotasks like setTimeout. Common mistake: not returning the promise from .then() breaks the chain — the next .then() receives undefined. Best practice: always return promises from chains; handle rejection at the end of the chain (not per-link); use Promise.all for parallel work.

async functions always return a Promise. await pauses execution until the awaited promise settles — but only within the async function (the caller continues). Common mistake: calling async functions without awaiting them — they still run but you lose the return value and error handling. Best practice: wrap await calls in try/catch for error handling; use Promise.all for independent parallel async operations (sequential await is slower); top-level await works in ES modules.

fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise<Response>. Always check response.ok — fetch only rejects on network errors, not HTTP errors. GET is default; POST/PUT/PATCH require method and body. Common mistake: not checking response.ok — a 404 resolves successfully. Best practice: always check .ok and throw for non-2xx; use AbortController for timeout/cancellation; set Content-Type for requests with body.

The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model — single-threaded but non-blocking. Eloquent JavaScript explains: 'when a program needs to wait, it schedules a callback and continues running other code'. The call stack runs synchronously; async callbacks go to the task queue. Promises and async/await use the microtask queue (higher priority than macrotasks like setTimeout). This means promise callbacks run BEFORE timer callbacks, even zero-delay timers. Crockford says: 'understanding the event loop is essential — everything in JavaScript happens in a single thread, and if you block it, the whole page freezes'.

Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread — they can't access the DOM, window, or parent scope. Communicate with the main thread via postMessage() and onmessage. Workers are great for CPU-intensive tasks (image processing, data parsing, encryption). Common mistake: trying to access DOM or window inside a worker — not available. Best practice: use workers for expensive computations that would block the UI; use structuredClone or Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) for efficient data passing; terminate workers when done to free resources.

Async iteration (for await...of) consumes async iterables with [Symbol.asyncIterator] that returns promises from next(). async function* defines an async generator. Useful for streaming data (paginated APIs, WebSocket messages, file chunks). Common mistake: using for...of instead of for await...of on async iterables — for...of doesn't await promises. Best practice: use async generators for streaming scenarios; handle errors inside the loop with try/catch.
Share code with import/export syntax, and run modules in modern browsers or bundlers.
Expand iterable values into arrays or function calls, and merge object properties effortlessly.

Optional chaining (?.) short-circuits to undefined if the value before ?. is null or undefined — without throwing. Works with property access (?.), method calls (?.()), and dynamic access (?.[]). Common mistake: thinking ?. prevents 'undefined is not a function' for methods that don't exist — it does, but only when the object itself is null/undefined. Best practice: combine ?. with ?? for safe deep access chains; don't overuse — if a value should always exist, let it throw (fail fast).

?? returns the right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined. Unlike || which returns the right operand for ANY falsy value (0, '', false). Common mistake: using || for defaults when 0 or '' are valid values — || treats them as absent. Best practice: use ?? for default values when the left side could be a valid falsy value (empty string, zero, false); use || for truly absent values (when undefined/null and falsy should both get the default).

import() is a function-like expression that dynamically loads a module at runtime. It returns a Promise resolving to the module namespace object. Enables code splitting (load only what's needed), lazy loading (load on user interaction), and conditional imports (platform detection). Common mistake: dynamic imports are NOT hoisted — they execute when reached. Best practice: use dynamic imports for large libraries not needed on initial load (charts, editors, heavy utilities); combine with top-level await in module scripts.

Promise.all waits for ALL promises — rejects fast if ANY rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for ALL to settle (resolve or reject) — never rejects, returns results with status. Promise.race returns the first settled promise. Promise.any returns the first fulfilled promise — rejects only if ALL reject. Common mistake: using Promise.all when one failure shouldn't fail the whole batch — use allSettled. Best practice: use all for dependent parallel work (must all succeed), allSettled for independent results, race for timeouts, any for fastest success.

Records and Tuples (Stage 2 proposal) add immutable compound primitives. Records (#{}) are like frozen objects; Tuples (#[]) are like frozen arrays. Compared by value, not reference. Use === naturally. Nested objects must be Records/Tuples. Polyfill available via @bloomberg/record-tuple. Browsers: enable via experimental flags.

React is a component-based UI library. Components return JSX (JavaScript XML) describing what to render. Props pass data from parent to child; state manages component-local data that triggers re-renders. Common mistake: mutating state directly (this.state.x = 5) instead of using setState or the state setter. Best practice: prefer functional components with hooks (useState, useEffect) over class components; keep components small and focused; lift shared state to the closest common ancestor.

Vue is a progressive framework with reactive templates and a component system. Options API uses data(), methods, computed, and watch. Composition API (setup) provides better code organization. Common mistake: using normal variables in data() instead of reactive ref() or reactive() — Vue can only track reactive objects. Best practice: prefer the Composition API for complex logic reuse; use computed for derived state instead of methods in templates; use v-bind:key in v-for for efficient re-rendering.

Express is a minimalist Node.js web framework. Define routes with app.get/post/put/delete. Middleware functions (app.use) process requests in order — they can modify req/res, end the request, or call next(). Common mistake: forgetting to call next() in middleware — the request hangs. Best practice: structure routes with express.Router() for modularity; use error-handling middleware (4 args) for centralized errors; parse bodies with express.json() middleware.

Next.js is a React framework for production with file-based routing (pages/ or app/), SSR/SSG, and API routes. Pages/ directory: each file becomes a route. App Router (app/) uses layouts, loading states, and server components. Common mistake: fetching data in client components when server components would be more efficient. Best practice: use server components for initial data fetching (rendered on server, smaller JS bundle); use getStaticProps (Pages Router) for SSG; leverage Suspense boundaries for streaming.

NestJS is a progressive Node.js framework built with TypeScript that uses decorators for controllers, providers, modules, and middleware. It supports Express or Fastify under the hood. Common mistake: forgetting to register providers in module decorators — unregistered providers cause runtime injection errors. Best practice: use modules to organize features; keep controllers thin (delegate logic to services); leverage dependency injection for testability.

Vite is a fast build tool that uses native ES modules for dev (instant HMR) and Rollup for production builds. Supports JS, TS, JSX, CSS, and assets out of the box. Common mistake: thinking Vite only works for frontend frameworks — it works with vanilla JS and library development too. Best practice: use vite.config.js for custom configuration (aliases, plugins, proxy); leverage HMR for fast iteration.

JSON.parse converts JSON strings to objects; JSON.stringify serializes objects to JSON strings. Essential for data exchange and API communication. Common mistake: JSON.parse throws on invalid JSON — always wrap in try/catch or use a safe parser. Best practice: use JSON.stringify's replacer and space arguments for controlled serialization; avoid storing undefined, BigInt, or circular references — they're silently dropped or throw.

Math provides constants and methods for math operations: random, floor, round, ceil, max, min, abs, pow, sqrt, sin, cos, PI, E. Number offers parseInt, parseFloat, isNaN, isFinite, isInteger, and EPSILON. Common mistake: using Math.floor for rounding — use Math.round for standard rounding and Math.trunc for integer truncation. Best practice: use Number.isNaN over global isNaN (global coerces, Number.isNaN doesn't); use Math.max/Math.min with spread for arrays; avoid floating-point equality checks — use epsilon comparison.

Date handles date/time operations: creation, formatting, arithmetic, and timezone handling. Months are zero-indexed (0 = January). Date objects are mutable — all set methods mutate in place. Common mistake: date parsing with strings is unreliable across browsers — use Date.parse cautiously or a date library. Best practice: use toISOString() for storage/serialization; use Intl.DateTimeFormat for localized display; use timestamps (Date.now()) for calculations to avoid month-index confusion.

Strings have built-in methods for manipulation: slice, substring, split, replace/replaceAll, toUpperCase/toLowerCase, trim, includes, startsWith, endsWith, repeat, padStart/padEnd, match, matchAll, and charAt. Strings are immutable — all methods return a new string. Common mistake: confusing slice (accepts negative indices) with substring (treats negative as 0). Best practice: use replaceAll (ES2021) over replace with global regex for simpler replacement; use template literals for concatenation; use includes over indexOf for readability.
Proxy wraps an object to intercept operations (get, set, delete, etc.) via traps. Reflect provides methods that mirror the default proxy behavior for forwarding.
Intl provides locale-aware formatting for dates, numbers, currencies, and collation. Intl.DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, and ListFormat are the most common.
TypedArrays provide views over raw binary data in an ArrayBuffer. Types include Int8Array, Uint8Array, Float64Array, and more for performance-critical work.
structuredClone creates a deep copy of an object, handling circular references and types like Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and Blob.

Intl API provides locale-sensitive formatting: Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.Collator, Intl.ListFormat, Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, Intl.PluralRules, Intl.Segmenter. The locale string ('en-US', 'de-DE', 'ja-JP') determines formatting rules. Use options for fine-grained control. Intl.DateTimeFormat handles timezone, calendar, numbering systems.

Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code execution. var declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined — accessing them before declaration returns undefined, not ReferenceError. let and const are hoisted but NOT initialized — they exist in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from block start until declaration, so accessing them throws ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted entirely (body included), so they can be called before their definition. Function expressions are NOT hoisted — use them only after the assignment line.

The global scope is the outermost scope. In browsers, window is the global object; in Node.js, it's global. Variables declared with var at the top level become properties of the global object. let, const, and class at the top level do NOT become global object properties — they exist in the global scope but are not properties of window/global. Relying on global variables is considered bad practice — they create naming conflicts and make code hard to reason about. The Good Parts: minimize global scope by using IIFEs or modules.

Lexical (static) scoping means a variable's scope is determined by its position in the source code, not by how functions are called at runtime. Inner functions can access variables from outer scopes, but not vice versa. This is the foundation of closures — a function remembers the scope in which it was defined. JavaScript has no dynamic scoping — this is not scope, it's context (determined by call pattern). Understanding lexical scope helps predict which variables are accessible at any point in the code.

TDZ is the region from block start to variable declaration where let/const/class variables exist but can't be accessed. ReferenceError: Cannot access before initialization. typeof also throws (unlike var/undeclared). TDZ prevents accessing variables before they're initialized. Class declarations are also hoisted but not initialized (TDZ applies).

Object.is (ES6) compares two values for equality. It behaves like === except for two edge cases: Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true (NaN === NaN is false), and Object.is(0, -0) returns false (0 === -0 is true). Use Object.is when you need NaN equivalence or need to distinguish signed zeros. For most cases, === is sufficient and more readable. Object.is does NOT perform deep object comparison — references must match. It's available on all modern platforms and polyfillable for older ones.

SameValueZero is an equality algorithm used by Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes. It behaves like Object.is but treats -0 and 0 as equal. This means NaN is considered equal to itself (unlike ===) but -0 equals 0 (unlike Object.is). It's not directly callable in user code but is used internally by Set.has(), Map.has(), and includes(). Understanding it helps explain why Set.has(NaN) returns true but indexOf(NaN) returns -1.

Object.is() compares value equality (SameValue algorithm), similar to === but with two differences: +0 !== -0, and NaN === NaN. SameValueZero (used in Map, Set, includes) treats +0 and -0 as equal. SameValue (Object.is) distinguishes them. Use Object.is for NaN-safe comparisons. Most algorithms use SameValueZero for consistency.

The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model: single-threaded, non-blocking, and asynchronous by necessity. The call stack runs synchronous code. When an async operation completes, its callback is queued. Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) go to the task queue. Microtasks (Promise.then, async/await, queueMicrotask) go to the microtask queue. After each macrotask, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue before processing the next macrotask. This means promise callbacks run before setTimeout callbacks, even zero-delay ones. Blocking the call stack with long synchronous work freezes the page.

Microtasks include Promise.then/catch/finally, MutationObserver, and queueMicrotask. Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, and UI rendering (browser). After every macrotask, the event loop processes all pending microtasks before the next macrotask or render. This is why Promise-based code runs before timer callbacks. queueMicrotask() explicitly schedules a microtask. Microtasks can starve the event loop if they continuously enqueue more microtasks — causing the page to become unresponsive despite no single long task.

A callback is a function passed to another function for later execution. They are the foundation of async JavaScript — used in setTimeout, event handlers, fs.readFile, and fetch. Callback-based code suffers from 'callback hell' (pyramid of doom) when nested. Modern alternatives: Promises and async/await. The error-first callback pattern (Node.js convention) passes error as the first argument: callback(err, result). Always handle errors in callbacks — unhandled errors silently disappear.

The event loop processes macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events) and microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver). Microtasks run immediately after the current macrotask, before the next macrotask. Await is syntactic sugar for .then(). process.nextTick (Node.js) runs before microtasks. requestAnimationFrame runs before repaint.

ES Modules (ES6) use import and export statements. Each module has its own scope — no global leakage. Named exports export multiple values with specific names. Default export exports a single main value per module. Dynamic import() (ES2020) loads modules on demand (returns a Promise). ESM is static — imports are hoisted and resolved before execution, enabling tree-shaking. Modules are strict by default. Use type='module' on script tags in browsers, or 'type': 'module' in package.json for Node.js.

CommonJS is Node.js's original module system using require() and module.exports. require() loads modules synchronously — fine for servers but not browsers. module.exports can be any value. exports is a shorthand reference to module.exports — reassigning exports breaks the reference. Node.js supports both CJS (file.js or .cjs) and ESM (.mjs or type='module' package.json). Use require() for dynamic conditional imports. CJS modules are not tree-shakeable because exports are determined at runtime.

Dynamic import() returns a promise for a module namespace. Enables code splitting (load on demand), reducing initial bundle size. import.meta provides module metadata. import.meta.url (file URL), import.meta.resolve (spec resolution). Dynamic imports are not statically analyzable — bundlers may need hints for splitting. Top-level await works in modules.

JavaScript manages memory automatically via garbage collection. The lifecycle: (1) Allocate — memory is reserved when you create values (objects, arrays, closures, DOM nodes); (2) Use — references point to the allocated memory as your code runs; (3) Release — when a value is no longer reachable, its memory becomes eligible for garbage collection. Reachability means the value can be accessed from a root (global object, current call stack, active closures). Values can become unreachable when all references go out of scope, are reassigned, or set to null.

Modern JavaScript engines use generational garbage collection. Young generation: new objects are allocated here — collected frequently (minor GC) since most objects die young. Old generation: objects that survive multiple GC cycles are promoted here — collected less often (major GC). The mark-and-sweep algorithm: starting from roots (global object, stack, DOM), the GC marks all reachable objects, then sweeps (frees) unmarked objects. Common memory leaks: detached DOM elements (referenced in JS but removed from DOM), forgotten timers holding references, global variable accumulation, and closures retaining large unnecessary data.

WeakRef holds a weak reference to an object (doesn't prevent GC). Use .deref() to access (may return undefined). FinalizationRegistry registers cleanup callbacks when objects are garbage collected. Use cases: caching, DOM node lifecycle, resource cleanup. Not meant for general use — GC timing is unpredictable. Avoid in performance-critical paths.

Browser DevTools console is essential for debugging. console.log() prints values. console.error() and console.warn() print with severity icons and stack traces. console.table() renders arrays/objects as sortable tables. console.time()/timeEnd() measures execution. console.group()/groupEnd() nests logs. console.count() counts calls. console.trace() prints the call stack. Using debugger; statement pauses execution. For real debugging, use Sources panel breakpoints — they're more precise than console.log scatterguns.

Performance debugging identifies slow code. Use the Performance panel to record activity: look for long tasks (>50ms block main thread), forced reflow (reading layout properties after DOM mutations), and layout thrash (alternating reads/writes in loops). Lighthouse audits performance. Use performance.now() for precise timing. The Network panel shows request timing and waterfall. Avoid: forcing layout with offsetWidth/Height in loops, heavy synchronous work on the main thread, and excessive DOM manipulations without batching.

Memory leaks cause page slowdown and crashes. Use the Memory panel to take heap snapshots — compare 'before' and 'after' to see retained objects. Common patterns: detached DOM nodes (elements referenced in JS but removed from DOM), closures holding large data, global caches without cleanup, forgotten timers/intervals, and event listeners not removed. Look for 'Detached HTML elements' in heap snapshots. The Performance panel's memory timeline shows heap growth over time — steady growth indicates a leak.
k8s.json: Introduction to k8s and its ecosystem.
Kubernetes clusters consist of a control plane managing worker nodes. The control plane runs the API server, scheduler, controller manager, and etcd as core components.
Pods are the smallest deployable units, containing one or more containers with shared storage and network. Each pod gets a unique cluster IP.
kubectl is the CLI for controlling Kubernetes clusters. Common commands manage resources, view logs, exec into containers, and port-forward.
Namespaces provide virtual cluster isolation for multi-tenant environments. Resources in one namespace are invisible to other namespaces by default.
ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs or files that pods consume as environment variables or volumes.
Secrets store sensitive data like passwords and API keys base64-encoded. They are injected into pods as environment variables or mounted volumes.
Environment variables in pods reference ConfigMaps and Secrets directly or via configMapKeyRef and secretKeyRef selectors.
ResourceQuotas limit total resource consumption per namespace, preventing any single team or app from exhausting cluster resources.
LimitRanges set minimum and maximum resource constraints per pod or container within a namespace, preventing runaway resource usage.
Deployments manage ReplicaSets and provide declarative updates with rolling updates, rollbacks, and scaling capabilities.
StatefulSets manage stateful applications with stable network identities, ordered deployment, and persistent storage per pod.
DaemonSets ensure all or selected nodes run a copy of a pod, ideal for logging, monitoring, and networking agents that run on every node.
Jobs run a pod to completion, useful for batch processing and migrations. CronJobs run jobs on a recurring schedule using cron syntax.
ClusterIP exposes a service on an internal cluster IP accessible only within the cluster. It is the default Service type for internal communication.
NodePort exposes a service on each node's IP at a static port, making it accessible externally via nodeIP:nodePort.
LoadBalancer provisions an external load balancer from cloud providers and assigns a public IP for internet-facing services.
Ingress exposes HTTP/S routes to services with host/path-based routing, TLS termination, and virtual hosting.
Network Policies control traffic flow between pods using label selectors and port rules. By default all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed.
Container volumes provide temporary or persistent storage attached to pods. Volume types include emptyDir, hostPath, and cloud disks.
PersistentVolumes are cluster-wide storage resources provisioned by administrators or dynamically via StorageClass.
PersistentVolumeClaims request storage resources from a PersistentVolume, binding to matching volumes based on capacity and access modes.
StorageClass provisions PersistentVolumes dynamically based on cloud provider storage types like SSD, HDD, or custom parameters.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically scales pod replicas based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics from Prometheus.
Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts CPU and memory requests for pods based on actual usage, improving resource efficiency.
Cluster Autoscaler automatically adds or removes nodes in a cloud provider's node group based on pending pod resource requests.
Helm is the Kubernetes package manager. Charts package YAML templates into reusable, configurable releases with versioning.
Helm charts follow a standard directory structure. Values.yaml provides defaults, and templates use Go templating for dynamic resource generation.
Helm templates use Go template syntax with Sprig functions. Values are injected from values.yaml or --set CLI flags.
Hooks run actions at specific points in a release lifecycle: pre/post install, upgrade, delete. Useful for database migrations and validation.
Custom Resource Definitions extend the Kubernetes API with custom resources that behave like built-in objects.
Operators automate application management by extending Kubernetes with custom controllers. They watch CRD resources and reconcile desired state.
Service meshes like Istio provide traffic management, security, and observability for microservices. They use sidecar proxies to intercept network traffic.
Role-Based Access Control restricts API access via Roles (namespace-scoped) and ClusterRoles (cluster-scoped) bound to users or ServiceAccounts.
ServiceAccounts provide identities for pods to authenticate with the Kubernetes API, used with RBAC for fine-grained permissions.
Pod Security Standards (restricted, baseline, privileged) enforce security contexts at the namespace level, preventing privileged containers.
Metrics Server collects resource utilization data from kubelet and exposes it via the Metrics API, enabling kubectl top and HPA.
Prometheus monitors Kubernetes with time-series metrics collection, alerting, and Grafana dashboards for visualization.
Logging in Kubernetes uses fluentd or Loki to collect container logs and forward them to Elasticsearch, Loki, or cloud logging services.

Kubernetes security: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) for API permissions, Pod Security Standards (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted) for pod capabilities, NetworkPolicies for traffic isolation, and OPA/Gatekeeper for admission control. ServiceAccounts should have minimal permissions. Secrets encrypted with KMS. Pod Security Admission (PSA) replaces PSP (deprecated in 1.21). NetworkPolicy defines ingress/egress rules with pod/namespace selectors. Seccomp, AppArmor profiles restrict syscalls.
kt.json: Variables and data types in Kotlin.
Input and output operations in Kotlin.
Kotlin is a modern, statically-typed language that runs on the JVM, JS, and Native targets. It's concise, safe, and fully interoperable with Java.
Kotlin omits semicolons and uses `fun` for functions, `val` for read-only references, and `var` for mutable ones. Types come after colons.
Kotlin infers types. `val` (immutable like final) and `var` (mutable). Basic types: String, Int, Long, Double, Float, Boolean, Char, Byte, Short.
Kotlin eliminates null pointer exceptions with nullable types (`?`), safe calls (`?.`), Elvis operator (`?:`), and the not-null assertion (`!!`).
The Kotlin Playground is an online IDE to experiment with Kotlin code. It supports multiplatform targets, embedded snippets, and sharing via URLs.
Kotlin Multiplatform shares business logic across JVM, JS, iOS, Android, and Native. Write once in shared modules; platform code in target modules.
Standard Kotlin projects use Gradle with `src/main/kotlin` and `src/test/kotlin`. Multiplatform adds `commonMain`, `jvmMain`, `iosMain` source sets.

Kotlin/Native compiles to native binaries (no JVM required) via LLVM. Targets: Windows (Mingw), Linux, macOS, iOS, Android NDK, WebAssembly. Use `konanTargets` in Gradle. Kotlin/Wasm targets WebAssembly with Kotlin/Wasm compiler. Native supports Kotlin's standard library subset, including coroutines and serialization.
`if` and `when` are expressions that return values. `when` replaces Java's switch and supports smart casts, ranges, and arbitrary conditions.
`for` iterates over ranges, collections, or anything with an iterator. `while` and `do..while` work as expected. Ranges use `..`, `until`, `downTo`, `step`.
Ranges (`1..10`) define intervals. Progressions control step direction. Use `in` to check membership, `until` for exclusive end.
`==` calls `equals()` (structural equality). `===` checks referential identity. `!=` and `!==` are the negated forms.
Use `try-catch-finally`. Kotlin has no checked exceptions. `catch` blocks can filter by exception type, and `finally` always executes.
`try` is an expression in Kotlin. It returns the last expression in the `try` block or the matching `catch` block. Use `finally` for side effects.

Ranges: `a..b` (inclusive), `a..<b` (exclusive, Kotlin 1.9+), `a downTo b`, `a..b step c`. Check containment with `in` operator. Progressions: IntProgression, LongProgression, CharProgression. Empty ranges: `10..1` (empty). `until` extension: `0 until 10` = `0..9`. Indices of collections. Iterate over ranges with for loops.
Functions use `fun` with explicit return types. Expression bodies omit braces. Single-expression functions infer the return type automatically.
Parameters can have default values. Named arguments allow skipping or reordering parameters, improving readability for functions with many parameters.
Lambdas are function literals. Higher-order functions take or return functions. Trailing lambda syntax removes parentheses for clean DSL-like code.
Add new functions to existing classes without inheritance. Extensions are resolved statically — they don't actually modify the class.
Infix functions are called without dot or parens. Single-parameter member or extension functions marked with `infix`. Common in DSLs.
Kotlin allows overloading operators like `+`, `-`, `*`, `[]`, `()` via functions named `plus`, `minus`, `times`, `get`, `invoke`.
`tailrec` optimises recursive functions into iterative loops when the recursive call is in tail position. No stack overflow risk.
`inline` inlines the function body at call sites, avoiding lambda object allocation. Use for higher-order functions with lambda parameters.

Destructuring decomposes an object into variables: val (name, age) = person. Works for data classes, Pair, Triple, Map.Entry, and classes with componentN() operators. Use _ for unused components. In lambdas: map.forEach { (key, value) -> }. Destructuring in for loops: for ((k, v) in map). ComponentN is an operator function: operator fun component1(): Type.
`listOf` creates read-only lists, `mutableListOf` for mutable. `arrayOf` for arrays. Lists are covariant; arrays are invariant.
`mapOf`/`mutableMapOf` for key-value pairs. `setOf`/`mutableSetOf` for unique elements. Immutable by default.
Sequences provide lazy evaluation for collection chains. Use `asSequence()` for large datasets to avoid intermediate list allocations.
Kotlin provides rich functional APIs: map, filter, reduce, fold, flatMap, sortedBy, distinct, zip, unzip, associate, and more.
`groupBy` groups elements by a key selector. `partition` splits into two lists based on a predicate. `groupingBy` for eager grouping.
`chunked(size)` splits collection into fixed-size lists. `windowed(size)` creates sliding windows. Both support partial windows and steps.

Sequences (Sequence<T>) provide lazy evaluation: intermediate operations don't execute until terminal operation. Collections are eager. Use `.asSequence()` for chains of `map/filter/take` to avoid intermediate collections. Sequences are ideal for large datasets, infinite series, and chaining many operations. Generate with `sequence { yield() }`, `generateSequence`, `asSequence`.
Classes use `class` with a primary constructor in the header. Properties declared in the constructor are automatically generated with getters/setters.
Classes are final by default — use `open` to allow inheritance. Override methods with `override`. Interfaces can have abstract and default implementations.
`data class` automatically generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions. Perfect for DTOs and value objects.
Sealed types restrict hierarchies to a fixed set of subclasses defined in the same file. Perfect for representing states or algebraic data types.
`object` declares a singleton. `companion object` defines static-like members inside a class. Objects can also implement interfaces as anonymous instances.
`value class` wraps a single value without heap allocation overhead. Use `@JvmInline` for JVM interop. Prevents primitive boxing in many cases.
Type aliases provide alternative names for existing types, improving readability without introducing new types. Useful for function types and complex generics.
`by` delegates interface implementation to another object. `by lazy` for lazy initialization. Delegated properties via `observable`, `vetoable`, or custom delegates.
Abstract classes can have constructors, state, and both abstract and concrete methods. Nested/inner classes differ by whether they hold an outer reference.

Value classes wrap a single value with minimal overhead (no heap allocation in most cases). Declare with `@JvmInline value class`. Can have methods and computed properties but no backing fields, no `init` blocks, no class delegation. Inline classes replace primitive wrapper types with type safety. Also useful for type-safe IDs, units, domain primitives.
Generics enable type-safe code with type parameters. Functions and classes can be parameterised with one or more type parameters.
`out T` makes a type covariant (producer). `in T` makes it contravariant (consumer). Declaration-site variance avoids wildcards.

Reified type parameters (inline fun <reified T>) preserve generic type information at runtime. Works only with inline functions. Enables `T::class`, `is T`, `as T`. Bypasses JVM type erasure of generics. Common use: type-safe Gson/Jackson deserialization, type checks, `instanceof`-style pattern matching.
`*` for unknown type arguments. `MutableList<*>` is a mutable list of unknown type — safe to read as `Any?`, but not to write.
`T : UpperBound` constrains type parameters. Multiple bounds use `where` clause. Use `Nothing` for impossible values.
`launch` fires a fire-and-forget coroutine. `async` starts a coroutine that returns a `Deferred` result via `await()`. Both are non-blocking.
Dispatchers determine thread pools: Default for CPU, IO for I/O, Main for UI, Unconfined for testing. `withContext` switches dispatchers.
Coroutines lifetime ties to parent scope. Cancellation propagates downward; errors bubble up. `coroutineScope` waits for all children to complete.
supervisorScope isolates child failures: one child's exception doesn't cancel siblings or parent. Use for parallel independent work.
CoroutineContext combines Dispatcher, Job, and elements. `CoroutineScope` manages lifecycle. `Job` tracks lifecycle of a coroutine.
Cancellation is cooperative — check `isActive` or use `yield()`. `withTimeout` throws TimeoutCancellationException. `withTimeoutOrNull` returns null.
Uncaught exceptions cancel parent. Use `try-catch` inside coroutine, or `CoroutineExceptionHandler` for top-level exceptions.
`coroutineScope` suspends without blocking a thread. `runBlocking` blocks the current thread for bridge mode. Use coroutineScope in suspend functions.

Dispatchers determine coroutine execution threads. Dispatchers.Default: CPU-bound work (thread pool = #cores). Dispatchers.IO: I/O-bound work (expandable pool). Dispatchers.Main: UI thread (Android, JavaFX). Dispatchers.Unconfined: runs in current thread until first suspension. `newSingleThreadContext`/`newFixedThreadPoolContext` for custom pools. `withContext` changes dispatcher within a coroutine.
Flow is a cold async stream. Use `flow { }` builder with `emit()`, collect with `collect()`. Cold means nothing happens until collected.
Additional builders: `flowOf` for fixed values, `asFlow` on collections/ranges, `channelFlow` for concurrent emission, `callbackFlow` for callback APIs.
Intermediate operators: map, filter, transform, take, drop, debounce, sample, distinctUntilChanged, flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, flatMapLatest.
StateFlow holds observable state. Hot flow — always has a value. Emits only distinct values. Ideal for ViewModels and UI state.
SharedFlow emits events to multiple collectors. Hot flow with replay cache. Use `MutableSharedFlow` for one-shot events like toasts.
callbackFlow bridges callback-based APIs into Flows. Use `send()` inside, `awaitClose()` to clean up. Context preserving.
`zip` pairs elements one-to-one. `combine` merges latest values. `merge` interleaves multiple flows into one.

Flow operators: map, filter, transform, take, drop, distinctUntilChanged, debounce, sample, flatMapConcat/Merge/Latest, buffer, conflate, catch, retry, retryWhen, onCompletion, combine, zip. Terminal operators: collect, toList, toSet, first, single, count, reduce, fold. Operators are cold (start on collect). Use flowOn to change context. Buffer for concurrent processing. catch recovers from upstream errors.
Context receivers declare dependency on context types without inheritance. Functions can receive multiple contexts for modular APIs.
Contracts tell the compiler about function behavior. Use `callsInPlace`, `returnsNotNull`, `implies` for smarter analysis and fewer warnings.
`@JvmInline` marks inline classes on JVM. `@JvmStatic`, `@JvmOverloads`, `@JvmField`, `@Throws` control Kotlin-to-Java interop.
JVM erases generic types at runtime. `inline` + `reified` preserves them. `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")` for manual casts.
Kotlin reflection (`::class`, `::memberProperty`) inspects types at runtime. Use `memberProperties`, `functions`, `annotations` for meta-programming.
Kotlin annotations: `@Target`, `@Retention`, custom annotation classes. Apply to classes, functions, properties, or expressions with `@file:`, `@get:` etc.
Destructuring decomposes objects into variables with `componentN()` functions. Data classes auto-generate them; custom classes can implement operator fun componentN().

Inline functions copy their body to call sites, avoiding function call overhead. Use for lambdas (reduces object creation). `crossinline` prevents non-local returns, `noinline` prevents inlining specific parameters. `value class` + inline functions = zero-overhead abstractions. Over-inlining increases code size; use judiciously for small, frequently-called functions.
Kotlin Multiplatform shares logic across platforms. Business logic, data models, and networking in commonMain; platform UIs in platform-specific source sets.
`expect` declares platform-agnostic API in common code. `actual` provides platform-specific implementations. Compiler ensures all expects have actuals.
CommonMain uses Kotlin stdlib-common, kotlinx.coroutines, kotlinx.serialization. Shared data models, repository logic, and ViewModels live here.
Platform source sets (jvmMain, iosMain, jsMain) provide actual implementations. Access platform APIs and libraries from each target.
KMP has a growing ecosystem: Ktor for networking, SQLDelight for databases, Koin for DI, kotlinx.serialization, and Compose Multiplatform for UI.

expect/actual declares platform-specific APIs. `expect` in common code defines the interface, `actual` in platform modules provides the implementation. Works for functions, properties, classes, objects, type aliases. Platform source sets: `commonMain`, `jvmMain`, `jsMain`, `nativeMain`, `iosMain`, etc. Use `@OptionalExpectation` for annotations.
`kotlin.test` provides `@Test`, `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertNull`, `assertThrows`. Annotations work with JUnit 4/5, and multiplatform testing.
Kotest is a multiplatform test framework with behavior specs, property-based testing, matchers, and data-driven tests.
MockK is a Kotlin-first mocking library. Supports coroutines, spies, relaxed mocks, capturing, and verification with expressive DSL.
Property testing verifies invariants across many random inputs. Kotest and kotlin-check use generators (`Arb`) and properties (`forAll`).
`kotlinx-coroutines-test` provides `runTest`, `TestScope`, and virtual time. `advanceTimeBy`, `advanceUntilIdle` skip delays instantly.
Kotlin works seamlessly with JUnit 5. Use `@ParameterizedTest`, `@MethodSource`, `@ValueSource` with Kotlin collections and lambdas.

Kotest property testing generates random inputs to verify invariants. `forAll`, `forNone`, `forAtLeast`. Generators: `Arb.int()`, `Arb.string()`, `Arb.list(Arb.int())`. Custom generators with `arbitrary { }`. Shrinking finds minimal failing case. Combine with table testing for specific cases. IntSeededRandom for reproducibility.

MockK is Kotlin's mocking library designed for Kotlin features: coroutines, extension functions, object mocks, private functions. Key features: `mockk<T>()`, `every { } returns`, `coEvery { } coReturns`, `verify { }`, `slot`, `capture`, `relaxed mock`. Use `mockkStatic` for companion/static, `spyk` for partial mocks. `confirmVerified` ensures all calls were verified.

Gradle Kotlin DSL is the idiomatic build configuration for Kotlin projects. Uses `.gradle.kts` files. Type-safe accessors for configurations, tasks, extensions. Key plugins: kotlin("jvm"), kotlin("multiplatform"), kotlin("plugin.serialization"), application. Version catalogs (libs.versions.toml) for dependency management. Convention plugins for shared build logic.
Version catalogs in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` centralise dependency versions. Access via `libs.some.dependency` in build scripts.
buildSrc stores shared build logic as Kotlin sources. Convention plugins apply common configurations across modules — DRY for multi-module projects.
KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing) is a compiler plugin for annotation processing. K2 compiler (1.9+) offers faster compilation and improved type inference.
Dokka generates Kotlin documentation (KDoc). Supports multiplatform projects, HTML/MD/JavaDoc outputs. Often used with Gradle's `dokka` plugin.

Scope functions: `let`, `run`, `with`, `apply`, `also`. Key differences: context object (it vs this), return value (context vs lambda result). `let`: `it` + result for transformations/chaining. `apply`: `this` + context for configuration. `run`: `this` + result for computing with context. `also`: `it` + context for side effects. `with`: `this` + result (extension function, non-null). Combine thoughtfully for readable code.

Lambda with receiver allows calling methods on an implicit `this` inside the lambda. The `receiver` type is the context. Used by `apply`, `run`, `with`, `buildString`, and custom DSLs. From Kotlin in Action.

Type-safe builders use lambdas with receivers for declarative construction. @DslMarker restricts implicit receiver access to prevent ambiguity with nested builder contexts. Common: HTML builders, Gradle DSL, Compose UI. Builder pattern with apply/also. Context receivers (Kotlin 1.6+) for multiple receivers in scope.

Single Abstract Method (SAM) conversion lets you pass a lambda where a Java functional interface is expected. Kotlin has built-in function types, so SAM conversion mainly applies to Java interop. From Head First Kotlin.

Kotlin is 100% interoperable with Java. Key annotations: `@JvmStatic` for static methods, `@JvmOverloads` for overloaded methods, `@JvmField` for fields, `@Throws` for checked exceptions, `@JvmName` to resolve signature clashes.

Common Kotlin idioms from Head First Kotlin and Kotlin in Action: default arguments for builders, `require`/`check` for preconditions, `use` for Closeable, `takeIf`/`takeUnless` for conditional returns, `TODO()` for stubs, `runCatching` for try-catch expressions.

Jetpack Compose is Kotlin's declarative UI framework for Android. `@Composable` functions describe UI. State: `mutableStateOf`, `remember`, `derivedStateOf`, `collectAsState`. Layout: Column, Row, Box, LazyColumn, LazyRow. Modifier chain for styling. Side effects: LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect. Compose uses Kotlin coroutines for animations and async operations.
ViewModel survives configuration changes. Use `viewModel()` in Compose, expose `StateFlow`, and collect as Compose state with `collectAsState()`.
LiveData is lifecycle-aware. StateFlow is the coroutines-native alternative. Use `asLiveData()` to bridge StateFlow to LiveData for legacy code.
Room is a SQLite ORM. Use `@Entity`, `@Dao`, `@Database`. Coroutines support via suspend functions and Flow return types in DAOs.
Retrofit type-safe HTTP client used with Kotlin coroutines. Define `suspend` functions in API interfaces. Use kotlinx.serialization or Moshi for JSON.
Navigation Compose provides type-safe navigation in Compose. Define routes with `NavHost`, navigate with `navController.navigate()`, pass safe args.

Ktor Client is Kotlin multiplatform HTTP client. Features: coroutine-based, pluggable engines (OkHttp JVM, Darwin iOS, JS), content negotiation, kotlinx.serialization, auth, cookies, WebSockets. Build with HttpClient { install(ContentNegotiation) { json() } }. Requests: get, post, put, delete. Streaming with HttpStatement.
lua.json: Variables and data types in Lua.

pcall(f, ...) calls function f in protected mode (like try-catch). Returns true + results on success, or false + error message on failure. pcall catches all errors and prevents them from propagating. Common mistake: not checking the first return value of pcall — always check if the call succeeded. Best practice: use pcall for operations that might fail with expected error types.

xpcall(f, err_handler, ...) is like pcall but with a custom error handler function. The handler receives the error message and can augment it with debug information. Common mistake: forgetting that the error handler runs in protected mode too — errors in the handler are caught. Best practice: use xpcall with debug.traceback to get detailed stack traces.

error(message, level) raises an error that terminates the current function unless caught by pcall/xpcall. The level parameter (1 = caller of error, 2 = caller's caller, etc.) controls where the error traceback points. Common mistake: not providing helpful error messages — good error messages include expected and actual values. Best practice: use descriptive error messages that help diagnose the problem.

assert(condition, message) combines assertion and error handling. If condition is truthy, returns it. If falsy, raises an error with the message (default: 'assertion failed!'). Common mistake: using assert for validation in production code — assert can be stripped in some contexts. Best practice: use assert for input validation and preconditions, not for runtime error handling.
Input and output operations in Lua.

Weak tables allow the garbage collector to reclaim objects even though they're referenced in the table. Modes: __mode = 'k' (weak keys), 'v' (weak values), or 'kv' (both). Used for memoization, object associations, and caching without preventing GC. Common mistake: using weak tables with non-collectible keys (numbers, booleans) — they don't support weak references. Best practice: use weak-value tables for caches and weak-key tables for object properties.

Lua uses incremental garbage collection. collectgarbage(opt) controls the collector: collectgarbage('collect') forces a full cycle, collectgarbage('count') reports memory in KB, collectgarbage('stop') pauses the collector. Lua 5.4 introduced generational mode. Common mistake: assuming collectgarbage('count') returns bytes — it returns kilobytes. Best practice: let the GC run automatically; only intervene for latency-sensitive code.

Lua 5.2+ uses _ENV to control the environment of a chunk. _ENV is a table that stores global variables. Changing _ENV enables sandboxing and module isolation. Common mistake: assuming _ENV affects the entire Lua state — it only affects the current chunk/function. Best practice: use _ENV for creating restricted execution environments and sandboxes.

The debug library provides introspection capabilities. debug.getinfo(f) returns a table with function metadata. debug.getlocal(f, i) and debug.getupvalue(f, i) inspect local/upvalue variables. debug.traceback() returns a stack trace string. debug.sethook sets function hooks for profiling. Common mistake: using debug library in production code — it's designed for debugging and development. Best practice: restrict debug library usage to development tools and testing.

Lua's C API allows embedding Lua in C/C++ programs and writing C libraries for Lua. Key concepts: lua_State (interpreter state), stack-based API (lua_push*, lua_to*, lua_get*), lua_pcall (protected call from C). The Lua C API follows a disciplined stack protocol. Common mistake: forgetting to balance the Lua stack after operations. Best practice: use the Lua Reference Manual as the definitive guide for C API functions.

LuaJIT is a Just-In-Time compiler for Lua 5.1. Much faster than PUC Lua. FFI library for direct C interop. JIT compilation for hot paths. Use `luajit` instead of `lua`. Pitfalls: JIT can't compile some constructs (calls to C functions, string manipulation in loops). Use --dump and --jv.dump to see compiled traces. NYI (Not Yet Implemented) calls force fallback to interpreter.

Lua is a lightweight, high-level, dynamically typed scripting language designed for embedded use in applications. Created in 1993 at PUC-Rio in Brazil, it's widely used in game development (World of Warcraft, Roblox), embedded systems, and configuration scripting. Common mistake: confusing Lua's simplicity with lack of power — Lua's metatables and first-class functions enable sophisticated programming patterns. Best practice: use local variables by default, avoid global pollution, and leverage Lua's table-as-structure paradigm.

Lua uses keywords instead of curly braces for blocks, and whitespace is not significant (unlike Python). Statements can end with semicolons but they're optional. Blocks are delimited with keywords like then/end, do/end, and function/end. Common mistake: forgetting the 'then' keyword after if/elseif conditions. Best practice: use semicolons only to separate statements on the same line; omit them otherwise for cleaner code.

Lua supports single-line comments with -- and multi-line comments with --[[ ]]. Multi-line comments can be nested with additional brackets. Common mistake: forgetting that --[[ ]] comments cannot contain the sequence ']]' unless you use an equal sign format. Best practice: use --[[ ]] for commenting out blocks of code during debugging, and -- for explanatory comments.

The print() function outputs text to stdout with a trailing newline. Multiple arguments are separated by tabs. Common mistake: forgetting that print adds a tab between arguments — use io.write() for exact output control. Best practice: use print() for quick debugging and io.write() for formatted output where you need precise control.

Lua's REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) lets you execute code interactively by running 'lua' with no arguments. Use dofile() to load and execute a Lua file, and loadfile() to compile without running. Common mistake: expecting the REPL to persist local variables between input lines — each line is a separate chunk. Best practice: use dofile() during development to reload modules without restarting the REPL.

Lua versions: 5.1 (most compatible, used by LuaJIT, World of Warcraft), 5.2 (environments changed), 5.3 (integers, bit32), 5.4 (generational GC, const/close, to-be-closed vars). LuaJIT is a JIT-compiled implementation compatible with Lua 5.1. Luau is Roblox's variant with typed Lua. Check _VERSION to detect version at runtime.

Lua is dynamically typed — variables don't have types; values do. A variable can hold any type of value at any time. There's no variable declaration keyword (unlike 'let' or 'var'); assigning a value creates the variable globally unless 'local' is used. Common mistake: forgetting 'local' creates a global variable, even inside loops and functions. Best practice: always use local for variables that should be scoped to the current block.

nil is Lua's "no value" type, representing the absence of a value. Global variables default to nil, table keys with no value are nil, and assigning nil to a table key removes it from the table. Common mistake: treating nil as false in comparisons — nil is falsy, but is not the same as false. Best practice: use x == nil to check for nil explicitly, not just if x then, since false is also falsy.

Lua's boolean type has two values: true and false. Only nil and false are falsy; everything else (including 0 and empty string) is truthy. Common mistake: assuming 0 or empty string is falsy — they are not in Lua. Best practice: use explicit comparisons like x == nil for clarity instead of relying on truthiness.

All Lua numbers are double-precision floating-point by default. Lua 5.3+ also provides integers (64-bit) that are used internally when appropriate. Arithmetic operations automatically choose between integer and float representations. Common mistake: assuming integer division truncates — use // (floor division) for integer division. Best practice: be aware that large integers (> 2^53) lose precision due to double representation.

Strings in Lua are immutable byte sequences. You can use single quotes, double quotes, or long brackets [[ ]] for multi-line strings. Escape sequences work inside quoted strings (\n, \t, \", \'). Common mistake: using # on strings counts bytes, not characters — for UTF-8 strings, use utf8.len(). Best practice: use [[ ]] for strings containing quotes or line breaks to avoid escaping.

The type() function returns a string describing the type of a value. Lua automatically coerces strings to numbers in arithmetic and numbers to strings in concatenation. Common mistake: relying on automatic coercion in comparisons — '10' == 10 is false (no coercion in equality). Best practice: use tonumber() and tostring() explicitly for clarity.

Lua supports simultaneous multiple assignment: `a, b = 1, 2`. Right-hand values are adjusted to match left-hand variables: extra values discarded, missing values become nil. Useful for swapping: `a, b = b, a`. Function calls can return multiple values captured by multiple assignment.

Lua provides standard arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, ^ (exponentiation), // (floor division, Lua 5.3+), and % (modulo). The modulo operator always takes the sign of the divisor. Common mistake: using / when you want integer division — use // (floor division) instead. Best practice: understand that % in Lua is defined as a % b == a - (a // b) * b, which differs from C's remainder.

Lua's relational operators are: == (equal), ~= (not equal), <, >, <=, >=. They always return a boolean. Tables and userdata are compared by reference, not by value. Common mistake: using == to compare tables — it checks reference equality, not structural equality. Best practice: implement custom comparison via metamethods if table equality is needed.

Lua's logical operators are: and, or, not. They use short-circuit evaluation: 'and' stops at the first falsy value; 'or' stops at the first truthy value. Common mistake: assuming logical operators always return booleans — they return one of their operands. Best practice: use the 'a or b' idiom for default values.

The .. operator concatenates strings (coercing numbers). The # operator returns the length of a string or array-like table. Common mistake: using # on tables with nil gaps — # returns an undefined result for non-sequence tables. Best practice: only use # on tables that are proper sequences (consecutive integer keys starting at 1, no nil values).

Lua's operator precedence (highest to lowest): ^, unary - not #, * / // %, + -, .., < > <= >= ~= ==, and, or. Exponentiation is right-associative; all others are left-associative. Common mistake: assuming bitwise operators exist — Lua 5.3+ has them in bit32 library, not as operators. Best practice: use parentheses generously for complex expressions.

Lua's if statement ends with 'end' and uses 'then' after conditions. Use 'elseif' (one word) for multiple branches. Conditions must be boolean or use truthiness. Common mistake: using 'else if' instead of 'elseif' — 'else if' requires a nested if/end block. Best practice: keep conditions simple; use local variables to store complex conditions.

The while loop executes as long as the condition is true. The condition is checked before each iteration. Common mistake: forgetting to update the loop variable, causing infinite loops. Best practice: use while for loops with variable conditions and for loops when the iteration count is known.

The repeat/until loop always executes its body at least once before checking the condition. This differs from while loops that may never execute. Common mistake: confusing repeat/until with while — the condition is checked AFTER the body. Best practice: use repeat/until when you need guaranteed at-least-once execution.

The numeric for loop: for var = init, limit, step do end. The loop variable is local to the loop body. Step defaults to 1 if omitted. The limit is evaluated once before the loop starts. Common mistake: modifying the loop variable inside the body — it will be reset each iteration. Best practice: don't modify the loop variable; use a separate variable if needed.

The generic for loop iterates over iterators like pairs(), ipairs(), and custom iterators. It uses the pattern: for var-list in iterator, state, initial-value do. Common mistake: using pairs() when you need ordered iteration — pairs() doesn't guarantee order. Best practice: use ipairs() for array-style tables and pairs() for dictionaries.

The break statement terminates the innermost enclosing loop (for, while, or repeat). Lua does NOT have continue — you must use conditional wrapping to skip iterations. Common mistake: trying to use 'continue' — it doesn't exist in Lua. Best practice: use if/else blocks to skip iterations instead of continue.

Tables are Lua's sole data structuring mechanism, combining arrays, dictionaries, objects, and modules. They're created with {} and are dynamically resizable. Tables are reference types — assigning a table to another variable creates a reference, not a copy. Common mistake: assuming tables are 0-indexed — Lua arrays conventionally start at index 1. Best practice: always start array indices at 1 for compatibility with #, ipairs(), and table library functions.

Table constructors create and initialize tables in a single expression. Use curly braces with comma-separated values. Common mistake: mixing key-value and array-style constructors can produce confusing results. Best practice: use array-style ({1, 2, 3}) for sequences and key-value style ({x=1, y=2}) for records.

Lua arrays are 1-indexed and can hold any value type. The # operator returns the length of a sequence. Array indices are conventional — Lua internally uses any value type as a key. Common mistake: assuming # gives the count of elements in a table with gaps — it doesn't. Best practice: maintain tables as proper sequences (no nil gaps) when using array operations.

The table library provides: table.insert(t, pos, val), table.remove(t, pos), table.sort(t, comp), and table.concat(t, sep). These modify the table in-place. Common mistake: table.insert with pos shifts all subsequent elements — O(n) operation. Best practice: use t[#t+1] = val for appending (faster than table.insert).

Use ipairs() for sequential iteration over array-style tables (stops at first nil). Use a numeric for loop for complete control. Common mistake: using pairs() for arrays — it doesn't guarantee order. Best practice: use ipairs() when you need ordered index-value pairs; use a numeric for loop when you need to modify elements during iteration.

Tables can use any value (except nil) as a key. String keys can be set with dot notation (t.key) or bracket notation (t['key']). Bracket notation is required for non-string keys or keys with spaces. Common mistake: using t.key when key contains spaces or special characters — use t["key name"] instead. Best practice: prefer bracket notation for dynamic keys and dot notation for literal string keys.

Tables can contain other tables as values, creating nested structures like multi-dimensional arrays, trees, and graphs. Access nested values by chaining brackets or dots. Common mistake: creating a shallow copy with = when you need a deep copy — = only copies the reference. Best practice: write a recursive copy function for deep copies of nested tables.

pairs() iterates over all key-value pairs in a table, including array-style indices. The iteration order is NOT guaranteed. For ordered iteration, collect keys into a sorted array first. Common mistake: relying on pairs() to visit keys in insertion order — it doesn't. Best practice: use pairs() for dictionary-style tables and ipairs() or numeric for for arrays.

The # operator only works reliably for sequences (consecutive integer keys from 1 with no nil gaps). For dictionaries, use next() to count elements. Common mistake: using # on a dictionary — it returns 0 or an arbitrary value. Best practice: write a table.size() helper using next() for non-array tables.

Lua allows mixing array-style and dictionary-style entries in a single constructor. Array items get integer keys starting at 1; dictionary items get string keys. Understanding how Lua assigns keys is crucial for predictable results. Common mistake: expecting array-style indices to skip over dictionary items — array indices are assigned based on position counting only array items.

table library provides: table.insert, table.remove, table.sort, table.concat, table.pack, table.unpack, table.move. table.sort accepts comparator function. table.concat efficiently joins string arrays. table.pack creates array from varargs with .n field. table.unpack expands table into values. These work on array-like tables (consecutive integer keys starting at 1).

Functions are first-class values in Lua, created with the function keyword or as anonymous functions. The return keyword exits a function and optionally returns values. Common mistake: forgetting 'return' — functions without an explicit return return nil. Best practice: declare local functions for internal use and assign to global variables for public APIs.

Functions can return multiple values using the 'return' keyword with comma-separated expressions. If a function doesn't hit a return statement, it returns nil. Common mistake: capturing multiple returns with a single variable — extra returns are discarded. Best practice: use multiple assignment to capture all return values.

Several built-in functions return multiple values: string.find returns start and end positions, pairs returns key and value, ipairs returns index and value. The unpack() function (table.unpack in Lua 5.3+) returns all elements of an array as individual values. Common mistake: wrapping a multi-return function in parentheses discards all but the first value. Best practice: use table.pack() to capture multiple returns in a table.

Variadic functions accept any number of arguments using the ... (three dots) syntax. Use {...} to capture args in a table, or select() to access individual args. Common mistake: using {...} when arguments may contain nil — nil values will be lost in the table. Best practice: use table.pack(...) to capture variadic args including nil values.

Lua supports lexical scoping: inner functions can access outer function's local variables (upvalues). Each invocation of the outer function creates a new closure with its own upvalues. Common mistake: assuming closures capture values by copy — they capture variables by reference. Best practice: use closures for function factories, callbacks, and iterators.

Lua proper tail calls: when a function ends with return func(args), the current stack frame is reused, preventing stack growth. This enables recursive algorithms without stack overflow. Common mistake: any operation after the call (like return func() + 1) prevents tail call optimization. Best practice: use tail calls for state-machine implementations and recursive algorithms.

Lua functions are closures — they capture local variables (upvalues) from their enclosing scope. Each closure instance has its own upvalue set. Closures enable function factories, callbacks, and encapsulation (private state). The upvalues persist even after the outer function returns.

Lua strings are immutable byte sequences. Indexing with # gives byte length, not character count. String positions start at 1 (not 0). Escape sequences in quoted strings: \n (newline), \t (tab), \\ (backslash), \" (double quote), \' (single quote). Common mistake: using string indexing syntax s[i] — Lua doesn't support this; use s:sub(i, i) instead. Best practice: use [[ ]] for multi-line or escape-heavy strings.

Use .. for string concatenation. Lua automatically coerces numbers to strings in concatenation context. For large-scale concatenation, use table.concat() which is much more efficient than repeated .. operations. Common mistake: using .. in a loop for building large strings — O(n^2) due to immutable string allocation. Best practice: collect parts in a table and use table.concat() for batch concatenation.

The string library provides: len(s), sub(s, i, j), upper(s), lower(s), rep(s, n), char(...), and byte(s, i). Methods use colon notation: s:upper(). Common mistake: confusing string.byte (returns numeric codes) with string.char (creates string from codes). Best practice: use colon notation (s:method()) for readability — it passes s as the first argument.

string.match(s, pattern) extracts captures from a string based on a Lua pattern. Returns the first match or nil. Anchored patterns start with ^ (beginning) or end with $ (end). Common mistake: using Lua patterns with regex metacharacters like ? or + — Lua patterns use a different syntax. Best practice: test patterns incrementally, starting simple and adding constraints.

string.gmatch(s, pattern) returns an iterator that yields all matches (with or without captures) of a pattern in a string. Use it in for loops or collect all matches into a table. Common mistake: forgetting that gmatch returns captures if the pattern has them, or the full match otherwise. Best practice: use gmatch with captures to extract structured data.
