string.gsub(s, pattern, replacement) performs global search-and-replace, returning the modified string and a count of replacements. Replacement can be a string, a table (keyed by captures), or a function. Common mistake: forgetting that gsub returns TWO values — the new string and the replacement count. Best practice: use a function replacement for complex transformations.

Lua patterns are simpler than regular expressions. Character classes: %a (letter), %d (digit), %s (whitespace), %w (alphanumeric), . (any). Uppercase means negation: %D = non-digit. Quantifiers: + (one or more), * (zero or more), - (lazy zero or more), ? (zero or one). Captures with (). Common mistake: using regex syntax like \d or [0-9] — use Lua %d or [09] instead. Best practice: use the () (empty capture) to capture positions.

print() is a simplified output function that adds a tab separator between arguments and a newline at the end. io.write() provides lower-level output with no automatic formatting. Common mistake: using print() when you need exact formatting control — print always adds separators and newlines. Best practice: use print() for quick debugging and io.write() for formatted, precise output.

io.read() reads input from stdin. Formats: '*l' (line, default), '*a' (entire file), '*n' (number), or a number (read that many characters). Returns nil on EOF. Common mistake: io.read('*n') reads a number but stops at whitespace — the newline remains in the buffer. Best practice: use io.read() for line input and tonumber() for numeric conversion.

Use io.open(filename, mode) to open files. Modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write, overwrites), 'a' (append), 'r+' (read/write). Returns a file handle or nil + error message. Methods: handle:read(), handle:write(), handle:close(), handle:lines(). Common mistake: forgetting to close files — use a pcall/finally pattern to ensure cleanup. Best practice: use io.lines() for line-by-line reading without manual close.

string.format(format, ...) provides C-style printf formatting. Specifiers: %d (integer), %f (float), %s (string), %x (hex), %e (scientific). Width and precision can be specified: %10s (min width 10), %.2f (2 decimal places). Common mistake: using %d for floats or %f for integers — both work but may give unexpected results. Best practice: use specific format specifiers for clarity.

Lua's I/O: io.open(mode) returns file handle or nil+errmsg. Modes: "r" (read), "w" (write), "a" (append), "r+"/"w+"/"a+" (read+write), "b" suffix (binary). Methods: read(format), write, lines, seek, flush, close. read formats: "*a" (all), "*l" (line), "*n" (number), or byte count.

require(name) loads and executes a module, returning the module table. It searches package.path for Lua files and package.cpath for C libraries. Modules are cached in package.loaded — subsequent require calls return the cached version. Common mistake: requiring a module returns the module table but forget to assign it. Best practice: always assign the result of require to a local variable.

The standard Lua module pattern: create a local table, add functions to it, and return it at the end. Use local variables for private/internal functions. Common mistake: polluting the global namespace — module internals should be local. Best practice: follow the standard pattern of returning a table with only public functions.

package.path controls where Lua looks for Lua modules. The default path uses ?.lua and ?/init.lua patterns. LUA_PATH environment variable overrides it. You can manipulate package.path at runtime to add search paths. Common mistake: module files not found because they're not in package.path — always check the search path. Best practice: use the LUA_PATH environment variable or add paths programmatically.

Lua modules should return a table, use local variables for private members, and avoid polluting the global namespace. Use 'local' by default. Name modules in lowercase with underscores. Place modules in a clear directory structure. Common mistake: defining module functions as globals — this pollutes the global namespace and can cause conflicts. Best practice: encapsulate all module code in a local table and return it.

Metatables control table behavior through metamethods (events). setmetatable(t, mt) assigns a metatable to table t; getmetatable(t) retrieves it. Metamethods are triggered by operations like indexing, arithmetic, and comparison. Common mistake: trying to set metatables on non-table types (numbers, strings) — only tables and userdata can have metatables in standard Lua. Best practice: use metatables sparingly for domain-specific behaviors.

__index is the most commonly used metamethod. It provides fallback behavior when a key doesn't exist in a table. It can be a table (lookup in that table) or a function (called with table and key). Common mistake: confusing __index with __newindex — __index handles MISSING key reads; __newindex handles MISSING key writes. Best practice: use __index with a table for simple inheritance and with a function for computed lookups.

__newindex intercepts assignments to keys that don't exist in the table. It can be a table (writes go to that table) or a function (receives table, key, value). Common mistake: __newindex doesn't prevent writes to EXISTING keys — it only fires for MISSING keys. Best practice: combine __index and __newindex for controlled table access patterns.

The __call metamethod makes a table callable as a function. The metamethod receives the table as the first argument, followed by any call arguments. Common mistake: forgetting that the table itself is passed as the first argument to __call. Best practice: use __call for function objects (functors) that maintain state.

Lua supports arithmetic metamethods: __add, __sub, __mul, __div, __mod, __pow, __unm (unary minus), __concat, and __tostring. These enable operator overloading on tables. Common mistake: forgetting to handle both operand orders — __add only fires when the first operand has the metatable. Best practice: define all relevant metamethods for consistent behavior.

Lua implements object-oriented programming through prototype-based inheritance using metatables. The colon syntax (obj:method()) is syntactic sugar for (obj.method(obj)) — it automatically passes the object as 'self'. Common mistake: forgetting 'self' parameter or colon syntax when calling methods. Best practice: always use colon syntax for method definitions (:method) and method calls (:method()).

Coroutines allow cooperative multitasking: a coroutine can yield (pause) execution and be resumed later from where it left off. coroutine.create(f) creates a coroutine. coroutine.resume(co, ...) starts or resumes it. coroutine.yield(...) suspends execution and returns values to the resumer. Common mistake: trying to resume a dead (finished) coroutine — it will return false + error message. Best practice: check the first return value of resume (true = success, false = error).

coroutine.status(co) returns the state: 'suspended' (created or just yielded), 'running' (currently executing), 'dead' (finished or errored), or 'normal' (resumed another coroutine). Common mistake: calling status from within the running coroutine — it returns 'running'. Best practice: use status() to check if a coroutine can be resumed before calling resume.

coroutine.wrap(f) creates a coroutine and returns a function that resumes it. Unlike coroutine.resume, errors are propagated as exceptions instead of returning false. Common mistake: wrap returns a function that throws errors — use pcall around it for error handling. Best practice: use wrap for simple iterator-like coroutines where you don't need error handling per step.

Coroutines excel at the producer-consumer pattern: a producer yields values as they become available, and a consumer resumes the producer to get the next value. Common mistake: not handling the end-of-production condition properly. Best practice: use a sentinel value (like nil) to signal end of production.

Coroutines are useful for: generators (lazy sequences), cooperative multitasking (game loops), state machines (each state is a yield point), and asynchronous I/O simulation. Common mistake: using coroutines for CPU-bound parallelism — Lua's coroutines are cooperative, not preemptive; they don't use multiple cores. Best practice: use coroutines for I/O-bound or event-driven programming.

The math library provides standard mathematical functions. Key functions: math.abs, math.max/min, math.floor/ceil, math.random, math.sin/cos/tan, math.sqrt, math.log. Constants: math.pi, math.huge (infinity). math.randomseed() seeds the random generator. Common mistake: forgetting to call math.randomseed() before using math.random() — you'll get the same sequence every run. Best practice: use math.randomseed(os.time()) for different sequences per run.

The os library interfaces with the operating system. Key functions: os.time (current time as timestamp), os.date (format time), os.clock (CPU time), os.execute (run command), os.exit (terminate), os.tmpname (temp file name). Common mistake: os.clock returns CPU time, not wall-clock time — use os.time for wall time. Best practice: use os.date with format strings for readable timestamps.

The io library provides input/output facilities beyond stdin/stdout. io.stdin, io.stdout, io.stderr are predefined file handles. io.popen runs a command and returns a file handle connected to its input/output. io.type checks if a handle is valid. Common mistake: mixing io.read/io.write with file handle methods — use file:read/file:write for file handles. Best practice: use the implicit handle (io.read/write) for stdin/out and explicit handles for files.

The table library provides essential table manipulation functions. Key functions: table.insert, table.remove, table.sort, table.concat, table.unpack (Lua 5.3+), and table.move (Lua 5.3+). table.unpack returns all elements of an array as separate values. table.move copies elements within or between tables. Common mistake: table.sort is unstable — equal elements may not preserve their original order. Best practice: combine table.sort with a comparison function for complex sorting.

The bit32 library (Lua 5.2+) provides bitwise operations: bit32.band, bit32.bor, bit32.bxor, bit32.bnot, bit32.lshift, bit32.rshift, bit32.arshift (arithmetic shift), bit32.rol, bit32.ror (rotate). All operations work on 32-bit unsigned integers. Common mistake: using bitwise operators (&, |, ^) that don't exist in Lua — use the bit32 library functions. Best practice: use bit32 for flags, permissions, and low-level data manipulation.

Busted is the standard Lua testing framework. Describe/it blocks structure tests. Assertions: assert.equals, assert.is_true, assert.is_nil, assert.truthy, assert.error. Setup/teardown: before_each, after_each, before, after. Pending tests, spy mocking, and async support. Run with `busted` command.
mobile.json: Test on a representative device matrix covering: low-end (2GB RAM, 720p), mid-range (4GB, 1080p), high-end (8GB+, 1440p), and different GPU families (Adreno, Mali, Apple). Use Firebase Test Lab for automated testing across 50+ Android devices. For iOS, use Xcode Cloud or AWS Device Farm. Test for: crash-on-start, memory leaks after 30 minutes, thermal throttling after 15 minutes of gameplay, touch input accuracy at screen edges, notch/cutout rendering, and audio latency. Run automated UI tests with Unity Test Framework or XCTest.
.Mobile Testing & Deployment.App Store & Google Play Submission[0]

Google Play requires: signed AAB (Android App Bundle), store listing (icons, screenshots, feature graphic, description), content rating questionnaire, privacy policy (if collecting data), and testing track (internal → closed alpha → open beta → production). App Store requires: signed IPA via Xcode archive, App Store Connect listing (screenshots for required sizes: 6.5-inch, 5.5-inch, iPad), privacy nutrition label, and review. Common rejection reasons: crashes, broken links, placeholder content, insufficient information. Budget 1-3 business days for review.

Mobile crash reporting is essential. Unity's Cloud Diagnostics captures native crashes (iOS/Android) and managed exceptions. Firebase Crashlytics provides real-time crash reporting with symbolication (mapping minified stack traces to source). Track: crash-free session rate (target > 99.5%), ANR (Application Not Responding) rate on Android, OOM (Out of Memory) kills, and custom breadcrumbs (player was in level 3, just opened inventory). Symbolicate iOS crashes with dSYM files. Upload Android ProGuard mapping files for obfuscated stack traces.

Mobile gaming is the largest segment of the games industry. Phones and tablets offer unique constraints: touch input, limited battery, thermal throttling, fragmented hardware, and interrupt-driven usage (calls, notifications). Success requires designing for short sessions, efficient resource use, and broad device compatibility. The major engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot) all support mobile export with platform-specific optimizations.

Unity dominates mobile with 60%+ market share — excellent cross-platform support, massive asset store, and C# scripting. Unreal Engine targets high-end mobile with stunning visuals but heavier APK sizes and higher device requirements. Godot is lightweight, open-source, and exports to Android/iOS with minimal overhead but a smaller mobile community. For 2D mobile games, Godot or Unity 2D are great choices. For 3D, Unity balances quality and performance; Unreal excels on flagship devices.

Building for mobile involves multiple steps: code compilation, asset compression, texture format conversion (ETC2 for Android, PVRTC/ASTC for iOS), architecture-specific binaries (ARM64, ARMv7), and final packaging. Unity uses the Build Settings window or command-line builds. Android produces APK or AAB (Android App Bundle). iOS produces IPA via Xcode. Each platform requires specific SDKs, NDKs, and provisioning profiles.

Mobile input is fundamentally different from mouse/keyboard. Touch events provide position, phase (began/moved/ended/cancelled), and a unique finger ID for multi-touch. The screen is a direct manipulation surface — what you touch is what you interact with. Input latency on mobile typically ranges from 40-100ms. Always handle the cancelled phase (system interrupts like calls). Maximum simultaneous touches varies from 5-10 depending on device.

Common mobile gestures: tap, double-tap, long-press, swipe, pinch-to-zoom, rotate, drag, flick. Implement gesture recognizers that track touch state over time. A tap is a brief touch/release within a distance threshold (usually < 10px) and time threshold (< 300ms). A swipe requires minimum velocity and distance. Pinch tracks two touch points' distance changes. Use dead zones (small ignored movements) to prevent jitter from noisy touch input.

Virtual controls overlay the screen with touch zones mapped to game actions. Joysticks track a touch point within a radius — the normalized offset from center becomes the input vector. Buttons trigger on touch began within their rect. Place controls in the lower screen thirds (thumb zones) and avoid the notch/camera cutout area. Consider configurable layouts for accessibility. Scale controls relative to screen resolution and aspect ratio.

Haptic feedback improves immersion and confirms actions. Android uses VibrationEffect with amplitude control. iOS uses UIImpactFeedbackGenerator, UINotificationFeedbackGenerator, and UISelectionFeedbackGenerator for different haptic patterns. Unity's Handheld.Vibrate() provides basic support; plugins like Lofelt provide advanced haptic design. Use haptics sparingly — overuse drains battery and annoys players. Respect system-level haptic settings.

Mobile devices throttle performance when overheating. CPU/GPU intensive tasks, background networking, and inefficient rendering drain battery. Profile thermal impact: measure temperature rise per operation. Key strategies: reduce CPU frame time (< 16ms for 60fps), minimize GPU overdraw, batch draw calls (< 100), use efficient physics (fewer colliders, simpler shapes), and reduce WiFi/cellular polling. iOS reports thermal state via ProcessInfo.thermalState. Android monitors via PowerManager.

Mobile has limited RAM (2-8GB shared with OS). Texture memory is the biggest consumer: a 2048x2048 RGBA texture = 16MB. Android's onTrimMemory() warns of impending kill. iOS issues memory warnings via didReceiveMemoryWarning. Load assets progressively, unload unused scenes, use mipmaps (saves ~33% GPU memory), and compress textures (ETC2/ASTC). Avoid large contiguous allocations — they fragment the heap. Pool and reuse objects instead of allocate/free cycles.

Device capabilities vary enormously. Measure GPU fill rate, RAM, and screen resolution at startup, then set quality tiers. Use a quality profile that adjusts: shadow resolution, anti-aliasing, post-processing, texture resolution, draw distance, particle count, and LOD bias. Re-evaluate periodically and when thermal state changes. Unity's QualitySettings and Godot's OS methods support runtime quality changes.

Mobile games must manage download size and memory. Asset bundles (Unity) or resource packs (Godot) let you split content into on-demand chunks. Initial download should be under 150MB. Stream additional levels, textures, and audio on demand. Use addressable assets for runtime loading with reference counting. Cache downloaded bundles to device storage. Prioritize essential assets (first level, UI) and defer high-res textures and later levels. Use LZ4 compression for faster runtime decompression.

Mobile screens range from 320x480 (old budget) to 1440x3040 (flagship). Use anchor-based layouts that scale relative to screen edges. Avoid absolute pixel positions. Calculate UI scale based on reference resolution (typically 1080p for mobile). Handle safe areas (notch, camera cutout, status bar, gesture bar). Unity's Canvas Scaler with 'Scale With Screen Size' handles most cases. For Godot, use Control nodes with anchors. Always test on a variety of screen sizes.
.Mobile UI & UX.Mobile UX Patterns for Games[0]

Mobile games thrive on simplicity: short sessions (3-5 minutes), clear goals, immediate feedback. Thumb zones: top = less reachable (menus, info), bottom = thumb-friendly (actions, navigation). Avoid right-edge swipe (system gesture conflict on iOS). Use touch-friendly targets (minimum 44x44pt, ideally 48x48pt). Provide visual feedback on touch (press state, animation). Use onboarding tutorials that respect player agency — let them skip or replay.

Mobile games are frequently interrupted: incoming calls, notifications, app switcher, low battery. Save game state aggressively — on every significant action, not just on graceful exit. Handle OnApplicationPause (Unity) or _notification() with NOTIFICATION_APPLICATION_PAUSED (Godot). Serialize critical state (player position, score, inventory, quest progress) to persistent storage. Use auto-save with a cooldown (every 30s or on checkpoint). On resume, restore state seamlessly without reloading the entire scene.

Mobile networks are unreliable: high latency (100-500ms cellular), packet loss, IP address changes, and frequent disconnections (tunnels, elevators). Design for offline-first with sync-on-reconnect. Use TCP for reliable state updates and UDP for real-time gameplay with interpolation/extrapolation. Implement reconnection with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...). Detect connection type (WiFi vs cellular) to adjust data usage. Respect metered connections — offer low-data mode.

Offline-first architecture lets players continue without connectivity. Queue actions locally, sync when online. Use a local database (SQLite via Unity's SQLite plugin, or IndexedDB for web). Track a sync version per record to resolve conflicts. Last-write-wins works for simple data; CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) for complex multiplayer. Show clear indicators for online/offline state. Never block gameplay waiting for network — use optimistic updates and reconcile later.

Mobile real-time multiplayer faces latency, connection drops, and data costs. Use UDP with reliability layers (like ENET or KCP) for fast-paced games. Implement client-side prediction and server reconciliation. For turn-based games, use WebSocket with JSON payloads. Photon, Mirror (Unity), and Nakama are popular mobile netcode solutions. Matchmaking should consider ping (prefer < 100ms), skill rating, and platform (iOS vs Android cross-play). Use delta compression to minimize data per packet.

Mobile ads come in several formats: banner (static, low eCPM), interstitial (full-screen between levels, medium eCPM), rewarded video (player opts in for reward, highest eCPM), and native (integrated into UI). Major networks: AdMob (Google), Unity Ads, AppLovin, ironSource. Mediation platforms (AdMob Mediation, ironSource) maximize fill rate by routing to the highest-paying network. Implement ad frequency capping (max 3 interstitials per 10 minutes). Never show ads during gameplay — place them at natural breaks (level transitions, menu screens).

IAPs include consumables (gems, coins, extra lives), non-consumables (remove ads, full game unlock), and subscriptions (weekly/monthly pass). Apple takes 30% (15% for small businesses under $1M). Google takes 15-30%. Use Unity IAP or a cross-platform purchase library. Always validate receipts server-side to prevent fraud. Implement a store UI that shows prices in local currency. Provide a 'restore purchases' button (required by Apple). Never make the game unplayable without IAP — monetize ethically.

Track player behavior: session length, retention (D1/D7/D30), conversion rate, average revenue per daily active user (ARPDAU), and funnel analysis (tutorial completion → first purchase → level 5). Use Firebase Analytics, Unity Analytics, or GameAnalytics. Implement event tracking with consistent naming: level_start, level_complete, iap_purchase. Send push notifications for re-engagement (daily rewards, new content). Use A/B testing for pricing and feature changes. Respect GDPR/CCPA privacy requirements.

Mobile GPUs use tile-based deferred rendering (TBDR) — they split the frame into tiles (typically 16x16 or 32x32), process geometry per tile, then render. This differs from desktop immediate-mode GPUs. Key implications: minimize overdraw (tiles pay for hidden pixels), use fewer but larger triangles, batch draw calls, avoid alpha blending (forces multiple passes), and use power-of-two textures. Apple GPUs (A-series) are TBDR; Qualcomm Adreno uses a hybrid approach. Mali GPUs (ARM) are also tile-based.

Mobile texture formats: ETC2 (mandatory for OpenGL ES 3.0+ Android), ASTC (universal, best quality, supported by iOS 9+/Android 10+), PVRTC (legacy iOS), and ETC1 (old Android, no alpha). ASTC is preferred — it offers flexible bitrates (4-12 bpp) and good quality. Always generate mipmaps for 3D scenes (saves GPU memory bandwidth). Compress GUI textures too — uncompressed RGBA at 1080p = 8MB per full-screen texture. Use sprite atlases to batch UI draw calls.

Mobile shaders are constrained by instruction count (32-128 instructions), limited texture samples (8-16), and no dynamic branching on many GPUs. Use the #pragma target 3.0 minimum. Reduce precision: fixed (11-bit) for colors, half for positions/UVs, float only when necessary. Avoid pow, exp, log, sin, cos in fragment shaders (use lookup textures). Precompute lighting in vertex shaders. Use fewer lights — ideally 1 directional + 0-1 point lights. Bake lighting into lightmaps when possible.

OGG uses Vorbis compression for music (good quality/size), MP3 is universally supported but slightly older, AAC offers better quality than MP3 at same bitrate, ADPCM is lossless-ish and fast for short SFX. On mobile, Unity's AudioImporter lets you choose compressed (OGG) for long clips vs ADPCM for short SFX to balance memory vs CPU decode cost. Streaming loads from disk instead of RAM but adds I/O overhead.

Ambisonics captures full-sphere surround sound; HRTF filters simulate 3D direction using head-related transfer functions. iOS spatial audio leverages AirPods motion tracking for fixed-position sounds. Android spatial audio uses Google's Resonance Audio or Oboe. FMOD and Wwise provide cross-platform spatial audio with occlusion, reverb zones, and dynamic mixing channels tuned for mobile CPU budgets.

iOS audio latency is minimized via AVAudioSession with category .playAndRecord and preferredIOBufferDuration (e.g. 0.005). Android uses Oboe or AAudio for low-latency paths. Unity's AudioMixer groups duck music under SFX, apply DSP effects (low-pass on pause), and profile via Audio Profiler. Streaming avoids loading entire clips into RAM but can stutter if I/O spikes; preload short clips as CompressedInMemory.

ARCore (Android) and ARKit (iOS) enable motion tracking, environmental understanding, and light estimation. ARCore uses visual-inertial odometry (VIO) — fusing camera imagery with IMU data. ARKit uses Visual Inertial Odometry + scene reconstruction with LiDAR on Pro devices. Both provide: plane detection (horizontal/vertical), point clouds, image tracking, object detection (ARKit 3+), and face tracking. Unity AR Foundation abstracts both APIs into a single workflow. Anchor virtual content to real-world positions using trackables.

AR games blend digital content with the real world. Design principles: surface alignment (content sits on tables/floors), scale matters (virtual objects should look physically sized), occlusion (hide objects behind real walls — LiDAR helps), lighting consistency (match virtual light to real environment), and persistent anchors (save object positions across sessions). User education is critical — show onboarding that demonstrates scanning surfaces and moving around. Handle low-light conditions gracefully (ARKit provides light estimation). Always provide a non-AR fallback mode.

Apple Core ML converts models from PyTorch/TF via coremltools for on-device inference — image classification (MobileNet), object detection (YOLO), pose estimation (OpenPose). Google ML Kit provides ready-to-use APIs for text recognition, face detection, barcode scanning, and pose detection with no custom model needed. In mobile games, use these for photo-based character creators, AR overlays, or cheater detection via screen analysis.

Unity Sentis runs ONNX neural networks directly in Unity on mobile GPUs via compute shaders. Load a .sentis model asset, create a Worker (GPUCompute or CPUShader), pass input tensors via TensorFloat, execute inference, and read output tensors. Use cases: real-time pose detection for avatar mirroring, style transfer for visual effects, or AI-driven NPC behavior without server calls.

Quantization reduces model size and speeds inference: FP16 halves size with minimal accuracy loss, INT8 is 4x smaller but needs calibration. Pruning removes near-zero weights. Core ML conversion uses coremltools with ct.quantize_weights(). TFLite supports dynamic range, FP16, and INT8 quantization. For mobile games, prefer FP16 quantized models (<10MB) to stay under app store limits and hit 30fps inference.

MFi (Made for iPhone) controllers, Xbox Wireless, and PlayStation DualShock/DualSense pair via Bluetooth. Unity's Input System auto-detects controllers and maps to common layouts (left stick = Vector2, A/B/X/Y = button). Use Gamepad.current to poll and InputAction bindings for cross-platform prompts; detect device type to switch glyphs (e.g. 'A' on Xbox vs 'X' on PlayStation).

Accelerometer measures linear acceleration (g-force), gyroscope measures angular rotation rate, magnetometer acts as digital compass. Unity's Input.gyro gives attitude as a Quaternion for tilt steering (racing games), userAcceleration for step counting, and rotationRate for camera look. Must enable Input.gyro.enabled and typically set Input.compensateSensors = true for screen orientation.

Foldable devices (Samsung Galaxy Z Fold, Pixel Fold) require handling screen continuity (activity recreates on fold), hinge angle sensor (half-fold mode for laptop-style gameplay), and display cutout (notch/punch-hole) insets. Samsung DeX and multi-window mean the game must handle arbitrary aspect ratios. Unity's Screen.safeArea gives the non-cutout rect; use OnApplicationFocus or ScreenOrientation changes to relayout.

Use .po/.json/.resx files for string storage. Unity Localization package provides StringTable assets and LocalizedString variables. Plural rules handle locale-specific forms via Smart Strings. Format strings with {0} placeholders and pass variables at runtime. Set locale from system language or player preference.

Arabic and Hebrew require right-to-left text rendering. TextMeshPro provides the RTL Editor for correct shaping of Arabic/Persian/Urdu. Hindi uses Devanagari script with complex ligatures — TMP handles OpenType shaping. CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) text needs appropriate fallback fonts assigned in TMP Font Asset. Set text direction via TMP_Text.isRightToLeft. Build fallback chain fonts for missing glyphs.

Adapt content for regional sensitivity — avoid offensive imagery, flags, or political symbols. Format dates per culture: en-US uses MM/dd/yyyy, most EU uses dd/MM/yyyy. Format currency with ISO 4217 codes and locale-aware symbols ($, Euro, Yen). Set regional pricing tiers (e.g., India, Brazil, Turkey have different purchasing power). Pseudolocalization wraps strings with accents to test layout expansion.

FCM sends push notifications via Firebase. On Android 8+ you must register notification channels with importance levels. Data messages (onMessageReceived in background) vs notification messages (auto-displayed). Manage instance tokens for targeted push; subscribe to topics for group broadcasts. Unity Firebase SDK handles token registration and message forwarding to the game object.
.Push Notifications & Deep Linking.Apple Push Notification Service[0]

APNs delivers notifications to iOS devices via device tokens. Implement UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate to handle incoming pushes. Notification Content Extensions allow custom UI within notification banners. Define notification categories with actions (accept/decline/snooze). Rich media attachments include images, video, and audio in the notification payload.

Android App Links (verified HTTP intents) and iOS Universal Links open your app directly from URLs. Deferred deep linking attributes installs: user clicks a link before installing, then gets routed to the correct content post-install. Firebase Dynamic Links handle this cross-platform. Handle incoming links at runtime by parsing query parameters and navigating to the relevant screen.

GPGS v2 for Unity provides sign-in, achievements, leaderboards, and Saved Games. Authenticate via PlayGamesPlatform.Instance.Authenticate. Report achievements incrementally or unlock them. Submit scores to leaderboards. Saved Games use ISavedGameClient with conflict resolution. Real-time multiplayer sends reliable/unreliable messages. Player Stats API returns session metrics.

GKLocalPlayer.local.authenticateHandler triggers the sign-in dialog. Report scores via GKLeaderboard and achievements via GKAchievement. Real-time matchmaking uses GKMatchRequest and GKMatchmaker; turn-based matches use GKTurnBasedMatch. Listen for player state changes and match events. Leaderboard and achievement IDs must match App Store Connect configuration.

Abstract social services behind a platform-agnostic interface so game code never calls GPGS or Game Center directly. The abstraction exposes sign-in, achievements, leaderboards, cloud saves, friend lists, and invites. Each platform (Google, Apple) implements the interface. The game logic calls the singleton SocialManager, making porting to new platforms trivial.
.Advanced Monetization & Economy.Battle Pass & Season Pass Design[0]

A battle pass has tiers (50-100 levels) each requiring set XP. Free track gives basic rewards; premium track (one-time purchase per season) adds exclusive skins, currency, and items. FOMO (fear of missing out) drives engagement as season-exclusive content disappears. Analytics track pass completion rate, tier drop-off, and average XP earned per day to tune progression.

Define soft currency (gold, coins) earned via gameplay and hard currency (gems) from purchases. Premium currency bridges free and paid. Inflation occurs when too much currency enters the system — sinks (upgrade costs, cosmetics) drain it; faucets (quest rewards, daily login) inject it. Balance sinks vs faucets per player segment. Price virtual goods based on perceived value.

Apple auto-renewable subscriptions use StoreKit 2 with SKProduct. Periods: weekly, monthly, yearly. Introductory pricing (free trial, discounted period) increases conversion. Subscription groups allow users to subscribe to one of several options. Track retention via renewal rate and churn. Offer subscriber-only perks (daily bonus multiplier, exclusive items, no ads).

Protect your Unity game from reverse engineering by applying ProGuard/R8 rules to strip unused code and obfuscate managed assemblies. Use IL2CPP over Mono to convert C# to C++ before native compilation, making memory inspection far more difficult. Compute runtime integrity checks via SHA256, and detect rooted/jailbroken devices by checking for common binary paths and su binaries.

Implement SSL pinning to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks by embedding the server certificate or public key hash directly in the client. On Android use OkHttp's CertificatePinner; on iOS implement URLSession didReceiveChallenge to validate the server trust against a known key. Encrypt payloads with AES-GCM before sending, add timestamps and nonces to prevent replay attacks.

Detect memory scanners by checking for suspicious process maps. Guard against speed hacks by comparing deltaTime against wall-clock time across multiple frames. Detect emulator environments by inspecting Build.FINGERPRINT, Build.HARDWARE, and Build.MODEL on Android. Encrypt and obfuscate memory values at runtime to reduce the attack surface.

Streamline your Unity mobile deployment pipeline with Fastlane lanes for building, testing, code signing, and uploading. Use match to manage iOS certificates and provisioning profiles across your team via a private Git repo. The gym action compiles your iOS .ipa, scan runs XCTests, and pilot uploads to TestFlight. For Android use gradle and supply to publish to Play Console.

Define reusable YAML workflows that build Unity games for both iOS and Android triggered by pushes, pull requests, or nightly runs. Use matrix strategies to test across device families and Unity versions. Cache the Library folder to cut build times by 50%. Store .ipa and .aab files as workflow artifacts, then deploy to TestFlight or Play Console via Fastlane.

Run game-loop tests on Firebase Test Lab to validate core gameplay across hundreds of real Android devices. For iOS, automate XCUITest flows that simulate taps, swipes, and IAP purchases via Xcode Cloud or Fastlane scan. Execute Unity Test Framework tests on device by building a test runner APK/IPA. Compare screenshots per-commit against golden images to catch visual regressions.

Optimize your Google Play title (30 chars), subtitle (30 chars), and short description (80 chars) to include high-volume, low-competition keywords. On iOS the keyword field (100 chars) is comma-separated. Use Sensor Tower, AppTweak, or Google Play Console keyword reports to discover competitor terms. Refresh metadata seasonally and when launching new content.

Design an app icon that reads well at small sizes: single bold subject, vibrant colors, no text. Create screenshot templates showcasing top 3-5 gameplay moments, overlaying UI at the bottom third to avoid safe-area clipping. Produce a preview video (15-30s) that loops automatically. Use Google Play Store Listing Experiments to A/B test icons and screenshots. Localize all assets per region.

Prompt users for ratings at natural engagement milestones (level complete, match win, first purchase) using SKStoreReviewController on iOS and In-App Review API on Google Play. Implement a rate limiter (max once per month) and only show on happy paths. Respond to negative reviews within 24 hours. Track rating trends per build version; investigate if dropping below 4.0 stars.

Bridge Unity C# with Android Java/Kotlin code using AndroidJavaClass and AndroidJavaObject to call methods on the JVM. Package your Kotlin code as an AAR with dependencies declared in the Gradle file, then place it in Assets/Plugins/Android/. Extend UnityPlayerActivity or use UnityAndroidApplication to hook into the activity lifecycle. Use UnityPlayer.UnitySendMessage from Java to invoke C# methods on GameObjects.

Expose Objective-C/Swift functionality to Unity by writing C-style function wrappers in .mm files that Unity's P/Invoke system can call. Declare [DllImport("__Internal")] extern functions in C# and implement in Objective-C using extern "C" linkage. Embed the static library (.a) or framework in Assets/Plugins/iOS/. For Swift interop, create an Obj-C bridging header that wraps your Swift classes.

Design your native plugin with a singleton manager that initializes once on app start, wires up lifecycle callbacks (OnApplicationPause, OnApplicationQuit), and dispatches events back to the Unity main thread using ConcurrentQueue. Keep a weak reference to the Unity GameObject. Marshal strings and byte arrays carefully across the managed/native boundary. Wrap all native calls in try/catch.

Android Studio is the official IDE. Install via JetBrains Toolbox or direct download. SDK Manager provides platform SDKs (target Android 14/API 34 minimum), build tools, NDK (for native C/C++ code), and emulator system images. AVD Manager creates virtual devices for testing. The recommended project structure uses Gradle with Kotlin DSL. Key SDK paths: $ANDROID_HOME, NDK in $ANDROID_NDK_HOME. Use SDK command-line tools (sdkmanager) for CI environments.

The AndroidManifest.xml configures your game: screen orientation (landscape or portrait), hardware features (android.hardware.touchscreen required), permissions (vibrate, internet, wake lock), and Google Play Services. For games, set android:hardwareAccelerated="true", disable screenshots in secure contexts, and use immersive mode to hide system UI. Declare required OpenGL ES version. For Unity, the manifest is auto-generated; overlay it via Plugins/Android/AndroidManifest.xml.

Android App Bundles (AAB) are the required publishing format. They split your APK into base + configuration APKs (different densities, CPU architectures, languages). This reduces download size by 30-40%. Adaptive icons consist of a foreground layer (200x200dp) and background layer (color or gradient) — the system masks them into various shapes (circle, squircle, rounded square). Generate icons for all densities: mdpi (48x48), hdpi (72x72), xhdpi (96x96), xxhdpi (144x144), xxxhdpi (192x192). Use Android Studio's Image Asset Studio.

Xcode is required for iOS development. Download from Mac App Store. Create an Apple Developer account ($99/year). Provisioning profiles and certificates authenticate your app: Development certificates (running on test devices), Distribution certificates (App Store), and Push notification certificates. Xcode manages signing automatically with 'Automatically manage signing' — it creates provisioning profiles on-the-fly. For CI, export signing certificates and provisioning profiles as files. Use fastlane match to sync signing across your team.

Xcode build settings critical for games: enable Bitcode (reduced binary size), set iOS Deployment Target (iOS 14 minimum for broad compat), configure Metal API Validation (debug only), disable NSAppTransportSecurity for development (allow HTTP), set UIViewControllerBasedStatusBarAppearance to NO for full-screen games, and configure Required Background Modes if needed. For Metal performance, enable 'Metal Validation' in debug. Set 'Enable Thread Sanitizer' off (games are highly concurrent). Optimize for size with 'Optimization Level' set to 'Fastest, Smallest' (-Oz).

App Store Connect manages app metadata, builds, pricing, and releases. Upload builds via Xcode Archive or Transporter app. TestFlight enables internal testing (up to 100 testers, no review) and external testing (up to 10,000 testers, requires Beta App Review). Manage versions with build numbers — each uploaded build increments. Set 'What's New' text per version. Use phased releases (7-day gradual rollout) to catch issues. Monitor crash reports and ratings in App Store Connect Analytics.

React Native enables cross-platform iOS/Android development with React. JavaScript thread runs JS code, while native threads handle UI rendering. The bridge (or JSI in new architecture) communicates between JS and native. Key concepts: Virtual DOM diffing for native views, Flexbox layout (converted to Yoga), Metro bundler for JS bundling, and Hermes JS engine for Android. Performance optimization: use FlatList instead of ScrollView, NativeDriver for animations, useMemo/useCallback for render optimization, and avoid bridge bottlenecks. New Architecture (Fabric + TurboModules) improves performance with synchronous native calls and better interop.

Flutter uses Dart and compiles to native ARM code via Skia/Impeller rendering engine. No JS bridge — framework paints directly to canvas for consistent 120fps performance. Key concepts: Widgets (StatelessWidget, StatefulWidget), BuildContext, RenderObjects, Element tree, and InheritedWidget for state propagation. State management: Provider, Riverpod, Bloc, or GetX. Flutter's widget tree rebuilds on setState, but const constructors and RepaintBoundary optimize rendering. Platform channels communicate with native (MethodChannel, EventChannel, BasicMessageChannel). Impeller engine (replacing Skia in newer versions) reduces jank.

Mobile testing covers unit tests (business logic), widget/component tests (UI rendering), integration tests (multi-screen flows), and E2E tests (real device/simulator). Tools: Jest/Vitest (RN unit), flutter_test (Flutter unit), Detox (RN E2E), Patrol (Flutter E2E), Maestro (cross-platform E2E), and Firebase Test Lab (device farm). Physical device testing catches real-world issues: notch cutouts, gesture conflicts, keyboard handling, and thermal throttling. Test on multiple OS versions and screen sizes. CI/CD integration with GitHub Actions or Bitrise for automated device testing.
.App Store Deployment & CI/CD.App Store Connect & Google Play Console[0]

App Store deployment involves Apple App Store Connect and Google Play Console. iOS requires: Apple Developer Program ($99/year), code signing certificates, provisioning profiles, and App Store Connect app record. Android requires: Google Play Console account ($25 one-time), keystore for signing, and app signing by Google Play. Key metadata: app icon (multiple sizes), screenshots (various devices), description, keywords, privacy policy URL, and age rating. In-app purchases and subscriptions use StoreKit (iOS) and Billing Library (Android). TestFlight (iOS) and internal testing tracks (Android) enable pre-release distribution.
.App Store Deployment & CI/CD.Code Push & Over-the-Air Updates[0]

Over-the-air (OTA) updates push JS bundle/asset changes without App Store review. React Native: CodePush (Microsoft App Center) or EAS Update (Expo). Flutter: Shorebird Code Push. OTA updates work only for JS/bundle changes, not native code (Swift/Kotlin/Java/ObjC). Native changes require full app store submission. Strategy: OTA for bug fixes and UI tweaks, app store for major features and security updates. Rollback mechanisms: push a previous bundle version or use feature flags to disable problematic features. EAS Update supports branches and channels for staged rollouts.

On-device ML runs models directly on the device for privacy, offline use, and low latency. iOS: CoreML with Neural Engine acceleration. Android: TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) with GPU/NNAPI delegates and ML Kit for common tasks. Apple's MLX framework provides ML research capabilities on Apple Silicon. Model formats: CoreML (.mlpackage), TFLite (.tflite), and MLX (.safetensors). Convert models from PyTorch/TensorFlow using coremltools or TFLite Converter. Quantization (FP16, INT8) reduces model size 2-4x with minimal accuracy loss. Use benchmarks like MLPerf Mobile to compare device performance.

Mobile AR/VR uses device cameras, sensors, and GPUs for immersive experiences. Apple ARKit (iOS) and Google ARCore (Android) provide motion tracking, environmental understanding, and light estimation. Unity's AR Foundation provides cross-platform abstraction. Key concepts: world tracking (6DoF), plane detection, image tracking, object scanning, and people occlusion. Reality Composer Pro (Apple) and Sceneform (Google) simplify 3D asset creation. Performance: use LODs, occlusion culling, reduce draw calls, and target 60fps minimum. Apple Vision Pro brings spatial computing with visionOS.

Mobile performance profiling identifies bottlenecks: slow UI rendering, memory leaks, network latency, and battery drain. iOS: Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations, Leaks, Energy Log), Xcode Organizer for crash/energy data. Android: Android Studio Profiler (CPU, Memory, Network, Energy), Perfetto for system tracing, and Firebase Performance Monitoring for production. Key metrics: FPS (target 60/120), frame drop rate, launch time (cold/warm/hot), APK/IPA size, memory usage (resident/pss), and ANR (Application Not Responding) rate. Profile on lowest-spec target device, not your flagship.
mongodb.json: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like BSON documents. It's schema-less, horizontally scalable, and designed for modern applications with dynamic data models. Supports replica sets for HA and sharding for distributed data.

Documents are JSON-like structures with field-value pairs. Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, nested objects, dates, ObjectIds, and more. Max document size is 16MB. Nested fields use dot notation for access.

BSON extends JSON with types: ObjectId (12-byte unique id), Date (64-bit millisecond timestamp), NumberInt/NumberLong, Decimal128 (exact precision), Binary, Regex, Code, Timestamp, and MinKey/MaxKey for comparison.

MongoDB 7.0+ (latest) with improved queryable encryption, change streams, and aggregation. Editions: Community (free), Enterprise (advanced security, auditing, Ops Manager), and Atlas (cloud-managed).
MongoDB Atlas offers free M0 clusters, auto-scaling, backups, monitoring, global clusters, serverless instances, and Atlas Search. Provision via web UI, API, or Terraform.
Standard format: `mongodb://host:port/db`. Atlas SRV format: `mongodb+srv://cluster.mongodb.net/db`. Options: retryWrites, w, readPreference, maxPoolSize, connectTimeoutMS, tls.
mongosh supports full JavaScript scripting with variables, loops, functions, and print helpers. Write scripts and load them with `load()`. The `--eval` flag runs inline expressions.
MongoDB supports SCRAM (default, password-based), x.509 (certificate), LDAP (enterprise), and Kerberos (enterprise). SCRAM-SHA-256 is the default mechanism, more secure than SCRAM-SHA-1.
Roles define permissions. Built-in: `read`, `readWrite`, `dbAdmin`, `userAdmin`, `clusterAdmin`. Create custom roles with specific actions on specific resources. Use `--auth` flag to enable.
Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE) encrypts fields before they reach the server. Supports deterministic (supports queries) and random (more secure) encryption. Uses a local or remote KMS.

Enterprise feature that logs all auth events, DDL operations, and CRUD operations. Output to console, syslog, JSON file, or BSON. Configure in mongod.conf. Essential for compliance (SOC2, HIPAA, PCI).
Enable TLS for encrypted client-server communication. Use PEM certificates. MongoDB supports snappy, zlib, and zstd compression to reduce network bandwidth. Configure both on mongod and client side.
Bind IP to specific interfaces (not 0.0.0.0). Use firewalls, VPCs, and security groups. Enable `--auth`. Rotate users' passwords. Use SCRAM-SHA-256. Monitor with audit logs. Enable TLS everywhere.

`insertOne()` inserts a single document, `insertMany()` inserts multiple in one round-trip. Each document auto-receives an `_id` (ObjectId) if not provided. `insertMany()` is ordered by default; use `{ ordered: false }` to continue on error.

`find()` returns a cursor to matching documents. `findOne()` returns the first matched doc. Filter object selects documents; projection object limits returned fields. Use `.pretty()` for formatted output in shell.

`updateOne()` updates the first matching doc. `updateMany()` updates all matching docs. Use `$set`, `$unset`, `$inc`, `$push`, `$pull`, and more. The third parameter accepts options like `upsert: true`.
`deleteOne()` deletes the first match. `deleteMany()` deletes all matches. `drop()` removes the entire collection including indexes. Deletes are permanent — verify filters with `find()` first.
`bulkWrite()` performs multiple write operations (insert, update, replace, delete) in a single batch. Accepts an array of operation objects. Supports `{ ordered: false }` for parallel execution.

`findOneAndUpdate()`, `findOneAndDelete()`, `findOneAndReplace()` atomically find and modify a document. Options: `returnDocument: 'after'/'before'`, `sort`, `projection`, `upsert`. Useful for queues and counters.
`replaceOne()` replaces the entire document (except `_id`) matching the filter. Unlike `updateOne()` with `$set`, this replaces all fields. The replacement doc must not contain update operators.
`$push` adds to array. `$pull` removes matching items. `$addToSet` adds if not present. `$each` pushes multiple. `$position` inserts at index. `$slice` limits array size after push.
arrayFilters target specific array elements for update. upsert: true creates a doc if no match is found. Combined, they enable powerful conditional updates on nested arrays.
Write concern controls acknowledgment: `w: 0` (fire-and-forget), `w: 1` (primary acknowledged), `w: 'majority'` (majority of nodes), `w: <tag>` (custom tag set). `wtimeout` cancels if not met.
`$eq`, `$ne`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$in`, `$nin`. Combine multiple on the same field. `$in` accepts an array of values. Use `$ne` and `$nin` with indexes carefully (they scan broadly).
`$and`, `$or`, `$not`, `$nor`. Implicit AND is used for comma-separated conditions. Use explicit `$and` when conditions involve the same field or complex expressions.
`$all` matches arrays containing all elements. `$elemMatch` matches docs with an array element satisfying all conditions. `$size` matches exact array length. Combine for precise array queries.
`$exists` checks field presence. `$type` matches BSON type. `$expr` enables aggregation expressions in queries. `$mod` modulo match. `$regex` pattern matching.
Cursors provide `.sort()`, `.limit()`, `.skip()`, `.count()`, `.forEach()`, `.map()`, `.toArray()`. Projection `{ field: 1 }` includes; `{ field: 0 }` excludes. `_id` is included by default.
Use `.sort()` with `.skip()`/`.limit()` for pagination (inefficient at scale). For efficient pagination, use range-based with `$lt`/`$gt` on indexed fields. Avoid large skips.

Supports GeoJSON objects (Point, LineString, Polygon). Create a `2dsphere` index for spherical queries. Operators: `$near` (sorted proximity), `$geoWithin` (within shape), `$geoIntersects` (intersects shape).

`$text` query operator with `$search` performs full-text search on text-indexed fields. Supports `$language` for stemming, `$caseSensitive`, `$diacriticSensitive`. `$meta: 'textScore'` for relevance ranking.

`$expr` allows aggregation expressions in queries. `$$` references system variables (`$NOW`, `$ROOT`). `let` defines variables for use within `$expr`. Enables cross-field comparisons and computed conditions.

Indexes speed up queries at the cost of write performance and storage. `createIndex()` creates an index. Types: single-field, compound, multikey (array), text, geospatial, hashed. Use `getIndexes()` to inspect.
Compound indexes support queries on multiple fields. ESR rule: Equality fields first, Sort fields next, Range fields last. Prefix matching — a compound index can serve queries on its leading fields.
Text indexes enable full-text search with `$text`. A collection can have only one text index (can cover multiple fields). Supports stemming, stop words, weights for field ranking, and text scoring.

`.explain('executionStats')` shows query plans, scanned docs, index usage, and timing. Look for IXSCAN (good) vs COLLSCAN (bad). `winningPlan` shows the chosen plan; `rejectedPlans` shows alternatives.

TTL indexes auto-delete docs after a timeout. Sparse indexes skip null fields. Unique indexes enforce uniqueness. Partial indexes index only matching docs. Hidden indexes are not used by the query planner.
MongoDB can use multiple indexes to satisfy a query via index intersection. Use `$or` clauses or compound queries. The query planner evaluates intersection vs compound index to pick the best plan.
A covered query is fulfilled entirely from the index without reading documents. All queried and projected fields must be in the index. `explain()` shows `FETCH` stage is absent for covered queries.

Index builds can block reads/writes on the collection (foreground) or run in background. In replica sets, rolling index builds build on each member sequentially to avoid downtime. For large collections, use `createIndex()` with `{ background: true }`.
The aggregation pipeline processes documents through a sequence of stages. `$match` filters early (like find). `$group` groups by key and computes accumulators. Always put `$match` early.
`$sum` adds values. `$avg` averages. `$min`/`$max` find extremes. `$first`/`$last` get first/last doc per group (requires sort). `$push` collects into array. `$addToSet` collects unique values.
`$lookup` performs left outer join. `from` is the target collection, `localField` and `foreignField` define the join, `as` names the output array. `$unwind` deconstructs arrays (flattens).
`$bucket` groups documents into user-defined ranges. `$bucketAuto` auto-generates evenly-sized buckets. Both support `$output` with accumulators. Useful for histograms and distribution analysis.
`$facet` runs multiple sub-pipelines on the same input. `$graphLookup` performs recursive graph traversal for hierarchical data like org charts or social networks.
`$out` writes pipeline results to a new collection (replaces entire collection). `$merge` merges results into an existing collection with merge strategies: `replace`, `merge`, `keepExisting`, `fail`.
`$unionWith` combines results from multiple collections (like SQL UNION). `$setWindowFields` enables window functions: `$rank`, `$denseRank`, `$rowNumber`, `$shift`, and sliding window accumulators.

Expressions include arithmetic (`$add`, `$multiply`, `$subtract`, `$divide`, `$mod`), string (`$concat`, `$substr`, `$toLower`, `$toUpper`, `$trim`), date (`$year`, `$month`, `$dayOfMonth`, `$dateToString`), and conditional (`$cond`, `$ifNull`, `$switch`).

Embedding stores related data in the same document (fast reads, atomic updates). Referencing stores IDs and uses `$lookup` to join (avoids 16MB limit, reduces duplication). Prefer embedding for one-to-few, referencing for one-to-many.
One-to-one: embed or reference with unique constraint. One-to-many: embed (few) or reference (many). Many-to-many: array of references on either side or a junction collection.

Store different entity types in the same collection using a type discriminator field. Common for event sourcing, content management (articles, videos, podcasts), and product catalogs with shared base fields.

The bucket pattern groups related data into time-based or size-based buckets. Ideal for time-series data (IoT sensor readings) — reduces document count, improves index efficiency, and enables pre-aggregation.

Pre-compute aggregates and store them alongside or in separate collections. Use `$merge` for periodic rollups. Reduce computation at read time — ideal for dashboards, leaderboards, and trend analysis.

Track document versions using a version field or separate history collection. Pattern: store current doc in main collection, append versions to a history collection. Supports rollback and audit trails.

MongoDB supports JSON Schema validation (`$jsonSchema`) at collection level. Validate required fields, types, ranges, enums, and patterns. Use `validationLevel: 'strict' | 'moderate'` and `validationAction: 'error' | 'warn'`.

Set profiling level to capture slow queries. Level 0: off. Level 1: queries slower than `slowms`. Level 2: all queries. Results stored in `system.profile`. Analyze for full scans, missing indexes, and sort patterns.

Use `explain('executionStats')` and system.profile to diagnose. Key metrics: `COLLSCAN` (bad, full collection scan), `IXSCAN` (good), `nReturned` vs `totalDocsExamined`, `executionTimeMillis`, and `docsExamined`.
`mongostat` shows real-time metrics: inserts/sec, queries/sec, page faults, % locked. `mongotop` shows read/write time per collection. Run with `--discover` for replica set monitoring.

`db.serverStatus()` provides comprehensive server metrics: connections, network, operations, memory, locks, wiredTiger cache, and repl info. `db.currentOp()` shows running operations. Kill slow ops with `db.killOp()`.

Connection pooling reuses TCP connections to MongoDB. Default pool size is 100 per mongos/mongod. Monitor with `serverStatus().connections`. Tune with `maxPoolSize` and `minPoolSize` in connection string.

WiredTiger is the default storage engine. It uses a cache (default 50% of RAM - 1GB, min 256MB). Manages data with B-trees and MVCC. Monitor cache hit ratio, evictions, and dirty pages via `serverStatus()`.
Replica sets provide HA with automatic failover. Primary handles writes; secondaries replicate via oplog. Minimum 3 members (or 2 + arbiter). Use `rs.status()` and `rs.conf()` to monitor.

Elections occur when primary becomes unreachable. Nodes vote using a protocol based on Raft. The node with highest priority and most up-to-date oplog wins. `settings.electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s) controls detection speed.

The oplog (local.oplog.rs) is a capped collection recording all writes. Default size: 5% of free disk (min 990MB, max 50GB). If too small, secondaries can fall behind. Resize with `replSetResizeOplog`.

Read preference controls where queries are routed: `primary` (default, strong consistency), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary` (offload reads), `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest` (lowest latency). Use with `maxStalenessSeconds`.

Delayed members replicate data with a time lag (e.g., 1 hour) — protection against accidental drops/corruption. Hidden members are invisible to application queries — used for reporting, backups, or analytics workloads.

An arbiter participates in elections but holds no data. Use to achieve odd-number voting in a 2-node replica set. Never run arbiter on the same server as a data node. Minimum recommended: 3 data nodes instead of 2+arbiter.
Tags enable custom write concern and read preference routing. Define tags per member in `rs.conf()`. Use `w: 'majority'` with tag sets to require acknowledgments from specific data centers.

Sharding horizontally partitions data across shards. Components: mongos (router), config servers (metadata), shards (data). A shard key determines data distribution. Enable per-database, then per-collection.

Hashed shard keys provide even distribution (good for monotonically increasing fields like ObjectId). Ranged shard keys support range queries but can create hotspots. Zone sharding pins data to specific shards based on key range.
Jumbo chunks exceed the configured chunk size (default 64MB) and cannot be split or moved. Causes: poor shard key cardinality. Balancer migrates chunks between shards. Monitor with `sh.status(true)`.
Shard zones allow pinning data to specific shards based on shard key ranges. Useful for data residency (GDPR), hot data on fast SSDs, cold data on cheaper storage, and multi-region deployments.
Resharding changes the shard key of a collection after deployment. MongoDB 7.0+ supports live resharding without downtime. The old key remains until resharding completes. Monitor with `sh.status()`.

mongos routers are stateless and can be scaled horizontally. Place mongos close to application servers. Use connection pooling and load balancers in front of multiple mongos instances for HA and throughput.

Atlas provides fully-managed MongoDB on AWS, Azure, GCP. Free M0 cluster (512MB). Features: auto-scaling, automated backups, monitoring alerts, BI Connector, global clusters, and serverless instances.
Atlas Search is built on Lucene for full-text search. Supports fuzzy matching, autocomplete, synonyms, faceted search, highlighting, and compound queries. Create indexes via web UI or API.

Atlas Data Lake queries data across Atlas clusters, AWS S3, and Azure Blob Storage using the MongoDB Query API (including aggregation). No data movement — query in place with federated database instances.

Atlas App Services (formerly Realm) provides serverless backend: Functions (JS on Atlas), Triggers (DB/webhook/scheduled), GraphQL API, and Data Access Rules. Enables rapid app development without managing servers.
Online Archive automatically moves older data to cost-effective S3 storage (fully queryable). Serverless instances scale from 0 to 1M+ ops/sec without capacity planning. Pay per operation.
Global clusters distribute data across geographic regions for low-latency reads/writes worldwide. BI Connector (MySQL protocol) enables Tableau, Power BI, and other BI tools to query MongoDB via SQL.

Official drivers (Node.js, Python, Java, Go, etc.) provide low-level database access. Key concepts: MongoClient (connection pool), Database, Collection, Cursor. Events: `commandStarted`, `commandSucceeded`, `commandFailed`.

Mongoose provides schema-based modeling with middleware (pre/post hooks for save, validate, find, etc.), virtuals (computed properties), population (reference resolution), plugins, and custom validators.
Change streams provide real-time notifications of data changes (insert, update, replace, delete, drop, invalidate). Can watch a collection, database, or entire cluster. Resumable via resume token.

MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions (since 4.0). Must use replica set or sharded cluster. Session-based: start a session, execute ops within `withTransaction()`, automatic retry on transient errors.

Retryable writes automatically retry write operations on network errors (not on write conflicts). Must use replica set. Enable with `retryWrites=true` in connection string. Idempotent ops are automatically retried.

`mongodump` creates BSON binary backups. `mongorestore` restores them. Supports `--db`, `--collection`, `--query` (filtered dump), `--gzip`, `--archive`. For consistent backups on replica sets, use `--oplog` or read from secondary.

Atlas provides automated backups with configurable retention (1-35 days for M10+). Serverless and M0 have continuous backups. Restore via UI, API, or CLI. Supports point-in-time recovery (PITR) within the retention window.

Ops Manager (Enterprise) provides automated backup, monitoring, and DB management for on-premise MongoDB. Supports continuous block-level backups with incremental snapshots, queryable backups, and point-in-time recovery.

Continuous backups apply oplog entries on top of snapshots for point-in-time recovery within a window. Trade-off: higher storage cost vs granular recovery. PITR allows restoring to any second within the window.

Combine snapshot backups (mongodump/Atlas snapshots) with oplog-based continuous backup for PITR. Automate with cron/Ops Manager/Atlas. Test restores regularly. Store backups in different region. Consider compliance retention.
mysql.json: MySQL is the world's most popular open-source relational database. It uses SQL for querying and is commonly used with LAMP/LEMP stacks. Known for speed, reliability, and ease of use. Owned by Oracle, with MariaDB as a popular fork.

Install via package manager, official APT/YUM repos, Docker, or use XAMPP/MAMP for local dev. The mysql service must be running. Check status with systemctl. First-run setup: mysql_secure_installation.
The mysql CLI connects to a MySQL server. Options: -h host, -P port, -u user, -p password prompt. Use -e for inline queries. \q or exit to quit. Use \u db_name to switch databases.

MySQL supports many data types: INT, BIGINT, VARCHAR, CHAR, TEXT, DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP, FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, JSON, ENUM, SET, BLOB. Choose types carefully — VARCHAR(255) for short strings, TEXT for long, DECIMAL for money.

Indexes speed up SELECT queries at the cost of slower INSERT/UPDATE. CREATE INDEX on frequently queried columns. PRIMARY KEY is a clustered index. UNIQUE index enforces uniqueness. Use EXPLAIN to check if queries use indexes.

EXPLAIN shows how MySQL executes a query. Key fields: type (ALL=full scan, ref/eq_ref=index lookup), possible_keys (indexes MySQL could use), key (index actually used), rows (estimated rows examined), Extra (Using index=covered, Using filesort=bad).

Enable the slow query log to find performance issues. Set long_query_time (default 10s). Log queries that don't use indexes with log_queries_not_using_indexes. Analyze with mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest.

CREATE TABLE defines a new table. Specify columns with names and types, then constraints. ENGINE=InnoDB is default (supports transactions, FK). ENGINE=MyISAM is older (full-text search, no transactions). CHARACTER SET and COLLATE control encoding.

ALTER TABLE modifies an existing table: ADD, DROP, MODIFY, CHANGE columns, or rename table. Use ALTER to add/drop indexes, constraints, and change storage settings. Be careful with large tables — ALTER can lock the table.

DROP TABLE removes the table entirely (data + structure). TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure — faster than DELETE for whole-table removal, but can't be rolled back in some engines. Use with extreme caution.

Constraints enforce data integrity: PRIMARY KEY (unique identifier), FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity), UNIQUE (no duplicates), NOT NULL (required), CHECK (value validation), DEFAULT (fallback value). InnoDB supports FK constraints.

SELECT retrieves rows. Use * for all columns, or list specific ones. WHERE filters, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT restricts rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates. AS renames columns. Use EXPLAIN to check query performance.

INSERT adds rows. INSERT INTO ... VALUES for single row, INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...), for multiple. INSERT ... SET is an alternative syntax. LAST_INSERT_ID() returns the auto-generated id. Use ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for upsert.

UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE to avoid updating all rows. LIMIT restricts how many rows to update. Use JOIN in UPDATE to update based on values in other tables. Check affected rows with ROW_COUNT().
DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE or all rows are deleted. Use JOIN to delete from multiple tables. TRUNCATE is faster for clearing all rows. Check what you'll delete first with SELECT COUNT(*).

WHERE filters rows. Operators: =, !=, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL. Combine with AND, OR, NOT. Use parentheses for complex logic. LIKE uses % (any chars) and _ (single char). IN matches any value in a list.
ORDER BY sorts results (ASC ascending, DESC descending). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET skips rows (for pagination). For large pagination, use WHERE instead of OFFSET for better performance.
INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables. Use table aliases for readability. Always prefix columns with table name/alias in JOIN queries. INNER JOIN is the most common join type.
LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where right doesn't match. RIGHT JOIN is the opposite (rarely used — prefer LEFT JOIN). Useful for finding missing relationships.

CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product (every row of A × every row of B). SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using aliases. Used for hierarchies (employees/managers), date ranges, and adjacency lists.

UNION combines results from multiple SELECT queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL is faster but keeps duplicates. All SELECTs must have the same number of columns with compatible types. Column names come from the first query.

GROUP BY groups rows by column values. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) compute per-group stats. HAVING filters groups (like WHERE for groups). SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY or aggregate functions.

COUNT(*): row count. COUNT(col): non-null count. SUM(col): total. AVG(col): average. MIN(col): minimum. MAX(col): maximum. GROUP_CONCAT(col): concatenates values into a string. DISTINCT inside aggregates: COUNT(DISTINCT col).
WITH ROLLUP adds subtotal and grand total rows to GROUP BY results. GROUPING() distinguishes subtotal rows from regular rows. Useful for summary reports and dashboards.

MySQL has powerful string functions: CONCAT (join strings), SUBSTRING (extract part), LENGTH (byte count), CHAR_LENGTH (character count), UPPER/LOWER (case), TRIM (remove spaces), REPLACE (find/replace), LOCATE (position of substring).

Key functions: NOW() (current datetime), CURDATE() (date), CURTIME() (time). DATE_FORMAT for custom formatting. DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB for arithmetic. DATEDIFF for difference. EXTRACT for parts (YEAR, MONTH, DAY).

IF(condition, true_val, false_val) — simple ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END — multi-way branching. IFNULL(val, default) — coalesce null. COALESCE(val1, val2, ..., default) — first non-null.

Transactions group operations as atomic units: all succeed or all roll back. START TRANSACTION / BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT creates rollback points. InnoDB supports transactions (MyISAM does not).

Stored procedures are reusable SQL blocks stored on the server. DELIMITER changes the statement delimiter. IN, OUT, INOUT parameters. Variables with DECLARE. Handlers for error handling. Reduces network traffic for complex operations.

Views are saved SQL queries that act like virtual tables. Simplify complex queries, add security layers (restrict columns), and provide abstraction. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents inserts/updates that don't match the view condition.

Triggers automatically execute SQL when a table event occurs (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). BEFORE/AFTER timing. FOR EACH ROW per-row trigger. OLD/ NEW refer to row values. Useful for auditing, validation, and derived data.

MySQL has native JSON data type and functions: JSON_EXTRACT (or -> operator), JSON_UNQUOTE (or ->>), JSON_ARRAY, JSON_OBJECT, JSON_SET, JSON_KEYS, JSON_CONTAINS. Index JSON fields with generated columns.

Amazon RDS for MySQL is a managed MySQL service on AWS. Automates backups, patching, failover, and scaling. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Multi-AZ for HA with synchronous standby replica. Read replicas for read scaling. Storage auto-scaling up to 64TB. Encryption at rest with KMS. Performance Insights for query monitoring.

Amazon Aurora MySQL is AWS's cloud-native MySQL-compatible engine. Up to 5x faster than standard MySQL. Auto-scaling storage up to 128TB. 6-way replication across 3 AZs with 1/6th data written (quorum). Aurora Serverless v2 scales to zero. Global Database for cross-region replication. Backtrack rewinds DB without restore. Built-in connection pooling with RDS Proxy.

Cloud SQL is GCP's fully managed MySQL service. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Automated backups with point-in-time recovery. High availability with regional failover across zones. Read replicas (including cross-region). Cloud SQL Proxy for secure IAM-based auth without public IP. Integrates with Vertex AI for in-database ML predictions. 30TB max storage. Private networking via VPC.

Azure Database for MySQL is Microsoft's managed offering. Flexible Server mode: zone-redundant HA, stop/start, burstable SKUs. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Automated backups with 35-day retention. Azure Private Link for VNet integration. Azure Defender for threat detection. Read replicas (up to 10) within region and cross-region. Flexible Server supports up to 16TB storage.

Oracle HeatWave is MySQL on OCI with an integrated in-memory query accelerator. HeatWave engine runs analytics directly on MySQL data — no ETL. Up to 6.5x faster than Aurora at half the cost. Built-in ML: HeatWave AutoML trains models inside the database. Lakehouse: query object storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob, OCI) directly from MySQL. Consistent pricing across all global regions. Automatic in-memory caching of InnoDB buffer pool.

PlanetScale is a serverless MySQL-compatible platform built on Vitess (YouTube's MySQL sharding layer). Git-like database branching: create schema branches, test changes, deploy via deploy requests with zero-downtime. Automatic horizontal scaling via Vitess sharding. Deploy requests for schema change review. Non-blocking schema migrations using gh-ost. Point-in-time recovery. Global read replicas. Connect via standard MySQL protocol. Foreign keys limited (Vitess constraint). Free $5/mo starter plan.

DigitalOcean Managed Databases: simple managed MySQL with automated backups, HA failover, monitoring. Starts at $15/mo (1 vCPU, 1GB). Aiven: multi-cloud MySQL on AWS/Azure/GCP, with BYOC option. Free tier available. PlanetScale, Aiven, and DigitalOcean offer managed MySQL outside the big 3 clouds, often simpler pricing and less lock-in.

Strategies: dump-and-restore (mysqldump to cloud), logical replication, or physical migration (AWS DMS, GCP Database Migration Service, Azure DMS). For minimal downtime use CDC-based replication. Validate character sets, timezone, sql_mode differences. Plan for network latency — co-locate app and DB in same region. Use connection pooling (ProxySQL, RDS Proxy) for serverless apps.

Stored procedures are reusable SQL blocks stored on the server. Use DELIMITER to change the statement delimiter. IN parameters pass values in, OUT returns values, INOUT does both. Variables declared with DECLARE. DECLARE ... HANDLER for error handling. A common mistake is forgetting to reset DELIMITER back to ;. Procedures reduce network traffic by executing logic server-side.

Triggers execute automatically on table events: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. BEFORE triggers validate or modify data before the operation, AFTER triggers run after. OLD refers to pre-change values (UPDATE/DELETE), NEW refers to post-change values (INSERT/UPDATE). A common mistake is creating recursive triggers (a trigger on Table A that updates Table A again). Use triggers sparingly — they're invisible to applications and can make debugging hard.

Views are saved SELECT queries that behave like virtual tables. They simplify complex joins, restrict column access (security), and provide schema abstraction. Updatable views must map directly to a single table's columns. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents INSERT/UPDATE that would make rows disappear from the view. Views do not improve performance — they're just stored queries, not materialized (unlike materialized views in PostgreSQL).

MySQL supports BTREE (default, for =, >, <, BETWEEN, LIKE without leading %) and HASH (MEMORY engine only, for = only). Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule: index on (a, b, c) helps queries on a, a+b, a+b+c, but not b or c alone. Use EXPLAIN to verify index usage. Common mistakes: over-indexing (slows writes), indexing low-cardinality columns (e.g., gender), and not covering highly selective columns first.

START TRANSACTION begins a transaction. COMMIT saves changes permanently. ROLLBACK undoes all changes since START TRANSACTION. SAVEPOINT creates a named rollback point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes to that point. Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads), READ COMMITTED (default in most DBs, no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (default in MySQL/InnoDB, no non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (fully isolated, slowest). Higher isolation = less concurrency. A common mistake is forgetting that DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) implicitly commit the current transaction.

CREATE USER creates a new user with a host (e.g., 'user'@'localhost'). GRANT assigns privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALL PRIVILEGES. REVOKE removes privileges. FLUSH PRIVILEGES reloads the grant tables (not needed if using GRANT/REVOKE directly, but needed after manual INSERT/UPDATE on mysql.user). Common mistake: creating 'user'@'%' (any host) when only localhost is needed — a security risk. Always use strong passwords. SHOW GRANTS to inspect current privileges.

mysqldump is the primary backup tool. Use --single-transaction for InnoDB consistency without locking. --routines, --triggers, --events include them. --all-databases or --databases for specific DBs. mysqlimport bulk-loads data from text files. SELECT INTO OUTFILE exports query results to a file on the server. Common mistake: forgetting --single-transaction on a live InnoDB DB (causes table locks). For large DBs, use Percona XtraBackup for physical/hot backups — mysqldump is too slow for >50GB.
next.json: Introduction to Next and its ecosystem.

The Pages Router is the original routing system in Next.js. Pages in the pages directory automatically become routes based on their file name, with index.js mapping to the root and nested folders creating nested paths.
Next.js supports dynamic routes using bracket syntax like [id].js. Links are created using the next/link component for client-side navigation with prefetching.
The App Router (app directory) is the modern routing system using React Server Components by default. Routes are defined by folders with page.js files, and layouts can be nested via layout.js.
Working with data and APIs in Next.
Vercel is the official deployment platform for Next.js, offering zero-config deploys from Git, automatic HTTPS, edge functions, and preview deployments for every pull request.
Next.js apps can be containerized with Docker for deployment on any container orchestration platform. A multi-stage Dockerfile optimizes for build speed and image size.
Next.js supports self-hosting on any Node.js server using the standalone output mode. The standalone folder includes only production dependencies, minimizing deployment size.

getServerSideProps runs on every request on the server, fetching data before rendering the page. It is used when you need fresh data on each request or access to request-time information like cookies.
getStaticProps runs at build time to fetch data for static generation. The generated HTML is reused for each request, making it ideal for content that changes infrequently.

Server Actions allow running server-side code directly from client components. They are functions defined with 'use server' that can be called via form actions or programmatically, handling mutations without building API routes.

Server-Side Rendering generates HTML on each request, delivering fully rendered pages to the client. This improves SEO and initial load performance at the cost of slower response times compared to static generation.

Static Site Generation pre-renders pages at build time into HTML and JSON files. These static files are served by CDN with near-instant load times, ideal for marketing pages, blogs, and documentation.

Incremental Static Regeneration allows updating static content after build without rebuilding the entire site. Pages are served from cache and regenerated in the background when the revalidation window expires.
