Locators can be filtered by text, by visibility, or by child elements. This narrows down selections without creating complex selectors.
Playwright clicks scroll elements into view, wait for actionability, and dispatch real browser events. Options include force, position, and modifier keys.
fill clears existing input and types new text. It dispatches input events for React and Vue change detection.
Navigation methods load URLs and wait for the page to reach a loaded state. Playwright supports back, forward, go, and reload.
Keyboard actions simulate key presses, combinations, and typing. Special keys are accessed via page.keyboard.
Playwright simulates drag and drop operations using locator.dragTo or manual mouse events for complex drag scenarios.
toHaveText asserts that an element's text content matches expected values, with options for exact or partial matching.
toBeVisible checks that an element is present in the DOM, not hidden, and within the viewport. It auto-retries until timeout.
Soft assertions continue test execution after failure, collecting all failures for reporting. The test fails at the end.
Negation with .not allows asserting the inverse condition, such as checking an element is hidden or doesn't contain text.
page.route intercepts and modifies network requests, enabling request blocking, response modification, and API mocking.
Request interception captures network traffic for inspection. Playwright waits for specific requests using request/response events.
API mocking returns fake responses without hitting the server, making tests fast and deterministic. Route patterns support wildcards.
Playwright's APIRequestContext tests APIs directly without a browser. Supports all HTTP methods, authentication, and request inspection.
Chromium is Playwright's primary browser, offering the fastest and most feature-complete support for modern web platform APIs.
Firefox support in Playwright enables testing in Gecko-based browsers with near-complete API parity to Chromium.
WebKit targets Safari's rendering engine, crucial for testing iOS Safari behavior and macOS-specific features.
Playwright emulates mobile devices with device descriptors for iPhone, iPad, and Android, including viewport, user agent, and touch events.
Screenshot testing captures an element or page and compares it against a baseline image. Useful for detecting unintended visual changes.
Configure screenshot thresholds, style masking, and animations to reduce false positives in visual regression testing.
Fixtures in Playwright Test inject reusable resources like page, context, and custom objects into tests with automatic setup and teardown.
Projects define browser configurations, device emulation, and retry policies. Multiple projects run in parallel for cross-browser coverage.
Global setup runs once before all test files for expensive operations like authentication, database seeding, or server startup.
Trace Viewer captures a full recording of the test including DOM snapshots, network logs, console output, and timing. Essential for debugging failures.
Playwright Codegen records user interactions in a browser and generates test code. Selectors are chosen automatically for resilience.
The inspector lets you step through selectors, see actionability checks, and debug locators interactively in a browser window.
The Playwright VS Code extension provides inline test running, time travel debugging, and locator picker without leaving the editor.
Playwright's official Docker image includes all browsers and system dependencies for reliable CI execution.
GitHub Actions runs Playwright tests with matrix strategy for parallel cross-browser execution across operating systems.
Playwright Test runs test files in parallel by default. Sharding splits tests across multiple CI machines for faster pipelines.
Playwright supports HTML, JSON, JUnit, and Allure reporters. The HTML reporter includes trace viewer, video, and screenshots.

Playwright supports component testing for React, Vue, Svelte, and Solid. Visual regression testing compares screenshots against baselines. toHaveScreenshot() captures element or page screenshots. playwright-ct runs components in real browsers. Component tests mount components directly: mount(MyComponent, { props: {...}, on: {...} }). Visual diff thresholds (maxDiffPixelRatio, maxDiffPixels) control sensitivity. Snapshot naming and updating:--update-snapshots. Git LFS for baseline images.
prisma.json: Introduction to prisma and its ecosystem.
The Prisma schema file (schema.prisma) defines data sources, generators, and models. It serves as the single source of truth for your database schema with a declarative DSL.
Prisma Migrate generates SQL migration files from schema changes and applies them to the database. Migrations track history and support rollbacks.
Prisma Client is an auto-generated, type-safe database client. It provides a fluent API for CRUD, filtering, pagination, relations, and transactions.
Models represent database tables with strongly-typed fields. Each field has attributes like @id, @unique, @default, and relation attributes. Native database types map to Prisma types.
Relations define connections between models using @relation and foreign keys. Supports one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many with both required and optional sides.
Attributes decorate fields with ID, default, uniqueness, constraint, and indexing metadata. Key attributes: @id, @default, @unique, @updatedAt, @map, @db.*, @@unique, @@index.
Prisma Client provides create, createMany, and upsert for inserting data. Nested writes create related records simultaneously in a single transaction.
Read operations include findUnique, findFirst, findMany, and count. They support filtering, sorting, pagination, relation inclusion, and field selection.
Update operations include update, updateMany, and upsert. Update modifies existing records matching the where condition with the provided data.
Delete operations include delete and deleteMany. Delete removes a single record by unique identifier, while deleteMany removes all matching records.
Nested writes create, update, or delete related records within a single operation. Prisma handles the transaction automatically across all related models.
Filter queries by relation conditions using some, every, none, and is. This enables complex queries like finding users with at least one published post.
Prisma supports offset pagination (skip/take) and cursor-based pagination (cursor/skip/take) for efficient navigation through large datasets.
Prisma groupBy enables aggregation queries with grouping, counting, summing, averaging, min, and max operations across specified fields.
Aggregate functions compute count, sum, avg, min, and max values across all matching records. Useful for dashboards and reporting.
Raw queries execute custom SQL for operations not supported by Prisma's query API. Use $queryRaw for SELECT and $executeRaw for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
Migration workflows: migrate dev for development (auto-generates and applies), migrate deploy for production (applies pending migrations), and migrate reset for testing.
Database seeding populates tables with initial or test data. Prisma seeding uses a seed script configured in package.json and runs with prisma db seed.
Prisma does not support automatic rollback, but you can revert by creating a new migration that reverses the previous changes, or by restoring the database from backup.
Prisma middleware (deprecated in favor of extensions) allows intercepting queries for logging, caching, access control, and input/output transformation.
Prisma Extensions (preview) enable model-scoped and client-scoped functionality including computed fields, access policies, and custom queries.
Prisma Client provides configurable logging for queries, info, warnings, and errors. Useful for debugging and performance monitoring in development.
Connection pooling via PgBouncer or Prisma Accelerate manages database connections efficiently, preventing connection exhaustion under load.
Prisma Edge Client is optimized for serverless environments like Cloudflare Workers and Vercel Edge. Uses HTTP-based Data Proxy instead of direct connections.
Production considerations: connection pooling, migration safety, timeouts, error-only logging, environment variables, and graceful shutdown.
Prisma Accelerate is a global cache and connection pooler that sits between your app and database. It caches queries at the edge, reduces connection overhead, and provides real-time analytics.
Accelerate supports TTL-based caching with swr and ttl options per query. Cached responses serve instantly from the edge while the database is updated asynchronously.
Accelerate replaces direct database connections with HTTP-based queries through a global connection pool, eliminating connection limits in serverless environments and cold starts.
Prisma Pulse provides real-time database change streaming. It emits events when rows are created, updated, or deleted, enabling reactive UIs without polling or WebSocket boilerplate.
Pulse works with Accelerate to stream changes through the edge network. Combined, they provide cached reads and real-time write propagation for globally distributed applications.
Prisma supports MongoDB as a data source provider with schemas, relations, and embedded documents. MongoDB models use @map and @db attributes for BSON type mapping.
MongoDB embedded documents are represented as JSON fields with @db.ObjectId for referencing. Prisma supports ObjectId, String, Int, Float, and Boolean BSON types for MongoDB fields.

MongoDB relations use ObjectId references with the same relation syntax as SQL databases. However, compound unique constraints are not supported, and referential actions are implemented at the application level.
Referential actions control what happens to related records when a parent record is deleted. Prisma supports Cascade, Restrict, NoAction, SetNull, and SetDefault for foreign key constraints.
onUpdate referential action specifies behavior when a parent's referenced field changes. These actions map to database-level ON UPDATE constraints and are validated during migrations.

Cascade propagates delete/update to related records. Restrict prevents delete if relations exist. NoAction defers to the database. SetNull sets foreign keys to NULL. SetDefault uses the default value.

Prisma middleware intercepts queries before/after execution. Use cases: soft deletes, audit logging, field encryption, multi-tenancy. prisma.$use() registers middleware. Prisma Client extensions (4.16+) provide type-safe computed fields, custom methods, and model helpers. $extends creates extended clients. Batch operations: createMany, updateMany, deleteMany. Raw queries with $queryRaw for complex SQL. Interactive transactions with $transaction([...]).
py.json: .Python Fundamentals.Variables & Types.exp

Variables & Types are named containers that store data values in memory. They allow programs to hold, reference, and manipulate data throughout execution, with rules governing naming, scope, and reassignment.
.Python Fundamentals.Numbers & Math.exp

Numbers & Math represent numeric data including integers, floating-point numbers, and specialized numeric types. They support arithmetic operations, mathematical functions, and have precision characteristics that vary by language.
.Python Fundamentals.Strings.exp

Strings are sequences of characters used to represent text data. They support operations such as concatenation, slicing, searching, replacing, and formatting, with immutability being a common characteristic.
.Python Fundamentals.String Formatting.exp

String Formatting enforces consistent code style including indentation, spacing, line breaks, and bracket placement. Automated formatters eliminate style debates and reduce cognitive load when reading code.
.Python Fundamentals.Lists.exp

Lists are ordered, mutable collections that can hold elements of varying types. They provide methods for adding, removing, searching, and sorting elements, and support indexing and slicing operations.
.Python Fundamentals.Tuples.exp
Tuples are ordered, immutable collections that can hold elements of different types. They are useful for grouping related values together and returning multiple values from functions.
.Python Fundamentals.Dictionaries.exp
Dictionaries are key-value mappings that provide efficient lookups by unique keys. They support insertion, deletion, and retrieval operations with average constant-time complexity.
.Python Fundamentals.Sets.exp
Sets are unordered collections of unique elements with no duplicates. They provide efficient membership testing and set operations like union, intersection, and difference.
.Python Fundamentals.Booleans & Comparisons.exp

Booleans & Comparisons compares values using operators like equality, inequality, greater than, and less than. Comparison results are booleans used to drive conditional logic and control program flow.
.Python Fundamentals.Type Conversion.exp

Type Conversion converts values from one data type to another, either implicitly by the runtime or explicitly by the programmer. Understanding type coercion and conversion is critical for avoiding subtle bugs.
.Control Flow.If Statements.exp
If Statements allow conditional execution of code blocks based on boolean expressions. If/else if/else chains enable multiple branching paths, and nested conditionals handle complex decision logic.
.Control Flow.For Loops.exp
For Loops iterate a specific number of times or over elements in a collection. They combine initialization, condition checking, and iteration in a single concise syntax.
.Control Flow.While Loops.exp
While Loops repeat execution as long as a specified condition remains true. They are useful when the number of iterations is not known in advance and depend on runtime conditions.
.Control Flow.Break & Continue.exp
Break & Continue skips the remaining statements in the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next iteration. It is useful for bypassing specific cases without exiting the loop entirely.
.Control Flow.List Comprehensions.exp
List Comprehensions provide concise syntax for creating collections by iterating and optionally filtering elements. They replace longer loop constructs with readable, expressive one-liners.
.Control Flow.Dict Comprehensions.exp
Dict Comprehensions provide concise syntax for creating collections by iterating and optionally filtering elements. They replace longer loop constructs with readable, expressive one-liners.
.Control Flow.Generator Expressions.exp

Generator Expressions is a minimal web framework for Node.js providing routing, middleware, and HTTP utilities. It simplifies building APIs and web applications with a rich ecosystem of middleware packages.
.Control Flow.Ternary Operator.exp
Ternary Operator is a special symbol or keyword that performs operations on operands. Common categories include arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, bitwise, and ternary operators.
.Control Flow.if-elif-else[0]

Branch execution based on boolean conditions. Python uses elif for else-if chains. Requires colons and indentation. Common mistake: forgetting the colon at the end of the condition. Best practice: avoid deep nesting by returning early or using guard clauses.
.Control Flow.Match Statement[0]

Structural pattern matching (Python 3.10+) enables elegant multi-way branching. Supports literal, class, sequence, and mapping patterns. Common mistake: forgetting that patterns match structurally, not by identity. Use wildcard _ as default case.
.Control Flow.for & range()[0]

Iterate across any iterable. range(stop), range(start, stop), range(start, stop, step). Common mistake: modifying a list while iterating over it — iterate over a copy instead. Best practice: use enumerate() when you need both index and value.
.Control Flow.for & range()[1]
.Control Flow.for & range()[2]
Data Structures::Lists
.Control Flow.while statement[0]

Loop as long as condition is True. Use with caution to avoid infinite loops. Common mistake: forgetting to update the loop variable. Best practice: prefer for-loops over while-loops when iterating over a known sequence.
.Control Flow.break, continue & else[0]

'break' exits the loop immediately. 'continue' skips to next iteration. The 'else' clause on loops runs only if the loop completed normally (no break). Common mistake: forgetting that loop-else runs after a normal finish — it does NOT run when break is hit.
.Functions.Function Basics.exp

Function Basics is a reusable block of code that accepts inputs, performs operations, and returns results. It enables modular programming, code reuse, better organization, and abstraction of complexity.
.Functions.Parameters & Arguments.exp

Parameters & Arguments are variables listed in a function definition that receive values when the function is called. Languages support positional, keyword, default, rest, and variadic parameters with different semantics.
.Functions.Lambda Functions.exp

Lambda Functions are reusable blocks of code that accept inputs, perform operations, and return results. They enable modular programming, code reuse, better organization, and abstraction of complexity.
.Functions.Decorators.exp
Decorators are functions that modify or enhance the behavior of other functions or methods. They are applied with a special syntax and are commonly used for logging, validation, and access control.
.Functions.Generators.exp

Generators are functions that can pause execution and yield multiple values over time, maintaining state between calls. They are ideal for lazy evaluation, infinite sequences, and asynchronous iteration.
.Functions.Iterators.exp
Iterators are objects that implement the iteration protocol, providing a way to traverse elements sequentially. They expose a next() method that returns value/done pairs until iteration completes.
.Functions.Definitions & Scopes[0]

Functions defined with 'def'. Variables follow LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Use 'global' and 'nonlocal' to rebind variables in outer scopes. Common mistake: assuming nested function can modify outer variables without 'nonlocal' — it creates a new local instead.
.Functions.Argument Logic[0]

Python supports positional, keyword, default, *args, and **kwargs parameters. Order: positional, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs. Common mistake: using mutable default arguments (e.g., def f(x=[])) — the default is evaluated once at definition time. Best practice: use None as default and create mutable inside.
.Functions.Lambda Expressions[0]

Inline anonymous functions limited to a single expression. Useful with sorted(), map(), filter(), and key functions. Common mistake: trying to use statements (print, return) inside lambdas — only expressions are allowed. Best practice: use lambdas for simple operations only; define named functions for complex logic.
.Functions.Recursion[0]

Functions calling themselves. Python has a default recursion limit of 1000 — use sys.setrecursionlimit() with caution. Common mistake: forgetting the base case leads to RecursionError. Best practice: prefer iteration over recursion for deep recursion; consider lru_cache for memoization.
.Functions.Docstrings[0]

Triple-quoted strings as the first statement in a function/class/module. Accessed via .__doc__ or help(). Common mistake: documenting 'what' instead of 'why' — docstrings should describe behavior, parameters, return values, and raised exceptions. Best practice: follow PEP 257 conventions or use Google/NumPy style.
.Functions.Type Hints in Functions[0]

PEP 484 annotations for parameters and return types. Not enforced at runtime — checked by static type checkers (mypy, pyright). Common mistake: thinking annotations affect runtime behavior — they don't. Best practice: always annotate public function signatures.
.Error Handling.Try Except.exp
Try Except provides structured error handling where potentially failing code runs in a try block and errors are caught in except blocks. Finally blocks execute cleanup code regardless of success.
.Error Handling.Custom Exceptions.exp

Custom Exceptions allow defining application-specific error types that carry relevant context. Custom exception classes extend base exception types and can include additional properties for error details.
.Error Handling.Exception Hierarchy.exp
Exception Hierarchy organizes exception types in a class hierarchy where more specific exceptions inherit from general ones. Catch blocks can target specific exception types or broader categories.
.Error Handling.Assertions.exp
Assertions verify that actual values match expected values in tests. When an assertion fails, it throws an error with a descriptive message indicating what went wrong.
.Error Handling.Context Managers.exp
Context Managers provide a convenient way to manage resources that need proper setup and cleanup. The with statement ensures resources are acquired and released correctly even when exceptions occur.
.Error Handling.Raising Exceptions.exp
Raising Exceptions are objects that represent exceptional conditions requiring special handling. They propagate up the call stack until caught, allowing errors to be handled at appropriate levels.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Classes & Objects.exp

Classes & Objects are blueprints for creating objects with shared properties and methods. They encapsulate data and behavior, support inheritance hierarchies, and are fundamental to object-oriented programming.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Inheritance.exp
Inheritance enables a class to derive properties and methods from a parent class. It promotes code reuse, establishes type hierarchies, and enables polymorphic behavior across related classes.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Polymorphism.exp

Polymorphism allows objects of different types to be treated uniformly through a common interface. It enables code to work with objects based on their shared capabilities rather than their specific types.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Encapsulation.exp

Encapsulation bundles data and methods that operate on that data within a single unit, restricting direct access to internal details. It is achieved through access modifiers like private, protected, and public.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Properties.exp

Properties are class members that provide controlled access to internal data through getter and setter methods. They allow validation, computed values, and lazy initialization while maintaining a simple access syntax.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Magic Methods.exp

Magic Methods are special methods with double underscores that define how objects behave with built-in operations. They enable operator overloading, string representation, iteration, and context manager support.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Class Methods.exp
Class Methods is a function that belongs to an object or class. Methods operate on the data contained within the object and can access other methods and properties through the object context.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Static Methods.exp
Static Methods is a function that belongs to an object or class. Methods operate on the data contained within the object and can access other methods and properties through the object context.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Abstract Classes.exp
Abstract Classes classes cannot be instantiated directly and are designed to be base classes for inheritance. They may contain abstract methods that must be implemented by concrete subclasses.
.Object-Oriented Programming.Dataclasses.exp
Dataclasses are simplified classes designed primarily for storing data with minimal boilerplate. They automatically generate methods like init, repr, and eq based on declared fields.
.Modules & Packages.Import System.exp
Import System governs how modules are discovered, loaded, and cached in the runtime environment. It searches predefined paths, resolves dependencies, and ensures modules are initialized only once.
.Modules & Packages.Package Structure.exp
Package Structure is a directory of related modules that provides organized functionality. It includes initialization code and can be nested to create hierarchical namespace structures.
.Modules & Packages.Standard Library.exp
Standard Library is the collection of built-in modules that ship with the language runtime. It provides essential functionality for file I/O, networking, data processing, system calls, and more.
.Modules & Packages.Virtual Environments.exp
Virtual Environments are isolated Python environments with their own dependencies and interpreter. They prevent conflicts between projects requiring different package versions.
.Modules & Packages.pip.exp
pip is the package installer for Python that downloads and manages third-party packages from the Python Package Index. It handles dependencies, version resolution, and package updates.
.Modules & Packages.Requirements Files.exp
Requirements Files files list project dependencies with optional version constraints. They enable reproducible installations across different environments and are essential for project portability.
.File I/O.Reading Files.exp
Reading Files loads data from files into memory for processing. Files can be read entirely, line by line, or in chunks depending on size and use case requirements.
.File I/O.Writing Files.exp
Writing Files persists data from memory to files on disk. Writing modes include creating new files, overwriting existing content, and appending to existing files.
.File I/O.File Modes.exp
File Modes determine how a file is opened, including read, write, append, and binary modes. File mode flags control whether the file is truncated, created, or positioned at the end.
.File I/O.CSV Files.exp
CSV Files store tabular data as comma-separated values, a common format for data exchange. Reading and writing CSV files requires handling delimiters, quoting, and escaping rules.
.File I/O.JSON Files.exp
JSON Files store structured data using JavaScript Object Notation, a lightweight data interchange format. JSON supports nested objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null values.
.File I/O.Binary Files.exp
Binary Files store data as raw bytes rather than human-readable text. Binary file operations handle byte sequences for images, executables, compressed archives, and proprietary formats.
.File I/O.Path Operations.exp
Path Operations manipulate filesystem paths for cross-platform compatibility. Path libraries handle joining, splitting, normalizing, and resolving paths without manual string manipulation.
.Advanced Python.Itertools.exp
Itertools is a fundamental concept in advanced python development. Understanding how itertools works, its common patterns, and best practices enables writing more robust and maintainable code in py.
.Advanced Python.Functools.exp
Functools is a fundamental concept in advanced python development. Understanding how functools works, its common patterns, and best practices enables writing more robust and maintainable code in py.
.Advanced Python.Collections.exp
Collections are data structures that store groups of related items. Common collections include arrays, lists, sets, maps, and queues, each with different performance characteristics and use cases.
.Advanced Python.Concurrency.exp

Concurrency enables multiple tasks to execute in overlapping time periods, improving resource utilization. Techniques include threads, async/await, coroutines, and multiprocessing for parallel execution.
.Advanced Python.Async/Await.exp
Async/Await provides a syntactic way to work with asynchronous operations. The async keyword declares an async function, while await suspends execution until a promise or future resolves.
.Advanced Python.Type Hints.exp
Type Hints are annotations that specify expected types for variables, function parameters, and return values. They enable static type checking, better IDE support, and self-documenting code.
.Advanced Python.Metaclasses.exp
Metaclasses are classes whose instances are themselves classes. They control class creation, attribute access, and method resolution, enabling powerful metaprogramming capabilities.
.Advanced Python.Descriptors.exp

Descriptors is a fundamental concept in advanced python development. Understanding how descriptors works, its common patterns, and best practices enables writing more robust and maintainable code in py.
.Getting Started.What is Python[0]

Python is an interpreted, high-level, dynamically typed language optimized for readability and rapid deployment. Used for web development, data science, automation, scripting, and AI/ML. Common mistake: confusing dynamic typing with weak typing — Python is strongly typed (no implicit coercion between incompatible types like '5' + 3 which throws TypeError). Best practice: use virtual environments for every project to isolate dependencies; follow PEP 8 for consistent style.
.Getting Started.Python Syntax[0]

Python relies on whitespace indentation instead of curly braces to define blocks. Use 4 spaces per level — never mix tabs and spaces. Statements end without semicolons. Common mistake: inconsistent indentation causes IndentationError; mixing tabs and spaces causes hard-to-debug TabError. Best practice: configure your editor to use 4 spaces per indent and convert tabs to spaces; use a linter (flake8, pylint) to catch style issues early.
.Getting Started.Variables[0]

Variables are created on assignment. Types are inferred dynamically. Common mistake: assuming variables are passed by reference — Python uses assignment semantics (object references). Mutable objects can be modified in-place; reassignment creates a new reference.
.Getting Started.Comments & Docstrings[0]

Use # for single-line comments. Triple-quoted strings serve as docstrings for modules, classes, and functions — they're accessible via help() and .__doc__. Unlike regular comments, docstrings are preserved as runtime attributes. Common mistake: using block comments where docstrings are appropriate — docstrings enable tooling (autodoc, IDEs), while comments are ignored. Best practice: always write docstrings for public modules, classes, and functions; use comments only for internal implementation notes.
.Getting Started.Basic I/O[0]

print() outputs to stdout with automatic newline. Use sep and end parameters for custom formatting. input() reads a line from stdin as a string. Common mistake: forgetting to convert input() result to int/float for numeric operations.
.Operators.Arithmetic[0]

Standard math operators: + - * / // % **. // is floor division (rounds down), ** is exponentiation. Common mistake: using / when integer division is needed — / always returns a float. Best practice: use // for integer division and % for modulo.
.Operators.Bitwise[0]

Operators that manipulate raw bits: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT), << (left shift), >> (right shift). Common mistake: confusing & with 'and', or | with 'or' — bitwise operators have higher precedence than logical operators.
.Operators.Assignment[0]
Combine operation with assignment: +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **=, &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>=. Common mistake: using = instead of == in conditions — = always assigns, which can lead to subtle bugs.
.Operators.Comparison[0]

Python supports ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= and chained comparisons (e.g., a < b < c). Common mistake: using == to compare floats — use math.isclose() instead due to floating-point precision. Best practice: use 'is' for None, True, False comparisons, not ==.
.Operators.Logical[0]

and, or, not operate on boolean values. Short-circuit evaluation: 'and' stops at first falsy value; 'or' stops at first truthy value. Common mistake: assuming logical operators return bool — they return the last evaluated operand.
.Operators.Identity & Membership[0]

'is' checks object identity (same memory), not equality. 'in' checks membership in iterables. Common mistake: using 'is' for value comparison instead of ==. Best practice: use 'is' only for singletons (None, True, False, sentinels).
.Data Structures.Lists[0]

Ordered, mutable sequences. Hold mixed types. Methods: append, extend, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse. Common mistake: using append() when extend() is needed — append adds one element; extend adds each element of the iterable. Best practice: use list comprehensions instead of manual loops for simple transformations.
.Data Structures.Tuples[0]

Ordered, immutable sequences. Can serve as dictionary keys. Support unpacking. Common mistake: forgetting the trailing comma for single-element tuples — (1) is just an int; (1,) is a tuple. Best practice: use tuples for fixed, heterogeneous data (like database rows); use lists for homogeneous sequences.
.Data Structures.Dictionaries[0]

Key-value mappings with O(1) average lookup. Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples of immutables). Methods: get, setdefault, keys, values, items, update, pop. Common mistake: using dict[key] when key may not exist — use .get() to avoid KeyError. Best practice: use collections.defaultdict for missing-key handling.
.Data Structures.Sets[0]

Unordered collections of unique, hashable elements. Support mathematical operations: union (|), intersection (&), difference (-), symmetric difference (^). Common mistake: using {} for an empty set — {} creates a dict; use set(). Best practice: use sets for O(1) membership testing and deduplication.
.Data Structures.Slicing[0]

Extract subsequences using start:stop:step syntax on lists, tuples, strings. Negative indices count from end. Common mistake: confusing start:stop — stop is exclusive. Best practice: use [::-1] to reverse; use [::2] for every second element.
.Data Structures.collections.deque[0]

Double-ended queue from collections module. O(1) append/pop from both ends. Common mistake: using list.pop(0) for a queue — lists have O(n) pop from front. Best practice: use deque for stacks/queues with operations on both ends.
.Data Structures.namedtuple[0]

Lightweight, immutable data containers with named fields. from collections import namedtuple. Common mistake: forgetting that namedtuples are immutable — use _replace() to create modified copies. Best practice: use dataclasses for mutable data with methods; namedtuple for simple immutable records.
.Comprehensions.List Comprehensions[0]

Concise syntax for creating lists: [expr for item in iterable if condition]. Common mistake: making comprehensions too complex (nested loops with multiple conditions) — prefer regular loops for readability beyond 2-3 clauses. Best practice: prefer comprehensions over map()/filter() for readability.
.Comprehensions.List Comprehensions[1]

squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]
evens = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
pairs = [(a, b) for a in range(3) for b in range(2)]
print(squares)
print(evens)
print(pairs)
.Comprehensions.List Comprehensions[2]
Control Flow::for & range()
.Comprehensions.Dict & Set Comprehensions[0]

Comprehension syntax extends to dictionaries {k: v for ...} and sets {expr for ...}. Common mistake: using dict comprehension with duplicate keys — last value wins silently. Best practice: use dict comprehensions for transforming one dict into another.
.Comprehensions.Generator Expressions[0]

Like list comprehensions but with () instead of [] — produce values lazily one at a time, saving memory. Common mistake: passing a genexp to str.join() or sum() works fine (they consume iterables), but don't reuse a generator — it's exhausted after iteration.
.Comprehensions.Nested Comprehensions[0]

Comprehensions can nest, but readability suffers quickly. Common mistake: confusing nesting order — the leftmost 'for' is the outer loop. Best practice: flatten with itertools.product() or break nested comprehensions into multiple lines.
.Classes.Class & Objects[0]

Classes are blueprints for objects. __init__ is the constructor. self refers to the instance. Common mistake: forgetting 'self' as the first parameter of instance methods — causes TypeError when called. Best practice: keep __init__ focused on attribute initialization only.
.Classes.Methods & Variables[0]

Instance variables are unique per object; class variables are shared. Use cls for classmethod, self for instancemethod, and no special first param for staticmethod. Common mistake: modifying a mutable class variable via one instance affects all instances.
.Classes.Inheritance[0]

Single and multiple inheritance. Use super() to call parent methods. MRO (Method Resolution Order) determines lookup order (C3 linearization). Common mistake: forgetting to call super().__init__() in subclasses. Best practice: prefer composition over inheritance; use abstract base classes for interfaces.
.Classes.dataclasses[0]

Auto-generate __init__, __repr__, __eq__, __hash__, __order__ from annotations. Use @dataclass decorator with field() for defaults, init=False, repr=False. Common mistake: assuming dataclasses are immutable by default — use frozen=True. Best practice: use dataclasses for data containers with behavior.
.Classes.@property Decorator[0]

Define methods accessed like attributes. Enables computed properties, validation, and encapsulation. Common mistake: writing trivial properties that just return an attribute — use @property only when you need computation, validation, or to maintain backward compatibility. Best practice: use the setter for validation logic.
.Classes.Magic Methods[0]

Dunder methods defining operator and built-in behavior: __add__, __str__, __repr__, __len__, __getitem__, __call__, __enter__/__exit__. Common mistake: defining __str__ but not __repr__ — __repr__ should be unambiguous; __str__ should be readable. Best practice: always implement __repr__ for debugging.
.Classes.Abstract Base Classes[0]

Define interfaces with abc module. Use @abstractmethod to enforce subclass implementation. Common mistake: forgetting that ABCs cannot be instantiated directly. Best practice: use ABCs to define interfaces; use collections.abc for built-in abstract types (Iterable, Sequence, Mapping).
.Modules & Errors.Modules & Packages[0]

Organize code into .py files (modules) and directories with __init__.py (packages). Use 'import module' or 'from module import name'. Common mistake: circular imports — restructure or use lazy imports inside functions. Best practice: use explicit imports over 'from module import *'; use absolute imports over relative.
.Modules & Errors.Handling Exceptions[0]

Use try/except/else/finally. 'else' runs if no exception; 'finally' always runs. Catch specific exceptions, not bare 'except:'. Common mistake: catching all exceptions with bare 'except:' which also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. Best practice: catch the most specific exception type.
.Modules & Errors.Raising Exceptions[0]

Use 'raise' to throw exceptions. Can re-raise current exception with bare 'raise'. Chain exceptions with 'raise ... from ...'. Common mistake: raising a generic Exception instead of a specific type. Best practice: create custom exception classes for your domain.
.Modules & Errors.Custom Exceptions[0]

Define domain-specific exceptions by inheriting from Exception. Common mistake: creating a huge exception hierarchy — keep it flat and pragmatic. Best practice: use a base exception for your application and inherit from it.
.Modules & Errors.pip & Virtual Environments[0]

pip installs packages from PyPI. venv creates isolated environments. Use pip freeze > requirements.txt to lock dependencies. Common mistake: committing .venv/ to version control — add it to .gitignore. Best practice: use pip-tools or Poetry for dependency management.
.Modules & Errors.if __name__ == '__main__'[0]

Guard that runs code only when file is executed directly, not on import. Common mistake: putting code that should be reusable outside this guard — it will run on import. Best practice: put minimal code in the guard; delegate to a main() function.
.Modules & Errors.with Statement (Context Managers)[0]

Manages resources via __enter__/__exit__ protocol. Use for files, locks, connections, and temporary settings. Common mistake: nesting with statements instead of using a single with with multiple context managers. Best practice: use contextlib.contextmanager to create custom context managers from generator functions.
.Files & Inputs.Reading & Writing[0]

Open files with open() in various modes: 'r', 'w', 'a', 'x', 'rb', 'wb'. Always use 'with' for automatic cleanup. Common mistake: opening files in text mode for binary data or vice versa. Best practice: specify encoding explicitly (encoding='utf-8') for text files.
.Files & Inputs.Terminal Input[0]

input() reads a line from stdin as a string. Use with care in scripts intended for automation. Common mistake: not stripping newline or trailing whitespace from input(). Best practice: provide a clear prompt and validate/convert input immediately.
.Files & Inputs.Binary Files[0]

Open with 'rb' or 'wb' for binary data. Essential for images, audio, serialized objects. Common mistake: using text mode on binary files corrupts data (newline translation). Best practice: use struct module for structured binary data.
.Files & Inputs.File Modes & Positions[0]

File modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write, truncate), 'a' (append), 'x' (exclusive create), '+', 'b' (binary), 't' (text, default). Use tell() for current position and seek() to move. Common mistake: opening in 'w' mode by accident — it truncates existing content. Best practice: use 'x' mode for creating new files safely.
.Additions.pass & Ellipsis[0]

'pass' is a no-op placeholder. '...' (Ellipsis) is also a valid placeholder. Common mistake: using pass when a docstring better communicates intent. Best practice: use pass for syntactic placeholders; use ... as a stub marker in type stubs.
.Additions.Generators[0]

Functions with 'yield' that produce values lazily. Each call to next() resumes execution until the next yield. Common mistake: trying to reuse a generator — generators are single-use iterators. Best practice: use generator functions for infinite sequences or large data streams; prefer generator expressions for simple cases.
.Additions.f-strings & Formatting[0]

f-strings (Python 3.6+) embed expressions with {}. Support format spec: alignment (< > ^), padding, precision, type conversion (!r, !s, !a). Common mistake: using f-strings with user input that contains braces — double braces {{}} for literal braces. Best practice: prefer f-strings over .format() and %-formatting for new code.
.Additions.Ternary Expression[0]

Inline conditional: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. Common mistake: nesting ternaries — they become unreadable quickly. Best practice: use ternaries only for simple conditions; use if/else blocks for complex logic.
.Additions.enumerate & zip[0]

enumerate() yields (index, value) pairs. zip() pairs elements from multiple iterables. Both return lazy iterators. Common mistake: using range(len(list)) instead of enumerate(). Best practice: use enumerate() when you need indices; use zip() to iterate multiple iterables in parallel.
.Additions.any & all[0]

any() returns True if at least one element is truthy. all() returns True if all elements are truthy. Both short-circuit. Common mistake: passing a generator expression instead of comprehension — both work but generator is more memory-efficient. Best practice: use with generator expressions for memory efficiency.
.Standard Libraries.json[0]

Serialize/deserialize Python objects to/from JSON. Use json.dumps() and json.loads(). Common mistake: trying to serialize non-serializable types (datetime, Decimal) — use a custom default handler or cls encoder. Best practice: use indent=2 for readable output; use sort_keys=True for deterministic output.
.Standard Libraries.re (Regular Expressions)[0]

Powerful text pattern matching. Key functions: re.match(), re.search(), re.findall(), re.sub(), re.split(). Compile patterns with re.compile() for reuse. Common mistake: confusing re.match() (anchored at start) with re.search() (anywhere). Best practice: use raw strings r'pattern' to avoid escaping backslashes.
.Standard Libraries.math, random & statistics[0]

math: advanced math functions, constants (pi, e). random: pseudo-random number generation. statistics: mean, median, stdev. Common mistake: using random for security-sensitive applications — use secrets module instead. Best practice: set random.seed() for reproducible results in tests.
.Standard Libraries.datetime[0]

date, time, datetime, timedelta classes for date/time manipulation. timezone-aware vs naive datetimes. Common mistake: doing arithmetic with naive datetimes across DST boundaries — use timezone-aware datetimes with zoneinfo (Python 3.9+). Best practice: always store and process UTC; convert to local time for display only.
.Standard Libraries.collections[0]

Specialized container datatypes: deque, Counter, defaultdict, OrderedDict, ChainMap. Common mistake: assuming OrderedDict is unnecessary in Python 3.7+ — dicts maintain insertion order, but OrderedDict has order-sensitive methods like move_to_end(). Best practice: use Counter for counting; use defaultdict for grouping.
.Standard Libraries.os & sys[0]

os: OS-level operations (environ, path, listdir, getcwd). sys: Python interpreter interaction (argv, path, exit, stdout). Common mistake: using os.path instead of pathlib for modern code. Best practice: prefer pathlib over os.path; use os.environ.get() with defaults for environment variables.
.Async Python.async/await[0]

asyncio enables concurrent I/O. 'async def' defines a coroutine; 'await' yields control to the event loop. Common mistake: calling async def directly returns a coroutine object, not the result — must use await. Best practice: use asyncio.run() as the entry point; never call it from inside a running event loop.
.Async Python.asyncio.gather[0]

Run multiple coroutines concurrently and collect all results. Results are in the same order as the input coroutines. Common mistake: not handling exceptions — one failure doesn't cancel others unless return_exceptions=True. Best practice: use return_exceptions=True when tasks can fail independently; wrap in try/except for critical tasks.
.Async Python.Async Context Managers[0]

Use 'async with' for async resources (connections, streams). Define with __aenter__ and __aexit__. Common mistake: forgetting that async context managers need 'async with', not regular 'with'. Best practice: use contextlib.asynccontextmanager for simple async context managers.
.Async Python.asyncio.TaskGroup[0]

Python 3.11+ TaskGroup provides structured concurrency. Tasks run concurrently; if any task fails, all are cancelled. Common mistake: mixing asyncio.gather with TaskGroup — use TaskGroup for structured error handling. Best practice: prefer TaskGroup over gather() when tasks have dependencies or need structured cancellation.
.Async Python.Async Generators[0]

Functions using 'yield' inside 'async def' produce values asynchronously. Iterate with 'async for'. Common mistake: using 'for' instead of 'async for' with async generators. Best practice: use async generators for streaming data (pagination, WebSocket messages, log tailing).
.File System & Paths.pathlib[0]

Object-oriented path manipulation. Path objects with / operator, .read_text(), .write_text(), .iterdir(), .glob(), .resolve(). Common mistake: concatenating paths with + instead of /. Best practice: use pathlib exclusively for all path operations in new code.
.File System & Paths.shutil[0]

High-level file operations: copy2 (preserves metadata), move, copytree, rmtree, make_archive. Common mistake: using shutil.copy() instead of shutil.copy2() — copy2 preserves timestamps. Best practice: always use shutil.rmtree() with caution (destructive).
.File System & Paths.glob (file patterns)[0]

Pattern-based file matching. Supports wildcards: *, ?, [chars], ** (recursive with recursive=True). Common mistake: forgetting recursive=True for ** patterns. Best practice: use pathlib.Path.glob() for an object-oriented approach, or the stand-alone glob module for simple cases.
.File System & Paths.tempfile[0]

Create temporary files and directories safely. tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile, TemporaryDirectory. Files are automatically cleaned up when closed. Common mistake: creating temp files without using context manager — they may not be cleaned up on errors. Best practice: always use with statement for automatic cleanup.
.Logging.logging module[0]

Built-in logging framework with levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. Configurable loggers, handlers, and formatters. Common mistake: using print() for debugging instead of logging — logging provides levels, timestamps, and easy redirection. Best practice: get a module-level logger with __name__; configure once at application entry point.
.Logging.Logging Configuration[0]

Configure logging via dictConfig for complex setups: multiple handlers (file, console, syslog), different levels per handler, formatters. Common mistake: modifying the root logger globally in libraries — libraries should use a NullHandler. Best practice: load config from a YAML/JSON file via dictConfig.
.Logging.Logging Handlers & Filters[0]

Built-in handlers: StreamHandler, FileHandler, RotatingFileHandler, TimedRotatingFileHandler, SysLogHandler, SMTPHandler. Filters allow selective logging. Common mistake: forgetting to configure handlers — no output without at least one handler attached to the logger or its ancestors. Best practice: use RotatingFileHandler for production apps to avoid huge log files.
.Itertools & Functools.itertools[0]

Iterator combinator library: chain, cycle, repeat, permutations, combinations, product, groupby, islice, count, accumulate. Common mistake: trying to use groupby on unsorted data — groupby only groups consecutive identical keys. Best practice: use itertools for memory-efficient iteration patterns; avoid converting to list unless necessary.
.Itertools & Functools.functools[0]

Higher-order functions: lru_cache, cache (3.9+), partial, reduce, singledispatch, wraps. Common mistake: not using functools.wraps on decorators — loses the original function's metadata. Best practice: use @functools.cache for simple memoization; use partial for pre-filling function arguments.
.Itertools & Functools.contextlib[0]

Context manager utilities: contextmanager (from generator), suppress (ignore specific exceptions), ExitStack (dynamic cleanup), redirect_stdout. Common mistake: using suppress(Error) instead of try/except when you need to log or handle the exception. Best practice: use @contextmanager for simple context wrappers; use ExitStack for dynamic context management.
.Itertools & Functools.operator module[0]

Functional equivalents of operators: itemgetter, attrgetter, methodcaller, add, mul, etc. Useful with sorting and itertools. Common mistake: writing lambda x: x[1] when operator.itemgetter(1) is clearer and faster. Best practice: use operator functions as key functions for sorted(), max(), min(), and groupby().
.Decorators & Closures.Function Decorators[0]

Functions that take a function and return a wrapped function, using @syntax. Used for logging, timing, access control, memoization. Common mistake: forgetting to return the wrapper function from the decorator — the original function is replaced by None. Best practice: always use functools.wraps in your decorators to preserve metadata.
.Decorators & Closures.Decorators with Arguments[0]

Decorators that accept parameters need three levels: outer function (params) -> decorator -> wrapper. Common mistake: confusing the call signature when adding parameters to an existing decorator. Best practice: use a decorator factory pattern: make_parametrized_decorator(param) returns the actual decorator.
.Decorators & Closures.Class Decorators[0]

Decorators applied to classes (not methods). Can modify class attributes, add methods, or register classes. Common mistake: class decorators don't handle inheritance well — consider using metaclasses instead. Best practice: use class decorators for simple modifications (registering, adding attributes); use metaclasses for complex class customization.
.Decorators & Closures.Closures[0]

A function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope even after the outer function has finished. Used for data hiding, factory functions, and decorators. Common mistake: late-binding in closures with loops — all closures refer to the last value of a loop variable. Best practice: use default arguments or functools.partial to capture loop variables.
.Decorators & Closures.Nested Functions & nonlocal[0]

Functions defined inside other functions. Use 'nonlocal' to rebind variables in the enclosing scope. Common mistake: forgetting 'nonlocal' when modifying a variable from the outer function — creates a new local variable instead. Best practice: minimize nesting depth; use classes for stateful closures.
.Decorators & Closures.@wraps (functools.wraps)[0]

functools.wraps copies __name__, __doc__, __module__, __annotations__ from the wrapped function to the wrapper. Essential for decorators. Common mistake: omitting wraps makes debugging harder — the decorated function loses its name and docstring. Best practice: always apply @functools.wraps(func) to the inner wrapper function of any decorator.
.Testing & Debugging.doctest[0]

Tests embedded in docstrings. Run with python -m doctest module.py. Common mistake: doctests are fragile — whitespace and output formatting must match exactly. Best practice: use doctest for simple examples and documentation; use pytest for comprehensive test suites.
.Testing & Debugging.unittest[0]

Built-in test framework with TestCase, assert methods, setUp/tearDown, and test discovery. Common mistake: forgetting to call super().setUp() in subclasses. Best practice: use unittest.mock for mocking; use parameterized tests with subTest for similar test cases.
.Testing & Debugging.pytest[0]

Modern testing framework with fixture system, parameterization, and powerful assertion introspection. No need to wrap in classes. Common mistake: using unittest-style classes when pytest functions suffice. Best practice: use pytest fixtures for shared setup; use pytest.mark.parametrize for multiple test cases.
.Testing & Debugging.pdb (Debugger)[0]

Built-in debugger. Use breakpoint() (Python 3.7+) to set breakpoints. Commands: n(ext), s(tep), c(ontinue), l(ist), p(rint), pp, q(uit). Common mistake: leaving breakpoint() calls in production code — use environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 to disable all breakpoints. Best practice: use breakpoint() for interactive debugging; use IDE debuggers for complex debugging sessions.
.Testing & Debugging.cProfile & Profiling[0]

Measure execution time of Python code. Use cProfile.run() or python -m cProfile script.py. Common mistake: optimizing before profiling — always profile first to find real bottlenecks. Best practice: use pstats to sort results by cumulative time; use snakeviz or py-spy for visualization.
.Testing & Debugging.unittest.mock[0]

Replace parts of a system with mock objects. Mock, patch, MagicMock, PropertyMock, side_effect. Common mistake: patching the wrong path — always patch where the name is looked up (the module under test), not where it's defined. Best practice: use patch as a context manager; use spec=True to catch attribute typos.
.Packaging & Distribution.setuptools & setup.py[0]

Traditional packaging tool. Define metadata in setup.py: name, version, packages, install_requires, entry_points. Common mistake: forgetting to include package data files (non-Python files). Best practice: use pyproject.toml for modern projects; setup.py is only needed for editable installs or dynamic metadata.
.Packaging & Distribution.pyproject.toml[0]

PEP 517/518 build system configuration. Declarative format replacing setup.py. Used by setuptools, flit, pdm, poetry. Common mistake: mixing [build-system] and [project] sections incorrectly. Best practice: use pyproject.toml exclusively; choose one build backend (setuptools, flit, or poetry).
.Packaging & Distribution.Wheels & sdist[0]

sdist (.tar.gz) is source distribution; wheel (.whl) is a built distribution (faster install). Build with: python -m build. Common mistake: distributing platform-specific wheels without implementing proper build variants for different OS. Best practice: publish both sdist and wheel to PyPI; use cibuildwheel for platform wheels with C extensions.
.Packaging & Distribution.pip install -e (Editable Installs)[0]

Install a package in development mode with pip install -e . Changes to source are reflected immediately without reinstalling. Common mistake: forgetting the trailing . (current directory). Best practice: always use editable installs during development; combine with a dev virtual environment.
.Packaging & Distribution.Namespace Packages[0]

Packages split across multiple directories. Python 3.3+ supports implicit namespace packages (no __init__.py needed). Common mistake: mixing regular packages (with __init__.py) and namespace packages in the same distribution. Best practice: use implicit namespace packages for large projects split across repos; avoid __init__.py in namespace package directories.
.Working with Data.CSV[0]

Read/write comma-separated values with csv module. Use DictReader and DictWriter for named columns. Common mistake: not handling quoted fields containing commas or newlines — csv module handles this correctly. Best practice: always specify delimiter and quoting; use utf-8-sig encoding for Excel compatibility.
.Working with Data.JSON[0]

Lightweight data interchange format. json.dumps(obj), json.loads(str), json.dump(obj, file), json.load(file). Common mistake: JSON only supports strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, objects — Python-specific types (datetime, Decimal) need custom encoders. Best practice: use json module for configuration files and API communication; use orjson for better performance.
.Working with Data.YAML[0]

Human-readable data serialization, common for config files. Requires PyYAML package (pip install pyyaml). Supports comments, multi-line strings, and complex nesting. Common mistake: YAML's truthy values (yes, on, true) — always use true/false for booleans. Best practice: use safe_load() instead of load() to avoid arbitrary code execution.
.Working with Data.SQLite[0]

Lightweight embedded SQL database via sqlite3 module (built-in). No separate server needed. Common mistake: using string formatting for SQL queries — use parameterized queries (?) to prevent SQL injection. Best practice: use context managers for auto-commit/rollback; use row_factory = sqlite3.Row for dict-like access.
.Working with Data.pickle[0]

Python object serialization (pickling). Serialize any Python object to bytes. Common mistake: unpickling untrusted data — pickle can execute arbitrary code during deserialization. Best practice: never unpickle data from untrusted sources; use json or other safe formats for untrusted data; use protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL for efficiency.
.Working with Data.XML & ElementTree[0]

Parse and generate XML with xml.etree.ElementTree. Supports find(), findall(), iter(), and XPath-like expressions. Common mistake: namespace handling is tricky — use {uri}tag or register_namespace(). Best practice: prefer json/yaml over XML when possible; use lxml for advanced XML features (XSLT, schema validation, complete XPath).
.Concurrency Deep Dive.threading[0]

Run functions in separate threads for I/O-bound tasks. GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) limits CPU-bound parallelism. Use threading.Thread, Lock, Semaphore, Event. Common mistake: assuming threads are safe for shared data — use Lock or Queue to prevent race conditions. Best practice: use threading for I/O-bound work; use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work.
.Concurrency Deep Dive.multiprocessing[0]

Run processes in parallel, bypassing the GIL for CPU-bound tasks. Pool, Process, Queue, shared memory. Common mistake: trying to share complex objects between processes — use Queue or Manager for safe sharing. Best practice: use Pool.map() for parallel data processing; avoid sharing mutable state between processes.
.Concurrency Deep Dive.ThreadPoolExecutor & ProcessPoolExecutor[0]

High-level concurrent.futures interface. submit() returns Future; map() for parallel iteration; as_completed() for partial results. Common mistake: using ThreadPoolExecutor for CPU-bound tasks — GIL prevents true parallelism. Best practice: use ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O; ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU; set max_workers based on the workload type.
.Concurrency Deep Dive.Queues (threading/multiprocessing)[0]

Thread-safe FIFO queues for producer-consumer patterns. queue.Queue for threads, multiprocessing.Queue for processes. Common mistake: using queue.task_done() without corresponding queue.get() or without queue.join(). Best practice: use Queue for decoupling producers and consumers; use join() to wait for all items to be processed.
.Concurrency Deep Dive.asyncio.Queue[0]

Async-compatible queue for asyncio applications. asyncio.Queue, task_done(), join(). Use in async producer-consumer patterns. Common mistake: performing blocking operations inside async code — use asyncio.to_thread() for blocking I/O. Best practice: prefer asyncio.Queue over threading.Queue in async applications; set maxsize for backpressure.
.Web & APIs.requests[0]

HTTP library with human-friendly API. Methods: get, post, put, delete, patch. Handles sessions, auth, timeouts, redirects. Common mistake: not setting timeouts — requests can hang indefinitely. Best practice: always set timeout; use Session() for connection reuse; raise_for_status() to check HTTP errors.
.Web & APIs.httpx[0]

Modern HTTP client supporting async/await, HTTP/2, and both sync/async APIs. Install with pip install httpx. Common mistake: mixing sync and async usage — use httpx.Client() for sync; httpx.AsyncClient() for async. Best practice: prefer httpx over requests for new projects (async support, HTTP/2, better API).
.Web & APIs.FastAPI Basics[0]

Modern async web framework with automatic OpenAPI docs, type validation via Pydantic, and high performance. Install: pip install fastapi uvicorn. Common mistake: not using Pydantic models for request/response validation. Best practice: use dependency injection for shared logic; use async endpoints for I/O; let FastAPI handle validation via type annotations.
.Web & APIs.Flask Basics[0]

Lightweight WSGI web framework for small to medium applications. Simple routing, request handling, and template rendering. Install: pip install flask. Common mistake: using the development server in production — use gunicorn or uwsgi instead. Best practice: use blueprints for modular applications; use the app factory pattern for testability.
.Web & APIs.aiohttp[0]

Async HTTP client/server library. Good for high-concurrency scraping and microservices. Install: pip install aiohttp. Common mistake: creating a new ClientSession per request — reuse sessions for connection pooling. Best practice: use a single ClientSession per application; use async with for proper cleanup.
.Type Hints.Basic Types & Annotations[0]

PEP 484 type hints for variables, parameters, and return types. Checked by mypy/pyright, not at runtime. Common mistake: thinking type hints affect performance — they're completely erased at runtime. Best practice: annotate all public APIs; use mypy --strict for rigorous checking.
.Type Hints.Optional & Union[0]

Optional[X] means X | None (Python 3.10+) or Union[X, None]. Union[X, Y] means either X or Y. Common mistake: thinking Optional[str] means 'optional string parameter' — it means 'str or None'. Best practice: use X | Y syntax (Python 3.10+) for brevity; use Optional[X] when specifically X or None.
.Type Hints.Generics & TypeVar[0]

Create reusable, type-safe functions and classes with TypeVar and Generic. Common mistake: over-constraining type variables — use proper bounds with bound= or constraints. Best practice: use generic types for collections, data structures, and functions that work with multiple types while preserving type safety.
.Type Hints.Protocol (Structural Subtyping)[0]

PEP 544 — static duck typing. Define an interface via Protocol that any class with matching methods satisfies. Common mistake: thinking Protocol requires explicit inheritance — it doesn't; structural subtyping is implicit. Best practice: use Protocols for loose coupling; use ABC for formal interface inheritance.
.Type Hints.TypedDict[0]

PEP 589 — type hints for dictionaries with specific keys and value types. Supports total=False for optional keys. Common mistake: defining TypedDict but still using dict[key] access without checking — mypy catches missing keys. Best practice: use TypedDict instead of plain dict for structured data with known keys.
.Type Hints.Literal, Final & Type Aliases[0]

Literal[X, Y] restricts a value to specific literals. Final prevents reassignment. Type aliases shorten complex annotations. Common mistake: mixing up Final (const) with final (inheritance). Best practice: use Literal for function arguments that accept only specific strings/numbers; use Final for constants.
.Performance.Profiling & Optimization[0]

Always profile before optimizing. Tools: cProfile, py-spy, snakeviz, pyinstrument. Common mistake: optimizing without profiling — you'll optimize the wrong things. Best practice: focus on hot spots (where time is actually spent); measure before and after each optimization; algorithmic improvements trump micro-optimizations.
.Performance.__slots__[0]

Reduce memory usage of classes by declaring a fixed set of attributes. Prevents __dict__ creation per instance. Common mistake: forgetting slots don't prevent adding new attributes — they just define the allowed attributes. Best practice: use __slots__ for classes with many instances (millions) to reduce memory; avoid in small-scale code.
.Performance.Generators vs Lists[0]

Generators produce values lazily (one at a time); lists store all values in memory. Generators save memory but have per-item overhead. Common mistake: converting a generator to a list unnecessarily — defeats the memory advantage. Best practice: use generators for large data streams and infinite sequences; use lists for small datasets and when you need random access.
.Performance.C Extensions (Cython & ctypes)[0]

Speed up Python with C. Cython compiles Python-like code to C extensions. ctypes calls C libraries from Python. Common mistake: assuming Cython always speeds up code — pure Python with many function calls can be slower. Best practice: use Cython for numeric-heavy loops; use ctypes for calling existing C libraries; consider numpy first for array operations.
.Performance.timeit & Benchmarking[0]

Measure small code snippets with timeit module. Use from the command line: python -m timeit '...'. Common mistake: using time.time() for micro-benchmarks — timeit handles garbage collection and repeat counts automatically. Best practice: use timeit for micro-optimizations; use real-world data and realistic workloads for macro-benchmarks.
.Performance.Memory Management & GC[0]

Python uses reference counting + cyclic garbage collector. Circular references are freed by the GC (can be slow). Use gc module to monitor/inspect. Common mistake: assuming del x frees memory immediately — it decrements the refcount; memory may not be returned to the OS. Best practice: use weakref for caching circular references; use __del__ with caution (can cause resurrection).
.Automation & Browsing.Web Scraping with BeautifulSoup[0]

Parse HTML/XML documents and extract data. Install: pip install beautifulsoup4 requests. Common mistake: not handling pagination or rate limiting — always respect robots.txt and add delays between requests. Best practice: use BeautifulSoup with a parser (lxml or html.parser); use requests.Session() for cookies/session persistence.
.Automation & Browsing.Selenium & Browser Automation[0]

Control real browsers for JavaScript-heavy sites and automation. Install: pip install selenium. Requires a WebDriver (ChromeDriver, GeckoDriver, or use webdriver-manager). Common mistake: not using WebDriverWait for dynamic content — elements may not be immediately available. Best practice: use webdriver-manager for automatic driver management; prefer explicit waits over implicit; use headless mode for CI.
.Automation & Browsing.Working with PDFs (PyMuPDF)[0]

Extract text, merge, split PDFs with PyMuPDF (fitz). Install: pip install PyMuPDF. Common mistake: PDF text extraction is unreliable for scanned docs — use OCR (pytesseract) for those. Best practice: use PyMuPDF for fast text extraction; use pypdf for simple merge/split; use pdfplumber for table extraction.
.Automation & Browsing.Excel (openpyxl)[0]

Read/write/style .xlsx files. Install: pip install openpyxl. Supports formulas, charts, conditional formatting. Common mistake: modifying large files in-memory uses lots of RAM — use read_only=True for big files. Best practice: use openpyxl for .xlsx; use pandas read_excel for quick analysis.
.Automation & Browsing.Word Documents (python-docx)[0]

Create/modify .docx files. Install: pip install python-docx. Supports paragraphs, tables, images, headers/footers, styles. Common mistake: forgetting to save after modifying. Best practice: use python-docx for report generation; use templates for complex documents.
.Automation & Browsing.Email (smtplib)[0]

Send emails with SMTP, attachments, HTML content using built-in modules. Common mistake: hardcoding credentials — use env vars. Best practice: use email.mime for multipart messages; use context managers for SMTP.
.Automation & Browsing.Scheduled Tasks (schedule)[0]

Run functions on a schedule. Install: pip install schedule. Common mistake: blocking tasks delay subsequent runs — run long tasks in threads. Best practice: use schedule for simple cron-like needs; use APScheduler for production.
.Automation & Browsing.GUI Automation (PyAutoGUI)[0]

Control mouse, keyboard, take screenshots. Install: pip install pyautogui. Common mistake: not adding safety delays — use PAUSE=1 and FAILSAFE=True. Best practice: include failsafe (move mouse to corner); add explicit pauses.
.Automation & Browsing.Image Manipulation (Pillow)[0]

Open, manipulate, save images with Pillow (PIL fork). Install: pip install Pillow. Supports resize, crop, filter, draw, text overlay, format conversion. Common mistake: forgetting RGBA vs RGB when saving JPEG. Best practice: use thumbnail() for preserving aspect ratio; convert to RGB before JPEG.
.Automation & Browsing.CLI Tools (argparse & click)[0]

Build command-line interfaces. argparse is built-in; click uses decorators. Install click: pip install click. Common mistake: not providing helpful error messages. Best practice: use argparse for simple scripts; use click for complex multi-command CLIs.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.Python Data Model (Dunder Methods)[0]

The Python data model makes objects behave like built-in types. By implementing __getitem__, __len__, __iter__, __contains__ your objects work with for, in, slicing, and more. Fluent Python calls this 'Python's superpower'. Common mistake: implementing __len__ but not __bool__ — Python falls back to __len__ (0 = False). Best practice: implement __repr__ first (debugging), then __str__ (display), then data model methods for your domain.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.__getattr__ & __setattr__[0]

__getattr__ called when normal lookup fails. __setattr__ called on every assignment. Fluent Python warns: __setattr__ is tricky — must call super() to avoid recursion. Common mistake: infinite recursion via self.x = val in __setattr__. Best practice: use __setattr__ for validation; prefer @property for individual attributes.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.__call__ & Callable Objects[0]

Make instances callable via __call__. Used for decorators, factories, strategies. Fluent Python shows this for function-like objects with state. Common mistake: overusing __call__ when a method is clearer. Best practice: use __call__ for objects representing a single action (callbacks, factories).
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.Descriptors[0]

Descriptors control attribute access via __get__, __set__, __delete__. Examples: @property, classmethod, staticmethod. Fluent Python calls descriptors 'the most important tool for framework builders'. Common mistake: descriptors only work as class attributes — instance-level assignment disables them. Best practice: use __set_name__ (3.6+) to auto-generate storage attribute names.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.Metaclasses[0]

Metaclasses are classes of classes — intercept class creation via __new__/__init__. Use cases: ORMs, registries, class validation. Fluent Python says 'metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% should ever use'. Common mistake: using a metaclass when a class decorator suffices. Best practice: prefer class decorators; keep metaclasses single-purpose.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.ABC Advanced (subclasshook)[0]

ABCs support virtual subclasses via register() and __subclasshook__(). Virtual subclasses are recognized by isinstance() without inheritance. Fluent Python shows this for duck typing with safety. Common mistake: registering too many virtual subclasses slows isinstance checks. Best practice: prefer collections.abc over custom ABCs; use __subclasshook__ for protocol-like behavior.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.Operator Overloading Advanced[0]

Python supports a fixed set of operator methods: __add__, __radd__, __iadd__, __eq__, __lt__, etc. Fluent Python emphasizes returning NotImplemented (not raising) for unsupported types. Common mistake: forgetting __hash__ when defining __eq__. Best practice: use @total_ordering to fill in missing comparisons; always return NotImplemented for unsupported operands.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.Context Managers Advanced[0]

Beyond basic with: contextlib.contextmanager (generator-based), ExitStack (dynamic cleanup), suppress (ignore exceptions), redirect_stdout. Fluent Python covers these in depth. Common mistake: using @contextmanager without try/finally — cleanup won't run on exception. Best practice: always wrap yield in try/finally; use ExitStack for dynamic contexts.
.Fluent Python Deep Dive.Coroutines & yield from[0]

Generator-based coroutines use yield to receive values via send(). yield from delegates to a subgenerator, forwarding send() and throw(). Fluent Python shows this as the foundation of asyncio. Common mistake: confusing generators (produce values) with coroutines (consume via send). Best practice: use async/await for new code; understand the coroutine model for framework-level work.
.Data Science & AI.NumPy Basics[0]

N-dimensional arrays with vectorized operations, broadcasting, linear algebra. Install: pip install numpy. Common mistake: using Python lists for numeric ops — NumPy is 10-100x faster. Best practice: avoid for-loops; use vectorized ops; set dtype for memory efficiency.
.Data Science & AI.Pandas Essentials[0]

DataFrame and Series for tabular data. Install: pip install pandas. Key ops: read_csv, groupby, merge, filter, pivot. Common mistake: for-loops over rows — use vectorized ops. Best practice: use .query() for readable filters; use category dtype for low-cardinality strings.
.Data Science & AI.Matplotlib & Visualization[0]

Foundational plotting library. Use OOP API (fig, ax) for fine-grained control. Install: pip install matplotlib. Common mistake: plotting in loops without clearing the figure. Best practice: use OOP API; use seaborn for statistical plots; save as SVG for scalable graphics.
.Data Science & AI.Seaborn Statistical Plots[0]

High-level statistical visualizations with nice defaults. Works with pandas DataFrames. Install: pip install seaborn. Common mistake: passing wide-format data instead of tidy/long format. Best practice: keep data tidy; use hue for grouping; use PairGrid for exploration.
.Data Science & AI.scikit-learn ML Basics[0]

Consistent ML API: fit, predict, transform, score. Covers classification, regression, clustering, preprocessing. Install: pip install scikit-learn. Common mistake: data leakage — always split before preprocessing; use Pipeline. Best practice: use train_test_split + Pipeline + cross_val_score + GridSearchCV.
.Data Science & AI.Pandas Data Wrangling[0]

Clean, transform, reshape messy data. Handle missing values, duplicates, string ops, datetime parsing, pivot/melt. Common mistake: using inplace=True everywhere. Best practice: use method chaining with .pipe(); use .melt() for wide-to-long; use .pivot_table() for summaries.
.Data Science & AI.PyTorch Deep Learning[0]

Tensor computation with GPU, autograd, nn.Module. Install: pip install torch. Key concepts: tensors like NumPy on GPU; autograd for gradients; Dataset/DataLoader for data. Common mistake: not moving data/model to same device. Best practice: use .to(device); use DataLoader for batching; use torch.compile() for speed.
.Data Science & AI.Transformers & Hugging Face[0]

Pre-trained models for NLP, vision, audio via transformers library. Install: pip install transformers torch. Pipeline API for quick inference; AutoModel for fine-tuning. Common mistake: wrong tokenizer for model — always use AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained. Best practice: use pipeline() for quick tasks; use datasets library for data loading.
.Data Science & AI.NumPy Linear Algebra[0]

np.linalg for matrix ops: solve, inv, det, eig, svd, qr. Common mistake: using np.inv(A) @ b instead of np.linalg.solve(A, b). Best practice: use solve() for linear systems (more stable); use @ operator for matrix multiplication.
.Data Science & AI.Feature Engineering & Preprocessing[0]

Transform raw data for ML: scaling, encoding, imputation, polynomial features. scikit-learn ColumnTransformer applies different transforms to different columns. Common mistake: fitting scaler on full dataset before split. Best practice: use Pipeline + ColumnTransformer; fit only on training data.
.Data Science & AI.Model Evaluation & Validation[0]

Prevent overfitting with proper evaluation: train/test split, cross-validation, metrics (precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC). Common mistake: evaluating on test set multiple times. Best practice: hold out final test set; use StratifiedKFold for classification; use learning_curve to diagnose bias/variance.
.Data Science & AI.Time Series Analysis[0]

Analyze time-series data with pandas date ranges, rolling windows, resampling, and statsmodels for decomposition and forecasting. Common mistake: forgetting to set index as datetime before resampling. Best practice: use pd.to_datetime() on parse; use .asfreq() for regular intervals; use seasonal_decompose for trend/seasonality/residual.
.Data Science & AI.Gradient Boosting[0]

Gradient boosting builds an ensemble of weak learners (decision trees) sequentially. XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost are optimized implementations with regularization, GPU support, and monotonic constraints. Best practice: use early_stopping_rounds; tune learning_rate + n_estimators + max_depth first.
.Data Science & AI.Unsupervised Learning[0]

Extract hidden patterns from unlabeled data. Clustering (K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical) groups similar points. Dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) projects high-dim data to 2/3D for visualization and noise reduction. Common mistake: assuming clusters exist — always validate with silhouette score.
.AI & LLM Engineering.LLM Foundations (Tokenization & Embeddings)[0]

LLMs tokenize text into tokens (subwords via BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece). Embeddings map tokens to dense vectors capturing semantic meaning. Attention mechanism weighs token relationships. From Hands-on LLM: understand tokenization granularity and embedding dimensionality for your use case.
.AI & LLM Engineering.Prompt Engineering[0]
