Craft inputs to guide LLM outputs. Components: system prompt (role/constraints), user prompt (task), few-shot examples. Techniques: chain-of-thought (step-by-step reasoning), zero-shot chain-of-thought ('Let's think step by step'), structured outputs (JSON mode). From Hands-on LLM: systematic prompt iteration is key to reliable LLM apps.
.AI & LLM Engineering.RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)[0]

RAG grounds LLM responses in external knowledge: chunk documents, embed chunks, store in vector DB, retrieve relevant chunks at query time, generate with context. From Hands-on LLM: chunk size, overlap, embedding model, and retrieval top-k are critical hyperparameters.
.AI & LLM Engineering.Fine-tuning with LoRA/QLoRA[0]

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) updates only a small set of adapter weights. LoRA decomposes weight updates into low-rank matrices. QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization. From Hands-on LLM: LoRA rank r=8-64, alpha=16-32, target modules depend on architecture.
.AI & LLM Engineering.LLM Evaluation & Guardrails[0]

Evaluate LLM outputs: automated metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore), LLM-as-judge, human evaluation. Guardrails enforce constraints (topic, format, safety). From Hands-on LLM: evaluation should cover relevance, accuracy, faithfulness, and safety.
.AI & LLM Engineering.AI Agents & Tool Use[0]

LLM agents use function calling to interact with tools (APIs, search, code execution). ReAct pattern: Thought → Action → Observation → Thought. From Hands-on LLM: define tools with clear schemas; implement safety checks; handle tool errors gracefully.
.AI & LLM Engineering.LLM API Integration & Streaming[0]

Integrate LLM APIs with streaming for responsive UIs. Support system/user/assistant messages, token usage tracking, structured outputs (JSON mode), retry with exponential backoff. From Hands-on LLM: streaming reduces perceived latency; structured outputs enable reliable parsing.
.AI & LLM Engineering.Data Collection for AI (Web Scraping Pipelines)[0]

Collect training/evaluation data via web scraping. Use requests + BeautifulSoup for static pages, Playwright/Selenium for JS-heavy sites. From oxylabs-ai-studio: build robust pipelines with retry, caching, proxy rotation, and structured output schemas.
.AI Engineering Pro.Embeddings & Vector Databases[0]

Vector databases store and search embedding vectors by similarity (cosine, dot product, L2). Chroma is lightweight and local; Pinecone/Qdrant are production-grade. Chunk documents, embed with sentence-transformers, index in vector DB, retrieve by semantic similarity. Common mistake: using wrong distance metric for your embedding model.
.AI Engineering Pro.LangChain & LlamaIndex[0]

Frameworks for building LLM applications: document loading, chunking, embedding, retrieval, chains, agents. LangChain is modular with many integrations; LlamaIndex excels at data indexing/retrieval. Common mistake: over-abstraction — start with direct API calls, add frameworks when complexity demands it.
.AI Engineering Pro.Multimodal AI[0]

Multimodal models process text + images + audio. CLIP embeds images and text jointly. LLaVA/GPT-4V reason about images. Use cases: image captioning, visual QA, document parsing. Common mistake: resizing images without maintaining aspect ratio degrades performance.
.AI Engineering Pro.Structured Output from LLMs[0]

LLMs can output structured data (JSON, types) using constrained decoding, JSON mode, or function calling. Instructor library provides Pydantic-integrated structured extraction with automatic retries and validation. Common mistake: relying on prompt engineering alone for consistent structured output.
.AI Engineering Pro.AI Agent Frameworks[0]

Multi-agent systems coordinate specialized agents for complex tasks. CrewAI uses role-based agents with defined goals; AutoGen enables agent-to-agent conversation; LangGraph builds stateful graphs of agent steps. Common mistake: making agents too autonomous without human-in-the-loop checks.
.AI Engineering Pro.Prompt Caching & Optimization[0]

Optimize LLM calls: cache identical prompts (exact match or semantic), batch similar inputs, compress long contexts (LLMLingua), use shorter system prompts. Anthropic Prompt Caching caches repeated prefix tokens for 50% cost reduction. Best practice: implement LRU cache for exact matches; use semantic caching for similar queries.
.AI Engineering Pro.Synthetic Data Generation[0]

Generate training/evaluation data using LLMs. Techniques: prompt-based generation (seed → variations), self-instruct (generate instructions + responses), evolving complexity (easy → hard). Validate quality with human review or LLM-as-judge. Common mistake: low diversity — vary prompts, temperature, and few-shot examples.
.AI Engineering Pro.Model Serving & Deployment[0]

Deploy open-weight LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Phi) for inference. vLLM provides PagedAttention for high-throughput serving; TGI (Text Generation Inference) by HuggingFace; Ollama for local development. Quantization reduces memory: 4-bit (GPTQ/AWQ) or 8-bit. Common mistake: serving without load testing — use Locust/Vegeta for benchmarking.
.AI Engineering Pro.AI Evaluations (Advanced)[0]

Systematic evaluation of LLM outputs beyond simple metrics. BLEU/ROUGE for text similarity; BERTScore for semantic similarity; LLM-as-judge for nuanced quality assessment; human evaluation for gold standard. Build eval datasets, track regressions, maintain leaderboards. Common mistake: single metric optimization — use composite evaluations.
.AI Engineering Pro.MLOps for LLMs[0]

MLOps for LLMs covers experiment tracking, prompt versioning, data management, monitoring. MLflow tracks parameters/metrics/artifacts; Weights & Biases for experiment dashboards; LangSmith for LLM-specific tracing and evaluation. Common mistake: not tracking prompt versions alongside model versions.
.AI Engineering Pro.AI Safety & Alignment[0]

Build responsible AI: content filtering, bias detection, adversarial robustness, jailbreak prevention. Techniques: RLHF/DPO for alignment; prompt injection detection; output guardrails; red-teaming. Common mistake: relying solely on system prompts for safety — use layered defenses. From Hands-on LLM: evaluate for toxicity, bias, and hallucination before deployment.
rails.json: Introduction to Rails and its ecosystem.

Ruby on Rails (often just Rails) is a full-stack web application framework written in Ruby by David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH). It follows the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern and emphasizes convention over configuration, DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), and rapid development. Rails includes everything needed to build database-backed web applications: ORM (ActiveRecord), routing, templating, testing, asset pipeline, and more. First released in 2004, Rails popularized many modern web development practices.

Rails follows the Model-View-Controller pattern. Models (ActiveRecord) handle data and business logic. Views (ActionView) render HTML/JSON templates. Controllers (ActionController) process requests, interact with models, and render views. The router maps URLs to controller actions. Additional layers: mailers, helpers, channels, jobs, libraries.

A Rails project has a standardized directory structure. app/ contains models, views, controllers, helpers, jobs, mailers, channels. config/ has routes, database, environments. db/ holds migrations and schema. public/ serves static assets. test/ (or spec/) for tests. Gemfile lists dependencies. The rails command and Rake tasks handle most development operations.

config/routes.rb defines URL patterns. The router maps HTTP verbs + paths to controller actions. resources generates RESTful routes (index, show, new, create, edit, update, destroy). singular_resource for non-ID routes. Nested resources for hierarchical data. Member and collection routes for custom actions. Concerns share reusable route groups.
Working with data and APIs in Rails.

Rails supports Minitest natively (test/ directory) and RSpec (via gem). Test types: unit tests (models), functional tests (controllers), integration tests (full stack), system tests (browser with Capybara). Fixtures and factories (FactoryBot) for test data. Assertions: assert_equal, assert_response, assert_redirected_to, assert_select, assert_difference.

ActiveRecord is Rails' Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) layer. Each model class maps to a database table. Instances map to rows. Columns become attributes automatically. Convention: table names are plural snake_case, model names are singular CamelCase. Foreign keys: user_id. Primary keys: id (auto-increment). ActiveRecord handles CRUD, validations, associations, queries, and migrations.

Validations ensure data integrity before saving to the database. Common validators: presence, uniqueness, length, format, numericality, inclusion, acceptance, confirmation. Custom validations via validate or custom validator classes. Validations run automatically on create/save/update. Check validity with valid?/invalid? which populate errors.errors.full_messages.

ActiveRecord associations define relationships between models. Types: belongs_to, has_many, has_one, has_many :through, has_one :through, has_and_belongs_to_many (HABTM). Polymorphic associations allow a model to belong to multiple models. Dependent options: :destroy, :delete_all, :nullify, :restrict_with_error. Counter cache for performance.

Migrations are versioned changes to the database schema. Rails tracks which migrations have run via schema_migrations table. Key generators: rails generate migration, rails generate model. Migration methods: create_table, change_table, add_column, remove_column, change_column, add_index, remove_index, create_join_table, add_reference, change_table. Rollback with rails db:rollback.

Controllers process HTTP requests. Each public method is an action. params hash contains request data (query string, form data, URL segments). Strong parameters protect against mass assignment. Filters (before_action, after_action, around_action) run before/after actions. Flash messages for user notifications. Session and cookies for state. Respond_to for content negotiation.

Strong Parameters protect against mass assignment vulnerabilities. params.require(:model) ensures the key exists. .permit(:field1, :field2) whitelists allowed attributes. Nested parameters require nested permit. Arrays, hashes, and scalars have different permit syntax. Never trust user input — always whitelist permitted parameters.

ActionView renders templates. Default template engine is ERB (.html.erb). <% %> executes Ruby code without output. <%= %> executes and outputs. Layouts wrap templates (yield). Partials (_partial.html.erb) share reusable view fragments. Helpers keep templates clean. Content_for yields named content. Link_to, form_for, image_tag are common view helpers.

Rails form helpers generate HTML forms with CSRF protection, error handling, and correct field names. form_for / form_with (Rails 5.1+). form_with can work with models or URLs. Collection helpers: collection_select, collection_check_boxes. Date/time select helpers. Fields for nested attributes. Strong parameters integration.

Rails API mode (rails new app --api) strips browser middleware for JSON APIs. Serializers: ActiveModelSerializers, jsonapi-rb, or jbuilder. GraphQL-Ruby gem integrates GraphQL into Rails. Authentication with devise-jwt or doorkeeper (OAuth). Rate limiting with rack-attack. Versioning via namespaced routes (namespace :api { namespace :v1 { ... } }). Testing with RSpec + FactoryBot. Background jobs with Sidekiq. API documentation with Rswag (OpenAPI).
rb.json: Variables and data types in Ruby.

Ruby's exception hierarchy: Exception (top) > StandardError (what you should rescue) > RuntimeError (default for raise), NoMethodError, TypeError, ArgumentError, ZeroDivisionError, IOError, and more. Never rescue Exception directly — you'll catch SignalException, SystemExit, and NoMemoryError. Rescue specific types for precise handling. Use the exception's backtrace for debugging.

Ruby uses begin/rescue/ensure/else for exception handling. rescue catches exceptions by class. Multiple rescue blocks for different exceptions. ensure always runs (like finally). else runs if no exception. raise/throw to trigger errors. $! contains last exception, $@ contains backtrace. StandardError is the common superclass (most code should rescue StandardError, not Exception).

Creating custom exception classes by inheriting from StandardError. Custom exceptions can carry additional data (attributes). Use meaningful class names that describe the error. Rescue specific exceptions rather than generic StandardError. Exception hierarchies allow fine-grained error handling.

ensure runs regardless of exception — use for cleanup (closing files, releasing locks). retry restarts the begin block, useful for transient failures. retry without limit can create infinite loops — always use a counter. catch/throw is for non-local control flow, not error handling (like a labeled break).

raise is for exceptions (error conditions). throw/catch is for control flow (early exit from nested loops). Only rescue StandardError subtypes. Never rescue Exception (catches everything including SignalException). Always specify an exception class with raise. Use throw with a symbol label for non-local control flow.
Input and output operations in Ruby.

Ruby's standard library includes Time (built-in), Date, and DateTime (require 'date'). Time handles seconds since epoch, timezones, and formatting. Date handles calendar dates without time. DateTime combines date and time. ActiveSupport (Rails) provides extensive additions like 1.day.ago, 2.hours.from_now. Use strftime for custom formatting.

IRB (Interactive Ruby) is Ruby's built-in REPL. Launch with `irb` in terminal. Features: history, tab completion, auto-indent, and inspection. Pry is a more powerful alternative with syntax highlighting, runtime invocation, and ls/show-source commands. Use `_` to access last result, `Ctrl+R` for history search, `Ctrl+D` to exit.

Ruby Version Managers like rbenv and RVM let you install and switch between multiple Ruby versions. rbenv is lightweight (recommended), RVM is more feature-rich. Key commands: rbenv install 3.2.2, rbenv global 3.2.2, rbenv local 3.1.0 (per-project), ruby -v. Use .ruby-version files for project-specific versions. Bundler integrates with both.

Ruby is a dynamic, interpreted, reflective, object-oriented programming language created by Yukihiro Matsumoto (Matz) in 1995. It combines syntax inspired by Perl and Smalltalk with object-oriented features. Everything in Ruby is an object — even integers and booleans. Ruby follows the Principle of Least Surprise (POLS), meaning the language behaves as you'd expect. It's known for its elegant syntax, powerful metaprogramming, and the Ruby on Rails web framework.

Ruby uses English-like, minimalist syntax. Parentheses are optional for method calls. Blocks defined with do/end or {}. Class and method names follow conventions: SNAKE_CASE for files/variables, CamelCase for classes, snake_case for methods. Files end with .rb. Comments use # for single line and =begin/=end for multi-line. Indentation is 2 spaces (convention, not enforced).

Ruby is dynamically typed. Local variables (name), instance variables (@name), class variables (@@name), global variables ($name), and constants (NAME). Basic types: Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, Boolean, Nil. Type checking occurs at runtime — no static type declarations needed. Symbols (:name) are immutable, lightweight identifiers used for keys and method names.

Ruby strings can be single-quoted (no interpolation) or double-quoted (supports interpolation and escape sequences). #{expression} interpolates any Ruby expression. Strings are mutable. Common methods: length, upcase, downcase, capitalize, reverse, split, join, gsub, strip, include?, empty?. << or + for concatenation.

Arrays are ordered, integer-indexed collections. Can hold mixed types. Index starts at 0. Negative indices count from end (-1 = last). Common methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, first, last, length/ size, include?, empty?, sort, reverse, join, map/collect, select/filter, reject, each, each_with_index. Arrays created with [] or Array.new.

Hashes are key-value dictionaries. Keys can be any object type, but symbols are most common (memory efficient, immutable). Two syntaxes: hash-rocket (=>) for any key type, and JSON-style for symbol keys (Ruby 1.9+). Default values can be set. Common methods: keys, values, key?, has_key?, has_value?, fetch, merge, select, each, except, slice.

Symbols are immutable, reusable identifiers represented as :name. Unlike strings, every instance of a symbol with the same name refers to the same object in memory (same object_id). This makes them ideal for hash keys and method references. Symbols are not garbage collected, so be careful about creating them dynamically from user input. Convert: to_sym / intern, to_s.

Ruby variables are dynamically typed. Local variables start with a lowercase letter or _, instance variables with @, class variables with @@, and global variables with $. Understanding scope rules prevents subtle bugs. Local vars are scoped to the current block/method; instance vars belong to an object instance; class vars are shared across the hierarchy; globals are visible everywhere (avoid when possible).
Constants in Ruby start with a capital letter. They are not truly immutable — Ruby warns but doesn't prevent reassignment. Use them for values that logically shouldn't change.
Ruby's core types: Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, true/false (TrueClass/FalseClass), nil (NilClass). Everything is an object — even nil has methods.
Ruby provides explicit conversion methods: to_s, to_i, to_f, to_a, to_sym. Implicit conversion is rare — Ruby prefers raising errors to silent coercion.
Standard + - * / % **. Integer division truncates. ** is exponentiation.
&& || ! (or and not). and/or/not have lower precedence than &&/||/!. Short-circuit evaluation applies.
Ruby ranges: inclusive (..) and exclusive (...). Used in iteration, slicing, and case conditions.

Ruby's ternary operator (?:) is a compact if/else expression. Statement modifiers (postfix if/unless/while/until) add conditionals at the end of a single statement. Use ternary for simple binary choices. Use statement modifiers for guard clauses and concise loops. Avoid nesting — readability matters more than brevity.

Ruby uses if, elsif, else, unless, and ternary (?:). unless is the opposite of if and reads naturally for negative conditions. if/unless can be used as statement modifiers (postfix). All conditionals return a value. Only nil and false are falsy — everything else (including 0, empty strings, empty arrays) is truthy.

Ruby's case/when is more flexible than switch/case in other languages. It uses === (case equality operator) for comparison, which can match classes, regexp, ranges, and procs. when can have multiple values separated by commas. else is the default. Returns the value of the last evaluated expression.

while executes while condition is truthy. until executes while condition is falsy (opposite of while). Both can be used as statement modifiers. begin/end versions guarantee at least one execution. Loop control: break (exit loop), next (skip iteration), redo (rerun current iteration), retry (restart from beginning).

Ruby has for/in loops but they're rarely used — each and friends are preferred. for/in iterates over enumerables but doesn't create a new scope for the variable (leaks it). each and the Enumerable module provide a rich set of iteration methods with proper scoping. Range literals (1..10) are commonly used for iteration.

Keyword arguments (Ruby 2.0+) let you pass arguments by name, making method calls self-documenting and order-independent. Required keyword args have no default, optional ones do. Double splot (**) captures extra keyword args. Use keyword args for methods with 3+ parameters, especially when multiple boolean options are needed.

Method arguments can have default values evaluated at call time. Use expressions, method calls, or even previous arguments. Defaults are evaluated left-to-right. Avoid side effects in defaults — they run every call. Use ||= inside the method body for more control over default initialization.

Methods defined with def/end. Parentheses optional. Return last evaluated expression implicitly or use explicit return. Method names can end with ? (predicates, return boolean), ! (dangerous/mutating version), = (setter). Arguments can have default values. Keyword arguments (Ruby 2.0+) for named parameters. Splat (*) captures multiple args. Double splat (**) captures keyword args.

The splat operator (*) captures a variable number of positional arguments into an array. It can also expand an array into individual arguments when calling a method. The double splat (**) captures keyword arguments into a hash. Place the splat parameter last in the parameter list to avoid ambiguity.

Ruby controls method visibility with public, private, and protected. public is the default. private methods can only be called without an explicit receiver (self is implied). protected methods can be called by any instance of the same class. Use private for internal helpers, protected for shared implementation in inheritance chains.

Refinements are a way to scope monkey-patches to specific files or modules. Defined with refine inside a module, activated with using. Refinements only affect code after the using statement and within the current scope. They don't pollute the global namespace, making them safer than outright monkey-patching.

Blocks are chunks of code passed to methods. They are not objects by themselves — they become Procs when captured. Use yield to invoke a block from within a method. Blocks can be defined with do/end (multi-line) or {} (single-line). The block_given? method checks if a block was passed.

Proc objects encapsulate blocks into first-class objects. Create with Proc.new or proc. Call with .call, .[], or .(). Procs don't check argument count (missing args become nil, extra args are ignored). They return from the enclosing method (not just the proc itself). Use procs when you need to pass a block to another method or store it for later.

Lambdas are defined with -> or lambda. Unlike Procs, lambdas check argument count strictly and return from the lambda itself (not the enclosing method). Lambdas are closer to method semantics. Use lambdas when you want strict argument checking and predictable return behavior.

Both Procs and lambdas are closures — they capture the local variables from the scope where they were defined. The binding retains access to those variables even after the enclosing scope has exited. This enables powerful patterns like generators, callbacks, and lazy evaluation.

Enumerable is Ruby's most powerful mixin. Include it + define each and you get map, select, reject, reduce, any?, all?, none?, one?, count, group_by, partition, sort_by, first, take, drop, min, max, min_by, max_by, each_slice, each_cons, cycle, detect/find, grep, flat_map, zip, chunk, and many more. Lazy enumerators (lazy) for infinite sequences.

map, select, and reduce form the core of Ruby's functional programming toolkit. map transforms each element. select filters. reduce accumulates. They can be combined with symbol-to-proc (&:method) shorthand. Chain them for powerful data processing pipelines.

Ruby arrays go beyond basic operations. Advanced techniques include: array intersections (&), unions (|), differences (-), Cartesian products (product), flattening (flatten), compacting (compact), transposing (transpose), sampling (sample), filling (fill), repeating (cycle), and combinations/permutations.

Advanced Hash techniques: fetch with default block, transforming keys/values, hash slicing, nested hash access with dig, custom defaults with Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = {} }, merging with block for conflict resolution, and converting to/from arrays.

Set is a collection of unique elements (require 'set'). It provides fast membership testing, mathematical set operations (union, intersection, difference), and automatic deduplication. SortedSet maintains elements in sorted order. Sets are useful for membership queries, deduplication, and set algebra.

Enumerable methods can be chained to build expressive data pipelines. Lazy evaluation with lazy avoids intermediate arrays. Method chains read left-to-right as transformation pipelines. Be mindful of performance — each chain method creates a new array (unless using lazy).

Ruby has an extensive set of string methods. Core methods: chomp/chop (remove trailing chars), gsub/sub (global/substitute), scan (extract matches), partition/rpartition (split around match), tr (character replacement), ljust/rjust/center (padding), delete (remove chars), squeeze (remove consecutive duplicates), count (character counting).

Ruby regex uses /pattern/ syntax with powerful features. Match operator =~ returns index or nil. Regexp.last_match ($~) for match data. Named captures (?<name>pattern). Modifiers: i (case-insensitive), m (multiline), x (extended). Common methods: match, scan, gsub with block, split with regex.

Ruby offers multiple ways to format strings: #{expr} for expression interpolation, sprintf/format/% for formatted output, and String#% for template formatting. Format specifiers: %s (string), %d (integer), %f (float), %x (hex). Precision and width control for alignment and padding.

String concatenation with + creates new strings (O(n²) in loops). Use << or concat for mutable appending. String interpolation (#{}) is optimized and preferred. For heavy building, use Array#join (fastest) or StringIO. Frozen string literals (# frozen_string_literal: true) reduce allocations. Use dup for mutable strings from frozen sources.

Ruby supports multiple string encodings via Encoding class. Strings have an encoding attribute (UTF-8 by default). Use force_encoding to change encoding, encode to convert. Common encodings: UTF-8, ASCII-8BIT, ISO-8859-1. String#valid_encoding? checks validity. Handle encoding errors with :invalid => :replace or :replace => ''.

Every Ruby object has a hidden singleton class (eigenclass) that holds methods unique to that object. Use class << obj to open it. This enables per-object behavior, class methods (methods on Class objects), and DSLs. The singleton class sits between the object and its real class in the method lookup chain.

Ruby is pure object-oriented. Classes defined with class/end. Constructor is initialize. Instance variables (@name) are private by default. attr_reader, attr_writer, attr_accessor create getters/setters automatically. self refers to the current object. Class methods defined with self.method_name. Every class inherits from Object (which inherits from BasicObject).

Ruby supports single inheritance with the < operator. Modules provide multiple inheritance-like behavior via mixins. super calls the parent method with the same arguments. Method resolution order (MRO) follows the lookup path: object -> class -> modules (reverse order of include) -> superclass. ancestor chain shows inheritance.

Modules collect methods and constants. They cannot be instantiated. Use include for instance methods (mixins), extend for class methods, and prepend to override methods (prepended module methods are called first). Namespacing: MyModule::MyClass. The include lookup checks modules in reverse order of inclusion. Enumerable and Comparable are built-in mixin examples.

Ruby provides metaprogramming shortcuts for attribute accessors. attr_reader creates a getter (@name -> name). attr_writer creates a setter (@name = value -> name = value). attr_accessor creates both. These can be customized by accepting multiple symbols. Use attr_reader for read-only attributes, attr_writer for write-only, attr_accessor for read-write.

super calls the parent method with the same arguments. super() calls with no arguments (empty). super(a, b) calls with specific arguments. It's used in initialize to chain constructors, in overridden methods to extend behavior, and around_alias for method wrapping. Know the difference between super (forwards args) and super() (no args).

Struct is a built-in class for creating plain old Ruby objects with attributes. Define with Struct.new(:name, :age). Creates a class with accessors, ==, to_a, and initialize. OpenStruct (require 'ostruct') creates objects on the fly with dynamic attributes (slower, flexible). Use Struct for data objects with known shape. Use Data.define (Ruby 3.2+) for immutable data objects.

Ruby uses duck typing: if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck. Objects are defined by what methods they respond to, not their class. This enables polymorphic behavior without explicit interfaces. Use respond_to? to check method availability. Duck typing leads to flexible, loosely coupled code.

Ruby provides three ways to load code. require loads a file once (preferred for gems/libraries). require_relative loads relative to the current file. load reloads a file every time (rare, only for development). autoload (deprecated in Ruby 2.0+) loads on first use. The $LOAD_PATH ($:) lists directories searched by require.

RubyGems is Ruby's package manager. Gems are packaged libraries installed via gem install. Bundler manages dependencies through Gemfile. Gemfile.lock locks exact versions. Key commands: gem install, gem list, gem search, bundle install, bundle exec, bundle update. Gemfile groups (development, test, production) control environment-specific dependencies.

Bundler provides a reliable dependency management workflow. Key concepts: Gemfile (declarative dependencies), Gemfile.lock (snapshot of exact versions), bundle exec (run in locked context), binstubs (bundle binstubs for wrappers). Use bundle outdated to check for updates. bundle viz generates dependency graphs. bundle doctor checks for issues.

Tempfile creates temporary files that auto-delete on garbage collection. StringIO provides an in-memory IO-like object (treat strings as files). Both implement the IO interface (read, write, gets, each_line, rewind, close). Useful for tests (capture stdout), file upload processing, and scratch data. Use Tempfile for actual file system operations, StringIO for in-memory.

File operations with File class. Block form auto-closes. Modes: r (read), w (write, truncate), a (append), r+ (read/write), w+ (read/write, truncate), a+ (read/append). Binary mode: rb, wb. Common methods: File.read, File.write, File.readlines, File.foreach (memory efficient for large files). Dir for directory operations. Pathname for path manipulation.

Ruby's standard library includes CSV and YAML for data file parsing. CSV provides read/write with headers support. YAML is used for configuration files. Both handle encoding and type conversion. Use CSV.foreach for memory-efficient processing of large files. YAML.load_file for loading config safely (with permitted_classes).

The Dir class provides directory operations. Dir.glob for file pattern matching (uses shell-style patterns). Dir entries for listing. Dir.mkdir/rmdir for creation/deletion. Dir.chdir for changing working directory. Dir.tmpdir for temporary files. Pathname (require 'pathname') provides an OO interface combining File and Dir operations.

Ruby's metaprogramming power comes from dynamic method dispatch. send invokes methods by name (string or symbol). define_method creates methods at runtime. public_send respects visibility (vs send which bypasses private). These enable DSL construction, dynamic proxies, and automatic delegation. Use them carefully — they bypass normal type checking.

method_missing is called when a method is not found. It enables ghost methods, dynamic proxies, and delegation patterns. Always call super (not defined?) for the default NoMethodError behavior. respond_to_missing? must be overridden alongside method_missing for respond_to? to work correctly. Use carefully — it makes debugging harder.

Domain Specific Languages (DSLs) are a Ruby specialty. Using blocks, method_missing, define_method, and instance_eval, you can create expressive DSLs. Examples: RSpec's describe/it, Rails routes, Rake tasks. The pattern: a class collects DSL calls, instance_eval evaluates blocks in the DSL context, method_missing handles undefined methods.

RubyGems is the package manager for Ruby libraries (gems). Bundler manages gem dependencies via Gemfile. Key commands: gem install, gem list, bundle init, bundle install, bundle exec. Gemfile specifies sources and gems. Gemfile.lock locks versions. gemspec for gem development. Popular gems: rails, sinatra, rspec, devise, sidekiq, nokogiri, httparty.

Ruby's standard testing library is Minitest (built-in, no install needed). RSpec is the most popular third-party testing framework (BDD-style). Minitest uses assert methods. RSpec uses describe/it/expect syntax. Both support before/after hooks, let helpers, and matchers. Test-driven development is common in the Ruby community.

RSpec uses a nested DSL. describe groups tests, it defines examples, expect sets expectations. Matchers: eq, be_true, be_falsey, include, match, change, raise_error. before/after/around hooks run at example or context level. let/lazy evaluation defines memoized helpers. subject defines the object under test.

Ruby projects commonly use GitHub Actions, CircleCI, or Travis CI. Standard CI pipeline: lint (rubocop), test (rspec/minitest), and sometimes type check (sorbet/rbs). Parallel test execution with knapsack or CI matrix for multiple Ruby versions. Use .github/workflows/ci.yml for GitHub Actions. Cache gems with actions/cache for faster runs.

RSpec mocking enables isolated testing. double creates test doubles. allow(...).to receive(...) sets up stubs. expect(...).to receive(...) sets expectations on method calls. instance_double verifies method signatures against real classes. spy records calls without setting expectations upfront. Use mocks sparingly — prefer real objects when practical.

Thread safety in Ruby requires careful synchronization. The GVL (Global VM Lock) protects Ruby internals but doesn't guarantee your code is thread-safe. Use Mutex (mutual exclusion) with synchronize to protect critical sections. ConditionVariable for signaling between threads. Avoid sharing mutable state across threads — prefer message passing.

Ractors are Ruby 3+'s answer to parallel execution without GVL limitations. Each Ractor has its own execution context and doesn't share mutable objects. Communication via send/receive (message passing). Objects passed to ractors are deeply copied or must be shareable (frozen, no references to unshareable objects). Ractors enable true CPU-bound parallelism.

Fibers are lightweight concurrency primitives for cooperative multitasking. Unlike threads, fibers yield control explicitly via Fiber.yield. The async/await pattern in Ruby uses fibers under the hood (Async gem by Samuel Williams). Fibers are ideal for streaming, generators, and non-blocking I/O with explicit scheduling.

Common concurrent patterns in Ruby: thread pools (ConnectionPool gem), promises (concurrent-ruby gem), actors (concurrent-ruby), and queues (Queue class is thread-safe). The concurrent-ruby gem provides high-level abstractions: Concurrent::Future, Concurrent::Promise, Concurrent::Actor, Concurrent::Map, and Concurrent::TimerTask.

Rack is the foundation of Ruby web servers. It defines a simple interface: call(env) returns [status, headers, body]. Middleware are Rack components that wrap requests/responses. Popular Rack-based frameworks: Sinatra, Rails, Roda. Use config.ru for Rack configuration. Rack middleware enables cross-cutting concerns like logging, auth, and caching.

Sinatra is a DSL for quick web applications. Core concepts: routes (get/post/put/delete/ patch), params hash, before/after filters, sessions, helpers, templates (ERB/Haml/Slim), and error handling. Sinatra::Base for modular apps (easier testing). Sinatra::Namespace for route grouping. Sinatra is ideal for APIs, microservices, and prototypes.

Ruby on Rails is a full-stack MVC framework. Model (ActiveRecord) handles data/database, View (ActionView/ERB) handles presentation, Controller (ActionController) handles request logic. Convention over configuration, DRY, and RESTful design are core principles. Key generators: rails generate model/user scaffold/product. Rails includes ActionMailer, ActiveJob, ActionCable (WebSockets), and ActiveStorage.

Grape is a REST-like API framework for Ruby. It's designed for building APIs separate from web views. Features: DSL for routes, parameter validation, content negotiation, versioning, and mounting on Rack or within Rails. Ideal for API-only services or microservices. Combine with Entity for JSON serialization.

ActiveRecord is Rails' ORM (Object-Relational Mapping). Maps database tables to Ruby classes. Key features: migrations (schema evolution), validations, associations (belongs_to/has_many/has_one), callbacks, scopes, query interface (where/order/joins/includes), and eager loading (includes/preload/eager_load). Chain query methods lazily — queries execute when results are needed.

Sequel is a lightweight, thread-safe ORM alternative to ActiveRecord. Key features: DSL for queries, model support, migrations, dataset chaining, eager loading, and excellent performance. Sequel's dataset API is more SQL-like and transparent. Works with SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and others. Popular for non-Rails Ruby apps.

Ruby connects to databases via gems: sqlite3 gem for SQLite, pg gem for PostgreSQL, mysql2 for MySQL. Establish connection, execute queries, handle results. Use connection pooling for production. Sequel and ActiveRecord handle connection management automatically. Environment-specific configs for development/test/production databases.

RuboCop is the standard Ruby linter and formatter. Enforces community style guides (Ruby Style Guide, Rails Style Guide). Integrates with editors via LSP. Run rubocop (check), rubocop -a (auto-fix safe offenses), rubocop -A (auto-fix all). Configuration in .rubocop.yml. Custom cops for project-specific rules. Use with pre-commit hooks and CI.

Pry is the de facto Ruby debugger. Features: binding.pry to pause execution, ls to list methods, cd to navigate objects, show-source to view implementation, wtf? for exception trace, edit to open in editor, and play to replay code. Byebug is an alternative with step/next/continue commands. Use binding.irb (built-in) for simple debugging.

Ruby provides built-in profiling tools. Benchmark module for timing code blocks. The stackprof gem for sampling CPU profiler. rack-mini-profiler for web request profiling. memory_profiler for memory allocation tracking. Derailed benchmarks for Rails apps. Profile before optimizing — measure, identify bottlenecks, then optimize.

YARD is Ruby's documentation tool (replaces RDoc). Uses @tag annotations for structured docs. Key tags: @param, @return, @raise, @yield, @example, @see, @deprecated, @since. Inline docs use # Comments above definitions. Generate HTML docs with yard doc. YARD types: String, Array<String>, Hash{Symbol=>Integer}, #method, DuckType#method.

Ruby supports threading (Thread class) and fibers (Fibers for cooperative concurrency). Threads run concurrently (with GIL limitation in CRuby). Fibers are lightweight control structures for cooperative multitasking. Ractors (Ruby 3+) provide parallel execution without GIL. Use threads for I/O-bound work, ractors for CPU-bound, fibers for generators/streaming.

Rake is Ruby's build tool (like Make). Tasks defined with desc + task. Namespaces group related tasks. Task dependencies via =>. Default task runs with plain `rake`. Rakefile in project root. File tasks for file generation. Rake is commonly used for database migrations, test running, asset compilation, and deployment automation.

Sinatra is a lightweight web framework. Routes are methods decorated with HTTP verbs. Params hash for input. ERB/Haml templates. before/after filters. Sessions with enable :sessions. Helpers for shared logic. Extensions for modular organization. Sinatra is ideal for APIs, microservices, and simple web apps.
react.json: Context API provides a built-in way to share values across the component tree without prop drilling. It's best suited for low-frequency updates like theme, locale, or auth state.

Redux is a predictable state container with a single store, immutable updates via pure reducers, and actions dispatched to trigger state changes. The Redux Toolkit simplifies boilerplate significantly.
Zustand is a minimal state management library with a hook-based API, no boilerplate, and support for middleware. It's ideal for projects that need simple global state without Redux overhead.
Code splitting breaks your bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial load time. React.lazy and Suspense make code splitting declarative and easy to implement.
Lazy loading defers loading of non-critical resources until they are needed. Combined with Suspense, it shows a fallback UI while the lazy component loads asynchronously.
React.memo is a higher-order component that prevents re-rendering when props haven't changed. useCallback memorizes callback functions to maintain referential equality across renders.

JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML and allows you to write markup inside your components. It gets transpiled to React.createElement calls under the hood by tools like Babel.
Components are reusable, self-contained pieces of UI that can be either function-based or class-based. Modern React favors functional components with hooks.
Props (short for properties) are read-only inputs passed to components from their parent. They enable parent-to-child communication and make components configurable.
useState is a hook that adds local state to function components. It returns a stateful value and a function to update it, triggering a re-render when called.
useEffect lets you perform side effects in function components such as data fetching, subscriptions, or DOM manipulation. The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs.
useRef returns a mutable ref object whose .current property persists across renders without causing re-renders. It's commonly used to access DOM elements directly.
useContext consumes a context value created by React.createContext, allowing deep prop drilling to be avoided. It re-renders the component when the context value changes.
useReducer is an alternative to useState for complex state logic involving multiple sub-values or when the next state depends on the previous one. It follows the reducer pattern from Redux.
useMemo memoizes the result of an expensive computation, recomputing only when its dependencies change. Use it to optimize performance by avoiding unnecessary recalculations.
CSS Modules scope CSS class names locally by default, preventing naming collisions across components. Files are imported like JavaScript objects and class names are accessed as properties.
Styled Components is a CSS-in-JS library that lets you write actual CSS inside your JavaScript using tagged template literals. It automatically handles vendor prefixing and scoping.
Tailwind CSS is a utility-first framework providing low-level classes for rapid UI building. It pairs well with React through class composition and tools like clsx for conditional classes.
In controlled forms, form elements derive their value from React state and update via onChange handlers. This gives React single source of truth for form data and enables validation.
React Router is the standard routing library for React apps, enabling navigation between views while keeping the UI in sync with the URL. It supports nested routes, params, and lazy loading.
Jest is a delightful JavaScript testing framework with zero configuration, built-in assertions, mocking, and code coverage. It's the default test runner in Create React App.
React Testing Library builds on top of DOM Testing Library and encourages testing components from the user's perspective. It queries rendered output rather than testing implementation details.
Cypress is an end-to-end testing framework that runs in the browser, providing real-time reloads, time travel debugging, and automatic waiting. It's ideal for integration and E2E tests.
useTransition marks state updates as non-urgent transitions, keeping the UI responsive during expensive re-renders. The isPending flag shows a loading state without blocking user input.
useDeferredValue lets you defer re-rendering a non-urgent part of the tree. The deferred value lags behind the real value, allowing urgent updates (like input typing) to stay responsive.
React Server Components run exclusively on the server, never sent to the client. They reduce bundle size by keeping heavy dependencies server-side and can directly access databases and file systems.
Server Actions are async functions that run on the server, invoked from client components. Use 'use server' to mark them, enabling direct mutations without building API routes.
Error Boundaries catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree, displaying a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. Class components with componentDidCatch are required.
Use key props to reset error boundaries. Changing the key unmounts and remounts the component tree, clearing the error state without a full page refresh.
Portals render children into a DOM node outside the parent component's hierarchy, useful for modals, tooltips, and dropdowns that need to escape overflow or z-index clipping.
TypeScript with React provides type safety for props, state, hooks, and event handlers. Use generic types for useState, useRef, and forwardRef for stricter typing.

React Server Components render on the server, reducing client bundle size by sending only the rendered output. RSC can directly access databases, files, and backend services without exposing secrets to the client. 'use client' directive marks client components. Server components cannot use hooks, event handlers, or browser APIs. App Router (Next.js 13+) uses RSC by default. Benefits: direct backend access, zero client JS for static content, automatic code splitting, and streaming HTML. Streaming with Suspense sends UI progressively as data loads, improving perceived performance.

Advanced React hooks for complex state management: useReducer for state with complex transitions (like Redux without the boilerplate). useCallback memoizes functions to prevent child re-renders. useMemo memoizes expensive computations. useRef stores mutable values across renders without causing re-renders. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations. useTransition marks state updates as non-urgent. useDeferredValue debounces rapidly-changing values. Custom hooks compose these primitives. The React Compiler (React Forget) automatically memoizes values, making explicit memoization optional.
redis.json: Introduction to redis and its ecosystem.
Redis can be installed via package managers, compiled from source, or run via Docker. The default configuration listens on port 6379 and stores data in memory with optional persistence to disk.
Redis supports Strings, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Hashes, Bitmaps, HyperLogLogs, Streams, and Geospatial indexes. Each type has optimized commands for specific use cases and data access patterns.

The `redis-cli` command-line interface connects to Redis servers for interactive or scripted use. It supports command execution, monitoring, slow log analysis, and server administration with built-in help.

Strings are the most fundamental Redis data type, capable of storing text, numbers, or binary data up to 512MB. SET stores a key-value pair, GET retrieves it, and commands like `SETNX` help with distributed locks.

Redis provides atomic increment/decrement operations that are essential for counters, rate limiting, and real-time analytics. Commands like `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`, and `INCRBYFLOAT` operate on string values holding numbers.
TTL (Time To Live) automatically removes keys after a specified duration. `EXPIRE`, `TTL`, and `PERSIST` manage key lifetimes. Expiry is crucial for caching, temporary tokens, and session management.
Lists are ordered sequences of strings, efficient for queue and stack implementations. LPUSH adds to the left, RPUSH adds to the right; LPOP and RPOP remove and return elements from either end.

Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. SADD adds members, SREM removes them, SMEMBERS returns all members, and SISMEMBER checks existence. Sets are ideal for tagging, deduplication, and relations.
Set operations enable powerful data analysis: SUNION combines sets, SINTER finds common elements, and SDIFF finds differences. These are used for recommendations, permissions, and social features.
Hashes store field-value pairs within a single key, ideal for representing objects. They provide memory-efficient storage with commands for individual field CRUD, bulk operations, and field counting.

Sorted Sets associate each member with a numeric score, maintaining order by score. ZADD adds or updates members, ZRANGE retrieves by rank, and ZRANK gets position. Perfect for leaderboards and priority queues.

Sorted Sets excel at real-time leaderboards with atomic score updates, range queries, and pagination. Combined with aggregation commands like ZCOUNT and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, they handle ranking systems efficiently.
RDB (Redis Database) performs point-in-time snapshots at configurable intervals. It creates compact single-file backups, ideal for disaster recovery, but may lose data written between snapshots.

Append-Only File (AOF) logs every write operation for durability. It provides finer-grained persistence than RDB with fsync policies (every write, every second, or OS-controlled) and can be rewritten to compact.

Redis backup involves copying RDB/AOF files, or using `redis-cli --rdb` for live snapshots. Restore requires stopping the server, placing the backup file correctly, and restarting. SLAVEOF enables replication-based recovery.

Pub/Sub implements the publish-subscribe messaging pattern where publishers send messages to channels without knowledge of subscribers. SUBSCRIBE listens on channels, PUBLISH sends messages, and UNSUBSCRIBE stops listening.

PSUBSCRIBE enables subscription to channels matching a glob-style pattern. This allows listening to multiple related channels (e.g., `user:*`, `orders:*`) with a single subscription for efficient message routing.

Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no message persistence; subscribers only receive messages sent after subscription. For reliable messaging, use Redis Streams which support consumer groups, acknowledgment, and message history.

Redis Sentinel provides high availability through automatic failover, monitoring, notifications, and service discovery. A Sentinel cluster monitors master/replica instances and promotes a replica when the master fails.

Redis Cluster automatically shards data across multiple nodes using hash slots (0-16383). Each node handles a subset of slots, providing horizontal scalability and automatic rebalancing when nodes are added or removed.

Hash slots distribute keys deterministically: `HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384`. Client-side sharding is also possible for simpler setups, but Redis Cluster handles routing transparently with MOVED redirections.

Redis caching improves application performance by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Common patterns include cache-aside (lazy loading), write-through, and TTL-based expiry with automatic cache invalidation.

Redis enables efficient distributed rate limiting using INCR with TTL. The sliding window algorithm tracks request counts per time window, and the token bucket algorithm offers more flexible rate control.

Redis is an ideal session store for distributed applications because of its speed, built-in TTL, and atomic operations. `connect-redis` or `ioredis-session` replace the default in-memory session store for persistence across restarts.
Redis Lists provide the foundation for lightweight job queues. `LPUSH` + `BRPOP` implement reliable FIFO queues with blocking pops. Bull and Kue are popular Node.js queue libraries built on Redis.

Redis Pub/Sub enables real-time messaging with fire-and-forget semantics. Channels are created on first publish. Subscribe with SUBSCRIBE command. Redis Streams (5.0+) provide persistent, ack-based messaging with consumer groups. Stream entries are identified by IDs (timestamp-sequence). Consumer groups enable load-balanced processing with message acknowledgment. Stream features: XREAD for reading, XADD for adding, XREADGROUP for group reads, XACK for acknowledgment. Streams support blocking reads and message delivery guarantees.
remix.json: Introduction to Remix and its ecosystem.
Remix uses a file-based routing system in the app/routes directory. Each file represents a route segment, with dot and folder conventions creating nested URL structures automatically.
Nested routes in Remix allow multiple components to render on the same URL. The parent route's layout wraps child routes through the <Outlet /> component, enabling complex UI hierarchies.
Layout routes use the special app/root.tsx file and route-specific layout.tsx files. Layouts wrap child routes and persist across navigation, preventing full page re-renders.
Working with data and APIs in Remix.
Fly.io is the recommended deployment target for Remix, offering global edge regions and effortless scaling. Remix apps deploy as Docker containers running close to users worldwide.
Vercel supports Remix via the @remix-run/vercel adapter. It automatically optimizes serverless functions and delivers assets through Vercel's edge network.
Netlify deploys Remix apps using the Netlify adapter, providing serverless functions for the Remix server and global CDN for static assets via Netlify Edge.
The Cloudflare Workers adapter runs Remix on Cloudflare's edge network. It uses Workers KV for sessions and Durable Objects for real-time state.
Loaders are server-side functions that fetch data before rendering a route. They run on every request, returning data that becomes available to the component via the useLoaderData hook.
useLoaderData returns the typed data from the nearest route loader. It provides type safety when used with TypeScript and the typeof loader generic pattern.
Params give access to dynamic segments from the URL pattern. They are available in loaders and actions via the params argument, matching the bracket syntax in the route filename.
Actions handle form submissions and data mutations on the server. They run on POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE requests and can return data, redirects, or errors to the client.
The <Form> component submits data without JavaScript by default. When JS loads, it progressively enhances to use fetch, providing optimistic UI and pending states without full page reloads.
useFetcher allows submitting actions or loading data without navigational transitions. It is ideal for non-blocking interactions like add-to-cart buttons or inline search suggestions.
Remix embraces Web Fetch API standards. Loaders and actions receive native Request objects and return Response objects, making routes portable across server environments.
Headers in Remix can be set at the route level for caching, security, and content negotiation. The headers export controls both document and resource route responses.
Remix provides a cookies API that integrates with the Web Fetch standard. Cookies are created, read, and written using the cookie utilities from @remix-run/node.
ErrorBoundary catches unexpected rendering errors in a route. When an error is thrown, Remix renders the closest ErrorBoundary instead of the default component, showing a fallback UI.
CatchBoundary handles expected error responses from loaders and actions. It receives the thrown Response object, allowing different UI for 404, 403, and other status codes.
Remix manages CSS through the links export, which adds link tags to the document head. This enables route-level CSS loading and automatic cleanup when navigating away.
Route styles in Remix support both traditional CSS files and CSS-in-JS solutions. CSS files can be imported in links functions, with automatic scoping via CSS Modules.
Remix supports Tailwind CSS through the conventional PostCSS setup. The @tailwind directives are processed during build, generating optimized CSS with unused class purging.
Resource Routes return non-HTML content such as JSON, images, PDFs, or sitemaps. They handle requests without rendering a component, functioning as pure API endpoints within the routes system.
Real-time features in Remix are achieved through WebSocket integrations. While Remix does not include WebSockets natively, it pairs well with libraries like Socket.io or PartyKit.
Remix leverages HTTP caching extensively. The headers export allows setting Cache-Control headers per route, and loaders can implement conditional requests with ETags for efficient revalidation.
Remix now ships as a Vite plugin for faster builds, HMR, and streamlined configuration. The vite.config replaces remix.config with a familiar Vite API and automatic React Fast Refresh.
The Remix Vite plugin accepts options for server entry, routes directory, future flags, and build output. It integrates with other Vite plugins like Tailwind and MDX for a unified build pipeline.
Vite-powered HMR updates Remix route components in milliseconds without losing page state. React Fast Refresh preserves component state across edits, dramatically improving the dev feedback loop.
Cookie session storage encodes session data directly in encrypted cookies, suitable for small payloads. It requires no database and is the simplest session strategy for Remix apps.
createSessionStorage allows custom backing stores (database, Redis) for larger session data while using a cookie only for the session ID. This scales beyond cookie size limits.
Flash messages are one-time session values that are cleared after being read, ideal for success or error notifications after form submissions. They use the session's flash method.
useLoaderData infers the return type of the route's loader using typeof loader. This provides end-to-end type safety from the server to the client without manual type definitions.
useActionData provides type-safe access to action return values. Combine with typeof action for compile-time checking of error messages, form data, and mutation results.
Remix's SerializeFrom type unwraps Promise and Response types from loaders, providing a cleaner type for client-side hooks when the loader uses async patterns.

Remix provides nested routing with shared layouts. Files in app/routes/ follow directory-based routing. app/root.tsx is the root layout. _layout.tsx files create shared layouts. Outlets render child routes. Nested routes load data in parallel via loader functions. useLoaderData, useRouteLoaderData, and useMatches access data from any route. shouldRevalidate optimizes data reloads. Error boundaries per route (ErrorBoundary). Pending UI with useNavigation. Optimistic UI with useFetcher form submissions.

Remix resource routes return non-HTML responses: JSON APIs, files, redirects, and webhooks. Resource routes don't render components — they only export loader (GET) and action (POST/PUT/DELETE). app/routes/api.products.$id.tsx becomes /api/products/:id. Webhook handlers verify signatures and process events. File uploads with unstable_parseMultipartFormData. RSS feeds, sitemaps, and PDF generation. response helpers: json, redirect, defer (streaming). CORS headers for public API routes.
rnative.json: Introduction to Rnative and its ecosystem.
JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML and is compiled to React.createElement calls. It allows writing UI components declaratively in React Native.
Components are reusable building blocks in React Native, defined as functions returning JSX. They accept props and manage their own state using hooks.
StyleSheet provides a way to define styles with performance benefits through abstraction. It validates and optimizes style objects, and styles are only sent to native once.
Expo is the recommended framework for building React Native apps. It provides managed workflows, over-the-air updates, and access to native APIs without Xcode or Android Studio.
Working with data and APIs in Rnative.
iOS deployment requires an Apple Developer account, Xcode configuration, and provisioning profiles. The app is archived and uploaded via Xcode or Transporter.
Android deployment generates a signed APK or AAB using keystore credentials. The build is created with Gradle and uploaded to the Play Console.
Expo Application Services (EAS) Build compiles and signs your app in the cloud without requiring Xcode or Android Studio installed locally.
View is the fundamental container component supporting flexbox layout, styling, touch handling, and accessibility. It maps to UIView on iOS and View on Android.
Text is the only component that renders text in React Native. It supports nesting, styling, and event handling like onPress.
Image displays images from local assets, network URLs, or data URIs. It requires explicit dimensions when loading from network sources.
ScrollView is a scrolling container for multiple components and views. It loads all content upfront and is best for smaller amounts of content.
Pressable is the modern touch handling component that provides feedback for different press states. Use instead of TouchableOpacity for more control.
Modal presents content on top of the app, useful for alerts and forms. StatusBar controls the device status bar appearance per screen.
React Navigation is the standard navigation library for React Native apps, providing stack, tab, and drawer navigators with native transitions.
Stack navigator manages a navigation stack where screens are pushed and popped. It provides native-like transitions and header customization.
Tab navigator provides bottom or top tab navigation with icons and labels. Each tab maintains its own navigation state for independent back stacks.
Drawer navigator creates a side menu that slides in from the left, supporting nested navigators and custom drawer content.
Expo Router provides file-based routing similar to Next.js. Files in the app/ directory automatically become routes with support for layout files and deep linking.
Fabric is the new rendering system that uses JSI (JavaScript Interface) instead of the Bridge. It enables synchronous communication and better performance for UI updates.
TurboModules replace the old Native Modules system, allowing lazy loading of native modules and efficient type-safe communication via JSI.
JavaScript Interface (JSI) enables direct, synchronous communication between JavaScript and native code without the Bridge. It eliminates the serialization overhead of the old architecture.
useState is a React hook that adds local state to functional components, returning a state variable and a setter function.
AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value storage system for persisting data across app restarts on both iOS and Android.
Zustand is a minimal state management library with a hook-based API. It works well in React Native for global state without boilerplate.
MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage by Tencent. It's significantly faster than AsyncStorage and ideal for performance-critical persistence.
React Native's built-in Animated API provides declarative animations using Animated.Value and timing/spring configurations. It drives animations natively on the UI thread.
Reanimated provides gesture-driven animations that run entirely on the UI thread using worklets. It enables smooth 60fps animations for complex interactions.
Gesture Handler replaces PanResponder with native gesture processing. It supports pan, pinch, rotation, tap, long press, and custom gesture compositions.
The Fetch API provides a native way to make HTTP requests in React Native. It returns promises and supports JSON, text, and binary responses.
Axios is a promise-based HTTP client with interceptors, automatic JSON parsing, and request cancellation. It provides a cleaner API than fetch.
React Query (TanStack Query) manages server state with automatic caching, refetching, pagination, and optimistic updates.
WebSocket enables full-duplex real-time communication over a persistent TCP connection, ideal for chat apps, live updates, and gaming.
React Native Camera provides device camera access with support for photos, videos, barcode scanning, and custom camera UI.
Geolocation APIs provide device location through GPS or network positioning, supporting high-accuracy and background location tracking.
Push notifications allow sending alerts to user devices even when the app is closed. Firebase Cloud Messaging is the standard solution.
FlatList efficiently renders large lists by virtualizing rows, recycling components, and rendering only visible items. It supports headers, footers, and pull-to-refresh.
React Native optimization includes using PureComponent, useMemo, avoiding inline functions in render, and minimizing re-renders with React.memo.
Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine optimized for React Native, reducing app startup time, memory usage, and APK/IPA size.
InteractionManager schedules tasks to run after animations or navigation transitions complete, preventing dropped frames during critical UI updates.
React Native Skia provides a high-performance 2D graphics canvas for custom drawing, image manipulation, and complex animations using the Skia graphics library.
CodePush enables over-the-air JavaScript bundle updates without going through the App Store review process, allowing instant bug fixes and small feature updates.
AppState tracks whether the app is in foreground, background, or inactive state. Use it to pause/resume timers, network requests, and animations.

React Navigation is the standard navigation library. Stack, Tab, Drawer, and native stack navigators. Deep linking maps URL schemes to screens (myapp://product/123 or universal links). Linking configuration registers URL patterns. Push notifications trigger navigation via deep links. NavigationContainer handles linking. useLinkProps creates accessible links. useLinkTo navigates programmatically. Auth flow: conditional navigation based on auth state. Screen tracking for analytics via onStateChange. Screen focus detection with useFocusEffect.

React Native provides multiple animation systems: Animated (imperative), react-native-reanimated (runs on UI thread for 60fps), react-native-gesture-handler (native gesture processing). Reanimated 3 uses worklets (JS functions that run on the UI thread). Shared values, animations, and gestures compose for smooth interactions. Layout Animations for enter/exit transitions. GestureDetector for pan, pinch, tap, rotation. runOnJS calls JS thread from worklets. Skia (react-native-skia) for custom drawing and animations.
rust.json: Variables and data types in Rust.
`Result<T, E>` for recoverable errors. `Option<T>` for nullable values. `?` operator propagates errors. `unwrap()` and `expect()` extract values or panic. `ok_or()` converts Option to Result.
`?` unwraps `Result` or `Option`, returning early on error/None. Converts error types via `From` trait. Only works in functions returning Result, Option, or types implementing `FromResidual`.
`panic!()` unwinds the stack (or aborts with `panic = "abort"`). Use for unrecoverable states. `unwrap`, `expect`, `unreachable!()`, `todo!()`, `unimplemented!()` all panic on use.
Implement `std::error::Error` for custom errors. Requires `Display` + `Debug`. `source()` method for error chaining. `Box<dyn Error>` for type-erased error handling.
thiserror derives `std::error::Error` with minimal boilerplate. Supports `#[error("...")]` for Display, `#[source]` for error chaining, and `#[from]` for automatic From impls.

anyhow provides `Result<T, anyhow::Error>` for application-level error handling. `bail!()` and `ensure!()` macros. Context method `.context()`. eyre is a similar alternative with better error reports.
Errors chain via `source()` or `.context()`. The `?` operator auto-converts via `From`. Libraries define specific error types; apps use anyhow/eyre. `Error::source` iterates the chain.
`map`, `map_err`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `ok`, `err`, `transpose` — these combinators transform Results without explicit match.
Input and output operations in Rust.
Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, speed, and concurrency. It guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector through its ownership system and zero-cost abstractions.

Rust uses `fn` for functions, `let` for variables, and macros with `!`. Semicolons end expressions, blocks use curly braces. `main` is the program entry point. Statements vs expressions distinction is key.
Variables are immutable by default. Use `mut` to make them mutable. `const` for compile-time constants. Shadowing redeclares a variable with `let`, allowing type changes.
Four scalar types: integers (i8-u128, i64, usize), floats (f32, f64), bool, char. Integer overflow wraps in release, panics in debug. Underscores improve readability: `1_000_000`.
rustup manages Rust toolchains. Switch between stable, beta, nightly. `rustup target add` for cross-compilation. `rustup component add` for tools. `rustup show` displays active toolchain.
Cargo is Rust's build system and package manager. `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`, `cargo check`, `cargo clean`. Cargo.toml defines metadata and dependencies.
rustfmt auto-formats code according to style guidelines. `cargo fmt` formats the whole project. `rustfmt --check` verifies formatting in CI. Configure with `rustfmt.toml`.
Clippy is Rust's linter with 550+ rules. `cargo clippy` catches common mistakes, non-idiomatic code, and performance pitfalls. `#[allow(clippy::...)]` silences specific lints.
rust-analyzer provides IDE support: code completion, goto-definition, type hints, inlay hints, rename, diagnostics. LSP server used by VS Code, Neovim, Emacs, and Zed.
Conditions must be `bool` — no truthy/falsy coercion. `if` is an expression, assignable with `let`. All arms must return the same type. Blocks evaluate to their last expression.
`loop` repeats forever until `break`. `while` loops on a condition. `for` iterates over iterators. `for (0..n)` is range syntax. Use `continue` to skip to next iteration.
`match` is Rust's powerful pattern matching. Arms must be exhaustive. Patterns can bind, match ranges (`..=`), use `|` for alternatives, and guards with `if`.
`if let` combines `match` for a single pattern, ignoring others. Useful with `Option`, `Result`, and enums. Reduces boilerplate when only one arm matters.
`while let` repeatedly matches a pattern until it fails. Common with iterators, `Option`-producing functions, and mutable borrow patterns.
Loop labels (`'label`) disambiguate nested loops. `break 'label` exits the named loop. `continue 'label` skips to the next iteration of the named loop.
`loop` can return a value with `break value`. `break` with no value returns `()`. Useful for retry logic or initializing values from fallible operations.
Each value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. Ownership can be moved. This guarantees memory safety without GC.
Assigning or passing a value moves ownership unless the type implements `Copy`. Stack-only types (integers, bools, floats, chars, tuples of Copy types) are copied.
References borrow values without taking ownership. `&T` (immutable, shared). `&mut T` (mutable, exclusive). References must never outlive their referent.
At any time: either one mutable reference, or any number of immutable references. References must always be valid. The borrow checker enforces this at compile time.
Rust allows borrowing different fields of a struct simultaneously. The borrow checker tracks borrows at the field level, enabling mutable access to disjoint fields.
NLL makes the borrow checker smarter: borrows end when they're last used, not at the end of the scope. This reduces friction with the borrow checker significantly.
Slices are dynamically-sized views into contiguous sequences. `&str` is a string slice. `&[T]` is an array slice. They are fat pointers (ptr + length) and never own data.
Interior mutability allows mutating data through shared references. Provided by `Cell<T>` (Copy types, no threads), `RefCell<T>` (runtime borrow checking, no threads), and `Mutex<T>` (thread-safe).
RefCell enforces borrow rules at runtime — panics on violation. `borrow()` returns `Ref<T>`, `borrow_mut()` returns `RefMut<T>`. Useful when the compiler can't verify correctness.
Functions use `fn` with snake_case naming. Parameters require type annotations. Return type is `-> Type`. The last expression in a block is implicitly returned. Early return with `return`.
Methods are functions defined in `impl` blocks with a `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` parameter. Associated functions (like constructors) don't take `self` and are called with `::`.
Closures are anonymous functions that capture their environment. `||` syntax. Traits: `Fn` (immutable capture), `FnMut` (mutable capture), `FnOnce` (consume capture). Each closure has a unique type.
`!` (never type) indicates a function that never returns. `panic!()`, `loop {}`, `todo!()`, `unreachable!()` all diverge. Used in match arms that must match any type.
`fn(T) -> U` is a function pointer type, not a closure. Cannot capture environment. Useful for callbacks and FFI. Coerces from closures that don't capture.
`where` clauses specify trait bounds after the function signature. More readable for complex generics. Same semantics as inline bounds. Required for some complex bound patterns.
Functions can take closures as parameters using generic bounds. Iterator adapters like `map`, `filter`, `fold` enable functional pipelines. Combinators compose nicely.
Tuples group values of different types. Fixed length. Destructure with pattern matching or index syntax `.0`, `.1`. Unit tuple `()` is the empty tuple, representing absence of value.
Arrays have fixed length `[T; N]`. Stored on stack. Bounds-checked at runtime. Slices `&[T]` borrow array elements. `[0; 100]` creates an array filled with the same value.
`Vec<T>` is a growable heap-allocated array. Use `vec![]` macro. Amortized O(1) push. `Vec::with_capacity(n)` pre-allocates. `drain`, `retain`, `splice` are powerful methods.
`&str` is a borrowed string slice (UTF-8). `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer. `&str` to `String` via `.to_string()` or `String::from()`. Strings are not `Index` due to UTF-8.
Structs define custom data with named fields. Use `impl` blocks for methods. Field init shorthand when variable matches field name. Struct update syntax `..other` fills remaining fields.
Tuple structs have unnamed fields accessed by position. Newtype pattern wraps a single type. Good for type safety without field name overhead. `struct Wrapper(T)`.
Unit structs have no fields — act as markers or flags. Zero size. Useful for implementing traits without data, or as phantom types with `PhantomData`.
Enums define sum types with variants. Variants can hold data (tuple or struct). `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` are the most common enums. `match` enforces exhaustive handling.
Generics abstract over types, enabling code reuse. Monomorphization generates specialized code per concrete type at compile time. Type parameters are declared with `<T>`.
Traits define shared behavior (like interfaces). Types implement traits with `impl Trait for Type`. Traits can provide default method implementations. Must be in scope to use methods.
`#[derive(...)]` auto-implements common traits: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default, PartialOrd, Ord. Saves boilerplate and ensures correctness.
Supertraits express that one trait extends another. `trait A: B` means types implementing A must also implement B. Used with `where Self: SuperTrait` for method access.

Trait objects enable dynamic dispatch via vtable. `dyn Trait` is unsized — must be behind a pointer (`&dyn Trait`, `Box<dyn Trait>`). Objects must be object-safe (no generic methods, no Self by value).
`impl Trait` in argument position is like a generic. In return position, it returns an opaque type implementing Trait. Cannot return multiple types. Useful for returning closures/iterators.
Associated types define placeholder types within a trait. One implementation per type — unlike generics which allow multiple impls. Used extensively in Iterator, Deref, and operator traits.
Blanket impls implement a trait for all types satisfying bounds. `impl<T: Display> ToString for T {}` is a blanket impl. They allow adding methods to all types meeting criteria.
Trait bounds constrain generics. Multiple bounds: `T: Clone + Debug`. `where` clauses improve readability. `impl Trait` as shorthand. `?Sized` opts out of the implicit Sized bound.

`Vec<T>` is the primary sequence type — growable, heap-allocated, contiguous. Amortized O(1) push/pop. O(n) insert/remove. `with_capacity` pre-allocates. `drain`, `splice`, `retain` for advanced operations.
`VecDeque<T>` is a double-ended queue with O(1) push/pop at both ends. Ring buffer internally. Use for queue/sliding window patterns. `make_contiguous()` for slice access.
`HashMap<K, V>` stores key-value pairs with O(1) average lookup. `HashSet<T>` is a set of unique values. Both require keys to implement `Hash + Eq`. `entry()` API handles insert-or-update.
`BTreeMap` / `BTreeSet` maintain sorted order with O(log n) operations. Keys must implement `Ord`. Use when order matters or for range queries. `range()` returns entries within bounds.
`BinaryHeap<T>` is a max-heap priority queue. O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop. Use `Reverse<T>` for min-heap. `into_sorted_vec()` drains in order.
`LinkedList<T>` is a doubly-linked list. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Split/append operations. Generally slower than Vec/VecDeque due to cache behavior. Use for heavy splitting.
`Box<T>` allocates on the heap. Used for recursive types (linked lists), trait objects (`Box<dyn Trait>`), and large data moved infrequently. Derefs to `&T` / `&mut T`.
`Rc<T>` enables shared ownership within a single thread. `Rc::clone()` increments reference count. `strong_count` / `weak_count`. `Weak<T>` prevents cycles. Use `Arc` for threads.
`Arc<T>` is `Rc` + atomic reference counting — thread-safe. `Arc::clone()` is atomic. Pair with `Mutex<T>` for mutable shared state. `Arc<[T]>` for shared slices.
`Cell<T>` provides interior mutability for Copy types (no borrow checking — just copy in/out). `RefCell<T>` provides interior mutability for any type, checking borrows at runtime.
`Cow<'a, B>` abstracts borrowed vs owned data. `Cow::Borrowed(&str)` / `Cow::Owned(String)`. Call `.to_mut()` to get mutable access, cloning if borrowed. Ideal for read-mostly APIs.
`Pin<T>` ensures a value is never moved again. Required for self-referential structs and async generators. `Pin<&mut T>` / `Pin<Box<T>>`. Unsafe to construct. Foundation of async Rust.
Variables drop in reverse declaration order. Struct fields drop in declaration order. `std::mem::forget` skips Drop. `ManuallyDrop` controls Drop. Nested values: outer drops first, then inner.
`Mutex<T>` guards shared data across threads. `RwLock<T>` allows concurrent reads / exclusive writes. `Condvar` blocks threads until a condition is met. `PoisonError` on panic.
