`std::sync::mpsc` provides multi-producer, single-consumer channels. `Sender` clones for multiple producers. `Receiver` has `recv`, `try_recv`, `iter`. `crossbeam` offers multi-consumer variants.

Pin ensures a value won't be moved in memory. Essential for self-referential structs (e.g., async Futures). `Pin<Box<T>>` (heap-pinned), `Pin<&mut T>` (stack-pinned via `pin!` macro). Once pinned, cannot safely move. `Unpin` auto-trait: most types are Unpin (move OK). Async blocks/futures are `!Unpin` (not Unpin). Unsafe `get_unchecked_mut` to mutate pinned data. PhantomPinned marker make a type !Unpin.
`mod` declares a module. Files and directories mirror modules. `pub` controls visibility. `super` / `crate` / `self` keywords for paths. `pub(crate)` restricts to crate.
`pub use` re-exports items at a different path, making them part of the public API. Useful for flattening module hierarchies and renaming. `pub(crate) use` for internal re-exports.
Modules can be nested inline or in files. `mod foo;` looks for `foo.rs` or `foo/mod.rs`. `mod foo { ... }` for inline. The 2018 edition uses the `foo.rs` convention.
Crate types: `bin` (binary), `lib` (library), `cdylib` (C-compatible dynamic lib), `staticlib`, `proc-macro`. `edition` field selects Rust edition. `[profile.*]` for optimization settings.
Dependencies from crates.io, git, or path. `features` enable conditional compilation. `default-features = false` to opt out. `[target.'cfg(...)'.dependencies]` for platform-specific deps.
Workspaces manage multiple crates in one project. Shared `target/` and `Cargo.lock`. Members listed in `[workspace]`. `cargo build -p specific-crate` to build a single member.
`#[cfg()]` gates code on target, feature, or OS. `cfg!()` is a runtime boolean. `#[cfg_attr(...)]` conditionally applies attributes. `cfg(test)` gates test-only code.
Lifetimes (`'a`) annotate how long references are valid. Prevent dangling references. The borrow checker validates lifetimes at compile time. Elision rules handle common patterns automatically.

Three elision rules: 1) each input reference gets its own lifetime. 2) with one input lifetime, output gets that lifetime. 3) with `&self`/`&mut self`, output gets self's lifetime. These cover 95%+ of cases.
`'static` references live for the entire program. String literals have type `&'static str`. `Box::leak` produces `&'static mut`. Const items are effectively static.
`'a: 'b` means 'a outlives 'b (is a subtype of 'b). Required when one lifetime must strictly outlive another. Common in structs and complex function signatures.
HRTBs with `for<'a>` express that a bound must hold for all lifetimes. `Fn(&i32)` is sugar for `for<'a> Fn(&'a i32)`. Required for trait objects and closure bounds.
Variance describes how lifetimes compose: `&'a T` is covariant in 'a, `&'a mut T` is invariant in 'a, `fn(T) -> U` is contravariant in T. `Cell<T>` makes T invariant. Important for type safety.
Rust coerces shorter lifetimes to longer ones when safe. `&'a T` coerces to `&'b T` if `'a: 'b`. String `&str` to `&str` with shorter lifetime. Occurs implicitly at coercion sites.
NLL (Non-Lexical Lifetimes) allows borrows to end before the scope ends. Two-phase borrows let reborrowing during method calls. The borrow checker uses a location-aware analysis.
`async fn` returns a `Future`. `.await` polls the future to completion. Futures are lazy — they do nothing until awaited or polled. An executor is required to drive futures.
Tokio provides a multi-threaded (work-stealing) or single-threaded runtime. `#[tokio::main]` attribute sets up the runtime. Key components: reactor (I/O events), scheduler (tasks), timers.
Async traits require nightly or workarounds. `async-trait` crate desugars to `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`. Upcoming native async traits in Rust will remove this overhead.
`tokio::select!` waits on multiple futures, completing when the first finishes. `futures::join!` awaits multiple futures concurrently. `try_join!` returns on first error.
`futures::future::join_all` awaits a collection of futures, returning all results. `FuturesUnordered` polls a set of futures, yielding results as they complete — ideal for dynamic workloads.
`Stream` trait is the async version of `Iterator`. `StreamExt` provides `next()`, `map`, `filter`, `fold`. `tokio_stream` and `futures` libraries. `async-stream` macro creates streams.

Pin projection allows safely accessing fields of a pinned struct using `pin_project` or `pin_utils`. Critical for self-referential async state machines. `#[pin_project]` attribute handles the unsafe parts.
Tokio provides async-aware synchronisation: `Mutex` (hold across .await), `RwLock`, `Semaphore`, `Barrier`, `Notify`, `watch`, `broadcast` channels. Never hold a std::sync::Mutex across .await.

`*const T` and `*mut T` are raw pointers with no safety guarantees. Can be null, dangling, or aliased. Dereferencing requires `unsafe`. Create from references with `as *const T`. Used for FFI and perf.
`unsafe fn` marks an unsafe function that callers must wrap in `unsafe {}`. `unsafe` blocks opt into: deref raw pointers, call unsafe fns, access mutable statics, implement unsafe traits.
`extern "C"` declares functions from C libraries. `#[link(name = "...")]` links native libs. `#[no_mangle]` prevents name mangling. `unsafe` to call. `libc` crate provides C type aliases.
`#[repr(C)]` lays out struct fields like C (no reordering). `#[repr(transparent)]` wraps a single field with same layout. `#[repr(packed)]` removes padding. `#[repr(align(n))]` sets alignment.
`#![no_std]` removes the standard library for embedded/kernel targets. Use `core` and `alloc` crates. `#[global_allocator]` replaces the default allocator. `alloc_error_handler` for OOM.
`#[link(name = "foo", kind = "static")]` links native libraries. `extern "C"` (or "system", "stdcall") blocks declare foreign functions. `#[link_name = "actual_name"]` overrides the symbol name.
`#[no_mangle]` with `extern "C"` exposes Rust functions to C. `CString` creates null-terminated strings. `Cargo.toml` needs `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]`. FFI-safe types only.
Builder pattern constructs complex objects with many optional parameters. Methods return `&mut Self` or `Self` for chaining. `build()` consumes the builder and produces the final value.
RAII ties resource lifetime to scope. Files, locks, and memory are released in `Drop`. `MutexGuard`, `File`, `Box` all use RAII. Cannot forget to release — the compiler handles it.
Wrap a single type in a tuple struct for type safety and trait impls. Zero-cost abstraction — the wrapper is optimized away. Used for units, IDs, and implementing external traits on external types.
Implementing `Deref<Target=U>` allows smart pointers to behave like references. `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, `Arc<T>` all deref to their inner type. `DerefMut` for mutable deref. Chains `.` auto-derefs.
Struct fields drop in declaration order. Tuple fields drop in index order. Slices/vectors drop elements front-to-back. Closures drop their captures when the closure drops.

Typestate encoding uses the type system to enforce state transitions. Methods consume the current state and return the next. Invalid transitions are compile-time errors. Common in builders and protocols.

Interior mutability: mutate data through shared references. Types: Cell<T> (Copy types, no sync), RefCell<T> (non-Copy, runtime borrow checking, no sync), OnceCell<T> (write once, no sync). Sync versions: Mutex<T>, RwLock<T>, AtomicBool/isize/ptr, OnceLock<T>. RefCell borrows checked at runtime — panics on double borrow. Rc<RefCell<T>> for shared mutable ownership (single-thread). Arc<Mutex<T>> for multi-thread.
Unit tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file. Test functions are annotated with `#[test]`. Assert with `assert!`, `assert_eq!`, `assert_ne!`. `#[should_panic]` for expected panics.
Integration tests live in `tests/` directory at crate root. Each file is a separate crate. They test the public API only. `cargo test --test integration_test_name` runs a specific file.
Doc tests are code blocks in `///` or `//!` docs. Run with `cargo test`. Code blocks with ` ``` ` are compiled and run. ` ```ignore ` skips compilation. ` ```no_run ` compiles but doesn't run.

`#[cfg(test)]` only compiles test modules. `#[test]` marks a test. `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]`. `#[ignore]` skips a test. `#[bench]` for benchmarks (nightly). `cargo test -- --nocapture` for stdout.
`cargo bench` runs benchmark functions with `#[bench]` (nightly). Or use the `criterion` crate (stable). Criterion measures time, generates reports, and detects performance regressions.
proptest generates many random inputs to verify properties. `proptest!` macro defines strategies. `#[proptest]` is an alternative. Checks invariants hold for all inputs. Finds edge cases.
Mock objects simulate dependencies. `mockall` crate generates mock types from trait definitions. `#[automock]` for single methods. Use with dependency injection for isolated tests.
`macro_rules!` matches patterns and generates code. Metavariables: `$expr`, `$ty`, `$ident`, `$stmt`, `$pat`, `$tt`. Repetition with `$()*`, `$()+`, `$()?`. Hygiene prevents name collisions.
Designators: `block`, `expr`, `ident`, `item`, `lifetime`, `literal`, `meta`, `pat`, `path`, `stmt`, `tt`, `ty`, `vis`. `tt` (token tree) is the most flexible — matches any single token group.
Procedural macros operate on the token stream. Three kinds: `#[derive]`, attribute-like `#[...]`, function-like `name!()`. Defined in proc-macro crates. `proc_macro::TokenStream` as input/output.
Derive macros automatically implement traits. Custom derive macros use `#[proc_macro_derive(Name)]`. Generate impl blocks. The `syn` crate parses token streams. `quote` crate generates output tokens.
Attribute macros customize items they annotate. `#[proc_macro_attribute]` receives the attribute arguments and the annotated item tokens. Used for `#[tokio::main]`, `#[async_trait]`, etc.
`cargo expand` (cargo-expand) shows macro expansion output. `log_syntax!()` prints tokens during expansion. `trace_macros!()` logs all macro invocations. `stringify!()` converts to string.

Advanced macro_rules! patterns: TT muncher (recursive token tree processing), internal rules, hygiene control, token types (ident, expr, ty, pat, stmt, block, literal, tt, meta, lifetime, vis). Common: vec! (repeated expr), hashmap! (key=>value pairs), builder patterns. Repetition: `$($x:expr),*` (zero+), `$($x:expr),+` (one+). Use `@` for internal rules. Export with `#[macro_export]`.
scala.json: Variables and data types in Scala.

`Try[T]` represents computations that may throw. Pattern: `Try(...) match { case Success(v) => ... case Failure(e) => ... }`. Chaining: `.map`, `.flatMap`, `.filter`. Recovery: `.recover`, `.recoverWith`.

`Either[L, R]` with convention: `Left` is error, `Right` is success. `.map`, `.flatMap`, `.fold`. `.toTry`, `.toOption`. Cats' `Validated` accumulates multiple errors (unlike Either which fails fast).
Model errors as sealed ADTs (algebraic data types) for exhaustive handling. Use case classes extending a sealed trait. Combine with Either or Try for type-safe error propagation.
Manage resources (files, sockets, connections) with `using` pattern or Scala 3's `using` rework. The loan pattern ensures proper cleanup even with exceptions.
Input and output operations in Scala.
Scala is a statically-typed language that blends OOP and functional programming on the JVM. It interoperates fully with Java and powers systems like Apache Spark and Apache Kafka.
Scala uses `def` for methods, `val` for immutable references, and `var` for mutable ones. Types are inferred but can be declared after colons. No semicolons required.
`val` creates an immutable binding (like final), `var` creates a mutable one. Basic types: Int, Long, Double, Float, Boolean, Char, Byte, Short, String.
Scala infers types from expressions. You can omit type annotations when the compiler can deduce them. Explicit types help with readability and API contracts.
The Scala REPL provides interactive evaluation. Scala Worksheets in IDEs auto-evaluate on save. Both are great for experimenting with code snippets.
Scala projects typically use sbt with `src/main/scala` and `src/test/scala`. Scala CLI supports single-file scripts. Maven and Gradle also support Scala via plugins.
Install Scala via Coursier (`cs setup`), SDKMAN, or download from scalalang.org. Verify with `scala -version`. Coursier is the recommended tool for managing Scala versions and tools.
`if` is an expression in Scala that returns a value. Ternary-style: `val x = if (cond) a else b`. The else branch is optional but Unit is returned without it.
`match` is Scala's powerful pattern matching — like switch on steroids. It returns a value and supports type matching, destructuring, and guards.
`for` loops iterate over collections. For-comprehensions (`for` with `yield`) produce new collections. Multiple generators and guards are supported.
`while` and `do-while` loops work as expected for imperative code. Prefer recursion or functional approaches in idiomatic Scala.
Exceptions use `try-catch-finally`. `try` is an expression returning a value. `catch` clauses use pattern matching for different exception types.
By-name parameters and higher-order functions enable custom control structures. Common patterns: `measure`, `timed`, `using` (resource management), `repeat`, custom loops.
Methods use `def` with explicit parameter types and optional return type. Expression-bodied methods omit braces. Parentheses can be omitted for nullary methods.
Parameters can have default values. Named arguments allow reordering or skipping parameters. Combine both for flexible APIs.
Lambda syntax: `(params) => expr`. Short form `_` for single-use params. Lambdas are first-class values with function types.
Functions that take or return other functions. `map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `fold` are core HOFs. Methods can be lifted to functions with `_`.
Methods can have multiple parameter lists. Partial application binds some args leaving others free. Currying transforms multi-arg functions into chains of single-arg functions.
By-name parameters (`=> T`) are evaluated only when used, not at call site. Useful for custom control structures and short-circuit logic.
`@tailrec` annotation ensures a recursive method is compiled into a loop. The recursive call must be in tail position (last operation).
`List` is an immutable linked list (head + tail). `::` prepends, `:::` concatenates. Rich API: map, filter, flatMap, fold, reduce, and more.
`Map` for key-value pairs (immutable by default). `Set` for unique elements. `+` adds entries, `++` merges, `-` removes keys.
`Seq` is the base trait for ordered collections. `Vector` offers O(log32) indexed access. `IndexedSeq` is the preferred type for random access sequences.
Core collection operations: map, filter, flatMap, foldLeft, foldRight, reduce, scan, partition, span, groupBy, sortBy, distinct, zip, unzip.
`LazyList` (formerly Stream) provides lazy, potentially infinite sequences. Elements are computed on demand and memoized. Use `#::` for construction.
`Option[T]` represents optional values: `Some(value)` or `None`. `Either[L, R]` represents a value that can be one of two types (typically success or error).
Array is a mutable, fixed-size sequence backed by JVM array. ArrayBuffer is a mutable, resizable sequence. Use `Array` for performance, `ArrayBuffer` for flexible sizing.
`View` provides lazy evaluation for collection operations. Transformations are deferred until forced. Avoids intermediate collections. Use `.view` to create, `.force` or `.toList` to materialize.
Classes have primary constructors in the class signature. Auxiliary constructors use `def this()`. Fields become public by default.
`object` declares a singleton. A companion object (same name as a class, same file) holds static-like members and factory methods. `apply` methods allow `new`-less construction.
Traits are like interfaces with concrete methods and fields. A class can mix in multiple traits. Traits support linearization (stackable modifications).
Case classes are immutable with auto-generated `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy`, and pattern-matching extractors. Perfect for data modelling.
Sealed classes restrict subtyping to the same file. The compiler knows all subtypes, enabling exhaustive pattern matching. `abstract class` provides base with constructor params.
Scala 3 enums provide algebraic data types with parameterized cases and methods. More concise than sealed trait + case class patterns.

Scala visibility: `public` (default), `protected` (subclass + companion), `private` (class + companion only). Scoped access: `private[this]`, `private[package]`. Companion objects access private members.

Self-type annotations (`_: Trait =>`) declare that a trait must be mixed into a class extending another type. Enables dependency injection via cake pattern. Use `this: Dependency =>` to require a dependency.
Pattern matching destructures and matches values. Supports constants, type tests, guards, and deep matching on case classes and collections.
Guards with `if` add conditional logic to patterns. Combine destructuring with boolean checks for precise matching.
Custom extractors use `unapply` methods on objects. They enable custom destructuring in pattern matching. `unapplySeq` for variable-length extractions.
For-comprehensions with `yield` desugar to `flatMap`, `map`, and `withFilter`. This works with any type providing these operations — enabling monadic composition.
The compiler checks exhaustiveness for sealed types — warns if a match is non-exhaustive. Use `sealed trait` or `enum` for ADTs. The `@unused` or wildcard `_` satisfies remaining cases.
Scala encourages immutable data and pure functions. `val` over `var`, immutable collections by default. Immutability simplifies reasoning and concurrency.
Pure functions have no side effects and depend only on their inputs. They're deterministic, testable, and composable. Referential transparency is the key principle.
`Option`, `Try`, `Either`, `Future` are monads — they support `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, and for-comprehensions. Chaining operations safely without null checks.
`Functor` provides `map`. `Applicative` provides `pure` and `ap` (`<*>`). Cats library provides typeclass hierarchy. Scala's standard library gives basic functor support via `map`.
Type classes use implicit parameters and implicit classes. Pattern: trait + implicit instances + interface methods. Enables ad-hoc polymorphism.
Scala 3 replaces `implicit` with `given`/`using`. `given` defines instances, `using` declares requirements. More explicit and safer than Scala 2 implicits.
For-comprehensions desugar to `foreach`, `map`, `flatMap`, `withFilter`. Any type providing these methods works in for-comprehensions. Custom monads can use for-comprehensions.

Recursion schemes generalize recursion patterns. `fold` (catamorphism) collapses data. `unfold` (anamorphism) generates data. Scala supports via `cats.Recursive`. Manual implementation with F-algebras.
Type parameters in square brackets. Variance annotations: `+T` (covariant), `-T` (contravariant). Bounds: `T <: Upper`, `T >: Lower`. Multiple bounds with `with`.
`+T`: covariant — `Box[Child] <: Box[Parent]`. `-T`: contravariant — `Printer[Parent] <: Printer[Child]`. Invariant (no annotation) is the default.
Upper bound: `T <: UpperType`. Lower bound: `T >: LowerType`. View bounds (deprecated): `T <% U`. Context bounds: `[T: TypeClass]`.
Ad-hoc polymorphism via type classes lets you define behavior for types without inheritance. Pattern: trait with type parameter + implicit instances + summon method. Scala 3 uses `given`/`using`.
`Future` represents an asynchronous computation. Use `Future.apply` to start, `map`/`flatMap` to transform, `onComplete` for callbacks. Requires an implicit `ExecutionContext`.
`Promise` completes a Future manually. `Future.sequence` runs multiple futures. `Future.traverse` maps and sequences. `Future.firstCompletedOf` races futures.
`Try[T]` represents a computation that may fail: `Success(t)` or `Failure(e)`. Use `.recover`, `.recoverWith`, `.getOrElse` for fallback logic.
Akka implements the Actor model for distributed concurrency. Actors encapsulate state and communicate via messages. `ActorSystem`, `Props`, and `tell/ask` patterns.
Future combinators: `zip` (pair of results), `foldLeft`/`sequence` (list of futures), `traverse` (map + sequence), `firstCompletedOf` (race), `fallbackTo` (fallback). Use `andThen` for side effects.
`java.util.concurrent.atomic` provides lock-free thread-safe primitives: AtomicInteger, AtomicReference, etc. Scala's `scala.concurrent.util.Unsafe` or Java's Atomic classes for shared mutable state.
sbt (Scala Build Tool) uses `build.sbt` for project config. Key tasks: `compile`, `run`, `test`, `console` (REPL). Dependencies are declared in `libraryDependencies`.
Scala CLI is a modern tool for running Scala scripts and projects without sbt. Supports single-file scripts, multiple files, dependencies with `//> using` directives.
ScalaTest supports multiple styles: `FlatSpec`, `WordSpec`, `FunSuite`. Matchers provide readable assertions. `should`/`must` methods with descriptive failure messages.
The Scala ecosystem includes: Apache Spark (data processing), Akka (actors/streams), http4s/Play (web), Cats/Zio (functional effects), Circe/UPickle (JSON), Doobie/Slick (database).
sbt supports multi-module builds and incremental compilation. Use `subproject` definitions, `dependsOn`, and `aggregate`. sbt's incremental compiler tracks dependencies for minimal recompilation.
Scala 3 uses significant indentation (like Python) as an alternative to braces. `if`, `for`, `match`, class bodies use indentation to define blocks.
Union types (`A | B`) accept either type. Intersection types (`A & B`) require both. Useful for flexible APIs and type-safe composition.
Scala 3's `CanEqual` type class prevents unsafe comparisons. Use `given` to opt-in to equality between types. Catches bugs at compile time.
Extension methods add functionality to existing types without implicit conversions. Defined with `extension` keyword and type parameter.
Scala 3 allows top-level definitions (methods, given, extensions) without wrapping in an object or class. Simplifies scripting and module structure.

Opaque type aliases (Scala 3) create new types at compile time without runtime overhead. `opaque type UserId = Long`. Only the companion object can access the underlying type. Enforces domain constraints.
Export clauses (Scala 3) forward selected members from a given value. Richer than inheritance — you choose exactly what to expose, rename, or exclude.
Scala supports string interpolation with `s` (expressions), `f` (formatting), `raw` (no escaping). Triple quotes """ for multi-line strings with no escaping needed.
Scala numeric types: Byte, Short, Int, Long, Float, Double. Implicit widening works. Conversion methods: `.toInt`, `.toDouble`, `.toLong`. Rich operations via implicit conversions.
Tuple groups values of possibly different types. `(a, b, c)` syntax up to Tuple22. Access with `._1`, `._2`. Destructuring in pattern matching. `Unit` (from `()`) is like `void`.
Scala type hierarchy: `Any` (top), `AnyVal` (primitives), `AnyRef` (objects). `Nothing` (bottom) is subtype of all types. `Null` is subtype of all AnyRef. `null` is dangerous — prefer Option.

Rich String API: `split`, `replaceAll`, `matches`, `stripMargin`, `toInt/toDouble`, `format`, `take/drop`, `slice`, `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `interpolate`. Strings are `java.lang.String` — full Java API available.
`scala.util.matching.Regex` provides pattern matching, find/replace, and extraction. Create with `.r` on strings. Use `findFirstIn`, `findAllIn`, `replaceFirstIn`, `replaceSomeIn`.

StringBuilder for efficient string building in loops. Pre-allocate capacity for performance. String concatenation with `+` creates intermediate strings — avoid in hot paths. Use `mkString` on collections.
Read/write files with `scala.io.Source`, `java.nio.file.Files`, `PrintWriter`. Source reads from files, URLs, and stdin. Java NIO Files provides concise read/write methods.
Java NIO provides non-blocking I/O, channels, buffers, and selectors. `FileChannel` for file transfer, `ByteBuffer` for data, `Selector` for multiplexing. Useful for high-performance I/O.
Serialize data with Java Serialization (binary, fragile), Circe/UPickle (JSON), or Scala Pickling. Circe is the most popular Scala JSON library. UPickle is simpler and faster.
ScalaCheck generates random test inputs. Define properties with `forAll` and generators. Test many edge cases automatically. Combined with ScalaTest for seamless integration.
ScalaMock and Mockito provide mocking for Scala tests. Mock traits/classes to isolate units. ScalaMock generates mocks from traits. Mockito works with Scala with fewer limitations.

Scala collections hierarchy: `Iterable` → `Seq`/`Set`/`Map`. Mutable and immutable versions. `Traversable` deprecated in 2.13. Prefer immutable by default. The 2.13 collections are simplified and more consistent.
Scala uses `java.time` (Java 8+) for date/time. Key classes: `LocalDate`, `LocalTime`, `LocalDateTime`, `ZonedDateTime`, `Instant`, `Duration`, `Period`. Scala no longer has its own date API.
Access JVM system properties (`sys.props`), environment variables (`sys.env`), and process control (`sys.exit`, `sys.addShutdownHook`). `scala.sys.process` for external process execution.

Implicit conversions (Scala 2) auto-convert between types. Used for extending libraries. Scala 3 replaces with `given` conversions. Use sparingly — can cause confusing behavior. Prefer extension methods.

Implicits are resolved using the type at compile time. Search order: local scope, imported scope, companion objects of type and type parameters. The `implicitly[T]` method summons an implicit value of type T.
Context bounds `[T: TypeClass]` desugar to `(using TypeClass[T])`. The type class pattern provides ad-hoc polymorphism. `implicitly[TC[T]]` or `summon[TC[T]]` retrieves the instance.
Use `scala.concurrent.blocking` for blocking operations in ForkJoinPool. Java Flight Recorder (JFR) for profiling. sbt-jmh for microbenchmarks. Measure, don't guess.

JVM memory tuning: -Xms/-Xmx for heap, -XX:NewRatio for young/old gen. G1GC is default. Avoid allocations in hot paths. Use `-XX:+PrintGCDetails` for diagnostics. Scala-specific: avoid boxing with specialized methods.
Java libraries work seamlessly. Use Java collections (convert with `asScala`), Java streams (`asScala`), Optional (`toOption`). Annotations, beans, and functional interfaces are fully compatible.

Call Scala code from Java. Scala objects appear as `ClassName$.MODULE$`. Methods with special chars are mangled. Scala collections need conversion. Case classes get `apply`, `copy`, `toString` methods.

Scala is a functional-first language. Immutability means variables declared with val cannot be reassigned. Pure functions have no side effects — they depend only on inputs and return only outputs. Benefits: easier reasoning, thread safety, testability. Scala encourages immutable data structures in scala.collection.immutable package. Use var sparingly, only when mutation is required for performance. final in Java translates to val in Scala. Pure functions enable referential transparency — any expression can be replaced with its value without changing program behavior.

Higher-order functions take functions as parameters or return functions. This is central to functional programming. Common higher-order functions on collections: map (transform each element), filter (keep matching elements), flatMap (map then flatten), foldLeft/foldRight (accumulate), reduce (combine without initial value). Anonymous functions (lambdas) use concise syntax: (x: Int) => x * 2. Placeholder syntax _ shortens common patterns: list.map(_ * 2). Method eta-expansion converts methods to functions: val f = add _.
.Functional Programming Deep Dive.Pattern Matching & Case Classes[0]

Pattern matching is Scala's powerful replacement for switch statements. Match against values, types, case class extractors, sequences, tuples, and custom extractors. Patterns can be: literal, variable, constructor, sequence, tuple, type test, and regex. Guards with if add conditions. Patterns are checked for exhaustiveness at compile time. Case classes automatically provide unapply methods for pattern matching, copy, equals, hashCode, and toString. Sealed hierarchies enable exhaustive matching.

A monad is a design pattern that provides a way to sequence computations. In Scala, common monads include Option, Either, Try, Future, and List. For-comprehensions provide syntactic sugar for chaining monadic operations: for (x <- expr1; y <- expr2) yield (x, y) desugars to expr1.flatMap(x => expr2.map(y => (x, y))). Monads must satisfy three laws: left identity, right identity, and associativity. In practice, monads enable safe error handling (Option/Either), asynchronous programming (Future), and collection operations.

Type classes in Scala provide ad-hoc polymorphism — the ability to add behavior to existing types without modifying them. A type class is defined as a trait with type parameters. Implicit parameters and implicit conversions provide the mechanism for type class dispatch. The implicit keyword marks parameters that are automatically filled by the compiler. Scala 3 (Dotty) uses given/using instead of implicits. Common type classes: Ordering, Numeric, JsonWriter, Show, Eq. Context bounds [T: Ordering] are syntactic sugar for implicit parameters.

Variance describes how generic types relate to subtype relationships. List[+T] is covariant: if Dog extends Animal, then List[Dog] is a subtype of List[Animal]. Contravariant[-T]: if Dog extends Animal, then Printer[Animal] is a subtype of Printer[Dog]. Invariant[T]: no relationship. Use covariance for immutable collections (producers), contravariance for consumers (functions), invariance for mutable data. The Liskov Substitution Principle guides variance: if a type can be used where a parent type is expected, it should be covariant. The compiler checks variance annotations for type safety.

Scala's type system supports advanced constructs: path-dependent types distinguish types based on instance paths. Dependent method types allow return types to depend on value parameters. Higher-kinded types abstract over type constructors (trait Functor[F[_]]). Existential types (deprecated in Scala 3) abstract over type parameters. Union types (Scala 3): Int | String. Intersection types (Scala 3): A & B. Match types (Scala 3): type-level computation. Opaque types (Scala 3): zero-cost type abstractions without runtime overhead.
spring.json: Introduction to Spring and its ecosystem.

Spring is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications. Spring Boot simplifies Spring development with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter dependencies. Key modules: Spring Core (DI/IoC), Spring MVC (web), Spring Data (databases), Spring Security (auth), Spring Cloud (microservices). Spring Boot's opinionated defaults reduce boilerplate while remaining configurable. Convention over configuration with auto-configuration classes. Starter POMs bundle related dependencies.

Spring Boot projects follow a layered architecture. Typical structure: controller (REST endpoints), service (business logic), repository (data access), model/entity (domain objects), dto (data transfer objects), config (configuration classes), exception (custom exceptions), util (utilities). Resources folder contains application.yml, static files, and templates. The @SpringBootApplication main class is typically at the root package. Package structure by feature or by layer.

Spring Boot externalizes configuration via application.properties or application.yml. YAML is more readable for hierarchical config. Profile-specific files: application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml. Active profiles via spring.profiles.active. Custom properties with @ConfigurationProperties (type-safe). @Value for simple injection. Environment variables override properties. Random values with ${random.int}. Command-line args override file properties. Spring Cloud Config for centralized config.
Working with data and APIs in Spring.

Spring Boot provides comprehensive testing support. @SpringBootTest for integration tests. @WebMvcTest for controller layer (loads only web beans). @DataJpaTest for repository layer (in-memory DB). @MockBean for mocking dependencies. TestRestTemplate or MockMvc for HTTP testing. @TestContainers for real database integration tests. AssertJ for fluent assertions. Test slices reduce startup time by loading only relevant beans.

Inversion of Control (IoC) is Spring's core - the container manages object creation and wiring. Annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController register beans. @Autowired injects dependencies (by type). @Primary resolves conflicts when multiple beans of same type. @Qualifier specifies exact bean. @Bean for explicit declaration in @Configuration classes. @Scope controls bean lifecycle (singleton, prototype, request, session). @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy for lifecycle callbacks.

@RestController combines @Controller + @ResponseBody for REST APIs. Request mapping annotations: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping. Extract data with: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @RequestHeader. @Valid for request validation. ResponseEntity for full HTTP response control. @ExceptionHandler for controller-level exception handling. @InitBinder for custom data binding.

Global exception handling with @ControllerAdvice. @ExceptionHandler for specific exceptions. Custom error response DTO for consistent API errors. HTTP status code mapping: 400 (bad request), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict), 500 (internal error). Field-level validation errors with MethodArgumentNotValidException. ResponseEntityExceptionHandler provides default Spring exceptions.

Spring Data JPA simplifies database access. Entities are POJOs with @Entity annotation. @Table customizes table name. @Id + @GeneratedValue for primary keys. @Column for column customization. Relationships: @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany. @JoinColumn for foreign key. Cascade types: ALL, PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE. Fetch types: LAZY (default for collections), EAGER. @Embeddable for value objects. @Enumerated for enums. @PrePersist/@PreUpdate for lifecycle callbacks.

Spring Data JPA generates implementations at runtime. Extend JpaRepository<T, ID> for full CRUD. Custom query methods via method naming: findBy, findByFieldNameContaining, findByFieldNameBetween, countBy, existsBy. @Query for custom JPQL/SQL. @Modifying + @Transactional for update/delete. Specifications for dynamic queries. Projections for partial data. @EntityGraph for eager fetching. Pageable for pagination.

Spring Boot makes building REST APIs straightforward. Use @RestController with request mappings. Content negotiation via produces/consumes. HATEOAS with links for discoverability. Versioning via URL, header, or content type. CORS with @CrossOrigin or global config. HTTP method support: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove). @Valid for request body validation. DTOs to decouple API from entities.

Springdoc OpenAPI generates API documentation automatically. Add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui dependency. Access at /swagger-ui.html and /v3/api-docs. Customize with @OpenAPIDefinition, @Info, @Tag, @Operation, @ApiResponse. Group APIs with GroupedOpenApi. Spring Boot 3.x uses springdoc v2. Configuration via application.yml. OAuth2 security scheme definition. Request/response examples with @Schema.

Spring Security provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common attacks. Add spring-boot-starter-security dependency. Core concepts: SecurityFilterChain (filter pipeline), AuthenticationManager (auth processing), UserDetailsService (user lookup), PasswordEncoder (password hashing). @EnableMethodSecurity for method-level security with @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured. CSRF protection (enabled by default for non-REST, disable for REST APIs with stateless JWT). CORS, headers, and exception handling configured in SecurityFilterChain bean.

JWT (JSON Web Token) is commonly used for stateless REST API authentication. Flow: User logs in with credentials, server validates and returns JWT token, client sends token in Authorization header on subsequent requests, server validates token on each request. Use io.jsonwebtoken (jjwt) library. JWT contains claims (sub, iat, exp, roles). Access tokens (short-lived) and refresh tokens (long-lived) pattern. Blacklist for token revocation.

Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready monitoring and management endpoints. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency. Key endpoints: /health (app health), /info (app info), /metrics (metrics), /env (environment), /loggers (logging levels), /httptrace (HTTP trace), /beans (all beans), /mappings (route mappings). Custom health indicators, metrics with Micrometer, and info contributors. Expose via HTTP or JMX. Integrate with Prometheus/Grafana for monitoring.

Spring profiles activate different configurations per environment. Use @Profile on beans or profile-specific YAML/properties files. Set active profiles via spring.profiles.active. Logging with Logback (default). Configure levels per package: logging.level.com.example=DEBUG. Logback-spring.xml for advanced config. Logstash encoder for JSON logging (ELK stack). Distributed tracing with Micrometer Tracing + Zipkin. Structured logging for better observability.

Spring Cloud provides tools for building microservices. Service discovery with Netflix Eureka or Consul. API Gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway. Load balancing with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer. Circuit breakers with Resilience4j. Distributed configuration with Spring Cloud Config. Distributed tracing with Micrometer + Zipkin. Event-driven communication with Spring Cloud Stream. Feign/WebClient for inter-service HTTP calls. Centralized logging with ELK stack.

Spring WebFlux provides reactive programming support for non-blocking, event-driven applications. Built on Project Reactor (Mono and Flux types). Reactive MongoDB, Cassandra, R2DBC for databases. WebClient for non-blocking HTTP calls. Reactive WebSockets. Functional endpoints with RouterFunctions. Backpressure handling. Better scalability for I/O-bound applications with fewer threads. Netty is the default embedded server for WebFlux.
sqlite.json: SQLite is a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration SQL database engine. It's the most widely deployed database in the world — embedded in browsers, phones, IoT devices. The entire database is a single file. No separate server process needed.
SQLite comes pre-installed on macOS and most Linux distros. On Windows, download from sqlite.org. Or use a package manager: apt, brew, or compile from source. The sqlite3 CLI tool is all you need.
The sqlite3 CLI is the main interface. Dot-commands start with . (not SQL). Key commands: .tables, .schema, .databases, .import, .output, .mode, .dump, .quit. SQL statements end with ;.

SQLite uses dynamic typing: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB. Type affinity (flexible): INTEGER affinity for whole numbers, REAL for floats, TEXT for strings, BLOB for binary. BOOLEAN stored as INTEGER 0/1. No separate DATE type — use TEXT, INTEGER (Unix), or REAL (Julian).

No concurrent writes (single writer, shared lock). No user management/authentication. 64-bit ROWID limit (~9 quintillion rows). 140TB max DB size (pragma page_size * max_pages). Limited ALTER TABLE (DROP COLUMN was added in 3.35, but no MODIFY COLUMN).

SQLite has full ACID transactions. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT for nested transactions (savepoints). IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE transaction types control locking. WAL mode allows concurrent reads during a write.

Views: saved queries acting as virtual tables. CREATE VIEW, DROP VIEW. Triggers: automatic SQL execution on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. BEFORE/AFTER and INSTEAD OF (for views). FOR EACH ROW (only option — no FOR EACH STATEMENT).

CREATE INDEX speeds up queries. Types: single-column, composite, UNIQUE, partial (WHERE clause), DESC. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows query execution. ANALYZE collects statistics for better query planning. Use WHERE clause indexes.
SQLite's FTS5 extension provides full-text search. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE using fts5. MATCH for searching. Supports stemming, ranking (bm25), prefix queries, and content tables (external content).

SQLite has JSON functions: json_extract, json_set, json_remove, json_array, json_object, json_each (table function), json_type. The -> and ->> operators work like MySQL. Use json_valid to check JSON validity.

WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) allows concurrent readers during a write. PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL. Better performance for many reads + occasional writes. Checkpoint moves WAL content to main DB. PRAGMA synchronous controls durability vs speed.

VACUUM rebuilds the database file, reclaiming space and defragmenting. AUTO_VACUUM is incremental but less effective. PRAGMA auto_vacuum = 1 enables incremental vacuum. PRAGMA integrity_check verifies database health.

CREATE TABLE defines a table. Column constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK. SQLite auto-creates INTEGER PRIMARY KEY as ROWID alias (auto-increment). WITHOUT ROWID tables use the PRIMARY KEY as the B-tree key.

SQLite supports limited ALTER TABLE: RENAME TABLE, RENAME COLUMN (3.25+), ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN (3.35+). Cannot MODIFY, ALTER, or ADD CONSTRAINT after creation. Workaround: create new table, copy data, drop old, rename.
DROP TABLE removes the table entirely. SQLite has no TRUNCATE TABLE — use DELETE FROM without WHERE. For large tables, DROP and recreate with same schema, or use DELETE and VACUUM to reclaim space.

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON enables FK enforcement (off by default!). Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY. ON DELETE/UPDATE: CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT, NO ACTION.
SELECT retrieves rows. Support for WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING. SQLite's LIMIT/OFFSET syntax is standard. Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to check optimization.

INSERT adds rows. Standard VALUES syntax. Multi-row INSERT supported (3.20+). INSERT OR REPLACE / INSERT OR ROLLBACK / INSERT OR ABORT / INSERT OR FAIL / INSERT OR IGNORE for conflict handling. last_insert_rowid() returns the auto-generated id.
UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports UPDATE FROM (joins in UPDATE) since 3.33. No LIMIT in UPDATE — use a subquery or WHERE with ROWID.
DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports DELETE FROM JOIN USING (since 3.35) and RETURNING clause (3.35+) to return deleted rows.
Standard WHERE operators: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, GLOB, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL. LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII. GLOB uses Unix wildcards (*, ?). Combine with AND, OR.

ORDER BY sorts results. NULLs sort first by default (change with NULLS FIRST/LAST). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET for pagination. For efficient pagination, use WHERE on indexed column instead of OFFSET.
SQLite has practical string functions: || for concatenation, LENGTH, UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTR, REPLACE, TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM, INSTR (find substring), LIKE/GLOB, || for concatenation. No CONCAT() — use ||.

SQLite has no date/time storage type. Use TEXT (ISO-8601), INTEGER (Unix timestamp), or REAL (Julian day). Functions: date(), time(), datetime(), strftime(), julianday(). strftime uses C-style format strings.

IIF(condition, true_val, false_val) — ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END for multi-way. IFNULL(val, default) replaces NULL. COALESCE returns first non-null. Math: ABS, ROUND, RANDOM, TOTAL, AVG, COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX.
Python's sqlite3 module is part of the standard library. No external dependencies. Connection, cursor, execute, commit, close pattern. Use ? placeholders for parameterized queries (never f-strings!).
Use better-sqlite3 (synchronous, fast) or sql.js (WASM, browser-compatible). better-sqlite3: prepare, run, get, all, iterate. No async — synchronous is fine for SQLite's speed.
Use mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO) or modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go). Standard database/sql interface. Placeholder: ?. WAL mode for concurrency.
sql.js compiles SQLite to WebAssembly for in-browser use. Also: OPFS (Origin Private File System) with SQLite WASM builds from sqlite.org. Great for offline-first apps, demos, and tools.
The sqlite3 CLI is powerful: .mode for output (column, csv, json, html), .headers on/off, .output file, .import for CSV loading, .dump for backup, .read for script execution, .timer for timing.

Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them like GROUP BY. ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique number, RANK() allows ties with gaps, DENSE_RANK() allows ties without gaps. LEAD() accesses the next row's value, LAG() accesses the previous row's value. OVER() defines the window; PARTITION BY splits into groups, ORDER BY orders within each group. SQLite has supported window functions since version 3.25. A common mistake is forgetting ORDER BY inside OVER for functions that depend on order (like ROW_NUMBER).

CTEs (Common Table Expressions) use WITH to define a named subquery that can be referenced multiple times. WITH RECURSIVE allows self-referencing CTEs for traversing hierarchical or graph data. The recursive CTE has two parts: the anchor (initial rows, no recursion) and the recursive member (references the CTE itself). Must use UNION ALL. SQLite limits recursion depth with PRAGMA recursive_triggers and an internal max depth of 1000 (configurable). Common mistake: forgetting the UNION ALL between anchor and recursive members.

FTS5 is SQLite's full-text search extension. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE USING fts5 creates the search index. MATCH performs the search. Supports prefix queries (*), phrase queries ("in double quotes"), and NEAR proximity searches. The bm25() function ranks results. FTS5 can use an external content table (content=) to avoid duplicating data. Use snippet() to get highlighted excerpts. Common mistake: forgetting that FTS5 is an extension that may not be available in all builds (check with PRAGMA compile_options).

Triggers in SQLite run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. BEFORE and AFTER control timing. INSTEAD OF triggers are used on views (since views aren't directly updatable). FOR EACH ROW is the only option (no FOR EACH STATEMENT). OLD.column and NEW.column access row values. Use RAISE(ABORT, 'message') to cancel an operation. Common mistake: triggers that recursively fire (Table A trigger updates Table A, firing the trigger again) — SQLite stops at recursion depth limit.

Views encapsulate complex queries as virtual tables. Indexes speed up lookups at the cost of write speed. Partial indexes index only rows matching a WHERE condition — saves space and improves speed for filtered queries. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether indexes are being used. The WITH clause can be used inside views. Common mistake: assuming a view with ORDER BY guarantees order (it doesn't — wrap in SELECT ... FROM (view) ORDER BY). Always use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to verify index usage.

SQLite has two journaling modes: DELETE (default) and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging). DELETE mode: changes go to a rollback journal, readers and writers block each other. WAL mode: changes are appended to a separate WAL file, readers can read the old DB while a write is in progress — much better concurrency. Checkpoints merge the WAL into the main DB (automatic or manual). WAL is faster for most workloads. Trade-off: WAL requires more file descriptors and is slightly worse for very large transactions. PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL is safe with WAL and faster than FULL. Common mistake: not setting WAL mode in applications with concurrent reads.

SQLite has robust JSON support since 3.9.0. json_extract() extracts values, json_set() updates values, json_remove() deletes keys. The -> and ->> operators (3.38+) provide shorthand: -> returns JSON, ->> returns SQL text/integer/real. json_each() expands a JSON array into rows (table function). json_group_array() aggregates values into a JSON array. json_group_object() aggregates into a JSON object. Common mistake: assuming JSON values in TEXT columns are validated — SQLite does not validate JSON on insert unless you use a CHECK(json_valid(data)) constraint.
svelte.json: Introduction to Svelte and its ecosystem.

Svelte's reactivity is compiler-driven: assignments to variables automatically trigger DOM updates without a virtual DOM or manual state management. The compiler instruments variable assignments to invalidate dependencies.

Svelte templates extend HTML with {expression} bindings, {#if} blocks, {#each} loops, and {#await} for promises. The template syntax is concise and compiles to highly optimized imperative DOM operations.
Svelte provides logic blocks ({#if}, {:else if}, {:else}) and loops ({#each}, {:else}) within templates. Loops support destructuring and index tracking without special directives.
Working with data and APIs in Svelte.
Vitest integrates seamlessly with SvelteKit projects for fast unit and integration testing with Vite-powered HMR, Jest-compatible API, and native ESM support.
Playwright is the recommended E2E testing framework for SvelteKit, providing cross-browser automation, network interception, and component testing across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.
Props in Svelte are declared with the export keyword inside a component script, allowing parent components to pass data. Props can have default values and are reactive when reassigned.
Slots allow parent components to inject content into a child's layout. Named slots and slot props enable flexible component composition and scoped content distribution.
Svelte uses the createEventDispatcher helper to forward custom events from child to parent components. DOM events are bound directly with on: directives like on:click.
Writable stores are the most basic store type, providing set, update, and subscribe methods. They allow cross-component state sharing without prop drilling and auto-subscribe in Svelte templates.
Derived stores compute values from one or more dependent stores, updating automatically when their sources change. They support transformations and can produce derived writable stores.
Custom stores encapsulate logic by wrapping the store primitives and exposing a controlled API. They hide implementation details while providing the same subscribe contract for template binding.
onMount is the most commonly used lifecycle function, executing after the component is first rendered. It's ideal for data fetching, DOM measurements, and cleanup via returned teardown functions.
beforeUpdate runs before the DOM is updated after state changes, making it useful for reading the DOM before Svelte patches it. It's the counterpart to afterUpdate.
afterUpdate runs after the DOM has been updated following state changes, suitable for DOM measurements or scrolling to newly rendered elements. It fires after every component update.
onDestroy registers a callback that runs when a component is unmounted, making it the right place for cleanup like clearing timers, unsubscribing from stores, or canceling network requests.
Tweened stores smoothly interpolate numeric values over time, creating animated transitions between states. They support configurable easing functions and interpolation durations.
Spring stores simulate physics-based animations using stiffness, damping, and mass parameters. They create natural-feeling motion that responds dynamically to changing target values.

Svelte's built-in transitions (fade, slide, scale, fly) and custom transition functions provide declarative enter/exit animations. They work with the transition: directive and support in/out modifiers.
Svelte's animate: directive enables FLIP-based animations for list reordering, automatically calculating position changes and animating elements to their new positions smoothly.

Actions are Svelte's approach to integrating with DOM elements imperatively, similar to use:action. They receive the element and optional parameters, returning lifecycle methods like destroy for cleanup.
The context API allows passing data to a component and all its descendants without prop drilling. setContext and getContext are scoped to the component tree, not globally like stores.
Svelte provides special elements like <svelte:body>, <svelte:head>, <svelte:window>, and <svelte:options> for declaring side effects and configuration directly in templates.
SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where each +page.svelte file in src/routes creates a route. Dynamic parameters are captured with [bracket] notation in directory names.
Endpoints are server-only API routes defined as +server.js files exporting request handlers. They handle GET, POST, PUT, DELETE requests and return JSON or other responses.
SvelteKit renders pages server-side by default, generating HTML on the server for fast initial loads and SEO. SSR can be disabled per route or globally for fully client-rendered apps.

Svelte 5 introduces runes — explicit reactive primitives that replace the Svelte 4 let / export let / $: magic. $state() creates reactive state. $derived() creates derived values that update automatically. $effect() runs side effects when tracked dependencies change. $props() explicitly declares component props. Runes work both in .svelte files and .svelte.js/.svelte.ts modules, enabling shared reactive logic outside components. $bindable() creates two-way bindable props. Runes make reactivity explicit and TypeScript-friendly.

Svelte 5 introduces snippets ({#snippet}) for reusable template fragments, replacing slots in many cases. Event handlers use callbacks (onclick={handler}) instead of on:click. Event modifiers are attached with function calls. Cross-component state uses runes in .svelte.ts files. onMount/onDestroy lifecycle functions are now imported. bind:value works with $bindable() for two-way bindings. class and style attributes support objects and arrays.
Snippets are reusable template fragments defined with {#snippet name} and rendered with {@render name}. They accept parameters and can be passed between components as first-class template values.
Snippets passed as props allow parent components to inject template content into children, replacing slot-based composition with a more explicit and type-safe pattern.
The implicit children snippet captures default content between component tags. It provides a cleaner alternative to the default slot for wrapping content in layout components.
sveltekit.json: Introduction to Sveltekit and its ecosystem.
Create a new SvelteKit project with the CLI, choosing from demo app, skeleton project, or minimal setup. The project includes Vite, TypeScript, ESLint, and Prettier out of the box.
SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where files in src/routes map to URL paths. +page.svelte files define pages, +layout.svelte wraps nested routes, and dynamic params use [bracket] directories.
Layout components wrap child routes with shared UI like headers and footers. Nested layouts inherit from parent layouts, and +layout.js can run data loading for an entire route segment.
Working with data and APIs in Sveltekit.
Adapters configure SvelteKit for deployment on various platforms by transforming the build output. Each adapter optimizes for the target platform's capabilities and constraints.
The Vercel adapter deploys SvelteKit apps to Vercel's serverless edge network with automatic CDN caching, ISR, and serverless function support for dynamic routes.
The Netlify adapter deploys to Netlify's platform with serverless functions, split testing, and form handling. It supports on-demand builders for incremental static regeneration.
The Node adapter creates a standalone Node.js server for traditional hosting environments. It produces a single output with middleware support, ready for PM2 or Docker deployment.
The load function runs before a page or layout renders, fetching data on the server during SSR and on the client during client-side navigation. It returns data passed to the page as $page.data.
Page data from load is available in +page.svelte via $page.data. Data is typed automatically when using TypeScript, and re-fetched reactively when load dependencies change via depends().
Layout load functions in +layout.js combine data for all child routes using merge strategies, accessible from any child page or layout. This is ideal for fetching shared resources like user profiles.
GET handlers in +server.js return data from the server, typically JSON. They receive request event with params, url, fetch, and locals, making them ideal for API routes.
POST handlers accept request bodies for creating resources, validating input, and returning appropriate status codes. They're used for REST APIs and can handle multipart uploads.
API routes in SvelteKit are server-only endpoints defined alongside pages, sharing the same filesystem routing. They can use server-side secrets and databases without exposing them to the client.
Form actions handle POST form submissions with progressive enhancement, running on the server to mutate data and return validation errors or success responses without JavaScript required.
SvelteKit supports SSR (default), prerendering (SSG), and CSR modes configurable per route or globally. SSR renders on the server on each request, SSG pre-builds static HTML at build time.
Prerendering generates static HTML files at build time for routes that don't need server data, suitable for marketing pages and blogs. Prerendered routes can be served from CDN with zero server cost.
Client-side rendering skips server rendering entirely, loading the page as a shell and fetching data on the client. Useful for authenticated dashboard pages or apps that need minimal server load.

SvelteKit sessions can be managed with cookies, JWTs, or server-side stores accessible via the event.locals object in hooks. Authentication libraries like Lucia or Auth.js integrate seamlessly with the hooks pattern.
SvelteKit provides a cookies API in server contexts for reading, setting, and deleting cookies with configurable options for path, maxAge, secure, httpOnly, and sameSite.

OAuth authentication flows are handled server-side using endpoints or form actions, redirecting users to providers and exchanging authorization codes for tokens. Libraries like Lucia provide OAuth adapters.
Hooks are server-side middleware that intercept every request in handle, or module-level functions like handleError and handleFetch. They enable session management, redirects, and error tracking.

Params matchers validate and transform dynamic route parameters before load runs, preventing invalid requests from reaching data loading logic. Built-in matchers include int, uuid, and custom matchers.
SvelteKit provides structured error handling with error/is-error utility, custom error pages (+error.svelte), and the handleError hook for logging and monitoring integration.
SvelteKit integrates with the View Transition API for smooth page transitions on client-side navigation. The onNavigate lifecycle runs before navigation, enabling transition setup.
Cross-document view transitions work across full page loads by defining @view-transition CSS rules. SvelteKit handles the JavaScript enhancement for seamless cross-page animations.
Individual elements can have their own view-transition-name for independent animation. Paired with the View Transition API, elements morph smoothly between pages without layout shifts.
$env/static/private provides build-time environment variables accessible only on the server. These are inlined at build time and reserved for secrets like API keys and database URLs.
$env/static/public exposes build-time environment variables prefixed with PUBLIC_ to both client and server code. These are safe for the browser and inlined during build.
$env/dynamic/private and $env/dynamic/public load environment variables at runtime instead of build time. Dynamic env vars are useful when the same build deploys to multiple environments.
Link options control prefetching behavior. data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover" starts loading data when the user hovers over a link, reducing perceived navigation time.
data-sveltekit-reload forces a full page navigation instead of client-side routing, useful when the target page uses different global CSS or needs a clean JavaScript context.
data-sveltekit-keepfocus preserves the currently focused element across navigation, improving accessibility for keyboard users on single-page applications.

SvelteKit form actions handle form submissions without JavaScript. Forms use method="POST" (or PUT/DELETE) and the use:enhance action for progressive enhancement. Server-side load functions receive form data via request.formData(). Actions return {success: true} or {error: string}. use:enhance gracefully upgrades to JS: forms work without JS (full page reload) and enhance with JS (AJAX, loading states). superforms library adds validation. fail() function returns validation errors with preserved form data.

SvelteKit provides powerful data loading: load functions run on server for initial renders and client for navigation. +page.server.ts runs only on server, +page.ts runs on both. +layout.server.ts loads data for all child routes. invalidate() and invalidateAll() re-run load functions. invalid and depends control cache invalidation. Stream promises in load functions for progressive rendering. entries function generates static pages at build time (SSG). HTTP caching headers (Cache-Control, ETag) can be set in load functions.
swift.json: Variables and data types in Swift.
Errors are thrown with `throw` from `Error` conforming types. `try` calls throwing functions. `do/catch` handles errors. Catch specific cases before generic. `defer` runs cleanup on scope exit.
`try?` converts throwing expressions to optional (nil on error). `try!` disables error propagation, crashing on failure. Use `try?` for optional handling, `try!` only when guaranteed.
`Result<Success, Failure>` captures either a success value or error as a value. Useful for async callbacks, composeable error handling, and mapping over errors.
Properties can throw errors by delegating to throwing functions in their getter. Computed properties marked with `get throws` (Swift 5.9+).
Subscripts can throw errors (Swift 5.9+). Access elements with `try` when the subscript can fail. Useful for safe collection access beyond bounds.
`rethrows` indicates a function only throws if its closure parameter throws. The function itself never throws directly. Enables higher-order functions that preserve throw behavior.
`defer` schedules code to execute when the current scope exits, regardless of errors or early returns. Multiple defers execute in reverse order (stack-like).
Custom error types conform to the `Error` protocol (or `Swift.LocalizedError`). Use enums with associated values for structured error information.
Input and output operations in Swift.

Swift is Apple's modern programming language for iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and beyond. It combines the performance of compiled languages with the expressiveness of scripting languages. Open-sourced in 2015.
Swift uses `var` for mutable variables, `let` for constants. No semicolons needed. Parentheses around conditions are optional. Braces are required for all control flow.
`let` declares constants (immutable binding). `var` declares variables (mutable). Type inference is common, but types can be annotated explicitly. Swift is type-safe with no implicit conversions.
Swift's fundamental types: Int, Double, Float, Bool, String, Character. Collection types: Array, Set, Dictionary. All types are strongly inferred and strictly checked at compile time.
Xcode is the official IDE for Swift development. Playgrounds provide interactive coding environments with live results, timeline views, and inline visualization of values.
Swift evolves rapidly. Swift 5.9 introduced macros and parameter packs. Swift 5.10 completed actor isolation. Swift 6 enhances concurrency safety and enables strict concurrency checking by default.
Swift has an interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop) for quick experimentation. `swift format` auto-formats code. `swiftc` compiles directly. Run with `swift` in terminal.
Swift infers types from literal values and expressions. The compiler deduces the type without explicit annotations. Inference works across function returns, closures, and complex expressions.
Swift is a type-safe language. Every value has a known type at compile time. Type mismatches produce compiler errors, preventing runtime type errors. No implicit type conversions.
Tuples group multiple values into a single compound value. Values can be accessed by position (.0, .1) or by name. Tuples are value types useful for returning multiple values.
`typealias` creates an alternative name for an existing type. Improves code readability and abstracts complex types like closures or generic types.
Swift offers Int (signed), UInt (unsigned), Int8/16/32/64, Float (32-bit), Double (64-bit), and CGFloat. Use `.random(in:)` for randomization. Overflow trapping prevents silent truncation.
Bool has `true` and `false`. Character is a single Unicode grapheme cluster. `String` is a collection of Characters. Use toggle() to flip a Bool value.
`Any` can represent any type (including functions and optionals). `AnyObject` represents any class instance. Avoid using these in favor of generics and protocol types for type safety.
`if` and `else` work as expected. Conditions must be Bool expressions (no truthiness). Swift supports `if let` for optional binding and `if case` for pattern matching.
`switch` supports pattern matching, ranges, tuples, value binding, and where clauses. No implicit fallthrough — use `fallthrough` explicitly. Must be exhaustive with `default` or all cases covered.
`for-in` iterates over sequences, ranges, and collections. `while` loops on a condition. `repeat-while` guarantees at least one execution. Use `break` and `continue` for flow control.
`if case` pattern-matches without a full switch. `guard let` unwraps optionals with early exit, reducing nested `if-let` blocks. `guard` must transfer control (return, break, throw).
`for where` filters loop iterations inline. Combines iteration with condition without nesting an `if` inside the loop body.
Labels identify loops and switch statements for precise `break` and `continue` control. Useful for breaking out of nested loops.
`#available` checks API availability at runtime. `@available` marks declarations with minimum platform versions. Guard against using unavailable APIs on older OS versions.
`#warning` emits a compiler warning. `#error` emits a compiler error, preventing compilation. Useful for TODOs, reminders, and blocking incomplete code from shipping.
Functions use `func` keyword. Parameters have argument labels (external) and parameter names (internal). `_` omits the external label. Return type with `->`. Functions are first-class types.
Closures are anonymous function literals. Syntax: `{ (params) -> ReturnType in body }`. Trailing closure syntax omits parameter labels. Shorthand: `$0`, `$1`. Closures capture surrounding context.
`inout` parameters allow functions to modify variables passed as arguments. Use `&` prefix when calling. The parameter is copied-in, modified, and copied-out (copy-in copy-out).
`@discardableResult` suppresses the unused-result compiler warning. Use when a function performs work through side effects and the result is optional to consume.
`@autoclosure` wraps an expression in a closure automatically, delaying evaluation until called. Useful for short-circuiting, lazy evaluation, and assertion-style APIs.
Custom types can implement operators as static functions. Precedence groups define evaluation order. Define both prefix/postfix/infix and assignment variants.
Variadic parameters accept zero or more values of the same type. Use `...` after the type. Inside the function, the parameter is an array. Only one variadic per function.
Functions can be defined inside other functions. Nested functions capture variables from the enclosing scope (closures). Useful for helper logic that is only relevant within a single function.
Optionals represent values that may be nil. `Type?` is syntactic sugar for `Optional<T>`. Unwrap with `!` (force), `if let`, `guard let`, or nil-coalescing `??`.
Optional chaining (`?.`) safely accesses properties and methods on optional values. Returns nil if any link in the chain is nil. Can be chained multiple levels deep.
Optionals conform to map/flatMap. `map` transforms an optional's value if non-nil, preserving nil. `flatMap` flattens nested optionals. Chains transformations without unwrapping.
IUOs (`Type!`) automatically force-unwrap when accessed. Used for properties that start nil but are set before use (e.g., IBOutlets). Safer to use regular optionals in new code.
`??` unwraps an optional with a default value. `??` can chain multiple fallbacks. Combine with ternary and `?:` for concise optional handling.
Optionals integrate with switch-case pattern matching. Match `.some` and `.none` directly, or use optional pattern `let x?`. Works with `if case` and `for case`.

Optional chaining (`?.`) short-circuits if nil. Can chain multiple levels: `person?.address?.city`. Returns optional at each level. Use `!` only when guaranteed non-nil. `??` nil-coalescing provides default. Combine with map/flatMap on optionals for functional transformations. Multiple optional binding: `if let a = x, let b = y { }`. Optional pattern matching in switch.
Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Type-safe and grow dynamically. Methods: append, insert, remove, map, filter, reduce, sort, forEach, first, last.
Unordered collections of unique values. `Set<Element>`. Efficient membership testing with `contains`. Set operations: union, intersection, subtracting, symmetricDifference.
Key-value collections with hashable keys. `[Key: Value]`. Access and modify with subscript. `updateValue(_:forKey:)` returns optional old value. Use `default` subscript for safe access.
Array slices are lightweight views into portions of an array. They share memory with the original. Use Array(slice) to create a new array. Preserves indices of the original.
`lazy` defers computation until elements are accessed. Avoids creating intermediate arrays. Chain multiple transformations efficiently with lazy evaluation.
`allSatisfy` checks if every element meets a condition. `contains(where:)` checks if any element matches. `first(where:)` finds the first match.
`reduce(into:)` accumulates into a mutable result (usually a collection). More efficient than `reduce` for building arrays/dictionaries since it avoids copying.
`zip(_:_:)` pairs elements from two sequences into tuples (stops at shortest). `sequence(first:next:)` and `sequence(state:next:)` generate infinite/lazy sequences.
Structs are value types. They receive automatic memberwise initializers. Properties can have observers (willSet, didSet). Mutating methods can modify self. Copy on write for performance.
Classes are reference types. Support inheritance, deinitializers, and multiple references to the same instance. ARC manages memory. Use `===` for identity comparison.
Stored properties hold values. Computed properties calculate on access. Property observers willSet/didSet watch changes. lazy properties initialize on first access.
Value types cannot modify their properties in methods by default. Mark methods `mutating` to allow self-modification. Mutating methods can reassign self entirely.
Types can have static subscripts, enabling type-level subscript access. Useful for registry patterns, default values, and lookup tables.
Classes support single inheritance. Override methods with `override` keyword. `final` prevents overriding. `super` accesses parent. `required` init ensures subclasses implement it.
`convenience init` calls another init (delegating). `required init` forces subclasses to implement it. `failable init?` returns nil. `designated init` is the primary initializer.
`@objc` exposes Swift declarations to Objective-C runtime. Required for target-action patterns, KVO, and some UIKit APIs. `dynamic` enables method swizzling via ObjC dispatch.
Protocols define blueprints of methods, properties, and requirements. Structs, classes, and enums can adopt protocols. Protocols can have default implementations via extensions.
Extensions add functionality to existing types. Add computed properties, methods, initializers, subscripts, and protocol conformance. Cannot override existing or add stored properties.
Protocol composition combines multiple protocols into a single requirement using `&`. A type must conform to all composed protocols. Use with type annotations and generic constraints.
Associated types (`associatedtype`) define placeholder types within protocols. Concrete types are resolved by the conforming type. Use `where` clauses for additional constraints.
Types can conform to protocols only under certain conditions using `extension: where`. Enables powerful composability like Array: Equatable only when Element: Equatable.
`some` keyword hides the concrete return type while preserving protocol conformance. The compiler knows the concrete type. Enables abstraction without generics at the call site.
`any` keyword creates an existential box for protocol types. Unlike `some` (opaque), `any` can hold any conforming type at runtime with a performance cost of the existential container.
Protocol extensions provide default method implementations. Conforming types can override or use the default. Combine with constrained extensions for conditional defaults.
Enums define a common type for a group of related values. Can have methods, computed properties, and initializers. Cases are first-class values.
Enum cases can carry associated values of any type. Each case can have different associated types. Enables tagged unions and the Result pattern.
`indirect` enables recursive enums where a case references the enum itself. Required for recursive data structures like lists and trees. Mark individual cases or the whole enum.
`CaseIterable` protocol auto-generates an array of all enum cases. Access via `AllCases`. Works for enums without associated values. Useful for menus, pickers, and iteration.
`@unknown default` handles future enum cases without breaking exhaustive switches. The compiler warns if all known cases are not covered. Use alongside explicit cases.
Enums can have raw values of String, Character, Int, or floating-point types. Raw values are unique per case. Auto-increment for Int if unspecified. Access with `.rawValue`.
Generic functions work with any type. Type parameters (`<T>`) represent placeholders. Type constraints (`where T: Equatable`) restrict allowed types. Swift infers type parameters at call sites.
Generic types like `Array<T>` work with any element type. Define custom generic structs, classes, and enums with type parameters. Methods can add their own generic parameters.
`where` clauses add constraints to generic parameters and associated types. Specify conformance, inheritance, and equality relationships between types.
Extensions on generic types can be constrained with `where` clauses. Methods and properties inside constrained extensions are only available when the constraints are met.
Phantom types are generic parameters not used in the struct's stored properties. They add type-level state without runtime overhead. Enforce invariants at compile time.
Type erasure wraps a concrete generic type into an abstract type, hiding the generic parameter. Common patterns: AnySequence, AnyPublisher. Implement via a box/wrapper class.

`some` (opaque types, Swift 5.1) hides the concrete return type: `some View`. The compiler knows the concrete type; caller doesn't. `any` (existential types, Swift 5.6) erases the concrete type: `any Equatable`. Caller can store heterogeneous values. `some` enables efficient polymorphism (no box); `any` has runtime overhead from existential containers. Opaque types preserve identity; existentials don't.
Key paths (`\Type.property`) provide type-safe references to properties. `WritableKeyPath` for mutable access. Useful for functional programming, sorting, and binding.
`@dynamicMemberLookup` enables dot-syntax access to arbitrary properties via a `subscript(dynamicMember:)` method. Useful for JSON handling, scripting, and DSLs.
Result builders (formerly function builders) construct complex values from a block of statements. Power SwiftUI's DSL, AttributedStringBuilder, and custom DSLs.
Property wrappers encapsulate getter/setter logic. Custom wrappers use `@propertyWrapper` with `wrappedValue`. `projectedValue` provides additional API via `$` prefix.
`Codable` (Encodable & Decodable) auto-generates serialization. Custom keys with `CodingKeys` enum. Custom encoding/decoding via `encode(to:)` and `init(from:)`.
Swift 5.7+ introduces native regex literals `/pattern/`. `Regex<Output>` type with type-safe captures. Use `firstMatch`, `wholeMatch`, and `matches` for matching.
`some` (opaque) preserves concrete type identity at compile time. `any` (existential) boxes the type at runtime. Some types work for return values; any types work for heterogeneous collections.
Swift 5.7+ allows `some` in function parameter position (like `some View`). Equivalent to a generic parameter with a protocol constraint but written more concisely.

Swift macros (Swift 5.9+) generate code at compile time. Freestanding macros (#stringify, #warning). Attached macros (@Observable, @Test, @MainActor). Declared with `@macro` or via external module. Built-in: #Preview, #Predicate. Macro roles: @freestanding(expression), @freestanding(declaration), @attached(member), @attached(conformance), @attached(peer).
Swift's structured concurrency uses async functions and await calls. async functions can suspend and resume, freeing the thread. Building block for all modern Swift concurrency.
Actors protect mutable state with actor isolation. Only one task accesses actor state at a time. `nonisolated` for methods that don't access actor state. `isolated` parameters for cross-actor calls.
Task groups create structured concurrency trees. Tasks added run in parallel. Group collects all results before returning. `withThrowingTaskGroup` for throwing tasks.
`async let` launches a child task that runs concurrently with the current task. All async let bindings must be awaited before the enclosing scope exits.
`@MainActor` ensures code runs on the main actor (main thread). Mark types, functions, or closures. `await` required when calling from non-main context.
Global actors provide shared concurrency isolation across types. Define with `@globalActor`. All properties/methods of an actor-isolated type share the same executor.
`Sendable` protocol guarantees a type is safe to share across concurrency domains. Value types are implicitly Sendable. Classes must be final with immutable state or use actor isolation.
AsyncSequence provides asynchronous iteration over values over time. `AsyncStream` creates custom async sequences. `AsyncAlgorithms` package adds zip, merge, combineLatest.
Task-local values propagate through the async task hierarchy. Scoped to specific task trees. Useful for logging context, request IDs, and configuration that follows async flow.
